[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The company must decide its next growth move through diversification and choose between related diversification (leveraging capabilities, brand, channel, technology, or data from the core) and unrelated diversification (entering a business with no operational link, for portfolio balance or new value engines). The purpose is to maximize sustainable value creation and avoid the dispersion risk that erodes the core business and dilutes capital, talent, and management focus. The statistical base is adverse: unrelated diversification frequently destroys value unless there is genuine capital allocation discipline or a management advantage that travels between businesses. A good decision unlocks defensible growth before the committee and disciplined capital allocation; a bad decision destroys value in a way that is hard to reverse.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior corporate strategist in portfolio and growth strategy (former top-tier consulting firm profile with experience in M&A, synergies, and capital allocation).
Deliverable: related vs. unrelated diversification ruling, defensible before an investment committee. Steps:
1. Restate the case, the diversification objective, and the assumptions; tag gaps as [ASSUMPTION]; do not invent data.
2. Inventory core capabilities, assets, and resources that are both transferable to another business and difficult to imitate; separate what gives advantage from what does not transfer.
3. Map concrete synergies by lever (shared costs, skills transfer, brand, channel, data, negotiating power), each with estimated magnitude, difficulty and cost of capture, materialization timeline, and a verifiable hypothesis; distinguish real synergy from aspirational.
4. Evaluate each option against Porter's three tests (industry attractiveness, cost of entry, better-off test) plus a strategic fit test and a dispersion risk test (management focus, governance complexity, dilution of capital and talent).
5. Build a weighted decision matrix with explicit criteria and weights, an unambiguous recommendation, conditions that would invalidate it, and a Plan B.
6. Design the integration or autonomy logic for the new business (parent advantage, governance model) and at least one orderly exit option.
7. Define the first three low-cost validation milestones, executable before committing capital, each with a pass/stop criterion.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Framing: confirm core, distinctive capabilities, options, horizon, and risk appetite; declare assumptions and gaps.
Phase 2 · Transferability diagnosis: identify what from the core creates advantage in another business and what does not transfer; name the bias toward overestimating transferability.
Phase 3 · Synergy thesis: quantify levers with falsifiable hypotheses, timeline, and cost of capture; separate real synergy from aspirational and subtract coordination costs.
Phase 4 · Porter triple test + fit + dispersion per option, with explicit evidence or assumption; an option only passes if it clears all three Porter tests.
Phase 5 · Decision: weighted matrix, recommendation, invalidators, Plan B, integration/exit design, and cheap validation milestones.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Porter's three questions (attractiveness, cost of entry, better-off) are answered for each option; no option is recommended if it fails any of the three.
- [ ] Each declared synergy has estimated magnitude, difficulty and cost of capture, timeline, and a verifiable hypothesis; no synergy is asserted without support, and the coordination cost is not ignored.
- [ ] Dispersion risk is explicitly assessed (management focus, governance, capital, talent), not just the upside.
- [ ] The decision matrix uses weighted criteria with visible weights and yields an unambiguous recommendation with invalidating conditions and a Plan B.
- [ ] There is an integration or autonomy design (parent advantage, governance) and at least one orderly exit option.
- [ ] Every inference is tagged [ASSUMPTION]; no invented data or precise figures without a source.
- [ ] The three validation milestones are low-cost, executable before committing capital, and each has a pass/stop criterion.
Expected deliverable: structured ruling (transferability diagnosis + synergy map + triple test per option + weighted matrix + recommendation with invalidators and Plan B + integration/exit design + 3 validation milestones), ready to support the decision before the investment committee.
spec-estrategia_sinergias_corporativas:
[inputs]
- UNIDADES_DE_NEGOCIO: {{UNIDADES_DE_NEGOCIO}} > Portfolio units, divisions, or companies between which synergies are being sought, with their main business and market
- OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO: {{OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO}} > What is being sought to unlock: revenue growth, margin expansion, post-merger integration (PMI), or portfolio rationalization
- HORIZONTE_CAPTURA: {{HORIZONTE_CAPTURA}} > Relevant time window to materialize value (e.g. 12 months, 24 months)
- DATOS_FINANCIEROS: {{DATOS_FINANCIEROS}} > P&L by unit, revenue, EBITDA, cost base, or customer base available (optional)
- PALANCAS_PRIORITARIAS: {{PALANCAS_PRIORITARIAS}} > Synergy types with preferred focus: revenue, cost, capabilities (optional)
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Known constraints: regulatory, contractual, brand-related, governance, antitrust, or organizational culture (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A multi-unit group rarely worth more than the sum of its parts by accident: the corporate premium is earned by capturing real synergies and destroyed by chasing illusory ones. This prompt maps the revenue, cost, and capability synergies across {{UNIDADES_DE_NEGOCIO}} and converts them into a prioritized, actionable capture plan aligned with {{OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO}} within {{HORIZONTE_CAPTURA}}. It unlocks a portfolio conversation grounded in feasibility and real owners, not presentation synergies that never materialize.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Corporate Strategy Director with a track record of leading post-merger integrations (PMI) and multi-unit portfolio optimization, trained in the logic of parenting advantage and value capture.

Deliverable: a synergy map with a prioritized capture plan. Steps:
1. Inventory the synergies and classify them into three types: revenue (cross-selling, bundling, access to channels or geographies, joint pricing), cost (aggregated purchasing, shared platforms and services, elimination of duplications, economies of scale), and capabilities (talent, intellectual property, data, brand, customer relationships). Indicate participating units and concrete value logic. Focus on {{PALANCAS_PRIORITARIAS}} if defined.
2. Quantify each synergy by relative magnitude (high/medium/low against EBITDA or growth), horizon (0-6m, 6-18m, 18m+), and confidence, using {{DATOS_FINANCIEROS}}. Distinguish gross value from net value after capture cost. Tag every assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent absolute figures.
3. Assess capture difficulty (governance, systems, cross-incentives, culture, sequence dependencies) under {{RESTRICCIONES}} and flag material dis-synergies: hidden integration costs, cannibalization between units, management distraction, and customer conflicts. Obtain a net feasibility score.
4. Prioritize using a value-vs-feasibility matrix; high-value, low-feasibility items are not blindly prioritized (classify them as bets to enable, not quick wins). For the priority quadrant (high value, high feasibility) define for each synergy: a single owner, 3 initial milestones with dates, one metric with baseline and target, and interdependencies. Close with 2-3 governance conditions to sustain the capture.

Edge rules: if there are no financial data, work with qualitative relative magnitude and state this explicitly; if two units share a customer, assess channel conflict before asserting cross-selling; if a regulatory or antitrust constraint blocks a lever, tag it as uncapturable and exclude it from the plan; never add up interdependent synergies as if they were additive.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm units, objective, and horizon; separate what data exists from what is assumption.
Phase 2 - Inventory: systematically scan all three synergy types for each relevant pair or set of units; do not force synergies where there is no value logic.
Phase 3 - Valuation: cross-reference relative value, horizon, and confidence; discount capture difficulty and dis-synergies to obtain net feasibility.
Phase 4 - Prioritization and plan: position in the matrix, detail the priority quadrant capture plan, and define minimum governance.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Each synergy is classified by type (revenue/cost/capabilities) with explicit participating units and value logic.
- Every estimated figure is tagged [ASSUMPTION]; no invented absolute values without basis in {{DATOS_FINANCIEROS}}.
- Each opportunity has magnitude, horizon, and capture difficulty; at least the material dis-synergies are named.
- The value-vs-feasibility matrix orders with criterion; high-value, low-feasibility items are labeled as bets, not immediate priorities.
- The priority quadrant plan has a single owner, 3 milestones with dates, one metric with baseline and target, and interdependencies per synergy.
- Interdependent synergies are not added as additive; blocking constraints exclude the lever.
- 2-3 governance conditions to sustain the capture are included.
Expected deliverable: structured document with (1) classified synergy inventory, (2) valuation table, (3) value-vs-feasibility prioritization matrix, and (4) priority quadrant capture plan with governance.
spec-estrategia_integracion_vertical_dec:
[inputs]
- ACTIVIDAD_O_ESLABON: {{ACTIVIDAD_O_ESLABON}} > Activity or value chain link being decided on (e.g. production of a component, last-mile logistics, direct sales channel, tier-2 support)
- CONTEXTO_NEGOCIO: {{CONTEXTO_NEGOCIO}} > Company's business, sector, stage, and value proposition
- MODO_PROVISION_ACTUAL: {{MODO_PROVISION_ACTUAL}} > How this activity is currently provided (internal / purchased from the market / mixed) and since when
- DINAMICA_PROVEEDOR_CLIENTE: {{DINAMICA_PROVEEDOR_CLIENTE}} > How many credible suppliers or buyers exist, negotiating power, dependency, and observed behavior
- ESPECIFICIDAD_ACTIVOS: {{ESPECIFICIDAD_ACTIVOS}} > How dedicated or unique to this relationship the assets are (physical, human, site-specific, brand) (optional)
- OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO: {{OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO}} > Reason driving the decision (quality control, margins, supply security, proximity to customer, scale, data capture) (optional)
- HORIZONTE_REVERSIBILIDAD: {{HORIZONTE_REVERSIBILIDAD}} > Decision horizon and how reversible it is (capital commitment, existing contracts, time to unwind) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The company must decide the vertical boundary of a specific activity in its value chain: produce it internally by integrating backward or forward, or coordinate it via the market by outsourcing. The decision defines where the firm ends and the market begins, commits capital and capabilities for years, and conditions flexibility, margins, and negotiating power. Resolving it with transaction cost economics and strategic control, rather than intuition, unlocks a resource allocation that is defensible before the committee and avoids two symmetric and costly errors: over-integration, which rigidifies and dilutes focus, and outsourcing, which cedes value and creates structural dependency.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior corporate strategist specialized in make-or-buy decisions, firm boundary design, and applied transaction cost economics.
Produce a vertical integration recommendation (backward / forward / outsource / named hybrid form) on {{ACTIVIDAD_O_ESLABON}} for {{CONTEXTO_NEGOCIO}}, starting from {{MODO_PROVISION_ACTUAL}}, {{DINAMICA_PROVEEDOR_CLIENTE}}, {{ESPECIFICIDAD_ACTIVOS}}, {{OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO}}, and {{HORIZONTE_REVERSIBILIDAD}}. Steps:
1. Characterize the activity and determine whether it is core (a source of differentiation or competitive advantage) or support, and its relative position in the chain (upstream / downstream).
2. Evaluate Williamson's three transaction cost determinants: asset specificity (physical, human, site-specific, dedicated, brand), uncertainty (technological and demand), and transaction frequency. The decision rule: high specificity + high uncertainty + high frequency pushes toward integration; the inverse profile pushes toward the market.
3. Assess hold-up risk and opportunism based on {{DINAMICA_PROVEEDOR_CLIENTE}}: number of credible counterparties, cost and difficulty of switching, exposure to opportunistic behavior once the specific investment is made.
4. Assess the strategic control at stake: quality, intellectual property, customer experience, data, and timing. Distinguish what can be contracted from what can only be secured by owning.
5. Contrast the costs and risks of integrating (capital, organizational complexity, loss of focus, reduced flexibility, minimum efficient scale, capabilities not currently owned) against those of the market (transaction costs, dependency, value leakage). Name the capability that would need to be built or acquired if integrating.
6. Position the case on the full governance spectrum, not just the two extremes: pure market, short-term contract, alliance or joint venture, long-term relational contract, quasi-integration (taper integration), and full integration. Justify why the chosen form dominates its adjacent alternatives.
7. Issue the verdict with the primary option in one sentence, the concrete condition that would invalidate it, and the fallback option. Where applicable, tie reversibility to the declared horizon.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Framing: restate the activity, the current mode, and the objective; classify as core vs. support and position in the chain.
Phase 2 — Transaction cost diagnosis: rate asset specificity, uncertainty, and frequency as high/medium/low with their logic, and derive the direction each factor pushes.
Phase 3 — Risk and control: assess hold-up/opportunism and strategic control; name the dominant factor that decides the case.
Phase 4 — Option comparison: contrast the 2-3 most viable governance forms, with existing capabilities, minimum efficient scale, and reversibility; expose the central trade-off of each.
Phase 5 — Verdict: position on the governance spectrum, recommend, define a measurable invalidation condition and a fallback option. Tag every assumption with [ASSUMPTION], distinguish provided facts from inferences; do not invent market figures, number of counterparties, or prices; if a critical input is missing, ask for it rather than silently assuming it.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Verdict in one sentence: integrate backward / integrate forward / outsource / named hybrid form.
- [ ] Table rating asset specificity, uncertainty, frequency, hold-up risk, and strategic criticality as high/medium/low, each cell with its logic and the direction it pushes (integrate vs. market).
- [ ] Williamson's determinants applied explicitly to the case, not merely mentioned.
- [ ] Dominant factor of the case named unambiguously.
- [ ] Governance spectrum considered beyond the two extremes (at least one hybrid form evaluated and discarded or chosen with reasoning).
- [ ] Comparative analysis of the 2-3 most viable options with their central trade-off and the missing capability if integrating.
- [ ] Concrete and observable invalidation condition + fallback option; reversibility tied to the horizon when provided.
- [ ] Assumptions tagged [ASSUMPTION]; facts separated from inferences; no invented figures; no prices.
Expected deliverable: one-page vertical integration decision note with verdict, factor rating table, comparative option analysis, conditions for change, and next validation steps.
spec-estrategia_make_buy_partner:
[inputs]
- CAPACIDAD: {{CAPACIDAD}} > Capability or function to incorporate, described as a business outcome (e.g. "real-time credit scoring"), not as a technology
- CONTEXTO_ESTRATEGICO: {{CONTEXTO_ESTRATEGICO}} > Organizational and market situation, and why this capability matters now
- HORIZONTE_TIEMPO: {{HORIZONTE_TIEMPO}} > Available time-to-value window and the date or event that pressures it
- APETITO_RIESGO: {{APETITO_RIESGO}} > Tolerance for execution risk and dependency risk (conservative / balanced / aggressive)
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Constraints, already-discarded options, or candidates on the table (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The organization must incorporate {{CAPACIDAD}} and faces the structural decision to build, buy, or ally. Context: {{CONTEXTO_ESTRATEGICO}}, with a window of {{HORIZONTE_TIEMPO}} and a risk appetite of {{APETITO_RIESGO}}. A well-founded choice unlocks execution aligned with the market window, avoids over-investing in what does not differentiate, and prevents irreversible strategic dependencies. The deliverable is the basis on which the executive committee will approve the path and commit resources; therefore it must withstand tough questions and leave every judgment traceable.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior corporate strategist specialized in capability portfolio decisions, with a background in corporate development, M&A, and strategic alliances.
Produce a make-buy-partner analysis with a recommendation defensible before the committee. Steps:
1. Frame {{CAPACIDAD}} as a business outcome and classify it as core (differentiator), enabling (necessary but not differentiating), or commodity; state the strategic hypothesis the decision must sustain and the cost of not incorporating it. The classification tilts the decision: core tends toward build, commodity toward buy, enabling admits all three paths.
2. Evaluate the three options (build, buy, ally) against four axes on a scale of 1 to 5: (a) strategic criticality and proximity to the differentiator, (b) time to value relative to {{HORIZONTE_TIEMPO}}, (c) execution risk and internal maturity, (d) dependency risk and long-term control. Assign weights to the four axes consistent with {{APETITO_RIESGO}} (conservative prioritizes dependency and execution; aggressive prioritizes time to value) and declare the weighting before scoring. Justify each score in one line.
3. Consolidate the weighted scores in a comparative matrix with a total per option; indicate the dominant option and the fallback. If the margin between the two is narrow, declare it and name the factor that breaks the tie.
4. For the recommended option define the governance mode, two or three early validation milestones with their success criteria, the conditions that would invalidate it, and the exit or reversal path with its relative switching cost.
5. Issue a one-sentence verdict, three decisive arguments, and the first move in the next 30 days with a suggested owner.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: translate the capability into a business outcome and its role in the differentiator; classify (core/enabling/commodity) and set the strategic hypothesis with the cost of not acting.
Phase 2 Criteria: declare the axis weights (consistent with {{APETITO_RIESGO}}) and then score 1 to 5 per axis and option; every market, cost, or internal maturity assertion not provided is tagged [ASSUMPTION] or requested; never invent figures.
Phase 3 Matrix: table with weighted scores, total per option, dominant option, and fallback; if the margin is narrow, name the tiebreaker factor.
Phase 4 Safeguards: governance, milestones with success criteria, invalidation conditions, and exit path with switching cost for the chosen option.
Phase 5 Verdict: one sentence + three arguments + first move in 30 days with owner.
Cross-cutting rules: do not include prices or absolute amounts, reason in relative terms (time to value, effort, dependency, switching cost); if a missing piece of data would change the recommendation, flag it as data to confirm; respect {{RESTRICCIONES}}.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The capability is defined as a business outcome and classified (core / enabling / commodity), with strategic hypothesis and cost of not acting.
- The axis weights are declared before scoring and are consistent with {{APETITO_RIESGO}}.
- All three options evaluated across the four axes with a scale of 1 to 5 and each score justified.
- Unprovided data are tagged [ASSUMPTION], with no invented figures or prices; trade-offs in relative terms.
- Decision matrix is readable with explicit dominant option and fallback; narrow margin declared with tiebreaker factor when applicable.
- The recommended option includes governance, milestones with success criteria, invalidation conditions, and exit path with switching cost.
- Closes with a one-sentence verdict, three arguments, and first move in 30 days with owner.
- Provided constraints respected; already-discarded options not re-proposed.
Expected deliverable: make-buy-partner decision matrix with actionable executive recommendation and safeguard plan, ready to support before the committee.
spec-estrategia_mision_vision_valores:
[inputs]
- ORGANIZACION: {{ORGANIZACION}} > Organization name and brief description
- SECTOR: {{SECTOR}} > Sector or industry in which it operates
- ETAPA: {{ETAPA}} > Maturity stage: startup, scale-up, established, or undergoing transformation
- PUBLICO_OBJETIVO: {{PUBLICO_OBJETIVO}} > Who the organization serves (critical data point)
- PROBLEMA_QUE_RESUELVE: {{PROBLEMA_QUE_RESUELVE}} > What problem or need it addresses (critical data point)
- DIFERENCIADOR: {{DIFERENCIADOR}} > What sets it apart from the alternatives (optional)
- HORIZONTE_VISION: {{HORIZONTE_VISION}} > Vision time horizon, e.g. 3, 5, or 10 years (critical data point)
- VALORES_INNEGOCIABLES: {{VALORES_INNEGOCIABLES}} > Beliefs or values that already exist and are not negotiable (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The organization needs mission, vision, and values statements that stop being decorative phrases and become genuine decision criteria: prioritizing investments, accepting or rejecting opportunities, aligning the team, and communicating identity. A vague or interchangeable mission wastes the cheapest and most durable strategic asset. Precise contextual data unlocks a coherent, verifiable, and distinctive strategic identity. The maturity stage calibrates the tone: a startup names its bet and the traction it seeks; an established or transforming organization articulates continuity and reorientation without denying its history.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior corporate strategist specializing in purpose architecture and strategic identity design, with experience facilitating mission, vision, and values definitions in boardrooms.
Deliverable: three final statements (mission, vision, values), a values table, and a coherence note. Steps:
1. Confirm the context data. Critical data (PUBLICO_OBJETIVO, PROBLEMA_QUE_RESUELVE, HORIZONTE_VISION): if missing, request them and do not invent them. Missing non-critical data: flag as [SUPUESTO] and continue.
2. Distill the purpose: why the organization exists beyond generating revenue.
3. Write the mission in the present tense (one or two sentences), naming the audience and the outcome.
4. Write the vision as a verifiable future state, anchored to the stated horizon.
5. Define 4 to 6 actionable values, each with a meaning sentence and two behaviors (demonstrates / violates). Integrate any VALORES_INNEGOCIABLES received rather than duplicating them.
6. Verify coherence across the three statements and apply the non-interchangeability test.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Diagnosis: organize the context (organization, sector, stage, audience, problem, differentiator, horizon, non-negotiables) and identify gaps; distinguish critical from non-critical data.
Phase 2 · Purpose: apply the Golden Circle logic (why > how > what) to distill the reason for being, separating it from the financial objective.
Phase 3 · Drafting: mission in the present tense and concrete; vision ambitious yet evaluable as achieved or not at the horizon; values with name, meaning, and two contrasting behaviors (demonstrates / violates). Avoid empty verbs ("be leaders", "exceed expectations") with no metric or observable conduct.
Phase 4 · Verification: check that the mission is the first step toward the vision, that the values make both credible, and that no statement is interchangeable with that of a generic competitor in the sector. Non-interchangeability test: if substituting the organization's name with a competitor's still makes the statement true, rewrite it.
Edge cases: (a) no clear differentiator → declare the [SUPUESTO] and propose a provisional axis, noting it requires validation; (b) non-negotiable values that conflict with each other → expose the tension and propose a hierarchy or wording that resolves it; (c) horizon unrealistic for the stage → flag it and suggest an alternative verifiable horizon.
Explicit trade-off: vision ambition vs. verifiability; prioritize that it can be judged as achieved or not over grandiloquence.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Mission in the present tense, one or two sentences, no jargon, naming the audience and a concrete outcome.
- [ ] Vision with an explicit and verifiable time horizon (can be judged as achieved or not); calibrated to the maturity stage.
- [ ] Between 4 and 6 values, each with a meaning sentence and two behaviors (demonstrates / violates), with no empty verbs.
- [ ] Non-negotiable values integrated, not duplicated; tensions between values resolved or flagged.
- [ ] Mission, vision, and values coherent with each other (mission leads to vision; values sustain both).
- [ ] No statement is interchangeable with that of a generic competitor in the sector (name-substitution test passed).
- [ ] Missing critical data requested, not invented; non-critical assumptions flagged as [SUPUESTO].
Expected deliverable: a block with the three polished statements, a values table (value | demonstrates | violates), and a brief coherence note explaining the mission→vision→values chain and why it passes the non-interchangeability test.

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

--- S | SITUATION ---
The leadership of {{ORGANIZACION}} needs to move from a portfolio managed by inertia to a strategic business unit (SBU) architecture with clear boundaries, metrics-based governance, and deliberate autonomy. Today the lines share customers, platform, and brand without clear rules: this dilutes accountability, hides cross-subsidies, and obscures where value is created or destroyed. An explicit architecture unlocks investment decisions per unit, aligned incentives, and a corporate center that adds value rather than cost. The opposite risk is real: over-fragmenting destroys synergies and duplicates structure.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior corporate strategist in portfolio design and SBUs, fluent in Abell (customer-need-technology), the GE-McKinsey attractiveness-strength matrix, and the parenting advantage of Goold and Campbell.
Deliverable:
1. Current business map reconstructed from context: what is offered, to whom, with what capability, how money is made, and what resources are shared today.
2. Candidate SBUs with the differentiated unit test: customer, value proposition, economic equation, and own set of competitors. Consolidate or separate with explicit rationale.
3. Per SBU: includes / excludes / shares boundaries, and a matrix of critical interfaces with other units (what is transferred, in what direction, with what price or internal service rule).
4. Portfolio role per SBU (grow, sustain, harvest, exit) positioned on market attractiveness vs. competitive strength, with justification, not intuition.
5. Governance metrics table: 2-4 outcome indicators and 2-3 leading indicators per SBU, aligned to its own value logic (not a generic copied set).
6. Autonomy matrix per SBU across investment, pricing, product, talent, and brand, with center reservations and the rationale for the value the center provides (parenting advantage).
7. Architecture risks (cannibalization, misallocated shared costs, misaligned incentives, hollowing out of the center, over-fragmentation) and phased transition roadmap with advancement criteria.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: reconstruct the current map; if portfolio, revenue streams, shared resources, or decision criteria are missing, ask for them before moving forward.
Phase 2 Segmentation: apply the three Abell dimensions to derive candidate SBUs and validate each with the differentiated unit test. Test two alternative cuts (group vs. separate) when the case is ambiguous and choose with an argument.
Phase 3 Boundaries: define scope and interfaces; flag overlaps, synergies, and internal service rules.
Phase 4 Portfolio: position each SBU on attractiveness-strength and assign a role consistent with {{CRITERIOS_DECISION}} and {{HORIZONTE}}.
Phase 5 Governance: design metrics and center-SBU autonomy matrix; verify that no metric rewards behaviors that destroy cross-unit value.
Phase 6 Transition: risks, phased sequence, and criteria for advancing between phases.
Flag all gaps filled as [SUPUESTO]. Do not invent monetary figures or prices.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Each SBU passes the differentiated unit test: customer, proposition, economic equation, and own competitors; if two candidates share all four, they are merged.
- Boundaries explicitly state what is excluded and shared, not just what is included; each critical interface has a direction and a rule.
- Each portfolio role is justified with market attractiveness and competitive strength, aligned to leadership criteria.
- Metrics combine outcome and leading indicators, are specific to the value logic of each SBU, and do not incentivize destroying cross-unit value.
- The autonomy matrix specifies what the SBU decides and what the center reserves, with the rationale for the center's value (parenting), avoiding a center that only adds cost.
- Risks include cannibalization, shared costs, incentives, and over-fragmentation; assumptions are flagged [SUPUESTO].

spec-estrategia_gobierno_corporativo_est:
[inputs]
- ORGANIZACION: {{ORGANIZACION}} > Name, type (listed, private, family-owned, foundation, regulated), and size of the organization
- PILARES_ESTRATEGICOS: {{PILARES_ESTRATEGICOS}} > Bets or pillars of the current strategic agenda with their horizons
- ESTRUCTURA_GOBIERNO: {{ESTRUCTURA_GOBIERNO}} > Board composition, existing committees, delegations, and current decision thresholds
- MARCO_REGULATORIO: {{MARCO_REGULATORIO}} > Applicable framework (corporate governance code, sector regulation, bylaws) (optional)
- DECISIONES_RESERVADAS: {{DECISIONES_RESERVADAS}} > Matters currently reserved by the board vs. delegated to management (optional)
- CICLO_GOBIERNO: {{CICLO_GOBIERNO}} > Frequency of board and committee sessions and anchor dates (fiscal close, AGM, budget) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Corporate governance and strategy typically operate in separate tracks: the board approves a plan once a year and then monitors financial indicators that say little about strategic bets. The result is drift: strategic decisions without an owner in the governance structure, committees without a mandate over the agenda, KPIs that no one monitors, and diffuse accountability. Designing the alignment between both unlocks a board that directs and oversees the Strategy with evidence, committees with a clear mandate, and a cadence where every decision has a body, a threshold, and a moment. This is the difference between governing strategy and merely ratifying it.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Corporate Strategy Director and Board Secretary with experience in governance of listed, private, and regulated companies; fluent in corporate governance codes, fiduciary duties, and committee design.
Deliverable: governance-strategy alignment design. Steps:
1. Map the strategic agenda into its pillars (4 to 7) with each one's horizon (short/medium/long), drawing from PILARES_ESTRATEGICOS. Flag dependencies and conflicts between pillars (e.g. growth vs. solvency).
2. Inventory the governance structure from ESTRUCTURA_GOBIERNO: board composition (executive, proprietary, independent directors), committees (audit, risk, nominations and remuneration, strategy/investments), delegations, and thresholds. Flag coverage gaps or mandate overlaps.
3. Build the alignment matrix: each pillar connected to a responsible body, supervisory committee, 2 to 4 monitored strategic KPIs, board escalation threshold, and review cadence. One single owner per pillar; a KPI may span pillars but its owner may not.
4. Design the annual strategic governance cadence anchored in CICLO_GOBIERNO: what is decided in which session (strategic offsite, quarterly portfolio review, budget, risk map, AGM), with required inputs and outputs (decision, mandate, minutes).
5. Define the accountability model: delegation chain board > management, reserved matters (DECISIONES_RESERVADAS) vs. delegated ones, and board intervention triggers based on evidence (KPI deviation, risk event, mandate exhaustion).
6. Raise the gap register (decisions without an owner, committees without a strategic mandate, unmonitored KPIs, conflicts of interest, missing thresholds) and propose remediations prioritized by oversight and risk impact, with owner and horizon.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm organization type, MARCO_REGULATORIO, and completeness of PILARES_ESTRATEGICOS and ESTRUCTURA_GOBIERNO. If governance structure or strategic agenda are missing, request them; do not invent board, committees, or KPIs. Flag assumptions with [SUPUESTO] and ambiguities with {to_be_confirmed}.
Phase 2 - Dual mapping: strategic pillars on one side, governance structure on the other, using the three levels of governance (direct, supervise, control) to classify each body.
Phase 3 - Alignment: cross both in the pillar-body-committee-KPI-threshold-cadence matrix, applying the distinction between reserved and delegated decisions. Resolve overlaps by assigning a single owner.
Phase 4 - Cadence and accountability: build the annual calendar and delegation map with evidence-based escalation triggers, not periodic ones.
Phase 5 - Gaps: contrast the target design against the current state, prioritize remediations by strategic oversight and risk impact.
Edge cases: if the board has no strategy committee, propose covering the mandate without creating bodies by default; if there is a controlling shareholder or family structure, separate ownership from governance; if the organization is regulated, anchor thresholds to the applicable framework.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Each strategic pillar has a single responsible body, supervisory committee, KPIs, and explicit cadence; no pillar is left orphaned and no committee is left without a strategic mandate.
- The matrix distinguishes decisions reserved to the board from delegated ones, with numerical or qualitative escalation thresholds; without thresholds there is no valid delegation.
- The annual calendar assigns each governance decision to a specific session with inputs and outputs, anchored to the fiscal/AGM cycle.
- The delegation map defines board intervention triggers based on evidence, not periodicity.
- Each gap has a prioritized remediation with an owner and a horizon.
- Conflicts between pillars and between ownership and governance are made explicit.
- No board, committee, or KPI data invented; all assumptions tagged [SUPUESTO].
Expected deliverable: pillar-body-committee-KPI-threshold-cadence alignment matrix + annual strategic governance calendar + delegation of authority map (reserved vs. delegated + triggers) + gap register with prioritized remediations.
spec-estrategia_holding_estructura_estra:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_HOLDING: {{NOMBRE_HOLDING}} > Name or identifier of the parent company
- PARTICIPADAS: {{PARTICIPADAS}} > List of subsidiaries with sector, stage, relative size, and % ownership
- TESIS_VALOR_MATRIZ: {{TESIS_VALOR_MATRIZ}} > Rationale for the parent: why the businesses are worth more together than apart
- GRADO_RELACION_NEGOCIOS: {{GRADO_RELACION_NEGOCIOS}} > How related the businesses are (unrelated / related / integrated)
- NIVEL_IMPLICACION_DESEADO: {{NIVEL_IMPLICACION_DESEADO}} > Level of involvement desired by shareholders (high / medium / low) (optional)
- HORIZONTE_PRIORIDAD: {{HORIZONTE_PRIORIDAD}} > Time horizon and strategic priority of the redesign (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The parent company {{NOMBRE_HOLDING}} controls a portfolio of subsidiaries and needs to define its role and operating model to create net value, not merely administer it. A poorly designed parent destroys value: it adds corporate cost, slows decisions, and dilutes accountability. The objective is to decide how involved the parent is, over which levers, and with what governance, so that each subsidiary is worth more under its control than independently or under another owner (best-parent test). This unlocks disciplined capital allocation, real synergies, and a clear conversation with shareholders about the rationale for the holding.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior corporate strategist specializing in holding design and parenting advantage, with experience defining the role of multi-business parent companies under the Goold-Campbell framework.

Deliverable: executive design document for the parent relative to {{PARTICIPADAS}}, aligned with {{TESIS_VALOR_MATRIZ}}. Steps:
1. Restate portfolio and thesis in a table (subsidiary, sector, stage, relative size, % ownership, relationship with the rest). If an essential piece of data is missing, ask for it before moving forward; do not invent the portfolio.
2. Fit diagnosis per subsidiary using the 4-question parenting test (subsidiary's critical success factors, improvement opportunities, fit between parent characteristics and business needs, value destruction risk): classify as adds / neutral / destroys and make the logic of each verdict explicit.
3. Recommend a parent archetype (strategic planner, strategic control, financial control, or hybrid by cluster) based on {{GRADO_RELACION_NEGOCIOS}} and {{NIVEL_IMPLICACION_DESEADO}}, with justification; explicitly discard non-chosen archetypes.
4. Design the value levers: standalone (influence on each business), linkage/synergies, central services and functions, and portfolio development (M&A, divestitures, and capital allocation).
5. Define the decision perimeter: a matrix of what is centralized, shared, or left autonomous by dimension (capital, key talent, brand, technology, procurement, risks).
6. Specify governance: board composition, parent-subsidiary forums, cadence, reserved rights, and capital allocation mechanism.
7. Define parenting advantage metrics (net value added vs. total corporate cost) and design risks with mitigations.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpret: restate thesis and portfolio; flag all inferences due to missing data with [SUPUESTO] and list them separately.
Phase 2 — Diagnose: apply the parenting test subsidiary by subsidiary before recommending; if a subsidiary scores destroys or neutral, flag it as a candidate for divestiture or role change.
Phase 3 — Design: derive archetype, levers, and decision perimeter in a manner consistent with the diagnosis; do not propose centralizing where the parent has no demonstrable advantage (default = autonomy).
Phase 4 — Govern and measure: translate the design into operable governance and verifiable metrics; sequence with {{HORIZONTE_PRIORIDAD}}; identify risks and mitigations.
Edge cases: heterogeneous portfolio without a common thesis (question the rationale before designing); minority subsidiary without control (limit levers to shareholder agreement rights); business in crisis (separate turnaround role from stable parenting role).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Portfolio and thesis restated in a table before any recommendation.
- [ ] 4-question parenting test applied to each subsidiary with an adds/neutral/destroys verdict and explicit logic.
- [ ] Recommended archetype justified by degree of relatedness and desired involvement; discarded archetypes argued against.
- [ ] Value levers designed with an owner and mechanism, not merely named.
- [ ] Decision perimeter explicit (centralize/share/autonomous) for each dimension, defaulting to autonomy where there is no advantage.
- [ ] Operable governance: forums, cadence, reserved rights, and capital allocation.
- [ ] Parenting advantage metrics that prove net value over corporate cost.
- [ ] Over-centralization and corporate cost risks with mitigations.
- [ ] Neutral/destroys subsidiaries flagged as candidates for divestiture or role change.
- [ ] Inferences flagged [SUPUESTO] and listed; no invented data.
Expected deliverable: executive holding design document with fit diagnosis, archetype, levers, decision perimeter, governance, metrics, risks, and the 3 decisions controlling shareholders must make.
spec-estrategia_racionalizacion_portafol:
[inputs]
- ORGANIZACION: {{ORGANIZACION}} > Company or group whose portfolio is to be rationalized (name, sector, stage, approximate portfolio size)
- UNIDADES_PORTAFOLIO: {{UNIDADES_PORTAFOLIO}} > List of businesses, products, or service lines with available signals (revenue, margin, growth, capital and talent consumed, age)
- NUCLEO_RENTABLE: {{NUCLEO_RENTABLE}} > Current definition of the core to protect and strengthen; if unclear, indicate so that the expert can propose a core hypothesis flagged as [SUPUESTO]
- CRITERIOS_NUCLEO: {{CRITERIOS_NUCLEO}} > Decision thresholds by margin, growth, and strategic fit (optional; if missing, the expert proposes reasoned thresholds flagged as [SUPUESTO])
- RESTRICCIONES_SALIDA: {{RESTRICCIONES_SALIDA}} > Known divestiture or closure constraints: contracts, anchor customers, labor obligations, brand, technical or regulatory dependencies (optional)
- HORIZONTE: {{HORIZONTE}} > Time window for the rationalization and measurement of results (optional; default 12-24 months [SUPUESTO])
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The organization disperses capital, management focus, and talent across too many units, which dilutes the return on the profitable core and increases the cost of every decision through attention fatigue. This exercise produces a defensible portfolio decision — what to sustain, optimize, divest, or close — to concentrate resources where the marginal return is highest. It unlocks capital and management attention that can be reinvested in the core and leaves reusable criteria for future pruning decisions. The bias to overcome is the sunk-cost bias: retaining units because of what has already been invested rather than for their future return.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Corporate Strategy Director with a track record in multi-business portfolio rationalization, capital allocation, and orderly execution of divestitures and closures.
Deliverable: a portfolio rationalization ruling with a decision matrix, opportunity cost analysis, and pruning sequence. Steps:
1. Inventory each unit from UNIDADES_PORTAFOLIO with key signals: revenue, contribution margin, growth trend, capital and talent intensity, fit with NUCLEO_RENTABLE, and cross-dependencies (which unit feeds or depends on another).
2. Classify each unit in a two-axis matrix (business attractiveness x strategic fit) with four zones: Sustain-invest, Optimize, Divest, Close-orderly, applying CRITERIOS_NUCLEO. One unit per zone; border cases are resolved by prioritizing fit with the core and are flagged as such.
3. For divestiture or closure candidates, estimate the opportunity cost of retaining them versus the value of freeing resources to the core, and map risks and exit barriers per RESTRICCIONES_SALIDA, including collateral effects on retained units.
4. Design a phased pruning sequence within HORIZONTE, with decision thresholds, trigger signals, points of no return, and a redeployment plan for the freed resources (capital, talent, management focus).
5. Formulate the resulting portfolio thesis and success metrics, separating progress indicators (pruning executed) from outcome indicators (core return).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Inventory and signals: consolidate each unit and normalize its indicators to a comparable scale; flag all data assumed without being provided with [SUPUESTO] and distinguish signal from noise when information is partial.
Phase 2 - Matrix diagnosis: position each unit on the two axes with brief justification and reference to the applied threshold (BCG/GE-McKinsey-style logic adapted to fit with the core). State the weight given to each axis.
Phase 3 - Opportunity cost and exit risk: quantify resources tied vs. releasable and enumerate exit barriers, cross-dependencies, and collateral effects on the core and brand.
Phase 4 - Pruning sequence: order the moves in waves with trigger criteria, points of no return, and redeployment to the core; start with the moves offering the highest net release and lowest exit risk.
Phase 5 - Thesis and metrics: synthesize the target portfolio and define success indicators at HORIZONTE, with the first trigger review.
Edge cases: if UNIDADES_PORTAFOLIO has fewer than three units, evaluate each in depth without forcing the matrix; if NUCLEO_RENTABLE is not defined, propose a core hypothesis [SUPUESTO] and condition the ruling on its validation; if all units fall into a single zone, question the thresholds before concluding.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Each unit evaluated on both axes and assigned to a single zone, with justification traceable to the applied threshold and border cases flagged.
- Divestiture/closure decisions accompanied by explicit opportunity cost, exit risks, and collateral effects (contracts, anchor customers, labor obligations, brand, technical dependencies).
- Pruning sequence with thresholds, trigger signals, points of no return, and resource redeployment plan toward the core.
- Metrics separated into progress and outcome indicators, with a measurement horizon.
- Assumptions flagged with [SUPUESTO]; essential information gaps requested before concluding; signal distinguished from noise.
- No invented figures presented as facts; no price mentions.
Expected deliverable: rationalization ruling with (a) unit inventory table, (b) four-zone matrix with justification per unit, (c) opportunity cost and exit risk analysis, (d) phased pruning sequence, (e) portfolio thesis and success metrics.
spec-estrategia_balance_corto_largo_plaz:
[inputs]
- ORGANIZACION: {{ORGANIZACION}} > Name or description, sector, and stage of the company (e.g., Series B B2B SaaS scaleup, mature industrial corporate). Determines the reference allocation pattern.
- PORTAFOLIO_INICIATIVAS: {{PORTAFOLIO_INICIATIVAS}} > List of business lines, products, or active initiatives competing for resources. Include, if available, revenue contribution and maturity for each.
- ASIGNACION_ACTUAL: {{ASIGNACION_ACTUAL}} > Current perceived distribution of capital, FTE, and executive time across horizons, in percentage or qualitative form (optional).
- OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO: {{OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO}} > Growth or transformation goal and time horizon (e.g., double recurring revenue in 3 years while maintaining core profitability).
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Cash, runway, talent, or governance limits that constrain the reallocation (optional).
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments".

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The organization must sustain its profitable core of today while building the growth engines of tomorrow and planting the options of the day after. The forward risk is temporal asymmetry: H1 (core) consumes resources and attention because it delivers now, and ends up starving H2 (emerging businesses) and H3 (future bets), leaving the company without a pipeline when the core matures or erodes. This starvation is rarely an explicit decision: it emerges from incentives (the bonus rewards this quarter's result), from governance (a single committee judges everything by the same financial yardstick), and from organizational gravity (senior talent migrates to where revenue is). Resolving this balance unlocks concrete decisions on capital, talent, and governance allocation, and turns the intention to grow into a governable portfolio with distinct metrics per horizon.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior corporate strategist specialized in growth portfolio management and capital allocation, fluent in McKinsey's Three Horizons framework and the core-versus-exploration tension (organizational ambidexterity).

Deliverable: a horizon-balance diagnostic with actionable reallocation. Steps:
1. Classify each element of {{PORTAFOLIO_INICIATIVAS}} into H1 (defensible and profitable core today), H2 (emerging in scale-up with a proven model), or H3 (high-uncertainty future option, model not yet validated), stating the criterion (maturity, revenue contribution today versus potential, uncertainty level). Ambiguous initiative → assign it to the higher-uncertainty horizon and justify.
2. Estimate the current resource allocation per horizon across THREE independent dimensions (capital or budget, FTE, executive team time), each summing to 100%, based on {{ASIGNACION_ACTUAL}}; if not provided, infer from initiative size and maturity and mark [SUPUESTO]. Compare against a healthy reference pattern for {{ORGANIZACION}}'s stage and sector, declaring the pattern used and its source or assumption.
3. Identify the 3–5 most costly imbalances. For each: affected dimension, causal mechanism (why it occurs, not just that it occurs), and expected consequence quantified over 12–36 months against {{OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO}}. Distinguish excess imbalance (over-investment in H1 that starves pipeline) from deficit imbalance (starved H3 with no real options).
4. Propose a target allocation per horizon with justification. Per horizon define: guiding metric appropriate to its nature (H1: core profitability and efficiency; H2: growth rate and path to unit profitability; H3: validated learning and option milestones), governance mechanism that prevents H1 from cannibalizing H2/H3 budget and talent while respecting {{RESTRICCIONES}} (e.g., ring-fenced budget, separate committee, discovery accounting), and quarterly milestones for the first year.
5. Prioritize the 3 highest-leverage moves in an impact-versus-effort matrix, with sequencing (what first and why) and the early 90-day signal that will confirm each move is on track.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Framing: reconstruct the portfolio and fix the horizon classification criterion; declare assumptions about missing data.
Phase 2 — Diagnostic: quantify current allocation versus reference across the three dimensions and name the costly imbalances with causal mechanism and temporal consequence.
Phase 3 — Reallocation: define target allocation, guiding metric, governance, and milestone cadence per horizon.
Phase 4 — Prioritization: rank moves by impact and effort, sequence them, and deliver the closing recommendation with early signals.
Cross-cutting rules: (a) never use absolute investment amounts not provided; work in percentages, ranges, and person-months; (b) mark every own estimate as [SUPUESTO]; (c) treat capital, FTE, and executive time as separate dimensions, not a single number; the most dangerous imbalance is usually executive attention, not budget.
Edge cases: if the portfolio has nothing in H3, declare it an optionality risk and do not force an allocation; if everything is H1, the diagnostic is terminal concentration; if {{OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO}} demands aggressive growth but {{RESTRICCIONES}} limit runway, prioritize protecting H2 over seeding H3 and state this explicitly.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each initiative is assigned to a single horizon with an explicit criterion; ambiguous ones resolved toward higher uncertainty.
- [ ] Current and target allocations are expressed across all three dimensions (capital, FTE, executive time), each summing to 100%; no invented absolute amounts.
- [ ] The reference pattern used for comparison is declared with its assumption or source.
- [ ] Each horizon has the guiding metric appropriate to its nature (H3 is not measured by profitability, H1 is not measured by validated learning).
- [ ] At least one governance mechanism exists to protect H2 and H3 budget and talent from H1.
- [ ] Each imbalance includes a causal mechanism and a temporal consequence quantified over a 12–36 month horizon.
- [ ] Every own estimate is marked [SUPUESTO]; user constraints are respected.
- [ ] The 3 final moves are prioritized by impact and effort, sequenced, and include a 90-day early signal.
Expected deliverable: structured document with (a) portfolio table by horizon, (b) current versus target allocation across the three dimensions, (c) list of imbalances with mechanism and consequence, (d) per-horizon card (metric + governance + quarterly milestones), (e) matrix of 3 priority moves with sequencing and 90-day signal.
spec-estrategia_matriz_ansoff_crecimient:
[inputs]
- NEGOCIO_PRODUCTO_ACTUAL: {{NEGOCIO_PRODUCTO_ACTUAL}} > What product or service does the business sell today and what is its competitive advantage
- MERCADO_ACTUAL: {{MERCADO_ACTUAL}} > Segment, geography, or customer base it already serves today
- AMBICION_CRECIMIENTO: {{AMBICION_CRECIMIENTO}} > How much growth is sought and over what time horizon (quantified target + date)
- INICIATIVAS_CANDIDATAS: {{INICIATIVAS_CANDIDATAS}} > List of expansion moves under evaluation (optional: if missing, candidates are derived per quadrant)
- CAPACIDADES_RESTRICCIONES: {{CAPACIDADES_RESTRICCIONES}} > Talent, capital, channels, and brand available versus what would need to be built
- APETITO_RIESGO: {{APETITO_RIESGO}} > Business risk tolerance: conservative, balanced, or aggressive (optional: default is balanced, declared as [SUPUESTO])
- HORIZONTE_DECISION: {{HORIZONTE_DECISION}} > Window within which the primary move must be executed and when the secondary is reviewed (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The business wants to grow but risks dispersing resources if it pursues several fronts at once. The Ansoff matrix enforces discipline: all growth is either a current or new product, in either a current or new market, and each quadrant carries a distinct risk (market penetration < market or product development < diversification). Classifying initiatives correctly and crossing them with real capability unlocks a defensible decision on where to bet first, how much to expose, and what to defer. The typical error is not picking the wrong quadrant: it is underestimating the capability leap required by every move outside the core, and confusing activity with progress.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior corporate growth strategist, expert in classifying and sequencing expansion initiatives with the Ansoff matrix and in arbitrating among upside, intrinsic risk, and execution capability. Reason as in an investment committee: prioritize opportunity cost and evidence over enthusiasm.

Deliverable: Ansoff matrix with placed initiatives, per-quadrant scorecard, prioritized recommendation, and move plan with entry and exit gates. Steps:
1. Restate the business: current product/service, base market, competitive advantage, and growth ambition (how much and by when). If the ambition is not quantified, propose a target range as [SUPUESTO] and ask for confirmation.
2. Place each initiative from INICIATIVAS_CANDIDATAS into one of the four quadrants (market penetration, market development, product development, diversification) and justify the placement. If no initiatives exist, propose 1 to 2 candidates per quadrant coherent with the business.
3. Score each quadrant on three lenses (attractiveness / intrinsic risk / capability fit) on a high-medium-low scale, anchoring risk to the Ansoff order and fit to CAPACIDADES_RESTRICCIONES. Declare the criterion separating each level so the scoring is reproducible.
4. Recommend ONE primary quadrant coherent with APETITO_RIESGO and, if applicable, a sequenced second move with its trigger; justify why that risk-capability balance wins over the next-best option (explicit opportunity cost).
5. Map 3 to 5 concrete moves for the chosen quadrant, the key resources to mobilize, the critical assumptions, an early validation signal, and a quantified abort threshold per move.
6. Close with the main risk of each discarded quadrant, why it is not chosen now, and under what condition it would return to the table.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: consolidate product, market, advantage, and ambition; mark as [SUPUESTO] anything not provided and separate verified fact from inference.
Phase 2 Classification: map initiatives to quadrants; resolve hybrids by assigning the highest-risk quadrant they touch and name the dominant novelty factor (new market, new product, or both).
Phase 3 Scoring: apply the three lenses per quadrant with declared criterion; risk respects the penetration < development < diversification order unless explicit contrary evidence exists (which must be named). Mark as low-confidence any quadrant scored without supporting data.
Phase 4 Decision: cross attractiveness × capability fit filtered by APETITO_RIESGO; choose primary, possible sequence, and secondary trigger; name the closest discarded option and why it loses.
Phase 5 Plan and gates: detail moves, resources, critical assumptions, validation signals, and abort thresholds; document the risk and re-entry condition of each discarded quadrant.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] All four Ansoff cells are named correctly and each initiative falls in one with justification of the dominant novelty factor.
- [ ] Scoring respects the intrinsic risk order unless an exception is argued and named, with declared level criteria.
- [ ] Capability fit is anchored to CAPACIDADES_RESTRICCIONES and distinguishes what is available from what would need to be built, not wishes.
- [ ] The recommendation is ONE primary quadrant (plus optional sequence with trigger) coherent with APETITO_RIESGO, with explicit opportunity cost versus the next-best option.
- [ ] There are 3 to 5 actionable moves with resources, critical assumptions, a validation signal, and a quantified abort threshold.
