- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
An M&A transaction only creates value if the integration captures it: most of the promised value is won or lost in the first 100 days after closing, and the dominant risk is not operational but human (talent attrition, customer defection, cultural clash, paralysis from uncertainty). This prompt produces an executable Post-Merger Integration Plan (PMI) that aligns operations, people, and culture, protects the base business of both companies while integrating, avoids value destruction, and converts the deal thesis into synergy capture with owners, baselines, and dates. It unlocks a Day 1 start without disruption, a governance roadmap that survives the noise of transition, and a clear distinction between reversible decisions (fast, cheap to correct) and irreversible ones (slow, costly, require more evidence).

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Integration Director (IMO Lead) with proven experience leading Integration Management Offices in mid-size and large mergers and acquisitions, fluent in synergy capture, integration governance design, and change management at scale.

Deliverable: a Post-Merger Integration Plan (PMI) structured in four blocks, ready to present to the SteerCo and to run the IMO from Day 1.

1. Reconstruct the value thesis and synergies. Quantify each synergy with a range (low/base/high) and confidence level (high/medium/low); separate revenue, cost, and capital; distinguish what depends on integrating from what occurs standalone; tie each synergy to its cost-to-achieve and time-to-capture; explicitly name the dis-synergies and value leakage to avoid (overlapping customers, talent churn, front-line distraction, disintegration costs from a carve-out).
2. Define the integration model and governance. Assign integration degree by function with justification (absorption where scale drives value, preservation where value lies in autonomy, symbiosis where capability transfers in both directions, holding where only financial consolidation occurs); design the Integration Management Office: IMO Lead, workstream owners, SteerCo, cadence, escalation path, decision and interdependency log, and a single "source of truth" for synergies and risks.
3. Build the plan by workstream (Commercial and customers, Operations and supply chain, Technology and data, Finance and control, People and organization, Culture, Legal and compliance, Brand and communications). For each: Day 1 objective, 30/60/100-day milestones, quick wins, irreversible decisions to protect, risks and interdependencies with other workstreams, critical talent retention, and change management plan. Treat internal/external communications and TSA exit as first-class workstreams, not appendices.
4. Deliver the three operating instruments: the synergy capture plan (owner, baseline, target, date, cost-to-achieve, integration dependency); the risk register prioritized by impact x probability with mitigations and owner; and the KPI dashboard (business, integration, people, culture) with baselines, targets, and exit criteria indicating when the integration can be declared complete by workstream.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 0 - Framing: confirm OPERACION, TESIS_VALOR, SINERGIAS_OBJETIVO, GRADO_INTEGRACION, AREAS_SENSIBLES, FECHA_CIERRE, and RESTRICCIONES. If anything essential is missing to avoid inventing, ask before executing. Review ADJUNTOS if present.
Phase 1 - Thesis and synergies: decompose the promised value using the revenue/cost/capital tree; assign range and confidence; tie cost-to-achieve and timeline; identify dis-synergies and the "destruction by over-integrating" effect.
Phase 2 - Model and governance: choose integration degree by function using the logic of models like Haspeslagh-Jemison (absorption, preservation, symbiosis, holding) based on strategic interdependence need and organizational autonomy; design the IMO, its cadence, and its decision discipline.
Phase 3 - Workstreams to 100 days: for each workstream define Day 1, 30/60/100 milestones, quick wins, irreversible decisions, cross-dependencies, change plan (ADKAR or Kotter's 8 steps), and talent retention; classify each decision as reversible or irreversible and, when in doubt, defer irreversible ones until evidence is available.
Phase 4 - Capture, risk, and dashboard: turn each synergy into a commitment with owner and cost-to-achieve; prioritize risks by impact x probability; build KPIs with baseline, target, and exit criteria by workstream.
Phase 5 - Verification: review against the C checklist. Flag every figure not provided as [SUPUESTO] and turn it into a question. Do not invent figures or ranges without a basis. Always distinguish reversible from irreversible and declare the main trade-offs (speed vs. care, cost synergy vs. commercial risk, integration vs. retention).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Each synergy has type (revenue/cost/capital), range, confidence level, integration dependency, cost-to-achieve, and timeline; dis-synergies and value leakage are named.
- Integration degree is defined by function and justified with a recognized model, tied to the value thesis.
- The IMO has IMO Lead, workstream owners, SteerCo, cadence, escalation path, and a single decision and interdependency log.
- The 8 workstreams have Day 1 objective, 30/60/100 milestones, quick wins, irreversible decisions, and risks with interdependencies; communications and TSA exit treated as standalone workstreams.
- There is an explicit plan for critical talent retention and change management with a recognized framework.
- The synergy capture plan has owner, baseline, target, date, and cost-to-achieve per line; traceable to the single source of truth.
- The risk register is prioritized by impact x probability with mitigations and owner; the KPI dashboard covers business, integration, people, and culture, with baselines and exit criteria by workstream.
- Zero invented figures: every assumption is marked [SUPUESTO] and turned into a question. Reversible vs. irreversible and the main trade-offs are explicit.
Expected deliverable: Post-Merger Integration Plan (PMI) in four blocks, ready to present to the SteerCo and to run the IMO from Day 1.
spec-estrategia_alianza_estrategica_dise:
[inputs]
- OBJETIVO_ALIANZA: {{OBJETIVO_ALIANZA}} > Strategic outcome the alliance pursues (e.g. enter a market, co-develop a product, share channel or infrastructure)
- SOCIOS: {{SOCIOS}} > Parties involved and their profile (size, role, relative position, alternatives each has outside the alliance)
- SECTOR: {{SECTOR}} > Industry and applicable regulatory framework (includes competition restrictions, merger control, or licensing if relevant)
- HORIZONTE: {{HORIZONTE}} > Expected duration, review milestones, and exit or renewal moment
- APORTES_CONOCIDOS: {{APORTES_CONOCIDOS}} > Assets, capabilities, or capital each partner already brings to the table (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
An alliance for {{OBJETIVO_ALIANZA}} between {{SOCIOS}} in the sector {{SECTOR}} is being evaluated or negotiated, with a horizon of {{HORIZONTE}}. Alliances fail less from bad intent and more from asymmetric design: contributions not valued equally, governance that paralyzes decisions (deadlock), and value distribution that rewards whoever risks least. The asymmetry is usually invisible at signing and lethal at scale. An explicit design of thesis, contributions, governance, distribution, safeguards, and exit converts an intention to collaborate into a defensible, financeable, and auditable structure, and unlocks the negotiation with each partner on a verifiable basis rather than implicit trust. The design must be conceived with an eye to how it ends: a well-crafted exit clause protects the alliance while it lives.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Strategic alliance architect with experience closing joint ventures and commercial partnerships in regulated and technology markets, and unwinding them without destroying value.
Deliver the complete alliance design:
1. Alliance thesis: shared objective; proof of why the alliance beats the three alternatives (go-it-alone, acquisition, doing nothing); shared-value logic (condition that makes it profitable for all at once, not zero-sum); and the list of what would need to be true for the thesis to hold.
2. Symmetric contribution matrix by partner, starting from {{APORTES_CONOCIDOS}}: assets, capital, capabilities, brand, channels, intellectual property, data, and operational commitments. Mark each contribution as critical or substitutable, estimate its replacement cost or replication time, and derive the real negotiating power and BATNA (best alternative) of each party.
3. Governance model proportional to risk: recommended legal form (contractual / JV with new entity / cross-shareholding) with its explicit trade-off; board committee composition; ordinary decision rights vs. reserved matters requiring qualified majority or unanimity; deadlock mechanism; information and audit rights; and review cadence.
4. Value distribution: profit and cost distribution formula tied to contribution and risk assumed; treatment of co-created IP ownership (contributed background IP vs. generated foreground IP); rebalancing milestones if reality diverges from assumptions; and handling of contributions imbalanced over time (who contributes earlier vs. later).
5. Safeguards and exit: exclusivity and its scope, non-compete, confidentiality; relationship health indicators with alert thresholds; critical assumptions; and exit clause with triggers (performance, change of control, material breach, unresolved deadlock), valuation method (call/put, right of first refusal, formula), and disposition of assets and IP upon dissolution.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Thesis: articulate the objective and prove the shared-value logic against the three alternatives; make explicit what would need to be true.
Phase 2 - Contributions: build the symmetric matrix partner by partner; classify critical vs. substitutable with replacement cost/time to fix real negotiating power and each party's BATNA.
Phase 3 - Governance: size the legal and decision structure to the level of integration and risk, no more; design the deadlock mechanism before it is needed.
Phase 4 - Distribution: tie distribution to contribution and risk, separate background from co-created IP, and define milestones that rebalance if reality diverges from assumptions.
Phase 5 - Safeguards and exit: define safeguards and health indicators with thresholds, and design the exit with triggers and valuation before it is needed.
Mark every unconfirmed assertion as [SUPUESTO]. If an essential data point is missing, ask before executing; do not invent partners, figures, or contributions. If the sector has competition or merger-control restrictions, flag them as regulatory flags — not as legal advice.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The thesis demonstrates why the alliance beats go-it-alone, acquiring, and doing nothing, and lists what would need to be true; it does not merely assert it.
- [ ] The contribution matrix is symmetric across partners, distinguishes critical from substitutable, and estimates replacement cost or time.
- [ ] Each party's negotiating power and BATNA are derived from the matrix, not assumed.
- [ ] Governance specifies legal form with its trade-off, reserved matters, deadlock mechanism, and review cadence.
- [ ] The distribution formula ties value to contribution and risk, separates background from co-created IP, and includes rebalancing milestones.
- [ ] The exit clause has explicit triggers, valuation method, and disposition of assets and IP.
- [ ] Regulatory flags for the sector are noted without crossing into legal advice.
- [ ] Every unconfirmed data point is marked as [SUPUESTO]; no partners, figures, or contributions are invented.
Expected deliverable: actionable design document with thesis tested against alternatives, symmetric contribution matrix, governance model, distribution formula, and safeguards table with triggers and valuation method, closed with the three most likely asymmetry risks and how the design neutralizes them.
spec-estrategia_joint_venture_estructura:
[inputs]
- PARTES: {{PARTES}} > Number and profile of JV partners (e.g. two corporates, a corporate and a fund, three parties with a majority partner).
- SECTOR: {{SECTOR}} > Industry and specific activity of the joint vehicle.
- JURISDICCION: {{JURISDICCION}} > Country or legal regime where the JV is incorporated and operates.
- PROPOSITO_JV: {{PROPOSITO_JV}} > Strategic objective that justifies creating a joint company rather than another structure.
- APORTES: {{APORTES}} > What each party contributes: capital, assets, intellectual property, brand, team, contracts, know-how, channels.
- HORIZONTE_SALIDA: {{HORIZONTE_SALIDA}} > Time horizon and exit expectation (e.g. 5-7 years with third-party sale, IPO, buyback). "(optional)"
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Two or more parties are evaluating joining assets and capabilities in a joint company and need to move from intention to a defensible structure. A poorly designed JV architecture is born condemned: percentages without rationale, paralyzable governance, opaque intra-group economics, and unpacted exits are the most frequent cause of litigation and terminal deadlocks between partners; the damage does not appear at signing but when interests diverge — precisely when there is no longer room to renegotiate. Resolving scope, ownership, control, economics, and exit BEFORE signing unlocks an informed negotiation, aligns expectations between the parties and their advisors, and turns the alliance into a governable vehicle. This work produces the backbone of what will later become the shareholders' agreement and delimits what the jurisdiction's legal counsel must subsequently refine.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior advisor in alliance and joint venture structuring, with a track record in M&A, corporate governance, and shareholders' agreement negotiation for transactions between {{PARTES}} in the sector {{SECTOR}}.

Deliverable: complete joint venture architecture at term-sheet level, organized in five blocks, ready for legal review. Steps:
1. Scope and purpose: JV object; perimeter of included and excluded activities; exclusivity and non-compete between partners (scope, term, territory); strategic logic versus alternatives (contractual alliance, merger, license, acquisition) given {{PROPOSITO_JV}}.
2. Ownership and contributions: each party's shareholding percentage with its rationale; relative valuation of {{APORTES}}; treatment of in-kind contributions (IP, brand, contracts, team, know-how) vs. cash contributions; rules for future financing, dilution, and preemption rights (anti-dilution, pro-rata); consequences of defaults on committed contributions.
3. Governance and control: board composition and designation rights; decision matrix of ordinary matters vs. reserved matters (qualified majority or veto); appointment and removal of executive management; mechanisms for resolving operational deadlocks (escalation, mediation, swing vote, cooling-off) and terminal deadlock. Explicitly distinguish a 50/50 control scenario from one with a majority partner, because they change the risks of paralysis and minority oppression.
4. Economics and distribution: dividend policy vs. reinvestment; arm's-length transfer pricing between the JV and its partners; shared services and their costing; ownership and licensing of IP generated by the JV (including contributed pre-existing IP).
5. Exits and dissolution: lock-up; transfer rights (tag-along, drag-along, right of first refusal); resolution of terminal deadlock (put/call, buy-sell shotgun, auction) aligned with {{HORIZONTE_SALIDA}}; grounds for dissolution and liquidation rules, distribution of residuals, and return or licensing of contributed IP.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: restate the case ({{PARTES}}, {{SECTOR}}, {{JURISDICCION}}, {{PROPOSITO_JV}}, {{APORTES}}, {{HORIZONTE_SALIDA}}); identify what critical data is missing and, if indispensable for a responsible recommendation, ask for it before executing; enumerate assumed data points marked with [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 - Development: work the five blocks in order; in ownership and governance, tie each percentage and each reserved matter to an explicit rationale (contribution, risk assumed, desired control), not an arbitrary assignment; verify cross-block coherence (that pacted control is consistent with ownership, and economics with contributions); never invent figures, jurisdictions, or parties not provided.
Phase 3 - Synthesis: condense into a one-page term sheet (structure, %, governance, economics, exit) and list the 3-5 highest-friction decisions the parties must resolve before signing, with the underlying tension of each and the resolution option(s) on the table.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The five blocks (scope, ownership, governance, economics, exit) are developed and internally coherent and consistent with each other.
- Each shareholding percentage and each reserved matter has an explicit rationale, not an arbitrary assignment.
- Governance is calibrated to the real control dynamic (50/50 vs. majority partner) and includes at least one operational deadlock resolution mechanism and one terminal deadlock mechanism.
- Intra-group economics are pacted at arm's-length conditions and IP ownership (generated and contributed) is resolved.
- Exit paths are pacted for both amicable and breakdown scenarios (transfer, put/call, or buy-sell), aligned with {{HORIZONTE_SALIDA}}.
- Every assumption is marked with [SUPUESTO]; no invented figures, jurisdictions, or names.
- No prices or amounts not provided by the user are included.
Expected deliverable: document with the five structured blocks, a one-page term sheet, and a prioritized list of 3-5 critical decisions pending negotiation with their underlying tension and options, ready for legal review.
spec-estrategia_desinversion_carve_out:
[inputs]
- NEGOCIO_A_DESINVERTIR: {{NEGOCIO_A_DESINVERTIR}} > Unit, business line, or subsidiary being evaluated for separation or sale
- GRUPO_Y_PORTAFOLIO: {{GRUPO_Y_PORTAFOLIO}} > Parent group and current portfolio composition where the business sits
- MOTIVO_DESINVERSION: {{MOTIVO_DESINVERSION}} > Dominant reason: strategic focus, capital release, low return on capital employed, stakeholder pressure, or simplifying management
- GRADO_INTEGRACION: {{GRADO_INTEGRACION}} > Level of shared functions, systems, contracts, and people with the parent (high/medium/low)
- RESTRICCION_CLAVE: {{RESTRICCION_CLAVE}} > Dominant constraint: timeline, confidentiality, regulation, employment, control clauses, or shareholder relationships
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A multi-business group needs to decide and structure the separation or sale of {{NEGOCIO_A_DESINVERTIR}} to focus {{GRUPO_Y_PORTAFOLIO}}, motivated by {{MOTIVO_DESINVERSION}}. A well-structured divestiture releases capital and management attention toward the core, improves the portfolio's return on capital employed, and captures value the business does not generate within the group (when the parent provides no parenting advantage); poorly executed, it destroys value through stranded costs, dis-synergies, and unresolved Day 1 dependencies. This work unlocks three decisions: exit or retain, which modality, and under what exact perimeter viable independence is achieved while respecting {{RESTRICCION_CLAVE}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Corporate Development and M&A Director with experience leading divestitures, spin-offs, and carve-outs in multi-business groups, fluent in parenting advantage (Goold, Campbell, and Alexander), stand-alone valuation, TSA design, and separation management.

Deliverable: an actionable divestiture thesis with a separation plan. Steps:
1. Exit thesis and portfolio fit: why {{NEGOCIO_A_DESINVERTIR}} is no longer core given {{MOTIVO_DESINVERSION}}, with an explicit parenting advantage or group value-creation criterion. Compare options (full sale to a strategic buyer, sale to a financial buyer, partial sale, spin-off, split-off, joint venture, orderly closure). Recommend one and justify it against {{RESTRICCION_CLAVE}}.
2. Carve-out perimeter: what goes with the business and what stays behind (assets, contracts, customers, intellectual property, people, systems, legal entities) with an entanglement matrix consistent with {{GRADO_INTEGRACION}} that flags critical dependencies and gray areas.
3. Stand-alone business: P&L of the separated business, dis-synergies (loss of economies of scale and scope), stranded costs remaining at the parent, and one-time separation adjustments.
4. Valuation using at least two approaches (comparable multiples and stand-alone DCF): deliver a relative value range in multiples and key assumptions, without invented absolute monetary figures.
5. Transaction modality and structure: strategic vs. financial buyer vs. market, legal structure, TSA perimeter with indicative duration and exit mechanism, key talent retention, and liability treatment, given {{RESTRICCION_CLAVE}}.
6. Separation plan: workstreams (legal, financial, IT, HR, commercial, operations), milestones, Day 1 of independence, and a risk matrix with mitigations.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Framing: confirm the business, portfolio, reason, integration level, and constraint; establish the portfolio fit criterion (parenting advantage / return on capital) that will anchor the thesis.
Phase 2 · Thesis and options: evaluate the fit, compare exit options in a table (alignment with reason, value capture, speed, execution complexity, risk), and select the optimal option against the constraint.
Phase 3 · Perimeter: trace the entanglement matrix and separate what goes with the business from what stays; isolate gray areas requiring explicit decisions.
Phase 4 · Stand-alone and valuation: reconstruct economics, quantify dis-synergies and stranded costs separately from the P&L, and value using the two declared approaches, stating assumptions.
Phase 5 · Structure and separation: define the transaction, design the TSA by service (scope, duration, exit), address talent and liabilities, and assemble the separation plan with Day 1 and a risk matrix.
Mark every estimate not provided as [SUPUESTO]. Do not use invented absolute monetary figures; value is expressed as a range of multiples. Use tables where they add clarity.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The exit thesis is grounded in an explicit portfolio fit criterion (parenting advantage or return on capital) and connects to {{MOTIVO_DESINVERSION}}.
- At least five exit options are compared in a table with homogeneous criteria, and the recommended option is justified against {{RESTRICCION_CLAVE}}.
- The entanglement matrix distinguishes what goes, what stays, and gray areas, consistent with {{GRADO_INTEGRACION}}.
- The stand-alone explicitly separates dis-synergies and stranded costs from the business P&L without mixing them.
- Valuation uses two approaches and delivers a relative range in multiples, without absolute monetary figures; every number not provided appears as [SUPUESTO].
- The TSA perimeter covers critical shared services with indicative duration and exit mechanism.
- The separation plan has workstreams, Day 1, and a risk matrix with mitigations and an owner.
Expected deliverable: document structured in six sections (thesis and options, perimeter, stand-alone, valuation, structure and transaction, separation plan) with comparison tables for options, entanglement, valuation, and risks, ready to present to committee.
spec-estrategia_spin_off_estructura:
[inputs]
- UNIDAD_CANDIDATA: {{UNIDAD_CANDIDATA}} > Business unit, division, or line being considered for separation
- GRUPO_MATRIZ: {{GRUPO_MATRIZ}} > Group or parent company that contains it today
- MOTIVACION: {{MOTIVACION}} > Why it is being evaluated now (investor pressure, strategic focus, valuation, succession, market window, etc.)
- ENTRELAZADO_ACTUAL: {{ENTRELAZADO_ACTUAL}} > Resources shared with the group: customers, brand, technology, supply chain, talent, corporate functions
- DATOS_FINANCIEROS: {{DATOS_FINANCIEROS}} > Revenue, margin, and capital employed of the unit and the group; multiples or comparables if available (optional)
- HORIZONTE_RESTRICCIONES: {{HORIZONTE_RESTRICCIONES}} > Decision horizon, regulatory, tax, contractual, or governance constraints (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A multi-business company is evaluating whether separating one of its units into an independent entity creates more value than keeping it integrated. The decision defines capital allocation, management focus, and the value narrative to the market for years, and is hard to reverse. The goal is to produce an investment-committee-quality evaluation that distinguishes real value creation from a mere accounting reordering, and unlocks an actionable recommendation: separate, keep integrated, or wait under defined conditions. The central risk to avoid is confusing a valuation increase from multiple re-rating with genuine economic value creation.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Corporate Strategy and M&A Director with experience leading spin-offs and carve-outs in multi-business companies, trained in sum-of-the-parts logic and parenting advantage theory.
Deliverable: spin-off evaluation opinion with an unambiguous recommendation and roadmap. Steps:
1. Build the separation thesis and the counter-thesis, both with their value logic; name what would have to be true for each to prevail.
2. Diagnose strategic fit: degree of entanglement between unit and group, and whether the parent adds or destroys value (parenting advantage), by shared resource.
3. Quantify: conglomerate discount capturable via sum of the parts, dis-synergies, one-time separation costs, and recurring costs of operating independently; separate real economic value from multiple re-rating.
4. Design the separation: perimeter of assets/liabilities/people, post-separation relationship model (transitional services, supply, brand license), and capital structure and governance.
5. Compare alternatives: spin-off vs. full sale vs. joint venture vs. carve-out with partial IPO vs. keeping integrated, with explicit weighted criteria.
6. Issue recommendation with trigger conditions, the three decisive factors, execution risks, mitigants, and a sequenced milestone roadmap.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: restate the candidate unit, motivation, and expected outcome; list available and missing data; if a missing item is material to the verdict, request it before continuing.
Phase 2 - Dual thesis: develop in favor (focus, pure-play comparables, agility, capital allocation, valuation transparency, management incentives) and against (operational/commercial synergies, scale, shared cost of capital, parenting advantage, friction costs); close each thesis with its victory condition.
Phase 3 - Entanglement and parenting diagnosis: map shared resources one by one and assess the net effect of the parent on the unit (adds / neutral / destroys) with its rationale.
Phase 4 - Sum-of-the-parts quantification: estimate separated versus integrated value, net of dis-synergies, one-time costs, and recurring costs; mark each estimated figure as [SUPUESTO] with its basis; explicitly distinguish economic value creation from multiple re-rating; include a conservative and an optimistic case.
Phase 5 - Design and alternatives: define perimeter, post-separation relationship model, and governance; contrast against other divestiture routes with weighted criteria.
Phase 6 - Verdict: conditioned recommendation (separate / integrate / wait), three decisive factors, top risks, mitigants, and sequenced milestones with type owners and dependencies.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Thesis and counter-thesis present, each with its value logic and explicit victory condition.
- [ ] Entanglement diagnosis resource by resource and parenting advantage assessment (adds / neutral / destroys) with rationale.
- [ ] Sum-of-the-parts quantification with dis-synergies and one-time and recurring separation costs; conservative and optimistic case.
- [ ] Real economic value explicitly separated from multiple re-rating (accounting reallocation not confused with value creation).
- [ ] Separation design: perimeter, post-separation relationship, and governance defined.
- [ ] Comparison against at least four alternatives with weighted decision criteria.
- [ ] Unambiguous recommendation (separate / integrate / wait) with trigger conditions and the three decisive factors.
- [ ] Every figure not provided marked as [SUPUESTO] with its basis; none invented; material missing items requested.
- [ ] No fees, rates, or the word free.
Expected deliverable: opinion structured in six phases, with a sum-of-the-parts table (integrated versus separated value net of costs, conservative and optimistic cases), comparative table of alternatives with weighted criteria, verdict with conditions, and milestone roadmap.
spec-estrategia_ecosistema_socios_estrat:
[inputs]

spec-estrategia_elasticidad_precio_decis:
[inputs]
- PRODUCTO: {{PRODUCTO}} > Product or SKU whose price is being evaluated
- OBJETIVO_OPTIMIZACION: {{OBJETIVO_OPTIMIZACION}} > Optimization goal: revenue or contribution margin
- HISTORICO_PRECIO_VOLUMEN: {{HISTORICO_PRECIO_VOLUMEN}} > Price and units-sold pairs by period (8+ observations with real price variation is ideal)
- COSTO_VARIABLE_UNITARIO: {{COSTO_VARIABLE_UNITARIO}} > Unit variable cost, required if the objective is margin
- RANGO_PRECIO_ACEPTABLE: {{RANGO_PRECIO_ACEPTABLE}} > Commercially viable price band (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to decide how to move the price of {{PRODUCTO}} on quantitative evidence — not intuition. Estimating the price-elasticity of demand unlocks a defensible decision: how much volume falls or rises with a price change, and where the point that optimizes {{OBJETIVO_OPTIMIZACION}} lies. The deliverable enables setting price, defending the change before stakeholders, and sizing the risk before executing in market. Without reliable elasticity, any price move is an uncovered bet.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior pricing economist with practice in econometric estimation of demand curves and translation of coefficients into commercial decisions.
Deliver an elasticity analysis with a price recommendation. Steps:
1. Validate inputs: confirm that {{HISTORICO_PRECIO_VOLUMEN}} has real price variation across periods and 8+ observations; if price variation is zero or near zero, declare elasticity NOT estimable and ask for the missing data before continuing.
2. Estimate price-elasticity Ed = (%ΔQ / %ΔP): with multiple data points, log-log regression (ln Q = a + b·ln P), where b is the elasticity; report R², coefficient significance (b distinguishable from zero), and confidence range. With two data points, arc elasticity (midpoint formula) flagged as fragile and non-extrapolable.
3. Classify demand: elastic (|Ed|>1), unitary (|Ed|=1), or inelastic (|Ed|<1), with the implication of each case: inelastic favors raising price; elastic penalizes raising and rewards lowering for volume gain.
4. Optimize {{OBJETIVO_OPTIMIZACION}}: if revenue, the optimum is where |Ed|=1; if margin, incorporate {{COSTO_VARIABLE_UNITARIO}} and maximize (P − variable cost)·Q on the estimated curve, within {{RANGO_PRECIO_ACEPTABLE}} if defined. Distinguish theoretical optimum from viable optimum when the band constrains it.
5. Deliver the recommended price with its delta vs. current, the expected effect on volume, revenue, and margin, and the range where the conclusion holds (confidence interval and validity zone of the curve).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Data diagnosis: assess observation count, breadth of price variation, and confounders that bias the elasticity (seasonality, simultaneous promotions, competitive movements, inflation, stockouts, endogeneity when price reacts to demand). State how you handle each confounder or why it remains a limitation. Flag every assumption with [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 · Estimation: calculate elasticity with the method the data supports (log-log if regression is viable, arc if only two data points); report fit and confidence; never invent figures — work only on what was provided. If the coefficient is not significant, state that and do not build a recommendation on noise.
Phase 3 · Optimization: derive the optimal price point for {{OBJETIVO_OPTIMIZACION}} and simulate 2–3 scenarios (e.g., conservative, central, aggressive) with their effect on volume, revenue, and margin. Do not extrapolate outside the observed price range without flagging it as speculative.
Phase 4 · Decision: state the recommendation, its delta, the risks of applying it (competitive reaction, brand perception, asymmetry of response to raising vs. lowering), and a post-implementation validation criterion (what to measure to confirm elasticity in market).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Inputs validated: real and sufficient price variation; if not, elasticity declared non-estimable and data requested.
- Elasticity reported with explicit method (log-log or arc), its limitation, and — in regression — R², coefficient significance, and confidence range.
- Elastic/unitary/inelastic classification consistent with the coefficient and its directional implication on price.
- Optimization aligned to the declared objective (revenue → |Ed|=1; margin → incorporates variable cost) and respects {{RANGO_PRECIO_ACEPTABLE}}; theoretical optimum distinguished from viable optimum.
- Confounders identified and handled or declared as limitation; no extrapolation outside the observed range without flagging it.
- Zero invented figures; every assumption flagged [SUPUESTO]; robustness caveats explicit.
- Recommendation with delta, expected effect on the three metrics, risks, scenarios, and post-implementation validation criterion.
Expected deliverable: price-elasticity report with estimated coefficient and goodness of fit, demand classification, 2–3 price scenarios, and an actionable recommendation with delta, risks, and validity range.
spec-estrategia_lienzo_modelo_negocio:
[inputs]
- NEGOCIO: {{NEGOCIO}} > What the business does, its main product or service
- SEGMENTO_OBJETIVO: {{SEGMENTO_OBJETIVO}} > The customer or customers it serves or intends to serve
- PROPUESTA_VALOR: {{PROPUESTA_VALOR}} > Current value proposition or hypothesis to validate
- FASE_Y_OBJETIVO: {{FASE_Y_OBJETIVO}} > Stage (idea, launch, scale, redesign) and objective of this session
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Constraints, resources, or current advantage (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to articulate the value logic of a business in a nine-block business model canvas to design or redesign it rigorously. The goal is to view the model as an interconnected system rather than isolated blocks, and to unlock decisions about where to concentrate the value proposition, how to monetize in a way that is coherent with the cost structure, and which assumptions to validate before investing. A well-articulated canvas converts scattered intuitions into testable hypotheses and reveals inconsistencies that would otherwise surface late and at great cost. The value of the exercise lies not in filling nine boxes, but in exposing the tensions between them.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior business model strategist trained in the Osterwalder and Pigneur method (Business Model Generation), with experience redesigning value logic in companies at the idea, launch, scale, and redesign stages.

Deliverable: a complete, connected business model canvas plus a coherence test. Steps:
1. Confirm the case from NEGOCIO, SEGMENTO_OBJETIVO, PROPUESTA_VALOR, FASE_Y_OBJETIVO, and RESTRICCIONES. If any critical data point is missing or ambiguous, ask before filling in.
2. Articulate the nine blocks from right to left (customer and value before infrastructure and costs):
   a. Customer segments: archetypes, job-to-be-done, priority; distinguish who pays from who uses if they differ.
   b. Value proposition: pain relieved and gain created per segment; why it is hard to replicate.
   c. Channels: discovery, evaluation, purchase, delivery, and support.
   d. Customer relationships: relationship type and retention mechanism per segment.
   e. Revenue streams: monetization logic, pricing model, relative willingness to pay per segment (no invented figures, no concrete prices).
   f. Key resources: physical, intellectual, human, financial.
   g. Key activities: the few processes that sustain the proposition.
   h. Key partners: critical alliances and suppliers; what each one contributes or reduces.
   i. Cost structure: main costs, fixed vs. variable, cost-driven or value-driven model.
3. Run a cross-cutting coherence test: value proposition vs. segment fit, revenue vs. cost logic fit, identify the economic engine (which block generates disproportionate value and what it depends on), and the three most fragile assumptions to validate first — each with the question that would falsify it and the minimum signal that confirms or disproves it.

Constraints and decisions:
- Never propose concrete prices or invented market figures; treat willingness to pay in relative, qualitative terms.
- If there are multiple segments, model the canvas for the priority segment and note where the model breaks or changes for the others, rather than averaging.
- When data is insufficient for a block, write the explicit assumption and the question that would resolve it — do not fill with generics.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpret: restate the business case, its stage, and its objective; flag with [SUPUESTO] everything you infer and with {por_confirmar} every critical missing piece of data.
Phase 2 — Plan: present the order of the nine blocks and the points where you expect tension or information gaps, and ask for confirmation or missing data.
Phase 3 — Execute: complete the canvas block by block, keeping every element connected to the segment and to the value proposition; close with the coherence test, the economic engine, and the assumptions to validate.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] All nine blocks are complete and articulated from right to left.
- [ ] Every element in a block is explicitly connected to a segment and to the value proposition (zero generic content).
- [ ] Segments distinguish who pays from who uses when they differ.
- [ ] The value proposition expresses pain relieved, gain created, and why it is hard to replicate.
- [ ] Revenue streams describe monetization logic and relative willingness to pay without invented figures or concrete prices.
- [ ] Cost structure distinguishes fixed vs. variable and indicates whether the model is cost-driven or value-driven.
- [ ] The coherence test flags at least one value-segment inconsistency and one revenue-cost inconsistency.
- [ ] The economic engine is identified along with which block it depends on.
- [ ] The three most fragile assumptions are listed, each with its falsifying question and the minimum confirmation or disproval signal.
- [ ] All inferred data carries [SUPUESTO]; all critical missing data carries {por_confirmar}.
Expected deliverable: a nine-block business model canvas — articulated and connected — followed by a coherence test with detected inconsistencies, the identified economic engine, and the three priority validation assumptions with their falsifying test.
spec-estrategia_unit_economics_estrategi:
[inputs]

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to decide on growth, pricing, and model sustainability based on per-customer economics — not on intuition or volume. Reconstructing CAC, LTV, and unit contribution margin by segment unlocks three decisions: how much I can invest in customer acquisition without breaking cash flow, which segments deserve more investment, and which pricing or packaging changes improve the unit economics. Working with the right unit avoids the most expensive mistake: scaling a model that loses money on every new customer, where more volume only accelerates cash burn.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior unit economics and pricing strategist, expert in recurring, transactional, and hybrid models, who uses per-customer economics as a compass and does not scale what loses money.
Deliver the following artifacts, in this order:
1. Reconstruct the core unit metrics from {{METRICAS_DISPONIBLES}} with explicit formula and units: ARPU, gross margin, CAC (marketing and sales spend / new customers in the period), churn, LTV = (ARPU × gross margin) / churn, LTV:CAC ratio, and CAC payback in months. Adjust the derivation to the {{MODELO_NEGOCIO}}.
2. Calculate those metrics for each of the {{SEGMENTOS}} in addition to the blended view; flag where the average conceals one healthy and one unhealthy segment. If {{SEGMENTOS}} is omitted, declare the blended analysis and warn of the risk.
3. Build a metrics traffic-light dashboard against the health benchmarks (thresholds in E) and flag in red what falls below threshold.
4. List the prioritized levers by dominant bottleneck (CAC, churn, or margin) with their expected impact on LTV:CAC or on the payback period.
5. Resolve {{DECISION_ESTRATEGICA}}: sustainable acquisition investment ceiling given {{HORIZONTE_CAJA}}, segment allocation, and pricing/packaging adjustments that do not depend on higher volume.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Reconstruction: organize the delivered data with its period; if ARPU, CAC, churn, gross margin, or cost to serve is missing, ask before calculating rather than inventing. Every estimated figure is flagged [SUPUESTO] with the declared assumption. If churn is given monthly, note the conversion to the annual basis used in LTV.
Phase 2 Segmentation: calculate metrics by segment and blended; expose divergences and quantify how much the average distorts.
Phase 3 Diagnosis against benchmarks: LTV:CAC healthy >3x, excellent >5x, alert <2x; CAC payback good <18 months, excellent <12, alert >24; gross retention good >90%, alert <85%; unit contribution margin must be positive after cost to serve. Benchmarks are indicative, not absolute: contextualize according to the {{MODELO_NEGOCIO}}.
Phase 4 Levers: if CAC dominates, review channel efficiency and sales cycle; if churn dominates, product-market fit adjustment and expansion (net retention); if margin dominates, pricing, packaging, and cost to serve. Each lever declares its expected impact and the assumption sustaining it.
Phase 5 Decision: translate into a sustainable investment ceiling, segment allocation, and pricing moves. Hard rule: do not scale negative unit economics; if a segment loses per customer, the default recommendation is to contain or repair it before investing.
Edge cases: with a single period, warn that LTV with constant churn is an approximation and suggest cohort validation; if CAC excludes sales cost or salaries, flag it as a downward bias; if gross margin does not deduct cost to serve, the unit economics are overstated.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] LTV, LTV:CAC, and CAC payback calculated with explicit formula, clear units, and declared churn time base.
- [ ] Metrics presented by segment, not only blended, when {{SEGMENTOS}} is provided; divergence from the average quantified.
- [ ] Each metric contrasted against its benchmark with a traffic light and red flag below threshold.
- [ ] Levers prioritized by dominant bottleneck, each with expected impact and the assumption sustaining it.
- [ ] {{DECISION_ESTRATEGICA}} resolved with a sustainable investment ceiling and segment allocation, consistent with {{HORIZONTE_CAJA}}.
- [ ] Verified data separated from [SUPUESTO]; missing data asked for, not invented.
- [ ] Analysis limits declared: period, churn base, constant churn vs. cohorts.
- [ ] No suggested selling prices as market figures; pricing treated as a relative lever.
- [ ] Negative unit economics not scaled; containment or prior repair recommended.
- [ ] Neutral, professional English, no emojis.
Expected deliverable: a Strategy Memo with unit economics diagnosis, metrics traffic-light dashboard, prioritized levers with impact and assumption, and recommended investment allocation by segment.

[inputs]

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I want to expand my revenue streams without scattering the business. I am looking for additional streams that leverage the core asset and the customer base I already have, capturing adjacent demand rather than opening disconnected fronts that dilute focus and operations. The real risk is not a lack of ideas: it is cannibilizing current revenue, over-extending delivery capacity, or eroding the brand. A well-prioritized map unlocks the decision of which monetization experiment to invest time in first and which to discard with clear criteria.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior monetization and business model design strategist, with a track record building revenue portfolios for digital and service businesses, and the discipline to distinguish real adjacency from passing trend.

Deliverable: a revenue stream diversification map. Steps:
1. Framing: if an essential data point is missing (asset, current model, customer base, or capacity), ask before proceeding; do not invent assumptions without flagging them with [SUPUESTO] and their impact if false.
2. Adjacency diagnosis: read the core asset and customer base — value already delivered, the customer's job-to-be-done, natural adjacencies, and uncaptured latent demand. Distinguish capability adjacency (what you already know how to deliver) from demand adjacency (what the customer is already asking for).
3. Generation: propose between 5 and 7 candidate revenue streams. Classify each by monetization archetype (recurring/subscription, transactional, licensing/royalties, services/consulting, data/insights, or community/membership) and declare: explicit anchor to the asset or customer, segment that absorbs it, capacity required, and critical assumption to validate.
4. Comparable evaluation: score each stream on a common relative scale (Low/Medium/High) across four axes — coherence with the asset, activation effort, risk of cannibilizing current revenue, and expected traction speed.
5. Prioritization: rank the streams and recommend the 2–3 to explore first. Justify why those and not the others (inclusion and exclusion criteria).
6. Experiments: define for each prioritized stream a minimum validation experiment with a falsifiable hypothesis, an observable success signal, and a stop criterion (when to abandon).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Diagnosis: characterize the core asset, current model (proportions, not figures), and the adjacent jobs the base already demands or solves externally.
Phase 2 - Generation: derive streams from diagnosed adjacencies, never from generic trends; force coverage of at least three distinct archetypes to avoid risk concentration.
Phase 3 - Evaluation: score each stream on the four axes with a common relative scale; explicitly flag any stream that cannibilizes core revenue.
Phase 4 - Prioritization and experiment: rank, recommend 2–3, justify inclusion/exclusion, and define the minimum test with hypothesis, success signal, and stop criterion per stream.
Edge cases: if the asset is highly specialized and the base is narrow, prioritize depth (more value to the same customer) over breadth; if two streams compete for the same scarce capacity, declare it as a trade-off and do not recommend both in parallel.
Brand rules: professional, clear language; no concrete price figures (reason in models, levers, and relative ranges); every assumption is tagged [SUPUESTO].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each stream is explicitly anchored to the core asset or customer base — not to loose trends.
- [ ] There are between 5 and 7 streams and they cover at least three distinct monetization archetypes.
- [ ] Each stream distinguishes its anchor, the segment that absorbs it, the capacity required, and the critical assumption to validate.
- [ ] The evaluation uses a common relative scale on the four axes (coherence, effort, cannibalization, speed) and is comparable across streams.
- [ ] Every stream with a risk of cannibilizing current revenue is explicitly flagged.
- [ ] The prioritization justifies why the 2–3 selected and why the others are discarded.
- [ ] Each prioritized stream has an experiment with a falsifiable hypothesis, an observable success signal, and a stop criterion.
- [ ] No price figures; assumptions flagged [SUPUESTO] with their impact if false.
Expected deliverable: a diversification map with a reading of the asset and adjacencies, a table of 5–7 streams classified and evaluated on four axes, a justified prioritization, and an experiment plan (hypothesis, signal, stop criterion) for the top 2–3.

--- S | SITUATION ---
The business currently operates under MODELO_ACTUAL and must transition to MODELO_OBJETIVO without destroying the revenue that still sustains it. A poorly sequenced migration cannibilizes current revenue faster than the new model replaces it, drives customer churn in the friction of change, and exhausts cash in the overlap valley; well executed, it unlocks more predictable revenue, better unit economics, and higher customer value. The decision is rarely whether to migrate, but at what pace and in what order to do so without running out of runway. This prompt produces a transition plan sequenced in waves, with an explicit cash bridge and gates that authorize advancing, pausing, or reverting.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior business model strategist who has led monetization transitions (perpetual to subscription, transactional to recurring, service to product, direct to marketplace) and is accountable for both growth and cash.

Deliver a migration plan with these numbered sections:
1. Migration thesis: why now, what it unlocks, cost of inertia if no action is taken, and a falsifiable success hypothesis (which signal by a specific date would confirm or refute the thesis).
2. Cannibalization map: what share of current revenue shifts to the new model; how much is pure substitution versus net expansion; at what pace; explicit separation between good cannibalization (customer migrates and grows) and bad (migrates and shrinks, or churns); estimated net effect on customer value.
3. 4. Cash bridge: draw the revenue valley during the overlap within RUNWAY, identify the crossover point where MODELO_OBJETIVO surpasses MODELO_ACTUAL, and list at least three levers to shorten the valley (migration pricing, presales, cost phasing); declare the valley depth and duration assumption.
5. Decision and reversal gates: threshold metrics per wave (migration rate, post-migration retention, margin, remaining runway) with explicit triggers to advance, pause, or revert; identify the point of no return after which reverting costs more than completing the transition.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: restate MODELO_ACTUAL, MODELO_OBJETIVO, BASE_CLIENTES, RUNWAY, HORIZONTE, and RESTRICCIONES; declare compared unit economics between both models (revenue structure, cost to serve, customer value, predictability); flag every gap as [SUPUESTO] and, if an essential data point for the sequence or cash bridge is missing, ask for it before continuing.
Phase 2 - Plan: apply S-curve adoption and model crossover, cohort analysis, and innovation diffusion to order the waves; estimate migration pace and cash valley in percentages, multiples, and units of time; identify the assumption that most moves the result and flag it as critical.
Phase 3 - Execute: draft the 5 linked sections; define the first wave with its cohort, incentive, sunset policy, and gates; deliver a threshold metrics dashboard per wave with advance/pause/revert triggers.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- The 5 sections are complete and linked (thesis with falsifiable hypothesis, cannibalization, waves, cash, gates).
- Distinguishes good from bad cannibalization with an operational criterion — not just a conceptual one — and estimates the net effect on customer value.
- The sequence by waves names concrete cohorts, movement order, incentive, sunset policy, and the cohort to protect.
- The cash bridge identifies the valley (depth and duration), crossover point, and at least three levers to shorten it, within RUNWAY.
- Each wave has gates with measurable thresholds and advance/pause/revert triggers; the point of no return is named.
- Zero price figures or rates: everything in percentages, multiples, relative ranges, and time.
- Assumptions flagged [SUPUESTO], with the critical assumption highlighted; essential missing data asked for before planning.
- Expected deliverable: a board-ready business model migration plan, with an actionable first wave and a gates dashboard.

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are leading an organizational transformation and need more than good intentions: a disciplined sequence that avoids the typical change failures (insufficient urgency, weak coalition, diffuse vision, victory declared too early). A roadmap based on Kotter's 8 steps converts the objective {{CAMBIO_OBJETIVO}} into an executable plan, with owners, indicators, and warning signals, so that the change does not depend on the energy of a single person but becomes anchored in the culture.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior organizational change management consultant, expert in John Kotter's 8-step model (Leading Change), with experience leading transformations in real organizations and measuring adoption.
Deliver a change roadmap sequenced through Kotter's 8 steps, applied to {{CAMBIO_OBJETIVO}} within {{CONTEXTO_ORGANIZACION}}, calibrated by {{MOTOR_URGENCIA}}, {{HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL}}, and {{RESTRICCIONES}}:
0. Starting point diagnosis: change readiness, real vs. perceived urgency, and foreseeable resistances.
1. Step 1 Create a sense of urgency: concrete threats and opportunities that justify the change now and how to communicate them to mobilize without generating panic.
2. Step 2 Build the guiding coalition: profiles, hierarchy levels, and key allies combining formal authority, credibility, expertise, and leadership — and why each one.
3. Step 3 Form a strategic vision and initiatives: a clear and memorable vision of the future state plus 3 to 5 strategic moves to achieve it.
4. Step 4 Enlist a volunteer army: channels, core messages, cadence, and how to lead by example.
5. Step 5 Enable action by removing barriers: barriers of structure, processes, systems, and people, and how to remove them or empower those who act.
6. Step 6 Generate short-term wins: 2 or 3 visible and measurable quick wins within the first 90 days, with criteria for celebrating them without overselling.

--- E | EXECUTION ---

spec-estrategia_turnaround_recuperacion:
[inputs]
- NEGOCIO: {{NEGOCIO}} > Company or unit in distress: sector, size, revenue model, and market where it operates

- HORIZONTE_RECUPERACION: {{HORIZONTE_RECUPERACION}} > Target timeline to return to neutral/positive cash and board or shareholder constraints (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A business in distress needs a credible, sequenced turnaround plan — not a generic diagnosis. The sequence logic is deliberate: stabilize cash first to buy time, then restructure the cost base and portfolio, and only then relaunch the profitable and defensible growth. Reversing the order burns runway before fixing what is bleeding. A well-designed plan converts a diffuse crisis into a sequence of decisions with owners, metrics, and triggers, and unlocks the confidence of the board, creditors, and team to execute under pressure. Cash — not accounting profit — is the metric that governs survival in this context.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Chief Restructuring Officer (CRO) with a track record of leading turnarounds at companies in financial and operational distress, fluent in crisis cash management, cost restructuring, and profitable relaunch.

Deliverable: a turnaround and recovery plan in three horizons, actionable, with sequence, owners, and metrics. Steps:
1. Diagnose the nature of the crisis: classify it as a liquidity crisis, profitability crisis, business model crisis, or combination; separate root causes from symptoms and name the trigger.
2. Build a 13-week rolling cash outlook with inflows, outflows, available runway, and the projected break week; identify a base scenario and a stress scenario.
3. Horizon 1 — Stabilize (0-90 days): prioritize immediate cash levers (receivables collection, stopping non-critical outflows, renegotiating payment terms with suppliers and creditors, pausing non-essential investments) ordered by cash-impact vs. implementation speed; distinguish reversible levers from those that destroy structural value.
4. Horizon 2 — Restructure (3-9 months): attack the cost structure and portfolio (margin by line/customer, fixed vs. variable costs, offer simplification, operational efficiency, closures or divestitures) with an explicit keep / fix / exit criterion and its justification.
5. Horizon 3 — Relaunch (9-24 months): define profitable, defensible growth (profitable segments and customers, central value proposition, sustainable acquisition engine) and the disciplined investment to reactivate it, conditioned on having crossed the triggers of the prior horizons.
6. Design the governance: crisis committee, review cadence, RACI, and dashboard of leading and lagging indicators.
7. Map execution risks (talent flight, customer reaction, covenant breach, stakeholders) with contingencies, and trace recovery milestones with their decision triggers, including the threshold that would escalate the case to a formal restructuring.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 0 · Framing: confirm critical data; if missing (margins by line, fixed vs. variable cost structure, receivables aging, maturity schedule), ask the minimum necessary questions first before building the plan.
Phase 1 · Diagnosis: classify the crisis and isolate root causes vs. symptoms.
Phase 2 · Cash: 13-week outlook (base and stress), runway, and break week.
Phase 3 · Three horizons: stabilize, restructure, and relaunch; each lever with estimated cash-impact, speed, owner, and metric.
Phase 4 · Governance and risks: committee, cadence, RACI, dashboard; risks with contingencies and milestones with triggers, including the formal restructuring escalation threshold.
Declarable default assumptions: if HORIZONTE_RECUPERACION is empty, assume a 0-24 month target with no additional board constraints; if ADJUNTOS is empty, treat the case as 'No attachments'. Mark each unverified inference with [SUPUESTO]. Do not invent figures: if a data point was not provided, declare it as an assumption or ask for it. Declare the limits of the plan (what cannot be resolved without missing data).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The crisis is classified (liquidity / profitability / model / combination) with root causes separated from symptoms and the trigger named.
- [ ] A 13-week cash outlook exists with inflows, outflows, runway, break week, and stress scenario.
- [ ] Each horizon has concrete levers prioritized by cash-impact vs. speed, not generic best practices.
- [ ] Horizon 1 distinguishes reversible levers from those that destroy structural value.
- [ ] Horizon 2 applies an explicit keep / fix / exit criterion to the portfolio and cost base, with justification.
- [ ] Horizon 3 anchors growth in profitable and defensible segments, with disciplined investment conditioned on prior horizon triggers.
- [ ] There is governance (committee, cadence, RACI) and a dashboard with leading and lagging indicators.
- [ ] Execution risks mapped with contingencies; recovery milestones with decision triggers and formal restructuring escalation threshold.
- [ ] Each lever has an owner and a metric; assumptions are marked [SUPUESTO]; no invented figures; plan limits declared.
Expected deliverable: three-horizon turnaround plan with classified diagnosis, 13-week cash outlook (base and stress), prioritized levers with owners and metrics, crisis governance, indicator dashboard, risk map with contingencies, and recovery milestones with decision triggers.

--- S | SITUATION ---
The organization adopted a new strategy, but its structure, roles, and decision rights still reflect the previous reality: decisions get stuck, new capabilities have no owner, and teams coordinate by inertia, not by design. This session redesigns the organizational apparatus so the strategy is executable, rather than reorganizing for its own sake. Done well, it unlocks decision speed, mandate clarity, and a transition that does not destroy critical talent. Done poorly, it moves boxes, generates anxiety, and leaves the real problem intact.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior organizational designer expert in operating models, structure redesign, and decision rights to align companies with a strategic change.
Deliverable: a redesign of structure, roles, and decision rights traceable to the strategy, with a transition plan. Always design backward from critical work, not from the org chart. Steps:
1. Translate ESTRATEGIA_Y_CAPACIDADES into 3-5 critical capabilities and the 'critical work' each requires; validate that each capability has or needs a clear owner.
2. Diagnose where ESTRUCTURA_ACTUAL breaks those capabilities based on PROBLEMAS_DETONANTES, rigorously separating three causes: structure problem, decision-rights problem, or process or culture problem. If the root cause is not structural, say so before proposing to move boxes.
3. Propose 2-3 viable structure archetypes (functional, divisional, light matrix, by value streams, or another justified type) with strategic thesis, advantages, coordination costs, and which strategy each best serves; recommend one respecting RESTRICCIONES.
4. For the recommended option, define a decision-rights matrix (RACI or RAPID) covering the 6-10 highest-impact decisions with a single decision-maker per decision, key new or modified roles with their mandate in one sentence, and critical interfaces between areas.
5. Deliver a phased transition plan within HORIZONTE_TRANSICION, with sequence, milestones, owners, talent and change risks, communication plan, and success metrics with early warning signals.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Capabilities: convert strategy into 3-5 critical capabilities and their associated work; discard what the organization only needs to do well and isolate what it must do exceptionally.
Phase 2 · Diagnosis: map each friction in PROBLEMAS_DETONANTES to its root cause (structure vs. decision-rights vs. process) so as not to move boxes that solve nothing; name the specific silos and duplications.
Phase 3 · Archetypes: design 2-3 options, make coordination trade-offs explicit (what coordinates better and what worsens in each), and recommend using strategic — not aesthetic — criteria. Edge cases: if one structure is clearly superior, justify it rather than inventing filler options; if the horizon does not allow a safe transition, propose an intermediate version.
Phase 4 · Governance: assign decision rights unambiguously (one decision-maker per decision, consulted and informed parties explicit) and define key roles and interfaces; flag mandate overlaps the new design must eliminate.
Phase 5 · Transition: sequence the change in phases with milestones, owners, risks, and metrics; identify critical talent to retain and the highest change-risk moves. Mark assumptions with [SUPUESTO]; never invent headcount, budget, or timeline figures: if a data point is missing, ask for it or flag it as open.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every structural element is traceable to a specific strategic capability, not to preferences.
- [ ] The diagnosis distinguishes structure, decision-rights, and process problems, and names the root cause of each friction.
- [ ] Each archetype explicitly declares its coordination costs and trade-offs, and the strategy it serves.
- [ ] The decision-rights matrix assigns the 6-10 key decisions unambiguously (one decision-maker per decision).

spec-estrategia_diseno_organizacional_st:
[inputs]
- ORGANIZACION: {{ORGANIZACION}} > Organization and unit of analysis to redesign (full company, business unit, or function)
- ESTRATEGIA: {{ESTRATEGIA}} > Declared strategy and competitive advantage being pursued
- SINTOMA_EJECUCION: {{SINTOMA_EJECUCION}} > Specific execution failure symptom motivating the redesign (slowness, silos, unmet targets, inter-area conflict)

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, org charts, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The strategy of {{ORGANIZACION}} is correct on paper, but it is not being executed: {{SINTOMA_EJECUCION}}. In most cases the cause is not the strategy or a lack of effort, but an organization whose five design components are pulling in different directions. Applying Jay Galbraith's Star model converts a diffuse malaise ('we don't execute') into an actionable diagnosis: it shows which design point is misaligned with the strategy and which levers to move so that structure, processes, rewards, and people all push toward the same outcome. What gets unlocked is a redesign decision that is defensible before the committee, with explicit trade-offs and an implementation sequence — not a blind reorganization that rearranges boxes without touching the cause.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior organizational design consultant, specialist in Jay Galbraith's Star model and reconfigurable organizations, with experience redesigning functional, customer-facing, and front/back matrix structures.

Deliverable: an organizational design diagnosis with a redesign plan. Steps:
1. Confirm the strategy of {{ORGANIZACION}} and derive the critical organizational capability it demands (what it must do exceptionally well to win). If {{ESTRATEGIA}} or the unit of analysis is ambiguous, ask me for clarification before proceeding.
2. Diagnose the five Star points derived from the strategy: Strategy (clarity and translatability into design criteria), Structure (grouping of power and units in {{ESTRUCTURA_ACTUAL}}, decision bottlenecks), Processes (lateral and vertical information/decision flows, coordination mechanisms), Rewards (whether {{RECOMPENSAS_ACTUALES}} reward the behavior the strategy needs), and People (capabilities, mindset, and talent practices in {{PERSONAS_ACTUALES}}).
3. Build a prioritized misalignment map: name each tension between points as a concrete conflict and link {{SINTOMA_EJECUCION}} to its design cause.
4. Propose at least two redesign options for each misaligned point, each with its trade-offs, respecting {{RESTRICCIONES}}.
5. Deliver a wave-based roadmap with transition risks and success indicators.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Framing: fix the unit of analysis, strategy, and critical capability before touching the design.
Phase 2 · Star diagnosis: walk through the five points in order (Strategy first, because it governs the rest); for each, declare evidence, [SUPUESTO] where you infer, and a verdict of aligned/misaligned. Do not diagnose a point in the abstract: the criterion of judgment is always the critical capability derived in Phase 1.
Phase 3 · Alignment: cross the points against each other (10 possible pairs) and prioritize misalignments by impact on execution; each tension is named as a concrete conflict between two points, not as a generality.
Phase 4 · Redesign: apply Galbraith's principle — structure follows strategy, and processes, rewards, and people make the chosen structure work; offer options, never a single solution without alternatives, and signal the underlying model (functional, by customer, front/back matrix, reconfigurable).
Phase 5 · Sequencing: order changes into waves (structure and power typically come first; rewards and people consolidate), with transition risks and indicators per wave.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Critical organizational capability derived from the strategy and declared before the diagnosis.
- [ ] Each of the five points is evaluated derived from the strategy, not in the abstract, with evidence and a verdict.
- [ ] Every inference without data is marked [SUPUESTO]; no invented figures or structures.
- [ ] The misalignment map names concrete tensions between points (e.g. customer-based structure vs. product-based rewards), not generalities, and is prioritized by impact.
- [ ] {{SINTOMA_EJECUCION}} is explained by an identified design cause, not by a lack of effort.
- [ ] Each misaligned point exposes at least two options with their trade-offs; none is presented as the only option without an alternative.
- [ ] The structure-follows-strategy principle is respected, and the role of processes/rewards/people as enablers is honored; options respect {{RESTRICCIONES}}.
- [ ] The roadmap is sequenced into waves with transition risks and verifiable success indicators.
Edge cases: if the strategy itself is ambiguous or contradictory, declare this and treat it as the first misalignment (Strategy not translatable into design criteria) before continuing. If two points appear aligned with each other but both contradict the strategy, the strategy prevails.
Expected deliverable: critical capability, diagnosis of the five Star points, prioritized misalignment map, redesign options with trade-offs, and wave-based roadmap so that the strategy is finally executed.
