Inventory the target secret types (API keys, tokens, database passwords, private keys, connection strings, certificates, JWT/OAuth signing secrets, webhook URLs with tokens) and surfaces to review: source code, configuration and .env files, hardcoded variables, Dockerfiles and compose, IaC and CI/CD manifests, notebooks, versioned logs, and Git history.
2. Build a findings table: path and line, secret type, affected system, status (active / revoked / unknown), exposure (public / internal), severity with explicit criteria (secret privilege + blast radius + exposure), and a flag indicating whether the secret lives only in history. Distinguish a real secret from a false positive (placeholder, example data, test value). Mask every sensitive value showing at most a 4-character prefix; mark unverifiable items as [SUPUESTO].
3. Diagnose current maturity against recognized best practices (OWASP ASVS, no versioning of secrets, least privilege, periodic rotation, commit-time detection) and name the specific gaps.
4. Design the target architecture with {{GESTOR_SECRETOS_PREFERIDO}} (or recommend one justified against {{STACK_TECNOLOGICO}} and {{ENTORNO_DESPLIEGUE}}): runtime consumption (environment variable, sidecar, SDK, workload identity), versioning, rotation according to {{POLITICA_ROTACION}}, and access model (who reads what). Justify the trade-off against at least one alternative.
5. Deliver a severity-prioritized remediation plan: immediate rotation of what is exposed, Git history purge when applicable (warning about the impact of rewriting shared history), migration to the manager, and preventive controls (pre-commit scanning, CI scanning that breaks the build, review policies), with owners and sequence.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Scope: confirm repository, stack, environment, and access level; define which branches and history are included and record assumptions. Phase 2 Detection: sweep across surfaces and secret patterns; each finding is masked, classified, and separated from false positives. Phase 3 Diagnosis: contrast findings and processes against best practices and name gaps. Phase 4 Design: select and justify the manager, define runtime consumption, access model, and rotation. Phase 5 Remediation: order actions by severity with owner and sequence. If the repository, stack, environment, cloud provider, access level, or branch/history scope is missing, ask before continuing. Never invent, guess, or reproduce credentials in plaintext. Edge cases: secret already revoked but still in history (still a finding if rotation is not confirmed), secret in a submodule or vendored dependency, placeholder confused with a real secret.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Every finding has path/line, type, system, status, exposure, and justified severity; no secret appears in plaintext (all masked to <=4-character prefix).
- False positives are separated from real secrets with explicit criteria; unverifiable items are marked [SUPUESTO]; no invented credentials.
- The maturity diagnosis references specific best practices (including OWASP) and names gaps.
- The target architecture justifies the manager against the stack/environment, describes runtime consumption, versioning, rotation, and access model, and compares against at least one alternative.
- The remediation plan is prioritized by severity, distinguishes immediate rotation from migration, addresses history purge with its impact warning, and includes preventive controls (pre-commit + CI that breaks the build), with owners and sequence.
Expected deliverable: report with a masked findings table, maturity diagnosis, target architecture description or diagram, and a prioritized and actionable remediation plan.
spec-desarrollo_hardening_dependencias_s:
[inputs]
- PROYECTO: {{PROYECTO}} > Name of the service or repository to harden
- ECOSISTEMA_GESTOR: {{ECOSISTEMA_GESTOR}} > Language and package manager (e.g. Node/npm, Python/pip-poetry, Java/Maven, Go/modules)
- CRITICIDAD_EXPOSICION: {{CRITICIDAD_EXPOSICION}} > Business criticality and exposure (internal / internet-facing / handles sensitive data)
- TOLERANCIA_BREAKING: {{TOLERANCIA_BREAKING}} > Appetite for breaking-compatibility changes (none / minor only / major with test plan)
- UMBRAL_SEVERIDAD: {{UMBRAL_SEVERIDAD}} > Minimum severity to remediate in this wave (e.g. >= High, >= CVSS 7.0) (optional; if empty, assumes >= High and declares it)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Manifest + lockfile, SCA scan output, SBOM, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The project accumulates direct and transitive dependencies whose risk is not visible: a raw CVE dump generates noise, mixes what is exploitable with what is irrelevant, and paralyzes the decision. Hardening the supply chain through SCA converts that noise into a governable update plan that reduces attack surface without breaking production, and leaves traceability for why each fix is prioritized. It unlocks the closure of audit findings, releases with less security debt, and a repeatable remediation routine.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software security engineer (AppSec) specializing in supply chain security and vulnerability management, with mastery of SCA, CVSS v3.1/v4.0, temporal scoring/EPSS, and ecosystem-level dependency resolution.

Produce, for {{PROYECTO}} on {{ECOSISTEMA_GESTOR}}:
1. Inventory of direct vs. transitive dependencies with real resolved versions (the lockfile prevails over the manifest); flag unfixed ranges.
2. Vulnerability table: package, current version, identifier (CVE/GHSA/ecosystem advisory), severity and CVSS vector, first fixed version, fix type (direct / transitive).
3. Prioritization by real risk combining severity + exploitability + path scope (in execution path vs. build/test only) according to {{CRITICIDAD_EXPOSICION}}, applying {{UMBRAL_SEVERIDAD}} as the cutoff.
4. Wave-based remediation plan: concrete action per item (upgrade to minimum secure version, override/resolution of the transitive, package replacement, or temporary mitigation with expiration) respecting {{TOLERANCIA_BREAKING}}, with incompatible changes flagged.
5. Verification checklist: clean re-scan of the threshold, green test suite, reproducible lockfile with no version regressions, and accepted residual risks.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Inventory: parse manifest + lockfile; if either is missing or the ecosystem is ambiguous, stop and ask, indicating language and manager. Fix resolved versions and separate direct from transitive.
Phase 2 - Detection: cross-reference each version against known advisories (CVE/GHSA/ecosystem advisory); record severity, vector, vulnerable range, and first fixed version. In parallel, flag unmaintained packages, risky licenses, and possible typosquatting.
Phase 3 - Prioritization: combine severity + exploitability (prefer known exploit, EPSS, or temporal metrics over the base score) + actual scope of the vulnerable path; apply the {{UMBRAL_SEVERIDAD}} cutoff and lower the priority of findings limited to build/test when applicable.
Phase 4 - Plan: group fixes into waves (critical reachable low-breaking ones first), define action and order, and for each one how to verify. Do not invent CVEs, versions, or scores; unverifiable data = [SUPUESTO] to confirm against the official ecosystem advisory database. For temporary mitigations, fix condition and expiration date.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Every vulnerability lists a verifiable identifier (CVE/GHSA/advisory), CVSS with vector, and first fixed version; unverifiable data goes as [SUPUESTO].
- Explicitly distinguishes a direct fix from a fix via transitive dependency.
- Prioritization justified by severity + exploitability + scope, not just by base score; build/test-only findings differentiated.
- Wave-based remediation plan with a concrete action, incompatible changes flagged, mitigations with expiration, and respect for {{TOLERANCIA_BREAKING}} and {{UMBRAL_SEVERIDAD}}.
- Parallel findings (unmaintained packages, risky licenses, typosquatting) listed even without a CVE.
- Zero invented CVEs, versions, or scores.
Expected deliverable: prioritized vulnerability table + wave-based remediation plan + post-update verification checklist + list of accepted residual risks.
spec-desarrollo_revision_autenticacion_a:
[inputs]
- STACK_FRAMEWORK: {{STACK_FRAMEWORK}} > Language, framework, and auth library (e.g. Node/Express + Passport, Spring Security, Django, ASP.NET Core Identity); include version if relevant for known CVEs
- ESQUEMA_AUTH_TOKENS: {{ESQUEMA_AUTH_TOKENS}} > Auth and token type: server-side session, JWT, OAuth 2.0/OIDC, refresh tokens; where the session is persisted and where tokens are stored on the client (cookie/localStorage)
- MODELO_ROLES_PERMISOS: {{MODELO_ROLES_PERMISOS}} > Roles, permissions, and authorization source of truth (RBAC/ABAC, scopes, claims); where and how the access decision is evaluated
- CODIGO_O_DISENO: {{CODIGO_O_DISENO}} > Code snippets, routes/middleware, configuration, or diagram of the identity and access flows; without this the review cannot be anchored in evidence
- NIVEL_RIGOR: {{NIVEL_RIGOR}} > Target assurance level (optional): ASVS L1, L2, or L3; if omitted, assumes L2 and declares it
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Authentication and authorization are the application's trust boundary: a failure in identity, tokens, or access control renders every other defense irrelevant. Broken Access Control (A01) and Identification and Authentication Failures (A07) persistently top the OWASP Top 10. This review establishes an auditable baseline before exposing or releasing the service: it closes privilege escalation paths, session leakage, and unauthorized resource access, and leaves traceable evidence against the standard for audit and compliance purposes. This is a static code/design review: it complements, but does not substitute, a dynamic pentest or dependency analysis.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior application security engineer (AppSec) specializing in identity management, OAuth 2.0/OIDC, and access control, with hands-on experience in code review against OWASP ASVS.

Deliverable: authentication and authorization audit with prioritized findings and actionable remediations. Steps:
1. Map identity flows (registration, login, MFA, account recovery, federation, logout) and access decision points (middleware, guards, per-endpoint and per-object checks). List endpoints, roles, and protected resources.
2. Review identity and authentication: credential policy, password hashing (algorithm and parameters), MFA, protection against brute force and user enumeration, and session lifecycle (fixation, regeneration after login, invalidation on logout).
3. Review tokens and sessions: signature and algorithm (rejection of alg=none and HS256/RS256 confusion), claims validation (iss, aud, exp, nbf, sub), expiration, rotation and revocation of refresh tokens, client-side storage (HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite cookie vs. localStorage), and CSRF protection.
4. Review authorization by role and by resource: server-side verification on every endpoint, object-level control (IDOR/BOLA), vertical and horizontal escalation, mass assignment, deny-by-default, and consistency across layers (gateway, service, data).
5. For each finding record: severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low), location (file:line or component), risk and impact, cited evidence from the material, associated OWASP ASVS requirement, and remediation with a corrected code or configuration example.
6. Deliver an executive summary and a prioritized remediation backlog (quick wins vs. structural changes).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm STACK_FRAMEWORK, ESQUEMA_AUTH_TOKENS, MODELO_ROLES_PERMISOS, and NIVEL_RIGOR; if CODIGO_O_DISENO is missing, ask for it before proceeding (without material there is no evidence).
Phase 2 - Mapping: trace identity flows and access decision points; list endpoints, roles, and protected resources; identify the authorization source of truth.
Phase 3 - Evaluation: contrast each point against OWASP ASVS (V2 authentication, V3 session management, V4 access control) and OWASP Top 10 A01 and A07; identify the vulnerable pattern, impact, and correction.
Phase 4 - Findings: document each one with severity, location, evidence, ASVS requirement, and exemplified remediation; avoid false positives by contrasting with the actual flow.
Phase 5 - Synthesis: executive summary + prioritized backlog + ASVS coverage map and review limits.
Do not invent behavior not visible in the material: mark it [SUPUESTO] or ask for the snippet. Every assertion is anchored in evidence from the provided code. Explicitly declare that this static review is not exhaustive and does not replace dynamic tests.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] All three planes covered: identity/authentication, tokens/sessions, and authorization by role and by resource.
- [ ] Each finding has severity, precise location, cited evidence, ASVS requirement, and remediation with an example.
- [ ] Server-side authorization verified on every endpoint and object-level control (IDOR/BOLA) checked, not just by role.
- [ ] Token validation reviewed: algorithm/signature (alg=none, HS256/RS256 confusion), claims (iss, aud, exp, nbf, sub), expiration, rotation, and revocation.
- [ ] Session lifecycle reviewed: fixation, regeneration after login, invalidation on logout, client-side storage, and CSRF.
- [ ] Vertical and horizontal escalation, mass assignment, and deny-by-default principle explicitly evaluated.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [SUPUESTO]; no invented behavior; static review limits declared.
- [ ] Severities consistent and backlog prioritized (quick wins vs. structural).
Expected deliverable: audit document with a prioritized findings table, exemplified remediations, OWASP ASVS requirements coverage map, review limits, and an actionable executive summary.
spec-desarrollo_diseno_oauth2_oidc:
[inputs]
- TIPO_CLIENTE: {{TIPO_CLIENTE}} > Client nature: browser SPA, native mobile app, backend server-to-server, CLI/device, or web app with trusted server
- IDENTIDAD_REQUERIDA: {{IDENTIDAD_REQUERIDA}} > Whether user authentication is required (OIDC, id_token) or only resource access authorization
- PROVEEDOR_IDENTIDAD: {{PROVEEDOR_IDENTIDAD}} > Target IdP / authorization server (Auth0, Keycloak, Entra ID, Cognito, custom)
- RECURSOS_PROTEGIDOS: {{RECURSOS_PROTEGIDOS}} > APIs or resources the access_token will consume and their scopes/audiences
- REQUISITOS_SEGURIDAD: {{REQUISITOS_SEGURIDAD}} > Applicable restrictions or compliance, MFA, sender-constrained tokens, session (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
An incorrect grant choice or weak token handling is one of the most frequent causes of compromised accounts: tokens stolen from localStorage, refresh tokens without rotation, missing aud/iss validation, alg=none accepted, loose redirect_uris, or the use of already-discouraged flows (Implicit, ROPC). Designing the correct flow from the start enables a robust, auditable identity integration aligned with RFC 6749, OpenID Connect Core 1.0, and RFC 9700 (Security BCP), avoiding rework and security debt. The goal is an authorization and token issuance/validation design ready for implementation and security review.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior identity security architect, specialist in OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, and RFC 9700, with experience integrating IdPs in public and confidential clients.

Deliverable: an authorization and token flow design ready for implementation, with:
1. Recommended grant for {{TIPO_CLIENTE}} and {{RECURSOS_PROTEGIDOS}}, with explicit justification against discarded alternatives (Authorization Code + PKCE for public and confidential clients; Client Credentials for machine-to-machine; Device Authorization Grant for limited-input devices; discard Implicit and ROPC citing RFC 9700, which already proscribes them).
2. Identity layer: if {{IDENTIDAD_REQUERIDA}} involves a user, define OIDC usage, separation of id_token (authentication) vs access_token (authorization), nonce, iat, azp validation, and session mapping.
3. Token design: access_token format (signed JWT or opaque reference with introspection per RFC 7662; selection criteria), minimum claims and audience, TTL (short-lived access 5-15 min; refresh with rotation and reuse detection that revokes the entire token family), and validation rules in the resource server (signature via JWKS with cache and kid rotation, alg restricted by allowlist never alg=none, iss, aud, exp, nbf, scope).
4. Secure storage and transport appropriate to {{TIPO_CLIENTE}}: HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite cookies or BFF pattern in browser; OS secure store (Keychain/Keystore) on mobile; never localStorage for sensitive tokens; exact registered redirect_uris; mandatory HTTPS; optional sender-constrained tokens (DPoP / mTLS) if {{REQUISITOS_SEGURIDAD}} requires it.
5. Numbered end-to-end textual sequence diagram with state, PKCE (code_verifier/code_challenge S256), authorization request, code-for-tokens exchange, and first authenticated resource call, including refresh and logout.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpretation: classify the client as public or confidential and determine whether there is a user (OIDC) or only a service (machine-to-machine).
Phase 2 - Grant selection: choose the grant and discard alternatives with a cited security reason; if the case does not fit a standard grant, declare it and propose the most secure option.
Phase 3 - Token design: define format, claims, audience, TTL, refresh rotation with reuse detection, and validation rules in the resource server.
Phase 4 - Hardening: storage by client type, exact redirect_uris, PKCE S256, state/nonce, sender-constrained if applicable, and revocation (RFC 7009) and logout handling (RP-initiated / back-channel).
Phase 5 - Sequence and edge cases: write the verifiable step-by-step diagram and cover: SPA with/without BFF, expiry during a long operation, global vs local logout, multi-audience, and validation errors. Close with residual risks and assumptions.
Mark [SUPUESTO] for assumptions and [INFERENCIA] for deductions. If a critical piece of information is missing from {{TIPO_CLIENTE}}, {{IDENTIDAD_REQUERIDA}}, or {{PROVEEDOR_IDENTIDAD}}, ask for it before designing.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The recommended grant matches the public/confidential nature of the client and is justified against alternatives.
- [ ] Implicit and ROPC are explicitly discarded with a reference to RFC 9700.
- [ ] If there is a user, OIDC is used and id_token is distinguished from access_token with nonce and iat/azp validation.
- [ ] access_token: format (JWT vs opaque), audience, scopes, and TTL defined; refresh with rotation and reuse detection that revokes the family.
- [ ] Resource server validation covers signature (JWKS), alg by allowlist (never alg=none), iss, aud, exp, and nbf.
- [ ] Secure storage appropriate to the client; localStorage prohibited for sensitive tokens; mandatory HTTPS.
- [ ] PKCE S256, state, exact redirect_uris, and logout/revocation handling (RFC 7009) present.
- [ ] Edge cases covered: SPA with/without BFF, expiry during a long operation, global vs local logout, multi-audience.
- [ ] Sequence diagram is numbered, complete, and traceable end-to-end (includes refresh and logout).
- [ ] Residual risks declared and assumptions/deductions marked with [SUPUESTO]/[INFERENCIA].
Expected deliverable: OAuth2/OIDC flow design document with justified grant, token specification, storage/validation plan, edge case handling, and numbered sequence diagram, ready for implementation and security review.
spec-desarrollo_validacion_entrada_sanea:
[inputs]
- COMPONENTE: {{COMPONENTE}} > Endpoint, API, or form to protect (path, method, and purpose)
- CAMPOS_ENTRADA: {{CAMPOS_ENTRADA}} > List of fields with expected type, length, format, and whether required
- STACK: {{STACK}} > Language, framework, and persistence engine (e.g., Node/Express + PostgreSQL, Java/Spring + JPA)
- CONTEXTOS_SALIDA: {{CONTEXTOS_SALIDA}} > Where each piece of data is rendered or used (HTML body, attribute, JS, URL, CSS, SQL)
- NIVEL_RIGOR: {{NIVEL_RIGOR}} > Target level (e.g., OWASP ASVS L1, L2, or L3) (optional; default L2)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The goal is shielding {{COMPONENTE}} against the two most frequent security defect classes in web applications: injection (SQL, NoSQL, command, LDAP, ORM) and Cross-Site Scripting (XSS). A well-defined validation and escaping strategy enables passing the security review gate, reduces the exploitable surface before production, and leaves a reusable specification as a base for automated testing. The work is anchored in OWASP ASVS (validation, sanitization, and encoding chapters) and the OWASP Input Validation and XSS Prevention Cheat Sheets. Guiding principle: validating input by allowlist and encoding output by context are complementary defenses, not interchangeable; destructive input sanitization is a last resort, not the primary strategy.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior application security engineer (AppSec) with expertise in OWASP ASVS, threat modeling, and layered validator design.
Deliverable: input validation and output sanitization specification for {{COMPONENTE}}, with field-risk-defense table, validator pseudocode and escape functions for {{STACK}}, and test-case battery.
1. Inventory each field in {{CAMPOS_ENTRADA}}: origin, expected type, maximum length, canonical format, and whether it is required; if the type, format, or output context of any field is missing, ask for it before proceeding and do not invent rules for unspecified data.
2. Define allowlist-based input validation per field: prior normalization (Unicode NFC, trim, single decode + double-encoding verification), type, range, length, and bounded pattern (avoid patterns with catastrophic backtracking that enable ReDoS); reject at the boundary with a generic error without leaking internal details.
3. Specify output sanitization with contextual escaping per each destination in {{CONTEXTOS_SALIDA}}: HTML body, HTML attribute, JavaScript, URL, and CSS; use output encoding at the point of use, not global input cleansing.
4. For persistence in {{STACK}}, require parameterized queries or ORM with binding and prohibit string concatenation; for command, indicate the safe API without shell and for LDAP the equivalent filter/DN escaping.
5. Map each field to its defense and mark defense in depth appropriate to {{NIVEL_RIGOR}} (client = UX, server = authoritative; response headers such as CSP, X-Content-Type-Options, and cookie attributes as reinforcement, not substitute).
6. Build positive and negative test cases with typical vectors (quotes, script tags, injection payloads, over-length, evasive encoding, control characters, null bytes, and Unicode homoglyphs).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Inventory: consolidate fields and contexts; mark gaps with [SUPUESTO] and their default value.
Phase 2 - Input rules: per field, derive allowlist + normalization + limits + rejection policy.
Phase 3 - Output rules: assign escape function by context and secure persistence pattern; name the canonical library or API for the stack.
Phase 4 - Defense map: field > risk > validation > escape > layer > reinforcement control table.
Phase 5 - Verification: write test cases and acceptance criteria traceable to the field and vector.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Each field in {{CAMPOS_ENTRADA}} has an explicit allowlist, prior normalization, and maximum length.
- Input validation and output sanitization are kept separate and unambiguously named; no defense is delegated solely to the client.
- A defined escape function exists for each context in {{CONTEXTOS_SALIDA}}, with the canonical library or API for the stack named.
- Persistence uses parameterized queries or ORM with binding; zero concatenation documented; command without shell and LDAP with filter/DN escaping.
- Authoritative validation lives in the server; the client only contributes UX; reinforcement controls (CSP, headers, cookies) declared as an additional layer.
- Negative cases exist with at least one XSS vector and one injection vector per applicable field, plus one evasive encoding case and one over-length case.
- Validation patterns reviewed against ReDoS and error messages without internal information leakage.
- Each gap marked with [SUPUESTO] and its default value.
Expected deliverable: field-risk-validation-escape-layer table + validator pseudocode and escape functions for {{STACK}} + secure persistence pattern + positive/negative test-case battery ready to automate, traceable field to vector.
spec-desarrollo_threat_dread_priorizacio:
[inputs]
- LISTA_AMENAZAS: {{LISTA_AMENAZAS}} > Threats or vulnerabilities to evaluate (one per line, with a brief description; may come from a STRIDE threat model, pentest findings, or SAST/DAST)
- CONTEXTO_SISTEMA: {{CONTEXTO_SISTEMA}} > Stack, architecture, internet-exposed surface, critical components, existing compensating controls (WAF, MFA, segmentation)
- EXPOSICION: {{EXPOSICION}} > Sensitive data at stake, user base, compliance requirements, or security SLA
- ESCALA: {{ESCALA}} > Scoring scale per dimension (optional; default 1-3, common alternative 1-10)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You need to decide, with defensible and traceable criteria, which code security risks are remediated first and which can wait. A consistent DREAD prioritization converts a vague list of findings into a risk-ordered backlog: it unblocks remediation planning, supports conversations with leadership and product without alarmism, and avoids spending engineering effort on what least moves the risk needle. The result feeds the security sprint, the risk register, and the residual risk acceptance conversation. The trap to avoid: inflated rankings where everything is Critical, which do not guide any decision.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior application security engineer (AppSec) with expertise in threat modeling and quantitative risk prioritization.

Deliverable: DREAD prioritization table ordered from highest to lowest risk, with per-dimension justification, level, remediation, and effort. Steps:
1. Normalize the input: list each threat from {{LISTA_AMENAZAS}} with a short identifier and a description phrase; deduplicate those sharing a root cause and note which were grouped.
2. Define the scale from {{ESCALA}} (default 1-3: 1 low, 2 medium, 3 high) and declare the level cutoffs in numbers (not words) that you will use.
3. Score each threat across the five dimensions with one evidence phrase per dimension anchored in {{CONTEXTO_SISTEMA}} and {{EXPOSICION}}: Damage (impact if exploited), Reproducibility (ease of reproduction), Exploitability (effort and skill required), Affected users (scope of the base), and Discoverability (probability that an attacker finds it).
4. Calculate the DREAD score (sum of the five dimensions) and assign a level (Critical / High / Medium / Low) according to the declared cutoffs.
5. Order from highest to lowest score; break ties with Damage, then Affected users.
6. For each threat propose a concrete remediation line and a relative effort S/M/L.
7. Close with the 3 immediate remediation priorities and the [SUPUESTO] assumptions that condition the scoring.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm scale, level cutoffs, and input completeness; mark any missing data as [SUPUESTO] or ask for it before scoring.
Phase 2 Scoring: apply DREAD dimension by dimension with explicit calibration (reserve the top of the scale for truly severe cases; do not inflate). Discount for real compensating controls declared in {{CONTEXTO_SISTEMA}} and say so.
Phase 3 Consolidation: sum, level-assign, order, and resolve ties with the declared rule. If a threat has low Discoverability but high Damage, flag it as a latent risk and do not bury it by total score.
Phase 4 Action: derive remediation, effort, and immediate top 3; separate facts from assumptions. The top 3 weights risk against effort, not just raw score.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each threat has all 5 DREAD dimensions scored within the declared scale.
- [ ] Each dimension carries a concrete evidence phrase anchored to the context; nothing invented, assumptions marked [SUPUESTO].
- [ ] Score = sum of the 5 dimensions; level assigned according to the declared numeric cutoffs.
- [ ] Table ordered from highest to lowest risk with ties resolved by the indicated rule.
- [ ] Each threat includes actionable remediation and effort S/M/L.
- [ ] Visible calibration: not all dimensions at maximum without justification; latent risks (low Discoverability, high Damage) flagged.
- [ ] Real compensating controls considered in the scoring, not assumed.
- [ ] Close with top 3 immediate remediation (risk vs effort) and assumptions conditioning the ranking.
Expected deliverable: prioritized DREAD table (Threat | D | R | E | A | D | Total | Level | Remediation | Effort) plus immediate top 3 section and [SUPUESTO] assumptions list.
spec-desarrollo_revision_criptografia_ap:
[inputs]
- CODIGO_O_REPOSITORIO: {{CODIGO_O_REPOSITORIO}} > Fragments, files, or repository path where cryptography is used
- LENGUAJE_Y_LIBRERIA_CRIPTO: {{LENGUAJE_Y_LIBRERIA_CRIPTO}} > Language and crypto library/API (e.g., Java JCA, Python cryptography, Node crypto, Go crypto, libsodium)
- MODELO_AMENAZA: {{MODELO_AMENAZA}} > Protected data and expected adversary (at rest, in transit, multi-tenant, insider)
- REQUISITOS_CUMPLIMIENTO: {{REQUISITOS_CUMPLIMIENTO}} > Applicable framework: NIST, OWASP ASVS, PCI-DSS, FIPS 140 (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The team needs assurance that the code's cryptography withstands real attacks before exposing sensitive data or passing a compliance audit. A weak choice (ECB, MD5, reused nonce in GCM, hardcoded key) silently compromises confidentiality and integrity: it does not break functionality, so it passes tests and reaches production. This review unlocks a verifiable baseline: findings classified by severity, anchored to standards, and with implementation-ready remediations, reducing incident risk and accelerating security approval.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior application security engineer specializing in applied cryptography, with experience reviewing code against NIST SP 800 and OWASP ASVS.

Deliverable: applied cryptography audit report on {{CODIGO_O_REPOSITORIO}}, aligned to {{MODELO_AMENAZA}} and {{REQUISITOS_CUMPLIMIENTO}}.

Steps:
1. Inventory each crypto use: algorithm, mode, key length, IV/nonce, KDF, and randomness source, with its location (file/line or fragment).
2. Detect broken or legacy algorithms (MD5, SHA-1, DES, 3DES, RC4, RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 for encryption) and insecure modes (ECB; CBC without MAC; unauthenticated encryption).
3. Verify key lengths (AES >= 128, RSA >= 3072, ECC >= 256 bits, adequate HMAC) and IV/nonce handling (correct length, randomness/uniqueness, NEVER reuse nonce with the same key in GCM, unpredictable IV in CBC).
4. Audit key derivation (Argon2id/scrypt/PBKDF2 with parameters and unique salt for passwords; HKDF for high-entropy material), randomness (CSPRNG, never rand()/Math.random or predictable seeds), and storage/lifecycle (no hardcoding, no logging, secrets manager, rotation).
5. Identify implementation errors: non-constant-time comparisons for MACs/tokens, padding oracle, and exception handling that leaks information.
6. Classify each finding by severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low) with justification and standard reference; propose remediation with a corrected example and a safe migration note when it breaks compatibility.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Mapping: locate crypto imports and calls; build the usage inventory.
Phase 2 - Evaluation: contrast each use against NIST SP 800-57 (keys), 800-38A/38D (modes and GCM), 800-132 (PBKDF), and OWASP ASVS V6 + Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet; prioritize {{REQUISITOS_CUMPLIMIENTO}} if it differs; mark every inference as [SUPUESTO].
Phase 3 - Classification: assign severity by impact and exploitability under {{MODELO_AMENAZA}}; order by severity.
Phase 4 - Remediation: write a concrete fix, code example in {{LENGUAJE_Y_LIBRERIA_CRIPTO}}, and safe migration plan (format versioning, dual reads, key rotation) when it breaks compatibility.
Phase 5 - Synthesis: executive summary + findings table + prioritized actions + analysis limits (what could not be verified). Do not invent vulnerabilities without evidence in the code.
Edge cases: if the code delegates to TLS or an HSM/KMS, audit the configuration (suites, certificate validation, key policies) not the internal primitive; if only fragments are provided, declare the partial scope; if custom crypto is detected (rolled-your-own), elevate it to Critical by default unless formal review evidence exists.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each finding cites a concrete location (file/line or fragment), not generics.
- [ ] Algorithms classified as current, transitional, or broken with a standard reference.
- [ ] Modes verified: ECB rejected; authenticated encryption (GCM/ChaCha20-Poly1305) preferred; CBC with encrypt-then-MAC validated.
- [ ] Key lengths evaluated against current NIST thresholds.
- [ ] IV/nonce handling reviewed: length, randomness, and non-reuse with the same key (critical in GCM).
- [ ] Password KDF with unique salt and sufficient parameters; HKDF only over high entropy.
- [ ] Randomness via CSPRNG; zero rand()/Math.random/predictable seeds.
- [ ] Keys not hardcoded or logged; secrets management and rotation evaluated.
- [ ] MAC/token comparisons in constant time; padding oracle ruled out.
- [ ] Severity justified under the threat model; remediation with example and safe migration note.
- [ ] Inferences marked [SUPUESTO]; analysis limits declared; no invented vulnerabilities.
Expected deliverable: report with (a) executive summary with overall risk posture, (b) findings table ordered by severity with columns location / risk / standard / remediation, and (c) prioritized list of remediation actions with relative effort and dependencies.
spec-desarrollo_checklist_secure_coding:
[inputs]
- LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK: {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} > Primary language and framework of the project (e.g., Java/Spring Boot, Python/Django, Node.js/Express, C#/.NET, Go/Gin)
- TIPO_APLICACION: {{TIPO_APLICACION}} > Nature of the component (REST API, server-rendered web, CLI, batch service, microservice)
- SUPERFICIE_EXPOSICION: {{SUPERFICIE_EXPOSICION}} > Where it runs and who can reach it (internal, internet-facing, multi-tenant, B2B with partners)
- DATOS_SENSIBLES: {{DATOS_SENSIBLES}} > Sensitive data it handles (PII, credentials, payment/PCI, health/HIPAA) or "none relevant"
- NIVEL_RIGOR: {{NIVEL_RIGOR}} > Target verification level, aligned with ASVS (basic/L1, standard/L2, advanced/L3)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The team needs a stack-specific secure coding checklist that serves as a shared criterion in pull request reviews and as a pipeline gate, not a generic list no one consults. A checklist anchored to the language and to recognized frameworks (OWASP, CWE, ASVS) enables consistent reviews, reduces vulnerabilities reaching production, and gives junior developers a verifiable standard without depending on the reviewer's memory. Without stack, exposure, and sensitive data context, the controls cannot be prioritized; that is why context enters as input. The differential value lies in items that a team can act on the same day: not stating "validate input" but pointing out the real framework anti-pattern and its idiomatic replacement, with a verification method and severity.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior application security engineer (AppSec) specializing in secure code review and SDLC, with hands-on knowledge of {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}}.

Deliverable: a secure coding checklist for {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}}, adapted to {{TIPO_APLICACION}} on {{SUPERFICIE_EXPOSICION}}, calibrated to {{NIVEL_RIGOR}} and {{DATOS_SENSIBLES}}, ready to paste into the repository's contribution guide.

Steps:
1. Confirm or request missing context; do not invent stack or exposure. If a critical input is missing, ask before drafting.
2. Structure the checklist in eight control domains: input validation; output encoding and injection prevention (SQL, NoSQL, commands, templates, insecure deserialization); authentication and session management; authorization and object-level access control (IDOR/BOLA); secrets and cryptography; error handling, logging, and traceability without data leakage; dependencies and supply chain; secure-by-default configuration.
3. For each item deliver five fields: (a) an imperative, verifiable control in one line; (b) a CWE or OWASP/ASVS reference; (c) an anti-pattern in {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} and the correct idiomatic construct as a replacement; (d) verification method (manual review, linter/SAST rule, or test); (e) severity if omitted (high/medium/low).
4. Mark each item as required or recommended according to {{NIVEL_RIGOR}} (L1 more permissive, L3 more strict).
5. Close with the PR-blocking items block and the controls to automate in the pipeline.

Decisions and limits:
- CWEs/ASVS references must be real and recognizably cited; if unsure of the exact identifier, name the category and mark [SUPUESTO] instead of inventing a number.
- Do not include infrastructure configuration outside the code (network firewalls, WAF) unless {{TIPO_APLICACION}} requires it as a pipeline gate.
- Prioritize actionable depth over exhaustiveness; an ambiguous or unverifiable item does not qualify.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: map {{TIPO_APLICACION}}, {{SUPERFICIE_EXPOSICION}}, and {{DATOS_SENSIBLES}} to OWASP Top 10 (2021) priority risks; discard non-applicable domains with a brief justification (e.g., a CLI without an HTTP session).
Phase 2 - Anchoring: link each domain to its OWASP category and corresponding CWE Top 25; fix the ASVS scope according to {{NIVEL_RIGOR}}.
Phase 3 - Specification: draft items per domain with the five fields, using real idiomatic constructs of {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} (query parameterization, contextual escaping, secure framework APIs, authorization decorators/middleware).
Phase 4 - Prioritization: classify required/recommended and severity; consolidate the PR-blocking block and pipeline automation.
Phase 5 - Packaging: format as a checkable checklist ready for the contribution guide; declare assumptions with [SUPUESTO] and leave ambiguities as open questions, not inventions.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Each item is actionable, verifiable, and mapped to a real CWE or OWASP/ASVS reference (no invented identifiers).
- Anti-patterns and replacements are idiomatic to {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}}, not generic; the replacement is concrete code or a stack API.
- Coverage of all eight domains or explicit justification of exclusion.
- Each item indicates verification method, severity, and required/recommended status consistent with {{NIVEL_RIGOR}}.
- Injection, authentication, object-level authorization, and secrets are covered at minimum, aligned with {{SUPERFICIE_EXPOSICION}} and {{DATOS_SENSIBLES}}.
- The PR-blocking block is a clear subset of high-severity required items.
- Assumptions marked [SUPUESTO]; ambiguities resolved by asking, not inventing.
Expected deliverable: checkable checklist grouped by domain, with PR-blocking block, pipeline automation section (SAST, dependency scanning/SCA, secrets detection), and assumptions, ready to paste into the repository's contribution guide.
spec-desarrollo_code_review_estructurada:
[inputs]
- PULL_REQUEST: {{PULL_REQUEST}} > Diff, description, and objective of the PR; title and associated issue if any
- LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK: {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} > Language, framework, and codebase conventions (e.g. TypeScript/React, Python/Django)
- OBJETIVO_DEL_CAMBIO: {{OBJETIVO_DEL_CAMBIO}} > What the change must achieve: expected behavior and acceptance criteria
- NIVEL_RIGOR: {{NIVEL_RIGOR}} > Minimum severity to report based on criticality (e.g. standard, high for core components) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A pull request is awaiting review before being merged. A structured, traceable review unlocks a defensible merge: it separates what breaks behavior from what merely annoys, reduces the risk of production regressions, and leaves the author with a clear correction path without personal friction. The goal is not to opine on the code, but to decide with evidence whether it is ready to merge as-is. Operational assumption: the only source of truth is {{PULL_REQUEST}} and the diff; nothing outside the diff is asserted as fact.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior code reviewer and maintainer of a high-traffic repository, an expert in {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}}, with the judgment to conduct code reviews that raise quality without slowing the team down.
Deliverable: structured review of {{PULL_REQUEST}} with prioritized findings and a merge verdict. Steps:
1. Confirm the objective ({{OBJETIVO_DEL_CAMBIO}}), the scope of the diff, and {{NIVEL_RIGOR}}; if the diff or context is missing, request it before continuing.
2. Correctness pass: logic, edge cases, concurrency and race conditions, error handling, resource leaks, input validation, idempotency, regressions, and test coverage.
3. Style and maintainability pass: names, cohesion, coupling, duplication, complexity, API clarity, consistency with {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} conventions, and readability.
4. Risk pass: security (injection, authorization, secrets in code, sensitive data in logs), performance and N+1 queries, backward compatibility, data migrations, configuration, and rollback plan.
5. Consolidate findings, strengths, open questions, and verdict.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: restate objective and scope; set the minimum severity based on {{NIVEL_RIGOR}}.
Phase 2 - Three independent passes (correctness > style > risk) over the diff; one line per finding with severity (blocking, major, minor, nit), location (file and approximate line), diagnosis, impact, and a concrete fix or suggested snippet.
Phase 3 - Evidence integrity: do not invent lines outside the diff; missing context is marked [SUPUESTO] with what you would verify; distinguish what is demonstrated from what is inferred. Trade-off: when in doubt between blocking and major, escalate to the higher severity and record the assumption that supports it.
Phase 4 - Consolidation and single verdict. Verdict rule: a single blocking finding forces "request changes"; only minors/nits enable "approve with comments".
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] All three passes (correctness, style, risk) are explicitly covered.
- [ ] Each finding has severity, location, impact, and an actionable fix.
- [ ] No finding cites non-existent lines; context gaps go as [SUPUESTO] with a verification plan.
- [ ] What is demonstrated by the diff is separated from what is inferred.
- [ ] There are genuine strengths and open questions for the author.
- [ ] The verdict is single (approve / approve with comments / request changes) and justified in one sentence, consistent with the severity rule.
- [ ] Professional, direct, and respectful tone with the author: the code is critiqued, not the person.
Expected deliverable: (a) findings table sorted by severity, (b) list of strengths, (c) open questions, (d) verdict with justification.
spec-desarrollo_revision_pull_request_di:
[inputs]
- TITULO_Y_DESCRIPCION_PR: {{TITULO_Y_DESCRIPCION_PR}} > Title and description of the pull request, with the declared purpose of the change
- DIFF: {{DIFF}} > Unified diff to review (output of git diff or patch), with added and removed lines and hunk headers
- FOCOS_DE_RIESGO: {{FOCOS_DE_RIESGO}} > Axes to treat as critical: security, concurrency, performance, migrations, contract compatibility (optional)
- POLITICA_DE_MERGE: {{POLITICA_DE_MERGE}} > Team severity convention and approval threshold (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A pull request is awaiting review and needs an actionable merge verdict today. Reviewing only the diff and its impact radius, rather than auditing the entire codebase, concentrates scrutiny where real risk originates: the lines that change and what those lines touch downstream. A clear hunk-by-hunk verdict unlocks the merge, prevents regressions that reach production, and leaves the author with concrete corrections rather than opinions.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software engineer, expert code reviewer, with the judgment to distinguish what is blocking from what is cosmetic and to infer side effects outside the diff.
Deliverable: hunk-by-hunk review report + merge verdict.
1. Reconstruct the PR's intent from TITULO_Y_DESCRIPCION_PR and the set of hunks in DIFF. If the description is missing or the diff arrives truncated (unclosed headers, incomplete paths), ask for it before continuing rather than inferring.
2. Go through the DIFF hunk by hunk; for each hunk evaluate correctness and edge cases, error handling and nulls, concurrency and shared state, security (injection, plaintext secrets, authorization, input validation), performance (N+1, hot allocations, locks), contract compatibility (API, schema, serialization), and migrations (reversibility, deployment order), prioritizing FOCOS_DE_RIESGO.
3. Classify each finding as Blocking, Major, Minor, or Nit according to POLITICA_DE_MERGE (if not provided, use that scale by default). Blocking = corrupts data, opens a breach, or breaks a contract; Major = probable regression or dangerous debt; Minor = robustness improvement; Nit = preference.
4. Track the impact radius of each change: callers, tests, feature flags, contracts, and dependencies affected even if they do not appear in the diff; mark those inferences as [SUPUESTO] and state what evidence would confirm them.
5. Verify that every behavioral change has a test covering it; if coverage is missing or the test does not exercise the new path, log it as a finding with the minimum suggested test.
6. Issue a single verdict: Approve / Approve with minor changes / Request Changes, with the prioritized list of blocking items and the exact unblocking condition.
Limits: do not rewrite code outside the diff; do not propose large-scale refactors outside the change; one verdict, without ambivalence.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: reconstruct intent and scope; confirm the diff is complete and declare environment assumptions (language, framework, version) if not stated.
Phase 2 Hunk sweep: analyze each hunk against the risk axes; do not go into untouched code except to trace side effects.
Phase 3 Impact radius: for each relevant change list what is affected downstream and mark [SUPUESTO] for anything not verifiable in the diff.
Phase 4 Test coverage: cross-reference behavioral changes against present or absent tests; name the missing test.
Phase 5 Verdict: consolidate findings with severity and suggested patch, sort by severity, and close with the verdict and its unblocking condition.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The analysis is confined to the diff; untouched code only appears as a traced side effect.
- [ ] Each finding includes file:line, severity, why it is a problem, and a concrete suggested patch.
- [ ] All axes covered: correctness, errors/nulls, concurrency, security, performance, contract/migrations.
- [ ] Severities justified by their criterion (Blocking/Major/Minor/Nit), not assigned arbitrarily.
- [ ] Explicit impact radius (callers, tests, flags, dependencies); inferences marked [SUPUESTO] with evidence that would close them.
- [ ] Behavioral changes cross-referenced against coverage; missing tests named.
- [ ] No style nits already covered by a linter; no rewriting of code outside the diff.
- [ ] Single, clear verdict with prioritized list of blocking items and unblocking condition.
Expected deliverable: hunk-by-hunk report with classified findings and suggested patches, closed with an actionable merge verdict and its unblocking condition.
spec-desarrollo_redaccion_comentarios_pr:
[inputs]
- LENGUAJE_O_STACK: {{LENGUAJE_O_STACK}} > Language, framework, or stack of the PR (defines applicable conventions and anti-patterns)
- DIFF_O_CODIGO: {{DIFF_O_CODIGO}} > Unified diff or fragments to review, with line numbers if possible
- CONTEXTO_PR: {{CONTEXTO_PR}} > What the PR resolves: issue, objective, expected scope (optional)
- ESTANDARES_EQUIPO: {{ESTANDARES_EQUIPO}} > Team's style guide, conventions, and definition of done (optional)
- NIVEL_EXIGENCIA: {{NIVEL_EXIGENCIA}} > Rigor based on the author's maturity or module criticality: formative / standard / critical (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are reviewing a pull request and must transform observations into comments the author can act on without clarification meetings. A good comment accelerates the merge, transfers judgment, and preserves the relationship with the author; a vague one generates back-and-forth, defensiveness, and debt that slips through. The goal is feedback that is specific, anchored to code evidence, and oriented toward improvement, not judging the person. What gets unlocked: a review the author appreciates and resolves in a single cycle.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software engineer and code reviewer expert in constructive technical communication, with the judgment to separate what is blocking from what is optional.
Deliverable: a set of review comments ready to paste into the PR, plus a closing summary.
1. Read {{DIFF_O_CODIGO}} in the context of {{CONTEXTO_PR}}; if it arrives empty, unreadable, or without useful line numbers, stop and ask for it rather than inventing findings.
2. Identify real findings across six axes: correctness, security, performance, maintainability, public contract (API/signatures/backward compatibility), and tests; discard cosmetic noise covered by the linter or formatter.
3. Classify each finding by severity with explicit criteria: [blocking] prevents merge (bug, leak, contract break), [important] should be resolved before merging, [suggestion] optional improvement, [question] requires clarification before judging.
4. Write each comment with four parts: severity + observation anchored to the line/block + why/impact + actionable suggestion with a code snippet when applicable.
5. Prioritize: group nits, do not pile them on top of a blocking item; adjust the quantity and detail to {{NIVEL_EXIGENCIA}} (formative = explain the why and offer alternatives; critical = exhaustive on correctness and security).
6. Close with verdict (approve / approve with minor changes / request changes), count by severity, and the 1 to 3 points that block the merge.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: restate what the PR does, the stack {{LENGUAJE_O_STACK}}, and the applicable {{ESTANDARES_EQUIPO}}; if missing, assume industry standard for the stack and declare it as [SUPUESTO]. Same treatment for an empty {{NIVEL_EXIGENCIA}} (assume standard) and an absent {{CONTEXTO_PR}} (review only what is evident in the diff).
Phase 2 Plan: list the detected findings with their tentative severity before writing, to validate priority and avoid false positives.
Phase 3 Execute: write the definitive comments. Tone: describe the code, not the person; propose in the plural ('we could', 'it would be worth'); avoid 'always', 'never', 'obvious', 'simply'; mark optional items and separate fact from preference. One finding per comment, with its suggested snippet.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each comment carries explicit severity among the four categories.
- [ ] Each finding is anchored to a specific line or block, not generic.
- [ ] Each comment explains the impact (bug, security, performance, maintainability, contract) and proposes an actionable change.
- [ ] The tone describes the code, does not judge the person; no 'always/never/obvious/simply'.
- [ ] Optional items are marked; nits are grouped and do not compete with blocking items.
- [ ] No false positives: what the linter already covers is not commented; assumptions are declared.
- [ ] The closing summary includes verdict, count by severity, and the 1 to 3 real blocking items.
Edge cases: empty or lineless diff -> ask before reviewing; huge PR -> review the risky parts and declare what was not covered; public contract change without tests -> blocking with justification.
Expected deliverable: block of review comments in neutral English, each self-contained and pasteable into the PR, followed by the closing summary.
spec-desarrollo_revision_legibilidad_nom:
[inputs]
- CODIGO: {{CODIGO}} > Fragment, file, or pasted code to review
- LENGUAJE: {{LENGUAJE}} > Programming language (defines the native naming convention)
- CONVENCION_ESTILO: {{CONVENCION_ESTILO}} > Team's style guide (e.g. PEP 8, Google Style, Airbnb) or "no defined guide"
- NIVEL_PROFUNDIDAD: {{NIVEL_PROFUNDIDAD}} > "quick" (high severity only) or "exhaustive" (all findings) (optional, default exhaustive)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A code fragment is read and modified many more times than it was written. Opaque names and confusing structure are the main source of friction when maintaining software: they slow down readers, hide bugs, and inflate the cost of every future change. This review unlocks self-documenting code, faster onboarding, and less accumulated technical debt, without touching the program's behavior. Limited scope: readability, names, and structure only; functionality, correctness, security, and performance are out of scope.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software engineer specializing in maintainability and code review, with judgment shaped by Clean Code, Code Complete, and the language's style guides.

Deliver a readability and naming review of {{CODIGO}} in {{LENGUAJE}}, aligned to {{CONVENCION_ESTILO}}, with the detail indicated by {{NIVEL_PROFUNDIDAD}}. Steps:
1. Inventory identifiers (variables, constants, parameters), functions/methods, and structural blocks in the fragment.
2. Evaluate identifiers: revealed intention, absence of opaque abbreviations and generics (data, temp, info, aux), length proportional to scope, consistency with the language convention.
3. Evaluate functions/methods: the name describes what it does and returns, precise verb, consistent size and level of abstraction, single responsibility, readable parameters.
4. Evaluate structure: logical grouping, top-down reading, excessive nesting, absent guard clauses, comments that mask unclear code, style consistency.
5. For each finding record: location (line or symbol), severity (high/medium/low), why it harms maintainability, and a concrete proposal in before > after format.
6. Synthesize a renaming table and the three highest-impact improvements prioritized.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm language, convention, and scope; if CODIGO, LENGUAJE, or CONVENCION_ESTILO are missing, ask for them before proceeding; if CONVENCION_ESTILO is "no defined guide", adopt the native convention of {{LENGUAJE}} and state it.
Phase 2 Inventory: list the symbols and blocks to evaluate.
Phase 3 Diagnosis: apply the heuristics of the three dimensions symbol by symbol, without inventing non-existent defects; acknowledge what is done well.
Phase 4 Proposals: for each finding write the renaming or restructuring in before > after format, verifying it does not alter behavior.
Phase 5 Synthesis: build the renaming table and prioritize the three highest-impact improvements.
Edge cases: code with no relevant defects (state it, do not force findings); incomplete or truncated fragment (note what context is missing); collision with existing names in the proposed renaming (warn). Unresolved assumptions are marked {por_confirmar}.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each finding has location, severity, maintainability justification, and a before > after proposal.
- [ ] Proposed names reveal intention and respect the convention of {{LENGUAJE}} and {{CONVENCION_ESTILO}}.
- [ ] All three dimensions are covered: identifiers, functions/methods, and structure.
- [ ] Functionality and performance are not evaluated; focus is exclusively on readability and no change alters behavior.
- [ ] Non-existent problems are not invented; what is done well is acknowledged.
- [ ] Severities are consistent and improvements are prioritized by real impact.
- [ ] NIVEL_PROFUNDIDAD is respected (quick = high severity only).
Expected deliverable: report with findings classified by severity, table of suggested renamings (current > proposed > rationale), and prioritized top 3 improvements.
spec-desarrollo_revision_clean_code:
[inputs]
- CODIGO: {{CODIGO}} > Fragment, file, or module to audit (paste the code or reference the file)
- LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK: {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} > Language, version, and framework (e.g. Java 21 + Spring Boot, TypeScript + React)
- CONVENCIONES: {{CONVENCIONES}} > Team style guide or conventions (optional; uses the language's idiomatic ones if omitted)
- SEVERIDAD_MINIMA: {{SEVERIDAD_MINIMA}} > Minimum threshold to report: blocking, high, medium, or low (optional; default: all)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A team needs to raise the maintainability of its codebase before technical debt stalls feature delivery. A rigorous audit against Clean Code and SOLID unlocks safe refactors, reduces future change cost, and turns subjective reviews into verifiable criteria. The result enables prioritization decisions backed by evidence, not opinions, and leaves an actionable remediation path.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software engineer specializing in code review and refactoring, trained in Robert C. Martin's Clean Code principles and in SOLID.

Audit {{CODIGO}} and deliver a prioritized report. Steps:
1. Audit the Small functions axis: length, single responsibility per function, homogeneous abstraction levels, number of parameters, nesting depth, boolean flags, and duplication.
2. Audit the Clear intent axis: intention-revealing names, comments that compensate for poor code, magic numbers and strings, readability as prose, explicit vs. silent error handling.
3. Audit the Low coupling axis: rigid dependencies, Law of Demeter, dependency injection, hidden side effects, Single Responsibility Principle, and leaky abstractions.
4. Record each finding with: location (line or range), violated axis and principle, severity (blocking/high/medium/low), and impact on maintainability.
5. Justify the severity: blocking = compromises correctness or security; high = multiplies change cost in a hot zone; medium = locally degrades readability; low = cosmetic.
6. Propose a concrete refactor with a before/after block per relevant finding, naming the technique (extract method, introduce parameter object, replace conditional with polymorphism, etc.).
7. Build a remediation plan ordered by impact and regression risk, with recommended test coverage per item.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} and {{CONVENCIONES}}; if {{CODIGO}} or the language is missing, ask for it before continuing. Mark any domain assumption as [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 - Audit by axes: go through the code applying the three axes in order; do not infer behavior not present in the code or invent domain logic.
Phase 3 - Synthesis: prioritize findings by impact on maintainability crossed with refactor regression risk; filter by {{SEVERIDAD_MINIMA}} if specified; identify the three highest-risk zones.
Phase 4 - Delivery: produce the report in the CRITERIA block format.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Each finding cites exact location (line or range) and names the violated principle, not a generality.
- Each severity is justified by its criterion (correctness/security, change cost, readability, or cosmetic).
- Each refactor includes compilable before/after code, names the technique, and preserves observable behavior.
- No finding invents domain logic absent from the code; assumptions are marked [SUPUESTO].
- The remediation plan orders by impact, flags regression risk per item, and indicates recommended test coverage before touching each zone.
- Zero unsolicited complete rewriting; the focus is to audit and propose.
- If {{SEVERIDAD_MINIMA}} was specified, no finding below the threshold appears in the report.

Expected deliverable: report in sections (1) Executive summary with finding count by axis and severity and the three highest-risk zones; (2) Findings table [ID | location | axis | principle | severity | impact]; (3) Before/after refactors per relevant finding with named technique; (4) Prioritized remediation plan with regression risk and recommended test coverage.
spec-desarrollo_revision_solid:
[inputs]
- CODIGO_O_MODULO: {{CODIGO_O_MODULO}} > Source code, class, or module to review; paste the text or reference the file
- LENGUAJE: {{LENGUAJE}} > Language and version (e.g. Java 17, C# .NET 8, Python 3.12, TypeScript 5.x)
- CONTEXTO_NEGOCIO: {{CONTEXTO_NEGOCIO}} > What the module does and how it is expected to evolve (future variants, anticipated extension points)
- PRIORIDAD_FOCO: {{PRIORIDAD_FOCO}} > Priority axis: maintainability, testability, or extensibility (optional; default maintainability)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Object-oriented design erodes when classes accumulate responsibilities and dependencies couple to concrete implementations: every change breaks something distant, and tests become brittle. A rigorous review against SOLID converts vague "this smells off" intuitions into actionable findings, unlocks safe refactors, and reduces technical debt before it becomes structural. The result enables extending the system without fear and testing each piece in isolation. Without this, the team pays the cost in regression bugs, slow onboarding, and declining velocity.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software engineer, specialist in object-oriented design, GoF patterns, and test-driven refactoring.
Deliver a SOLID review report on {{CODIGO_O_MODULO}} ({{LENGUAJE}}), considering {{CONTEXTO_NEGOCIO}} and prioritizing {{PRIORIDAD_FOCO}}:
1. Brief inventory of detected classes, interfaces, and responsibilities, with the reason for change of each unit.
2. Principle-by-principle walkthrough (SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP) with findings for each; all five are reviewed even if one presents no findings.
3. Per finding: principle, exact location (class / method / lines), observable symptom, concrete risk, and proposed refactor with applicable pattern and minimum viable change.
4. Findings prioritization table by severity and impact on {{PRIORIDAD_FOCO}}, with relative estimated effort (S/M/L).
5. List of design decisions that look like violations but are justified (not flagged as issues), with the reasoning that supports them.
6. Suggested refactor sequence: a safe order that respects dependencies between findings and minimizes regression risk.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Mapping: identify classes, interfaces, dependencies, and the reasons for change of each unit.
Phase 2 - Detection by principle:
  SRP: one class, one reason for change; detect mixing of persistence, domain logic, and presentation.
  OCP: look for if/else or switch on types that force editing existing code when adding variants.
  LSP: verify that subtypes honor the parent's contract (no strengthened preconditions, no weakened postconditions, exceptions, and invariants).
  ISP: detect fat interfaces with empty methods, NotImplemented, or that no client uses in full.
  DIP: trace dependencies toward concrete classes that should point to abstractions; review dependency direction and where objects are constructed.
Phase 3 - Refactor: for each finding propose the appropriate pattern (Strategy, Factory Method, interface extraction, dependency injection, composition over inheritance) with the minimum viable change; warn if it breaks a public API or binary compatibility.
Phase 4 - Prioritization: rank by severity x impact on {{PRIORIDAD_FOCO}}; separate critical from cosmetic and estimate relative effort. Mark inferences as [SUPUESTO].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] All five principles reviewed explicitly, even if one presents no findings.
- [ ] Each finding cites an exact location (class / method / lines) verifiable in the provided code.
- [ ] Each refactor names a concrete pattern and the minimum viable change — no generic advice.
- [ ] Warning issued when a refactor requires breaking a public API or compatibility.
- [ ] Real violations are distinguished from deliberate justified decisions, with their reasoning.
- [ ] Findings prioritized by severity and impact on {{PRIORIDAD_FOCO}}, with relative effort and a safe refactor sequence.
- [ ] Inferences marked as [SUPUESTO]; nothing invented about code not provided.
Deliverable: structured report with inventory, findings by principle, prioritization table, justified decisions, and refactor sequence, ready to open tickets.

The {{EQUIPO_O_PRODUCTO}} team merges changes to the main branch without an explicit, verifiable "done" agreement, producing inconsistent quality across pull requests and reviews that depend on each reviewer's judgment. Formalizing a technical Definition of Done unlocks an objective merge gate: it converts tacit expectations into measurable checks, reduces rework and defects that escape to production, and enables automating part of the verification in the pipeline.
