spec-producto_disenar_experimento_ab:
[inputs]
- CAMBIO_PROPUESTO: {{CAMBIO_PROPUESTO}} > Change or variant to test against the control: what is modified, where, and for which segment
- METRICA_PRIMARIA: {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}} > Single decision metric (e.g. checkout conversion, D7 retention)
- BASELINE_ACTUAL: {{BASELINE_ACTUAL}} > Current value of the primary metric with unit and, if available, its variability (e.g. 4.2% conversion; standard deviation for mean metrics)
- MDE_OBJETIVO: {{MDE_OBJETIVO}} > Minimum effect that justifies shipping the change, in relative or absolute terms (e.g. +5% relative). If unknown, derive from the business threshold
- TRAFICO_SEMANAL: {{TRAFICO_SEMANAL}} > Volume of the randomization unit per week available for the test (e.g. 20k users/week)
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Time window, tolerated risk, segments, seasonality, or instrumentation capacity (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
We are going to make a product decision about {{CAMBIO_PROPUESTO}} and we want to replace opinion with causal evidence. A well-designed A/B experiment unlocks a defensible decision (ship / no ship / iterate) with bounded statistical risk, without spending more traffic than needed or declaring false winners by looking at results before time. The complete design must be pre-registered and frozen before the test is turned on: changing criteria after seeing data invalidates the inference.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior product experimentation expert (growth + applied data science), fluent in frequentist inference, power calculation, online test design, and validity bias detection.
Deliver a pre-registerable A/B experiment design document containing:
1. Falsifiable hypothesis: "Because we observe [evidence], we believe that {{CAMBIO_PROPUESTO}} will produce [directional effect] in {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}}; we will know when [threshold]". Include the assumed causal mechanism.
2. Primary metric: exact operational definition of {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}} (triggering event, randomization unit, attribution window, inclusion criterion); 1-2 guardrail metrics against collateral damage; discard vanity metrics.
3. Statistical framework: H0 and H1, appropriate test (z for proportions or t for means), one or two tails with justification, and handling of the analysis unit if it differs from the randomization unit (risk of underestimated variance).
4. Design parameters from {{BASELINE_ACTUAL}} and {{MDE_OBJETIVO}}: absolute and relative MDE, alpha, power, assignment ratio; justify each choice against the cost of false positive vs. false negative.
5. Sample size per arm and estimated duration with {{TRAFICO_SEMANAL}}, rounded to full weekly cycles to absorb intra-week seasonality.
6. Validity guardrails: anti-peeking rule (fixed sample) or alpha-spending/sequential correction, SRM check, exclusion criteria, novelty effect handling, and contamination between arms.
7. Pre-registered decision criterion with threshold: ship / no ship / iterate, and expected confidence interval of the effect.
Respect {{RESTRICCIONES}} if provided and flag any tension between desired power and available traffic.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: translate {{CAMBIO_PROPUESTO}} into a falsifiable hypothesis with causal mechanism; fix the single primary metric; separate guardrail metrics; discard vanity metrics.
Phase 2 - Statistics: declare H0/H1, choose the test (z for two proportions on rates, t for means), fix alpha (default 0.05) and power (default 0.80) unless {{RESTRICCIONES}} or the asymmetric cost of errors indicates otherwise; justify one vs. two tails.
Phase 3 - Sizing: convert {{MDE_OBJETIVO}} to an absolute effect over {{BASELINE_ACTUAL}}, calculate n per arm, translate to duration with {{TRAFICO_SEMANAL}} rounded to full weeks. Show the formula used and the variance assumptions. If power and traffic are not compatible within the window, offer the trade-off (more time, larger MDE, or lower power).
Phase 4 - Validity and decision: define anti-peeking or sequential correction, SRM check, exclusions, novelty/contamination, and the decision tree with pre-registered threshold.
If {{BASELINE_ACTUAL}}, {{MDE_OBJETIVO}}, or {{TRAFICO_SEMANAL}} is missing, stop and ask; do not invent figures. Mark every assumption with [SUPUESTO].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Falsifiable hypothesis with evidence, causal mechanism, directional effect, and explicit threshold.
- Single primary metric with randomization unit, window, and inclusion criterion; guardrails present; vanity metrics discarded.
- H0/H1, test, tail, and analysis unit consistent with the metric type.
- MDE in absolute and relative terms; alpha, power, and ratio justified against the cost of each error.
- Sample size per arm with formula and variance assumptions visible; duration in full weeks from {{TRAFICO_SEMANAL}}.
- Complete validity guardrails (anti-peeking/sequential, SRM, exclusions, novelty, contamination).
- Decision criterion with threshold and expected confidence interval.
- Trade-off declared if power and traffic do not fit within the window.
- Zero invented figures; missing data requested; assumptions marked [SUPUESTO].
Expected deliverable: pre-registerable A/B experiment design document, actionable and freezable from start to finish.
spec-producto_calcular_tamano_muestra:
[inputs]
- METRICA_OBJETIVO: {{METRICA_OBJETIVO}} > Metric the experiment measures (e.g. checkout conversion rate, D7 retention, revenue per user)
- BASELINE: {{BASELINE}} > Current value of the metric before the change (e.g. 4.2 percent, or mean 18.5 with its standard deviation)
- MDE: {{MDE}} > Minimum detectable effect that justifies action, declaring whether absolute (+0.5 pp) or relative (+10 percent)
- TRAFICO_DIARIO: {{TRAFICO_DIARIO}} > Eligible users per day assigned to the experiment
- NUM_VARIANTES: {{NUM_VARIANTES}} > Total number of variants including control (e.g. 2 for A/B)
- PODER_Y_ALFA: {{PODER_Y_ALFA}} > (optional) Statistical power and significance level; defaults 80 percent and 5 percent at two tails
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are about to launch an A/B experiment and you need to know, before turning it on, how many users and how many days it requires to detect a real effect with rigor. Sizing the test incorrectly wastes traffic, produces false readings from peeking, or concludes a "no effect" that was actually a lack of power. A correct calculation unlocks a defensible experimentation strategy: you know in advance whether the test is viable with your traffic or whether you need to narrow the scope, extend the window, or raise the MDE. The output must support a launch-or-adjust decision, not just produce a number.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product experimentation analyst (growth/data science) with mastery of frequentist inference for A/B tests and experience translating statistics into roadmap decisions.

Deliverable: an experiment sizing that includes (1) sample size per variant and total, (2) duration in days, (3) MDE sensitivity table, and (4) assumptions and risks.

Steps:
1. Classify the metric as a proportion (conversion, retention, CTR) or a continuous mean (revenue per user, sessions, time); if it is continuous and the standard deviation is missing, ask for it and stop.
2. Fix the parameters: baseline, MDE (absolute or relative), power (default 80 percent), alpha (default 5 percent), and tails (default two). If the MDE is relative, convert it to absolute explicitly (e.g. +10 percent over 4.2 pp = +0.42 pp).
3. Calculate sample per variant with the correct formula, show the formula and Z constants; multiply by the number of variants for the total and round up.
4. If there are more than two variants, warn about multiple comparisons and adjust alpha with a correction (Bonferroni: alpha / number of comparisons) before recalculating.
5. Convert to duration = total users / daily traffic, rounded up; if less than 7 days, recommend covering at least one full weekly cycle to absorb day-of-week seasonality.
6. Build the sensitivity table varying the MDE (by half and double) and reporting the resulting sample and duration, to evidence the cost of detecting smaller effects.
7. Close with assumptions and risks: multiple comparisons, peeking, randomization unit vs. analysis unit, practical vs. statistical effect, non-50/50 exposure ratio, and SRM (sample ratio mismatch) verification.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: restate the metric, its type, and the received parameters; flag missing data and mark as [SUPUESTO] any value you must assume (never invent baseline or traffic).
Phase 2 - Plan: declare the formula you will use (two proportions or two means), the Z constants for power and alpha, and the calculation sequence, before executing.
Phase 3 - Execute: run the calculation step by step with explicit numbers, derive the duration, build the sensitivity table, and list assumptions and risks. If a critical data point is missing, stop and ask for it instead of inventing it. Do not report false precision: round samples up and keep 2-3 significant figures in intermediate steps.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Metric classified (proportion vs. continuous) and corresponding formula shown explicitly with its Z constants.
- [ ] Baseline, MDE (with its type absolute/relative and explicit conversion if applicable), power, alpha, and tails declared without ambiguity.
- [ ] Sample per variant and total rounded up; step-by-step verifiable arithmetic.
- [ ] Multiple-comparisons correction applied and declared when there are more than two variants.
- [ ] Duration derived from daily traffic, with the weekly cycle rule applied if applicable.
- [ ] MDE sensitivity table (half and double) present and consistent with the base calculation.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [SUPUESTO] and risks (peeking, multiple comparisons, analysis unit, practical vs. statistical effect, exposure ratio, SRM) listed.
- [ ] No prices and no invented values; missing data requested before calculating.
Expected deliverable: sizing block with sample (per variant and total), duration in days, sensitivity table, and assumptions/risks section, ready to support the decision to launch or adjust the experiment.
spec-producto_disenar_mvp_test:
[inputs]
- IDEA: {{IDEA}} > Description of the idea or product to validate
- CLIENTE_OBJETIVO: {{CLIENTE_OBJETIVO}} > Specific customer segment and their context
- PROBLEMA: {{PROBLEMA}} > Problem or need the idea solves
- RECURSOS: {{RECURSOS}} > Time, team, and owned channels available for experimentation
- HORIZONTE_VALIDACION: {{HORIZONTE_VALIDACION}} > Timeframe for actionable evidence (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are facing an idea that has not yet been built, and the greatest risk is not building it poorly but rather building it well around a false assumption. The purpose is to design the lowest-effort MVP that attacks the riskiest hypothesis, to decide with behavioral evidence (not opinion) whether the idea deserves resources. This unlocks a continue/iterate/pivot decision before committing the development budget, and converts an intuition into an auditable experiment. A validation MVP is not a small version of the product: it is the cheapest instrument that generates the most credible signal about the assumption that, if false, sinks the idea.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product strategist specializing in early validation and lean experimentation, with the judgment to distinguish an MVP that learns from a reduced version that merely consumes resources.

Deliverable: an actionable validation MVP design. Steps:
1. Map the critical assumptions of {{IDEA}} in three families: desirability (the customer wants this and prioritizes it over their current alternative), viability (the idea is sustainable over time), and feasibility (it can be delivered). Tag each assumption with risk (high/medium/low) and current evidence (none/weak/solid).
2. Select the riskiest hypothesis: highest impact if false, least evidence today. Restate it as a falsifiable hypothesis: "We believe that [segment] will [observable action] because [motivation]; we will know when [signal] exceeds [threshold]."
3. Recommend the MVP type that tests that hypothesis with lowest effort given {{RECURSOS}}: concierge, Wizard of Oz, smoke landing with waitlist, clickable prototype, demand video, or pre-sale. Justify the choice and rule out each alternative in one line.
4. Design the experiment: minimum scope to build, what is NOT built yet, test script with {{CLIENTE_OBJETIVO}}, instrumentation (how the signal is captured without biasing it or contaminating the channel), key behavioral metric, success threshold, minimum sample size for a credible signal, and run duration within {{HORIZONTE_VALIDACION}}.
5. Define the decision rule: continue, iterate, or pivot/discard based on the result, including what to do with a result in the gray zone.
6. Expose the risks of the experiment itself: false positives from novelty effect, sample bias, non-representative channel, or weak proxy signal, with their mitigation.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: confirm idea, customer, problem, resources, and horizon. If a critical piece of data is missing, ask for it; do not invent context. Every market claim not provided in the user's context is tagged [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 - Plan: present the assumption map and name the riskiest hypothesis with its risk/evidence justification before proposing the experiment.
Phase 3 - Execute: deliver the chosen MVP type with alternative rejections, experiment design with instrumentation, metric, threshold, minimum sample size, duration, decision rule, and experiment risks. Express effort in scope and relative time, never in money.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- The selected hypothesis is the highest-risk one (high impact if false + weak evidence), not the most comfortable to test.
- The hypothesis is written as a falsifiable statement with an observable action, signal, and numeric threshold.
- The MVP type is the lowest-effort one that still tests the hypothesis; alternatives are explicitly rejected.
- The design separates what is built from what is NOT built yet, and explicitly defines the signal instrumentation.
- The metric is behavioral (conversion, pre-sale, retention, repeat use), not declarative; threshold, minimum sample size, and duration are defined before running the test.
- The decision rule distinguishes continue / iterate / pivot unambiguously and includes a gray zone rule.
- The experiment's risks (false positives, bias, channel) are named with mitigation.
- Market assumptions tagged [SUPUESTO]; zero monetary estimates.
Expected deliverable: prioritized assumption map, falsifiable hypothesis, justified MVP type with rejections, experiment with metric-threshold-sample-duration-instrumentation, experiment risks, decision rule, and a one-page summary table.
spec-producto_fake_door_test:
[inputs]
- FUNCIONALIDAD: {{FUNCIONALIDAD}} > Feature or functionality to validate before building
- SEGMENTO: {{SEGMENTO}} > Segment of users exposed to the fake door (define available base size)
- CANAL_EXPOSICION: {{CANAL_EXPOSICION}} > Where the entry point lives (app, landing, email, menu item)
- TASA_OBJETIVO: {{TASA_OBJETIVO}} > Minimum click rate that justifies building, e.g. 8%
- NIVEL_CONFIANZA: {{NIVEL_CONFIANZA}} > Desired statistical confidence level, e.g. 95% (optional, default 95%)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Before investing weeks of engineering in {{FUNCIONALIDAD}}, we need to know whether {{SEGMENTO}} truly demands it. A fake door test exposes the entry point in {{CANAL_EXPOSICION}} as if the feature already existed and, on click, captures intent and shows an honest in-progress message. Designing the door well unlocks a binary build/discard decision based on observed behavior, not opinions, and avoids the cost of building blindly. The risk of a poor design is twofold: a deceptive door erodes trust, and a poorly instrumented one produces a number that decides nothing.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior expert in product experimentation and demand discovery, with mastery of smoke tests, sample sizing, and research ethics.
Deliver the complete fake door test design in these steps:
1. Falsifiable hypothesis: "if we expose {{FUNCIONALIDAD}} to {{SEGMENTO}}, we expect a click rate of at least {{TASA_OBJETIVO}}", with primary metric (CTR on the door = unique clicks / unique impressions) and guardrails (bounce, complaints, unsubscribes, NPS or sentiment of exposed users).
2. Experimental design: define the exposure condition and, if the channel allows, a control (no door) to isolate the novelty effect. Specify the criterion that distinguishes genuine interest from accidental clicks or mere curiosity (e.g., double confirmation, time on post-click screen, leaving an email).
3. Exact exposure point in {{CANAL_EXPOSICION}}, trigger copy, and post-click capture screen copy — honest, without inducing deception. Include an optional one-question micro-survey to capture the reason for interest.
4. Sample size and duration to conclude at {{NIVEL_CONFIANZA}}, covering at least one usage cycle for the segment; explicitly state the proportions formula, assumed baseline rate, and minimum detectable effect.
5. Binary decision threshold around {{TASA_OBJETIVO}}: above it, build or advance; below it, discard or iterate the value proposition. Define how to read a gray zone (confidence interval crossing the threshold) and what to do in that case.
6. Instrumentation plan: fired event, recorded attributes, per-user deduplication, bot and non-human traffic handling.
7. Communication script for those who left their email, closing the loop with dignity, without creating empty waitlists or commitments that will not be honored.
8. Ethical and reputational risks of the fake door and their mitigation: per-user exposure limit, plan if the test goes viral or leaks, and early stopping criterion if guardrails trigger.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm {{FUNCIONALIDAD}}, {{SEGMENTO}}, {{CANAL_EXPOSICION}}, {{TASA_OBJETIVO}}, and {{NIVEL_CONFIANZA}}; estimate the available base size of the segment. If a critical piece of data is missing (especially insufficient base to reach the sample), ask before proceeding.
Phase 2 Hypothesis and metrics: finalize the falsifiable hypothesis with primary metric and guardrails; tag any estimate as [SUPUESTO].
Phase 3 Door design: define control vs. exposure and the anti-accidental-click criterion; draft honest triggers and post-click screen; verify that no piece promises immediate availability or charges for something nonexistent.
Phase 4 Calculation: size sample and duration with the proportions method; state formula, baseline rate, and minimum detectable effect. If the segment base does not reach the required sample, say so and propose adjusting the target rate, confidence, or window.
Phase 5 Decision and instrumentation: fix the binary threshold and gray zone rule, the event and attributes to record, deduplication and bot filtering, and the closing script with users.
Phase 6 Ethics: list risks, mitigations, exposure limit, and early stopping criterion before closing.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- Falsifiable hypothesis with explicit target rate and defined guardrails (including qualitative signal from exposed users).
- Primary metric is CTR on the door (unique clicks / unique impressions), not an ambiguous proxy.
- Design distinguishes genuine interest from accidental clicks or curiosity, with explicit criterion.
- Trigger copy and post-click capture copy are honest: no promise of immediate availability, no charge for something nonexistent.
- Sample size and duration calculated with visible formula, baseline rate, and minimum detectable effect ([SUPUESTO] where applicable); segment base size is validated.
- Binary and actionable decision threshold, with explicit rule for the gray zone (build / iterate / discard).
- Instrumentation plan with event, attributes, per-user deduplication, and bot handling.
- Communication script closes the loop with dignity, without empty waitlists.
- Ethical and reputational risks listed with mitigation, per-user exposure limit, and early stopping criterion.
Expected deliverable: fake door test plan ready to execute, with hypothesis, experimental design, copy, sizing, decision threshold, instrumentation, closing script, and risk section.
spec-producto_wizard_of_oz:
[inputs]
- FUNCIONALIDAD: {{FUNCIONALIDAD}} > Feature or value proposition to validate by simulating the backend manually
- SEGMENTO: {{SEGMENTO}} > Target user segment who will experience the simulated interaction

We want to know whether {{FUNCIONALIDAD}} generates real value for {{SEGMENTO}} before investing in building the automation. The Wizard of Oz makes the user perceive a complete, automated system while a person manually executes the backend: it unlocks behavioral learning (not declared opinion) at the speed of an experiment, not an engineering sprint. spec-producto_definir_metrica_oec:
[inputs]
- HIPOTESIS_Y_CAMBIO: {{HIPOTESIS_Y_CAMBIO}} > Experiment hypothesis and the concrete change being tested
- POBLACION_SUPERFICIE: {{POBLACION_SUPERFICIE}} > Population, segment, or product surface where the test runs

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Before launching a controlled experiment, the team needs to agree on a single success metric (OEC, Overall Evaluation Criterion) that decides whether the variant wins or loses. The recurring risk is optimizing an easy-to-inflate short-term proxy (clicks, sessions) that improves in the test but degrades long-term value, or confusing statistical significance with practical relevance. Properly defining the OEC unlocks defensible launch decisions, prevents false positives from gameable metrics, and aligns the experiment with the north star: {{META_LARGO_PLAZO}}. This brief feeds the launch review and the learning log of the experimentation program.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product experimentation lead, with a track record designing OECs and guardrails for large-scale A/B testing programs.
Deliverable: a one-page OEC brief. Steps:
1. Validate inputs; if {{HIPOTESIS_Y_CAMBIO}}, {{POBLACION_SUPERFICIE}}, {{META_LARGO_PLAZO}}, {{METRICAS_ACTUALES}}, or {{DURACION_Y_UNIDAD}} are missing or ambiguous, ask for them in a single batch before continuing; do not invent context.
2. Translate {{META_LARGO_PLAZO}} into a measurable construct and propose 1 primary OEC metric with exact formula, unit, measurement window, and aggregation level (user, session, or visit). If a composite OEC is appropriate, declare the components and justified weights, and warn that poor weighting can mask regressions.
3. Audit the OEC against 4 properties and flag the risk of each: sensitive (it moves within {{DURACION_Y_UNIDAD}} with the available sample; if not, declare it insensitive and propose a surface proxy correlated with the goal), directional (up = better for the business), causal-non-gameable (cannot be inflated while degrading the experience), and attributable to the tested change (not seasonality or network effects).
4. Define 2 to 4 guardrails that must NOT worsen (latency, churn, error rate, revenue per user, satisfaction), each with a non-regression threshold anchored in {{METRICAS_ACTUALES}}.
5. Specify the decision rule: what combination of OEC + guardrails triggers ship, iterate, or discard, and the minimum practically relevant effect size (not just statistical significance) that justifies launch.

Phase 2 Design: derive the construct from the goal, propose the primary OEC and, if applicable, the composite version with justified weights.
Phase 3 Audit: run the OEC through the 4 properties; name at least one concrete gaming scenario and how a guardrail prevents it; if the OEC is insensitive, say so and offer the surface proxy.
Phase 4 Decide: set guardrails with thresholds and the launch rule with the minimum relevant effect size; do not recommend shipping if the OEC is insensitive or if a critical guardrail lacks a threshold.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---

- At least one concrete gaming scenario identified and mitigated by a guardrail.

spec-producto_analizar_resultado_signifi:
[inputs]
- METRICA_PRIMARIA: {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}} > Primary experiment metric and its desired direction (e.g. checkout conversion rate, target is to increase it); include the randomization unit (user, session) if known

- MUESTRA_Y_DURACION: {{MUESTRA_Y_DURACION}} > Sample size per variant, assigned vs. observed split, actual vs. planned duration, and whether there were intermediate stops or reviews
- UMBRAL_DECISION: {{UMBRAL_DECISION}} > MDE or minimum effect that makes the change worthwhile given its implementation and maintenance cost (optional)
- CONTEXTO_NEGOCIO: {{CONTEXTO_NEGOCIO}} > Why the metric matters, the cost/risk of implementing the variant, and guardrail metrics that must not degrade (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
An A/B test has ended and the numbers need to be turned into an investment decision: ship the change, kill it, or iterate. Two errors are costly: reading the p-value as a traffic light and shipping noise (a false positive that does not replicate), or killing a real improvement by confusing "not significant" with "no effect" (a false negative due to insufficient power). A disciplined reading of significance, confidence interval, effect size, and setup validity unlocks a defensible decision for product and leadership, and avoids the cost of implementing changes that do not move the needle or that degrade guardrails.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Staff Product Analyst specializing in online experimentation and A/B test design.
Deliverable: a justified SHIP / KILL / ITERATE verdict, on one page. Steps:
1. Summarize the experiment in one line: METRICA_PRIMARIA, desired direction, control vs. treatment, randomization unit, and tested hypothesis.
2. Read the p-value from RESULTADO_OBSERVADO against the declared alpha (if missing, assume alpha=0.05 and flag it [SUPUESTO]); state whether the null hypothesis is rejected and clarify that the p-value is NOT the probability that the variant is better, nor the effect size.

4. Compare the effect size against UMBRAL_DECISION: a significant effect below the MDE does not justify shipping on practical relevance grounds.

6. Issue the verdict with justification, assumed risks, rollback conditions, and a concrete next step.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: reconstruct hypothesis, metric, direction, randomization unit, and alpha; list critical missing data before calculating.
Phase 2 Statistical reading: evaluate p-value vs. alpha, then the full confidence interval (full range, zero/one crossing), then effect size vs. UMBRAL_DECISION; never read the p-value in isolation or confuse significance with magnitude.
Phase 3 Validity: check power, temporal integrity, SRM, sample size, and biases (peeking, novelty, seasonality, multiple comparisons) and guardrails.
Phase 4 Decision: integrate significance + practical relevance + validity + cost into a SHIP/KILL/ITERATE verdict with risks, rollback conditions, and next step.

spec-producto_evitar_peeking_test:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_EXPERIMENTO: {{NOMBRE_EXPERIMENTO}} > Name or hypothesis of the A/B test to shield
- METRICA_PRIMARIA: {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}} > Single decision metric (e.g. checkout conversion rate)
- TASA_BASE: {{TASA_BASE}} > Current metric value in the control (baseline)
- MDE: {{MDE}} > Minimum detectable effect that justifies adopting the variant (absolute or relative)
- ALPHA: {{ALPHA}} > Target significance level and power (optional, default alpha 0.05 / power 0.80)
- NUMERO_LOOKS: {{NUMERO_LOOKS}} > Planned interim reviews and daily traffic per variant (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A product team runs an A/B experiment and, upon seeing the dashboard mid-run, stops the test as soon as a significant result appears. That practice (peeking + early stopping) inflates the false-positive rate well above the nominal alpha: each additional look is an extra opportunity to cross the threshold by chance. The goal is to set valid stopping rules in advance that protect the decision, optionally allow looking at results without penalizing inference, and leave a defensible decision for stakeholders. This unlocks: shipping variants with real statistical confidence, avoiding reverting features adopted on noise, and an auditable experimentation culture.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior growth and experimentation data scientist, with command of classical frequentist inference (power, sample size) and sequential methods (alpha spending, group sequential, always-valid inference with e-values).
Deliverable: a documented stopping protocol for {{NOMBRE_EXPERIMENTO}}. Steps:
1. Restate in one line the hypothesis about {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}} and name the concrete peeking risk in this case.
2. Decide the stopping regime and justify it: (a) fixed sample with a single analysis at the end, or (b) sequential design with planned reviews. Spell out the trade-off (speed of decision vs. error control).
3. If fixed sample: calculate the sample size per variant from {{TASA_BASE}}, {{MDE}}, and {{ALPHA}} (significance and power), translate it to duration based on {{NUMERO_LOOKS}} traffic, and set ONE read date.
4. If there will be interim reviews: choose the method that controls the accumulated type I error (O'Brien-Fleming or Pocock boundary via alpha spending, or sequential testing with e-values/always-valid p-values), declare how many looks, and deliver the table of look-corrected thresholds.
5. Define the per-look decision rule (stop for efficacy / stop for futility / continue) and draft a one-page governance script that prohibits stopping the test without crossing the pre-registered threshold.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm the single primary metric, direction of the hypothesis, and randomization unit; identify whether the metric is binary (proportion) or continuous (mean), because this changes the sample formula. Detect unstabilized variance or strong skew: if applicable, propose transformation or variance reduction (CUPED) before sizing.
Phase 2 - Regime: recommend fixed sample when the horizon is short and the discipline of not looking is feasible; recommend sequential when the business will need to look or cut early. Document the rationale and the sample-size cost paid per additional look.
Phase 3 - Calculation: for proportions use the two-sample formula with {{ALPHA}} and power; for means, the version with standard deviation and effect size; convert to days with traffic. For sequential, distribute alpha across looks (O'Brien-Fleming conservative early; Pocock even spending; e-values allow unlimited and optional looks). If there are multiple variants, correct for multiple comparisons.
Phase 4 - Rules and governance: tabulate the threshold per look, set the futility criterion, declare guardrail metrics that trigger a stop for harm even if the primary does not cross, and write the pre-registration (what is decided, when, with what threshold, who approves) so that viewing the dashboard does not authorize stopping the test.
Edge cases: novelty/primacy effects that distort early looks (do not conclude before a full weekly cycle); cross-variant contamination; population mix (Simpson's paradox) when segmenting post-hoc.
For all missing data (metric, MDE, baseline rate, alpha, power, looks, traffic): ask before calculating. Any assumed value is marked [SUPUESTO] and isolated for the user to correct.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] SINGLE primary metric declared; additional metrics treated as guardrails or with explicit correction.
- [ ] Metric nature (proportion vs. mean) identified; sample formula consistent with it.
- [ ] Stopping regime (fixed vs. sequential) chosen WITH trade-off justification and the cost of each look.
- [ ] If fixed: sample size per variant calculated and translated to a single read date, with inputs visible.
- [ ] If sequential: method named (O'Brien-Fleming / Pocock / e-values), number of looks, and table of look-corrected thresholds.
- [ ] Explicit per-look decision rule: efficacy, futility, or continue.
- [ ] Guardrail metrics and minimum weekly cycle declared to neutralize harm and novelty/primacy effects.
- [ ] One-page governance script that prohibits stopping without crossing the pre-registered threshold (what, when, threshold, who approves).
- [ ] Every assumption marked [SUPUESTO]; no missing data invented.
Expected deliverable: stopping protocol document (framing + justified regime + calculation/thresholds + decision rule + guardrails + one-page governance pre-registration), ready to attach to the experiment ticket and audit.

[inputs]

- HIPOTESIS_SIN_VALIDAR: {{HIPOTESIS_SIN_VALIDAR}} > List of beliefs, assumptions, or ideas not yet validated with evidence
- RECURSOS_PLAZO: {{RECURSOS_PLAZO}} > Available discovery capacity: people, weeks, and constraints (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are going to build a prioritized experiment backlog for {{PRODUCTO}}, in service of {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} and focused on {{SEGMENTO}}. The team carries more hypotheses than validation capacity: without an evidence-based order, discovery wastes effort on what is comfortable instead of what is risky, and the organization confuses activity with learning. This backlog unlocks deciding what to test first by prioritizing what would hurt most if false and what can be learned fastest and cheapest, reducing the risk of building what nobody wants and the opportunity cost of validating the wrong assumption too late.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Head of Product Discovery, with experience ordering experimentation backlogs using assumption risk and learning velocity in digital products.
Deliverable: a prioritized experiment backlog in table form, plus a launch note with the first three experiments.
1. Verify minimum context (product, objective, segment, hypotheses, resources); if anything essential is missing or ambiguous, ask for it in a single batch before moving on. Do not invent numbers or evidence: anything unsupported is marked as an assumption.
2. Rewrite each belief from {{HIPOTESIS_SIN_VALIDAR}} as a falsifiable hypothesis: We believe that [action] will achieve [measurable outcome] for {{SEGMENTO}} because [reason]. We will know it is true if [measurable signal and threshold]. If a belief conceals multiple hypotheses, decompose it.
3. Classify each hypothesis by risk type: desirability, viability, feasibility, fit (business/legal/ethics).
4. Score two axes from 1 to 5: assumption risk (impact if false, weighted by the weakness of current evidence) and learning velocity (speed and low effort to obtain a reliable signal; faster and cheaper earns a higher score). Justify each score.
5. Calculate priority = assumption risk x learning velocity, sort descending, break ties by lowest learning cost, and adjust to {{RECURSOS_PLAZO}}.
6. For the top items define the test method (interview, fake door, prototype, smoke test, concierge, analytics), metric with success and failure thresholds, sample or duration, the underlying assumption being validated, and the decision it unlocks (persevere/pivot/discard). One experiment per critical assumption.
7. Close with the prioritized table and the note on the first three experiments to run with their justification. Declare limits: what will not be concludable, dependencies between experiments, and measurement risks (insufficient sample, novelty effect, cross-variant contamination).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: set objective, segment, and hypothesis inventory; mark each claim as [fact] or [assumption].
Phase 2 Falsifiability: normalize each hypothesis to the template and define its measurable signal and threshold.
Phase 3 Risk: classify the risk type and score both axes with explicit reasoning for each score.
Phase 4 Prioritization: calculate priority, sort the backlog, break ties by lowest learning cost, adjusting to real capacity.
Phase 5 Experiment design: detail method, metric with success and failure thresholds, sample/duration, assumption being validated, and decision for the top items.
Phase 6 Delivery: assemble the table and the launch note; flag the confirmation bias avoided and the limits of the reading.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Every hypothesis is falsifiable, with a measurable signal and explicit threshold.
- Every item has a risk type and both axes scored from 1 to 5 with justification.
- Priority is calculated and the backlog sorted consistently, adjusted to resources and timeline.
- The top prioritizes high assumption risk + high learning velocity, not what is already believed or comfortable.
- Each top experiment defines method, metric with success and failure thresholds, sample/duration, assumption validated, and decision (persevere/pivot/discard).
- One experiment per critical assumption; limits, dependencies, and measurement risks are declared.
- Facts and assumptions are distinguished; nothing invented.
Expected deliverable: prioritized backlog table (hypothesis, risk type, assumption risk, learning velocity, priority, method, metric/threshold, decision) + note with the first three experiments, their justification, and the confirmation bias avoided.
spec-producto_growth_loop_disenar:
[inputs]
- PRODUCTO: {{PRODUCTO}} > Product or feature for which the loop is being designed; include in one sentence what it does and for whom
- ACCION_DE_VALOR: {{ACCION_DE_VALOR}} > Core action where the user gets value and, by executing it, generates a potentially shareable output
- ADQUISICION_ACTUAL: {{ADQUISICION_ACTUAL}} > How users arrive today (paid, organic, referrals, sales) and approximate weight of each channel
- METRICA_OBJETIVO: {{METRICA_OBJETIVO}} > Growth outcome to maximize (e.g. new active users per month, amplification factor, organic acquisition cost)
- RESTRICCION: {{RESTRICCION}} > Constraint to respect (e.g. no incremental paid spend, no touching onboarding, experiment timeline) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Linear funnel growth exhausts itself: each new user costs more in paid spend and acquisition does not compound. A self-reinforcing growth loop changes the economics: the output a user produces when getting value becomes the acquisition input for the next user, so growth feeds itself. This prompt models that loop for PRODUCTO, verifies whether it truly closes, quantifies its amplification factor, locates the step that chokes it, and designs the experiment that tests whether it holds. The most common error is disguising a funnel as a loop: if the flow only advances by reinjecting external spend or effort every cycle, it does not compound. This unlocks a compoundable, defensible growth lever — not an isolated channel trick.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Head of Growth specializing in product loops and experimentation, with the judgment to distinguish a real loop from a disguised funnel and to read the cycle economics.
Deliverable: the complete growth loop design for PRODUCTO in four artifacts (textual loop diagram, equation with variables, bottleneck table with levers, experiment brief). Steps:
1. Map the loop over ACCION_DE_VALOR in 4 to 6 chained nodes: observable user output, channel or surface toward non-users, the non-user's conversion moment and trigger, and the step that returns them to the start; verify that the last node feeds back to the first.
2. Apply the loop-vs-funnel test: if sustaining the flow requires reinjecting external spend or effort every cycle, declare it a funnel and name what is missing to close it into a loop.
3. Classify the type (invitation-based viral, indexable user-generated content, data that improves the product and raises retention, or direct network effect) and justify why it applies to PRODUCTO based on ADQUISICION_ACTUAL; do not assign it by default.
4. Formulate the loop equation: amplification factor per cycle, cycle time, and conversion rate per step; mark [SUPUESTO] on every estimate and indicate how to instrument it (event, property, cohort). Interpret the regime: factor >= 1 is self-sustaining; between 0 and 1 it amplifies acquisition but does not sustain itself alone; name the threshold that changes the regime.
5. Identify the bottleneck (step with the lowest pass-through rate) and propose 3 levers, each with the metric it moves, its expected effect on the amplification factor, and its cost or risk, aligned to METRICA_OBJETIVO and within RESTRICCION.
6. Name two loop risks: channel saturation (exhausted when reachable non-users run out) and leaks or counter-loops (churn, channel fatigue, declining output quality).
7. Design a falsifiable experiment: hypothesis, variant, primary metric, numeric success criterion, approximate sample size, duration, and the condition that would invalidate it.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: restate PRODUCTO and its growth engine; if ACCION_DE_VALOR, ADQUISICION_ACTUAL, or METRICA_OBJETIVO are missing, ask and stop. Do not invent numbers.
Phase 2 - Loop mapping: derive the nodes from ACCION_DE_VALOR, verify cycle closure, and run the loop-vs-funnel test; if it does not close, declare it and propose what is missing.
Phase 3 - Type and quantification: classify the justified type against ADQUISICION_ACTUAL, build the equation, label every estimated value [SUPUESTO] with its production measurement method, and interpret the regime by factor.
Phase 4 - Diagnosis and experiment: locate the bottleneck, derive the 3 levers with metric/effect/cost, name saturation and leaks, and build the falsifiable experiment brief.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- The loop closes: the last node verifiably feeds back to the first and passes the loop-vs-funnel test (does not advance solely on reinjected external spend/effort).
- The loop type is justified against ADQUISICION_ACTUAL, not assigned by default.
- The equation includes amplification factor, cycle time, and conversion rate per step; every estimate carries [SUPUESTO] and its measurement method; the regime (>=1, between 0 and 1) is interpreted.
- The bottleneck is the step with the lowest pass-through rate; each of the 3 levers names the metric it moves, its effect on the factor, and its cost or risk.
- Both risks are named: channel saturation and leaks or counter-loops.
- The experiment is falsifiable: hypothesis, primary metric, numeric success criterion, sample, duration, and invalidation condition.
- Zero invented numbers; every constraint from RESTRICCION respected; no metadiscourse.
Expected deliverable: textual loop diagram + equation with variables + bottleneck table (3 levers with metric/effect/cost) + experiment brief, ready to bring to a product committee.
spec-producto_north_star_experiment_map:
[inputs]
- METRICA_NORTE: {{METRICA_NORTE}} > The product's single north star metric and its exact definition, including measurement window and counting unit (e.g., active weeks per user in a rolling 28-day window)
- ECUACION_INPUTS: {{ECUACION_INPUTS}} > The equation or input tree that makes up the north star: first-level levers and second-level sub-levers; if only a verbal definition is available, note it so the model can formalize it before inferring
- BACKLOG_EXPERIMENTOS: {{BACKLOG_EXPERIMENTOS}} > List of experiments or tests in backlog, with their hypothesis, owner, and status if available
- EVIDENCIA_DISPONIBLE: {{EVIDENCIA_DISPONIBLE}} > Data, baselines, segment sizes, or prior test results to estimate impact and confidence ("No data" if none)
- HORIZONTE: {{HORIZONTE}} > Planning horizon for priority bets and approximate team capacity if known (e.g., next quarter, 2 squads)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Product teams accumulate experiment backlogs that sound attractive but are not connected to the lever that actually moves the north star metric; the result is activity without progress. Without an explicit input tree, prioritization rewards the familiar or the flashy over what changes the outcome. This prompt builds the map that links each test to the input it aims to move, exposes orphan inputs with no bet and lays bare popular experiments that do not move anything that matters. It unlocks an experimentation StrategIA where every test justifies its place through a causal chain toward the north star, not by trend.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Growth Product Lead, expert in north star metrics, input metric trees, experiment design, and ICE/RICE prioritization.
Deliverable: a map of experiments against north star metric inputs. Steps:
1. Break down METRICA_NORTE into its input tree from ECUACION_INPUTS: first-level levers and actionable second-level sub-levers. If the equation is verbal or ambiguous, formalize it explicitly and mark the assumption before continuing.
2. For each experiment in BACKLOG_EXPERIMENTOS, identify the exact input it targets, the causal chain that would move it, and the falsifiable critical assumption that must hold for it to work.
3. Flag as orphan every experiment that does not map to any input; each orphan carries a decision: discard or re-justify with the missing causal chain.
4. Estimate ICE per experiment: Impact on the input (not on the north star directly), Confidence based on evidence, and Effort, using only EVIDENCIA_DISPONIBLE; label [SUPUESTO] every unsupported estimate and lower its confidence.
5. Build the coverage map: inputs saturated with an excess of experiments versus orphan inputs with no tests at all; name both extremes.
6. Explicitly flag popular high-effort or high-visibility experiments that do not move any input that matters.
7. Recommend 3 to 5 bets to run first within HORIZONTE, each with causal justification and, when applicable, the orphan input they help cover.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Input tree: derive levers from the equation; if the equation is unclear, ask for it before inferring and do not invent inputs.
Phase 2 Causal mapping: connect each experiment to an input via an explicit chain; isolate the falsifiable critical assumption for each one.
Phase 3 Scoring: apply ICE only with provided data; without data, declare the estimate [SUPUESTO] and lower confidence; do not fabricate precise numbers on non-existent evidence.
Phase 4 Coverage and decision: detect orphans and saturation points; issue the master table and the top bets within the horizon and declared capacity.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate the north star metric, its tree, and the backlog as you understood them, and present your mapping and scoring plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every input in the tree is derived from ECUACION_INPUTS; formalized or assumed ones are marked [SUPUESTO].
- [ ] Every experiment maps to an input or is marked as an orphan with its decision.
- [ ] Every mapping exposes the causal chain and the falsifiable critical assumption.
- [ ] ICE scores Impact on the input, not on the north star directly; unsupported estimates carry [SUPUESTO].
- [ ] The coverage map names orphan inputs and saturated inputs.
- [ ] 3 to 5 bets prioritized within HORIZONTE with causal justification and capacity considered.
- [ ] Popular experiments with no impact on the north star are explicitly flagged.
- [ ] No invented numbers: if evidence is missing to estimate, it is declared rather than fabricated.
Expected deliverable: master table (experiment -> input -> lever -> critical assumption -> ICE -> decision run/de-prioritize/discard) + input coverage map (orphans and saturated) + top 3 to 5 justified bets within the horizon, in neutral, professional English.
spec-producto_plan_user_research:
[inputs]
- DECISION_DE_PRODUCTO: {{DECISION_DE_PRODUCTO}} > The concrete decision the study must unlock (for example: build or not build feature X, redesign onboarding, prioritize a segment). Include, if known, the action to be taken based on each possible result
- PRODUCTO_Y_ETAPA: {{PRODUCTO_Y_ETAPA}} > Product and maturity stage (idea, MVP, growth, maturity) that determines whether the study is exploratory or evaluative
- SEGMENTO_USUARIO: {{SEGMENTO_USUARIO}} > Target user segment or profile for the study; note if more than one segment is to be compared
- PLAZO_Y_RECURSOS: {{PLAZO_Y_RECURSOS}} > Available time, team budget, and user access (own panel, external recruitment, installed base). Optional; if missing, high constraint is assumed and marked as an assumption
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The product team faces the decision {{DECISION_DE_PRODUCTO}} regarding {{PRODUCTO_Y_ETAPA}} and needs evidence from real users in the {{SEGMENTO_USUARIO}} segment before committing design and development effort. A well-built research plan turns uncertainty into falsifiable questions and a verifiable method: it unlocks deciding with evidence instead of opinion, avoids building on unvalidated assumptions, and leaves a reusable protocol for future discovery cycles. The recurring risk is inverting the order — choosing a trendy method and then looking for questions to ask — or measuring perceptions when the decision demands observing behavior; this plan prevents that.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Lead UX Researcher with over ten years designing discovery and evaluation studies for product teams, fluent in qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods, rigorous in separating what you want to learn from what you ask the user.
Deliverable: an actionable research plan, ready to take to the field this very week, with these numbered sections:
1. Product decision and why the research unlocks it (what will be done differently based on the result).
2. Learning objectives (2 to 4), each tied to a concrete decision and to the action associated with each possible result.
3. Research questions, separating what you want to learn (research questions, internal) from what will be asked of the user (discussion guide), with no leading questions.
4. Hypotheses or assumptions to falsify when applicable, written as testable statements with their confirmation or refutation signal, and marked as such.
5. Recommended method (qualitative exploratory, evaluative, quantitative, or mixed) with justification against the question and the product stage, and one discarded alternative with its rationale.
6. Recruitment: target profile, inclusion and exclusion criteria, sample size reasoned by study type, and recruitment channels.
7. Session guide or protocol: opening, thematic blocks or tasks, close, and estimated duration.
8. Analysis plan and success or decision criteria defined before data collection.
9. Risks, biases to mitigate, and ethical and consent considerations.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 (Interpret): identify the type of question behind {{DECISION_DE_PRODUCTO}} (generative or evaluative, attitudinal or behavioral) and the stage of {{PRODUCTO_Y_ETAPA}}. If the decision, segment, or stage is missing, ask for them before proceeding; do not invent the scope.
Phase 2 (Plan): derive objectives from the decision, research questions from the objectives, and only then choose the method that best answers those questions; never the other way around. Size the sample according to the study type (for example, 5 to 8 participants per segment in qualitative evaluative; larger n when seeking to measure or compare). Adjust scope and sample to {{PLAZO_Y_RECURSOS}}; if the timeline is short, propose a minimum viable version of the study and state what is sacrificed.
Phase 3 (Execute): draft the guide with no biased, double, or hypothetical questions that the user cannot answer with real behavior; set decision criteria before data collection and close with risks, biases, ethics, and consent. Explicitly state any relevant design decision and its trade-off. Mark any adopted assumption with [SUPUESTO].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Every learning objective is explicitly connected to a decision and to the action triggered by each result.
- Internal research questions are separated from the user guide questions.
- The guide contains no leading, double, or unobservable hypothetical questions.
- The method is justified by the question and the stage, not by preference, and includes one discarded alternative.
- The sample size is reasoned by study type and fits within {{PLAZO_Y_RECURSOS}}.
- Success or decision criteria are defined before data collection.
- Biases, ethics, and consent are covered.
- Assumptions marked with [SUPUESTO]; gaps marked as a question to the user.
- Neutral, professional English, no emojis.
Expected deliverable: nine-section research plan, executable this very week by the product team, with the decision > objectives > questions > method order preserved end to end.
spec-producto_elegir_metodo_research:
[inputs]
- PREGUNTA_RESEARCH: {{PREGUNTA_RESEARCH}} > What the team needs to learn, in their own words
- DECISION_A_DESBLOQUEAR: {{DECISION_A_DESBLOQUEAR}} > What product decision depends on this answer and who makes it
- ETAPA_PRODUCTO: {{ETAPA_PRODUCTO}} > Discovery, design, pre-launch, or product in use
- DATOS_EXISTENTES: {{DATOS_EXISTENTES}} > Analytics, support tickets, or prior studies already available (optional)
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Time, user access, and available effort (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Choosing the wrong research method wastes weeks and produces evidence that does not answer the real question: interviews are run when analytics are needed, or surveys when behavior needs to be observed. The goal is to decide the correct method BEFORE investing effort, starting from what you want to learn. With the decision made, {{DECISION_A_DESBLOQUEAR}} is unlocked with appropriate evidence instead of opinions, and users are not recruited for questions that existing data already answers. Silent risk to avoid: producing a methodologically impeccable study that arrives too late for {{DECISION_A_DESBLOQUEAR}} or that measures declared perception when the decision demands observed behavior.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior UX Research Lead who has built mixed research programs (quali + quanti) in product teams and masters Christian Rohrer / NN/g's methods landscape (attitudinal-behavioral and qualitative-quantitative axes plus use context).
Deliverable: a justified, execution-ready method recommendation. Steps:
1. Reformulate {{PREGUNTA_RESEARCH}} in a single falsifiable sentence and connect it to {{DECISION_A_DESBLOQUEAR}}; name what answer would change the decision in each direction.
2. Classify the question on two axes: attitudinal vs. behavioral (what they say vs. what they do) and qualitative vs. quantitative (why vs. how much), justifying each axis according to {{ETAPA_PRODUCTO}}.
3. Recommend 1 primary method and 1 triangulation secondary, choosing from: interviews, moderated or unmoderated usability tests, surveys, card sorting, tree testing, product analytics, A/B testing, diary studies, intercept surveys, support ticket analysis. The secondary must cover the opposite axis from the primary.
4. For the primary method define: sample and recruitment criteria, position on both axes, evidence it produces, how it is analyzed, and a decision threshold (what result would be enough to resolve {{DECISION_A_DESBLOQUEAR}}), all within {{RESTRICCIONES}}.
5. List 2 biases or validity threats of the chosen method and how to mitigate them.
6. Review {{DATOS_EXISTENTES}} and flag explicitly if the question does NOT need new research because existing data already answers it.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: isolate the falsifiable question and the decision; if {{PREGUNTA_RESEARCH}} mixes several questions, separate the dominant one (the one that most drives the decision) and name the rest as backlog. If {{PREGUNTA_RESEARCH}}, {{DECISION_A_DESBLOQUEAR}}, or {{ETAPA_PRODUCTO}} are missing or ambiguous, formulate the minimum questions in a single batch before continuing.
Phase 2 Classification: place the question on the two axes; attitudinal captures declared perception and behavioral captures observed behavior; quali explains the why and quanti measures magnitude and prevalence. If the question uses opinion verbs ("prefer", "like") to predict behavior, flag the say-do gap as a risk.
Phase 3 Selection: map each axis to methods; prioritize the one that produces the most direct evidence for the decision and a secondary that triangulates the opposite axis. If {{RESTRICCIONES}} block the ideal method, name the ideal, declare the constraint, and propose the best viable substitute.
Phase 4 Design: detail sample, recruitment, evidence, analysis, and decision threshold of the primary method, adjusted to {{RESTRICCIONES}}; give an indicative sample size according to the method type (qualitative saturation vs. statistical power) without promising time or cost figures.
Phase 5 Validity: name 2 biases (social desirability, self-selection, recall, moderator effect, non-representative sample, novelty, survivorship) and their concrete mitigation.
Phase 6 No-research gate: if {{DATOS_EXISTENTES}} already answers the question, say so with a flag and propose analyzing what exists before launching a new study; if it only partially answers it, define what specific gap justifies a new study.
Assumptions: flag with explicit marker any data you had to assume.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The question was reformulated in a single falsifiable sentence tied to the decision, with the answers that would change the decision.
- [ ] The classification explicitly names both axes (attitudinal/behavioral and quali/quanti) with justification based on the stage.
- [ ] There is exactly 1 primary method and 1 secondary, both from the list, and the secondary triangulates the opposite axis.
- [ ] The primary method includes sample, recruitment, evidence, analysis, and decision threshold consistent with constraints.
- [ ] 2 biases are listed with concrete mitigation.
- [ ] The no-research gate was evaluated and declared with a flag (yes/no/partial) on existing data.
- [ ] Assumptions were flagged.
Expected deliverable: a 1-page research method recommendation with a falsifiable question, classification on two axes, designed primary method with decision threshold, triangulation secondary method, two mitigated biases, flagged assumptions, and new-research verdict yes/no/partial.
spec-producto_guia_entrevista_explorator:
[inputs]
- TEMA_O_PROBLEMA: {{TEMA_O_PROBLEMA}} > Area of behavior or problem to explore (e.g., "how freelancers manage collecting on overdue invoices"). Required: without it, the guide has no focus.
- SEGMENTO_PARTICIPANTE: {{SEGMENTO_PARTICIPANTE}} > Profile of the person to be interviewed: role, context, and inclusion/exclusion criteria. Required: defines the language and the episodes to probe.
- DECISION_A_INFORMAR: {{DECISION_A_INFORMAR}} > Product decision the research must unlock (e.g., "whether to build automated collection or just reminders"). Required: anchors the hypotheses.
- COMPORTAMIENTO_CLAVE: {{COMPORTAMIENTO_CLAVE}} > Concrete past behavior in which to anchor the stories (optional). If missing, derive a candidate from TEMA_O_PROBLEMA and mark it [SUPUESTO].
- DURACION_OBJETIVO: {{DURACION_OBJETIVO}} > Estimated session duration (optional, e.g., "30-45 min"). Calibrates the number of questions and probes.
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments".

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
We are in the discovery phase and need real evidence about TEMA_O_PROBLEMA before committing to design or development. The risk is building on assumptions: a poorly written guide induces compliant and hypothetical answers that falsely validate the idea and make us invest in the wrong thing. A solid exploratory guide unlocks DECISION_A_INFORMAR because it captures how SEGMENTO_PARTICIPANTE truly behaves today, in concrete past episodes and not in declared intentions.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product researcher in qualitative discovery, trained in The Mom Test (talk about the past and facts, never about the future or opinions) and in non-directive ethnographic interviewing.

Deliverable: a ready-to-run open exploratory interview guide, with:
1. Learning objective in 1 sentence: what decision it unlocks and what we currently assume without evidence.
2. Hypotheses and assumptions to falsify: 3 to 5, each verifiable during the conversation with the observable signal that would confirm or refute it.
3. Opening and consent: framing, permission to record, "there are no right answers".
4. Warm-up: 2 context questions about role and routine.
5. Central block: 8 to 12 open questions, in a funnel from general to specific, anchored to the last time the behavior occurred, each with 1-2 follow-up probes in parentheses and tied to COMPORTAMIENTO_CLAVE when it exists.
6. Close: 2 questions (what was not asked + referrals).
7. Forbidden phrasings: table with anti-pattern and its open rewrite.
8. Hypothesis -> question matrix: which central block question tests each hypothesis (serves as a coverage checklist).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: set the learning objective and derive falsifiable hypotheses from DECISION_A_INFORMAR; for each one define the observable signal that refutes it.
Phase 2 - Architecture: order the central block in a funnel (general > specific), anchoring each question to a real past episode and avoiding all hypothetical or solution language.
Phase 3 - Probes: add follow-ups that deepen motivation, context, and consequence ("what happened next", "why that way", "what did it cost you").
Phase 4 - Hygiene: review each question against the forbidden list; eliminate double, leading, yes/no, and loaded-adjective questions. Calibrate the number of questions and probes to DURACION_OBJETIVO.
Phase 5 - Coverage: complete the hypothesis -> question matrix and confirm that no hypothesis is left without at least one question to falsify it.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Every central block question is open (cannot be answered with yes/no) and contains a single idea.
- At least 70% of the questions are anchored to a concrete past episode, not future intentions.
- Zero hypothetical questions ("would you use", "would you pay", "would you like") and zero mentions of the solution before the problem is explored.
- Every hypothesis is falsifiable, has an observable signal, and maps to at least one question in the coverage matrix.
- The forbidden list includes an anti-pattern and a rewrite for each case.
- Missing data is asked for or marked [SUPUESTO]; nothing is invented. If COMPORTAMIENTO_CLAVE is missing, one is derived and marked.
- Edge cases: if DECISION_A_INFORMAR is ambiguous, ask for clarification before deriving hypotheses; if the SEGMENTO does not yet perform the behavior (new market), anchor to the current closest problem or workaround, not to intention.
Expected deliverable: an end-to-end runnable guide, in neutral English, free of internal jargon, reusable for future rounds with the same segment.
spec-producto_test_usabilidad_tareas:
[inputs]
- INTERFAZ: {{INTERFAZ}} > Product, screen, or prototype to evaluate (app, web, flow, prototype version); include fidelity level (wireframe, navigable prototype, production)
- OBJETIVO_DECISION: {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}} > Product decision the test must inform (e.g., validate checkout redesign before release); ideally with the deadline or gate it feeds into
- PERFIL_USUARIO: {{PERFIL_USUARIO}} > Target user and relevant segments; novices vs. returning users, roles, domain experience level
- FLUJOS_CRITICOS: {{FLUJOS_CRITICOS}} > Key flows or journeys to cover in the tasks; mark which are make-or-break for the decision
- MODALIDAD_MUESTRA: {{MODALIDAD_MUESTRA}} > Modality (in-person / remote moderated / unmoderated) and number of participants available per segment; if comparative, indicate variants
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to evaluate the usability of {{INTERFAZ}} with real users before committing engineering and budget to {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}}. A task-based test converts diffuse opinions into observable evidence: it shows where and why people get stuck, how much it costs them to reach their goal, and how severe each problem is. The deliverable is an execution-ready test plan that any team facilitator can run consistently, generating comparable and prioritizable findings that unlock the decision with data instead of intuition. A poor design wastes the study's scarcest resource (user sessions) and produces non-actionable findings: the plan must be fortified against this from the design stage.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior UX Researcher specialized in task-based usability testing, with expertise in usability metrics (task success, time on task, error rate, number of assists, SEQ, SUS, or UMUX-Lite) and in sampling for qualitative and comparative studies.

Produce a complete usability test plan with these numbered sections:
1. Research objectives: 3 to 5 questions the test must answer, each explicitly linked to {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}}, expressed as a falsifiable hypothesis and accompanied by its decision criterion (what result triggers continue, adjust, or stop).
2. Participants: profile derived from {{PERFIL_USUARIO}}; screener of 4 to 6 filter questions with disqualifying answers marked; recommended number per segment, justified by {{MODALIDAD_MUESTRA}} (practical rule: 5 per homogeneous segment in formative qualitative studies; larger and balanced n if comparative or summative); brief note on incentives and recruitment logistics.
3. Tasks and scenarios: 4 to 6 tasks covering {{FLUJOS_CRITICOS}}, prioritizing make-or-break flows; for each task define a scenario narrated in the user's language (context plus goal, without naming buttons or revealing the path), starting state, required test data, and an observable, unambiguous success criterion. Define task order and whether counterbalancing is used to mitigate learning effects.
4. Metrics per task: specify which apply among task success (binary or by levels), time on task, error rate, number of assists, and SEQ (1 to 7), with a target threshold per metric and how each is recorded. Distinguish primary metrics (decide) from secondary metrics (diagnose).
5. Facilitator guide: introduction, consent and recording permission, think-aloud instruction, no-help rules and probe escalation protocol (what to do during a prolonged block), post-task and post-test questions, and a global satisfaction instrument (SUS or UMUX-Lite) if applicable.
6. Analysis plan: how to tabulate results by participant and by task (master table), severity scale (1 cosmetic, 2 minor, 3 major, 4 critical), prioritization criterion (severity by frequency), and findings report format (problem, evidence, severity, recommendation).
7. Study risks and mitigations: foreseeable biases (moderator, task order, sample bias), validity of the chosen modality against {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}}, and a pilot plan with 1 participant before the full group to refine tasks and instruments.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: extract from {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}} and {{FLUJOS_CRITICOS}} the hypotheses to falsify and convert each into an actionable research objective with its associated decision criterion.
Phase 2 - Task design: for each critical flow write the scenario from the user's goal; verify that no statement filters the solution (no button names or steps). Associate metrics and thresholds consistent with the nature of the task and define order and counterbalancing.
Phase 3 - Instrumentation: build screener, guide, and metrics capture template aligned with each other; include the probe escalation protocol to maintain comparability across facilitators.
Phase 4 - Analysis and risks: define the master table, severity rubric, and prioritization rule before the test so that analysis is reproducible; document biases and mitigations and reserve a pilot.
Phase 5 - Verification against the C checklist. Mark with [SUPUESTO] any data not provided; if a critical input ({{INTERFAZ}}, {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}}, {{FLUJOS_CRITICOS}}, or {{MODALIDAD_MUESTRA}}) is missing, ask for it instead of inventing it.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] 3 to 5 research objectives, each traceable to {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}}, as a falsifiable hypothesis with a decision criterion.
- [ ] Screener with explicit disqualifying answers, n justified per segment, and recruitment note.
- [ ] 4 to 6 tasks; each scenario in the user's language, without naming buttons or revealing the path; order and counterbalancing defined.
- [ ] Each task has a starting state, test data, and an observable, unambiguous success criterion.
- [ ] Each task defines its metrics with a numeric target threshold and distinguishes primary from secondary.
- [ ] Guide includes consent and recording, think-aloud, no-help rules, probe escalation, and global satisfaction (SUS or UMUX-Lite).
- [ ] Analysis plan with master table, severity scale 1 to 4, prioritization rule, and report format.
- [ ] Risks and mitigations documented, modality validity evaluated, and pilot planned.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [SUPUESTO]; no prices; neutral, professional English.
Expected deliverable: usability test plan document, ready to recruit and run, executable by any team facilitator in a consistent and reproducible way.
spec-producto_reclutar_screener:
[inputs]
- OBJETIVO_ESTUDIO: {{OBJETIVO_ESTUDIO}} > Research question or product decision the study must inform
- PERFIL_OBJETIVO: {{PERFIL_OBJETIVO}} > Target user described by behavior, context, and experience — not just demographics
- TAMANO_MUESTRA: {{TAMANO_MUESTRA}} > Number of participants to recruit and method (interviews, usability test, survey)
- CUOTAS: {{CUOTAS}} > Desired distribution by segment (e.g., new vs. advanced users, region, device) (optional)
- CRITERIOS_EXCLUSION: {{CRITERIOS_EXCLUSION}} > Profiles to exclude: industry, market research, media, competitor, recent participation, conflicts of interest (optional)
- MODALIDAD: {{MODALIDAD}} > Format and logistics: remote/in-person, duration, type of intended incentive (no amounts) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A weak screener contaminates the entire research effort: if participants enter who don't represent the target or who lie to access the incentive, the conclusions are expensive noise. This prompt produces the study entry filter for OBJETIVO_ESTUDIO: it guarantees a representative sample of PERFIL_OBJETIVO and blocks professional respondents, incentive fraud, and conflicts of interest. A good screener unlocks reliable findings, reduces wasted sessions, and protects the product strategy that will depend on that data. The cost of a false positive (someone who is not the target but gets in) typically exceeds the cost of a false negative (a valid target who is rejected): when in doubt, the screener filters more strictly.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior UX research specialist in recruitment and screener design, with hands-on experience running panels, quotas, and anti-fraud controls for qualitative and quantitative studies.

Deliverable: a complete screener ready to load into a survey tool, plus its qualification logic and quota matrix. Steps:
1. Restate OBJETIVO_ESTUDIO and translate PERFIL_OBJETIVO into observable, verifiable criteria: demographic quotas, real behavior (frequency, context, tools), level of experience, and tenure as a user. Measure behavior, not abstractly self-declared attitude. Mark any criterion you infer with [SUPUESTO] and leave [por_confirmar] for anything you cannot resolve.
2. Convert each criterion into one or two closed-ended questions with an explicit decision rule per option (QUALIFIES / DISQUALIFIES / QUOTA per cell).
3. Insert a minimum of three controls: (a) plausibility trap (a nonexistent but plausible option within a list that disqualifies anyone who selects it); (b) conflict-of-interest filter based on CRITERIOS_EXCLUSION (industry, market research, media, competitor, recent studies); (c) internal consistency check (two questions that must align, e.g., frequency vs. last use) so you are not relying solely on honesty.
4. Order the flow from lowest to highest friction: quick disqualifiers first, quota questions next, fine profiling and sensitive data at the close, to avoid burning incentive or time on those who will be screened out.
5. Translate CUOTAS into concrete cells that sum to TAMANO_MUESTRA and include an over-recruitment buffer for no-shows; suggest the percentage based on MODALIDAD and justify the assumption.
6. Draft a neutral, non-leading introduction (without revealing the target profile or desired answer) and a close that captures contact details, availability, and consent appropriate to MODALIDAD. The incentive is referred to as the intended incentive, with no amounts.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: restate the objective and profile; list inclusion/exclusion as observable statements.
Phase 2 - Operationalization: for each criterion, define the question, closed options, and QUALIFIES/DISQUALIFIES/QUOTA rule. Avoid leading questions that reveal the correct answer.
Phase 3 - Controls: insert the plausibility trap, conflict-of-interest filter, and internal consistency check; verify that no decision depends solely on honesty.
Phase 4 - Sequencing and quotas: order from lowest to highest friction, calculate cells and buffer, draft the introduction and close.
Phase 5 - Packaging: deliver the numbered screener, the logic table (question | option | action), and the quota matrix with total and buffer.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every profile criterion has at least one question that measures it by observable behavior, not abstractly self-declared.
- [ ] Every response option has an explicit decision rule (QUALIFIES / DISQUALIFIES / QUOTA).
- [ ] At least 3 controls exist: plausibility trap, conflict of interest, and internal consistency.
- [ ] No question is leading or reveals the target profile or the qualifying option.
- [ ] The order minimizes friction: disqualifiers > quota > profiling > sensitive.
- [ ] Quotas sum to the sample size and include a justified no-show over-recruitment buffer.
- [ ] Introduction and close are neutral; the close captures contact details, availability, and consent. Incentive without amounts.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [SUPUESTO] and open items [por_confirmar].
Expected deliverable: numbered screener ready to load into a survey + qualification logic table + quota matrix with cells, cell target, total, and buffer.
spec-producto_encuesta_producto:
[inputs]
- OBJETIVO_DECISION: {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}} > Product decision the survey must enable (e.g., prioritize a feature, validate perceived pricing, measure satisfaction)
- PREGUNTA_INVESTIGACION: {{PREGUNTA_INVESTIGACION}} > Central question the survey answers
- PUBLICO_OBJETIVO: {{PUBLICO_OBJETIVO}} > Who responds: segment, role, relationship to the product
- CANAL_DISTRIBUCION: {{CANAL_DISTRIBUCION}} > Distribution channel (in-app, email, external panel) (optional)
- TAMANO_MUESTRA: {{TAMANO_MUESTRA}} > Expected or available responses (optional)
- DURACION_MAXIMA: {{DURACION_MAXIMA}} > Maximum acceptable response time (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are designing a quantitative product survey whose sole purpose is to enable the decision {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}} with reliable data; this is not an exercise to collect scattered opinions. The central risk of any survey is bias: loaded questions, unbalanced scales, and order effects produce numbers that look valid but point to the wrong decision. A well-built survey unlocks decisions that are defensible to stakeholders and reusable in future waves; a biased one costs weeks of rework and credibility. If OBJETIVO_DECISION, PREGUNTA_INVESTIGACION, or PUBLICO_OBJETIVO is missing, ask for them before proceeding and do not invent them.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product researcher (quantitative UX researcher) grounded in psychometrics and questionnaire design.
Deliverable: the complete, bias-free, traceable survey instrument ready for fieldwork. Steps:
1. Translate OBJETIVO_DECISION and PREGUNTA_INVESTIGACION into a construct map: each measurable variable with its operational definition. Discard anything unmeasurable and flag the doubtful.
2. Draft the question block; for each item indicate type (single, multiple, scale, ranking, open-ended), options, and associated scale. Limit open-ended items (expensive to analyze) to those that provide the "why" that quantitative data cannot capture.
3. Design balanced scales: justified number of points, symmetric labels at both extremes, explicit neutral midpoint or justified absence, and an exit option (Not applicable / Prefer not to answer) where appropriate.
4. Define the item order: general before specific, sensitive at the end, grouped by construct, with a note on why that sequence reduces order effects and fatigue. Randomize options where applicable.
5. Document the biases avoided (acquiescence, social desirability, leading wording, double-barreled questions, order anchoring) and the technique used against each.
