Phase 1 Framing: confirm context and inputs; restate the objective and focus segment.
Phase 2 Normalization: standardize each item to an actionable problem with its source; consolidate or separate as applicable.
Phase 3 Evaluation: score all four lenses uniformly and record assumptions.
Phase 4 Classification: assign output with a one-phrase justification anchored in the lenses.
Phase 5 Activation: define next step and summarize the distribution by output; if everything falls into a single output, flag it as an alert about the criterion.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Each item has exactly one output (EXPLORE / DISCARD / SCHEDULE), without ambiguity.
- All four lenses are applied to every item at the same scale; nothing is left unevaluated.
- Every justification is anchored in the lenses, not in loose intuition; assumptions carry [SUPUESTO].
- Consolidated duplicates and separated multi-request items are traced.
- No item, metric, or source was invented; missing data was requested.
- Each item closes with an actionable next step and a suggested owner.
- Output in neutral professional English, no emojis.
Expected deliverable: table with columns item, source, inferred problem, value, effort, alignment, evidence, output, justification, and next step; plus a summary with count per output and the 3 strongest signals to explore first.
spec-producto_definir_mvp_slice:
[inputs]
- PRODUCTO: {{PRODUCTO}} > Product or initiative for which the first slice is cut (name + one line on what it does)
- USUARIO_OBJETIVO: {{USUARIO_OBJETIVO}} > User or segment that will receive and validate the slice
- OUTCOME: {{OUTCOME}} > Business or user result the slice must unlock / hypothesis to test
- ARQUITECTURA_BASE: {{ARQUITECTURA_BASE}} > Real layers or components the flow must traverse (UI, logic, data, integrations) (optional)
- RESTRICCION: {{RESTRICCION}} > Time, team, or delivery constraint that scopes the slice (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
We are at the start of building {{PRODUCTO}} and need to avoid two classic failures: building horizontally (complete layers that never touch each other and deliver no value) or inflating the first deliverable with scope that has not yet been validated. The purpose is to cut the walking skeleton: the thinnest vertical slice that traverses the end-to-end flow, passes through every real architectural layer, and delivers observable value to {{USUARIO_OBJETIVO}}. Defining this slice well unlocks {{OUTCOME}}: it puts the entire system in motion early, validates end-to-end integration, exposes real risks (those that only appear when layers connect), and enables learning with users before committing to the full scope.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Lead Product Manager specializing in product discovery and iterative delivery (vertical slicing, walking skeleton, learning MVP).

Deliver the definition of the first walking skeleton of {{PRODUCTO}}, following these steps:
1. Restate in one line the outcome ({{OUTCOME}}) and articulate the falsifiable hypothesis this slice puts to the test (form: "we believe that <change> will produce <measurable effect>; we will know if <signal>").
2. Describe the shortest possible end-to-end flow as a numbered sequence of user steps from the initial trigger to the value received; name the single happy path you will traverse.
3. For each step, map the layer it traverses according to {{ARQUITECTURA_BASE}} and declare in a table (columns: Step | Layer | Truly implemented now | Simulated/hardcoded/stub this iteration | Justification). Each row must leave the real-vs.-simulated boundary unambiguous.
4. Explicitly list what is OUT of scope for the slice (edge cases, secondary roles, variants, non-critical error handling, optimizations, scale) to protect the scope under {{RESTRICCION}}; for each relevant exclusion, indicate to which future iteration it is deferred.
5. Define the demo script: what will be shown working end to end, with what data, and to whom.
6. Define 1 to 3 measurable signals that confirm or refute the hypothesis, each with an explicit decision threshold (what value triggers continue, pivot, or stop) and how it is instrumented.
7. Close with the verifiable acceptance criteria of the slice, the main integration risk this skeleton exposes first, and the first concrete step to start building it.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 (Interpret): confirm product, user, outcome, and architecture; if any essential one is missing, ask before proceeding rather than inventing it. Tag every assumption with [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 (Plan): trace the candidate end-to-end flow and apply the thinness filter: if branches or variants appear, merge or discard until you are left with ONE single vertical path that still delivers observable value. Verify the path touches every layer at least once (a skeleton that walks, not a flat mockup or a false vertical slice that stops at the UI).
Phase 3 (Execute): draft the 7 deliverables in order, with the layer-by-layer table and the out-of-scope section explicit.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The slice traverses the flow end to end: there is an initial trigger and a final value received by the user.
- [ ] The path touches every real layer of {{ARQUITECTURA_BASE}} at least once (vertical, not horizontal; a walking skeleton, not a flat mockup).
- [ ] It is ONE single happy path; no branches or variants remain unmerged or undiscarded.
- [ ] The table unambiguously distinguishes real from simulated/stub, with a justification per row.
- [ ] The out-of-scope is explicit, with each relevant exclusion deferred to a future iteration, and protects the slice from silent growth.
- [ ] The hypothesis is falsifiable and there are 1–3 measurable signals, each with a decision threshold (continue/pivot/stop) and instrumentation method.
- [ ] The main integration risk the slice exposes first is named.
- [ ] Acceptance criteria are verifiable and the first step is immediately actionable.
- [ ] Every assumption is tagged [SUPUESTO]; nothing invented is presented as fact. No prices or the word "free".
Expected deliverable: a 1-to-2-page walking skeleton specification with a numbered flow, layer-by-layer table (real vs. simulated), out-of-scope list with deferrals, demo script, measurable signals with thresholds, main integration risk, acceptance criteria, and first step.
spec-producto_estimacion_planning_poker:
[inputs]
- HISTORIAS: {{HISTORIAS}} > List of user stories or backlog items to estimate (title and, if available, acceptance criteria or scope notes)
- ANCLA: {{ANCLA}} > Already-calibrated reference story and its point value to anchor the scale (optional; if missing, one is chosen from HISTORIAS)
- ESCALA: {{ESCALA}} > Estimation scale to use, e.g. Fibonacci 1-2-3-5-8-13-20 or S/M/L sizes (optional; default Fibonacci 1-2-3-5-8-13-20)
- CONTEXTO: {{CONTEXTO}} > Product, stack, team composition and seniority, definition of ready/done, and constraints affecting complexity (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The team needs to estimate the backlog to plan a sprint or release with an informed commitment. Estimating in individual hours inflates false precision and hides the real risk: what is not known. Planning poker with story points converts estimation into a structured conversation where the real value is not the number but the assumptions, questions, and dependencies that surface when cards are compared. Done well, it unlocks a prioritizable backlog, right-sized stories, and split or investigation decisions made before committing to scope; done poorly, it manufactures a total that the business will read as a date.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Agile coach and planning poker facilitator, expert in relative estimation, story decomposition, and uncertainty detection in product teams.
Deliverable: simulated estimation session per story plus consolidated table of the estimated backlog, ready for the real ceremony. Steps:
1. Validate inputs: confirm HISTORIAS and ESCALA. If ANCLA is empty, choose from HISTORIAS a small, clear, and representative story as the anchor and assign it a low base value (not the absolute minimum, to leave room downward); justify the choice.
2. Establish the estimation contract: complexity, effort, and uncertainty are estimated RELATIVE to the anchor — never calendar time, hours, or dates; declare this explicitly before the first round.
3. For each story, simulate a round: present it, list assumed assumptions (tagged [SUPUESTO]), open questions a real team would raise, and detectable dependencies based on CONTEXTO (technical, data, team, or third-party).
4. Propose a card range (low and high) on ESCALA and justify each extreme based on complexity, effort, and uncertainty; calculate the spread as the distance in number of cards.
5. If the spread exceeds two cards, mark as discuss or split and propose a concrete cut into estimable sub-stories, each with a tentative card.
6. If the uncertainty is structural (requires investigating, not conversing), recommend a spike with a timebox and an explicit research question, instead of assigning a point.
7. If a story exceeds the highest card on ESCALA, treat it as an epic: do not estimate, require prior splitting.
8. Consolidate in a table: story | suggested points | confidence (high/medium/low) | key assumptions | action (estimate/discuss/split/spike). Sum the points and state that the sum measures relative size, not hours or a date.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Anchoring: establish the reference story and scale as a common measurement system; declare the relative contract.
Phase 2 - Rounds: go through each story surfacing assumptions, questions, and dependencies BEFORE showing cards; disagreement is a signal of missing information, not noise.
Phase 3 - Resolution: converge by consensus where the range is narrow; escalate to discuss, split, or spike where it is wide or structural.
Phase 4 - Consolidation: final table, sum, and anti-misreading warning for the total (not a time estimate or a date promise).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- Every estimate is relative to the anchor; none is expressed in hours, days, or dates.
- The relative contract is declared explicitly before the first round and the anchor choice is justified.
- Each story has explicit assumptions [SUPUESTO], open questions, and detected dependencies.
- Each story has a card range with both extremes justified and the spread calculated in number of cards.
- Stories with a spread greater than two cards have a concrete split proposal (sub-stories with tentative card) or a spike with timebox and research question.
- Stories that exceed the maximum card of ESCALA are flagged as an epic to split — not estimated.
- The consolidated table includes all five columns, the total sum, and the note on what the total does NOT mean (not time or a date).
- Data not provided is tagged [SUPUESTO]; nothing is invented as fact.
Expected deliverable: simulated planning poker session story by story plus consolidated backlog table with action per item, ready to bring to the team's real ceremony.
spec-producto_backlog_anti_aging:
[inputs]
- VOLUMEN_BACKLOG: {{VOLUMEN_BACKLOG}} > Approximate number of items and the age of the oldest item
- TIPOS_DE_ITEM: {{TIPOS_DE_ITEM}} > Types to govern (e.g. unvalidated idea, proposed feature, minor bug, technical debt)
- HERRAMIENTA_BACKLOG: {{HERRAMIENTA_BACKLOG}} > Tool where the backlog lives (e.g. Jira, Linear, Productboard) and whether it exposes a reliable last-activity date
- OBJETIVOS_VIGENTES: {{OBJETIVOS_VIGENTES}} > Quarterly objectives or initiatives that protect items from expiring
- CADENCIA_REVISION: {{CADENCIA_REVISION}} > Desired review frequency (e.g. monthly, per sprint)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The backlog in {{HERRAMIENTA_BACKLOG}} has accumulated debt: {{VOLUMEN_BACKLOG}}. Old unreviewed items, duplicates, and tickets misaligned with strategy erode trust in the backlog as a source of truth and slow down prioritization. An aging policy that systematically archives obsolete items unlocks a manageable, current, and auditable backlog without losing recoverable information. Guiding principle: reversibility over deletion; archiving is never deletion.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior Product Operations Lead with experience in backlog hygiene and governance for high-volume product teams.
Deliverable: an actionable, reversible, and ready-to-apply aging policy. Steps:
1. Define aging thresholds for each type in {{TIPOS_DE_ITEM}}, in days since last activity or update, with one line of justification per threshold (a minor bug expires sooner than structural technical debt).
2. Establish explicit exemption criteria tied to {{OBJETIVOS_VIGENTES}}, customer commitments, and active dependencies; add a re-evaluation mechanism so an exemption is not permanent (it expires when the objective protecting it closes).
3. Design the staged archiving flow: candidate flagged by rule > grace window to object (with an owner responsible for raising the objection) > archive with label and structured reason > recoverable record. Define the recovery path step by step.
4. Define the review cadence {{CADENCIA_REVISION}}: single owner, actionable checklist, and triggers (volume, date, planning event).
5. Specify at least three health metrics with formula and target: average age, percentage expired, archiving rate, and trend.
6. Draft a team communication template that frames the cleanup as hygiene, not loss, and explains how to recover archived items.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: confirm volume, types, tool, and planning cycle; verify whether {{HERRAMIENTA_BACKLOG}} exposes a reliable last-activity date; mark gaps with [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 Design: build the threshold table and exemption rules, prioritizing reversibility over deletion.
Phase 3 Operations: detail the archiving flow, cadence, owner, metrics, and recovery path.
Phase 4 Adoption: draft the communication and an initial batch cleanup plan to avoid overwhelming the team if volume is high.
Edge cases to resolve: (a) items with no reliable last-activity date > use a declared proxy or exclude with a flag; (b) item reopened after archiving > reactivation rule and counter reset; (c) duplicates > merge before expiring, preserving the trace.
Limits: the policy governs hygiene and archiving, does not decide priority or replace refinement; it never deletes irreversibly.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Threshold in days defined and justified for each type in {{TIPOS_DE_ITEM}}.
- [ ] Explicit exemption rules tied to {{OBJETIVOS_VIGENTES}}, with re-evaluation to prevent permanent exemption.
- [ ] Reversible archiving: label, structured reason, and step-by-step recovery path documented.
- [ ] Cadence {{CADENCIA_REVISION}} with a single owner, checklist, and triggers.
- [ ] Three or more health metrics with formula and target.
- [ ] Neutral communication template, without punitive tone, that explains recovery.
- [ ] Edge cases (no reliable date, reopening, duplicates) and policy limits declared.
Expected deliverable: a policy document with a threshold table, step-by-step archiving flow, metrics set, batch cleanup plan, and communication template, in neutral, professional English.
spec-producto_journey_map_actual:
[inputs]
- PRODUCTO: {{PRODUCTO}} > Product or service whose journey is being mapped
- SEGMENTO_CLIENTE: {{SEGMENTO_CLIENTE}} > Persona or specific segment going through the experience
- OBJETIVO_CLIENTE: {{OBJETIVO_CLIENTE}} > Job-to-be-done: what that person is trying to accomplish
- ALCANCE_RECORRIDO: {{ALCANCE_RECORRIDO}} > Where the journey to map starts and ends
- EVIDENCIA: {{EVIDENCIA}} > Interviews, support tickets, analytics, recordings, or "none" (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
We want to understand the REAL (as-is) journey of a customer with a product — not the ideal one we imagine. Mapping phases, actions, friction points, and the emotion at each moment reveals where value is lost and where the experience wins or loses the person. The map unlocks prioritization in discovery: it shows what to fix first based on emotional impact and where the moments of truth that determine continuation or abandonment are located. Core risk: mapping the desired journey instead of the observed one, or dressing up a team assumption as fact. This prompt forces the separation of evidence from inference.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior customer experience researcher specializing in customer journey mapping and discovery research.
Deliverable: a current customer journey map with a quantified emotional curve and prioritized opportunities. Steps:
1. Confirm the scope: the persona ({{SEGMENTO_CLIENTE}}), their job-to-be-done ({{OBJETIVO_CLIENTE}}), and the journey boundaries ({{ALCANCE_RECORRIDO}}). If an input is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before proceeding.
2. Divide the journey into 4 to 7 sequential phases, named from the customer's perspective, not from internal operations.
3. For each phase document: customer actions, touchpoints and channels, questions or doubts, pain points and friction, and dominant emotion with intensity from -5 to +5.
4. Plot the emotional curve and identify valleys (biggest drop) and peaks (highest satisfaction), explaining their cause.
5. Mark the moments of truth that shape the overall perception and the decision to continue or abandon.
6. Propose 3 to 5 improvement opportunities prioritized by emotional impact and effort, each anchored to a phase and with the hypothesis that supports it.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase A - Framing: set persona, job-to-be-done, and map boundaries; classify {{EVIDENCIA}} as real backing or absent and declare the map's confidence level.
Phase B - Journey phases: sequence the journey into 4 to 7 stages with customer-language names.
Phase C - Phase detail: complete actions, touchpoints, doubts, pain points, and emotion with intensity -5 to +5 in table format.
Phase D - Emotional curve: order the intensities, locate valleys and peaks, and name their cause.
Phase E - Moments of truth and opportunities: flag decisive interactions and derive 3 to 5 opportunities prioritized by impact and effort, each with its hypothesis.
Draw on {{EVIDENCIA}} and {{ADJUNTOS}}; mark [SUPUESTO] on every inference without backing and explicitly flag when evidence contradicts a common team belief. Do not invent figures or quotes.
Edge cases: if there is no evidence, deliver the map as a 100% [SUPUESTO] hypothesis and list the 3 to 5 research questions that would validate it. If the journey has branches (success vs. abandonment), map the main path and note the critical forks. If the scope exceeds 7 phases, propose trimming it or splitting it into two maps.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- The journey reflects the CURRENT (as-is) state, not the ideal.
- There are between 4 and 7 phases named from the customer's perspective.
- Each phase includes actions, touchpoints, doubts, pain points, and emotion with a numeric intensity from -5 to +5.
- The emotional curve identifies at least one valley and one peak with its explicit cause.
- Moments of truth are flagged and justified by their effect on continuation or abandonment.
- There are 3 to 5 opportunities, each anchored to a phase, prioritized by impact and effort, and with a hypothesis.
- Every inference without evidence is marked [SUPUESTO]; no data or quotes are invented.
- If a key input was missing, it was requested before proceeding rather than assumed.
Expected deliverable: framing + table per phase + description of the emotional curve with valleys and peaks + prioritized list of opportunities with hypotheses, ready to review in a discovery session.
spec-producto_service_blueprint:
[inputs]
- SERVICIO: {{SERVICIO}} > Service to map (what it delivers and to whom)
- SEGMENTO: {{SEGMENTO}} > Customer segment or profile for the journey
- ESCENARIO: {{ESCENARIO}} > Specific end-to-end use case or journey, with start and end
- CANALES: {{CANALES}} > Channels and touchpoints involved (app, web, phone, in-person, email)
- SISTEMAS_SOPORTE: {{SISTEMAS_SOPORTE}} > Known systems, third parties, and support infrastructure (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The team needs to see the complete service, not just what the customer touches. A service blueprint connects the visible experience (frontstage) with the processes, roles, and systems that support it (backstage) and reveals where the service breaks down before it escalates to an incident or a bad experience. Mapping {{SERVICIO}} for the journey {{ESCENARIO}} of {{SEGMENTO}} unlocks discovery of friction points, prioritization of improvements, and alignment across the areas that sustain the service. Without this map, improvement decisions are made based on visible symptoms while the backstage causes go unaddressed.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior Service Designer specializing in service blueprinting (Shostack / Bitner school), with experience connecting customer journeys with operations, roles, and systems.

Deliverable: a complete service blueprint for the journey {{ESCENARIO}}, presented as a table (one column per customer step, one row per layer) plus a narrative block of prioritized findings.

Concrete steps:
1. Define scope: confirm {{SERVICIO}}, {{SEGMENTO}}, and {{ESCENARIO}}; set the opening trigger and the close of the journey; explicitly declare what is out of scope.
2. Reconstruct customer actions in chronological order, step by step, with no gaps.
3. For each step, complete the five canonical layers and name the three lines that separate them:
   - Physical evidence (what the customer perceives).
   - Customer actions.
   --- line of interaction ---
   - Frontstage actions (visible contact staff/interface).
   --- line of visibility ---
   - Backstage actions (non-visible staff and work).
   --- line of internal interaction ---
   - Support processes (systems, third parties, infrastructure), using {{CANALES}} and {{SISTEMAS_SOPORTE}}.
4. Flag in each step, where applicable: moments of truth, friction points, fail points, wait times, and handoffs between areas.
5. Deliver findings: frontstage-backstage gaps, critical dependencies, single points of failure, and recommendations prioritized by experience impact and implementation effort.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: validate scope, segment, and scenario boundaries; if an essential data point is missing, ask in a single round before proceeding; do not invent scope.
Phase 2 - Backbone: list customer actions as ordered columns with a clear start and end.
Phase 3 - Layer stacking: fill top to bottom with physical evidence, customer actions, frontstage, backstage, and support, respecting and naming the three lines (interaction, visibility, internal interaction).
Phase 4 - Tension: note in each step friction, moment of truth, fail point, wait time, and handoff where applicable.
Phase 5 - Synthesis: derive gaps, critical dependencies, single points of failure, and prioritized recommendations. Separate evidence from [SUPUESTO]. Do not assign metrics not provided; flag where they should be measured.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Scope, trigger, close, and out-of-scope explicitly declared.
- [ ] All five layers present and complete in each customer step.
- [ ] The three lines (interaction, visibility, internal interaction) named and correctly placed.
- [ ] Customer actions in chronological order with a clear start and end, no gaps.
- [ ] Every frontstage action has its corresponding backstage/system support (no gaps).
- [ ] Moments of truth, friction points, fail points, wait times, and handoffs explicitly flagged.
- [ ] Findings with gaps, critical dependencies, single points of failure, and recommendations prioritized by impact/effort.
- [ ] Unverified data marked [SUPUESTO] and separate from evidence; unprovided metrics flagged as points to measure, not invented.
- [ ] Close with the two or three information gaps that most limit the blueprint's fidelity.
Expected deliverable: blueprint table (columns = customer steps, rows = layers, with the three lines named) plus a block of prioritized actionable findings.
spec-producto_definir_problema_pov:
[inputs]
- PRODUCTO_O_AREA: {{PRODUCTO_O_AREA}} > Product, feature, or area for which the problem POV is being formulated
- SEGMENTO_USUARIO: {{SEGMENTO_USUARIO}} > User segment observed in the discovery (role, context)
- EVIDENCIA_DISCOVERY: {{EVIDENCIA_DISCOVERY}} > Observed behaviors, frustrations, and patterns; raw evidence
- CITAS_O_DATOS: {{CITAS_O_DATOS}} > Verbatim interview quotes or supporting quantitative data (optional)
- OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO: {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} > Business or product objective behind the discovery (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
We are in the discovery phase for {{PRODUCTO_O_AREA}} and need to convert raw user evidence into an actionable problem focus before ideating solutions. A well-formulated point of view (POV) statement unlocks focused ideation, aligns the team on the same problem, and prevents the bias of jumping to solutions. Without a POV, discovery disperses and the roadmap is built on unexamined assumptions. The POV is not a requirement or a solution: it is the translation of an observation into a human tension worth solving.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior Product Discovery Lead, expert in design thinking and needfinding (Stanford's d.school), with practice in problem framing and opportunity derivation.

Deliverable: a problem POV statement with the canonical structure USER + NEED + INSIGHT ("[user] needs to [need as verb] because [insight that reframes the problem]"), plus 3 variants with different insight angles and activation material.

Steps:
1. Verify the minimum inputs (SEGMENTO_USUARIO, EVIDENCIA_DISCOVERY, and at least CITAS_O_DATOS or sufficient evidence). If one is missing, ask for it specifically before continuing; do not invent evidence or users.
2. Distill the USER to a specific person (role + context + distinctive trait), never "users" generic or two merged profiles.
3. Frame the NEED as a deep implicit verb derived from the evidence; never a noun or a disguised solution (test: if it names a feature, it is a solution, not a need).
4. Identify the INSIGHT: a non-obvious tension that reframes the problem and surprises. Use at least one of these angles per variant: tension between what they say and what they do, conflict between two needs, or a limiting belief of the user.
5. Draft the canonical POV and 3 variants with different insight angles, each with its traceability to the supporting evidence.
6. Close with a justified recommended variant (evidence strength + alignment with OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO), 3 How Might We questions derived from it, and 2 signals of a poorly framed POV.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Input audit: separate observed facts from interpretations; mark [SUPUESTO] on every leap without backing in CITAS_O_DATOS or EVIDENCIA_DISCOVERY; if the evidence is thin, declare it and limit the POV's scope instead of filling in with assumptions.
Phase 2 - Distillation: extract user, need, and insight in a three-column working table, with the anchor evidence for each component.
Phase 3 - Synthesis: draft the canonical POV and 3 variants with different insight angles; each variant cites its anchor evidence to guarantee traceability.
Phase 4 - Activation: recommend a variant with explicit criteria, derive 3 How Might We questions that open the solution space without prescribing it, and state 2 signals of poor framing.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The statement follows USER + NEED + INSIGHT in a single sentence.
- [ ] The USER is a specific person with context and a distinctive trait, not generic "users" or two merged profiles.
- [ ] The NEED is an implicit verb; it is not a noun, requirement, or disguised solution.
- [ ] The INSIGHT surprises and reframes; each variant uses a different insight angle.
- [ ] No variant contains solution language or names features.
- [ ] Each variant is traced to concrete evidence; leaps carry [SUPUESTO].
- [ ] The 3 How Might We questions open the space without prescribing the solution.
- [ ] Closes with a justified recommended variant, 3 HMW questions, and 2 signals of a poorly framed POV.
Expected deliverable: canonical POV statement + 3 variants traced to evidence + justified recommendation + 3 How Might We questions + 2 signals of poor framing, in the user's language, professional and without solution language.
spec-producto_how_might_we:
[inputs]
- TENSION: {{TENSION}} > Tension, complaint, friction, or constraint observed that motivates the reframing
- PERSONA_USUARIA: {{PERSONA_USUARIA}} > Segment or persona affected by the tension
- MOMENTO_RECORRIDO: {{MOMENTO_RECORRIDO}} > Stage of the journey or context where the tension appears
- RESULTADO_DESEADO: {{RESULTADO_DESEADO}} > Business or experience outcome sought
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Scope, technical, or business constraints to respect (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
We are in product discovery and need to open the solution space before jumping to features. A poorly framed problem closes ideation (when too narrow it already contains the solution) or dilutes it (when too broad no one knows what to solve). Reframing the tension as How Might We questions unlocks divergent, actionable ideation centered on the user persona and produces a reusable input for the ideation workshop. The reframe lives before prioritization and before committing to scope: its job is to expand the field, not decide it.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Product Discovery Lead with experience in design thinking, Jobs to Be Done, and discovery workshop facilitation.
Deliverable: a set of 5 to 8 calibrated How Might We questions with their reframing angle and a recommended starting block. Steps:
1. Extract the core problem: separate the observable symptom of TENSION from the job PERSONA_USUARIA is trying to accomplish at MOMENTO_RECORRIDO. Distinguish cause from consequence; if TENSION already names a solution, trace back to the unresolved job that originates it.
2. Name the functional or emotional tension at play and the RESULTADO_DESEADO the reframe must enable. If functional and emotional compete, declare which one the set prioritizes and why.
3. Apply the Goldilocks test to the framing: discard what is too broad (invites vague solutions) and what is too narrow (hides a solution). Calibrate the level: the right framing admits several families of solution without naming any.
4. Generate 5 to 8 How Might We questions, each from a different angle: amplify the positive, remove the negative, explore the opposite, question the assumption, analogy from another domain, change who, change when. Cover at least four different angles before repeating.
5. For each question indicate the angle applied; recommend 1 or 2 questions to start ideation with a brief justification (why they open more space or connect more strongly with RESULTADO_DESEADO).
6. Close with a usage note for the workshop: how to read the set (it is not a ranking) and which question to hold if the group drifts toward premature solutions.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: restate TENSION, PERSONA_USUARIA, MOMENTO_RECORRIDO, and RESULTADO_DESEADO; mark with [SUPUESTO] any data not provided and do not invent context. If TENSION, PERSONA_USUARIA, MOMENTO_RECORRIDO, or RESULTADO_DESEADO are missing, ask for that data before continuing; empty RESTRICCIONES is treated as no declared constraints.
Phase 2 Plan: state the core problem in a sentence and list the reframing angles you will use, in order.
Phase 3 Execute: draft the questions. Rule per question: start with "How might we", name PERSONA_USUARIA, aim at RESULTADO_DESEADO, respect RESTRICCIONES, and do NOT mention any feature or specific solution (no feature names, technology, channel, or mechanism). Keep it to a single focus: one question, one job.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Between 5 and 8 questions, all starting with "How might we".
- [ ] No question contains a hidden feature or solution (Goldilocks test passed); none is so broad it admits any response.
- [ ] Each question names PERSONA_USUARIA and connects with RESULTADO_DESEADO.
- [ ] Each question declares its reframing angle; at least four different angles before repeating, and every repetition is justified.
- [ ] Each question has a single focus (does not chain two problems).
- [ ] Assumptions marked [SUPUESTO]; zero invented data; essential missing inputs requested before generating.
- [ ] 1 or 2 questions recommended to start, with justification.
- [ ] Usage note for the workshop included.
Edge cases: TENSION already contained a solution and was traced back to the unresolved job; functional and emotional tension in conflict resolved with a declared priority; empty RESTRICCIONES = no declared constraints.
Expected deliverable: a numbered list of 5 to 8 How Might We questions with an angle per question, plus a recommended starting block and a usage note, ready to take to the ideation workshop.
spec-producto_jobs_forces_diagram:
[inputs]
- PERFIL_CLIENTE: {{PERFIL_CLIENTE}} > Segment or persona making the switching decision.
- SOLUCION_ACTUAL: {{SOLUCION_ACTUAL}} > Product, tool, or habit the customer uses today (can be "doing nothing" or a spreadsheet).
- SOLUCION_EVALUADA: {{SOLUCION_EVALUADA}} > New product or service being considered for adoption.
- JOB_A_RESOLVER: {{JOB_A_RESOLVER}} > Progress the customer is trying to make, with its functional, emotional, and social dimensions when known.
- EVIDENCIA_DISPONIBLE: {{EVIDENCIA_DISPONIBLE}} > Interviews, verbatim quotes, usage data, or signals that support the analysis (optional).
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments".

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You need to understand why {{PERFIL_CLIENTE}} switches — or does not switch — from {{SOLUCION_ACTUAL}} toward {{SOLUCION_EVALUADA}} to achieve the job {{JOB_A_RESOLVER}}. The Four Forces of Progress model (Bob Moesta and Chris Spiek, within Jobs to be Done) pits the two forces that drive change (push from the current situation, pull of the new solution) against the two that slow it down (anxiety about the new, inertia or habit attachment). Change only happens when push + pull exceed anxiety + inertia. Mapping these forces unlocks concrete product, messaging, and experience levers, and explains why a funnel stalls despite a strong value proposition: almost always the bottleneck is in anxiety or inertia, not in pull.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product researcher specialized in Jobs to be Done and the Four Forces of Progress model by Moesta and Spiek, with experience in switch interviews and value proposition design.
Deliverable: a four-quadrant diagram (structured text) with net balance and actionable levers. Steps:
1. Restate the context: {{PERFIL_CLIENTE}}, {{SOLUCION_ACTUAL}}, {{SOLUCION_EVALUADA}}, and the job {{JOB_A_RESOLVER}}; name the switching moment analyzed (the event that triggers the search).
2. Classify evidence from {{EVIDENCIA_DISPONIBLE}} into the four forces; separate observed facts from inferences and mark anything unverified as [SUPUESTO]. Zero invented figures.
3. For each force (push, pull, anxiety, inertia) list the factors, estimate intensity high/medium/low with justification, and indicate the job dimension it touches (functional, emotional, social).
4. Build the net balance: push + pull versus anxiety + inertia; conclude whether the customer would switch and declare the confidence level based on evidence quality and quantity.
5. Deliver three to five actionable, prioritized levers: amplify push and pull, reduce anxiety and inertia; each tied to a force, to a product/messaging/experience decision, and to the signal that would confirm its effect.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Frame: confirm customer, current solution, evaluated solution, and job; if an essential input is missing, ask for it before continuing.
Phase 2 Classification: place each signal or quote in its force, back it with evidence, and label assumptions; if a signal applies to two forces, assign it to the dominant one and note the secondary.
Phase 3 Intensity and balance: weight each force, resolve the net balance, and declare confidence; distinguish a brake from anxiety (fear of the new, perceived risk) from a brake from inertia (switching cost, habit), because they require different levers.
Phase 4 Levers: translate the balance into prioritized interventions and, at the close, name the most critical evidence gap and the switch interview question that would close it.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- All four forces are present, clearly differentiated, and non-overlapping (push and pull drive; anxiety and inertia brake; anxiety distinguished from inertia).
- Each factor cites evidence from the input or is marked [SUPUESTO]; zero invented figures.
- Each force has intensity (high/medium/low) with explicit justification and associated job dimension.
- The net balance concludes traceably whether the customer switches and declares confidence level.
- Three to five actionable levers, each tied to a force, to a product/messaging/experience decision, and to a validation signal.
- The most critical evidence gap is named along with the switch interview question that would close it.
- Neutral, professional English, no prices.
Expected deliverable: four-quadrant diagram (structured text) with factors, intensity, and dimension per force; net balance verdict with confidence; prioritized lever list; and evidence gap note.
spec-producto_outcome_driven_innovation:
[inputs]
- JOB_FUNCIONAL: {{JOB_FUNCIONAL}} > Main functional job the customer is trying to solve, ideally in verb + object + context syntax
- SEGMENTO_CLIENTE: {{SEGMENTO_CLIENTE}} > Customer segment or archetype executing the job (defines the relevant outcome set)
- CONTEXTO_EJECUCION: {{CONTEXTO_EJECUCION}} > Situation, environment, or constraints under which the job is executed
- DATOS_ENCUESTA: {{DATOS_ENCUESTA}} > Available importance/satisfaction data (sample n, scale, source), or "No data" to estimate and mark as assumption (optional)
- NUM_OUTCOMES: {{NUM_OUTCOMES}} > Target number of outcomes to map, between 15 and 30 (optional, default 20)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You will apply Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) to convert a functional job into a prioritized desired-outcome map. The purpose is to unlock discovery: instead of asking for features, you measure how important and how satisfied the customer is with each outcome they pursue, and reveal the underserved outcomes where innovation opportunity and future product strategy are concentrated. ODI premise: the job is stable over time; solutions change, the customer's success metrics do not. That is why an outcome is measured, never proposed.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product strategist expert in Anthony Ulwick's Outcome-Driven Innovation and in Jobs To Be Done, with practice in quantitative outcomes research and anti-feature discipline.

Deliver a desired-outcome map prioritized by opportunity score. Steps:
1. Frame the functional job in canonical syntax: verb + object + context clarifier. If the input carries an implicit solution, strip it back to the underlying result.
2. Decompose the job into its execution stages (define, locate, prepare, confirm, execute, monitor, modify, conclude) and derive outcomes from each stage. Do not force outcomes into stages the job does not pass through.
3. Write each outcome with ODI structure: direction of improvement (minimize/increase) + metric (time, frequency, probability, number) + object + clarifier. Aim for {{NUM_OUTCOMES}} outcomes (15–30). No solutions, no technologies, no feature names.
4. Assign importance (1–10) and current satisfaction (1–10) to each outcome; use {{DADOS_ENCUESTA}} if available (cite n and source); if not, estimate by stage and mark every figure [SUPUESTO].
5. Calculate the opportunity score: importance + max(importance − satisfaction, 0). Show the calculation for the top 3–5 outcomes.
6. Rank from highest to lowest score and classify into zones: over-served (<10), well-served (10–15), underserved / high opportunity (>15).
7. Present table (outcome | importance | satisfaction | score | zone) + executive reading of the 3–5 underserved outcomes that guide the next cycle, with the strategic implication of each.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: validate that you have the job, segment, and context; if any is missing, ask before proceeding. If {{DATOS_ENCUESTA}} is present, record the scale and n; if it says No data, announce that all measurement will be [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 Job map: decompose the job into stages and list candidate outcomes per stage, without filtering yet.
Phase 3 ODI wording: normalize each outcome to minimize/increase + metric + object + clarifier. Eliminate duplicates and outcomes that are actually disguised solutions.
Phase 4 Measurement: score importance and satisfaction; mark [SUPUESTO] for every figure without real data from {{DATOS_ENCUESTA}}. Maintain scale consistency across comparable outcomes.
Phase 5 Prioritization: calculate opportunity score, rank from highest to lowest, and assign zone with its thresholds.
Phase 6 Synthesis: full table + executive reading of underserved outcomes and their implication for discovery. Close with 1 confidence note: how much of the map rests on assumptions versus real data.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Assumptions and limits:
- Without real data, prioritization is directional, not conclusive; the output signals where to investigate, it does not decide alone.
- One job per run; related jobs are mapped separately to avoid mixing outcome sets.
- The 1–10 scale is kept constant; mixing sources with different scales invalidates comparison.
Edge cases:
- If the job arrives as a solution (e.g., "use an app to..."), reframe it as the underlying result and announce the change.
- If fewer than 15 useful outcomes are available because the job is narrow, indicate this rather than padding with filler.
- If two outcomes tie on score, break the tie by higher importance.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- The job is in verb + object + context syntax, with no mention of solutions.
- There are between 15 and 30 outcomes (or a smaller number is justified), each with direction + metric + object + clarifier and no feature language.
- Each outcome has importance and satisfaction on a 1–10 scale; every estimate without real data is marked [SUPUESTO] and real data cites n/source.
- The opportunity score uses the formula importance + max(importance − satisfaction, 0) and the table is ranked from highest to lowest.
- Zones (over-served <10 / well-served 10–15 / underserved >15) are assigned with their thresholds.
- The executive reading names 3–5 actionable underserved outcomes, each with its strategic implication for the next cycle.
- A confidence note (assumption vs. data) is included and no features are proposed as outcomes.
Expected deliverable: prioritized outcome table + executive reading of underserved opportunities + confidence note, ready to feed the product strategy.
spec-producto_validar_problema_severidad:
[inputs]
- PROBLEMA: {{PROBLEMA}} > Problem or friction detected that needs validating (who it hurts and what the pain is)
- SEGMENTO: {{SEGMENTO}} > Segment or user type experiencing the problem
- EVIDENCIA: {{EVIDENCIA}} > Interviews, analytics, tickets, or available signals ("no evidence yet" if applicable)
- WORKAROUND_ACTUAL: {{WORKAROUND_ACTUAL}} > How they solve the problem today without the product (optional)
- FRECUENCIA_OBSERVADA: {{FRECUENCIA_OBSERVADA}} > How often the problem is observed according to data (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Before investing in designing a solution, you must confirm the problem deserves it. Validating severity and frequency avoids building for lukewarm or anecdotal pains: it separates the problem the user genuinely suffers from often from one they merely mention in passing. The result unlocks a evidence-based investment decision (continue discovery, archive the idea, or keep investigating) and a prioritization criterion defensible to stakeholders, replacing intuition with quantified evidence. Severity and frequency are independent axes: a sharp but rare pain and a mild but constant one require different decisions, and confusing them biases prioritization.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Product Discovery Lead, expert in problem research and evidence-based prioritization (discovery interviews, product analytics, ticket analysis).

Deliverable: a problem validation verdict with an actionable conclusion. Steps:
1. Restate PROBLEMA in one sentence with the structure: who experiences it (SEGMENTO), in what context, what task they are trying to accomplish, and what friction they encounter.
2. Rate SEVERITY on four axes (scale 1 to 5): impact on user outcome, emotional or effort intensity, cost of WORKAROUND_ACTUAL, and consequence of leaving it unresolved. Define each axis in one line so the score is reproducible.
3. Rate FREQUENCY: how often it occurs (supported by FRECUENCIA_OBSERVADA), what percentage of SEGMENTO experiences it, and trend (stable, growing, declining).
4. Cross severity by frequency on a matrix and place the problem in a quadrant; name the quadrant and what it implies.
5. Issue the verdict: continue, archive, or investigate, with its reason traceable to the matrix.
6. List the three pending questions or metrics of greatest value for reducing uncertainty, indicating what decision each one unlocks.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: restate the problem; if PROBLEMA or SEGMENTO are missing, or if EVIDENCIA, WORKAROUND_ACTUAL, or FRECUENCIA_OBSERVADA are needed to support any piece, ask for the data before proceeding.
Phase 2 - Severity: assign the four scores 1 to 5, each justified with cited evidence; mark [SUPUESTO] for every score not backed by data. Calculate aggregated severity (average of the four axes) and name the dominant axis.
Phase 3 - Frequency: estimate recurrence, reach within the segment, and trend; distinguish observed data from estimates [SUPUESTO]. If EVIDENCIA says "no evidence yet", the entire block is [SUPUESTO] and the default verdict leans toward investigate.
Phase 4 - Synthesis: build the severity-frequency matrix (high/low on each axis, threshold severity >=3.5 and frequency recurrent or growing), place the quadrant, derive the verdict, and prioritize the three questions/metrics of greatest uncertainty reduction.
Edge cases: if severity and frequency fall in opposite quadrants (one high, one low) the verdict is investigate, not continue. If most scores are [SUPUESTO], the verdict cannot be a definitive archive: archive is only appropriate with evidence that negates the pain.
Limit: this verdict validates the problem, it does not design or size the solution; it does not estimate build effort.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- The problem is in one sentence with sufferer, context, task, and friction.
- Severity has the four scores 1 to 5, each axis defined and each score with its explicit justification; aggregated severity calculated.
- Frequency distinguishes recurrence, reach within the segment, and trend.
- Every claim without data is marked [SUPUESTO]; evidence-backed claims are cited; observed data and estimates are never mixed.
- The matrix places the problem in an unambiguous quadrant with an explicit threshold.
- The verdict is one of continue/archive/investigate, with a reason traceable to the matrix and consistent with edge cases.
- The three pending questions or metrics are concrete, address the greatest uncertainty, and indicate what decision they unlock.
Expected deliverable: verdict with (1) restated problem, (2) severity table, (3) frequency table, (4) matrix with quadrant, (5) reasoned verdict, (6) three prioritized questions/metrics.
spec-producto_segmentar_jtbd:
[inputs]
- PRODUCTO: {{PRODUCTO}} > Product, service, or category whose market will be re-segmented
- BASE_CLIENTES: {{BASE_CLIENTES}} > Current or interviewed customers with usage evidence (interviews, data, cohorts)
- SENALES_DISPARO: {{SENALES_DISPARO}} > Situations, events, or behaviors that trigger the search for a solution (optional)
- ALTERNATIVAS_ACTUALES: {{ALTERNATIVAS_ACTUALES}} > Solutions, workarounds, or non-consumption that customers hire today (optional)
- OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO: {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} > Decision this segmentation must enable (prioritize roadmap, position, expand)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Demographic segmentation groups customers who look alike but buy for different reasons, which dilutes the roadmap and the message. Re-segmenting by jobs to be done reveals groups that share a sought progress and a common trigger, making discovery actionable. This unlocks product prioritization where the opportunity is real (important job, poorly solved) and positioning against the true competition: what the customer hires today, including non-consumption. A job is stable over time; the solution that resolves it changes. Business objective: {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} for {{PRODUCTO}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product strategist specialized in Jobs to be Done, trained in Clayton Christensen's framework and Anthony Ulwick's outcome-driven innovation.
Deliver a jobs-based segmentation of {{PRODUCTO}} starting from {{BASE_CLIENTES}}:
1. Articulate the jobs in the format when [situation], I want [progress verb], in order to [outcome]; separate the main job from related, emotional, and social jobs, and distinguish the job (stable) from the solution (changing).
2. Group customers into segments defined by a shared job and a shared trigger context; name each segment by its job, never by demographics or firmographics. A customer may appear in more than one segment if they hire the product for different jobs: record this and do not force exclusivity.
3. For each segment, map the trigger (from {{SENALES_DISPARO}}), solutions hired today with workarounds and non-consumption (from {{ALTERNATIVAS_ACTUALES}}), struggle or friction, and success metrics the customer uses to judge progress.
4. Prioritize with the opportunity score (job importance + dissatisfaction gap); declare the scale used (e.g., 1–10 per dimension) and flag over-served and underserved segments, aligned to {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}}.
5. Recommend where to start and formulate a falsifiable hypothesis per segment with its decision criterion (what evidence would confirm or discard the bet).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Articulate: extract progress verbs from evidence; distinguish job (stable) from solution (changing). Phase 2 Group: cluster by job + trigger, not by customer attributes; allow overlaps and record evidence density per segment. Phase 3 Map: complete trigger, alternatives, struggle, and metrics; where evidence is missing, ask and mark [SUPUESTO]. Phase 4 Prioritize: calculate opportunity by segment, declare the scale and rank; distinguish over-served (over-investing yields diminishing returns) from underserved (real opportunity). Phase 5 Decide: recommendation and one testable hypothesis per segment with decision criterion. Edge cases: if evidence is scarce for a segment, mark it as provisional and propose the validation question before issuing a firm score; if two jobs collapse into the same trigger and progress, merge them. Do not invent customer data or cite external figures without backing.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Each segment is named by its job, not by demographics or firmographics.
- Each job follows the when/want/in-order-to structure and separates functional from emotional and social.
- Job (stable) and solution (changing) are explicitly differentiated.
- Current alternatives include workarounds and non-consumption, not only direct competitors.
- The opportunity score combines importance and dissatisfaction, declares its scale, and justifies the ranking.
- Over-served and underserved segments are flagged with their implication for {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}}.
- Every unprovided data point is marked [SUPUESTO] or converted into a question; no customer data is invented.
- Each segment closes with customer success metrics and a falsifiable hypothesis with decision criterion.
Deliverable: segment-by-job table (job | trigger | current alternatives | struggle | success metrics | opportunity score | evidence density), prioritized recommendation of where to start, and falsifiable hypothesis per segment with its decision criterion.
spec-producto_definir_anti_personas:
[inputs]
- PRODUCTO: {{PRODUCTO}} > Product or service to focus (name and one line on what it does)
- PROPUESTA_VALOR: {{PROPUESTA_VALOR}} > Core value proposition and problem it solves
- USUARIO_OBJETIVO: {{USUARIO_OBJETIVO}} > Segment or persona the product DOES serve
- SENALES_ACTUALES: {{SENALES_ACTUALES}} > Observed tensions: misfit customers, out-of-scope requests, churn, disproportionate support (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Defining whom the product deliberately does NOT serve is a focus decision as strategic as choosing whom it does serve. Without explicit anti-personas, the roadmap dilutes by attending noisy profiles, positioning becomes generic, and prioritization yields to the customer who asks most even when they fit least. Opposite risk: over-excluding and killing a legitimate adjacent segment. Clarifying anti-personas, non-target users, and the gray zone unlocks faster decisions in discovery, commercial qualification, and backlog, and protects value proposition coherence without amputating real opportunity.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Product Strategist with experience in market discovery and JTBD segmentation, who has focused portfolios by actively deciding whom not to serve.

Deliverable: a set of anti-personas with actionable exclusion criteria, cost to serve, and focus implications. Steps:
1. Restate PRODUCTO, PROPUESTA_VALOR, and USUARIO_OBJETIVO in one line each to confirm understanding.
2. Distinguish anti-personas (they look like users but you decide not to serve them) from non-target users (out of scope by design), with the axis "could buy or use but should not" vs. "out of scope by design".
3. Build 3 to 5 anti-personas; each with six fields: (a) named and memorable archetype; (b) why they seem to fit but do not; (c) real need and why PRODUCTO does not resolve it well; (d) concrete cost of serving them (focus dilution, product debt, support burden, confused positioning, roadmap bias); (e) observable, early signal in sales, onboarding, support, or adoption; (f) verifiable exclusion criterion as an applicable rule.
4. Document 1 to 2 non-target users in one line each to fix the outer perimeter.
5. Add a gray zone: 1 ambiguous profile you cannot classify with certainty today, with the question or evidence that would resolve it, to avoid premature exclusions.
6. Close with three focus implications: what you stop building; what positioning message you reinforce; what watchdog metric you observe with its alert threshold. Add a review trigger (when to reconsider these exclusions).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm product, value proposition, target user, and signals; if a critical input is missing, ask before continuing.
Phase 2 - Contrast: classify profiles using the axis from step 2; separate what is excluded by decision from what is excluded by design.
Phase 3 - Construction: develop each anti-persona with its six fields, anchoring in SENALES_ACTUALES when they exist and marking inferences as [SUPUESTO].
Phase 4 - Perimeter and gray zone: fix non-target users and declare the ambiguous profile with its resolution criterion.
Phase 5 - Rules and focus: convert each anti-persona into an operable exclusion criterion and synthesize the three implications (stop building / position / watchdog metric) plus the review trigger.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Product, value proposition, and target user restated and confirmed before building.
- [ ] Anti-personas, non-target users, and gray zone clearly differentiated with the declared axis.
- [ ] 3 to 5 anti-personas, each with all six fields complete.
- [ ] Each anti-persona has a verifiable and operable exclusion criterion for discovery, sales, or prioritization.
- [ ] The cost of serving each profile is concrete, not generic, and the observable signal is early.
- [ ] 1 to 2 non-target users and 1 gray zone profile with its resolution criterion.
- [ ] Every inference marked [SUPUESTO]; decisions dependent on missing evidence flagged.
- [ ] Close with three focus implications (stop building / position / watchdog metric with threshold) and review trigger.
Expected deliverable: structured document with anti-persona table or cards, non-target user list, exclusion rules, gray zone, and focus implications block, ready for discovery, commercial qualification, and backlog prioritization.
spec-producto_mapa_competitivo_jtbd:
[inputs]
- PRODUCTO: {{PRODUCTO}} > Product or service whose competitive map is being built
- SEGMENTO_CLIENTE: {{SEGMENTO_CLIENTE}} > Specific customer segment whose perspective is adopted
- JOB_HIPOTESIS: {{JOB_HIPOTESIS}} > Initial hypothesis of the progress the customer seeks
- EVIDENCIA: {{EVIDENCIA}} > Interviews, usage data, or available research ("No evidence" if none) (optional)
- OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO: {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} > Positioning or growth decision the map must inform (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
We are mapping the real competition of {{PRODUCTO}} from the perspective of {{SEGMENTO_CLIENTE}}. The assumption to dismantle is that competition is category-bound: in reality the customer hires something to make progress in a situation, and everything that competes for that progress is competition — including solutions from other categories, DIY solutions, hiring someone else, and non-consumption. Mapping the job rather than the category unlocks positioning against the true competitor, uncovers hidden demand in non-consumption, and avoids the features war trap. Risks to avoid: defining the job too narrowly (ties it to the solution) or too broadly (stops discriminating); confusing the job with a task or a use case; treating the commercial category as the market boundary.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product strategist specialized in Jobs-to-be-Done, trained in Clayton Christensen's framework and Bob Moesta's theory of the forces of progress.
Deliverable: a job-based competitive map, actionable, with a comparative table and positioning implications. Steps:
1. Formulate the job-to-be-done from {{JOB_HIPOTESIS}} in the structure "when [situation], I want to [motivation], so that [expected outcome]" and separate the functional, emotional, and social jobs.
2. List the complete set of alternatives that {{SEGMENTO_CLIENTE}} considers or already uses, across four bands: direct same-category, other-category, DIY or manual, and non-consumption. Flag for each whether it is an observed or considered hire.
3. For each alternative document: progress delivered, hiring reason, push forces, and friction barriers.
4. Build a comparative table against the customer's success criteria (not features); for each criterion indicate which alternative leads today and where {{PRODUTO}} falls short.
5. Apply the four forces of progress (situational push, pull of the new, anxiety about the new, attachment to the current) and identify which one is currently blocking adoption.
6. Deliver three positioning implications aligned with {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}}: which real alternative to position against, what progress to promise, what friction to eliminate. Close with the 3 highest-value discovery questions to falsify the map.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Job framing: convert the hypothesis into a well-formed job and validate that it is stable over time and solution-agnostic. Quick test: if the job names your category or a technology, it is badly formulated; rewrite it.
Phase 2 - Alternatives sweep: think like the customer at the moment of struggle; list everything they have tried or considered, without filtering by category. Explicitly include non-consumption and, where applicable, "hire someone."
Phase 3 - Profile per alternative: progress, reason, push, friction. If a band is empty, declare it as a finding, not an omission.
Phase 4 - Table by customer success criteria and forces synthesis; distinguish functional criteria from emotional/social ones.
Phase 5 - Actionable positioning implications + discovery questions.
Draw on {{EVIDENCIA}} and {{ADJUNTOS}} when available; if not, work from hypotheses. Do not invent data: mark every assumption as [SUPUESTO] with its customer validation path and flag where evidence is weak. No prices or cost descriptions.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- The job is formulated as progress (when-I want-so that), is solution-agnostic, and separates the functional, emotional, and social dimensions.
- All four bands of alternatives are present and non-consumption appears as a full-fledged competitor.
- Each alternative has progress, hiring reason, push forces, and friction barriers.
- The table compares by customer success criteria (not features) and indicates the leader per criterion and where {{PRODUTO}} falls short.
- The four forces of progress are applied to the case and identify the force currently blocking adoption.
- There are three actionable positioning implications tied to {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}}, plus the 3 highest-value discovery questions.
- Every unverified piece of data is marked [SUPUESTO] with a validation path; zero prices.
Expected deliverable: job-based competitive map in structured format (job + four bands with profiles + comparative table + forces synthesis + three implications + discovery questions), ready to take into customer discovery.
spec-producto_pirate_metrics_funnel:
[inputs]
- PRODUTO: {{PRODUTO}} > Name and brief description of the product whose funnel is being diagnosed
- OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO: {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} > Business outcome the diagnosis is pursuing (e.g. raise revenue conversion, reduce effective CAC, improve early retention)
- DADOS_EMBUDO: {{DADOS_EMBUDO}} > Volume and conversion rate stage by stage for the last measurable period; operational definition of each stage; period and data source
- EVENTO_ACTIVACION: {{EVENTO_ACTIVACION}} > Event that counts as the user's 'aha moment' / activation
- CANALES_ADQUISICION: {{CANALES_ADQUISICION}} > Main user acquisition channels, with approximate mix if known (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The growth of {{PRODUTO}} is measured as an AARRR funnel (Dave McClure's Pirate Metrics: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue) and is pursuing {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}}. When overall conversion drops, the reflex is to inject more traffic at the top; almost always the real constraint is a mid-funnel stage that wastes already-paid traffic. This diagnosis unlocks an investment decision: knowing with evidence which stage to intervene in first so that each recovered point carries the maximum number of users through to revenue, rather than spending on acquisition that leaks downstream. A poor reading of the bottleneck costs quarters of misallocated budget.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Head of Growth, specialist in AARRR funnel diagnosis and conversion analytics for digital products.
Deliverable: funnel diagnosis with identified bottleneck, root-cause hypotheses, and prioritized experiments. Steps:
1. If any data from {{DADOS_EMBUDO}} or {{EVENTO_ACTIVACION}} is missing, ask for it before continuing; do not invent figures. Declare the period, source, and definition assumption for each stage.
2. Reconstruct the complete AARRR funnel with absolute volume per stage and pass-through rate between each pair of consecutive stages. If Referral or Revenue do not apply to {{PRODUTO}}'s model, declare it and work the effective funnel of active stages.
3. Calculate the leak per stage through two lenses: percentage drop and lost users in absolute terms.
4. Identify the bottleneck stage using the impact-per-point criterion: which one, by recovering X conversion points, carries the most users through to revenue. Justify why it is not just the lowest isolated rate.
5. Classify the problem as entry volume, traffic quality, or intra-stage friction, citing the data that confirms it or flagging it as [SUPUESTO]. Use {{CANALES_ADQUISICION}} to discriminate quality vs. friction when applicable.
6. Deliver 3 root-cause hypotheses ranked by evidence and 3 experiments for the bottleneck stage, each with a success metric, a decision threshold (advance / pivot / discard), and relative effort if estimable.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: validate stage definitions and the activation event; declare the period and source; warn if volume or time window makes the reading statistically weak; flag stages with ambiguous definitions or double-counting risk before calculating.
Phase 2 - Reconstruction: build the funnel table (volume, pass-through rate, percentage leak, absolute leak) using only provided data; anything not supported goes as [SUPUESTO].
Phase 3 - Diagnosis: apply impact-per-point to isolate the bottleneck and classify its nature (volume / quality / friction); if two stages tie on impact, prioritize the one closest to revenue and explain why.
Phase 4 - Action: derive 3 hypotheses ranked by evidence and 3 experiments with metric, decision threshold, and relative effort; close with a single prioritized intervention recommendation and the trade-off it assumes relative to the second option.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The funnel covers the active AARRR stages with absolute volume and pass-through rate between consecutive stages; inapplicable ones are declared.
- [ ] The leak is reported as both percentage and absolute lost users per stage.
- [ ] The bottleneck is justified using the impact-per-point criterion, not the lowest isolated rate; ties resolved by proximity to revenue.
- [ ] The problem is classified as volume / quality / friction, with the confirming data or marked [SUPUESTO].
- [ ] There are 3 hypotheses ranked by evidence and 3 experiments, each with a success metric and a decision threshold (advance / pivot / discard).
- [ ] A warning is given if the period or volume compromises the statistical reliability of the reading.
- [ ] No invented figures; missing data is requested or declared as a range; no prices.
Expected deliverable: AARRR funnel table + classified bottleneck stage + 3 hypotheses + 3 experiments with threshold + a single recommendation of where to intervene first with its trade-off.
spec-producto_modelo_aha_onboarding:
[inputs]
- PRODUTO: {{PRODUTO}} > What the product is, what problem it solves, and what platform it lives on (web, mobile, desktop, API)
- USUARIO_NOVO: {{USUARIO_NOVO}} > Profile of the user who signs up for the first time (role, context, intended use, urgency level)
- EVENTO_DE_VALOR: {{EVENTO_DE_VALOR}} > Concrete action you believe represents the first perceived value / aha moment (optional)
- FRICCION_CONOCIDA: {{FRICCION_CONOCIDA}} > Steps, forms, or waits you suspect cause abandonment today (optional)
- METRICA_ACTIVACION: {{METRICA_ACTIVACION}} > How you currently measure that a user is activated, if it exists (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The new user signs up but abandons before experiencing the product's real value. Every extra step, every form field, and every empty state between sign-up and the first perceived value is a drop-off point. Redesigning onboarding toward the aha moment shortens time-to-value, raises activation, and unlocks early retention: whoever lives the aha quickly stays; whoever does not, leaves silently. The goal is an actionable redesign of the journey with triggers and measurement — not a generic diagnosis or a list of best practices.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Product Growth leader specializing in activation and onboarding, with experience measuring time-to-value and designing aha moments in digital products.

Deliverable: onboarding redesign with the aha moment defined, current journey, target journey, triggers, and measurement plan. Steps:
1. Define the aha moment as a concrete, observable, and measurable action that best predicts retention (criterion: action that correlates with retention, not the flashiest feature). Express it with an operational threshold: what action, how many times, in what time window. If EVENTO_DE_VALOR is unclear or lacks evidence, propose 2–3 candidates and the data criterion for validating which one wins.
2. Map USUARIO_NOVO's current journey from sign-up to the aha, step by step, noting friction, cognitive effort, and probability of abandonment at each step; integrate FRICCION_CONOCIDA and flag the highest estimated drop-off step.
3. Design the target journey with reduce-reorder-reinforce: eliminate dispensable steps and justify each elimination, reorder the essentials along the shortest path to the aha, and specify at least one trigger per critical transition (message, empty state with pre-loaded example, smart default, visible progress, celebration of the first milestone). Defer until after the aha every step that is not a blocker (verification, full profile, invite team).
4. Deliver the measurement plan: define the activation metric with its threshold, compare step count before vs. after, declare the baseline, and formulate a verifiable hypothesis for an experiment.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Aha definition: translate the product's value into a single, measurable event with a threshold; discard vanity proxies (registration completed, tour viewed) that do not predict retention.
Phase 2 - Journey diagnosis: reconstruct the real flow step by step and quantify friction where possible; mark [SUPUESTO] when data is missing rather than inventing it.
Phase 3 - Redesign: apply reduce-reorder-reinforce; each elimination carries its reason and each critical transition its trigger.
Phase 4 - Measurement: close with the activation metric, step-count baseline, and a hypothesis ready to experiment (variable you change, metric you move, expected magnitude, horizon, and population).
Edge cases: if the product requires technical setup or external data before the aha (integrations, importing data), separate time-to-first-action from time-to-value and design an interim progress state. If there are multiple USUARIO_NOVO profiles with different ahas, prioritize one and name the others as variants to iterate.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
