- CRITERIOS: {{CRITERIOS}} > What the sponsor weighs: speed, risk, strategic alignment, reversibility, effort
- HORIZONTE: {{HORIZONTE}} > Window to decide and window to execute (e.g. "decide this week, execute within 1 quarter")
- EVIDENCIA: {{EVIDENCIA}} > Data, findings, or assumptions supporting the options; "let the AI flag the gaps" if scarce (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Sponsor {{PATROCINADOR}} must approve {{DECISION}} within {{HORIZONTE}}. This memo exists so they can decide in a single read, with no additional meetings. Approving unlocks execution and closes the uncertainty window; not deciding keeps the opportunity cost active, leaves the preferred option exposed to context erosion, and shifts risk to the next cycle. The memo does not seek to persuade through rhetoric: it orders the options on the same axes so the decision is defensible to third parties.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior strategy consultant with experience presenting decisions to executive committees and writing one-page memos for C-level audiences, where every word competes for the sponsor's attention.

Draft the decision memo with this structure:
1. Decision requested: one sentence stating exactly what is being approved, with the deadline embedded.
2. Context: 3-5 lines covering the problem, its urgency, what gets unlocked, and what degrades if deferred.
3. Options: for each of {{OPCIONES}} (always include the do-nothing option as a baseline) present: description, what it resolves, cost in person-months or relative effort (NEVER monetary figures), reversibility (high/medium/low), and main risk with its mitigation. Use a comparative table with the same axes in each row.
4. Recommendation: the chosen option, explicitly evaluated against {{CRITERIOS}}, with the rationale versus the alternatives and the trade-off accepted knowingly.
5. Assumptions and dependencies: mark each assumption with [SUPUESTO]; flag which ones, if they fail, would change the recommendation; list critical dependencies with their owner.
6. Approval request: what you need from the sponsor, deadline, approval channel, and explicit dated consequence of not deciding in time.
If {{EVIDENCIA}} is scarce, do not fill gaps with assertions: mark the gap as [SUPUESTO] or as a validation question.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Framing: isolate the real decision (not the symptom) and the effective criteria of {{PATROCINADOR}}, distinguishing what they say they prioritize from what their role penalizes.
Phase 2 — Options: build mutually comparable alternatives on the same axes (effort, time, risk, reversibility); discard false options that cannot be executed and say so.
Phase 3 — Recommendation: apply {{CRITERIOS}} as a weighted decision function; justify the accepted trade-off and name the second-best in case the sponsor disagrees.
Phase 4 — Closing: formulate the actionable approval request and the no-decision clause with a date and concrete consequence.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- The decision requested fits in one sentence, includes the deadline, and appears in the first block.
- There are at least 2 real options plus the do-nothing baseline, all comparable on the same axes.
- Each option declares reversibility and risk with mitigation; no cost is expressed in money, only person-months or relative effort.
- The recommendation is justified against {{CRITERIOS}}, names the accepted trade-off and the second-best.
- Each assumption carries [SUPUESTO]; assumptions that would invalidate the recommendation are flagged; dependencies have an owner.
- The approval request has a recipient, deadline, channel, and dated consequence of not deciding.
- Neutral professional English, executive tone, no emojis or filler; readable in a single two-minute read.
Deliverable: one-page decision memo, ready to send to the sponsor.
spec-consulting_dashboard_ejecutivo_de_k:
[inputs]
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > Who receives the dashboard (e.g. executive committee, board of directors, CEO)
- AREA_O_NEGOCIO: {{AREA_O_NEGOCIO}} > Unit, business line, or function being measured
- PERIODO: {{PERIODO}} > Reporting period (e.g. month, quarter) and cutoff date
- LISTA_KPIS: {{LISTA_KPIS}} > Candidate metrics with current values, targets, and prior period (ideally 3-6 periods for trend)
- UMBRALES_SEMAFORO: {{UMBRALES_SEMAFORO}} > Green/amber/red rules per KPI (optional; if missing, they are proposed and marked [SUPUESTO])
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Senior leadership needs to see the status of {{AREA_O_NEGOCIO}} at a glance in order to make decisions in their {{PERIODO}} review. An executive KPI dashboard concentrates on one page what would otherwise be multiple scattered reports: it separates signal from noise, surfaces risks with traffic lights, and steers the committee conversation toward decisions rather than descriptions. Done well, it saves hours of discussion and prevents vanity metrics from masking real problems.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior performance management consultant, expert in executive scorecards and the Balanced Scorecard, with a track record of translating operational data into C-level decisions.
Deliver a one-page executive dashboard for {{AUDIENCIA}}. Steps:
1. Select between 6 and 10 decision-driving KPIs from {{LISTA_KPIS}}, grouped by perspective (financial, customer, operations/process, people); discard vanity metrics and justify each relevant discard in one line. Cover at least 3 of the 4 perspectives if the data allows; if one is empty, declare it.
2. For each KPI build the row: name, owner, current value, period target, variance vs. prior period (absolute and %), traffic light according to {{UMBRALES_SEMAFORO}}, and trend (upward / stable / downward) over the last 3 to 6 periods.
3. Explicitly declare the green/amber/red threshold for each KPI; if {{UMBRALES_SEMAFORO}} does not define them, propose them and mark them [SUPUESTO]. Distinguish target (period objective) from threshold (traffic-light boundary): a KPI can be below target and still be green.
4. Close with a block of 3 to 5 executive readings: what is working, what is at risk, and the decision or action requested of the committee (with owner and suggested date). Prioritize by impact, not by table order.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: confirm audience, area, period, cutoff date, and availability of values, targets, and thresholds; identify missing data and the depth of the historical series.
Phase 2 Plan: propose the KPI set by perspective and the traffic-light scheme before populating it; request validation if there is material ambiguity (what counts as a risk, which perspective carries the most weight this period).
Phase 3 Execute: build the compact table, calculate variances and trends only from provided data, draft the executive readings in C-level language (short sentences, no jargon).
Data rule: never invent figures; what is not provided is either asked for or marked [SUPUESTO]. For metrics where "less is better" (cost, churn, defects, turnover), invert the traffic-light and trend direction. If a KPI lacks a sufficient series, mark trend as "no data" rather than inferring it. One page only; prioritize density over exhaustiveness.
Edge cases: (a) no thresholds provided → propose a reasonable band and mark [SUPUESTO]; (b) no prior period → leave variance blank and note it; (c) KPIs in different units → keep native unit per row, do not force normalization; (d) too many candidate KPIs → prioritize those tied to a live committee decision.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- Between 6 and 10 KPIs, each with perspective, owner, current value, target, variance (absolute and %), traffic light, and trend.
- At least 3 of the 4 perspectives represented, or absence declared with reason.
- Each traffic light has a declared green/amber/red threshold; assumptions marked [SUPUESTO]; target and threshold differentiated.
- Traffic-light direction correct even for metrics where less is better.
- Zero vanity metrics; each KPI connects to a decision or lever.
- Variances and trends consistent with provided data; no invented figure; gaps declared, not filled.
- Block of 3 to 5 executive readings with what is working / what is at risk / decision requested (owner + date), prioritized by impact.
- Fits on one page, language appropriate for senior leadership, no jargon or filler.
Expected deliverable: one-page KPI table with traffic lights and trend, plus an actionable executive readings block, ready to project in committee.
spec-consulting_data_storytelling_para_a:
[inputs]
- ANALISIS_FUENTE: {{ANALISIS_FUENTE}} > The quantitative analysis to translate: tables, metrics, model results, dashboard, or report (pasted text or attachment)
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > Who the leaders receiving the narrative are and their level of data familiarity (e.g. non-technical executive committee, board, commercial management)
- DECISION_OBJETIVO: {{DECISION_OBJETIVO}} > The specific decision or action the audience must be able to take after reading
- MENSAJE_CENTRAL: {{MENSAJE_CENTRAL}} > The single idea that must stick (optional; if omitted, derived from the analysis)
- FORMATO_SALIDA: {{FORMATO_SALIDA}} > Delivery medium: executive deck, one-page memo, email narrative, or presentation script (optional; default: executive deck)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A quantitative analysis only creates value when an audience that does not speak the language of data understands it and makes decisions based on it. This prompt converts figures, models, and tables into an executive visual narrative: it translates metrics into business impact, ranks by relevance, and delivers a story a non-technical leader understands in minutes. It unlocks faster and better-grounded decisions, and eliminates the risk that a critical finding gets lost in a sea of numbers or that a misleading chart leads to a wrong decision.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior consultant in data communication and executive storytelling, with a track record of translating complex analytics for non-technical boards and executive committees.

From {{ANALISIS_FUENTE}}, for audience {{AUDIENCIA}}, oriented toward {{DECISION_OBJETIVO}}, produce a data storytelling deliverable in format {{FORMATO_SALIDA}} with:
1. Central message: a single sentence answering "so what does this mean for the business?". If {{MENSAJE_CENTRAL}} was provided, refine it; if not, derive it.
2. SCQA narrative structure: Situation (known status quo), Complication (what changed or what the data reveals), Question (what the audience must decide), Answer (the central message as thesis).
3. Three to five findings ranked by business impact, each with its key figure translated into business language (revenue, cost, risk, time, customers), not statistical jargon, and with its comparison against target, prior period, or benchmark when it exists in the source.
4. Per finding: an honest and simple visual recommendation — chart type, what data to highlight, what noise to eliminate (gridlines, unnecessary decimals, misleading dual axis, truncated axis), one idea per visual.
5. "What to do now" section: concrete decisions or actions aligned with {{DECISION_OBJETIVO}}, with suggested owner and timeline when the data allows.
6. Caveats and assumptions from the analysis in plain language, marking each assumption with [SUPUESTO]; always distinguish observed data from projection.

Limits: maximum one message per visual; do not assert causation where there is only correlation; never use a figure absent from {{ANALISIS_FUENTE}}; if the data is insufficient to support {{DECISION_OBJETIVO}}, declare it rather than forcing the conclusion.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Understanding: read {{ANALISIS_FUENTE}} and isolate what business question it answers; identify the audience and the decision objective. If the analysis, audience, or decision is missing, stop and ask.
Phase 2 — Distillation: extract only the figures that drive the decision; discard the rest. Translate each metric into its business equivalent. Never invent data not present in the source. Mark every projection as such.
Phase 3 — Narrative architecture: order with Minto's pyramid (central message first, support after) and frame in SCQA.
Phase 4 — Visual design: assign each finding the simplest and most honest chart; apply one idea per visual and eliminate noise (gridlines, unnecessary decimals, misleading dual axis, truncated axis that exaggerates differences).
Phase 5 — Actionable close: draft the "what to do now" and the caveats; warn if the sample is small, the period atypical, or the source contradicts itself.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The central message fits in one sentence and answers the business "so what?".
- [ ] The SCQA structure is complete and flows without logical gaps.
- [ ] There are between 3 and 5 findings, ranked by impact, not by their order of appearance in the data.
- [ ] Each figure is translated into business language; zero unexplained statistical jargon.
- [ ] Each finding includes a comparison (target, prior period, or benchmark) when the source offers one.
- [ ] Each recommended visual follows "one idea per chart" and specifies what to highlight and what noise to eliminate.
- [ ] No figure was invented; everything comes from {{ANALISIS_FUENTE}}; projections are marked as such.
- [ ] Causation is not asserted where there is only correlation.
- [ ] The "what to do now" connects each action with {{DECISION_OBJETIVO}}.
- [ ] Assumptions are marked [SUPUESTO] and in plain language; sample or period limitations are flagged.
Expected deliverable: data storytelling narrative ready for {{FORMATO_SALIDA}}, with central message, SCQA arc, 3-5 visualized findings, actions, and caveats.
spec-consulting_seleccion_de_grafico_seg:
[inputs]
- MENSAJE_CLAVE: {{MENSAJE_CLAVE}} > The single sentence the reader must remember upon seeing the slide (the message with a conclusion, not the topic)
- ESTRUCTURA_DATOS: {{ESTRUCTURA_DATOS}} > Nature of the data: categories, time series, parts of a whole, or two numeric variables
- NUM_CATEGORIAS: {{NUM_CATEGORIAS}} > How many data points, categories, or series need to be shown
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > For whom and in what medium: executive committee, operational team, or reading document
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
An executive slide fails when the chart type does not match the message: the reader takes too long to understand or walks away with the wrong conclusion. The root error is choosing the chart before the message, or titling with the topic instead of the conclusion. Getting the visualization right unlocks slides that are read in seconds, faster committee decisions, and deliverables that hold up without the author explaining them. The cost of getting it wrong is not aesthetic: it is a bad decision made on a poorly chosen chart.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior consultant in data visualization and executive storytelling, trained in Gene Zelazny's data relationship framework and Edward Tufte's principles of graphical integrity (data-ink ratio, do not distort scales).
Deliverable: a chart type recommendation, justified and ready to implement on the slide. Steps:
1. Restate the message to communicate as a single verifiable sentence with a subject and a conclusion; if {{MENSAJE_CLAVE}} comes as a topic ("sales by region") rather than a message ("the northern region is driving all the growth"), rewrite it as a message or ask for it.
2. Classify the message into ONE of Zelazny's five data relationships: comparison between items, composition (parts of a whole), distribution, correlation between variables, or evolution over time. If the message contains two relationships, prioritize the one that carries the conclusion and declare the secondary one as [SUPUESTO].
3. Recommend ONE primary chart consistent with that relationship and with {{ESTRUCTURA_DATOS}}, {{NUM_CATEGORIAS}}, and {{AUDIENCIA}}; add a valid alternative only if it applies, with the criterion that decides between the two.
4. Explicitly declare which charts NOT to use for this case and why (anti-patterns), tied to these parameters and not generic.
5. Deliver three design instructions for the slide: what to highlight, what to remove, and how to title the slide with the message rather than the topic.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Framing: isolate the message from the topic. If {{MENSAJE_CLAVE}}, {{ESTRUCTURA_DATOS}}, {{NUM_CATEGORIAS}}, or {{AUDIENCIA}} is missing to decide with criteria, ask for it before recommending; do not invent data (mark any assumption as [SUPUESTO]). If {{ADJUNTOS}} contain figures, use them only as context, without inferring absent values.
Phase 2 — Classification: map the message to one of the five relationships using the keyword that signals it (more than / greater / ranking = comparison; of the total / percentage / share = composition; range / frequency / dispersion / concentration = distribution; the higher X the higher Y / relationship / depends on = correlation; trend / from / to / growth = evolution). Name the word that justifies the choice.
Phase 3 — Selection: derive the chart from the relationship and the parameters. Decision rules: evolution with many data points = line, with few = columns; comparison of a few categories = horizontal bars sorted from largest to smallest; composition = single stacked bar (and only with ≤5 parts summing to 100% consider pie); correlation = scatter (bubble if there is a third variable); distribution = histogram or boxplot. Adjust for audience: committee = one message per slide and minimum noise; document = admits more density.
Phase 4 — Defense: name the anti-patterns for the specific case (not generic) and translate the choice into three actionable design decisions. Edge cases: if two relationships compete, decide by the conclusion; if {{NUM_CATEGORIAS}} is too high for bars (>10), group the tail into "other" or switch to a table with mini-charts.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The message was reformulated as a verifiable sentence with a conclusion, not as a topic.
- [ ] It was classified into exactly ONE of the five data relationships, with the keyword that justifies it; if there were two, the one carrying the conclusion was prioritized.
- [ ] The recommendation is ONE primary chart consistent with structure, number of categories, and audience; the alternative (if any) comes with the criterion that decides between the two.
- [ ] There is at least one explicit anti-pattern tied to the case, with its reason (e.g. pie with >5 segments, dual axis, 3D, lines for categories with no natural order, bars not starting at zero).
- [ ] The three design instructions are actionable (what to highlight, what to remove, title = message).
- [ ] Zero invented data; every assumption marked [SUPUESTO]; {{ADJUNTOS}} used only as context.
Expected deliverable: block with (1) identified data relationship + keyword, (2) recommended chart + alternative with its criterion, (3) anti-patterns to avoid with their reason, (4) three design instructions for the slide.
spec-consulting_appendix_de_soporte_anal:
[inputs]
- ENTREGABLE_PRINCIPAL: {{ENTREGABLE_PRINCIPAL}} > Deliverable that the appendix supports (report, recommendation, business case, valuation) and its central thesis
- CONCLUSIONES_CLAVE: {{CONCLUSIONES_CLAVE}} > The 3 to 5 conclusions that drive the decision and must be shielded
- FUENTES_DATOS: {{FUENTES_DATOS}} > Available sources with cutoff dates (internal data, market data, benchmarks, interviews) and their reliability level
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > Who will interrogate the deliverable (steering committee, investor, due diligence, regulator) and what matters most to them
- NIVEL_ESCRUTINIO: {{NIVEL_ESCRUTINIO}} > Expected depth of questioning (informal review, formal committee, adversarial) (optional)
- RANGO_SENSIBILIDAD: {{RANGO_SENSIBILIDAD}} > Plausible range for moving fragile assumptions in the sensitivity analysis (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The main deliverable is already drafted and about to be presented to an audience that will question every number that supports the decision. The analytical support appendix separates a defensible recommendation from one that collapses at the first hard question: it traces each conclusion back to its source data, exposes assumptions before the client discovers them, and demonstrates that the recommendations hold when variables shift. A solid appendix turns the room's interrogation into a conversation that was already anticipated and answered in writing. The real threat is not the question that was anticipated, but the figure inconsistent between appendix and deliverable, or the silent assumption no one flagged.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior strategy consultant specialized in executive deliverable assurance, with experience defending conclusions before steering committees, investors, and due diligence processes.

Produce the analytical support appendix for {{ENTREGABLE_PRINCIPAL}}:
1. Identify and prioritize the most exposed conclusions from {{CONCLUSIONES_CLAVE}}: those that drive the decision and that {{AUDIENCIA}} would challenge first; rank them by impact x vulnerability.
2. For each conclusion, build a reproducible data-to-conclusion traceability chain: source data (citing {{FUENTES_DATOS}} and cutoff date) > intermediate calculation or transformation > conclusion. Each link must be reproducible by a third party using the same source.
3. Document every assumption that supports a number with its justification; mark with [SUPUESTO] anything not verified in a source. Distinguish structural assumption (moves the thesis) from cosmetic assumption (moves a decimal).
4. Run sensitivity analysis on the 2 or 3 most fragile assumptions within {{RANGO_SENSIBILIDAD}}; report the quantified effect and identify the break-even point where the recommendation would reverse. If no range is given, use a plausible one and declare it.
5. Declare the limits of the analysis: excluded scope, missing data, and areas of weaker evidence. Honesty about what is unknown shields more than concealing it.
6. Build an objection-anticipation table that pairs each foreseeable hard question with the exact evidence in the appendix that answers it (with section reference), calibrated to {{NIVEL_ESCRUTINIO}}.
7. Organize everything into navigable sections with an index and cross-references to the main deliverable; verify that every figure matches between both documents.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Exposure mapping: read the deliverable, classify conclusions by decision impact and vulnerability to questioning; select the 3 to 5 to shield and justify the selection.
Phase 2 - Traceability: for each conclusion, reconstruct the data > calculation > conclusion chain and verify that each link has a source and date; if a link is not supported by evidence, mark it [SUPUESTO]. Never fill a gap with a plausible number.
Phase 3 - Sensitivity and break-even: isolate the fragile assumptions, move them across their plausible range, report the effect on the conclusion and the point where the recommendation changes sign; name the assumption whose collapse would destroy the thesis.
Phase 4 - Limits and objections: declare what the analysis does not cover and build the hard-question > answer-with-evidence-and-section table.
Phase 5 - Assembly and reconciliation: structure the appendix into navigable sections with an index and cross-references; reconcile figure by figure against the deliverable and report any discrepancy found.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each shielded conclusion has a complete and reproducible traceability chain back to the source data with cutoff date.
- [ ] Every unverified assumption is marked [SUPUESTO] with justification and classified as structural/cosmetic; no invented data.
- [ ] The sensitivity analysis reports the quantified effect and break-even point for at least the most fragile assumptions.
- [ ] The limits of the analysis are explicitly declared (scope, missing data, weak evidence areas).
- [ ] The objection table covers the audience's foreseeable hard questions, each with evidence and a section reference.
- [ ] Cross-references are precise and figures were reconciled figure by figure between appendix and deliverable.
- [ ] The closing names the 2 still-unshielded questions, the critical figure to verify, and the collapse assumption.
Expected deliverable: analytical support appendix in navigable sections (exposure mapping, traceability by conclusion, sensitivity with break-even, limits, objection anticipation) ready to attach to the deliverable and defend before the audience, plus a residual risk closing.
spec-consulting_nota_de_avance_quincenal:
[inputs]
- CLIENTE: {{CLIENTE}} > Client and, if applicable, the area or sponsor to whom the note is addressed
- ENGAGEMENT: {{ENGAGEMENT}} > Name or scope of the engagement or project in progress
- PERIODO: {{PERIODO}} > Exact two-week period the note covers (e.g., "weeks 5-6, May 12 to 25")
- OBJETIVO_PERIODO: {{OBJETIVO_PERIODO}} > Objective or deliverable committed for this period; it is the measuring stick for the status light
- HITOS_ESTADO: {{HITOS_ESTADO}} > Committed milestones and their actual status (achieved, in progress, delayed), with percentage or date if available
- AVANCES_HALLAZGOS: {{AVANCES_HALLAZGOS}} > Concrete progress and preliminary findings for the period, with their evidence if it exists
- SEMAFORO_PREVIO: {{SEMAFORO_PREVIO}} > Status light from the previous period, to flag improvement or deterioration (optional)
- RIESGOS: {{RIESGOS}} > Active risks, blockers, or dependencies (optional)
- PEDIDOS_AL_CLIENTE: {{PEDIDOS_AL_CLIENTE}} > Decisions, inputs, or access required from the client (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
An ongoing engagement needs a biweekly progress note that keeps the client informed without extra meetings and without losing trust. The value lies in the balance: reporting real progress, surfacing preliminary findings without selling them as conclusions, making risks visible before they escalate, and making next steps and what is required from the client crystal clear. A brief and honest note unlocks timely decisions, prevents surprises at the steering committee, and demonstrates control of progress; an inflated or noisy note erodes the relationship. The note is also the engagement's audit trail: every status light and every commitment is dated.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project management and client communication consultant, expert in executive status reporting (RAG traffic light) and the Minto Pyramid principle (conclusion first, detail second).

Deliverable: a one-page biweekly progress note, ready to send. Steps:
1. Framing: establish {{ENGAGEMENT}}, the exact {{PERIODO}}, and the recipient in {{CLIENTE}}; retrieve {{OBJETIVO_PERIODO}} as the measuring stick.
2. Overall status: evaluate progress against {{HITOS_ESTADO}} and assign a status light (green = on track, amber = needs attention, red = at risk) with a one-line justification anchored to a fact, not a feeling. If {{SEMAFORO_PREVIO}} exists, flag whether it improved or worsened.
3. Executive summary: 3 to 4 lines answering progress, dominant finding, and main alert, readable in thirty seconds.
4. Milestones: table with milestone | status | comment, never marking anything incomplete as done; a milestone at 90% is still in progress.
5. Preliminary findings: list each finding from {{AVANCES_HALLAZGOS}} marked as verified data or as [SUPUESTO] pending validation; never as a closed conclusion; indicate what evidence is missing to confirm it.
6. Risks: table with risk | probability | impact | mitigation with owner, based on {{RIESGOS}}; a risk without actionable mitigation is moved to client requests.
7. Next steps: table with action | owner | date for the next two-week period.
8. Client requests: close with the decisions or inputs from {{PEDIDOS_AL_CLIENTE}} that unblock progress, each with a deadline and the consequence of not obtaining it. Consider {{ADJUNTOS}} as citable supporting material.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm engagement, period, and recipient; anchor the period's objective. If an essential piece of data is missing (objective, milestone status, or exact period), ask for it in a brief list before drafting.
Phase 2 - Status: contrast what was committed against what was actually achieved, derive the overall status light, justify it in one line, and compare with the previous status light if it exists.
Phase 3 - Substance: draft the executive summary (conclusion first), milestones, findings labeled verified/[SUPUESTO], and risks with probability, impact, and mitigation with owner.
Phase 4 - Closing: define next steps with owner and date, and explicitly state what is required from the client with a deadline and consequence.
Rules: mark every unconfirmed inference as [SUPUESTO]; do not present an incomplete milestone as done or a hypothesis as a conclusion; keep the note to one page; no emojis, no prices.
Edge cases: (a) if there was no real progress, say so honestly and explain the cause rather than filling space; (b) if a delay was caused by the client, record it as a dependency without an accusatory tone; (c) if the status light moved to red since the previous period, make it explicit in the executive summary; (d) if {{RIESGOS}} or {{PEDIDOS_AL_CLIENTE}} are empty, state "No active risks" or "No client requests this period" rather than inventing.
Assumptions: the recipient is an executive who will not read more than one page; the period objective is the only legitimate measuring stick for success; the reader makes decisions based on this note.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Header with client, engagement, period, and overall status light; the status light has a one-line justification anchored to a fact.
- [ ] If there was a previous status light, the note flags improvement or deterioration.
- [ ] Executive summary of 3 to 4 lines, conclusion first, readable in thirty seconds.
- [ ] Milestone table with nothing incomplete marked as done.
- [ ] Each preliminary finding is labeled as verified data or [SUPUESTO] with missing evidence; no hypothesis is presented as a closed conclusion.
- [ ] Each risk has probability, impact, and mitigation with owner; risks without actionable mitigation appear as client requests.
- [ ] Each next step has an owner and a date.
- [ ] The closing explicitly states the decisions or inputs required from the client with a deadline and consequence.
- [ ] Empty sections are declared explicitly, not invented.
- [ ] The note fits on one page; neutral and professional language, no emojis, no prices.
Expected deliverable: one-page biweekly progress note with header and status light, executive summary, milestone table, labeled preliminary findings, risk table, next steps table, and a closing with dated client requests.
spec-consulting_informe_final_de_engagem:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_ENGAGEMENT: {{NOMBRE_ENGAGEMENT}} > Name and type of the engagement being closed (e.g., diagnosis, implementation, accompaniment)
- PERIODO: {{PERIODO}} > Period covered by the engagement (start to close)
- OBJETIVOS_COMPROMETIDOS: {{OBJETIVOS_COMPROMETIDOS}} > Objectives or outcomes committed at the start, against which the closing is measured
- RESULTADOS_Y_ENTREGABLES: {{RESULTADOS_Y_ENTREGABLES}} > Deliverables produced and results or metrics achieved, with their evidence if it exists
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > Report audience (e.g., executive sponsor, committee, area lead)
- DIAGNOSTICO_INICIAL: {{DIAGNOSTICO_INICIAL}} > Initial situation or diagnosis that serves as the baseline (optional)

4. Sensitivity table: pessimistic, base, and optimistic scenarios moving the 2-3 most critical variables; report the NPV for each scenario and the break-even point that brings NPV to zero for each dominant variable (how far the benefit can fall or cost can rise before the case stops making sense).

--- S | SITUATION ---
A business decision must be made whose merit is not obvious: the figures are scattered, mixed with perceptions, and without a framework that makes them comparable. The purpose is to transform that decision into an auditable cost-benefit model that a committee can defend. A well-built model unlocks budget approval, aligns stakeholders around evidence, and leaves a trail of reviewable assumptions when conditions change. The risk to avoid: a single number with no traceability, intangibles that are inflated or ignored, and a verdict no one can defend under scrutiny.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior business analysis consultant specialized in business cases and investment evaluation, with command of applied corporate finance (NPV, ROI, payback) and disciplined separation of the quantifiable from the intangible.

Deliverable: a cost-benefit model with a one-page committee-ready summary table plus the model detail. Steps:
1. Restate DECISION_EVALUADA in one sentence; set HORIZONTE_ANIOS, TASA_DESCUENTO, and unit of time. If any of these three critical pieces of data are missing, ask for them before modeling.
2. Inventory total costs in four categories: initial investment (CapEx), recurring costs per period (OpEx), indirect and transition costs, and the cost of inaction (status quo). Distinguish sunk costs (ignored) from avoidable costs (counted).
3. Inventory benefits, strictly separating quantifiable (savings, incremental revenues, productivity, monetizable risk) from qualitative (reputation, satisfaction, competitive position, optionality). Flag those that depend on adoption or a fragile assumption.
4. Build the net flow period by period; calculate simple payback, NPV, and ROI, exposing the formula and assumption behind each figure.
5. Score the intangibles in a table with an explicit scale and weighting, without converting them to currency.
6. Run sensitivity on the 2-3 variables that move the result the most, with base, conservative, and optimistic scenarios.
7. Issue a GO / NO-GO / conditional GO recommendation with the threshold that reverses the decision and break-even conditions, respecting RESTRICCIONES.

--- E | EXECUTION ---

Phase 2 - Costs: populate the four categories; every piece of data not provided is marked [SUPUESTO] with justification and, where it exists, a plausible range. Separate sunk from avoidable.
Phase 3 - Benefits: populate quantifiable and qualitative separately; never mix a perception into a monetary cell; flag adoption dependencies.
Phase 4 - Model: build net flow, discount by period, calculate payback, NPV, and ROI; show the formula and assumption for each line; report NPV in addition to ROI so as not to reward returns without scale or time.
Phase 5 - Intangibles and sensitivity: score intangibles with scale/weighting; vary the 2-3 critical levers in three scenarios; name the break-even threshold.
Phase 6 - Verdict: GO/NO-GO/conditional GO, threshold that reverses the decision, conditions for the conditional case, and risks to monitor.

--- S | SITUATION ---
The operational viability of a product or service line is being evaluated: we need to know the minimum volume at which revenue equals total costs before any profit appears. Knowing that threshold unlocks decisions on pricing, fixed-cost sizing, sales targets, and tolerance for demand drops. A poorly estimated break-even leads to overcommitting capacity or pricing without a foundation; well estimated, it turns intuition into a defensible business case. This analysis uses the classic cost-volume-profit (CVP) model and assumes cost and price linearity within the relevant operating range.

2. Calculate the unit contribution margin (price minus unit variable cost) and the contribution margin ratio (unit margin over price).

4. Calculate the safety margin relative to {{VOLUMEN_ESPERADO}} (the percentage drop in sales the business can absorb before losing money) and the degree of operating leverage (total contribution margin / operating income).

A three-scenario model (base, optimistic, pessimistic) makes assumptions explicit, separates what is known from what is assumed, and converts uncertainty into an actionable decision range: how good it can get, how bad it can get, and what to watch to anticipate which way reality is trending. The value is not in predicting the number — it is in structuring the bet and its limits.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior strategy and business analysis consultant, with experience in financial modeling and planning under uncertainty (scenario analysis and sensitivity analysis).

Phase 2 - Drivers: decompose the result into its drivers and set the three values per driver with their labeled origin.

--- S | SITUATION ---
The business case for {{INICIATIVA}} in the {{SECTOR}} sector supports its return on hard benefits (savings, revenue, productivity), but leaves {{BENEFICIO_INTANGIBLE}} as a qualitative mention without an assigned value. This weakens the decision: the committee discounts what is not measured and the case figure ends up understated. Quantifying the soft benefit with defensible proxies, explicit assumptions, and ranges over a horizon of {{HORIZONTE}} unlocks a more robust case, an honest conversation with finance, and a baseline for measuring benefits realization afterward. --- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior business analysis and value engineering consultant, expert in building business cases that survive the scrutiny of a finance committee and in translating intangibles into CFO language.
Deliverable:

3. For each link, propose 2–3 concrete, measurable proxies and the data source that feeds them, prioritizing {{DATOS_DISPONIBLES}} over the ideal but inaccessible proxy.

spec-consulting_analisis_de_cadena_de_va:
[inputs]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A business needs to understand precisely where its margin really comes from and where it is being eroded — before investing in improvements, cutting costs, or repositioning. Porter's value chain analysis decomposes the firm into discrete activities to reveal sources of competitive advantage and cost pools that aggregated income statements hide. A rigorous diagnostic unlocks founded prioritization: what to reinforce, what to eliminate, and what gap to close to improve margin without destroying the differentiation that sustains the price. The risk to avoid is blind cutting: lowering cost in an activity the customer does value and eroding the price that justified that cost.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior competitive strategy consultant with practice in value chain analysis and advantage design, trained in Michael Porter's framework.
Deliver a value chain diagnostic with these steps:
1. Restate the business, the value proposition, and the basis of competition (cost, differentiation, or focus) based on {{NEGOCIO_Y_PROPUESTA}}, {{SECTOR_Y_MODELO}}, and {{BASE_COMPETENCIA}}; declare what data is missing and which gaps are critical for the diagnosis.
2. Map the five primary activities (inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, after-sales service) and the four support activities (infrastructure, human resource management, technology development, procurement): what is done today, relative weight in cost, and contribution to differentiation. If the business does not handle physical goods (services, software, digital), reinterpret inbound/outbound logistics as acquisition, orchestration, and delivery of information or service, and state this explicitly.
3. Identify the links where competitive advantage resides or is absent, and the connections between activities that create or destroy value (e.g., design that lowers after-sales cost, procurement that enables differentiating quality).
4. Locate the cost pools misaligned with what the customer values, contrasting {{ESTRUCTURA_COSTOS}} against the perception of value; separate cost that is necessary to differentiate from cost that only burdens margin.
5. Deliver a prioritized levers table by impact on margin and execution difficulty, classifying each lever as an advantage to reinforce, a cost to eliminate, or a gap to close, attending to {{VENTAJA_O_DOLOR}}; state the improvement assumption that underpins each lever.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpretation: reconstruct the business model and basis of competition; mark every inference with [SUPUESTO] and list the gaps, flagging which ones block the diagnosis.
Phase 2 — Decomposition: complete the nine-activity matrix with what/cost-weight/differentiation-contribution; use qualitative ranges (high/medium/low) when figures are missing and never invent amounts.
Phase 3 — Diagnosis: cross cost against perceived value, expose advantage links, inter-activity connections, and misalignments; distinguish cause from symptom.
Phase 4 — Prioritization: rank the levers by margin impact and effort, classify each, and state its improvement assumption; close with the data point that would most change the diagnosis if different.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- All nine Porter activities are covered without omissions or inventions; inbound/outbound logistics are reinterpreted and declared if the business does not deal in physical goods.
- Each advantage link is supported by an input data point or an explicit [SUPUESTO].
- Cost pools are contrasted against the customer's perceived value — not in the abstract; cost that differentiates is separated from cost that only burdens margin.
- Levers are prioritized (impact x effort) and classified (reinforce/eliminate/close), each with its improvement assumption.

The organization wants to rigorously understand at what maturity level the process {{PROCESO}} operates and how to scale it in a defensible way toward {{NIVEL_OBJETIVO}}. A solid diagnosis unlocks justified investment, prioritizes effort where it hurts most, and turns a vague perception of "the process is failing" into an actionable plan organized by horizons. The typical mistake is averaging strong and weak dimensions to inflate the verdict; here the ceiling is set by the weakest link. Context: {{CONTEXTO_ORGANIZACION}}. Evidence: {{EVIDENCIA}}. Constraints: {{RESTRICCIONES}}. Attachments: {{ADJUNTOS}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior operational excellence consultant specializing in process maturity models (CMMI levels 1–5 and Michael Hammer's PEMM) and continuous improvement.

Deliverable: process maturity diagnosis with an overall verdict justified by the weakest link and a prioritized improvement roadmap organized by horizons toward the target level.

1. Describe the process {{PROCESO}}: end-to-end scope, owner, evaluation triggers, and the business outcome it produces.
2. Assess five dimensions and assign each a level from 1 to 5 with supporting evidence:

Phase 1 Framing: fix the process, owner, objective, and horizon; if {{PROCESO}}, {{NIVEL_OBJETIVO}}, or {{EVIDENCIA}} are missing, request them in a single round before proceeding.

Phase 3 Overall verdict: level = weakest link; justify the ceiling and the risk of averaging.
Phase 4 Roadmap design: gap by dimension, quick wins vs. structural, sequence by horizons with dependencies and owner.
Phase 5 Risks and level-advance indicators (outcome, not just activity).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---

spec-consulting_analisis_make_or_buy:

- CRITERIOS_PRIORITARIOS: {{CRITERIOS_PRIORITARIOS}} > Criteria that carry the most weight in the decision (optional)
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Regulatory, compliance, data, or contractual constraints (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
An organization must decide whether to build internally (make) or outsource/buy (buy) {{CAPACIDAD_O_COMPONENTE}}. This is a high-impact sourcing decision: it determines total cost of ownership over several years, vendor dependency, control over intellectual property, and delivery speed. Well-grounded, it unlocks investment with executive committee confidence; poorly grounded, it generates costly lock-in, technical debt, or loss of differentiation. The deliverable is a structured analysis that supports a defensible recommendation before stakeholders, considering a horizon of {{HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL}} and current internal capacity ({{CAPACIDAD_INTERNA}}).

Common error to avoid: comparing only the initial construction cost while ignoring operation, maintenance, and exit; or treating make and buy with asymmetry (enthusiasm for one, skepticism for the other). Both cases are built with the same rigor.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior consultant in sourcing strategy and business decision analysis, with experience in TCO frameworks, vendor evaluation, and technology investment decisions before committee.

Deliver a complete make-or-buy analysis following these steps:
1. Define {{CAPACIDAD_O_COMPONENTE}}: what problem it solves, what it unlocks, strategic criticality, whether it is differentiating or commodity, and use horizon. Constraints ({{RESTRICCIONES}}) are applied first as eliminatory filters: if an option violates them fundamentally, it is eliminated before scoring.
2. Establish the decision criteria and weight them according to {{CRITERIOS_PRIORITARIOS}} with weights adding up to 100%: TCO (construction + operation + maintenance + exit/reversibility), internal capacity and maturity, time-to-market, criticality/differentiation, risk (technical, vendor, lock-in, continuity, compliance), and future flexibility.
3. Build the MAKE case: talent requirements relative to {{CAPACIDAD_INTERNA}}, effort in FTE-months by phase with ranges, assumptions, control and IP advantages, weaknesses, and learning curve/execution risk.
4. Build the BUY case: vendor archetypes or market options (without naming brands unless the user provides them), integration effort and contract governance in FTE-months, dependency/lock-in and reversal cost, speed advantages, weaknesses.
5. Evaluate the HYBRID or phased option (buy now and internalize later; or core make + periphery buy) as an explicit alternative, not a footnote.
6. Compare MAKE vs. BUY (vs. hybrid) in a criterion-by-criterion matrix with a consistent scale (1–5), justified scores, applied weights, and weighted result.
7. Issue the recommendation with validity conditions, thresholds that would reverse it, residual risks with mitigations, and the 3–5 data points to confirm before committing.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Framing: confirm the capability under decision, horizon, strategic criticality, and constraints; apply the eliminatory filter; identify missing data and request it if it blocks the analysis.
Phase 2 — Criteria and weights: define the matrix and assign explicit weights (sum 100%) justified by {{CRITERIOS_PRIORITARIOS}}; if none are provided, propose a default set and mark it [SUPUESTO].
Phase 3 — Parallel cases: develop MAKE, BUY, and hybrid with symmetric structure, effort in FTE-months and ranges, marking each unverified estimate as [SUPUESTO].
Phase 4 — Comparison: score criterion by criterion, apply weights, expose the weighted result and the sensitivity to the 2–3 assumptions that most affect the result (what would have to change to reverse the decision).
Phase 5 — Recommendation: decide, condition, identify reversal thresholds, and provide residual risk mitigations.
Rules: FTE-months and ranges, never absolute prices or monetary figures; never the word "free". Every unverified estimate is marked [SUPUESTO]. Neutral, professional English, no emojis.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Capability under decision and horizon defined with explicit strategic criticality (differentiating vs. commodity).
- [ ] Constraints applied as eliminatory filters before scoring.
- [ ] Decision criteria weighted with weights summing to 100%, justified, not arbitrary.
- [ ] MAKE, BUY, and hybrid cases are symmetric, with effort in FTE-months and ranges, without absolute prices.
- [ ] Risks covered in both cases: technical, vendor, lock-in, continuity, compliance, reversal cost.
- [ ] Criterion-by-criterion comparison matrix with score, weighted result, and sensitivity analysis.
- [ ] Clear recommendation with validity conditions, reversal thresholds, and mitigations.
- [ ] All unverified data marked [SUPUESTO]; 3–5 data points to confirm listed.
Expected deliverable: a make-or-buy decision document with framing, weighted criteria matrix, MAKE/BUY/hybrid cases compared with sensitivity, conditioned recommendation, and list of pending verifications, ready to present to the executive committee.
spec-consulting_modelo_de_capacidad_y_de:
[inputs]
- OPERACION: {{OPERACION}} > Process, line, or service to model (e.g. assembly line, support desk, packaging plant, logistics route)
- UNIDAD_CAPACIDAD: {{UNIDAD_CAPACIDAD}} > Common unit for normalizing demand and capacity (machine-hours, person-hours, transactions/shift, units/day)
- HORIZONTE: {{HORIZONTE}} > Period and granularity of the analysis (e.g. 12 months, 8 weeks, 20 shifts in a month)
- RECURSOS_CAPACIDAD: {{RECURSOS_CAPACIDAD}} > Theoretical capacity by resource or station and its downtime: calendar, maintenance, absenteeism, waste, efficiency/OEE; process sequence if known
- DEMANDA_PROYECTADA: {{DEMANDA_PROYECTADA}} > Demand by period with seasonality, known peaks, and confidence level (firm, forecast, optional)
- UMBRAL_UTILIZACION: {{UMBRAL_UTILIZACION}} > Utilization threshold that marks a bottleneck (optional, default 85%)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to anticipate where and when {{OPERACION}} will saturate before committing volumes, hiring, or investing. Contrasting installed capacity against projected demand turns the intuition of "we're going to run short" into a quantified bottleneck map by resource and period. The model unlocks planning decisions (shifts, leveling, subcontracting, investment) grounded in utilization and slack, not in loose assumptions. The value lies in separating the resource that truly limits the system from the noise of stations with slack.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior operations consultant, expert in capacity planning (S&OP) and the theory of constraints (Goldratt), with experience in manufacturing and service operations.
Deliverable: capacity-versus-demand model with a resource-by-period utilization dashboard, identified constraining resource, and actionable levers. Steps:
1. Define the horizon {{HORIZONTE}} with its granularity and normalize demand and capacity to {{UNIDAD_CAPACIDAD}}; declare each conversion factor.
2. Build effective capacity by resource from {{RECURSOS_CAPACIDAD}}: theoretical capacity minus non-working calendar days, scheduled downtime, maintenance, absenteeism, waste, and efficiency/OEE factor; label each discount as data or [SUPUESTO].
3. Project demand by period from {{DEMANDA_PROYECTADA}} incorporating seasonality, peaks, and confidence level (firm vs. forecast).
4. Calculate utilization (demand/effective capacity) for each resource-by-period cell; flag as a bottleneck if utilization is greater than or equal to {{UMBRAL_UTILIZACION}} or if capacity falls below demand.
5. Identify the system's constraining resource (it governs total throughput, not just the highest point utilization) and quantify the slack or deficit of each non-constraining station in the same unit.
6. Propose 3 to 5 levers (extra shifts, demand leveling, subcontracting, reallocation, capacity investment) with their estimated impact on the constraining resource's utilization and its critical period.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Normalization: fix the common unit and horizon; reexpress all inputs on that basis; tabulate the applied conversions.
Phase 2 - Effective capacity: derive available capacity by resource discounting downtime in cascade (theoretical > calendar > scheduled > efficiency); document each discount as data or [SUPUESTO] with its value.
Phase 3 - Demand: tabulate demand by period with seasonality, peaks, and confidence level; separate firm demand from forecast.
Phase 4 - Contrast and utilization: cross demand against effective capacity, calculate utilization for each resource-by-period cell, and apply the traffic light.
Phase 5 - Constraint and slack: locate the system's constraining resource, quantify deficit and slack, and simulate 3 to 5 levers with their effect on the constraining resource's utilization.
Rules: reason in physical units, hours, or percentages, never in prices or monetary costs. Distinguish data from assumption in each cell. If a critical input is missing (operation, unit, horizon, resources, or demand), ask before executing rather than inventing. If demand shifts the constraint between periods, report it: the constraint can migrate.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- Demand and capacity expressed in the same {{UNIDAD_CAPACIDAD}}, with explicit conversion factors.
- Effective capacity derived from theoretical in cascade, with each discount documented (data or [SUPUESTO] with value).
- Utilization calculated by resource and period, with traffic light: green below 75%, yellow 75–85%, red above 85%.
- System's constraining resource identified and justified by its effect on throughput, not by an isolated point utilization.
- Bottleneck reported with the exact period when demand exceeds capacity; constraint migration flagged if it occurs.
- Slack or deficit quantified by non-constraining station in the common unit.
- 3 to 5 actionable levers, each with estimated impact on the constraining resource's utilization and the assumptions behind that impact.
- Zero mentions of prices or monetary costs; reasoning only in units, hours, or percentages.
Expected deliverable: resource-by-period utilization dashboard (traffic light) + constraining resource profile + slack/deficit table + prioritized list of levers with estimated impact.
spec-consulting_analisis_de_canibalizaci:
[inputs]
- LANZAMIENTO: {{LANZAMIENTO}} > Product, service, or line to be launched: what it is, value proposition, projected sales or expected volume, and launch date
- PORTAFOLIO_EXISTENTE: {{PORTAFOLIO_EXISTENTE}} > Existing products or lines that could be displaced, with their historical revenue performance, share, and trend
- UNIDAD_ANALISIS: {{UNIDAD_ANALISIS}} > Level of analysis: product, SKU, customer segment, channel, or geography
- HORIZONTE: {{HORIZONTE}} > Evaluation period (e.g. first 12 months, 3 years) and whether the interest is in the stabilized steady state or the cumulative total
- MARGEN_RELATIVO: {{MARGEN_RELATIVO}} > Margin difference between the new product and the displaced one, in points or as a ratio (optional; marked [SUPUESTO] if missing)
- SOLAPAMIENTO_PUBLICO: {{SOLAPAMIENTO_PUBLICO}} > Degree of target audience and usage occasion overlap between new and existing products (optional)
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Capacity, commercial budget, strategic intent (defend vs. expand), trade spend, or channels with caps (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A launch may appear successful by gross revenue yet still destroy value if most of that revenue would have been captured anyway with the existing products. Before committing capacity, budget, and commercial focus, I need to separate the truly incremental revenue from the revenue simply reallocated within the portfolio. The analysis unlocks a well-grounded go/no-go decision, a tolerable cannibalization threshold for setting internal transfer targets and prices, and a reading of whether the cannibalization is deliberate defense or value leakage.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior commercial strategy consultant specializing in portfolio management, incrementality, and source-of-volume analysis.

Deliver a cannibalization analysis with:
1. Restatement of the launch, the portfolio at risk, and the unit of analysis; confirmation of the horizon and strategic intent (defend vs. expand).
2. Decomposition of the launch's source of volume into three origins summing to 100 percent: new demand or category expansion, switching from competitors, and switching from own products (cannibalization).
3. Cannibalization rate = own displaced revenue / gross launch revenue, separating planned cannibalization (deliberate migration) from unplanned, and distinguishing permanent displacement from pull-forward (temporary purchase acceleration).
4. Net incremental revenue = gross launch revenue minus own displaced revenue, adjusted by relative margin and by halo (positive pull-through) and dilution effects on the rest of the portfolio.
5. Three scenarios (base, optimistic, pessimistic) explicitly varying cannibalization rate and capture of new demand, with the driver that distinguishes each scenario.
6. Verdict: creates value / neutral / destroys value, with the indifference cannibalization threshold beyond which the launch stops making sense, the 3 levers to reduce it, and the early signal that would confirm or refute the base scenario in the first weeks.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: fix the unit of analysis, horizon, and portfolio boundary at risk; list elasticity assumptions, audience overlap, and usage occasion. If the launch projection, displaced product history, or relative margin are missing, request them in a single round before quantifying.
Phase 2 - Source of volume: decompose the launch volume into new demand, competitor switching, and own cannibalization; reason the split from audience overlap, usage occasion, and price/positioning proximity, not by default.
Phase 3 - Quantification: calculate cannibalization rate and net incremental revenue, adjusting for margin difference so as not to count gross revenue as value; separate planned from unplanned cannibalization.
Phase 4 - Second-order effects: estimate halo (positive pull-through) and dilution on the rest of the portfolio, and distinguish permanent displacement from pull-forward.
Phase 5 - Scenarios and verdict: model base/optimistic/pessimistic, derive the indifference cannibalization threshold, issue the recommendation, and define the early verification signal.
Every data point without a real source goes as [SUPUESTO] with its sensitivity on the verdict; reason in percentages and share, without inventing absolute prices.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- [ ] Unit of analysis, horizon, and strategic intent confirmed before quantifying.
- [ ] Source of volume decomposed into the three origins and summing exactly to 100 percent.
- [ ] Distinguishes planned from unplanned cannibalization and permanent displacement from pull-forward.
- [ ] Net incremental revenue adjusted by margin, not just by gross revenue.
- [ ] Considers halo and dilution effects on the rest of the portfolio.
- [ ] Three scenarios with cannibalization rate and new demand as explicit variables.
- [ ] Verdict with indifference cannibalization threshold, 3 mitigation levers, and one early verification signal.
- [ ] Every assumption marked [SUPUESTO] with its sensitivity; zero invented absolute prices.
Expected deliverable: structured cannibalization report with source-of-volume table, cannibalization rate, net incremental revenue by scenario, and an actionable go/no-go verdict with the indifference threshold.
