1. Issue a global status verdict in a single line with its color (red/amber/green), the dominant reason that determines it, and the trend versus the previous period (improving / stable / deteriorating) if there is a basis for comparison.
2. Build a dimension-by-dimension traffic-light dashboard: scope, schedule, budget, risks, and quality, each with its color.
3. Assign each color against an explicit criterion derived from {{UMBRALES_TOLERANCIA}} (green: within tolerance, no action; amber: contained deviation with an active plan; red: outside tolerance, requires a committee decision). Cite the applied threshold next to the color.
4. For each dimension draft a narrative of exactly three sentences: evidence supporting the color, root cause, and corrective action underway or requested (with owner if known).
5. List the decisions or support requested from the committee, each linked to the dimension that originates it, with the recommended option and the consequence of not deciding in this period.
6. Close with milestones committed for the next two weeks, each with owner and target date.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: confirm project, period, audience, and map data from {{ESTADO_DIMENSIONES}} to the five dimensions; mark every absent datum as [SUPUESTO] or ask for it before drafting if it is critical for the color.
Phase 2 Calibrate: apply {{UMBRALES_TOLERANCIA}} to assign color by dimension; if no thresholds are provided, propose standard thresholds and mark them [SUPUESTO]; derive the global color by weighted worst-case per {{PESOS_DIMENSIONES}}, never by averaging (a high-weight red dimension forces a justified global red or amber — it is never diluted by greens).
Phase 3 Draft: write global verdict with trend, dashboard and three-sentence narrative per dimension; consolidate decisions (with consequence of not deciding) and milestones (with owner and date).
Phase 4 Verify: check that every color has traceable evidence, that no green is complacent, that there is no watermelon effect, that the global color is consistent with the dimensions, and that every decision is actionable and linked to its source.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Global verdict in one line, with color, dominant reason, and trend vs. prior period.
- [ ] All five dimensions (scope, schedule, budget, risks, quality) have an assigned color.
- [ ] Each color is justified against an explicit tolerance criterion with the threshold cited, not by opinion.
- [ ] Each dimension has a narrative of exactly three sentences: evidence, root cause, corrective action.
- [ ] The global color is derived by weighted worst-case and is consistent with the dimensions; no watermelon effect.
- [ ] Every unsupported figure is marked [SUPUESTO]; zero invented data.
- [ ] Requested decisions are actionable, linked to their source dimension, with the consequence of not deciding.
- [ ] Milestones for the next two weeks with owner and target date.
- [ ] Executive, neutral tone, professional English, without emojis.
Expected deliverable: a one-page RAG status report with global verdict and trend, five-dimension traffic-light dashboard with a three-sentence narrative for each, a block of requested decisions with the consequence of not deciding, and milestones for the next two weeks with owner — ready to bring to the committee.
spec-gestion-proyectos_flash-report-hito:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_HITO: {{NOMBRE_HITO}} > Name of the milestone being communicated (e.g., "UAT closure for billing module")
- PROYECTO: {{PROYECTO}} > Project name or code
- ESTADO_HITO: {{ESTADO_HITO}} > Reached / At Risk / Deviated
- FECHA_PLANEADA: {{FECHA_PLANEADA}} > Baseline date for the milestone
- FECHA_REAL: {{FECHA_REAL}} > Actual date achieved or projected closure date
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > Recipients (e.g., sponsor, committee, client)
- IMPACTO_Y_CONTEXTO: {{IMPACTO_Y_CONTEXTO}} > Root cause, known impact on scope/cost/team, dependencies (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A milestone for {{PROYECTO}} has just closed or deviated and {{AUDIENCIA}} needs to be informed immediately, before the next formal report. The flash report ensures that in under one minute the reader understands what happened, its effect on the triple constraint (scope, schedule, budget), and what comes next — preventing rumors and delayed decisions. A Reached milestone unlocks dependent work; one At Risk or Deviated activates early containment and, sometimes, a sponsor decision. The value lies in speed and precision: an erroneous figure here propagates to the committee.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Project Director, PMP-certified, expert in executive communications and milestone management by triple constraint.
Produce a flash report of maximum 200 words, ready to send, with this numbered structure:
1. One-line subject: [FLASH] {{NOMBRE_HITO}} - {{ESTADO_HITO}}.
2. Verdict in one sentence: {{FECHA_REAL}} versus {{FECHA_PLANEADA}}, with the exact variation in days (positive = delay, negative = early).
3. What is now unblocked (if Reached) or what remains blocked and its root cause (if At Risk/Deviated).
4. Impact on the three constraints: scope (no change/expanded/reduced), schedule (days of variation vs. baseline and effect on critical path or subsequent milestones), budget (no impact/reserve consumption/cost overrun, in relative magnitude).
5. Three concrete next steps, each with a named owner and committed date.
6. One single decision or question for {{AUDIENCIA}}, only if the reader's action is required.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1: Validate that milestone name, status, and both dates exist. If one essential item is missing, ask for everything in one batch and stop. Do not invent data; mark inferences with [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2: Calculate the variation in days (actual minus planned) and classify the impact on each constraint. If {{IMPACTO_Y_CONTEXTO}} is empty, derive the impact from the dates alone and state the limits.
Phase 3: Draft in neutral, professional English, without emojis or filler, short sentences, active voice. Never invent money figures; use relative magnitude.
Phase 4: Trim to <=200 words prioritizing verdict, impact, and next steps. If the reader's action is not required, omit point 6 and state so.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] One-line subject with milestone name and explicit status.
- [ ] Verdict includes actual date, planned date, and variation in days with interpreted sign.
- [ ] Point 3 consistent with the status: unblocking if Reached, blocking + root cause if At Risk/Deviated.
- [ ] Impact covers all three constraints; schedule references critical path or subsequent milestones.
- [ ] Three next steps, each with a named owner and date.
- [ ] Maximum one decision/question for the audience, omitted if no action is required.
- [ ] <=200 words, without emojis, without filler, neutral English, active voice.
- [ ] Zero invented data; assumptions marked [SUPUESTO]; no invented money figures.
Expected deliverable: a single block of text, copyable to email or chat, that communicates the milestone in under one minute of reading time, closed with the word count.
spec-gestion-proyectos_minuta-reunion-ac:
[inputs]
- PROYECTO: {{PROYECTO}} > Name of the project or initiative to which the meeting belongs
- NOMBRE_REUNION: {{NOMBRE_REUNION}} > Type or title of the meeting (e.g., kickoff, weekly check-in, change committee)
- FECHA_REUNION: {{FECHA_REUNION}} > Date and, if known, start/end time of the meeting
- ASISTENTES: {{ASISTENTES}} > People present with their roles; indicate the facilitator and, if noted, excused absences
- NOTAS_REUNION: {{NOTAS_REUNION}} > Raw notes, topics discussed, decisions, and commitments mentioned
- PROXIMA_REUNION: {{PROXIMA_REUNION}} > Tentative date of the next meeting (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A project meeting only creates value if its conversations are turned into trackable commitments. I need to transform the notes from the {{NOMBRE_REUNION}} meeting for the {{PROYECTO}} project into professional minutes ready to distribute to attendees and stakeholders. Well-crafted minutes unlock follow-up: everyone knows what the team decided, what needs to be done, by when, and under whose responsibility — preventing misinterpretations and vague commitments. The risk to neutralize is twofold: agreements without an owner or date that no one executes, and attribution of commitments that were never made.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Project Manager (PMP) with experience in project governance, meeting facilitation, and agreement-tracking discipline.

Draft meeting minutes with this structure:
1. Header: meeting name, project, date, start/end time, location or channel, facilitator, and list of attendees with their roles; separate those present from excused absences if the notes indicate this.
2. Meeting objective in a single sentence.
3. Topics discussed: summary by item, without transcribing the conversation.
4. Decisions made: each decision with a brief justification and, if noted, who approved it.
5. Agreements and action items table with columns: Action | Owner (single) | Commitment date | Priority (High/Medium/Low) | Status (starts as Pending).
6. Open items / parking lot: unresolved points requiring future follow-up.
7. Risks or dependencies mentioned, if any (if none, omit the section).
8. Next meeting: tentative date ({{PROXIMA_REUNION}} if provided; otherwise [TO BE CONFIRMED]).

Hard rules: each action has a single named owner and a concrete date; if {{NOTAS_REUNION}} does not specify an owner or date, write [TO BE CONFIRMED] and do not invent one. Always distinguish a decision (closed) from an action item (executable commitment) from an open item (pending). If a note is ambiguous or contradictory, mark it [VERIFY] rather than resolving it at your own discretion. Clearly separate what was decided from what is open; use neutral and verifiable language, without attributing commitments not in the notes. Do not include figures, amounts, or costs that do not appear literally in the notes.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpret: extract from {{NOTAS_REUNION}} the topics, decisions, and commitments; classify each item as a decision, action item, or open item; detect gaps in owner/date and contradictions.
Phase 2 — Plan: build the header with {{PROYECTO}}, {{FECHA_REUNION}}, and {{ASISTENTES}}; map each action to a single owner and a date, marking gaps as [TO BE CONFIRMED] and ambiguities as [VERIFY]; present the section outline and list of gaps before drafting.
Phase 3 — Execute: draft the full minutes; validate that no action lacks an explicit owner and date (real or [TO BE CONFIRMED]) and that no decision is mixed with an open item.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Complete header: meeting, project, date, schedule, location/channel, facilitator, attendees with roles (present and excused absent if noted).
- [ ] Objective in a single sentence.
- [ ] Decisions separated from open items, without mixing them; each decision with justification.
- [ ] Action table with 5 columns; each row with a single owner, date, and priority (or [TO BE CONFIRMED]).
- [ ] Each action has exactly one named owner; no orphaned actions.
- [ ] Zero invented commitments, figures, or data not in {{NOTAS_REUNION}}; ambiguities marked [VERIFY].
- [ ] Neutral, professional language, no emojis.
- [ ] Next meeting indicated or marked [TO BE CONFIRMED].
Expected deliverable: meeting minutes in distributable format (structured text with agreements and action items table), ready to send to attendees and stakeholders, with the action table as the anchor for subsequent follow-up.
spec-gestion-proyectos_comunicado-cambio:
[inputs]
- CAMBIO: {{CAMBIO}} > Change from the project to announce (what is being modified: process, tool, structure, scope, dates)
- MOTIVO: {{MOTIVO}} > Problem or opportunity driving the change and what it unlocks
- AUDIENCIAS_AFECTADAS: {{AUDIENCIAS_AFECTADAS}} > Impacted groups and how the change affects them (e.g., sales team, operations, internal clients)
- FECHA_VIGENCIA: {{FECHA_VIGENCIA}} > Effective date of the change
- SOPORTE: {{SOPORTE}} > Channels, training sessions, and points of contact available to support the transition
- REMITENTE: {{REMITENTE}} > Who signs the announcement (role or name of the sponsor/leader)
- CANAL_TONO: {{CANAL_TONO}} > Delivery channel and formality level (e.g., formal email, team message, town hall) or "Not specified"
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A project underway is introducing a change ({{CAMBIO}}) that affects {{AUDIENCIAS_AFECTADAS}} starting {{FECHA_VIGENCIA}}, in response to {{MOTIVO}}. The communication vacuum is not neutral: rumor fills it. Without a clear announcement, resistance, rework, and productivity loss emerge during the transition, and trust in the project team erodes. A well-built announcement reduces uncertainty, accelerates adoption, and preserves trust: each person understands why things are changing, what happens to their day-to-day work, and who to turn to. The announcement informs and enables the decision to adopt; it does not replace one-on-one conversations when the change touches sensitive employment conditions.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior organizational change management (OCM) leader with hands-on experience in transformation projects and mastery of the ADKAR model.

Deliverable: an official one-page announcement ready to send, signed by {{REMITENTE}}, adjusted to {{CANAL_TONO}}. Build it in these steps:
1. Subject line and headline that name the change without euphemisms (ADKAR Awareness).
2. Purpose and context: {{MOTIVO}} and what it unlocks; connect the change to a credible benefit for the recipient (Desire).
3. Exactly what is changing and from {{FECHA_VIGENCIA}}; be specific about the before and after states.
4. Differentiated impact for each group in {{AUDIENCIAS_AFECTADAS}}, in language about their day-to-day work (what they stop doing, what they start doing, what they learn).
5. What is NOT changing, to contain fear and separate fact from rumor.
6. Support: channels, training sessions, points of contact, and where to resolve questions, with the first concrete action for each person (Knowledge and Ability).
7. Next steps with explicit owners and dates.
8. Closing that acknowledges the effort of the transition (Reinforcement) and {{REMITENTE}}'s signature.
Reference {{ADJUNTOS}} where they add value (guide, FAQ, calendar). If a critical data point is missing, declare the assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and flag it for validation; do not invent names, dates, or figures.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpret: confirm change, audiences, reason, date, support, sender, and channel/tone. If a critical data point is missing, ask for it; whatever you assume, mark it [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 — Plan: map each block of the announcement to ADKAR logic and to the three questions (why, how does it affect me, where is support); present the outline before drafting.
Phase 3 — Execute: draft the full announcement in neutral language, professional, empathetic, and honest tone, naming the real discomforts instead of minimizing them. Short paragraphs; no emojis. If {{CAMBIO}} touches sensitive employment conditions (roles, locations, working hours, compensation), prepend a note stating that the message requires prior review by {{REMITENTE}} and, where applicable, by the legal or people teams.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Clearly answers the three questions: why are we changing, how does this affect me, where do I find support.
- [ ] Covers all 5 ADKAR states (Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement) and the mapping is visible in the prior outline.
- [ ] Names the change without euphemisms; acknowledges real discomforts without minimizing them.
- [ ] Differentiated impact for each group in {{AUDIENCIAS_AFECTADAS}}, with the first concrete action for each one.
- [ ] Includes a section on what is NOT changing.
- [ ] {{FECHA_VIGENCIA}}, {{SOPORTE}}, and next steps with explicit owners and dates.
- [ ] Adjusted to {{CANAL_TONO}}; {{ADJUNTOS}} referenced where they add value.
- [ ] If it touches sensitive employment conditions, includes a prior-review note (sponsor and, if applicable, legal/people).
- [ ] Neutral language, no emojis, short paragraphs, signed by {{REMITENTE}}.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented names, dates, or figures.
Expected deliverable: official one-page announcement ready to send, with subject line, body structured in the 8 sections, and signature, preceded by the validated ADKAR outline.
spec-gestion-proyectos_one-pager-ejecuti:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_PROYECTO: {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} > Project name and responsible sponsor or leader
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > Recipient of the one-pager (steering committee, board, executive sponsor) and the decision expected from the committee
- PERIODO_REPORTE: {{PERIODO_REPORTE}} > Period covered by the report (week, month, sprint, cutoff date)
- ESTADO_AVANCE: {{ESTADO_AVANCE}} > Current progress: percentage vs. plan, milestones achieved, upcoming milestones with dates
- RIESGOS_BLOQUEOS: {{RIESGOS_BLOQUEOS}} > Active risks, blockers, and incidents with their owner and impact if known
- DECISIONES_PENDIENTES: {{DECISIONES_PENDIENTES}} > Decisions made in the period and those requiring leadership
- PEDIDOS_DIRECCION: {{PEDIDOS_DIRECCION}} > (optional) What you need from the committee: approvals, resources, unblocking actions
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Leadership has minutes, not hours, to understand a project and act. An executive one-pager condenses status, health, risks, decisions, and requests into a single scannable page so the committee can decide without reading the full plan. Done well, it unlocks approvals, resources, and mitigations in the same meeting; done poorly, it generates more questions than answers. This covers the period {{PERIODO_REPORTE}} for the project {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} before {{AUDIENCIA}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior PMO Director with experience presenting portfolios to steering committees, trained in executive communication and risk management.
Deliverable: a single page with six blocks in this order, with what demands action first:
1. Header: project, sponsor, period, and global traffic light (green/yellow/red) with one line of justification.
2. Progress vs. plan from {{ESTADO_AVANCE}}: percentage completed vs. expected, milestones achieved in the period, upcoming milestones with dates.
3. Health by dimension: mini-table for scope, schedule, budget, and team, each with a traffic light and brief note; dimensions must support the global traffic light.
4. Top 3 from {{RIESGOS_BLOQUEOS}}: exactly three, each with impact, probability, owner, and mitigation in progress. If two are tied in severity, prioritize the one blocking an upcoming milestone.
5. Decisions: those made in the period and the {{DECISIONES_PENDIENTES}} requiring leadership, kept separate.
6. Requests to the committee from {{PEDIDOS_DIRECCION}}: each as an action with a suggested owner and deadline.
Consider {{ADJUNTOS}} as input. If {{PEDIDOS_DIRECCION}} is empty, deduce the requests from the risks and pending decisions and mark them as proposed.
Assumed limit: fits on one page even if detail is sacrificed; non-essential content goes to the 'detail available on request' note.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpret: restate the report's objective and the specific decision the committee must make. Identify what data is missing (status, risks, decisions, dates, requests) and ask for it before drafting; never invent figures or traffic lights.
Phase 2 — Plan: prioritize content by relevance to the decision; what demands action goes first. Define what goes on the page and what moves to the 'detail available on request' note.
Phase 3 — Execute: draft the six blocks in executive language, short sentences, zero unnecessary technical jargon. Assign traffic lights that are coherent between the global and the dimensions. Close by verifying everything fits on one page.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Fits on a single page; non-essential content is in the detail-on-request note.
- [ ] What demands action (critical risks, decisions, requests) appears first.
- [ ] Global traffic light coherent with the four dimension traffic lights; the worst dimension is never below the global without explanation.
- [ ] Progress expressed as completed vs. expected, not just as an absolute percentage.
- [ ] Exactly the 3 most relevant risks, each with impact, probability, owner, and mitigation.
- [ ] Decisions separate what has been decided from what is pending with the committee.
- [ ] Each request to leadership is an action with an owner and a deadline; deduced ones are marked as proposed.
- [ ] Zero invented figures or traffic lights; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION].
- [ ] Executive language, no emojis, no unnecessary technical jargon, neutral language.
Expected deliverable: a single-page executive one-pager ready to present to the committee, with what demands action first.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-mala:
[inputs]
- DESVIACION: {{DESVIACION}} > Bad news to communicate and its magnitude against the baseline (e.g., "the integration milestone is delayed by 3 weeks" or "the cost exceeds the budget by 12%")
- CAUSA_RAIZ: {{CAUSA_RAIZ}} > Why it happened, in factual terms without blaming individuals
- IMPACTO: {{IMPACTO}} > Effect on time, cost, scope, or quality, and what remains intact
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > Message recipient and their level of power and interest (e.g., "executive sponsor, high power/high interest" or "development team"). May list multiple audiences
- PEDIDO: {{PEDIDO}} > Decision, approval, or backing you need from the recipient
- PLAN_RECUPERACION: {{PLAN_RECUPERACION}} > Recovery options you already have in mind (optional)
- CANAL: {{CANAL}} > Message medium: email, meeting, spokesperson, chat (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A delay or cost overrun that is poorly communicated destroys more trust than the deviation itself: the sponsor does not react to the problem — they react to feeling that there is no control. I need to convert a bad news event into a message that maintains credibility, anchors the recipient in facts, and leads them to a decision rather than an alarm. A structured announcement with context, impact, and an action plan transforms a defensive conversation into one of project governance: it unlocks the decision I need, preserves the stakeholder relationship, and leaves a record that the deviation was managed transparently.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project director (PMP), expert in stakeholder management, expectation communication, and difficult conversations, with mastery of the Minto pyramid.

Produce the bad news communication plan with these components:
1. Reframe {{DESVIACION}} as a factual statement against the baseline, without euphemisms, without exaggeration, and without attributing blame to individuals.
2. Main message in three labeled blocks:
   - CONTEXT: what was expected (baseline), what changed, and the {{CAUSA_RAIZ}} in terms of process or circumstance, not of individuals.
   - IMPACT: quantified effect of {{IMPACTO}} on time/cost/scope/quality and, explicitly, what is NOT affected to contain perceived damage. If applicable, distinguish impact already materialized vs. projected impact.
   - ACTION PLAN: 2 to 3 recovery options starting from {{PLAN_RECUPERACION}}, each with its cost/time/risk trade-off; the recommended option justified; and the {{PEDIDO}} with a response deadline and the cost of not deciding in time.
3. Apply the Minto pyramid: conclusion and request go first; detail goes after. Adjust depth to the power and interest of {{AUDIENCIA}} and to {{CANAL}}.
4. Short version of 3 to 4 lines for a quick channel, with the same request and the same deadline.
5. Objections anticipation note: 3 to 5 probable reactions from the recipient and a suggested fact-based response to each one.
If {{AUDIENCIA}} groups opposing interests (e.g., sponsor and team), indicate what to reframe or omit per audience rather than using a single message.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Frame: establish the fact of the deviation against the baseline; eliminate euphemisms, exaggerations, and personal blame; separate observed fact from interpretation.
Phase 2 — Structure: draft CONTEXT, IMPACT, and ACTION PLAN; quantify the impact, explicitly contain what remains stable, and trace each recovery option to its cost/time/risk.
Phase 3 — Adapt: order with the Minto pyramid (conclusion and request at the start) and calibrate the level of detail to the power and interest of {{AUDIENCIA}} and {{CANAL}}; produce the short version without losing the request or the date.
Phase 4 — Anticipate: list probable objections and prepare a response for each; verify direct, responsible tone, oriented toward the next action.
Mark any unconfirmed figure or effect as [ASSUMPTION]; never present an estimate as a closed data point. If an essential data point is missing (magnitude, root cause, impact, audience, or request), ask for it in a brief list before drafting.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- The message opens with the conclusion and the request (Minto), not with a preamble that delays the news.
- The deviation is stated as a fact against the baseline, without euphemisms, dramatization, or blame toward individuals.
- The IMPACT block quantifies the effect and contains what is NOT affected.
- The ACTION PLAN offers 2 to 3 options with cost/time/risk trade-offs, a justified recommendation, and a request with a deadline and the cost of not deciding.
- The level of detail is calibrated to the audience's power and interest and to the channel.
- Every unconfirmed figure is marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented data.
- The tone conveys control without minimizing or dramatizing; no emojis; neutral and professional language.
- Includes a short version (3 to 4 lines) and an objections anticipation note with a response for each one.
- If the audience groups opposing interests, there is a note on what to reframe or omit per audience.
Expected deliverable: main message ready to send (subject line + three labeled blocks + closing with request and date), short version of 3 to 4 lines, and a separate objections anticipation note with a response for each one.
spec-gestion-proyectos_matriz-asignacion:
[inputs]
- PROYECTO: {{PROYECTO}} > Name and objective of the project to which the matrix belongs
- ACTIVIDADES: {{ACTIVIDADES}} > List of activities or deliverables to assign (one per line)
- ROLES: {{ROLES}} > Roles or team members that will be the matrix columns
- FASE: {{FASE}} > Phase or time scope covered (e.g., initiation, execution, closure)
- GOBERNANZA: {{GOBERNANZA}} > How decisions are made and approved; who has final authority (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
In {{PROYECTO}}, during the phase {{FASE}}, the team needs a RACI matrix that eliminates ambiguity about who executes, who approves, who is consulted, and who is informed for each activity or deliverable. A well-built matrix unlocks faster decisions, avoids duplicated work, prevents orphaned approvals, and documents the governance model for auditing and onboarding. The cost of not having one: rework due to late approvals, authority conflicts, and deliverables without a clear owner.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project director (PMP) expert in organizational design and the RACI model.
Produce, in this order:
1. RACI matrix as a table: rows = each activity from {{ACTIVIDADES}}, columns = each role from {{ROLES}}; each cell contains R, A, C, I, or is empty if the role does not participate.
2. Operational definition of each letter as applied to this project (R executes, A is accountable and approves — unique per row —, C contributes input before the decision, I receives subsequent communication).
3. Integrity validation: confirm row by row that there is exactly one A and at least one R; list the rows that fail along with their proposed correction.
4. Gaps and conflicts: activities without a single approver or without an owner, roles overloaded with A or R, excess C's slowing decisions, and poor executor/approver separation.
5. Three actionable recommendations to unblock the governance according to {{GOBERNANZA}}, executable this week.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpret: restate the project, phase, activity list, and roles; flag missing or ambiguous data. If the essentials are missing (activities, roles, or approval criteria), ask for the data rather than inventing it.
Phase 2 — Plan: define the assignment criterion for the A's according to {{GOBERNANZA}}, group related activities, and anticipate where authority conflicts could arise.
Phase 3 — Execute: fill the matrix cell by cell, run the integrity rules (one A per row, at least one R, no empty rows, no overload), document gaps with corrections, and issue recommendations.
Explicit assumptions (mark if applied): a single A per activity — no co-decision —; R and A can fall on the same role only when internal controls allow it; functional roles, not individual names; activity granularity level is fixed according to {{ACTIVIDADES}}.
Limits: do not invent roles or activities not provided; do not assign final authority that {{GOBERNANZA}} does not support; no emojis; no real individual names if not provided.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each activity from {{ACTIVIDADES}} is a row and each role from {{ROLES}} is a column.
- [ ] Each row has exactly one A and at least one R; no row is empty.
- [ ] No role concentrates a proportion of A's or R's that makes it a bottleneck.
- [ ] Every C or I cell is justified; no decorative consulted or informed parties.
- [ ] The executor/approver separation is respected where controls require it.
- [ ] Each detected gap includes its proposed correction, not just the diagnosis.
- [ ] The three recommendations are specific to {{GOBERNANZA}} and executable this week.
- [ ] Applied assumptions are marked as such.
Expected deliverable: RACI matrix as a table ready to validate with the sponsor, plus an integrity report, gap and correction diagnosis, and three governance recommendations, in professional language.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-recu:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_PROYECTO: {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} > Name of the project to which the plan belongs
- OBJETIVO_PROYECTO: {{OBJETIVO_PROYECTO}} > Brief project objective and scope (what is being built or delivered)
- FASES_PROYECTO: {{FASES_PROYECTO}} > Schedule phases or milestones with approximate dates or durations
- ENTREGABLES: {{ENTREGABLES}} > Main deliverables or work packages to which responsibility is assigned
- EQUIPO_DISPONIBLE: {{EQUIPO_DISPONIBLE}} > Roles, people, or profiles already available and their current dedication
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Capacity constraints (FTE cap, hours, unavailability windows, hiring policies) (optional)
- VENTANA_TIEMPO: {{VENTANA_TIEMPO}} > Project time horizon (start and end date or horizon in months) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are planning the resources for project {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} ({{OBJETIVO_PROYECTO}}). A solid Resource Management Plan is what prevents the schedule from collapsing due to late arrivals, over-allocated profiles, or missing competencies. This document unlocks hiring decisions, availability negotiations with functional areas, and the baseline for measuring team load across the phases {{FASES_PROYECTO}} within the horizon {{VENTANA_TIEMPO}}. In matrix organizations availability is not a given — it is negotiated, which is why acquisition dates and owners are as critical as the list of roles.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Project Manager (PMP), expert in resource planning under the PMBOK standard (Resource Management knowledge area), with experience in matrix organizations.
Deliverable: a Resource Management Plan in titled sections. Build, in this order:
1. Resource identification: human resources by role and physical resources (equipment, materials, facilities, licenses) required by {{ENTREGABLES}}, with an effort estimate (FTE, hours, or person-months) or quantity for each. Using {{EQUIPO_DISPONIBLE}} as the baseline, flag each resource as available, partially available, or missing (gap).
2. RACI matrix in table form: cross each deliverable or work package in {{ENTREGABLES}} against team roles, assigning R (Responsible), A (Accountable, unique per row), C (Consulted), and I (Informed). Hard rule: no row with two Accountables, no row without a Responsible, no role-column without at least one assignment. Avoid overloading a single role with too many simultaneous Responsibles.
3. Acquisition strategy: for each missing role or resource, state the source (internal, contracted, or outsourced), target incorporation date, owner, and acquisition critical path (steps and lead time), respecting {{RESTRICCIONES}}. Flag which incorporations are on the schedule's critical path.
4. Resource calendar in table form: availability window and dedication level (full, partial, on-demand) of each resource across the phases {{FASES_PROYECTO}}; flag demand peaks and over-allocation conflicts (any resource above 100 percent capacity in a window), and the dependency between each incorporation and the phase that requires it.
5. Training and release: competency gaps with a closing plan (action, owner, deadline), and the criteria and process for releasing each resource when their participation ends (knowledge handover, documentation, reassignment).
Close with a brief resource risk block: 2 or 3 risks (late incorporation, over-allocation, dependency on a single key resource) with their mitigation action.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Inventory: start from {{EQUIPO_DISPONIBLE}} and {{ENTREGABLES}} to list required vs. available resources and identify gaps.
Phase 2 — Assignment: build the RACI and validate the single-Accountable-per-row rule, R presence, and no orphan roles.
Phase 3 — Acquisition and calendar: define source, date, and owner for each missing resource, then project availability across phases and detect over-allocations and dependencies with the schedule.
Phase 4 — Development and release: cover competency gaps and define release criteria.
Phase 5 — Assumptions and risks: tag as [SUPUESTO] everything assumed due to missing data, with its impact if false, and close with the resource risks. If essential data is missing, request it in a single numbered list before drafting. Do not use monetary cost figures; express capacity in FTE, hours, or person-months.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- All five blocks present and in order: identification, RACI, acquisition, calendar, training and release.
- Identification distinguishes available, partial, and missing resources; each with effort or quantity.
- RACI with exactly one Accountable per row, at least one Responsible per row, and no orphan roles.
- Each acquisition resource has a source, target date, owner, and lead time; items on the critical path are flagged.
- The calendar shows dedication by phase and explicitly flags peaks, over-allocation conflicts (>100% of capacity), and dependencies with the schedule.
- Every competency gap has an action, owner, and date; each resource has a release criterion.
- Block of 2–3 resource risks with mitigation.
- Zero monetary cost figures; capacity expressed in FTE, hours, or person-months.
- Assumptions tagged [SUPUESTO] with impact; ambiguities resolved with questions, not invented.
Expected deliverable: document "Resource Management Plan — {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}}" in titled sections, with tables for RACI and calendar, ready for sponsor review.
spec-gestion-proyectos_planificacion-cap:
[inputs]
- PERFILES_Y_HORAS: {{PERFILES_Y_HORAS}} > Team profiles or roles and gross hours available per person/period (e.g., 2 developers 160h/month, 1 QA 160h/month)
- HORIZONTE_Y_PERIODO: {{HORIZONTE_Y_PERIODO}} > Planning horizon and period granularity (e.g., next 3 months in monthly periods; or 6 bi-weekly sprints)
- AUSENCIAS_Y_DEDICACION: {{AUSENCIAS_Y_DEDICACION}} > Vacations, holidays, recurring support/meetings, and project dedication factor by profile (e.g., QA at 60 percent, dev at 75 percent)
- DEMANDA_POR_INICIATIVA: {{DEMANDA_POR_INICIATIVA}} > Committed initiatives or deliverables with estimated effort by profile and the period in which they fall (e.g., Module A: 120h dev + 40h QA in period 1)
- PRIORIDADES_Y_RESTRICCIONES: {{PRIORIDADES_Y_RESTRICCIONES}} > (optional) Priority order, immovable committed dates, dependencies between initiatives, and hiring/onboarding-ramp limits
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Committing to dates without contrasting demand against real capacity leads to silent over-allocation, delays, and team burnout. This exercise produces a capacity plan that makes visible, by profile and by period, where demand exceeds supply and where slack exists, so leveling decisions can be made before promising dates rather than after missing them. The unit of analysis is the profile x period cell: the team may have aggregate slack and yet a specific profile may be saturated in a given period; averages lie, the cell does not.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior resource manager (capacity planner) in a PMO, with expertise in capacity planning, resource leveling, and the theory of constraints.
Deliverable: a capacity plan by profile and period. Steps:
1. Calculate net capacity per cell (profile x period): gross hours minus absences, meetings, and support, adjusted by the dedication factor (realistic effective availability 70–80 percent unless specific data is provided).
2. Consolidate demand per cell by summing the estimated effort of committed initiatives falling in each period and profile.
3. Build the net balance matrix = net capacity minus demand, per cell; classify each cell as over-allocated, balanced, or slack using an explicit threshold.
4. Identify the bottleneck profile-period and quantify the shortage or surplus in hours and percentage; also flag idle periods.
5. Propose prioritized leveling options (reschedule within the horizon, redistribute across profiles, adjust scope, or add capacity) with their impact on dates, assumption, and side effect.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Capacity: derive net hours per cell and keep the deductions and dedication factor visible. If a profile has multiple people, aggregate by profile but retain individual-level detail when a specific absence distorts it.
Phase 2 — Demand: map each initiative to profile and period; if an estimate lacks a profile breakdown, tag it [SUPUESTO] and state the allocation criterion. Distinguish committed demand from desired or tentative demand; only committed demand weighs in the baseline balance.
Phase 3 — Balance: cross both in a profile x period matrix with row and column totals. Default threshold: balanced between -10 and +10 percent of the cell's net capacity; over-allocated above, slack below (declare the threshold and adjust if specific data is provided).
Phase 4 — Diagnosis: name bottlenecks, idle periods, and the critical period of the horizon. Apply the constraint: a shortage in a bottleneck profile limits throughput even if other profiles have slack; do not compensate hours across non-interchangeable profiles.
Phase 5 — Leveling: translate the diagnosis into at least 3 actions with quantified impact on dates. Respect dependencies and immovable dates from PRIORIDADES_Y_RESTRICCIONES; if adding capacity implies onboarding, deduct the ramp (reduced capacity in the first weeks).
Edge case: if total committed demand for the horizon already exceeds total net capacity, declare it upfront: no internal leveling will suffice and the decision is escalated to scope, timeline, or capacity. Any data not provided is requested; nothing is invented. Tag assumptions with [SUPUESTO].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Net capacity justified: gross hours, deductions, and dedication factor are visible per cell.
- [ ] Complete profile x period matrix with net balance and row and column totals.
- [ ] Each cell classified as over-allocated / balanced / slack with an explicit threshold.
- [ ] Bottleneck identified and shortage quantified in hours and percentage; idle periods flagged.
- [ ] Committed demand distinguished from desired; constraint applied (no compensating across non-interchangeable profiles).
- [ ] At least 3 leveling options with impact on dates, assumption, and side effect; dependencies and immovable dates respected.
- [ ] If total demand exceeds total capacity, declared upfront as a scope/timeline/capacity decision.
- [ ] Assumptions tagged [SUPUESTO]; missing data requested, not invented.
Expected deliverable: capacity-vs-demand matrix by profile and period, bottleneck and slack diagnosis, and prioritized leveling plan with impact on dates.
spec-gestion-proyectos_histograma-recurs:
[inputs]
- EQUIPO: {{EQUIPO}} > People or roles to analyze, with a readable identifier (name, alias, or role). Allows the same person to appear across multiple projects
- CAPACIDAD_DISPONIBLE: {{CAPACIDAD_DISPONIBLE}} > Net capacity per person and period (hours or percentage of FTE) after deducting vacations, recurring meetings, and non-assignable time; always use net, never gross
- ASIGNACIONES: {{ASIGNACIONES}} > Tasks or projects assigned to each person with hours or dedication percentage and their start and end period
- HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL: {{HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL}} > Date range to cover (start and end)
- GRANULARIDAD: {{GRANULARIDAD}} > Histogram period unit: week, fortnight, or month
- UMBRALES_UTILIZACION: {{UMBRALES_UTILIZACION}} > (optional) Limits for under-utilized, optimal, and over-allocated; defaults: below 70 percent, 70 to 100 percent, above 100 percent
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Visualize the real workload of each team member over time to anticipate over-allocation (risk of delay, cost overrun, and burnout) and under-utilization (reassignable idle capacity). A well-built histogram unlocks leveling and smoothing decisions before committing to dates, and provides an objective basis for capacity conversations with the sponsor and functional leaders. Without a histogram you negotiate blind: over-allocation is discovered only when there is already a delay, and slack is wasted without reassignment.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior PMO Resource Manager, expert in capacity planning and in the resource optimization techniques of the project management standard: leveling (resource leveling, reschedules to avoid exceeding capacity and may move dates) and smoothing (resource smoothing, redistributes within float without touching milestones).

Deliverable: a resource assignment histogram with diagnosis and adjustment plan. Steps:
1. Validate inputs: if EQUIPO, CAPACIDAD_DISPONIBLE, ASIGNACIONES, HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL, or GRANULARIDAD are missing or ambiguous, request them explicitly before continuing; do not invent figures.
2. Normalize capacity and assignments to a common unit (hours or percentage of FTE) and declare it.
3. Calculate, per person and period, assigned workload, available capacity, and utilization percentage; aggregate totals by person and by period.
4. Render the histogram as a period x person table and as proportional text bars, with each cell's status according to UMBRALES_UTILIZACION.
5. List over-allocation peaks and under-utilization valleys with the tasks causing them and the excess or slack quantified.
6. Propose leveling and smoothing actions with period, affected person, moved task, and expected effect on utilization; flag which ones impact dates and milestones.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Normalization: convert all capacity and assignments to the same unit; consolidate by person and period. If a person appears in multiple projects, sum their total workload before judging utilization.
Phase 2 — Calculation: utilization = assigned workload / available capacity per cell; totals by person and by period. If net capacity is zero or negative in a period (full absence), do not calculate a percentage and mark the cell as unavailable.
Phase 3 — Visualization: matrix table + proportional text bars; code status (under-utilized, optimal, over-allocated) per thresholds.
Phase 4 — Diagnosis: identify peaks and valleys, quantify excess or slack in the common unit, and trace the tasks causing them.
Phase 5 — Optimization: leveling (reschedule tasks to avoid exceeding capacity, accepting possible impact on dates) and smoothing (redistribute within float without moving milestones); quantify the effect of each action and prioritize by urgency (peak magnitude) and effect (utilization recovered).
Edge cases: task with no clear period = mark as unplaceable and exclude from the calculation, declaring it; always work with net capacity, not gross. Tag with [SUPUESTO] any figure estimated due to authorized missing data. Do not report prices or monetary costs; reason in capacity, time, and dedication.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] All capacity and assignments are in a declared common unit and are net capacity.
- [ ] The workload of anyone appearing in multiple projects is consolidated before judging utilization.
- [ ] Each cell shows workload, capacity, and utilization percentage; periods with no net capacity are marked as unavailable.
- [ ] Each cell's status respects UMBRALES_UTILIZACION.
- [ ] Each over-allocation peak indicates person, period, quantified excess, and causing tasks.
- [ ] Each under-utilization valley indicates available slack quantified.
- [ ] Actions distinguish leveling from smoothing, quantify the effect on utilization, and flag which ones impact dates and milestones.
- [ ] Actions are prioritized by urgency and effect.
- [ ] Estimated figures are tagged [SUPUESTO]; no invented data or monetary figures.
Expected deliverable: period x person histogram (table + text bars) with a diagnosis section for peaks and valleys traced to their tasks and an adjustment plan with prioritized leveling and smoothing actions.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-staffing-ram:
[inputs]
- PROYECTO_Y_HORIZONTE: {{PROYECTO_Y_HORIZONTE}} > Project name, objective, and total time horizon (e.g., 9 months, May 2026 to Jan 2027)
- FASES_HITOS: {{FASES_HITOS}} > Phases with their durations and key milestones that trigger workload changes
- ROLES_PERFILES: {{ROLES_PERFILES}} > Required roles and profiles (seniority, specialty) and, if known, their intensity by phase
- LEAD_TIMES: {{LEAD_TIMES}} > Recruitment/assignment and onboarding lead time by role (e.g., senior backend: 6 weeks) (optional)
- RESTRICCIONES_CAPACIDAD: {{RESTRICCIONES_CAPACIDAD}} > FTE cap, available talent pool, shared with other projects, or seasonality (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I am planning the human resources of a project and need people to join and leave following the real demand profile, not a flat-team assumption. A solid staffing plan and ramp curve unlocks: committing to milestones with realistic capacity, avoiding over-staffing (people assigned without useful work) and under-staffing (bottlenecks that delay deliveries), anticipating recruitment with enough lead time, and giving the PMO and the sponsor a defensible month-by-month view of demand vs. capacity. The plan must be auditable: every demand level and every entry or exit date is justified, not asserted.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior PMO Resource Manager, expert in capacity planning, resource leveling, and project team ramp curves (ramp-up/ramp-down).

Deliverable: a staffing plan with ramp curve. Produce, in order:
1. Monthly demand curve by role derived from FASES_HITOS, in FTE or person-months, justifying why each phase requires that level and flagging peaks and valleys. State the unit and the assumed hours/month per FTE.
2. Ramp-up plan: target incorporation month by role, working backward from the need using LEAD_TIMES (recruitment + onboarding) and applying a learning curve (reduced productivity in the first weeks; declare the assumed factor, e.g., 50% weeks 1–2, 80% weeks 3–4).
3. Ramp-down plan: when and how to release or rotate each person as demand drops, with a knowledge-preservation mechanism (handover, documentation, exit overlap) and the overlap duration.
4. Month-by-month table: planned demand vs. available capacity by role, a gap column (shortage/surplus in FTE), and a corrective action, respecting RESTRICCIONES_CAPACIDAD. Distinguish nominal from effective capacity (deduct vacations, holidays, and fragmentation due to partial dedication).
5. Staffing risks (key person, long lead time, talent seasonality, shared-pool dependency, unplanned turnover) with a concrete mitigation and an activation trigger.
6. Explicit assumptions tagged [SUPUESTO] wherever information is missing.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpret demand: translate phases, milestones, and profiles into a role x month demand matrix in FTE; identify peaks and valleys and the critical personnel path (the role whose absence blocks the milestone).
Phase 2 — Offset supply: apply lead times and learning curve to set entry dates prior to the need; plan exits with handover overlap. If a lead time makes covering a peak infeasible, flag the recruitment decision deadline.
Phase 3 — Level and contrast: build the demand-vs-capacity table, detect gaps, propose corrections (pull/push entries, redistribute assignment, smooth the curve, move work between months) without violating RESTRICCIONES_CAPACIDAD. State the trade-off of each correction (e.g., pulling forward = bench cost; pushing back = milestone risk).
Phase 4 — Risks and assumptions: list staffing risks with mitigation and trigger; consolidate [SUPUESTO]. Always reason in person-months, FTE, and assignment percentages; never in rates or prices. If a critical input is missing (phases/durations, milestones, roles, lead times, constraints), ask before continuing instead of inventing.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The demand curve derives explicitly from phases and milestones, with justified peaks/valleys and declared unit/hours-per-FTE.
- [ ] Each ramp-up date works backward from the need using lead time + onboarding and declares the learning curve factor.
- [ ] The ramp-down preserves critical knowledge (handover/overlap with duration), not just releases people.
- [ ] The month-by-month table shows demand, capacity (nominal vs. effective), gap, and corrective action by role.
- [ ] Each correction states its trade-off; none violates RESTRICCIONES_CAPACIDAD.
- [ ] Staffing risks include a concrete mitigation and an activation trigger.
- [ ] All reasoning in FTE/person-months/percentages; zero rates or prices.
- [ ] Information gaps are tagged [SUPUESTO] or converted into questions.
Expected deliverable: staffing plan with demand curve by role, ramp-up and ramp-down plan, month-by-month demand-vs-capacity table with gaps and actions, and risk and assumptions log, ready for review with the sponsor and PMO.
spec-gestion-proyectos_matriz-habilidade:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_PROYECTO: {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} > Name or code of the project to which the team belongs
- ALCANCE_Y_ENTREGABLES: {{ALCANCE_Y_ENTREGABLES}} > Scope, key deliverables, and phases with their dates or sequence
- INTEGRANTES_Y_EXPERIENCIA: {{INTEGRANTES_Y_EXPERIENCIA}} > List of team members with role, seniority, and relevant experience per person
- HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL: {{HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL}} > Project window and upcoming milestones that condition the urgency of gap closure
- ESCALA_DOMINIO: {{ESCALA_DOMINIO}} > (optional) Mastery scale to use; default 0 none / 1 awareness / 2 supervised application / 3 autonomous / 4 expert-mentor
- PREFERENCIA_ESTRATEGIA: {{PREFERENCIA_ESTRATEGIA}} > (optional) Bias toward train, borrow, or hire and constraints (hiring freeze, mentor availability, shared dedication)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The delivery of {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} depends on the team having the right competencies at the right time. When skills gaps are discovered late, they translate into rework, single-person dependency, and milestone slippage. Mapping required competencies against available ones before each phase unlocks early decisions on training, reinforcement, or hiring, and turns team capacity into a manageable variable rather than a surprise. This analysis feeds the resource plan, the RACI matrix, and the risk register, and serves as evidence to support team reinforcements with the sponsor.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project manager (PMP) and technical talent development specialist, with experience in team capacity planning and competency frameworks.
Deliver a skills matrix and an actionable gap analysis, following these steps:
1. Derive required competencies from {{ALCANCE_Y_ENTREGABLES}}, classifying them as technical, domain, and soft skills; flag which are critical to the delivery path and which deliverable or phase each one serves. Do not conflate concrete tools with capabilities: the tool is evidence of the competency, not the competency itself.
2. Define the required level per competency per {{ESCALA_DOMINIO}} and record each team member's current level from {{INTEGRANTES_Y_EXPERIENCIA}}. With ambiguous experience, assign the conservative level and record the reason; do not inflate levels based on seniority alone.
3. Build the people x competencies matrix; per cell, show current, required, and gap (required minus current, truncated to zero for closing purposes), and per column, coverage (number of people who reach or exceed the required level). Distinguish nominal coverage (at least one person reaches it) from resilient coverage (at least two).
4. Identify critical gaps: zero coverage, single point of failure (only one person covers a critical competency), or overloading (one person is the sole source of multiple critical competencies simultaneously). Prioritize them by the proximity of the dependent deliverable within {{HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL}}.
5. Propose a closing plan per gap with a train / borrow / hire strategy aligned with {{PREFERENCIA_ESTRATEGIA}}: owner, concrete action, horizon, verifiable success signal, and relative effort indicator (low/medium/high). When the deliverable horizon is shorter than the plausible training time, recommend borrowing or hiring as a bridge and training in parallel. Never include prices or monetary costs.
6. Close with a capacity risk map (gap, impact, probability, trigger, mitigation linked to the closing plan) and the list of decisions requiring escalation to the sponsor or committee, each with the specific question to be resolved.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Framing: confirm scope, deliverables by phase, team members, and the mastery scale; if any of the four mandatory inputs is missing, request it before continuing. Do not invent competencies, team members, or levels; tag each inference with [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 — Requirements: derive and classify competencies and set required levels linked to deliverables.
Phase 3 — Inventory: record current levels per person from the provided experience, with a conservative and traceable criterion.
Phase 4 — Analysis: calculate gaps and coverage, detect single points of failure and overloading, and prioritize by criticality and urgency.
Phase 5 — Plan: design the train-borrow-hire closure, adjust bridges when time is insufficient, and consolidate the risk map and escalation decisions.
Edge case: if the team is too small to avoid all single points of failure, state this explicitly and present the capacity decision to the sponsor rather than forcing a fictitious coverage.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each competency is classified (technical / domain / soft) and linked to a specific deliverable or phase, without conflating tool with capability.
- [ ] Every critical competency is flagged and justified by its effect on the delivery path.
- [ ] The matrix uses a single consistent mastery scale; each cell shows current, required, and gap.
- [ ] Coverage per competency is calculated and distinguishes nominal from resilient; single points of failure and overloading are flagged.
- [ ] Each critical gap has a closing plan with strategy (train/borrow/hire), owner, horizon, verifiable success signal, and relative effort; cases with insufficient time propose a bridge.
- [ ] The risk map links each risk to its mitigation in the closing plan; each escalation includes the decision question.
- [ ] No prices, monetary costs, or the word "free" appear anywhere.
- [ ] Assumptions are tagged [SUPUESTO] and missing data was requested, not invented.
Expected deliverable: people x competencies matrix with gaps and coverage, prioritized list of critical gaps, train-borrow-hire closing plan, and capacity risk map with escalation decisions, in a format ready to integrate into the project resource plan.
spec-gestion-proyectos_modelo-desarrollo:
[inputs]
- EQUIPO_Y_CONTEXTO: {{EQUIPO_Y_CONTEXTO}} > Size, team tenure, modality (in-person/remote/hybrid), project type and stage in the life cycle
- SENALES_OBSERVABLES: {{SENALES_OBSERVABLES}} > Observed behaviors: climate, nature of conflicts, role clarity, leader dependency, autonomy, quality and pace of deliverables
- ESTILO_LIDERAZGO_ACTUAL: {{ESTILO_LIDERAZGO_ACTUAL}} > How the person managing the team leads today (directive, persuasive/coaching, participatory, delegating)
- OBJETIVO_CRITICO: {{OBJETIVO_CRITICO}} > Upcoming deliverable or milestone that demands team performance
- HORIZONTE_TIEMPO: {{HORIZONTE_TIEMPO}} > Available window to reach the required performance level (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A project team goes through maturation phases before performing at its peak; forcing results without reading the correct phase produces friction, rework, and turnover. The most costly mistake is applying the wrong leadership style for the phase: giving autonomy to a team that has not yet established norms, or micromanaging one that is already mature. Accurately diagnosing the point in the Tuckman model unlocks the central leadership decision: which style to apply and what to intervene on now to accelerate the path to high performance before the next critical milestone.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior high-performance team facilitator and project leadership coach, expert in Bruce Tuckman's group development model (Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing, Adjourning) and in situational leadership (Hersey-Blanchard: directing, coaching, supporting, delegating).

Deliverable: a phase diagnosis with an actionable intervention plan. Produce:
1. Phase diagnosis: place the team in a primary phase and, if the evidence supports it, a transition phase (e.g., Storming -> Norming), justified with concrete behaviors extracted from SENALES_OBSERVABLES, not with generalizations. If two adjacent phases are compatible with the evidence, declare the ambiguity and name the data that would resolve it instead of forcing a conclusion.
2. Phase reading: what is normal and expected behavior, what is an alarm signal requiring action, and what is the concrete risk of stagnating in that phase.
3. Intervention plan: 4 to 6 leadership actions to advance to the next phase; each with what to do, responsible party, observable success signal, and suggested time horizon. Align the recommended style to the phase (more directive/structuring in Forming-Storming; more participatory/delegating in Norming-Performing) and contrast with ESTILO_LIDERAZGO_ACTUAL naming the gap to close.
4. Progress signals: 3 to 5 observable and verifiable indicators that confirm the move to the next phase, tied to OBJETIVO_CRITICO and HORIZONTE_TIEMPO.
5. Regression risks: events that can push the team back to a previous phase (turnover, addition of a member, scope change, new leader, unresolved conflict, schedule pressure), each with its mitigation.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: read EQUIPO_Y_CONTEXTO and SENALES_OBSERVABLES; if key data for diagnosis is missing (size, tenure, conflicts, role clarity, modality, leader dependency), ask before continuing. Do not invent absent signals; mark assumptions as [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 - Diagnosis: map each observed signal to its corresponding Tuckman criterion (orientation/dependency, conflict/positioning, cohesion/norms, productivity/autonomy, closure/disengagement) and derive the phase with traceable signal-by-signal evidence.
Phase 3 - Intervention design: select actions and leadership style consistent with the phase and with the gap against ESTILO_LIDERAZGO_ACTUAL; prioritize by impact on phase advancement and proximity to OBJETIVO_CRITICO.
Phase 4 - Closure: define progress signals and regression risks tied to OBJETIVO_CRITICO and HORIZONTE_TIEMPO.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The assigned phase is justified with concrete signals from SENALES_OBSERVABLES, not with generic statements.
- [ ] Each observed signal was mapped to an explicit Tuckman criterion.
- [ ] The transition phase is named only if the evidence supports it; ambiguity between two phases is declared with the data that would resolve it.
- [ ] Each intervention has what to do, responsible party, success signal, and time horizon.
- [ ] The recommended leadership style corresponds to the phase and is contrasted with the current one naming the gap.

--- S | SITUATION ---
A poorly designed recognition plan reinforces the wrong behaviors: it rewards visible results and ignores the person who flags a risk on time or unblocks a colleague. The purpose is to design incentives and recognition aligned to the behaviors that sustain a healthy team and a project that delivers. A good plan raises engagement, retains talent, and makes observable what would otherwise go unnoticed. A deliberate, equitable, and sustainable system of reinforcement is unlocked — not isolated gestures. Underlying risk: poorly calibrated recognition erodes intrinsic motivation (overjustification effect) or generates perceptions of favoritism; the design must protect against both.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project leader and evidence-based team motivation specialist (Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory: autonomy, competence, and relatedness; Daniel Pink's intrinsic motivation: autonomy, mastery, and purpose; behavioral reinforcement).
Deliverable: an actionable recognition and motivation plan. Steps:
1. Based on COMPORTAMIENTOS_DESEADOS and EQUIPO_Y_CONTEXTO, define 4 to 6 concrete behaviors to reinforce; if there is a problem to correct, frame the desired substitute behavior, not the prohibition.
2. For each behavior, specify an observable signal that demonstrates it occurred, avoiding gameable metrics or ones that reward individualism at the expense of the team; name the failure mode each signal could induce.
3. Propose a repertoire of recognition differentiated by effort and visibility: immediate micro-recognition, peer-to-peer, from the leader in ceremonies, and formal recognition before stakeholders; balance public and private according to the person and justify the mix.
4. Assign cadence (in the moment, weekly in the retro, per milestone) and responsible party to each, anchored to CADENCIA_Y_CEREMONIAS and respecting MEDIOS_Y_RESTRICCIONES.
5. Consolidate a behavior - signal - recognition - cadence - responsible party matrix.
6. List 3 anti-patterns to avoid and 3 indicators to evaluate whether the plan is working, with their reading and alert threshold.
7. Deliver a 30-day launch plan (what to activate first, what to observe, when to recalibrate).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: confirm team, context, and priority behaviors; mark as [SUPUESTO] any data not provided and ask for the minimum missing before proceeding.
Phase 2 Design: map each behavior to its observable signal and to the most proportional type of recognition, caring for autonomy, competence, and relatedness; avoid overjustifying what is already intrinsic.
Phase 3 Operation: define cadence, responsible parties, and anti-gaming safeguards; verify equity across roles, introverted/extroverted profiles, and remote/in-person modality.
Phase 4 Measurement: define the 3 indicators, their reading, alert threshold, and recalibration cycle.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- 4 to 6 concrete and observable behaviors, not vague traits; problems reformulated as desired behavior.
- Each signal is verifiable and resistant to gaming; none rewards individualism at the expense of the team; failure mode named.
- Recognition differentiated by effort and visibility; justified public/private mix sensitive to the person's profile.
- Each row in the matrix has clear cadence and responsible party, anchored to the ceremonies and within the given constraints.
- 3 anti-patterns and 3 indicators present, specific, and with reading/threshold.
- 30-day launch plan present.
- Assumptions marked [SUPUESTO]; no invented data about the team.

--- S | SITUATION ---
A distributed team loses hours to crossed time zones, decisions that dissolve in chat, and unwritten response-time expectations that generate friction and burnout. This working agreement (team working agreement) converts those implicit rules into a living and explicit contract: it unlocks decisions asynchronously, protects individual focus, and eliminates ambiguity about when, where, and how the {{NOMBRE_EQUIPO}} team communicates. It serves as the single onboarding reference and as the basis for continuous improvement in every retrospective.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior facilitator of distributed teams, with experience in remote agile frameworks, team working agreement design, and follow-the-sun coordination.
Deliverable: a Working Agreement ready to review, vote on, and sign. Produce, in this order:
1. Time-zone map: table of {{INTEGRANTES_Y_HUSOS}} with city, zone, and schedule from {{HORARIOS_LABORALES}}, and the calculated common overlap window expressed in {{ZONA_REFERENCIA}} (start time, end time, and total hours/minutes).
2. Synchronous window: protected hours for live meetings and decisions within the overlap, with the rituals from {{RITUALES_CADENCIA}} (purpose, duration, cadence, and time in {{ZONA_REFERENCIA}}). Mark which rituals can become async without losing value.
3. Tools by purpose: assign a single channel from {{HERRAMIENTAS}} to each type of communication (ephemeral chat, decisions and documentation, video, task management, code or deliverables) to avoid duplicated conversations.
4. Asynchronous rules: expected response times by channel and priority, criterion for what is resolved async versus synchronous, message format (context + question + deadline), and where decisions are recorded so they are traceable.
5. Coexistence rules: right to disconnect, notification-free windows, definition of real urgency and its exclusive channel, working language, and mechanism to update the agreement itself.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: confirm {{INTEGRANTES_Y_HUSOS}}, {{HORARIOS_LABORALES}}, {{HERRAMIENTAS}}, and {{RITUALES_CADENCIA}}. If any piece of data is missing or ambiguous, ask before drafting; do not invent time zones or names and mark any gap as [SUPUESTO] only if the user authorizes proceeding.
Phase 2 - Plan: calculate the overlap window in {{ZONA_REFERENCIA}} and propose the skeleton of the five blocks. If the overlap is less than two hours, warn of the risk and suggest an async-first model with written decisions and handoffs between zones; if there is no overlap, propose a follow-the-sun rhythm by documented relay.
Phase 3 - Execute: draft the full agreement in clear language, with tables for time zones and tools, and rules in actionable and verifiable sentences. Close with the adoption checklist and validity criterion.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- The overlap window is calculated and expressed in {{ZONA_REFERENCIA}} with start, end, and total — not just described.
- Each type of communication has a single assigned channel; there are no overlaps or channels without a purpose.
- Each asynchronous rule is verifiable: specific response time, priority, and format — not generic.
- The right to disconnect and the definition of real urgency are explicit and separate, with a single urgency channel.
- If the overlap is less than two hours, the agreement warns of this and explicitly adopts an async-first model.
- No time zone, name, or tool was invented: everything comes from the inputs or from an authorized [SUPUESTO].

--- S | SITUATION ---
The project {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} needs a Quality Management Plan that the sponsor can approve and the team can operate from day one. A clear plan unlocks unambiguous acceptance criteria, reduces rework, aligns the team on what "done with quality" means, and enables auditing deliverables in a traceable manner against requirements. Without it, quality becomes subjective, defects are detected late and at high cost, and the cost of non-quality escalates out of control.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: PMP-certified Project Quality Manager, grounded in the PMBOK Guide 7 (Delivery domain and quality models) and ISO 9001, with experience in quality assurance and control in technology and services projects.

Deliverable: an actionable Quality Management Plan with these sections in order:
1. Quality objectives: policies and expected outcomes, aligned with the objectives of the project {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} and sponsor expectations; name the cost of non-quality to be avoided.
2. Applicable standards and norms: list based on {{ESTANDARES_APLICABLES}}, with the reason for inclusion and the specific clause or requirement from each.
3. Quality metrics (table): for each deliverable or critical attribute from {{ENTREGABLES_CRITICOS}} define the metric, measurement formula or method, baseline if it exists, acceptance threshold, measurement frequency, responsible party, and data source.
4. Roles and responsibilities (RACI matrix): for defining standards, reviewing, approving, auditing, and correcting, using {{ROLES_EQUIPO}}; exactly one Approver (A) per row.
5. Quality assurance (QA): preventive, process-oriented processes and audits, with cadence and triggers.
6. Quality control (QC): inspections, tests, and reviews against acceptance criteria, with control points, records, and sampling calibrated to {{TOLERANCIA_DEFECTOS}}.
7. Non-conformance management and continuous improvement: log, severity classification, escalation, closure criteria, and the plan-do-check-act cycle.
8. Tools and records: dashboards, checklists, and logs, with where they live and who maintains them.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm scope, critical deliverables, and constraints; mark every inference with [SUPUESTO]; if the project type, critical deliverables, regulatory sector, or defect tolerance is missing, ask before drafting.
Phase 2 - QA/QC distinction: explicitly separate assurance (process, preventive) from control (deliverable, verification), without confusing or duplicating them.
Phase 3 - Traceability: link every metric and control point to a requirement or acceptance criterion, so nothing is left orphaned and no requirement is left without a metric.
Phase 4 - Criticality calibration: adjust the rigor of sampling, thresholds, and frequency to {{TOLERANCIA_DEFECTOS}} (life/safety requires full inspection and zero defects; experimental allows sampling and tolerant thresholds).
Phase 5 - Operability: ensure every activity has a responsible party, cadence, and record; verify RACI coherence (a single A per row, at least one R per activity).
Edge cases: with no applicable standards, explicitly state that control is based on internal acceptance criteria. If the roles are insufficient to segregate who executes from who approves, flag this as a governance risk.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] QA and QC are clearly differentiated (process vs. deliverable).
- [ ] Each metric has a formula/method, threshold, frequency, responsible party, and data source.
- [ ] The RACI matrix has exactly one Approver (A) and at least one Responsible (R) per row.
- [ ] Each metric and control point is traceable to a requirement or acceptance criterion; no critical requirement is left without a metric.
- [ ] QC rigor is calibrated to the declared defect tolerance.
- [ ] The continuous improvement cycle and the non-conformance flow are defined from start to closure, with severity and closure criteria.
- [ ] Every inference is marked with [SUPUESTO].
Expected deliverable: document structured in the 8 sections, with metrics table and RACI matrix ready for sponsor review and team operation.

--- S | SITUATION ---
The project {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} ({{TIPO_PROYECTO}}) needs to govern quality with evidence and not with perception. A quality metrics dashboard converts defects, rework, and conformance into actionable signals with alert thresholds, so the team intervenes before a problem escalates to a rejected delivery, cost overrun, or leak to production. It unlocks deliverable acceptance decisions, data-driven steering conversations, and measurable continuous improvement cycle by cycle. Without a dashboard, quality is discussed anecdotally and problems are detected late and at high cost.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project quality assurance manager, with mastery of PMBOK quality management, ISO 9001, and cost of quality (COQ).
Deliverable: a one-page quality metrics dashboard, ready to operate in cycle {{CICLO_MEDICION}}, prioritizing {{FAMILIAS_PRIORITARIAS}}.
1. Define the indicator catalog covering defects (defect density, defects by severity, defect leakage to production), rework (rework rate, rework effort as % of total effort), and conformance (deliverable conformance rate, cost of non-quality). 2. For each indicator specify: what it measures and why it matters, explicit formula, unit, data source and capture responsible party, frequency.

Phase 2 - Catalog: write each indicator with its full profile (definition, formula, unit, source, responsible party, frequency, direction).
Phase 3 - Thresholds: calibrate green/amber/red against {{METAS_CALIDAD}}, separating real data from [SUPUESTO]; define the trend rule.
Phase 4 - Governance: map response action and escalation owner by color, including the trend trigger.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
