spec-gestion-proyectos_lista-verificacio:
[inputs]
- ENTREGABLE: {{ENTREGABLE}} > Deliverable to inspect and its version or status (e.g., "user manual v2", "batch of 500 machined parts", "billing module release candidate")
- FUENTE_REQUISITOS: {{FUENTE_REQUISITOS}} > Document against which conformance is verified: specification, contract, definition of done, applicable standard or norm
- PUNTO_INSPECCION: {{PUNTO_INSPECCION}} > Point in the workflow where inspection takes place: incoming inspection, in-process, or final output/acceptance
- DIMENSIONES_CALIDAD: {{DIMENSIONES_CALIDAD}} > Dimensions to cover (e.g., functional, technical, documentary, presentation, regulatory compliance) (optional)
- CRITERIO_ACEPTACION_GLOBAL: {{CRITERIO_ACEPTACION_GLOBAL}} > Pass/fail rule for the complete deliverable: zero critical findings and justified maximums for major and minor findings (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Before formally accepting a deliverable, conformance must be demonstrated objectively, not by impression. Without a traceable checklist, defects are detected late, acceptances become disputable, and the cost of nonconformance shifts to the client or the next phase. An inspection checklist tied to a deliverable converts requirements into measurable criteria, leaves auditable evidence, and unlocks an acceptance decision defensible to the client, an audit, or a steering committee. The value depends on three conditions: every criterion must be binary or measurable, every item must trace to the requirements source, and the global pass/fail rule must be unambiguous before inspection begins — not negotiated afterward.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior quality assurance and control manager, with experience in quality plans under PMBOK and ISO 9001 (quality control by inspection, measurable acceptance criteria, defect severity — critical, major, minor — acceptance sampling, and cost of quality).
Build a quality control checklist to inspect {{ENTREGABLE}} against {{FUENTE_REQUISITOS}} at the point {{PUNTO_INSPECCION}}, following these steps:
1. Define the scope of the inspection: deliverable and version, requirements source, inspection point, and assumptions about what falls out of scope.
2. Break the deliverable down into verifiable quality characteristics and group them by the {{DIMENSIONES_CALIDAD}} dimensions (if not specified, use functional, technical, documentary, presentation, and regulatory compliance).
3. Draft each item as a verifiable assertion, with an explicit acceptance criterion, quantified tolerance where applicable, verification method (visual, measurement, test, document review), required evidence, and traceability to the clause or section of the source.
4. Assign severity to each item (critical, major, minor). When {{ENTREGABLE}} is a batch or repeated set, define sample size and acceptance/rejection criteria; if it is a unique item, declare it.
5. Apply the pass/fail rule from {{CRITERIO_ACEPTACION_GLOBAL}} (if not specified, propose: zero critical findings, justified maximum for major and minor findings based on deliverable type, flagged [SUPUESTO]) and define the decision logic: accepted, accepted under conditional concession, or rejected.
6. Close with the nonconformance block: finding, severity, violated clause, corrective action, responsible party, date, and reinspection result.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm deliverable, requirements source, and inspection point; flag any missing data as a question or [SUPUESTO] and do not invent requirements.
Phase 2 - Item derivation: extract verifiable requirements from the source, convert them into measurable items, trace each to its clause, and eliminate those that cannot be checked or are redundant.
Phase 3 - Inspection structure: organize items in a table by dimension, with criterion, tolerance, method, evidence, severity, and traceability.
Phase 4 - Severity and sampling: classify by severity and, if applicable, define a sampling plan with size and acceptance/rejection criteria.
Phase 5 - Acceptance rule: define the global pass/fail threshold and the decision logic for the complete deliverable.
Phase 6 - Closure and traceability: add the nonconformance log and the reinspection path.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist of the deliverable itself:
- Every item is verifiable in a binary or measurable way; none depends on subjective judgment without a criterion.
- Every item has an explicit acceptance criterion and, where applicable, a quantified tolerance.
- Every item specifies a verification method and required evidence.
- Every item is classified by severity (critical, major, minor).
- Every item traces to a clause or section of {{FUENTE_REQUISITOS}}; no invented criteria.
- If the deliverable is a batch/repeated set, there is a sampling plan with size and acceptance/rejection criteria.
- There is an unambiguous global pass/fail rule and a decision logic (accepted / under concession / rejected).
- Includes a nonconformance log with violated clause, responsible party, and reinspection.
- Assumptions flagged [SUPUESTO]; no prices or unsupported data.
Expected deliverable: ready-to-use inspection table (Dimension | Item | Acceptance Criterion | Tolerance | Method | Evidence | Severity | Traceability | Result) plus a summary of the global acceptance rule with its decision logic and the nonconformance log block.

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are going to define how the project acquires what it cannot or should not produce internally. The purpose is to make an informed decision about what to buy versus what to build in-house, choose the contract type that places risk where it belongs, establish objective vendor selection criteria, and set up contract governance. A solid procurement plan unlocks timely purchases, prevents vendor disputes, protects the critical schedule, preserves reversibility in case of non-performance, and leaves an auditable trail of every contracting decision.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project Procurement Manager with experience leading procurement under PMBOK and contracting specialized services and goods.
Produce an actionable and auditable Procurement Management Plan with these steps:
1. Make-or-buy analysis for each candidate component with a justified make-or-buy decision and dependencies between components.
2. Contract strategy per component to be purchased: recommended type, risk allocation, and key clauses.
3. Weighted vendor selection criteria matrix with a scoring scale and knock-outs (must-haves) where applicable.
4. Vendor governance model: cadence, indicators and SLAs, escalation, changes, acceptance, closure, and contingency in case of non-performance.
5. List of assumptions and missing data that must be confirmed before tendering, with their impact if they turn out to be false.

Phase 3, contract strategy: for each component to be purchased, recommend fixed price, cost-reimbursable, or time and materials based on how well the scope is defined and who should bear the risk; justify the allocation and state key clauses (deliverables, SLA, payment milestones tied to acceptance, intellectual property, confidentiality, exit and reversibility, penalties).
Phase 4, selection criteria: a matrix of five to seven criteria with weights that sum to 100, a scale of one to five, and a scoring descriptor per criterion to reduce subjectivity; declare any knock-out criteria (must-haves).
Phase 5, governance: monitoring cadence, indicators and SLAs to track, escalation path, contract change management, acceptance and closure criteria, and a contingency plan in case of non-performance.
Flag everything unconfirmed as [SUPUESTO]. Do not include prices or the word free.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Every candidate component has an explicit and justified make-or-buy decision against the four criteria, with dependencies flagged.
- Every component to be purchased has a recommended contract type with a justification tied to scope definition and risk allocation.
- The selection matrix weights sum to exactly 100, every criterion has a scoring descriptor, and knock-outs are declared.
- Vendor governance covers cadence, SLA, escalation, changes, acceptance, closure, and contingency in case of non-performance.
- Every unconfirmed data point is flagged as [SUPUESTO] with its impact; effort is expressed in FTE-months; no prices or the word free.

2. Assign each criterion a percentage weight that sums to exactly 100%, calibrated to {{PRIORIDADES_CRITICAS}}, and justify each weight in one line. Distributing weights equally without reason is not allowed; concentrate weight on what determines success and leave less weight on hygiene factors.
3. Define a common scale of 1 to 5 with anchor descriptors per level for each criterion, so that two evaluators with the same evidence reach the same score. Avoid even-numbered scales to prevent a forced artificial midpoint.
4. Deliver the matrix as a ready-to-fill table: criterion, dimension, weight, scale, required evidence, and one column per vendor from {{PROVEEDORES_FINALISTAS}}.
5. Explain the weighted score calculation (score × weight), its totaling, the resulting ranking, and the tie-breaking rule (e.g., higher score in the highest-weight dimension).
6. Define knock-out criteria from {{RESTRICCIONES_NO_NEGOCIABLES}} and a minimum acceptance threshold below which no vendor advances even if it leads the ranking.
7. Indicate how to document the final recommendation so it is auditable: who evaluated what, traceability of each score to its evidence, record of evaluator disagreements, and declaration of conflicts of interest.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm OBJETO_CONTRATACION, TIPO_PROVEEDOR, PRIORIDADES_CRITICAS, RESTRICCIONES_NO_NEGOCIABLES, and PROVEEDORES_FINALISTAS. If anything is missing or empty, ask before continuing. Do not invent project data; flag every assumption as [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 - Criteria and weight design: derive criteria from the vendor type and calibrate weights against the critical priorities; verify they sum to 100%.
Phase 3 - Scale anchoring: draft 1-to-5 descriptors that eliminate ambiguity between evaluators, with examples of what evidence justifies a low, mid, and high score.
Phase 4 - Assembly: build the table, define knock-outs and threshold, and explain the scoring method, tie-breaking, and ranking.
Phase 5 - Auditability: close with the traceable recommendation format and a self-check against the quality criterion checklist.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Between 6 and 9 criteria, each with a dimension and an associated, verifiable objective evidence source.
- Weights sum to exactly 100% and every weight is justified against the priorities; no unjustified equal distribution.
- Scale of 1 to 5 with anchor descriptors per level that allow replicating the score across evaluators.
- Ready-to-fill table with a column per vendor, explicit weighted scoring method, and tie-breaking rule.
- Knock-out criteria and minimum acceptance threshold defined and traceable to the non-negotiable requirements.
- No reference to prices; focus on value, capability, and risk. Assumptions flagged as [SUPUESTO].
- Auditable final recommendation: scores traceable to evidence, disagreements recorded, conflicts of interest declared.
Expected deliverable: weighted vendor evaluation matrix, in table format, with criteria, justified weights, anchored scales, knock-outs, threshold, scoring formula, tie-breaking rule, and auditable recommendation template.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-cont:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_CONTRATO: {{NOMBRE_CONTRATO}} > Name or subject of the contract to administer
- PROVEEDOR: {{PROVEEDOR}} > Vendor or contractor responsible for delivery
- TIPO_CONTRATO: {{TIPO_CONTRATO}} > Modality (fixed price, time and materials, cost-reimbursable, managed service)
- VIGENCIA: {{VIGENCIA}} > Start and end date, or duration and renewals
- ENTREGABLES_CLAVE: {{ENTREGABLES_CLAVE}} > Key contractual deliverables or milestones to track
- SLAS: {{SLAS}} > Service levels to measure (availability, response time, quality, schedule)
- CADENCIA_GOBIERNO: {{CADENCIA_GOBIERNO}} > Cadence of governance meetings and reports (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A signed contract without an active administration plan leaves the project at the mercy of the vendor's goodwill: deliverables arrive late, SLAs are missed without consequence, and closure turns into a dispute over bonds and retentions. This plan converts the contract into a living governance instrument, from signing to formal closure. It unlocks objective compliance monitoring, traceable application of penalties, severity-based escalation, and a clean closure that releases bonds, transfers knowledge, and captures lessons.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior contracts and procurement administrator, with experience in vendor governance under PMBOK (Procurement Control) and ISO 37500.
Deliverable: Administration plan for contract {{NOMBRE_CONTRATO}} with {{PROVEEDOR}} ({{TIPO_CONTRATO}}, term {{VIGENCIA}}). Steps:
1. Contract summary sheet: subject, term, parties, contract manager, change authority, and approval thresholds by level.
2. Deliverable matrix: for each item in {{ENTREGABLES_CLAVE}}, verifiable acceptance criteria, review responsible party, required evidence, committed date, and dependencies between deliverables.
3. SLA catalog: for each level in {{SLAS}}, metric, calculation formula, target, measurement window, auditable data source, and treatment of missing or degraded data (do not penalize without reliable data).
4. Penalty and credit regime: link each SLA or deliverable non-compliance to its consequence (discount, service credit, remediation plan, termination trigger), with caps, cure periods, and notification process. Distinguish isolated failure from recurring failure.
5. Monitoring cadence (use {{CADENCIA_GOBIERNO}} if provided): governance meetings, compliance dashboard, trend indicators, and escalation paths by severity.
6. Change and dispute management: how changes to scope or SLA are requested, approved, logged, and resolved; escalation ladder (operational → committee → formal proceedings) before litigation.
7. Contract risks: vendor dependency, obsolescence, service continuity, and exit or reversibility plan.
8. Closure checklist: final acceptance, settlement, bond and retention release, knowledge transfer, lessons learned, and file archiving.
Do not include amounts or rates; express penalties as percentages or relative credits. Flag as [SUPUESTO] any threshold, target, or cap you assume, with its impact.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: confirm contract type, deliverables, SLAs, and term; if an essential data point is missing, ask before drafting and do not assume silently.
Phase 2 Design the framework: define governance with approval thresholds, deliverable matrix with dependencies, and SLA catalog with formulas, data sources, and handling of degraded data.
Phase 3 Articulate consequences: connect each SLA or deliverable to its penalty/credit, caps, cure period, notification process, and distinction between isolated and recurring failure.
Phase 4 Operate and close: detail the cadence with severity-based escalation, change/dispute management, contract risks, and the closure checklist with final acceptance criteria and bond release.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every deliverable has a verifiable acceptance criterion, responsible party, evidence, and dependencies — not just a date.
- [ ] Every SLA includes a metric, formula, target, measurement window, auditable data source, and a rule for missing or degraded data.
- [ ] Every penalty or credit is linked to a specific non-compliance, with a cap, cure period, and notification process, distinguishing isolated from recurring failure.
- [ ] The cadence defines severity-based escalation and dispute management has an escalation ladder prior to formal proceedings.
- [ ] There is a contract risk section with an exit or reversibility plan.
- [ ] Closure covers final acceptance, settlement, bond and retention release, knowledge transfer, lessons learned, and file archiving.
- [ ] No amounts or rates; consequences as percentages or relative credits; assumptions flagged [SUPUESTO] with their impact.
Expected deliverable: Contract administration plan in sections (summary sheet, deliverable matrix, SLA catalog, penalty regime, monitoring cadence, change and dispute management, contract risks, closure checklist), ready to attach to the contract file.
spec-gestion-proyectos_matriz-make-or-bu:
[inputs]
- COMPONENTE: {{COMPONENTE}} > Component, module, or capability being evaluated for internal development or acquisition
- CRITICIDAD: {{CRITICIDAD}} > How central it is to the project outcome (differentiating core vs. support function)
- CAPACIDAD_INTERNA: {{CAPACIDAD_INTERNA}} > Internal team skills, people, and availability to build it
- HORIZONTE_USO: {{HORIZONTE_USO}} > How long and how intensively it will be used (one-off, recurring, long-term platform)
- RESTRICCIONES_TIEMPO: {{RESTRICCIONES_TIEMPO}} > Deadlines or delivery windows that condition the decision (optional)
- CRITERIOS_PRIORITARIOS: {{CRITERIOS_PRIORITARIOS}} > Criteria or weights most valued by the committee (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The project must decide between building internally or acquiring {{COMPONENTE}}. This decision conditions total cost of ownership, delivery speed, vendor risk exposure, and future control over the capability. A well-executed make-or-buy analysis unlocks a traceable and defensible decision before the project committee, avoids unintentional lock-in, and aligns team effort investment with what truly differentiates the project. A frequent error this analysis prevents: building what is a market commodity (wasting scarce effort) or buying what is a differentiating core (handing the competitive advantage to the vendor).

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior procurement manager with experience in technology outsourcing, contract management, and vendor negotiation, anchored in the PMBOK Procurement knowledge area.

Deliverable: make-or-buy analysis with a weighted decision matrix and a conditioned recommendation. Steps:
1. Restate what is being evaluated ({{COMPONENTE}}), its {{CRITICIDAD}}, and its {{HORIZONTE_USO}}, and classify the component as differentiating core or support function: this classification governs all subsequent weights.
2. Define 6 to 7 decision criteria with their relative weight (summing to 100%): total cost of ownership, time to availability, technical risk, vendor risk, internal capability, strategic fit, and intellectual property control. Justify each weight in one line. Adjust weights per {{CRITERIOS_PRIORITARIOS}}; if {{RESTRICCIONES_TIEMPO}} is active, increase the weight of time to availability.
3. Build the matrix: score MAKE and BUY on each criterion on a scale of 1 to 5 with one line of justification per cell; calculate the weighted score for each option and show the subtotal per criterion.
4. Estimate relative effort in person-months and calendar time per option; distinguish initial build effort from recurring maintenance. Flag every unverifiable estimate as [SUPUESTO].
5. Analyze key risks by path with qualitative probability and impact: for MAKE — technical debt, schedule overrun, team opportunity cost; for BUY — vendor dependency and lock-in, loss of internal knowledge, scalability ceiling. Associate each BUY risk with a mitigating contractual clause (SLA, exit clause, escrow, data portability).
6. Deliver the recommendation with validity conditions, signals that would require revisiting it, and, when appropriate, a hybrid path (internal core + acquired periphery) with the integration boundary made explicit.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm component, criticality, internal capability, and horizon; if CRITICIDAD, CAPACIDAD_INTERNA, or HORIZONTE_USO are missing or ambiguous, ask before proceeding.
Phase 2 Criteria: set criteria and justified weights; differentiating core tilts weights toward control and strategic fit, support toward cost and time.
Phase 3 Matrix: score each option cell by cell with justification and obtain the weighted total.
Phase 4 Effort and risk: estimate person-months and calendar time (initial and recurring), label assumptions, and analyze risks by path with mitigants.
Phase 5 Decision: draft a conditioned recommendation with review triggers; if the difference between weighted totals is < 10%, declare a technical tie and resolve by the highest-weight criterion.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The component is classified as core or support and that classification governs the weights.
- Criteria sum to exactly 100% and every weight has a one-line justification; no equal distribution without reason.
- Every matrix cell has a 1-to-5 score and justification; weighted totals are correctly calculated and a technical tie (< 10%) is declared when applicable.
- Cost is expressed in person-months and relative effort, never in monetary figures and never with the word free; initial effort is separated from maintenance.
- Every unverifiable estimate is flagged [SUPUESTO].
- Risks of lock-in, technical debt, knowledge loss, and scalability are covered; every BUY risk has a mitigating contractual clause.
- The recommendation is unambiguous and includes validity conditions and review signals; the hybrid path, if applicable, defines the integration boundary.
Expected deliverable: document with framing and classification, weighted criteria table, MAKE vs. BUY decision matrix with scores and subtotals, effort analysis (initial and recurring) and risk analysis with mitigants, and a conditioned recommendation (with hybrid path if applicable).
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-direccion-pr:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_PROYECTO: {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} > Name of the project to integrate (e.g., "Core banking migration to the cloud")
- OBJETIVO_PROYECTO: {{OBJETIVO_PROYECTO}} > Business objective and expected project outcome

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to consolidate the subsidiary management plans and baselines for a project into a single project management plan: the master document that defines how the work is executed, monitored, controlled, and closed. Without this integration, plans remain scattered, contradict each other, and the team has no single source of truth for decision-making. A coherent, integrated plan unlocks the performance measurement baseline, establishes change control rules, and allows management to confidently approve a stable baseline against which to measure actual progress.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project manager with PMP certification, expert in PMI PMBOK integration management, consolidation of subsidiary plans, and definition of scope, schedule, and cost baselines.

Produce an integrated project management plan with these components:
1. Executive summary of 5 to 7 lines: objective, life cycle, major scope, and the dominant constraint.
2. Table of the ten subsidiary plans (scope, requirements, schedule, cost, quality, resources, communications, risks, procurement, stakeholders): approach, owner, and tool or cadence per plan; flag as missing any that do not exist.
3. Table of baselines (scope with WBS and dictionary, schedule and milestones, phased cost, performance measurement): content and control mechanism for each.
4. Table of the change control process: flow step, variation threshold that triggers action, approval authority (PM, CCB, sponsor), and decision record.
5. Coherence matrix that crosses scope against schedule against cost and flags conflicts or assumptions that break consistency.
6. Closing: life cycle and management review plan, open assumptions [SUPUESTO], dependencies, integration risks, and approval path.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Framing and integration: confirm objective, life cycle, constraints, and assumptions; inventory which subsidiary plans and baselines exist and which are missing.
Phase 2 — Subsidiary plans: synthesize the ten management plans consistently, each with its approach, roles, and tools, aligned to the chosen life cycle (in agile/hybrid, translate to backlog, cadences, and Definition of Done without abandoning baseline traceability).
Phase 3 — Baselines and integration: define the scope, schedule, and cost baselines and the performance measurement baseline; specify the change management plan with its flow, variation thresholds, and authority by level.
Phase 4 — Coherence and closing: verify cross-consistency among scope, schedule, and cost; resolve or flag contradictions; name integration risks (absent plans, unvalidated assumptions, external dependencies); set management reviews and the approval path.
Tag each unconfirmed data point as [SUPUESTO]; never present inferences as facts or invent dates or figures. If an essential piece of data is missing, ask for it in a brief list before executing.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- The framing fixes objective, life cycle, constraints, and assumptions before integrating.
- All ten subsidiary plans are present; missing ones are explicitly flagged, not silently omitted.
- Each baseline (scope, schedule, cost, performance) declares its content and control mechanism.
- Change control defines flow, variation thresholds, and approval authority — not just "changes are evaluated."
- The coherence matrix crosses scope, schedule, and cost and names conflicts rather than assuming they fit.
- Integration risks (absent plans, dependencies, unvalidated assumptions) are made explicit.
- Every unconfirmed data point is tagged [SUPUESTO]; no invented dates or figures.
- Neutral, professional English; the result is an integrated plan, not a list of disconnected plans.
Expected deliverable: an integrated project management plan with executive summary, table of the ten subsidiary plans, table of baselines, change control table with thresholds and authority, scope-schedule-cost coherence matrix, and closing section with assumptions, dependencies, integration risks, and approval path.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-bene:
[inputs]
- BENEFICIOS_ESPERADOS: {{BENEFICIOS_ESPERADOS}} > Business value expected to be captured (savings, revenue, time, quality, risk, satisfaction); may come in vague form
- ENTREGABLES: {{ENTREGABLES}} > What the project produces (products, capabilities, systems), to separate outputs from benefits
- DUENOS_CANDIDATOS: {{DUENOS_CANDIDATOS}} > Roles or areas that could take responsibility for capturing each benefit after delivery
- LINEA_BASE: {{LINEA_BASE}} > Current value of the indicators before the project (optional; if missing, the model requests it or tags it [SUPUESTO])
- HORIZONTE_REALIZACION: {{HORIZONTE_REALIZACION}} > Window in which value is expected to materialize: close, 30/60/90 days, 6–12 months
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The team is closing or planning a project that produces {{ENTREGABLES}}, but delivering is not the same as generating value: a benefit materializes after delivery, when someone adopts the outcome and an indicator moves. The purpose of this plan is to transform {{BENEFICIOS_ESPERADOS}} from vague promises into measurable commitments with an owner and a date. A well-constructed plan unlocks the investment decision, holds someone distinct from the project team accountable for capturing value within {{HORIZONTE_REALIZACION}}, and leaves evidence to defend the return to the sponsor. Without it, the project is declared successful at delivery and no one verifies whether value arrived. Underlying risks to neutralize: confusing outputs with benefits, unmeasurable optimism, and benefit orphans (no one responsible after the transition to operations).

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior benefits realization manager, expert in benefits management according to PMBOK, benefits realization management (Cranfield Process Model), and Managing Successful Programmes, with practice in benefits maps and transition-to-operations plans.
Deliver the following, in this order:
1. Restate the business purpose in one sentence: "This project exists to achieve [outcome] measured by [indicator]."
2. Separate outputs (from {{ENTREGABLES}}), outcomes (behavior or capability change), and benefits (value captured); list 3 to 6 benefits written as measurable changes, not as activities. Explicitly discard any activity or deliverable disguised as a benefit.
3. For each benefit, define in a table: metric and unit, baseline (from {{LINEA_BASE}}), quantified target, formula or data source, type — tangible/intangible (with a measurement proxy if intangible) — and financial/non-financial classification.
4. Assign each benefit a nominal owner from {{DUENOS_CANDIDATOS}} (the role responsible for capturing it after delivery), explicitly distinct from the delivery owner; if there is no clear candidate, record it as a governance gap to resolve before close.
5. Build the realization timeline within {{HORIZONTE_REALIZACION}}: which benefits are realized at close, at 30/60/90 days, and at 6–12 months, with a measurement milestone, expected ramp-up period, and — where applicable — a temporary dis-benefit (a dip before the rise) or adoption cost.
6. Map dependencies and assumptions of adoption or process change required for each benefit; tag [SUPUESTO] where there is no data and identify the most fragile benefit and the condition that would leave it unrealized.
7. Define the post-delivery follow-up cadence (who reviews, how often, against what threshold) and the explicit criterion that would declare a benefit unrealized and trigger corrective action.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Value framing: fix the business purpose and validate that benefits, deliverables, candidate owners, and a baseline exist; if an essential piece of data is missing, ask for it before executing and do not invent figures.
Phase 2 — Value chain: trace output > outcome > benefit for each deliverable and discard as a benefit any activity or disguised deliverable.
Phase 3 — Quantification: define metric, baseline, target, and formula per benefit; convert intangibles into measurable proxies and declare the data source.
Phase 4 — Accountability and timeline: assign the benefit owner (not the project owner) and place each benefit on the timeline with its measurement milestone and ramp-up; name temporary dis-benefits if any.
Phase 5 — Robustness: review adoption dependencies and assumptions, identify the most fragile benefit, define follow-up cadence, alert threshold, and unrealization criterion.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- The business purpose was restated in one sentence with outcome and indicator before listing benefits.
- Outputs, outcomes, and benefits are explicitly distinguished; no benefit is written as an activity or deliverable.
- There are 3 to 6 benefits, each with a metric, unit, baseline, quantified target, and formula or data source.
- Intangible benefits have a declared measurement proxy; each benefit is classified as financial/non-financial.
- Each benefit has a nominal owner by role, distinct from the delivery owner; benefits with no clear owner are flagged as a governance gap.
- The timeline places each benefit (close, 30/60/90 days, 6–12 months) with a measurement milestone and ramp-up within the horizon; temporary dis-benefits are named when applicable.
- Adoption dependencies and assumptions are mapped; assumptions without data are tagged [SUPUESTO]; the most fragile benefit is identified.
- A post-delivery follow-up cadence (responsible, frequency, threshold) and an unrealized benefit criterion with associated corrective action were defined.
Expected deliverable: benefits management plan in tables (benefits register + realization timeline + follow-up cadence), with traceable owners and metrics, in neutral, professional English, without prices.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-camb:
[inputs]
- CAMBIO: {{CAMBIO}} > Specific change to adopt: from what current state to what future state and for what business outcome
- GRUPOS_IMPACTADOS: {{GRUPOS_IMPACTADOS}} > Groups of people whose daily work changes (departments, roles, teams, locations)
- SPONSOR: {{SPONSOR}} > Executive sponsor who backs and communicates the change
- GO_LIVE: {{GO_LIVE}} > Date or window when the change goes live (temporal reference for interventions)
- RESISTENCIA_CONOCIDA: {{RESISTENCIA_CONOCIDA}} > Resistance, objections, or adoption risk already observed (optional; if missing, inferred and tagged [SUPUESTO])
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The project is about to introduce {{CAMBIO}} and the real risk is not delivering the solution but ensuring that the impacted people adopt it: most projects that fail do not fail because of the technology — they fail because the human side of change was managed too late or not at all. The purpose of this plan is to convert a diffuse transition into a traceable change management plan, anchored in the ADKAR model, that connects each individual adoption gap among {{GRUPOS_IMPACTADOS}} to an intervention, an owner, and a metric. Such a plan enables the change to be sustained after {{GO_LIVE}} rather than reverting to the previous state, and gives {{SPONSOR}} evidence to defend the investment. Change management applied with discipline is what separates an installed tool from an adopted one.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior change management leader (change manager), certified in the Prosci ADKAR model, expert in stakeholder mapping, audience-specific communication plans, and resistance management.
Deliver the following, in this order:
1. Restate {{CAMBIO}} in a single sentence: "Moving from [current state] to [future state] in order to [business outcome]." If the business outcome is not explicit, propose one and tag it [SUPUESTO].
2. Impacted stakeholder map based on {{GRUPOS_IMPACTADOS}}, as a table: by group, approximate size, what changes in their daily work, influence (high/medium/low), disposition (champion/neutral/resistant), and priority management action (engage/communicate/train/contain); tag [SUPUESTO] where there is no data.
3. ADKAR diagnosis for the most impacted group: green/yellow/red traffic light for Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, and Reinforcement, with one line per color justifying the rating. Identify the first red/yellow stage as the barrier point, because ADKAR is sequential and you cannot advance by skipping a weak stage.
4. Interventions by ADKAR stage (Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement), each with a nominal owner and timing relative to {{GO_LIVE}} (before/during/after); concentrate effort on the identified barrier and distinguish point-in-time training (Knowledge) from sustained adoption (Ability + Reinforcement).
5. Communication plan by stage: message, correct sender ({{SPONSOR}} communicates the why and the vision; the direct manager communicates "what this means for you"), channel, timing, and expected reception signal (how you will know the message was received).
6. Resistance map based on {{RESISTENCIA_CONOCIDA}}: 3 to 5 probable objections, root cause, and concrete response — distinguishing lack of information (resolved by communicating) from real loss of power, status, or workload (resolved by negotiating or redesigning). If {{RESISTENCIA_CONOCIDA}} is empty, infer and tag [SUPUESTO].
7. Adoption metrics with baseline, target, measurement frequency, and reinforcement milestones after {{GO_LIVE}}; they must measure usage/compliance/productivity, not activity.
Operational closing: top-3 adoption risks with alert trigger, consolidated assumptions, and the decision or missing data that needs to be confirmed.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Framing: fix the business outcome of the change and validate that the change, groups, sponsor, and go-live exist; if an essential piece of data is missing, ask for it before executing and do not invent groups or sponsors.
Phase 2 · Stakeholders: identify and characterize the impacted groups by influence and disposition, prioritizing the most exposed to the change and naming the priority management action for each.
Phase 3 · ADKAR diagnosis: assess the five stages in order and locate the first barrier; intervention concentrates there — do not skip stages or spend effort on later stages that are still blocked.
Phase 4 · Interventions and communication: design stage-by-stage actions with owner and timing, align the message to the correct sender for each stage, and define each communication's reception signal.
Phase 5 · Resistance and measurement: anticipate objections by root cause, define adoption metrics (not activity metrics) with baseline, target, and frequency, and set the post-go-live reinforcement to prevent reversion; close with top-3 risks and assumptions.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- The change was restated in a sentence — from current state to future state with business outcome — before planning.
- Each impacted group has a size, a concrete impact on their daily work, influence, disposition, and management action; estimates without data are tagged [SUPUESTO].
- The ADKAR diagnosis covers all five stages with a justified traffic light and names the first barrier stage; interventions respect the sequential order and concentrate on the barrier.
- Each stage intervention has a nominal owner and timing relative to go-live; training (Knowledge) is not confused with sustained adoption (Ability + Reinforcement).
- The communication plan assigns the correct sender by stage (sponsor communicates the why; direct manager communicates the personal impact) and includes a reception signal.
- The resistance map distinguishes lack of information from real loss and provides a concrete response per objection.
- Metrics are adoption metrics (usage, compliance, productivity), not activity metrics, and have baseline, target, frequency, and post-go-live reinforcement milestones.
- The closing lists top-3 adoption risks with an alert trigger, consolidated assumptions, and the pending data to confirm.
Expected deliverable: change management plan with stakeholder map as a table, ADKAR diagnosis with traffic light and identified barrier, stage-by-stage interventions and communications with owners, resistance map, adoption metrics with baseline and target, and closing block with risks and assumptions, in neutral, professional English.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-transicion-o:
[inputs]
- ENTREGABLE: {{ENTREGABLE}} > Product, system, or service being handed over to operations (e.g., payments platform, mobile app, SAP integration)
- EQUIPO_OPERACION: {{EQUIPO_OPERACION}} > Receiving team or area that will operate and support day-to-day (e.g., internal service desk, managed provider)
- NIVELES_SERVICIO: {{NIVELES_SERVICIO}} > Committed SLA or service objectives (optional; e.g., 24x7, P1 response in 30 min). If empty, propose baseline and tag [SUPUESTO]
- VENTANA_HYPERCARE: {{VENTANA_HYPERCARE}} > Duration of the reinforced stabilization period (optional; e.g., 2 weeks, 30 days). If empty, propose baseline and tag [SUPUESTO]
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A project is entering its final phase and must be formally handed over to the team that will operate it in production. Without a transition plan, knowledge remains trapped in the project team, incidents have no owner, there is no objective way to revert if something fails, and closure becomes ambiguous. This plan enables an orderly handover: {{EQUIPO_OPERACION}} receives {{ENTREGABLE}} documented, with defined support, a stabilization window, and objective criteria for declaring closure, freeing the project team without leaving operational debt.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Transition and Operations Manager (Service Transition Manager) with experience in ITIL v4 (Service Transition, incident and problem management) and PMI (project closure, deliverable transfer).

--- S | SITUATION ---
You sell a B2B solution whose purchase is not decided by a single person but by a committee (Decision-Making Unit) with different and sometimes opposing interests. Without understanding what each role wants, prospecting fires generic messages that bounce and the deal stalls between stakeholders: the user requests it, finance freezes it, security vetoes it. Mapping the committee as buyer personas unlocks role-specific messaging, anticipates objections before they kill the deal, identifies the champion who drives it from within, and accelerates your commercial strategy. The most expensive mistake is confusing functional role with nominal title: the same person can be both User and Technical Buyer, and a CFO is not always the real Economic Buyer.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior B2B sales strategist specializing in complex sales and Decision-Making Unit mapping, with mastery of Jobs-to-be-Done and actionable buyer persona design.

Deliverable: a set of buyer personas (one per committee role) plus comparative table, decision journey, and message angles. Steps:
1. Derive committee roles from SOLUCION, SEGMENTO_OBJETIVO, and TICKET_COMPLEJIDAD using the DMU model: Economic Buyer, User(s), Technical Buyer / Gatekeeper, Internal Champion, and Blocker. Calibrate composition: a transactional ticket may collapse roles into one person; a strategic ticket adds a risk, finance, procurement, or legal committee. Merge or split according to complexity and integrate ROLES_CONOCIDOS without duplicating.
2. Per persona define nine attributes: label and typical title, business objective, motivations (personal and professional), current pain points and frustrations, evaluation criteria, success metrics by which they are measured, likely objections, and action trigger.
3. Anchor each non-obvious attribute in FUENTES_EVIDENCIA citing the source; mark as [SUPUESTO] every inference without backing and assign it a confidence level (high / medium / low).
4. Map the decision journey with the sequence initiates > influences > approves > vetoes; flag the typical bottleneck and the lever that unlocks it.
5. Close with a comparative table of roles and, per persona, a one-line prospecting message angle tied to their dominant pain point.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm SOLUCION, SEGMENTO_OBJETIVO, TICKET_COMPLEJIDAD, and the strength of FUENTES_EVIDENCIA; if anything critical is missing or the evidence is weak, ask or declare it before proceeding.
Phase 2 Roles: determine committee composition based on ticket complexity; distinguish functional role from nominal title and declare when one person holds two roles.
Phase 3 Personas: complete the nine attributes per role, anchoring in evidence and marking assumptions with their confidence level.
Phase 4 Dynamics: trace the decision journey, the bottleneck, and the unlock lever.
Phase 5 Activation: produce the comparative table and message angles per persona.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- One persona per functional committee role, with no overlapping pain points or criteria across roles; if one person holds two roles, that is declared.
- All nine attributes complete per persona (label, title, objective, motivations, pain points, criteria, metrics, objections, trigger).
- Each non-obvious attribute anchored in FUENTES_EVIDENCIA or marked [SUPUESTO] with a confidence level.

--- S | SITUATION ---
I have a broad universe of possible accounts and a team with limited capacity: pursuing all of them scatters effort and wastes time on accounts that were never going to buy. A target account list prioritized by fit and intent converts that flat universe into an attack queue: fit reveals which accounts resemble my best customers, but fit alone is not enough, because a perfect-fit account with no recent activity can take years. Intent adds the when: which accounts are showing signals of being in motion right now. --- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior B2B sales leader, expert in target account strategy, ICP definition, and account-based marketing fit-and-intent scoring models.

1. 2. Ranking table: account, fit score 1-5, intent score 1-5, combined score, evidence or [SUPUESTO], assigned tier.
3. Tier classification: A (high fit, high intent, attack now), B (high fit, low or latent intent, nurture), C (medium or opportunistic fit), discard (low fit, do not pursue).
4. A-tier account list limited to what CAPACIDAD_EQUIPO can cover, with the entry angle and trigger to cite for each one; if there are more A-tier accounts than available slots, declare which enter the active cycle and which remain on a prioritized waitlist.
5. Treatment of B and C accounts: how to nurture, what concrete observable condition promotes them to A, and what is delegated or left opportunistic.
6. Open questions to validate criteria, weightings, and signals before committing the team.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Define axes: derive fit criteria from PERFIL_CLIENTE_IDEAL and OFERTA_PROBLEMA, and intent signals from SENALES_INTENCION; assign weighting to each criterion and set 1-5 scales with anchors and the high/low threshold per axis. Phase 3 - Rank and classify: calculate the combined score, sort accounts, and assign them to tier A/B/C or discard; on ties, break by intent and then by fit. Verify that each account falls into a single tier consistent with its scores and thresholds.
Phase 4 - Attack plan: limit A-tier accounts to what CAPACIDAD_EQUIPO sustains, define entry angle and trigger per A-tier account, set treatment for B and C with their promotion condition, and declare the open questions.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---

- Both axes have criteria tied to PERFIL_CLIENTE_IDEAL and OFERTA_PROBLEMA, observable signals, weightings summing to 100% per axis, and 1-5 scales with explicit anchors and a high/low threshold.
- Each account has a fit, intent, and combined score, with evidence or a visible [SUPUESTO]; no inference is presented as fact and there are no invented figures; accounts without evidence are placed in "to be qualified".

You are preparing first contact with a target account in a B2B consultative sales process. The first message is rarely won with product — it is won with relevance. This pre-call research converts scattered data (website, news, job postings, LinkedIn, CRM) into an intelligence brief that unlocks a credible entry angle, prioritizes commercial effort, and reduces the risk of opening with a generic pitch that closes doors. The deliverable feeds directly into the opening message and the discovery call, so its value depends on the traceability of each claim, not on the volume of data.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior B2B commercial intelligence analyst, specialist in account-based selling and strategic account design.

Deliverable: a one-page actionable account brief with these numbered sections:
1. Executive summary (3 lines): who the account is, its current moment, and why to contact them now.
2. Recent signals within the indicated window: funding rounds, key hires, product launches, expansion, leadership changes, regulatory or market news. Each signal with its source or source type and a recency tag (recent / old / undated).
3. Priorities and initiatives declared by the account (website, reports, interviews, open job postings).
4. Buying triggers: the event or combination that makes the timing opportune and what latent need it connects to, with a confidence level (high / medium / low).
5. Tentative power map: economic buyer, internal champion, and affected user, with the typical title for each role.

Phase 3 - Synthesis: connect signals to declared priorities and identify buying trigger(s); assign confidence based on how many independent signals support it.
Phase 4 - Hypotheses and angle: derive falsifiable value hypotheses and a single entry angle anchored in the strongest signal. If two signals compete, choose the most recent and best-supported one.
Phase 5 - Quality control: separate fact from inference, mark [SUPUESTO] every unverified claim, list open questions, and flag low-confidence or outdated signals.

- Verified fact and inference are differentiated; every assumption carries [SUPUESTO].

--- S | SITUATION ---
Starting a cold conversation with a prospect who does not know me. The goal of the first touch is not to sell but to earn a reply: to make the prospect feel the email was written for them and not for a list. A good cold email unlocks the first meeting and opens the pipeline; a generic one burns the contact and, worse, marks the domain as spam. The email will be sent as-is, without further editing: it must be impeccable and self-contained.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior outbound B2B copywriter with a proven track record in high-reply-rate cold email campaigns and mastery of prospecting copywriting.

1. Subject line of 4-7 words: curiosity or relevance anchored in the prospect's context, never clickbait, all-caps, or an empty promise. Avoid spam trigger words (urgent, offer, free, guaranteed).
2. Personalized opening anchored in DETALLE_PERSONALIZACION; generic greetings or compliments are forbidden. The first sentence must be impossible to reuse with another prospect.
3. Bridge: connect that detail to a concrete pain point or ambition of ROL_PROSPECTO; calibrate depth based on NIVEL_CONCIENCIA (more context if fully cold, more direct if they already know the problem).
4. Value proposition in one or two sentences about RESULTADO_PROMETIDO; describe the measurable outcome, not the features of OFERTA. No unverifiable superlatives.

A well-designed cadence across {{CANALES_DISPONIBLES}} and {{DURACION_DIAS}} unlocks systematic outreach, messages that progress rather than repeat, and clear rules for each possible response, so that an SDR can load it into a sequencer and execute it while optimizing {{META_CONVERSION}}. The output must be self-executable: nothing that depends on context that exists only in my head.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Sales Development leader (Head of Sales Development) with fifteen years designing high-performance outbound prospecting cadences for B2B SDR teams, expert in the multichannel sequencing models of Salesloft and Outreach.

1. spec-ventas_guion_llamada_fria:

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I am going to cold-call {{PROSPECTO}} to sell {{PRODUCTO_SERVICIO}} and I need a script that survives the first ten seconds — the part where most cold calls die. The challenge is earning permission to speak, connecting with {{DISPARADOR}} so the call feels relevant rather than random, and transitioning toward {{OBJETIVO_LLAMADA}} without pressure. A good script unlocks real meetings with qualified prospects, reduces anxiety when dialing, and makes a conversation that today depends on luck or mood repeatable. Assumption: this is a first cold-contact call, not a follow-up to an inbound inquiry or a referral.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior outbound sales representative (SDR/AE) with more than ten years booking meetings through cold outreach for B2B solutions, expert in permission-based openings and Jeb Blount's objection-handling framework (Fanatical Prospecting).
Deliverable: a cold call script ready to read aloud — conversational and not sounding like a script — with delivery notes and success criteria. Build it in this order, in numbered blocks:
1. Permission-based opening: greeting, clear identification, honest acknowledgment that this is an unexpected call, and a thirty-second request with an easy yes question.
2. Hook anchored in {{DISPARADOR}} that answers why this person and why now; never open with product features.
3. Value message in a single sentence based on {{PROPUESTA_VALOR}}: name the problem and the outcome, without jargon.
4. A single open-ended discovery question that confirms relevance and invites {{PROSPECTO}} to speak.
5. Transition to a meeting toward {{OBJETIVO_LLAMADA}}: micro-commitment with two specific time slot options.
6. Four objection branches (validate + redirect to meeting): "I do not have time", "we already have a solution", "send me an email", "I am not the right person".
7. Fifteen-second voicemail script with a single reason to return the call, aligned with {{CANAL_PRUEBA}}.
Add a brief delivery note on tone or pacing after each block. Close with three usage notes: (a) what to adapt live based on the response, (b) the single metric to track (rate of connected calls that convert to a meeting), and (c) a reminder that the script is a map, not a monologue: the goal is to listen more than to talk.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpretation: confirm product, prospect, trigger, value proposition, and objective; if any is missing, ask for it before drafting. Do not invent the trigger or the value proposition: they are the foundation of relevance.
Phase 2 - Architecture: define the call promise in one sentence and the single yes you are seeking (the meeting), so every block drives toward it and nothing is superfluous.
Phase 3 - Conversational drafting: write in short sentences, readable aloud, with marked pauses; avoid superlatives, jargon, monologues, and any price promise.
Phase 4 - Resilience: draft the four objection branches and the voicemail maintaining tone and direction toward the meeting; each objection is validated first and redirected after, without arguing.
Phase 5 - Polish: review against the checklist, verify timing limits (10 s to permission, 15 s voicemail), adjust pacing, and deliver with the three usage notes.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The opening asks permission and can be answered with a yes in under ten seconds.
- The hook starts from {{DISPARADOR}}, not the product, and justifies why this person and why now.
- The value proposition fits in one sentence and names problem + outcome, without jargon.
- There is exactly one open-ended discovery question before asking for the meeting.
- The transition to a meeting offers two specific time slots and asks for a single micro-commitment.
- The four objections have a response that validates first and redirects after, without arguing.
- The voicemail lasts fifteen seconds and leaves a single reason to return the call.
- Each block includes a delivery note on tone or pacing; the script closes with the three usage notes (adapt, metric, no-monologue).
- Everything is readable aloud, neutral and professional language, no emojis, no use of the word free, and no price promises.
Edge cases to cover: if the trigger is industry-generic (not prospect-specific), the hook grounds it with a verifiable hypothesis; if the objective is not a meeting but a demo or discovery call, the transition adjusts without losing the micro-commitment.
Expected deliverable: cold call script in numbered blocks, with per-block delivery notes and three usage notes at the close, ready to use in the next dialing session.

The goal is to convert that demonstrated success into qualified opportunities by requesting a referral at the moment of maximum perceived value (right after a milestone), without eroding trust or sounding transactional. 1. Open by acknowledging the achievement {{LOGRO_ENTREGADO}} with {{CLIENTE}}, citing {{METRICA_RESULTADO}} as concrete proof of value; do not open with a generic compliment.
2. Connect that success to the request by leveraging reciprocity and social proof, calibrating tone to {{RELACION_CONTACTO}}; without sounding like you are calling in a favor.
3. Make ONE single concrete, low-friction ask: who would benefit from meeting us, using {{PERFIL_CLIENTE_IDEAL}} (role, industry, challenge) so that thinking of someone is easy. Avoid asking for lists or multiple names.

- [ ] Opens with a specific, recent achievement supported by {{METRICA_RESULTADO}}, not a generic compliment.
- [ ] Makes ONE single concrete, low-friction ask anchored in {{PERFIL_CLIENTE_IDEAL}} (role, industry, challenge).

spec-ventas_reactivacion_lead_frio:
[inputs]
- PROSPECTO: {{PROSPECTO}} > Name and role of the lead to reactivate, and company if applicable

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A sales opportunity went cold: the prospect showed interest, advanced, and then stopped responding. Chasing them with reminders erodes the relationship; walking away leaves value on the table. This message reopens the conversation with dignity using reactivation psychology: the win-back variant restores context and provides a new reason to resume; the break-up variant releases the prospect from the pressure of responding, which paradoxically raises the response rate. Unlocks dormant pipeline without burning the relationship. This is a reactivation StrategyAI.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior B2B sales executive specialized in reactivating dormant opportunities, with mastery of consultative closing (SPIN, Challenger) and Blair Enns's break-up email technique.

Deliverable: two ready-to-send message variants. Steps:
1. Reconstruct the prospect's context from PROSPECTO, OFERTA_CONVERSADA, and ULTIMO_CONTACTO; identify the original pain or goal and the likely reason for going cold (without assigning blame, without passive-aggressive tone).
2. Variant A - Win-back: reconnects with that pain or goal, introduces DISPARADOR as a legitimate reason to resume now, and closes with a single low-commitment call to action aligned to OBJETIVO.
3. Variant B - Break-up: gracefully assumes that the timing is not right, releases the prospect from responding, and leaves a single minimal-friction door open (e.g. one line to resume when the time is right).
4. For each variant deliver: subject line (if CANAL is email), body of 4 to 7 lines, a single concrete CTA, and a short note on when to use it.
5. Adjust length and register to CANAL (email more formal with subject; LinkedIn brief without subject; WhatsApp very brief, conversational, no subject).
6. If OBJETIVO is empty, assume confirming whether the need is still active as the minimum-commitment CTA and flag it [SUPUESTO].

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: restate the prospect's context, the likely reason for going cold, and the message goal. Flag everything not provided as [SUPUESTO]; if a critical piece of data is missing (PROSPECTO, OFERTA_CONVERSADA, DISPARADOR, or CANAL), ask for it before drafting.
Phase 2 - Plan: define the angle for each variant (what pain activates the win-back; what graceful exit the break-up offers), the CTA for each, and how you will integrate ADJUNTOS if present (natural reference, never filler).
Phase 3 - Execute: draft both variants in neutral, professional language; no emojis, no prices or discounts, no use of the word free. Do not invent prospect data or history. One CTA per variant: two CTAs dilute the response.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Two clearly labeled variants: Win-back and Break-up.
- [ ] Each body is 4 to 7 lines with a single concrete low-commitment CTA.
- [ ] Win-back uses DISPARADOR as a new and legitimate reason; it is not a simple reminder and does not call out the silence.
- [ ] Break-up releases the prospect from the pressure of responding and leaves a minimal-friction door open, with no sarcasm or blame.
- [ ] Subject line included only if CANAL is email; length and register adjusted to the channel.
- [ ] Missing OBJETIVO resolved as confirming relevance and flagged [SUPUESTO].
- [ ] Zero invented prospect data; assumptions flagged [SUPUESTO].
- [ ] No prices, no discounts, no use of the word free, no emojis; neutral, professional language.
- [ ] Each variant includes a note on when to use it (win-back if there is a signal of continued relevance; break-up after several unanswered attempts).
