spec-vibe-coding_descomposicion-en-histo:
[inputs]
- DESCRIPCION_FEATURE: {{DESCRIPCION_FEATURE}} > Description of the feature to decompose: what it should do, for whom, and why
- STACK_RESTRICCIONES: {{STACK_RESTRICCIONES}} > Technical stack, architecture, and constraints (language, framework, database, integrations, code conventions)
- ROL_OBJETIVO: {{ROL_OBJETIVO}} > User or role that receives the value of the feature
- GRANULARIDAD: {{GRANULARIDAD}} > Maximum acceptable size per story (e.g. "implementable in one agent session", "half a day") (optional; default: implementable and verifiable in one agent session)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A feature described as a block is not reliably implementable by a coding AI: the scope is ambiguous, dependencies are hidden, and there are no objective success criteria, which produces retries, scope drift, and code that cannot be verified. Decomposing it into INVEST stories with Gherkin criteria converts a fuzzy intention into a one-story-at-a-time executable backlog, where each piece has a single focus, a clear dependency order, and a checkable acceptance condition. This unlocks incremental, reviewable, and testable implementation: the Strategy of cutting before coding.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product engineer and tech lead experienced in breaking features into backlogs executable by coding agents, fluent in INVEST, Gherkin, and flow-oriented design.

Deliverable: a backlog of codeable user stories from {{DESCRIPCION_FEATURE}}, ready for an AI to implement and verify each story separately.

Steps:
1. Restate {{DESCRIPCION_FEATURE}} in a value sentence (as {{ROL_OBJETIVO}} I want [capability] so that [benefit]) and list assumptions, each tagged [SUPUESTO]. If critical context is missing (role, business rule, data constraint), ask before continuing instead of assuming it.
2. Trace the end-to-end flow and declare scope boundaries: what is in and what is explicitly out. Name the actors, states, and data that cross each step.
3. Slice into stories applying INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small implementable within {{GRANULARIDAD}}, Testable); divide by flow steps or business rules, never by technical layers. A story that still does not fit within {{GRANULARIDAD}} after slicing is declared and a subdivision proposal is provided.
4. Order by dependencies and mark them explicitly (Hn depends on Hm); verify no cycles. Identify the critical path (stories that unblock the rest).
5. For each story deliver: id, title, value narrative, acceptance criteria in Gherkin (happy path + at least one edge case or error, Given/When/Then format), implementation notes (probable modules/files and data contracts per {{STACK_RESTRICCIONES}}), and a definition of done verifiable by the AI (what command, test, or observable confirms it is done).
6. Close with a summary table (id, title, depends-on, size S/M) and flag the recommended first story with one line justifying why to start there (lowest risk, unblocks the most, validates a key assumption).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: restate value, fix [SUPUESTO] assumptions and scope boundaries; block if a critical piece of data is missing.
Phase 2 Slicing: derive stories from the flow and rules, validating each against the 6 INVEST criteria; merge what is trivial, split what does not fit within {{GRANULARIDAD}}.
Phase 3 Sequencing: order by dependencies, rule out cycles, mark critical path, and assign relative size S/M.
Phase 4 Specification: write Gherkin and a verifiable definition of done per story; record undefined rules as open questions instead of assuming them.
Accepted trade-off: if forcing Independence breaks the flow coherence, prioritize Testable and declare the residual dependency instead of inventing an artificial coupling.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Each story demonstrably meets the 6 INVEST criteria, especially Small (fits within {{GRANULARIDAD}}) and Testable.
- No story is sliced by technical layer (no separate "backend" vs "frontend" stories); the cut is by flow step or business rule.
- Each story has Gherkin with a happy path and at least one edge case or error, in Given/When/Then format.
- Dependencies are declared, the order respects them, and there are no cycles; the critical path is identified.
- Each story has a definition of done with a concrete observable (command, test, or state) that the AI can objectively verify.
- Assumptions are tagged [SUPUESTO]; undefined rules appear as open questions, with no invented requirements.
- Every story exceeding {{GRANULARIDAD}} is declared with a subdivision proposal.
Expected deliverable: prioritized story backlog (id, title, value, Gherkin, implementation notes, definition of done) + summary table (id, title, depends-on, size) + recommended first story with justification.

--- S | SITUATION ---
Before coding with an AI agent, most rework is born from two gaps: the AI starts without sufficient context, or it declares "done" something that does not comply. Setting an explicit Definition of Ready (DoR) and Definition of Done (DoD) converts those two moments into verifiable contracts. This unlocks predictable vibe coding sessions: the agent knows when it can start and when it can close, and back-and-forth, false completions, and silent regressions are reduced.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software engineer expert in task specification and human-agent collaboration, with mastery of verifiable acceptance criteria.
Deliverable: two separate checklists (Definition of Ready and Definition of Done) plus a start verdict. Steps:
1. Build the Definition of Ready (DoR) for {{OBJETIVO_TAREA}} in {{STACK_Y_REPO}}: verifiable preconditions (objective as an observable and measurable output; repo context and relevant files loaded; dependencies, permissions, and credentials available; {{CRITERIOS_ACEPTACION}} agreed; fixtures or test data identified; scope and {{RESTRICCIONES_Y_NO_ALCANCE}} delimited). Mark each item: met, pending, or blocker.
2. Build the Definition of Done (DoD): objective completion conditions (functionality meets {{CRITERIOS_ACEPTACION}}; tests passing per {{ESTRATEGIA_PRUEBAS}}; existing suite intact — no regression —; code aligned to repo style and linters; minimum docs and comments updated; no TODOs or loose ends; atomic changes ready to commit with a proposed message).
3. Issue the start verdict: cross-check the DoR against the real state, rule Ready to start yes/no, and list blockers with their resolution action.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Reading: interpret objective, stack, and criteria; detect critical gaps and risky assumptions.
Phase 2 - DoR: write each precondition as a verifiable assertion (not "understand the objective" but "objective expressed as an observable and measurable output").
Phase 3 - DoD: write each completion condition as an objective, not a subjective, test; include no-regression and commit state.
Phase 4 - Verdict: cross-check the DoR against the real state, issue Ready to start yes/no, and order blockers by unblocking priority.
Edge cases: if CRITERIOS_ACEPTACION = "To be defined", the first DoR blocker is to agree on them and the verdict is No; if ESTRATEGIA_PRUEBAS does not allow verifying the functionality, mark the DoD as undemonstrable and propose one; if non-scope is omitted, declare the assumption explicitly rather than inventing it.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Every DoR and DoD item is objectively verifiable, not a matter of opinion.
- DoR covers objective, repo context, dependencies/permissions, criteria, test data, and scope.
- DoD covers functionality, tests, no-regression, style/linters, docs, and commit state.
- Each item is marked met / pending / blocker, distinguishing blocker from pending.

- Essential missing items are asked for in a single batch; assumptions are declared explicitly, not silently assumed.

spec-vibe-coding_seleccion-de-stack-just:
[inputs]
- PROYECTO: {{PROYECTO}} > Name and one- or two-line description of the software to be built and who it serves
- REQUISITOS_CLAVE: {{REQUISITOS_CLAVE}} > Main functional requirements and quality attributes that matter most (e.g., low latency, scale to X users, ship in N weeks, low operational cost)
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Hard limits: team skills, timeline, operational budget, existing ecosystem or systems, compliance, self-hosted vs managed
- CRITERIOS_DECISION: {{CRITERIOS_DECISION}} > Criteria for weighing the options and their relative priority (optional; if missing, the architect proposes them and marks them as [SUPUESTO])
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to choose the technology stack for {{PROYECTO}} and be able to defend every choice to my team and stakeholders. The risk of choosing by trend or by familiarity is real: a stack poorly matched to {{RESTRICCIONES}} is paid for in time, operational cost, and rewrites, and the cost of reverting grows with every week of code written on the wrong foundation. A justified selection with a tradeoffs matrix turns an opinionated decision into a traceable one: it aligns the team on the same criteria, puts in writing which tradeoff was accepted and why, and unlocks the start of development, the foundational ADR, and the effort estimate on a defensible basis.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software architect who has chosen and operated multiple stacks in production under team, timeline, and cost constraints, and who decides based on evidence and contextual fit, not trends.

Deliverable: the recommended stack layer by layer, each backed by a weighted tradeoffs matrix and a prioritized recommendation, plus a full-stack coherence check and a validation plan. Steps:
1. Restate {{PROYECTO}} and {{REQUISITOS_CLAVE}} in your own words; derive the dominant quality attributes and prioritize the 1 to 3 that drive the decision; treat {{RESTRICCIONES}} as non-negotiable limits and distinguish hard constraints (non-negotiable) from preferences (negotiable). If a piece of information is missing that would change the decision (target scale, operational budget, skills, timeline, dependencies, compliance), ask for it before proceeding.
2. Set the decision criteria from {{CRITERIOS_DECISION}} and assign each a relative weight summing to 100 percent; if not provided, propose them and mark them as [SUPUESTO]. Include total cost of ownership dimensions: team learning curve, ecosystem and hiring, long-term maturity and support, and exit cost or lock-in.
3. For each applicable layer (language, backend framework, frontend if applicable, database and data model, messaging or queues if applicable, hosting and infrastructure, authentication, observability, CI/CD) propose 2 to 3 real candidates and build the matrix: rows equal candidates, columns equal weighted criteria, cell equals score 1 to 5 with a verifiable rationale phrase, plus the weighted sum per candidate. Explicitly mark inapplicable layers and explain why.
4. Deliver the context-prioritized recommendation per layer: primary option, fallback alternative, and conservative bet if risk is high; explain why the primary wins given {{RESTRICCIONES}} and name the accepted tradeoff.
5. Verify full-stack coherence: layer interoperability, single language where appropriate, reasonable total operational complexity; flag any friction between layers that the per-layer sum does not capture.
6. Define the validation plan: the minimum spike or proof of concept that confirms or refutes the riskiest choice before committing to it, with an explicit success criterion, and the objective signals (metrics, thresholds) that would force a stack reconsideration.
7. Close with a one-line summary per layer and the list of residual risks with their mitigation.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: consolidate project, requirements, quality attributes, and constraints into a verifiable statement; separate hard constraints from preferences; list the missing data that blocks the decision.
Phase 2 Criteria: define and weight the criteria (sum 100 percent); document each weight or [SUPUESTO]; include total cost of ownership and lock-in.
Phase 3 Evaluation: per layer, generate real candidates and complete the matrix with verifiable rationale; never invent benchmarks or figures (if you cite a data point, make it verifiable or mark it as [SUPUESTO]); do not recommend based on popularity.
Phase 4 Decision: write the context-prioritized recommendation, the accepted tradeoff, and the fallback; verify full-stack coherence.
Phase 5 Validation: specify the minimum spike with success criterion and decision-change signals; close with summary and mitigated residual risks.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The framing prioritizes 1 to 3 dominant quality attributes and separates hard constraints from preferences.
- [ ] Criteria are weighted with weights summing to 100 percent and include total cost of ownership and lock-in; assumptions are marked [SUPUESTO].
- [ ] Each applicable layer has 2 to 3 real candidates and a matrix with weighted criteria, scores 1 to 5, and weighted sum; inapplicable layers are marked with their reason.
- [ ] Each matrix cell has a verifiable rationale; no benchmark or figure is invented.
- [ ] The per-layer recommendation is prioritized (primary, fallback, conservative if applicable) and justified by the contextual constraints, not popularity; each primary choice names the tradeoff it accepts.
- [ ] There is a full-stack coherence check that flags friction between layers.
- [ ] There is a validation plan with a minimum spike, its success criterion, and objective signals that would force a stack reconsideration.
- [ ] If critical data was missing, it was asked before deciding rather than silently assumed.
Expected deliverable: a stack selection document with a per-layer tradeoffs matrix, context-prioritized recommendation, coherence check, validation plan, and mitigated residual risks, ready to underpin a foundational ADR.

I am about to build {{NOMBRE_PRODUCTO}} with vibe coding and I need a navigation contract before generating screens. Without an agreed route map, every generated screen invents its own structure, routes collide, error and permission states are left uncovered, deep links do not resolve, and I end up rewriting the navigation mid-project. spec-vibe-coding_modelo-de-datos-concept:
[inputs]
- DESCRIPCION_FUNCIONAL: {{DESCRIPCION_FUNCIONAL}} > Prose description of what the app does, its flows, and main screens

- ACTORES: {{ACTORES}} > Users or roles that interact with the system
- REGLAS_NEGOCIO: {{REGLAS_NEGOCIO}} > Known constraints and rules that affect the data (optional)

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I am in the specification phase of an app and I want to translate its functional description into a conceptual data model before writing code or defining tables. A solid conceptual model prevents the physical schema from carrying misunderstood business decisions: it clarifies the domain language, surfaces implicit rules, and delivers an artifact the team can validate with the business. Getting this right unlocks a physical design and an implementation that do not need to be redone. The costly mistake here is naming as an entity something that is actually an attribute, or leaving N:M relationships unresolved: both propagate into the physical schema and the code.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior data architect specializing in conceptual modeling and domain-driven design (DDD), with expertise in entity-relationship notation.

Deliverable: a conceptual data model of the described domain. Steps:
1. Extract the domain language: list the candidate nouns (entities) and candidate verbs (relationships) present in the description; preserve the exact domain term.
2. Identify the real entities: those that have their own identity and lifecycle; discard those that are merely attributes of another entity or catalog values, and justify each discard.
3. For each entity define its key attributes and its natural identifier (not a technical one). If no reliable natural identifier exists, declare it as a business ambiguity rather than inventing a technical key.
4. Establish relationships between entities with cardinality (1:1, 1:N, N:M) and optionality (mandatory or optional on each end); when a relationship carries its own data (date, quantity, status), note it.
5. Distinguish strong entities from weak or associative entities; resolve every N:M relationship by creating an intermediate entity with a domain name, not a technical name.
6. Record each assumption with the tag [SUPUESTO] and list ambiguities that require a business decision as actionable questions.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpretation: restate the purpose of the app and its actors; declare the model scope (which entities are in and which are out, and why). If an essential input (description, domain, or actors) is missing, ask for it before proceeding.
Phase 2 - Plan: present the preliminary list of candidate entities and relationships for confirmation before elaborating; flag decisions that depend on business answers.
Phase 3 - Modeling: develop entities, attributes, identifiers, and relationships; resolve all N:M relationships; stay at the conceptual level without physical types, engines, or technical keys. Honor REGLAS_NEGOCIO and adjust granularity to NIVEL_DETALLE.
Phase 4 - Validation: review the model against the criterion checklist, verify that every entity is reachable by at least one relationship or actor, and consolidate assumptions and open questions.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every entity has its own identity and lifecycle; no attribute or catalog disguised as an entity.
- [ ] Every entity declares key attributes and a natural identifier; if none exists, it remains as a question to the business.
- [ ] Every relationship has explicit cardinality and optionality on both ends.
- [ ] Every N:M relationship is resolved with an intermediate entity named in domain language; relationships with their own data are marked.
- [ ] Strong entities are distinguished from weak or associative ones.
- [ ] No entity is orphaned: all are connected by a relationship or by an actor.
- [ ] The model is conceptual: no physical data types, engine, or technical keys.
- [ ] Every assumption is tagged [SUPUESTO] and ambiguities are listed as questions to the business.
- [ ] Names use the vocabulary of the described domain.

spec-vibe-coding_contrato-de-api-primero:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_API: {{NOMBRE_API}} > Name or domain of the API to contract (e.g., "orders API", "identity service")
- RECURSOS: {{RECURSOS}} > Main domain resources/entities and their key relationships
- CONSUMIDORES: {{CONSUMIDORES}} > Who consumes the contract (web SPA, mobile app, backend team, third parties) and their needs

--- S | SITUATION ---
We are going to define the contract for the API {{NOMBRE_API}} BEFORE implementing anything, following the API-first approach: the contract is the artifact agreed upon first and becomes the single source of truth. A closed contract unlocks parallel work (backend implements, frontend mocks, QA writes tests, third parties integrate), eliminates ambiguity in integrations, and prevents costly rework from poorly modeled endpoints. What is decided here governs code, tests, and documentation downstream, and sets the cost of future changes: a well-versioned contract avoids breaking {{CONSUMIDORES}} already integrated.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior API Architect, specialist in REST/OpenAPI design and contract governance, with a focus on developer experience and evolutionary compatibility.
Deliverable: a valid OpenAPI 3.1 contract plus a human-readable guide and an approval checklist. Steps:
1. Model the resources from {{RECURSOS}} as plural nouns; define the REST route hierarchy and naming convention (paths kebab-case, JSON fields camelCase). Document the relationships (nesting vs reference by id) and justify the choice.
2. For each endpoint specify method, route, path/query parameters, headers, request body schema and response schema, with types, formats, mandatory vs optional, and real examples for {{CONSUMIDORES}}. Distinguish PATCH (partial) from PUT (full replacement) and declare which fields are sensitive and must never travel in responses.
3. Define the status code catalog per endpoint: success (200/201/202/204), client (400/401/403/404/409/422), rate (429), server (500/503), with a unified error schema (code, message, details, traceId). Differentiate 400 (malformed) from 422 (valid type, invalid for business) and 409 (conflict/uniqueness).
4. Establish cross-cutting policies per {{RESTRICCIONES}} and {{STACK}}: auth/authz, pagination (offset vs cursor), filtering/sorting, write idempotency via Idempotency-Key, rate limiting with quota headers, and versioning (URL or header) with a rule for compatible vs breaking changes and a deprecation policy (Deprecation/Sunset).
5. Close with request/response examples (including the empty case and the error case), an initial contract changelog, and an approval checklist.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 (Domain modeling): resource inventory, relationships, and operations; define naming, route structure, and nesting strategy.
Phase 2 (Per-endpoint specification): input/output payloads, parameters, headers, validations, and examples per consumer.
Phase 3 (Error and status contract): per-endpoint status code table and unified error schema with traceId for support.
Phase 4 (Cross-cutting policies): auth, pagination, filtering, idempotency, rate limiting, versioning, and deprecation.
Phase 5 (Assembly and verification): valid OpenAPI 3.1 + examples + changelog + approval checklist.
Mandatory edge cases: zero results in listings; uniqueness collision (409); semantic validation (422); safe vs unsafe retries; sensitive fields out of responses; field deprecation.
Tradeoffs to justify when applicable: URL versioning (cacheability/clarity) vs header versioning (stable URLs); offset pagination (simple, drifts with volatile data) vs cursor (stable); granular errors vs bounded catalog.
Do not invent business rules: mark assumptions as [SUPUESTO]; if {{RECURSOS}}, {{CONSUMIDORES}}, {{STACK}}, or {{RESTRICCIONES}} are missing or ambiguous, ask before continuing.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every endpoint declares method, route, parameters, request, response, and at least one success code and one error code.
- [ ] Unified and consistent error schema across all endpoints (code, message, details, traceId).
- [ ] Uniform naming: resources as plural nouns, paths kebab-case, fields camelCase.
- [ ] HTTP codes with correct semantics: 201 on creation, 204 with no body, 400 vs 422 properly differentiated, 409 on conflict.

--- S | SITUATION ---
I am about to start vibe coding of {{PRODUCTO_MVP}} for {{USUARIO_PRIMARIO}}, whose core action is {{ACCION_CENTRAL}}, within {{STACK_O_RESTRICCIONES}}. The risk is not what I forget to ask for, but what the agent adds on its own: complex authentication, admin panels, optimizations, integrations, handling rare edge cases that inflate the MVP and delay the first usable version. I need to fix the boundaries in writing BEFORE generating code. A clear non-goals document unlocks fast iterations: the agent knows exactly what not to touch and I know when to stop it.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product engineer expert at delimiting MVP scope and writing scope guards for coding agents.
Deliver a scope document in markdown that shields the MVP against scope creep, with these steps:
1. Restate the product, the primary user, and the core action as you understand them; if any is missing or ambiguous, ask before continuing and do not assume it.
2. List 3 to 5 MVP objectives (what IS in scope), each as an observable user capability aligned with {{ACCION_CENTRAL}}.
3. Declare 6 to 12 NON-GOALS grouped into five categories: deferred functionality, premature technical perfection, premature scale and performance, external integrations, edge cases and rare states. For each non-goal: what is excluded, why it is deferred, and the reconsideration signal (using {{HORIZONTE_RECONSIDERACION}} as a reference) so it is a "not yet" and not a "never".
4. 5. List 3 to 5 gray area decisions (neither clearly in nor out) that require my explicit confirmation before coding, each with the concrete question to answer.
6. Close with a one-line traceability matrix per category confirming that each non-goal arises by contrast with an objective, not in the abstract.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Understanding: paraphrase product/user/action and flag gaps.
Phase 2 Positive boundary: fix the minimum that IS in scope so non-goals can be defined by contrast, not in the abstract.
Phase 3 Negative boundary: derive exclusions by category, each with rationale and reconsideration signal.
Phase 4 Operationalization: convert exclusions into imperative and verifiable rules the agent can apply without interpretation.
Phase 5 Ambiguity: isolate what is not clearly in or out and escalate to human confirmation.
Phase 6 Traceability: verify that each non-goal is anchored to an objective and that no category is empty or overloaded.

- Product, user, and core action restated; gaps asked for, not assumed.

- 3 to 5 gray area decisions flagged for confirmation, each with its question.
- Traceability matrix present: each non-goal anchored to an objective by contrast.
- No prices or monetary amounts; inferences marked as [SUPUESTO].
- Deliverable: markdown document with the six sections plus a final Scope Done Definition line.

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I am in the specification and planning phase of a product and have not yet committed to an architecture. I want to anticipate the highest-impact technical uncertainties before writing structural code, so I do not discover late a hidden assumption that forces a ground-up rewrite. An early technical risk inventory unlocks three decisions: what to validate first, which architecture decisions it makes sense to defer, and where to invest proof-of-concept spikes before committing resources. The value lies in separating real risk (what can force a rewrite) from noise (what gets resolved on the fly).

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior software architect specializing in early technical validation and spike design, with experience eliminating architecture risks before the first structural commit.
Deliverable: a prioritized technical risk inventory with a spike-based mitigation plan. Steps:
1. Restate in one sentence what is being built and for whom, and which constraints you treat as given; list the inherited assumptions you accept as true.
2. Extract the real technical uncertainties grouped by category: integrations and external dependencies, data and domain model, performance and scale, security and compliance, operational costs, and stack or library maturity. Explicitly discard categories with no material risk for this product instead of padding them.
3. For each risk, produce a card: id, assumption that could fail, observable signal of materialization, probability (high/medium/low), architecture impact (high/medium/low), reversibility (easy/costly/irreversible if discovered late), and resulting priority.
4. Rank the risks in a probability x impact matrix and mark the architecture bets to validate first; when two risks tie in priority, break the tie by reversibility (irreversible items are validated first).
5. For each high-priority risk, design a spike: question to answer, minimum experiment, effort in time bands (hours/days), signals that count as evidence, and an exit criterion that defines whether the risk is retired, mitigated, or confirmed.
6. Close with the recommended validation sequence (order and dependencies among spikes), the architecture decisions to defer until evidence is available, and a re-evaluation trigger (what context change reopens the inventory).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm IDEA_PRODUCTO, RESTRICCIONES, and STACK_TENTATIVO; if any is missing, ask before continuing and do not invent data; label every assumption of your own with [SUPUESTO]; calibrate severity according to TOLERANCIA_RIESGO if provided.
Phase 2 - Detection: walk through the six categories and name only concrete risks from the product, not generic textbook risks; each risk must be able to fail in an observable way.
Phase 3 - Prioritization: assign probability, impact, and reversibility to each risk and place them in the matrix; if HORIZONTE_DECISION is short, prioritize risks that block imminent decisions.
Phase 4 - Spike design: for each high-priority risk, build the minimum experiment with a falsifiable exit criterion; the cheapest spike that retires the risk wins.
Phase 5 - Sequencing: order the validation respecting dependencies among spikes and declare which architecture decisions to defer and why, citing the specific uncertainty that blocks each.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Each risk names a specific product assumption and an observable signal of materialization, not generic formulations.
- Every card has probability, impact, and reversibility assigned; no risk is left unclassified.
- The probability x impact matrix explicitly identifies the architecture bets to validate first, with reversibility as a tiebreaker.
- Each high-priority risk has a spike with a question, minimum experiment, effort in time bands (never monetary costs), evidence signals, and a falsifiable exit criterion (retired/mitigated/confirmed).
- Architecture decisions to defer are justified by the specific uncertainty that blocks them.
- Categories with no material risk are explicitly discarded instead of padded.
- A re-evaluation trigger indicates when to reopen the inventory.

--- S | SITUATION ---
I am starting {{PROYECTO}} and the first structural decision shapes speed, CI, ownership, and cost of change for years: monorepo (one repository with workspaces and an internal dependency graph) or polyrepo (one repository per service/package with versioning and publishing between them). Choosing wrong forces a costly migration later. Solving this well unlocks scaffolding on which the team codes from day one without relitigating the structure, with CI and shared packages consistent with the choice. The most common mistake is deciding by trend or preference and discovering the cost at the first cross-cutting change or the first independent release.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior platform architect who has built and migrated repository structures (monorepo with pnpm/Turborepo/Nx and polyrepo with published packages) in product teams.

1. Verify the inputs; if APPS_Y_SERVICIOS, CODIGO_COMPARTIDO, ACOPLAMIENTO_RELEASE, or STACK_GESTOR are missing or ambiguous, ask before deciding. Do not assume silently.
2. Evaluate a weighted criteria matrix: shared-code coupling, release cadence and independence, cross-cutting change atomicity, tooling/CI overhead, governance and ownership, scale and build times. Assign each criterion a weight and a score per option, and show the total.
3. Recommend monorepo or polyrepo by deriving the decision from the matrix, not from preference. Write out the trade-offs we are accepting and at least one measurable trigger condition that would invalidate the decision in the future. Mark every assumption with [SUPUESTO].
4. Phase 1 - Framing: confirm inputs and flag critical gaps; do not proceed without the four decisive inputs.
Phase 2 - Decision: apply the weighted matrix, emit the recommendation with trade-offs and trigger condition.
Phase 3 - Scaffolding: produce tree, configs, sample shared package, root scripts, runtime/manager pin, and CI.
Phase 4 - Execution and future: deliver copyable commands and the bidirectional migration note.
Edge cases to cover when applicable: a single service with no shared code (favors the simpler option); compliance requiring per-repo permission isolation (may tip toward polyrepo even when the rest points to mono); polyglot stacks where the workspace manager does not cover all languages (declare the boundary with [SUPUESTO]).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- The recommendation (monorepo or polyrepo) is explicitly derived from the weighted matrix with visible totals, not from preference.
- Accepted trade-offs and at least one measurable trigger condition are written out.
- The scaffolding is consistent with the decision: if monorepo, there is a real workspace manager with an affected filter; if polyrepo, there is a versioning convention and a published shared package with its release flow.

I have a prototype, {{PROTOTIPO}}, that was born in {{HERRAMIENTA_ORIGEN}} and I need to move it to {{HERRAMIENTA_DESTINO}} to continue building it with version control and a real stack. The risk of the handoff is fidelity loss: the destination tool reconstructs "similar" but not identical because it is unaware of the design tokens, the interactive states, the exact dependencies, and the proprietary components from the origin. Three concrete causes of silent divergence: (a) implicit tokens that the origin resolves by convention and the destination does not inherit; (b) proprietary components from the origin runtime with no equivalent in the destination; (c) different library versions that change style or behavior defaults. An explicit handoff package converts the implicit knowledge of the prototype into a portable specification, so the destination reconstructs with verifiable parity instead of improvising. This unlocks continuing development without visual rework or behavioral regressions.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior platform engineer specializing in porting generative AI prototypes (v0, Lovable, Bolt) to real development environments, with hands-on experience in design systems, visual parity, and dependency management across runtimes.

2. Fidelity specification: per screen and component, the design tokens (color, typography, spacing, radii, shadows), responsive breakpoints, states (hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error, empty), animations/transitions, and expected behavior for each interaction, with focus on {{ELEMENTOS_CRITICOS}}.
3. Stack and dependency manifest: framework, package manager, exact versions, UI and icon library, fonts, environment variables, and differences between the {{HERRAMIENTA_ORIGEN}} runtime and {{STACK_DESTINO}} that break fidelity; every proprietary component with no equivalent in the destination is flagged and a replacement is proposed with its trade-off (fidelity vs. effort).
4. Reconstruction instructions: numbered steps to set up the project in the destination, file-by-file origin->destination mapping, copyable install commands, theme/fonts/assets configuration, and migration order (UI primitives -> components -> screens -> routes -> state/data).
5. Parity verification: checklist confirming identical render per screen, identical response per interactive state, absence of console errors and broken imports, and responsive match at the declared breakpoints.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 0 Framing: confirm that you have access to the exported code from the origin or, failing that, to screenshots and the file tree. If a critical input for the inventory or fidelity is missing, ask for it before continuing; do not reconstruct blindly.
Phase 1 Inventory: go through the origin and list the artifacts without interpreting them yet.

Phase 3 Stack and dependencies: fix real versions from the origin and contrast with {{STACK_DESTINO}}; isolate proprietary components and their replacements. If {{STACK_DESTINO}} is not provided, infer it from the origin and tag it [SUPUESTO].
Phase 4 Reconstruction: order the migration from least to most coupled and produce the mapping and commands.

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need the system prompt that will govern a custom coding agent for project {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}}, destined for {{HERRAMIENTA_DESTINO}}. A code agent without a behavioral contract improvises: it invents APIs, rewrites what it should not touch, and delivers changes that are impossible to review. A well-designed system prompt turns it into a predictable and auditable collaborator: it respects the stack, knows its hard limits, follows a fixed workflow, and always delivers in the same reviewable format. This unlocks delegating real coding work with confidence and enabling fast reviews.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior prompt engineer specializing in designing system prompts for code agents, with experience operating programming assistants in production repos and adapting contracts to different IDEs/agents.
Deliverable: the complete system prompt for the agent, in a single pasteable block, plus (a) a short list of assumptions [SUPUESTO] and (b) a mini acceptance checklist for the user to validate. Build the system prompt with these five explicit numbered sections inside the prompt:
1. Role and identity: define who the agent is, its seniority, and its mission in {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}}; establish that it prioritizes correctness and reviewability over speed.
2. Stack and conventions: fix the stack {{STACK_TECNICO}} and the conventions {{CONVENCIONES}} as mandatory (language, framework, package manager, runtime, linter/formatter, folder structure, patterns). Golden rule: when in doubt about a convention, imitate the neighboring existing code rather than introducing a new style.
3. Hard constraints: translate {{RESTRICCIONES_DURAS}} into explicit verifiable NEVER rules; include by default: do not invent APIs or signatures (if not present in the code or docs, declare it and ask for confirmation), do not delete or move files without confirmation, do not add dependencies without justifying a native alternative, do not expose or assume secrets (use placeholders), do not touch CI/CD configuration or data migrations without explicit approval, do not reformat entire files when the change is local.
4. Workflow: numbered steps the agent follows for each task (1-read relevant code before writing; 2-restate the task in one line; 3-present a short plan; 4-execute the minimum change; 5-self-verify: lint, build/tests, or manual review when no runtime is available) bounded by {{NIVEL_AUTONOMIA}}. Define behavior at each level: propose only / edit with confirmation / autonomous within scope.
5. Output format and clarifications: define exactly what it returns per {{FORMATO_SALIDA}} (diff, full file, explanation, test commands) and the protocol for asking for data when something is ambiguous rather than assuming (ask at most for the essential information and propose a reasonable default tagged accordingly).

Phase 2 - Design: draft the five sections in second-person imperative directed at the agent, with verifiable rules and no filler; resolve the edge case of conflict between {{NIVEL_AUTONOMIA}} and a hard constraint (the constraint wins) and the edge case of a missing convention (imitate neighboring code). Make the workflow always end in verification.
Phase 3 - Packaging: deliver the prompt in a single pasteable block; below it the list of assumptions [SUPUESTO] and a mini acceptance checklist (3-5 items). Do not include prices or the word free.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- The five sections (role, stack/conventions, hard constraints, workflow, output format) are present and numbered inside the system prompt.
- The constraints are in NEVER form, are verifiable, and are project-specific, not generic.
- The workflow explicitly includes reading before writing and verifying before closing, defines the three levels of {{NIVEL_AUTONOMIA}}, and resolves the constraint-vs-autonomy conflict in favor of the constraint.
- The output format is unambiguous: it defines what the agent returns and how it asks for clarifications with a reasonable default.

You need to package {{REPOSITORIO}} so the agent can execute {{TAREA_AGENTE}} with exactly the right context, within {{LIMITE_TOKENS}}. A good package enables the agent to start by locating the right touchpoints on the first attempt, without asking avoidable clarifying questions or breaking the repo's conventions. This is context engineering: the signal-to-token ratio — not volume — is what determines whether the agent succeeds.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior context engineer specializing in coding agents, with software architecture judgment and strict token-budget discipline.

Deliverable: a packaged context document in Markdown, ready to paste as the agent's initial instruction. Steps:
1. Map {{REPOSITORIO}}: folder structure, dominant language and framework, entry point, dependency manifests, configuration, and conventions; incorporate {{ARCHIVOS_PRIORITARIOS}} as an initial signal.
2. Classify files by relevance to {{TAREA_AGENTE}} into three levels: CRITICAL (read in full), REFERENCE (signatures/interfaces/schemas/load-bearing fragments only), and CONTEXT (one line stating existence and purpose).
3. For each CRITICAL file, extract what matters: public contract, invariants, side effects, and extension points; discard dispensable internal implementation.
4. Assemble the package: repo map, rules/conventions to respect, files by level, and an explicit list of omissions with their reason.

Phase 2 - Curation: score each file by relevance to {{TAREA_AGENTE}} and assign a level; the rule is maximum signal per token. A file is CRITICAL only if the agent needs to read it in full to succeed at the task.
Phase 3 - Distillation: summarize each critical file down to its contract and risks (invariants, side effects, extension points); preserve literal text only when it is load-bearing (signatures, schemas, invariants).
Phase 4 - Sanitization: remove or replace with placeholders every secret, credential, token, or PII before including any fragment.
Phase 5 - Assembly and budget: build the document and verify it fits within {{LIMITE_TOKENS}}; if not, demote levels (CRITICAL->REFERENCE, REFERENCE->CONTEXT) before trimming critical content, and document each cut with its reason.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:

- [ ] Each critical file exposes its contract, invariants, side effects, and extension points; no superfluous internal implementation.
- [ ] Conventions are derived from observed code; anything unverifiable is marked [SUPUESTO].
- [ ] Zero secrets, credentials, tokens, or PII in the package.
- [ ] The document fits within {{LIMITE_TOKENS}}; demotions and omissions are listed with their reason.

You are translating a functional description of an interface component into production code. The antipattern to avoid is speculative change: touching multiple things at once and not knowing which fix worked.

Phase 4 - Bisection: remove dependencies, layers, and lines one at a time, verifying after each cut that the failure persists; stop at the irreducible minimum.

spec-vibe-coding_analisis-de-fuga-de-mem:
[inputs]
- RUNTIME: {{RUNTIME}} > Runtime and version where the leak occurs (e.g. Node 20, Chrome 125, JVM 21, CPython 3.12, Go 1.22). Defines capture tool and GC root semantics.
- SINTOMA: {{SINTOMA}} > Observed symptom: shape of the heap or RSS curve, GC frequency, time to OOM, whether memory drops or not after work. Rising RSS with stable heap suggests native/fragmentation leak, not managed heap.
- ESCENARIO_REPRO: {{ESCENARIO_REPRO}} > Flow that triggers growth and steps to reproduce it: which action to repeat, how many times, initial state and logical capture state (same cycle point so snapshots are comparable).
- EVIDENCIA: {{EVIDENCIA}} > Two heap snapshots at the same logical state separated by several cycles of the suspect flow (preferred); or the module code if no snapshots are available (static diagnosis, lower confidence).
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments".

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A process consumes memory in a sustained manner and does not release it after completing work: the pattern points to a leak from retained references, not transient pressure. Closing the retention chain unlocks production stability: avoids OOM, eliminates defensive restarts, and halts the progressive latency degradation from more frequent and longer GC. The goal is to isolate the root cause down to the GC root with evidence, not patch symptoms. Confusions to avoid: transient pressure (heap rises and falls), bounded caches (they grow and stabilize), native leak outside the managed heap (RSS rises with flat heap), and allocator fragmentation.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior performance engineer specialized in memory management and heap diagnostics in garbage-collected runtimes.
Deliverable: leak diagnosis with retainer path to the GC root, pattern named, minimal fix, and verification that proves deallocation.
1. Validate inputs: if RUNTIME, SINTOMA, ESCENARIO_REPRO, or EVIDENCIA are missing or insufficient (a single snapshot, no reproduction steps), stop and ask for them before analyzing.
2. Confirm leak vs. pressure: compare the two snapshots by delta of live retained objects; require monotonic growth of the retained set; discard caches with limits and buffers that stabilize. If SINTOMA is rising RSS with stable managed heap, mark [SUPUESTO] of native/fragmentation leak and reorient.
3. Prioritize: sort constructors and types by growing retained size (not by shallow size); pick 1 to 3 dominant suspects and note their contribution to the delta.
4. Trace retainer path: for each suspect, follow the reference chain to the GC root (global, live closure, stack frame, listener, timer, singleton); if there are multiple paths, prioritize the one retaining the largest size.
5. Name the pattern: unremoved listeners, timers or intervals without clear, closures capturing large objects, cache without eviction or TTL, collection that only grows, global references, detached DOM nodes referenced, subscriptions without unsubscription.
6. Explain retention: why the reference keeps the object alive and at what point in the lifecycle it should be released.
7. Minimal fix: break that chain without touching what is not involved (remove listener in cleanup, clear the timer, WeakMap or WeakRef where applicable, bounded LRU cache, unsubscribe in teardown). If the fix risks regression (aggressive eviction, manual GC in hot path), declare the trade-off.
8. Verification: define the procedure (repeat N cycles, force GC, recapture snapshot, confirm retained delta at zero or stable) that demonstrates closure; include a quantitative acceptance criterion.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Confirmation: distinguish leak from pressure by monotonic retained delta between snapshots; discard bounded caches and native leak.
Phase 2 Isolation: rank by retained size and trace the retainer path of the dominant suspect to the GC root.
Phase 3 Root cause: name the pattern and justify the retention against the evidence; mark every inference not supported with [SUPUESTO].
Phase 4 Remediation and test: minimal targeted fix with declared trade-off + reproducible verification procedure that demonstrates deallocation.
If EVIDENCIA is code and not snapshots: explicit static diagnosis, lower confidence, and list of measurements to confirm it.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Explicit diagnosis: leak yes or no, justified by retained delta between the two snapshots (not by RSS alone).
- [ ] Confusions discarded: bounded cache, transient buffer, and native/fragmentation leak considered and excluded with reason.
- [ ] Suspect table sorted by retained size (not shallow) with its contribution to the growth.
- [ ] Retainer path of the dominant suspect annotated node by node to the named GC root; if there are multiple paths, the one with the greatest retention prioritized.
- [ ] Pattern identified with name from the list and location in the code or snapshot.
- [ ] Minimal fix targeted at breaking the chain, without out-of-scope changes, with declared trade-off if it introduces risk.
- [ ] Reproducible verification with quantitative criterion: steps to reconfirm retained delta at zero or stable after the fix.
- [ ] Inferences not supported by EVIDENCIA marked [SUPUESTO]; no heap data invented.
Expected deliverable: leak analysis report with diagnosis, discarded confusions, suspect table, retainer path to GC root, named pattern, minimal fix diff, and verification procedure with acceptance criterion that proves deallocation.
spec-vibe-coding_bisect-asistido-de-regr:
[inputs]
- SINTOMA: {{SINTOMA}} > Behavior that broke: what was expected, what happens now, and how it is observed (message, output, test failure, metric)
- TEST_DE_BONDAD: {{TEST_DE_BONDAD}} > Way to verify a commit: command, script, or manual steps that give an unequivocal good/bad verdict and, ideally, are repeatable
- COMMIT_MALO: {{COMMIT_MALO}} > Commit or reference where the regression is already present, normally HEAD
- COMMIT_BUENO: {{COMMIT_BUENO}} > Commit or reference where the behavior still worked (optional; if missing, help estimate it with tags, dates, or git log)
- STACK_Y_ENTORNO: {{STACK_Y_ENTORNO}} > Language, dependency manager, and how to install/compile/run the project at each commit; flakiness notes or setup steps (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A behavior that used to work broke at some point in history: {{SINTOMA}}. Reviewing commit by commit is unfeasible and reading the accumulated diff is noise. Binary search over history (git bisect) resolves this: given a bad commit ({{COMMIT_MALO}}) and a good one ({{COMMIT_BUENO}}), it halves the range at each step and isolates the first defective commit in approximately log2(N) iterations. The technique is only valid if the range is monotonic (a single good->bad transition) and the verdict per commit is stable; that is why the deterministic goodness test is the critical piece. Isolating the guilty commit unlocks root cause diagnosis, a targeted fix instead of a blind one, and a non-regression test that shields the system against the same failure.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software engineer expert in regression debugging with git bisect, with practice in designing deterministic goodness tests and root cause analysis on diffs.

Deliverable: the first defective commit isolated, with root cause explained, a concrete fix, and a non-regression test. Conduct the session one iteration at a time:
1. Reproduce and define goodness: based on {{SINTOMA}} and {{TEST_DE_BONDAD}}, formulate a deterministic, fast test with an unequivocal good/bad verdict for any commit; confirm reproducibility (at least two stable runs) before continuing. If the test depends on external state (network, data, date), propose it isolated.
2. Set the bounds: validate {{COMMIT_MALO}} and {{COMMIT_BUENO}}; if the good one is missing, help estimate a candidate with tags, dates, or git log and verify it is truly good before starting. Warn that the range must be monotonic; if {{COMMIT_BUENO}} also fails, the range is poorly bounded and you need to go further back.
3. Handle intermittency: if {{STACK_Y_ENTORNO}} suggests flakiness, propose mitigations (retries, pin versions, clean build/cache between steps, container, git bisect skip for commits that do not compile or do not apply).
4. Start: deliver git bisect start, git bisect bad {{COMMIT_MALO}}, git bisect good {{COMMIT_BUENO}}, and estimate the expected iterations (log2 of the number of commits in the range).
5. Iterate one at a time: at each step ask for {{TEST_DE_BONDAD}} to be executed on the active commit and the verdict reported; according to the real response deliver git bisect good or git bisect bad and the remaining commits. Do not assume verdicts. If a commit does not compile or does not apply, instruct git bisect skip.
6. Close and diagnose: upon the first defective commit, ask for git show; explain the root cause, propose a concrete and minimal fix and a non-regression test that fails before and passes after; remind git bisect reset to return to the original branch. If {{TEST_DE_BONDAD}} is automatable (exit code 0=good, !=0=bad), write the equivalent git bisect run to reproduce the session without intervention.

Edge cases to watch: the culprit is a merge commit (suggest git bisect with --first-parent or review parents); the bug was introduced and then masked (non-monotonic range); the bad and good commits are inverted; the goodness test changes definition between commits (pin the script from outside the tree).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm symptom, reproducible goodness test, and both bounds; ask for missing inputs before touching the history.
Phase 2 - Start: issue the bisect start commands and announce the estimated number of iterations.
Phase 3 - Iterative loop: one iteration per turn; wait for the user's real verdict, never assume it, and respond only with the next good/bad/skip command and the remaining commits.
Phase 4 - Close: isolate the first defective commit, analyze its diff, deliver root cause, fix, and non-regression test, remind git bisect reset and, if applicable, the automated git bisect run.
Mark as [SUPUESTO] every inference about commits, environment, or behavior not confirmed by the user. If a non-monotonic range, inverted bounds, a good commit that fails, or a merge as the culprit is detected, stop and ask for adjustment before continuing.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- The goodness test is deterministic, fast, and gives an unequivocal good/bad verdict for any commit; its reproducibility was confirmed before starting.
- The bounds were validated: the bad one fails, the good one passes, and the range is monotonic; a warning was issued if not.
- The git bisect commands are exact and in order (start, bad, good, good/bad/skip per iteration, reset at the end).
- The loop advances one iteration per turn and never assumes the user's verdict.
- Applicable edge cases are covered (intermittency with mitigations, commits that do not compile via skip, merge as culprit, automation with git bisect run).
- The close includes the first defective commit, root cause in plain language, a concrete and minimal fix, and a non-regression test that fails before and passes after.
- Unconfirmed inferences are marked [SUPUESTO]; neutral, professional English, no emojis.
Expected deliverable: a bisect session transcript that ends with the guilty commit identified, its root cause, the proposed fix, and the non-regression test, ready to apply.

A frontend request is being blocked by the browser and delivery has stopped: the data is not arriving, the user flow is broken, and the team is losing time because the console labels as "CORS" both genuine CORS failures and network, TLS, or mixed-content errors. The focus is systems and processes, never people: the question is not who made a mistake, but why the system allowed the error and how to structurally prevent it. This requires three disciplines the document must sustain together: factual reconstruction without interpretation, honest quantification of impact, and action-to-cause traceability.

I have a deployed application that responds on a temporary provider URL and I want to serve it from my own domain with valid HTTPS. The challenge is not just pointing the domain: it is doing so without downtime if traffic is already flowing, with the certificate properly issued and renewing automatically, and with a clear path back if something fails. Solving this correctly unlocks publishing the brand at its definitive URL, enabling email and stable links, and operating with confidence across every redeploy. A poorly thought-out cutover strategy produces minutes of downtime or a broken padlock that drives users away; a well-planned one is invisible.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior platform and DNS engineer, with experience in TLS/ACME certificates and zero-downtime production cutovers.
Deliver an executed and verified plan to connect {{DOMINIO}} on {{PROVEEDOR_DNS}} pointing to {{DESTINO_DESPLIEGUE}}, with SSL via {{METODO_SSL}}, considering {{TRAFICO_PRODUCTIVO}} and {{VENTANA}}. Steps:
1. Confirm missing or ambiguous data (ALIAS/ANAME or CNAME-flattening support at the apex, current TTL, port 80 exposure, existing CAA record, need for a wildcard) BEFORE modifying any record. If a piece of data blocks a decision, ask for it instead of assuming.
2. Reduce the TTL of the target record to a short value in advance and capture the current DNS state as a rollback baseline.
3. Issue the certificate validating all names (apex, www, wildcard if applicable) and confirm the complete chain.
4. Define apex (A/AAAA or ALIAS/ANAME) and www (CNAME), declare the canonical host, and configure the 301 redirect from the other.
5. Execute the cutover, verify resolution and TLS from several resolvers, raise the TTL to a stable value, and activate automatic renewal.

Phase 1 - Preparation and baseline: document current records with dig/nslookup (include CAA and authoritative NS); lower the TTL of the record being changed (e.g. 300 s) and wait for the old TTL to expire so the cutover propagates quickly.
Phase 2 - Certificate: choose validation based on the case (HTTP-01 if the origin exposes port 80; DNS-01 with TXT _acme-challenge if going through a CDN, dealing with an apex, or needing a wildcard); if the CA applies rate limits, test first against its staging environment; issue and verify SAN, dates, issuer, and fullchain.
Phase 3 - Name topology: apex via ALIAS/ANAME, CNAME-flattening, or A/AAAA depending on provider support; www as CNAME to the apex or the hosting hostname; declare canonical and set up the 301 redirect from the non-canonical one.
Phase 4 - Zero-downtime cutover: update the record to the new target only when the certificate is already valid at the destination; verify resolution from at least two independent resolvers, validate fullchain, test HTTPS, the HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect, and HSTS if applicable.
Phase 5 - Hardening and close-out: raise the TTL to a stable value (e.g. 3600 s), confirm automatic renewal (schedule an expiration alert as a safety net), and document the exact rollback (previous record, value, TTL, and reversion order).
Edge cases: apex without ALIAS/ANAME support -> use a canonical subdomain or flattening; CAA blocking the chosen CA -> adjust CAA before issuing; domain behind a proxy/CDN that terminates TLS -> the origin certificate may differ from the public one.

It also tends to produce plausible and well-presented code that hides the defect: correct names, clean structure, wrong behavior. The purpose is to separate what the code claims to do from what it actually does, in the context of {{CONTEXTO_TAREA}}, with the rigor required by {{NIVEL_CONFIANZA}}. 3. Layer 2 - False assumptions: what the code takes for granted without verifying (field always present, input already validated, network infallible, stable collection order, idempotence, assumed behavior or version of a library).
4. Layer 3 - Dangerous shortcuts: empty catch, secrets in plaintext, injection via concatenation of queries or commands, missing input validation, broad permissions, invented or nonexistent dependencies, sensitive data in logs, happy-path-only code.
5. Layer 4 - Maintainability: unnecessary complexity, duplication, misleading names, hidden coupling, absence of tests on critical paths.
6. Integration verdict: Ready to integrate / Integrate with corrections / Do not integrate, with the list of blockers and, if applicable, the 1-3 minimal tests that would close the decision.

2. Explain the root cause of each bottleneck linking it to its source: WHERE/JOIN predicates, implicit functions or casts that break sargability, missing useful index, stale statistics, low selectivity, ORDER BY/GROUP BY without a supporting index, or a suboptimal join order.
3. Propose concrete indexes (columns, order, covering or partial where applicable) and rewrites (remove SELECT *, make predicates sargable, reorder/condition joins, avoid correlated subqueries, materialized CTE vs inline, OR to UNION ALL when appropriate), each with justification and trade-off.
4. Deliver the rewritten query ready to execute and the exact CREATE INDEX statements for the declared engine.
5. Define how to validate the improvement: re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and compare plan, cost, and time before/after against the goal.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Plan reading: locate operations, their relative cost, and the estimated-vs-actual relationship.
Phase 2 - Diagnostic: rank bottlenecks from highest to lowest impact with their root cause.
Phase 3 - Proposal: design indexes and sargable rewrite; flag conflicts or redundancy with existing indexes.
Phase 4 - Delivery: optimized query + index DDL + assumptions marked [SUPUESTO].
Phase 5 - Validation: instructions to measure before/after and warning about the write and storage cost of new indexes on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE workloads.
Edge cases: if the plan is only an estimated EXPLAIN, state that mis-estimates cannot be confirmed and request EXPLAIN ANALYZE; if the slowness is not attributable to the query (locks, IO contention, server parameters), note it and do not force indexes; if a proposed index duplicates an existing one, prefer adjusting the existing one.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each cited bottleneck references a concrete node from the provided plan (no invented operations).
- [ ] Cardinalities and structure are not invented; anything assumed is marked [SUPUESTO].
- [ ] Proposed indexes specify table, columns, and order, are valid for the given MOTOR_VERSION, and do not duplicate existing indexes.
- [ ] The rewritten query is executable and preserves the exact semantics of the original result (same row set and ordering if the original guaranteed it).
- [ ] Each rewrite justifies why it improves sargability or reduces rows processed, with its trade-off.
- [ ] A before/after validation plan is included that is measurable against OBJETIVO_RENDIMIENTO, with a warning about the write cost of new indexes.
- [ ] If the cause is not the query (locks, IO, config), it is noted rather than forcing a solution.
Expected deliverable: prioritized diagnostic block + final SQL query + CREATE INDEX scripts + measurable verification steps against OBJETIVO_RENDIMIENTO.
spec-datos_sql_refactor_subqueries_a_cte:
[inputs]
- CONSULTA_SQL: {{CONSULTA_SQL}} > Original SQL query with nested subqueries to refactor
- MOTOR_SQL: {{MOTOR_SQL}} > Engine and version: PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, MySQL 8+, SQL Server, or other

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I have a SQL query ({{CONSULTA_SQL}}) on {{MOTOR_SQL}} whose nested subqueries in SELECT, FROM, WHERE, or HAVING have made it difficult to read, debug, and maintain. Common Table Expressions (the WITH clause from SQL:1999, now supported by PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, MySQL 8+, and SQL Server) let you decompose that logic into named, sequential blocks that read top to bottom. A faithful refactoring unlocks faster code reviews, step-by-step debugging, sub-result reuse, and a maintainable foundation for optimizing or evolving the query — without changing a single row of the result. The goal is readability and maintainability with exact equivalence, not execution-plan optimization: any performance change is reported but not pursued unless requested.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior data engineer with expertise in analytical SQL and query refactoring, with mastery of CTEs, execution plans, and dialect differences across database engines.

Deliverable: the query rewritten as modular CTEs, 100% equivalent to the original. Steps:
1) Inventory each nested subquery in {{CONSULTA_SQL}}, its clause, its purpose, its expected cardinality, and its dependencies.
2) Restate the intent of the query and lay out the decomposition plan before writing any SQL.
3) Convert each subquery into a named CTE per {{CONVENCION_NOMBRES}}, ordered so each depends only on prior CTEs, closing with a clean final SELECT.
4) Comment each CTE per {{NIVEL_COMENTARIOS}}: what it produces and why it exists.
5) Preserve exact semantics: same columns, types, filters, joins, aggregations, NULL handling, DISTINCT, LIMIT/OFFSET, and ORDER BY from the original.
6) Deliver an equivalence proof: EXCEPT/MINUS in both directions plus row counts, adapted to {{MOTOR_SQL}}.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Mapping: parse {{CONSULTA_SQL}} against {{ESQUEMA_TABLAS}} and list subqueries with their dependency graph; classify each as non-correlated, correlated, or scalar; if the engine or schema is ambiguous, ask before continuing.
Phase 2 Planning: order CTEs topologically (leaves first, then aggregations, rankings, and correlated ones) and name them self-descriptively, with no forward references or name collisions.
Phase 3 Rewriting: emit the WITH block with each CTE commented and the final SELECT; use only syntax valid for {{MOTOR_SQL}}. Sensitive cases: correlated subqueries (rewrite to join, LATERAL, or APPLY per engine while preserving row-by-row semantics); scalar subqueries in SELECT (ensure they still return at most one row); EXISTS/IN/NOT IN predicates (preserve NULL behavior, especially NOT IN with NULLs); rankings and tie-breaking (exactly replicate the ORDER BY clause and tie treatment).
Phase 4 Verification: mentally validate equivalence, generate the bidirectional EXCEPT/MINUS + count script, and declare as [SUPUESTO] any inference about NULLs, duplicates, or tie-breaking. Do not invent columns or tables outside {{ESQUEMA_TABLAS}} or {{CONSULTA_SQL}}. If a subquery cannot be faithfully converted to a CTE, declare it, do not force it, and propose the safest alternative.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every nested subquery in the original is mapped to exactly one CTE (or its merge or non-conversion is justified).
- [ ] CTEs are ordered with no forward references; each depends only on prior ones.
- [ ] Names follow {{CONVENCION_NOMBRES}}, are descriptive, with no collisions or opaque aliases.
- [ ] Each CTE carries a comment per {{NIVEL_COMENTARIOS}}.
- [ ] The final SELECT preserves columns, ordering, types, filters, aggregations, NULLs, DISTINCT, LIMIT/OFFSET, and ORDER BY from the original.
- [ ] Correlated, scalar subqueries, and EXISTS/IN/NOT IN predicates preserve their exact semantics, including NULL handling.
- [ ] Syntax is 100% valid for {{MOTOR_SQL}}; no functions from another dialect.
- [ ] Equivalence proof included (bidirectional EXCEPT/MINUS + row counts) returning zero differences.
- [ ] All inferences marked [SUPUESTO]; zero invented columns or tables.
Expected deliverable: (1) executable refactored SQL block, (2) CTE-by-CTE table (name, purpose, dependencies), (3) equivalence-proof script with expected result, (4) a brief note on limits: non-convertible subqueries, open assumptions, and any observed performance differences.
spec-datos_sql_window_functions_ranking:
[inputs]
- TABLA: {{TABLA}} > Source fact table or view (e.g. sales_facts)
- DIMENSION_PARTICION: {{DIMENSION_PARTICION}} > Column that defines the window partition group (e.g. region)
- ENTIDAD: {{ENTIDAD}} > Entity to rank within the partition (e.g. customer_id)
- METRICA: {{METRICA}} > Numeric column to order and accumulate (e.g. sale_amount)
- GRANO_TEMPORAL: {{GRANO_TEMPORAL}} > Column or expression for the ORDER BY time axis (e.g. month)
- MOTOR_SQL: {{MOTOR_SQL}} > Target engine: PostgreSQL | SQL Server | BigQuery | Snowflake
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to turn a fact table into actionable analytical metrics without collapsing the per-row detail: competitive ranking within each group, progressive running totals over time, and period-over-period comparisons. Solving this with window functions (instead of correlated subqueries or self-joins) unlocks dashboards, trend alerts, and cohort analysis with readable, performant queries. The result must be SQL ready to run and reusable as a team data pattern.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior data engineer specializing in analytical SQL and dimensional modeling, with mastery of the SQL:2003 window function standard and its differences across engines.
Deliverable: a complete, commented, and validated SQL query over {{TABLA}} for {{MOTOR_SQL}}. Steps:
1. Base CTE that selects {{DIMENSION_PARTICION}}, {{ENTIDAD}}, {{GRANO_TEMPORAL}}, and {{METRICA}} aggregated to the correct grain. First resolve whether the (entity + grain) key has duplicates: aggregate with SUM/COUNT before applying windows, so ROW_NUMBER does not operate on repeated rows.
2. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY {{DIMENSION_PARTICION}} ORDER BY {{METRICA}} DESC) as a unique ordered identifier, plus RANK() and DENSE_RANK() with the same ordering. Comment when to choose each in the presence of ties (unique row vs gaps vs dense) and add a secondary order column (e.g. {{ENTIDAD}}) for deterministic, reproducible tie-breaking.
3. Running total: SUM({{METRICA}}) OVER (PARTITION BY {{DIMENSION_PARTICION}} ORDER BY {{GRANO_TEMPORAL}} ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW). Explicit ROWS frame: justify that the default RANGE would sum all ties on the order value and distort the running total.
4. Period-over-period comparison: LAG({{METRICA}}, 1, 0) and LEAD({{METRICA}}, 1, 0) OVER (PARTITION BY {{ENTIDAD}} ORDER BY {{GRANO_TEMPORAL}}). Derive absolute and percentage change, protecting division by zero with NULLIF(prev, 0); decide and document whether a null/zero prior period yields NULL or an explicit default.
5. Flag all {{MOTOR_SQL}}-dependent syntax (date handling for {{GRANO_TEMPORAL}}, QUALIFY in BigQuery/Snowflake vs wrapping subquery in PostgreSQL/SQL Server, NULLS FIRST/LAST, numeric casts) and deliver a portable variant for all 4 engines.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Understand: confirm schema, actual grain of {{METRICA}}, type and continuity of {{GRANO_TEMPORAL}} (period gaps break positional LAG/LEAD), approximate volume, and desired tie treatment.
Phase 2 Build: aggregated base CTE, then windows in a second layer to maintain readability. Name each derived column by its semantics (rn, ranking, dense_ranking, running_total, prior_period, abs_change, pct_change).
Phase 3 Verify: each window has correct PARTITION BY and ORDER BY, explicit frame on the running total, LAG/LEAD with offset and default, and deterministic tie-breaking present.
If {{TABLA}}, {{DIMENSION_PARTICION}}, {{ENTIDAD}}, {{METRICA}}, {{GRANO_TEMPORAL}}, or {{MOTOR_SQL}} are missing, ask before writing SQL.
Default assumptions if not specified: ties resolved by {{ENTIDAD}} ascending; missing prior period treated as zero for abs_change and NULL for pct_change. Limit: window functions do not fill missing periods; if continuity is needed, suggest a calendar/spine as a prior step.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The base CTE aggregates to the correct grain and eliminates key duplicates before applying windows.
- [ ] Every window function declares PARTITION BY and ORDER BY explicitly and with justification.
- [ ] Ranking includes deterministic tie-breaking (secondary order column) and explains ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK in the presence of ties.
- [ ] The running total uses the ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW frame (not implicit RANGE), with justification.
- [ ] LAG and LEAD specify offset and default; the percentage change avoids division by zero with NULLIF.
- [ ] All {{MOTOR_SQL}}-dependent syntax (dates, QUALIFY, NULLS FIRST/LAST, casts) is flagged, and a portable variant for all 4 engines is included.
- [ ] The query is commented and executable as-is over {{TABLA}}.
Expected deliverable: executable, commented SQL block + validation note (control counts; verify that the last running-total value per group equals the group's full sum; confirm ROW_NUMBER generates no duplicates per partition).

--- S | SITUATION ---
Data lives in long format (one row per transaction), but decisions need a cross-tabulation: categories as columns, an aggregated metric per cell, ready to paste into an executive report or dashboard without manual post-processing in spreadsheets. A well-built PIVOT query unlocks immediate readability for leadership; its inverse UNPIVOT enables reconciliation and audit of the result against the source, closing the risk of figures that do not reconcile with the origin.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior data engineer specializing in analytical SQL and reporting, with expertise in dialect differences across database engines.
Deliverable: four executable, commented SQL blocks.
1. Main PIVOT query over {{TABLA_ORIGEN}}: groups by {{COLUMNAS_FILA}}, converts the values of {{COLUMNA_A_PIVOTAR}} (or {{VALORES_COLUMNA}} if provided) into columns, applies {{FUNCION_AGREGACION}}({{METRICA}}) per cell, with row subtotals and a grand total (GROUPING SETS / ROLLUP where the engine supports it).
2. Inverse UNPIVOT query that returns the cross-tab to long format (one row per row-column pair) to validate reconciliation against the source.
3. Portable version using aggregated CASE WHEN (SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN ... END)), valid in any engine without a native PIVOT operator.

Phase 1 Interpret: confirm engine and exact version, identify the source's long format, validate that {{COLUMNA_A_PIVOTAR}} has a reasonable cardinality for columns (ideally fewer than 50 distinct values), and that {{FUNCION_AGREGACION}} is consistent with the type of {{METRICA}}.
Phase 2 Plan: decide static pivot (known values in {{VALORES_COLUMNA}}) or dynamic (SQL generated at runtime); define aggregation, NULL policy, and deterministic ordering.
Phase 3 Execute: write all 4 blocks with the exact syntax of the declared dialect; mark as [SUPUESTO] any table/column name, data type, or category value not provided.
Phase 4 Verify: confirm that the UNPIVOT reconstructs the source count/total (the PIVOT's SUM total equals SUM(METRICA) from the source for SUM; equivalent counts for COUNT) and that row subtotals and grand total agree.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- [ ] Dialect and version of {{MOTOR_BD}} declared; syntax correct and executable for that engine.
- [ ] PIVOT aggregates {{FUNCION_AGREGACION}}({{METRICA}}) correctly for each {{COLUMNAS_FILA}} x {{COLUMNA_A_PIVOTAR}} intersection.
- [ ] Row subtotals and grand total present and reconciled; columns in deterministic order.
- [ ] UNPIVOT reconstructs the source with an explicit reconciliation criterion (which equality must hold).
- [ ] Portable CASE WHEN version included and equivalent in result to the native PIVOT.
- [ ] NULLs vs zeros handled explicitly based on whether the metric is additive.
- [ ] Static vs dynamic pivot decision justified for {{MOTOR_BD}} (BigQuery requires EXECUTE IMMEDIATE; MySQL has no native PIVOT; etc.).
- [ ] Assumptions marked [SUPUESTO]; no name, type, or value invented without a tag.
