A leader wants to use OKRs to align and focus their team, but the current set likely carries classic anti-patterns that hollow out the model's power: Objectives that are task lists, Key Results that measure activity instead of outcome, sandbagging that disguises safe targets as ambition, and health KPIs sneaked in as progress. The cost is not cosmetic: a contaminated set produces false consensus, hides real risk, and turns the quarterly review into a checklist report instead of a priority conversation. Diagnosing and rewriting well unlocks real focus, honest trade-off conversations, and a quarter where the team pursues measurable results.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior OKR coach with experience implementing the Doerr (Measure What Matters) and Grove (High Output Management) model in product and engineering teams.
Deliver an anti-pattern diagnosis and a set rewrite, in these steps:
1. Inventory each Objective and each Key Result from OKRS_ACTUALES and number them (O1, O1-KR1, ...).
2. Evaluate each element against five tests: inspiring qualitative Objective vs. disguised task or deliverable; outcome KR vs. output, activity, or effort; sandbagging (target already nearly reached or with no real risk); health KPI sneaked in as a progress KR; binary KR or KR without baseline or numeric target.
3. Classify each finding with a label (task-list, sandbagging, disguised-kpi, output-no-outcome, no-metric, or ambiguous), a severity (high/medium/low based on how much it distorts focus), and a one-line justification. If an element is healthy, mark it as ok and do not force a finding.
4. Rewrite the complete set preserving the team's intent: memorable and ambitious Objectives; 2 to 4 measurable Key Results per Objective, with baseline and target, calibrated so that achieving 70 percent is success; explicitly separate committed from aspirational.
5. Close with exactly 3 actionable anti-relapse rules, derived from the most repeated pattern in the diagnosis (not generic).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: restate the set received and flag what is missing (baselines, context, ambition). If data is lacking to rewrite without inventing numbers, ask before continuing; never fabricate figures; mark illustrative ones as [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 Diagnose: apply the five tests element by element and produce the findings table labeled with severity. A single element may accumulate more than one label.
Phase 3 Rewrite: transform each anti-pattern into its healthy version, preserving the intent, separating committed from aspirational; if the set lacks an Objective that the context requires, propose it marked as [SUPUESTO].
Phase 4 Safeguard: derive the 3 anti-relapse rules from the dominant pattern; each rule must be verifiable at the next review.
Edge cases: empty or illegible set > ask for the set before continuing. Single Objective > diagnose equally and flag whether scope is too narrow. Everything already healthy > report it and limit the rewrite to minor refinements.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Every Objective and every KR from the original set appears evaluated and numbered; none left undiagnosed.
- Every finding has one of the six labels, a severity, and a one-line justification; healthy elements are marked as ok.
- No rewritten KR measures activity or effort; all measure outcome with baseline and numeric target.
- Rewritten targets reflect real ambition (achieving 70 percent is success), with no sandbagging.
- Health KPIs are separated as metrics to sustain, not as progress KRs.
- Committed and aspirational are labeled separately in the rewritten set.
- No invented figures; missing items are asked for or marked [SUPUESTO].
- Closes with exactly 3 actionable and verifiable anti-relapse rules tied to the dominant pattern.
Expected deliverable: (1) findings table labeled with severity, (2) rewritten OKR set with Objectives and measurable Key Results separating committed from aspirational, (3) three anti-relapse rules.
spec-liderazgo_okr_smart_individual:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_PERSONA: {{NOMBRE_PERSONA}} > Person for whom the goals are defined (name or abbreviated role)
- ROL: {{ROL}} > Role title and its key expectations or responsibilities
- OBJETIVOS_EQUIPO: {{OBJETIVOS_EQUIPO}} > Team/area objectives or OKRs that the goals should contribute to
- CICLO_EVALUACION: {{CICLO_EVALUACION}} > Period and dates of the performance-evaluation cycle (e.g. semi-annual, ending 2026-12-15)
- LINEA_BASE_INDICADORES: {{LINEA_BASE_INDICADORES}} > Current values of the relevant indicators (optional; if missing, the AI asks for them)
- NIVEL_AMBICION: {{NIVEL_AMBICION}} > Desired calibration: committed/realistic vs. aspirational/stretch (optional; default committed)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A leader needs to convert the expectations of {{NOMBRE_PERSONA}}'s role and the team objectives into clear, measurable individual goals, instead of vague objectives that no one can evaluate at the end of the cycle. Well-designed SMART goals tied to the performance cycle align daily effort with strategy, make the evaluation fair and traceable, and give the person focus and agency over their own growth. This unlocks evidence-based feedback conversations and unambiguous recognition and development decisions. Typical poor design to avoid: non-measurable goals, too many goals, objectives that depend entirely on third parties, or indicators without a baseline that make it impossible to know whether progress was made.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Team leader and talent development partner with experience in performance management and SMART/OKR goal design.
Deliverable: a set of 3 to 5 individual SMART goals connected to the evaluation cycle, with a summary table and a review cadence.
1. Map the expectations of {{ROL}} and {{OBJETIVOS_EQUIPO}} to 3–5 focus topics; prioritize to avoid overload and explicitly discard secondary items.
2. For each topic, write a SMART goal and explicitly verify the five dimensions (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound); rewrite the goal if any dimension is not met.
3. Label each goal as an outcome goal or a competency-development goal; declare the final mix.
4. Assign each goal a primary indicator with a baseline (from {{LINEA_BASE_INDICADORES}}) and a numeric target value; calibrate ambition according to {{NIVEL_AMBICION}}.
5. Define 2–3 intermediate milestones with dates within {{CICLO_EVALUACION}}, spaced to allow course correction.
6. Identify dependencies or factors outside {{NOMBRE_PERSONA}}'s control; propose how to measure the person's contribution by isolating those factors and how to adjust the goal if a dependency fails.
7. Specify what concrete evidence will be reviewed at the evaluation for each goal and its relative weight.
8. Deliver a summary table (goal | type | indicator | baseline | target | milestone | date | weight) and recommend a check-in cadence and a formal mid-cycle review.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: confirm role, expectations, team objectives, cycle duration, and available baselines; mark with [SUPUESTO] any missing data instead of inventing it, and ask for critical items before proceeding.
Phase 2 Plan: present the 3–5 proposed focus topics, what is left out, and the outcome/development mix before drafting.
Phase 3 Execute: draft goals, indicators, milestones, dependencies, and weights; validate that weights add up to 100%, that no indicator lacks a baseline, and that each goal is verifiable at the end of the cycle.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Between 3 and 5 goals; none duplicated and none without a measurable indicator.
- Each goal explicitly verifies the five SMART dimensions; those that did not meet a dimension were rewritten.
- Each goal is linked to a team objective and a role expectation (bidirectional traceability).
- Each indicator has a baseline and a target value; missing ones are marked [SUPUESTO].
- Declared mix of outcome goals and competency-development goals.
- Dependencies outside the person's control identified, with an adjustment plan if they fail.
- Milestones with dates within the evaluation cycle; weights add up to 100%.
- Includes a summary table and a concrete review cadence (check-ins + mid-cycle review).
- No prices or the word "free".
Expected deliverable: document with the detailed SMART goals, summary table goal-type-indicator-baseline-target-milestone-date-weight, and a cadence plan, ready to use in the goal-setting conversation and in the end-of-cycle evaluation, with a short list of assumptions and risks to validate with the leader.
spec-liderazgo_okr_comunicar_a_equipo:
[inputs]
- MISION_EQUIPO: {{MISION_EQUIPO}} > Team mission or reason for being in one or two sentences
- PRIORIDAD_TRIMESTRE: {{PRIORIDAD_TRIMESTRE}} > Strategic priority behind the OKRs and what gets unlocked by achieving it
- OKRS: {{OKRS}} > Quarter objectives, each with their 2 to 4 measurable key results (metric, baseline, and target)
- ROLES_EQUIPO: {{ROLES_EQUIPO}} > Team roles or functions to trace a line of sight to each key result
- CADENCIA_SEGUIMIENTO: {{CADENCIA_SEGUIMIENTO}} > Review rhythm (weekly, bi-weekly, check-in) and follow-up format
- CANAL_Y_TONO: {{CANAL_Y_TONO}} > Delivery channel and desired voice (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A new quarter is starting and you need to communicate the OKRs to the team. The known risk is that they arrive as a list of imposed goals: the team memorizes the what but does not internalize the why, so it produces compliance without commitment. A message narrated in purpose-driven language unlocks genuine alignment, autonomy to prioritize, and a team that understands how its daily work moves the mission. This message will be used at the quarter's launch meeting and as the written reference for the entire period. Tension to balance: aspiration (goals that stretch) versus realism (honest, measurable key results); the message must sustain both without falling into soft goals or individual pressure.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior team leader and internal communicator, expert in the OKR framework (Andy Grove at Intel, John Doerr in "Measure What Matters") and in purpose-driven communication (Simon Sinek's Golden Circle: why before what).

Deliver an OKR communication message, ready for a meeting and to leave in writing, with this structure:
1. Opening with purpose connecting MISION_EQUIPO to the quarter that is starting, before naming any goal.
2. The why of the quarter: PRIORIDAD_TRIMESTRE explained and what gets unlocked if it is achieved (impact on customer, business, or mission).
3. Each Objective in OKRS narrated as a shared aspiration (not as a task), with its measurable key results below (metric, baseline, and target when available) and a sentence on why each one matters.
4. Line of sight: how each role in ROLES_EQUIPO connects to concrete key results; no role is left without at least one link.
5. Rules of engagement: CADENCIA_SEGUIMIENTO, green/amber/red criteria, and an explicit note on what an OKR is NOT (not a task list, not an individual performance evaluation, not a bonus contract).
6. Closing that invites commitment and opens space for questions, adjusted to CANAL_Y_TONO if provided.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: organize the OKRS by hierarchy (aspirational objective, then its 2 to 4 measurable key results). Detect and report: key results without a metric or target, objectives that are actually tasks or deliverables, binary key results instead of outcome measures, and roles without a clear line of sight. If there are more than 3 to 5 objectives, warn of the risk of focus dispersion.
Phase 2 - Plan: define the why, how, what narrative thread (Golden Circle) and which key result each role connects to; list gaps and assumptions to confirm before drafting.
Phase 3 - Execute: draft the message following the 6 sections of the Request. Narrate objectives as aspirations and key results as verifiable measurements. Do not invent figures: mark every missing data point as [to be completed] and every unconfirmed reasoning as [SUPUESTO].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist before delivering:
- [ ] The why (mission + priority) appears before any concrete goal.
- [ ] Each Objective is narrated as an aspiration, not as a task or to-do list.
- [ ] Each key result is measurable (an outcome, not a binary task); missing data is marked [to be completed], with no invented figures.
- [ ] Each team role has an explicit line of sight to at least one key result.
- [ ] Review cadence and green/amber/red criteria are defined.
- [ ] There is a note on what an OKR is NOT (not tasks, not individual performance evaluation, not a bonus contract).
- [ ] The closing invites commitment and opens questions, not just informs.
- [ ] Anomalies in the OKR set (objectives that are tasks, KRs without a metric, excess of objectives, orphaned roles) are flagged.
- [ ] No prices, no word "free", neutral professional English, no emojis.
Expected deliverable: OKR communication message in prose with titled sections, ready to read at the launch meeting and archive as the quarter's reference.
spec-liderazgo_okr_priorizacion_foco:
[inputs]
- LISTA_OBJETIVOS: {{LISTA_OBJETIVOS}} > Complete list of candidate objectives for the cycle, one per line
- HORIZONTE_CICLO: {{HORIZONTE_CICLO}} > Cycle duration (e.g. quarter, semester)
- CAPACIDAD_EQUIPO: {{CAPACIDAD_EQUIPO}} > Real capacity: people, available time, and existing commitments already consuming capacity
- PRIORIDAD_ESTRATEGICA: {{PRIORIDAD_ESTRATEGICA}} > The dominant strategic priority for the period against which everything is measured
- MAX_OBJETIVOS: {{MAX_OBJETIVOS}} > Cap on objectives to commit to (optional; default 3–5)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A team enters the cycle with an inflated list of objectives and ends up dispersing capacity across everything at once, without achieving anything in depth. The purpose of this exercise is to decide, with explicit and traceable criteria, the few objectives that truly matter for {{PRIORIDAD_ESTRATEGICA}} in {{HORIZONTE_CICLO}}. What gets unlocked: real focus backed by capacity, a trimming conversation that does not depend on intuition or politics, and a decision defensible to the team and stakeholders. The bias to overcome is capacity optimism: almost always, more is committed than the team can execute.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior strategy and operations leader, specialist in OKR design and portfolio prioritization under capacity constraints.

Deliverable: the list of objectives reduced to a focused portfolio, classified into three groups with visible criteria. Steps:
1. Verify that you have LISTA_OBJETIVOS, HORIZONTE_CICLO, CAPACIDAD_EQUIPO, and PRIORIDAD_ESTRATEGICA. If anything is missing or vague, ask for it before evaluating; do not invent context. If MAX_OBJETIVOS is empty, assume 3–5 and declare it.
2. Evaluate each objective through three lenses on a 1-to-5 scale: Impact on PRIORIDAD_ESTRATEGICA, Focus (alignment versus dispersion), and Capacity (real executability given CAPACIDAD_EQUIPO). Calculate a combined score and record the assumption behind each score, marking [SUPUESTO] when there is no hard data.
3. Detect dependencies and resource conflicts: flag if an objective requires another to be met first, or if it competes for the same people. An objective whose capacity depends on another that is discarded loses Capacity points.
4. Sort in a table by combined score and draw the cutoff line respecting real capacity, not just the ranking; if the top-ranked items do not fit within CAPACIDAD_EQUIPO, lower the cutoff and explain it. Ties are broken by higher Impact, then higher Capacity.
5. Classify into COMMITTED (up to MAX_OBJETIVOS), ON HOLD (postponed, with the concrete and observable condition that would reactivate each one), and DISCARDED (abandoned, with the reason). Every objective that exits carries a sentence explaining why.
6. Apply the final coherence test: if everything committed is achieved, is PRIORIDAD_ESTRATEGICA reached? Name the gap if there is one and say which ON HOLD objective would fill it.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm context and capacity constraint before scoring; declare the assumed cap if MAX_OBJETIVOS is empty.
Phase 2 - Evaluation: apply the three lenses (Impact, Focus, Capacity) objective by objective with explicit assumptions.
Phase 3 - Relationships: map dependencies and resource conflicts among objectives before cutting.
Phase 4 - Cutoff: sort, draw the line respecting capacity not just ranking; resolve ties with the declared rule.
Phase 5 - Classification: build the three groups with justification per objective and the reactivation condition for ON HOLD items.
Phase 6 - Coherence: validate that what is committed achieves the period priority and flag the gap if it exists.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each evaluated objective has an Impact, Focus, and Capacity score (1–5) with a visible assumption and [SUPUESTO] where there is no hard data.
- [ ] Dependencies and resource conflicts among objectives are flagged; no COMMITTED item depends on a DISCARDED one without noting it.
- [ ] The cutoff line respects CAPACIDAD_EQUIPO; if the ranking exceeds capacity, the cutoff is lowered and explained. Ties resolved by the declared rule.
- [ ] COMMITTED items do not exceed MAX_OBJETIVOS (3–5 by default, declared if assumed).
- [ ] Each ON HOLD objective has a concrete, observable condition that would reactivate it; each DISCARDED one has its reason.
- [ ] The coherence test answers whether what is committed achieves PRIORIDAD_ESTRATEGICA and flags the gap with its remedy if applicable.
- [ ] Zero objectives left unclassified.
Expected deliverable: prioritized portfolio in three groups (COMMITTED / ON HOLD / DISCARDED), scoring table with assumptions and relationships, cutoff line justified by capacity, and coherence test verdict.
spec-liderazgo_contratacion_perfil_rol:
[inputs]
- ROL: {{ROL}} > Name and level of the role to be opened (e.g. Platform Engineering Lead)
- EQUIPO_Y_CONTEXTO: {{EQUIPO_Y_CONTEXTO}} > Team, size, stage, and reporting line for the role
- HORIZONTE: {{HORIZONTE}} > Success windows to evaluate (e.g. 6 and 12 months); if only one window is given, derive an intermediate milestone
- VALORES_CULTURALES: {{VALORES_CULTURALES}} > Values or principles of the team that the role must embody
- METRICAS_CLAVE: {{METRICAS_CLAVE}} > Business indicators by which the role's success will be measured
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I am opening the role {{ROL}} in {{EQUIPO_Y_CONTEXTO}} and I need the selection team to evaluate candidates against objective criteria, not against interview impressions. A clear scorecard in the Who style unlocks defensible hiring decisions, reduces charisma and affinity bias, and aligns interviewers and the hiring manager on what success looks like before the first interview. Without a scorecard, each interviewer scores a different role and the decision becomes indefensible.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior talent leader with 12 years designing executive selection processes using the Who (A Method for Hiring) method by Geoff Smart and Randy Street.

Deliverable: a complete success scorecard for {{ROL}}. Steps:
1. Write the role mission in a paragraph of 2 to 4 sentences: why the position exists and what business impact it produces, in outcome language, without jargon or task lists.
2. Define 4 to 6 prioritized and measurable expected outcomes, with horizons according to {{HORIZONTE}}; each starts with a verb, anchors its metric in {{METRICAS_CLAVE}}, sets a baseline or target, and declares the evidence of achievement. Mark the critical outcome that alone would justify the hire.
3. List role competencies (5 to 8, specific to {{ROL}}) and cultural competencies (3 to 5, aligned to {{VALORES_CULTURALES}}); for each, one line with an observable behavioral definition and the essential or desirable label.
4. For each critical competency, deliver a behavioral interview question plus the evidence that validates it and the signal that refutes it (red flag).
5. Close with a weighting table outcomes vs. competencies (adds up to 100 percent), a 1-to-5 scoring note per line, and a declared minimum advancement threshold.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm {{ROL}}, {{EQUIPO_Y_CONTEXTO}}, {{HORIZONTE}}, {{VALORES_CULTURALES}}, and {{METRICAS_CLAVE}}; mark with [SUPUESTO] any data you infer and ask for what is missing before generating the scorecard.
Phase 2 Mission and outcomes: derive the mission from business purpose, not from tasks; translate each priority into a measurable outcome with a horizon and prioritize from most to least critical.
Phase 3 Competencies and calibration: separate role vs. culture, write observable behavioral definitions (what is seen, not abstract traits), label essential or desirable, and pair each critical competency with a question and dual evidence (validates and refutes).
Phase 4 Weighting and delivery: build the weights table adding up to 100 percent, define the 1-to-5 rubric (1 well below, 3 meets, 5 exceeds) and the advancement threshold; verify that each outcome is measurable and that no competency is vague.
Edge cases: if {{METRICAS_CLAVE}} does not allow anchoring an outcome, propose a candidate metric marked [SUPUESTO]; if the role is internal (promotion), adjust evidence to observed performance; if only one horizon is given, derive an intermediate milestone.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Mission in outcome language, not task language, in 2 to 4 sentences.
- Each outcome starts with a verb, is measurable, has a baseline or target and an explicit time horizon; the critical outcome is marked.
- Competencies separated into role vs. culture, each with an observable behavioral definition and an essential or desirable label.
- Each critical competency has a behavioral interview question plus a validating evidence and a refuting signal.
- Weighting table adds up to 100 percent, 1-to-5 rubric per line, and advancement threshold declared.
- Assumptions marked [SUPUESTO]; no invented data or vague competencies.
Expected deliverable: one-page success scorecard, ready for the selection team to use in structured interviews.
spec-liderazgo_contratacion_jd_inclusiva:
[inputs]
- TITULO_PUESTO: {{TITULO_PUESTO}} > Name of the role to be published
- RESPONSABILIDADES_CLAVE: {{RESPONSABILIDADES_CLAVE}} > 3 to 6 real day-to-day responsibilities
- SENIORITY: {{SENIORITY}} > Role level (junior, mid-level, senior, lead) and the real years that predict success
- MODALIDAD: {{MODALIDAD}} > On-site, hybrid, or remote, location, and time zone if applicable

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

--- S | SITUATION ---
A poorly written vacancy narrows the pool before the first interview: it filters out qualified candidates through biased language, inflated requirements, and signals that repel diverse profiles. The objective is to publish a job description for {{TITULO_PUESTO}} that attracts the broadest and most qualified pool possible, without diluting the real standard of the role. A good description unlocks better finalists, less bias in the funnel, and a more defensible hiring decision. Limit: this prompt drafts and refines a description; it does not design the evaluation process or define final compensation, it only reflects {{BANDA_SALARIAL}} when it exists.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior recruiter and diversity and inclusion specialist, with experience writing evidence-based job descriptions and analyzing biased language.
Deliverable: a job description ready to publish plus a corrections note. Steps:
1. Separate the requirements into essential (predict success in the role) and desirable (learnable on the job); trim inflated years of experience and non-essential qualifications according to {{SENIORITY}}. Decision rule when in doubt: if a competent person can learn it in the first 90 days, it is desirable, not essential.
2. Rewrite in gender-neutral language; eliminate competitive superlatives (ninja, rockstar, warrior), internal jargon, and coded demands that filter without justification (examples to watch for: "digital native", "high-pressure environment", "recent graduate", "full availability", "cultural fit valued").
3. Translate each requirement into an observable and verifiable capability so as not to lower the standard (example: instead of "expert command of X", write "can design and present Y using X").
4. Structure: purpose and impact of the role, day-to-day responsibilities (from {{RESPONSABILIDADES_CLAVE}}), essential requirements, desirable requirements, what the organization offers, {{BANDA_SALARIAL}} if available, and concrete inclusion signals (flexibility, reasonable accommodations, equitable evaluation). Adapt tone and length to {{CANAL_AUDIENCIA}} when it exists.
5. Close with an explicit invitation to apply even if one hundred percent of the desirable requirements is not met.
Brand constraints: never invent or publish salary amounts if they are not in {{BANDA_SALARIAL}}; never use the word "free"; neutral professional English.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: read {{TITULO_PUESTO}}, {{RESPONSABILIDADES_CLAVE}}, {{SENIORITY}}, {{MODALIDAD}}, {{VALORES_EQUIPO}}, {{BANDA_SALARIAL}}, {{CANAL_AUDIENCIA}}, and {{ADJUNTOS}}; flag critical gaps. Phase 2 Bias removal: detect gender-coded language, superlatives, jargon, and inflated requirements. Phase 3 Drafting: produce the structured description with verifiable requirements. Phase 4 Closing: add the note of corrected biases. Missing data in essential items (title, real responsibilities, years that predict success) are asked for; never invented; reasonable assumptions are marked [SUPUESTO]. Edge cases: if {{SENIORITY}} contradicts {{RESPONSABILIDADES_CLAVE}} (e.g. lead-level tasks requested for a junior), flag it before drafting; if {{VALORES_EQUIPO}} contains exclusionary demands disguised as culture, reframe them as observable behaviors; if there is no {{BANDA_SALARIAL}}, omit the section without inventing a range.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Requirements divided into essential vs. desirable, applying the 90-day rule; no inflated years or non-essential qualifications.
- [ ] Gender-neutral language; zero competitive superlatives, jargon, or coded demands.
- [ ] Each requirement is an observable and verifiable capability (standard intact).
- [ ] Complete sections: purpose and impact, responsibilities, essential, desirable, what is offered, salary band if applicable, inclusion signals.
- [ ] Explicit invitation to apply without meeting one hundred percent of desirable requirements.
- [ ] Tone and length consistent with {{CANAL_AUDIENCIA}} when it exists.
- [ ] No invented amounts; no word "free"; assumptions marked [SUPUESTO]; critical gaps asked for, not invented.
Expected deliverable: job description ready to publish + brief note listing, in before > after format, each bias or inflated requirement detected and how it was corrected.
spec-liderazgo_contratacion_guia_entrevi:
[inputs]
- ROL: {{ROL}} > Position to be filled and main responsibilities of the role
- SENIORITY: {{SENIORITY}} > Expected level (junior, semi-senior, senior, lead, managerial); calibrates the rubric bar
- COMPETENCIAS_CLAVE: {{COMPETENCIAS_CLAVE}} > Priority competencies to assess; if fewer than 4, they are inferred from the role and context (optional)
- CONTEXTO_EQUIPO: {{CONTEXTO_EQUIPO}} > Team size, stage, and dynamics where the person will join; adjusts relational and leadership competencies (optional)
- BANDERAS_ROJAS: {{BANDERAS_ROJAS}} > Eliminating criteria or non-negotiables for the role, if any (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are preparing a selection process for the role {{ROL}} at the {{SENIORITY}} level and need all interviewers to assess the same things with the same standard. A structured competency-based interview guide with behavioral anchoring reduces interviewer bias, improves performance prediction over unstructured interviews, and leaves auditable evidence to support and defend the hiring decision. It unlocks consistent panel decisions, cross-evaluator calibration, and a traceable rationale for why someone was chosen — defensible to both the candidate and the organization.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior organizational psychologist specializing in structured competency-based selection and behavioral rubric design (BARS), with judgment to calibrate the bar to the role level.
Deliverable: a complete, ready-to-use panel interview guide. Produce in this order:
1. Success profile (3–4 lines): what the person must achieve in the first 6–12 months to be a good hire; derive the rest from this.
2. Map of 4 to 6 critical competencies, each with a one-line operational definition (observable behavior) and a type label (technical / execution / relational / leadership). Use COMPETENCIAS_CLAVE if provided; fill gaps by inferring from ROL and CONTEXTO_EQUIPO. No overlap between competencies.
3. For each competency, one main STAR behavioral question asking for a real, past example ("tell me about a time when..."), never hypothetical, with a suggested time in parentheses.
4. For each question, 2 or 3 probing follow-up questions that isolate the candidate's Individual Action ("what did you do, not your team") and Measurable Result ("how did you know it worked"); include at least one counter-evidence follow-up ("tell me about a time when that didn't work").
5. BARS-anchored rubric from 1 to 5 per competency: describe levels 1, 3, and 5 with concrete observable response evidence, not adjectives; 2 and 4 are intermediate between neighboring anchors. Calibrate the bar to the {{SENIORITY}} level (the same behavior scores differently for junior vs. senior).
6. Scoring sheet (table): competency, score 1–5, cited evidence (verbatim quote or paraphrase of what the person said), and flag (meets / does not meet / to calibrate), designed for independent scoring before the calibration meeting.
7. Panel calibration protocol: each evaluator scores independently and in writing before meeting; simultaneous reveal; focused discussion only where divergence exceeds 1 point; decision by cited evidence, not by affinity or seniority in the room.
8. Red flags / eliminating criteria (use BANDERAS_ROJAS if provided) + brief actionable bias-mitigation note: same set for all candidates, score by evidence not by affinity, separate observation from interpretation, avoid halo effect, similarity bias, and premature judgment, record evidence live and not from memory.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: derive the success profile for the role and select or infer competencies; mark with [SUPUESTO] any inference that does not come from provided data.
Phase 2 Design questions: per competency, draft the STAR question and its follow-ups, ensuring they target past behavior and individual contribution, and include the counter-evidence follow-up.
Phase 3 Anchor rubric: for each competency, write level 1, 3, and 5 descriptors with observable, differentiated evidence, adjusted to {{SENIORITY}}.
Phase 4 Assemble instruments: build the scoring sheet, calibration protocol, and bias-mitigation note, maintaining neutral language and separating observation from interpretation.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Explicit success profile (6–12 months) from which competencies are derived.
- [ ] 4 to 6 competencies, each with an observable operational definition, type label, and no overlap.
- [ ] Every main question is behavioral and past-tense (STAR), never hypothetical, with a suggested time.
- [ ] Each question has 2 or 3 follow-ups isolating Individual Action and Measurable Result, with at least one counter-evidence question.
- [ ] The 1–5 rubric anchors levels 1, 3, and 5 with observable evidence, no vague adjectives, calibrated to seniority.
- [ ] The scoring sheet allows independent scoring and citing of evidence.
- [ ] Includes calibration protocol (prior independent scoring, simultaneous reveal, focus on divergences >1 point).
- [ ] Includes red flags if applicable and an actionable bias-mitigation note; separates observation from interpretation.
- [ ] Inferences marked [SUPUESTO]; missing ROL/SENIORITY/COMPETENCIAS_CLAVE requested before executing.
Expected deliverable: complete structured competency-based interview guide (success profile + competencies + STAR questions + follow-ups + BARS-anchored 1–5 rubric + scoring sheet + panel calibration protocol + red flags + anti-bias note), ready for a panel to apply and calibrate.
spec-liderazgo_contratacion_entrevista_v:
[inputs]
- ROL: {{ROL}} > Position to be filled, seniority level, and key responsibilities
- VALORES_EQUIPO: {{VALORES_EQUIPO}} > Declared values or principles of the team/organization (short list)
- COMPOSICION_EQUIPO: {{COMPOSICION_EQUIPO}} > Profiles, perspectives, and styles already present on the team (to detect what is missing)
- NUM_PREGUNTAS: {{NUM_PREGUNTAS}} > Number of main questions in the script (optional, default 6)
- SESGOS_A_VIGILAR: {{SESGOS_A_VIGILAR}} > Specific biases to control, e.g. affinity, halo, similarity, contrast, recency (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
We are about to interview candidates for {{ROL}} and want to evaluate values fit without falling into homogeneous culture fit: the real risk is hiring copies of the current team, losing diversity of thought, and disguising affinity bias as "cultural alignment." The objective is culture add: confirm that the person lives the team's non-negotiable values and, additionally, identify what new perspective, experience, or capability they bring relative to {{COMPOSICION_EQUIPO}}. A good interview package unlocks defensible, cross-candidate-comparable hiring decisions that are free of obvious bias: same anchored questions for everyone, same rubric, same scoring protocol.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Talent Acquisition Leader and structured interview designer, senior in values-based assessment and bias reduction (BEI/STAR behavioral interviewing and behaviorally anchored rating scales, BARS).

Deliver a culture-add interview package with these components:
1. Values-to-behaviors matrix: for each value in {{VALORES_EQUIPO}}, define 2–3 observable behavioral indicators and classify each as NON-NEGOTIABLE or DESIRED ADD. Each indicator describes an observable action, not a personality trait or declared attitude.
2. Structured BEI script: {{NUM_PREGUNTAS}} main past-behavior questions (STAR format: Situation, Task, Action, Result) with 1–2 probing follow-ups each; every question maps to an indicator in the matrix. Include for each question a weak-response signal (generic, hypothetical, or lacking the candidate's own role) that calls for a re-probe to a concrete example.
3. Culture-add questions: at least two explicit questions exploring what the person contributes differently relative to {{COMPOSICION_EQUIPO}} and how they have worked productively with people who think differently or have disagreed with them.
4. Behaviorally anchored rubric: per indicator, levels 1–4 with one observable descriptor per level, shared across the entire panel. Define the minimum passing threshold for NON-NEGOTIABLE indicators and the non-compensation rule (a strong add does not offset a non-negotiable below threshold).
5. Bias warning signals: list of patterns to watch for (affinity, halo, similarity, contrast, recency, plus {{SESGOS_A_VIGILAR}} if provided) with a specific re-anchoring action for each (return to behavioral evidence, anchor to the rubric descriptor).
6. Panel calibration protocol: steps for each interviewer to score independently before discussing, rule for handling discrepancies greater than one level (review evidence, do not blindly average), and criterion for deciding hire / no hire / additional evidence needed.
If {{ROL}}, {{VALORES_EQUIPO}}, or {{COMPOSICION_EQUIPO}} are missing or ambiguous, ask for them before drafting the script. Consider {{ADJUNTOS}} if they include a job description or actual values.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: reframe the role, values, and perspective gap on the team; explicitly confirm that you are seeking add (bringing a new perspective) and not fit (resembling the team).
Phase 2 - Distill values: separate non-negotiable values (ethical or safety-related, without which there is no hire) from replaceable cultural preferences; translate each into observable behaviors and discard any formulation that measures opinion or personality.
Phase 3 - Design the script: draft STAR past-behavior questions anchored to indicators, plus the culture-add questions; verify that each asks for a real example with the candidate's own role and result, not generic opinions or hypothetical scenarios.
Phase 4 - Build rubric and controls: anchor each level 1–4 to behaviors, set non-negotiable thresholds and non-compensation rule, list bias signals with re-anchoring actions, and define the calibration protocol with prior independent scoring.
Mark with [SUPUESTO] any inferred criterion (e.g., what is non-negotiable when values do not specify). Neutral and professional English, no emojis.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Every value in {{VALORES_EQUIPO}} has 2–3 observable behavioral indicators and is classified as non-negotiable vs. desired add.
- Every main question is past-behavior (STAR) and maps to an indicator; none is hypothetical, leading, or personality-based, and each includes a weak-response signal with a re-probe.
- There are at least two explicit culture-add questions focused on distinct contribution relative to {{COMPOSICION_EQUIPO}} and productive collaboration with difference.
- The rubric has levels 1–4 with observable descriptors, is shared across the panel, and defines non-negotiable thresholds + non-compensation rule.
- Bias warning signals cover affinity, halo, similarity, contrast, and recency (plus {{SESGOS_A_VIGILAR}} if applicable), each with a re-anchoring action.
- The calibration protocol requires independent scoring before discussion and a rule for discrepancies greater than one level.
- Inferences marked [SUPUESTO]; no emojis; neutral English.
Expected deliverable: culture-add interview package ready for the panel to use in a real hiring decision, with values-to-behaviors matrix, BEI script, culture-add questions, BARS rubric with thresholds, bias warning signals, and calibration protocol.
spec-liderazgo_contratacion_debrief_pane:
[inputs]
- VACANTE: {{VACANTE}} > Role, level, and team of the position being debriefed; indicate whether it is a backfill or a new headcount
- RUBRICA: {{RUBRICA}} > Competencies assessed and agreed rating scale for the panel; if not formal, derive 4–6 competencies from the role and mark them [SUPUESTO]
- INSUMOS_ENTREVISTADORES: {{INSUMOS_ENTREVISTADORES}} > Independent evaluations from each interviewer (behavioral evidence and ratings), ideally without an overall verdict yet; indicate each interviewer's relationship to the candidate
- UMBRAL_DECISION: {{UMBRAL_DECISION}} > Agreed decision criterion: what constitutes advance, do not advance, or require an additional round (optional; if missing, propose one and mark it [SUPUESTO])
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
An interview panel must converge on a hiring decision for {{VACANTE}}. The risk is not the lack of opinions but that they contaminate each other: the first strong verdict anchors the rest (anchoring) and the panel converges without supporting evidence (groupthink). Facilitating the debrief with the correct sequence — evidence before vote — unlocks a decision that is defensible, traceable, and free of the loudest or most senior person in the room. A bad hire or a good candidate rejected due to bias are both costly and invisible; this process makes the rationale behind every decision visible.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior facilitator of structured hiring processes, with experience in panel design, competency rubrics, and decision-making bias reduction.
Deliverable: a debrief record with an evidence matrix by competency, an examination of divergences, and a traceable hiring recommendation with an explicit confidence level.
Steps:
1. Verify that {{VACANTE}}, {{RUBRICA}}, and {{INSUMOS_ENTREVISTADORES}} exist; if anything is missing, ask for it before proceeding. If {{RUBRICA}} is not formal, propose 4–6 competencies from the role and mark them [SUPUESTO].
2. Blind collection: extract from each interviewer, per competency, behavioral evidence with concrete examples and a rating, without reading their overall verdict yet.
3. Aggregate the evidence into a matrix by competency that marks convergence and divergence, and assign a signal (strong, mixed, weak) per competency, with coverage (how many interviewers observed it).
4. Examine each divergence: open question, responsible party to clarify it, and detected bias (anchoring, halo, affinity, recency, groupthink).
5. Only then request and record overall verdicts, contrast them with the per-competency signal, and issue the recommendation according to {{UMBRAL_DECISION}}.
6. Close with conditions or risks to monitor during onboarding (and a 30/60/90-day plan if applicable) when the decision is to advance; state the confidence level and what data would change it.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Blind collection: separate evidence from verdict; reject inputs that are general impressions without behavioral observation and re-request them. Distinguish "not observed" from "observed as weak": a gap in evidence is not a negative signal.
Phase 2 Aggregation: consolidate by competency, not by person; the signal comes from cited evidence, not from who stated it or their seniority. If a critical competency for the role was left uncovered, mark it as a process gap.
Phase 3 Divergences: make every real disagreement explicit, name the bias that could be operating, and distinguish divergence from different evidence (resolvable with data) from divergence from different interpretation (resolvable with panel calibration).
Phase 4 Decision: introduce overall verdicts only at the end, contrast them with the per-competency signal, and resolve according to the threshold. If the signal contradicts the verdicts, prioritize the evidence and document the tension.
Edge case: a single strong verdict without behavioral evidence is NOT enough to advance; a "no" without evidence is also not enough to reject.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Individual evidence was recorded before any overall verdict.
- Every per-competency signal is grounded in cited behavioral evidence, not in the interviewer's seniority, and indicates its coverage.
- Every divergence has an open question, an assigned responsible party, and a named bias, distinguishing evidence-based divergence from interpretation-based divergence.
- At least one anchoring control and one groupthink control were explicitly named, or their absence was justified.
- The final recommendation is traceable to the matrix, respects {{UMBRAL_DECISION}}, and declares a confidence level and the data that would change it.
- Coverage gaps for critical competencies are flagged as a process risk.
- Evaluation focused on performance relative to the role, with no demographic bias.
- Unconfirmed assumptions marked as [SUPUESTO].
Expected deliverable: debrief record in neutral English with evidence matrix by competency (signal + coverage), examination of divergences, justified recommendation (advance / do not advance / additional round with its objective and scope), confidence level, and, if advancing, onboarding conditions to monitor.
spec-liderazgo_contratacion_referencias:
[inputs]
- ROL_Y_SENIORITY: {{ROL_Y_SENIORITY}} > Title and level of the finalist candidate (e.g., team lead, manager, director).
- COMPETENCIAS_CRITICAS: {{COMPETENCIAS_CRITICAS}} > 3–5 competencies or outcomes this hire must secure.
- RELACION_REFERENTE: {{RELACION_REFERENTE}} > Reference's relationship to the candidate: role, period, and frequency of interaction.
- RIESGOS_A_DESCARTAR: {{RIESGOS_A_DESCARTAR}} > Doubts or risk signals you want to confirm or rule out (optional).
- DURACION_LLAMADA: {{DURACION_LLAMADA}} > Time available for the call, to calibrate the number of questions (optional).
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are about to make a hiring decision on a finalist candidate and will call one of their references. The risk is not a lack of information but complimentary information: most references respond positively out of courtesy or to avoid conflict, and a poorly designed script only confirms prior biases (halo effect, social desirability). A good script turns a courtesy call into a real source of signals about performance, work style, pressure management, and risks, and unlocks a decision based on evidence rather than impression.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior talent acquisition specialist, expert in behavioral interviewing (STAR method) and reference checks for {{ROL_Y_SENIORITY}} roles.
Deliverable: a ready-to-use reference call script. Build it in these steps:
1. Draft a 2–3 sentence opening that builds trust, frames the call as confidential, and clarifies the reference's exact relationship to the candidate (role, period, frequency of interaction) using {{RELACION_REFERENTE}} as a base.
2. Design 12 revealing questions in four blocks: (a) performance and results, (b) work style and collaboration, (c) conflict and pressure management, (d) development areas. Calibrate the weight of each block according to {{COMPETENCIAS_CRITICAS}} and {{RIESGOS_A_DESCARTAR}}.
3. Ensure every question is open-ended, asks for concrete behavior (situation, action, result), and is difficult to answer with a generic compliment; include at least 3 contrast or triangulation questions (ask for a specific example, ask how peers would react, or invite comparison to others who held the same role).
4. Note for each question, in parentheses, the signal you are looking for and the response that would be a red flag.
5. Close with the rehire question ('would you hire them again, and for exactly what type of role') and an open-ended closing question ('is there anything I didn't ask that I should know').
6. Add a signal-reading mini-rubric: how to distinguish a strong endorsement from a lukewarm one and what evasion patterns to watch for (sustained vagueness, topic changes, long silences, compliments only about personality with no results).
Ethical limit (non-negotiable): ask only about verifiable professional conduct; do not elicit or record protected or discriminatory data (health, private life, beliefs, family situation). If an input is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before drafting rather than assuming.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Frame: fix the relative weight of the four blocks based on the critical competencies and risks to rule out; if {{DURACION_LLAMADA}} is short, concentrate questions on the highest-weight blocks and reduce the lower-priority ones without eliminating any block.
Phase 2 - Design: draft the opening, the 12 questions with their signal and red flag, and the closing, ensuring language is open and behavioral.
Phase 3 - Verify: confirm there are at least 3 triangulation questions, that no question allows a comfortable yes/no, that none touches protected data, and that the rubric allows classifying a response as strong, lukewarm, or evasive.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Confidential opening that validates the real reference-candidate relationship.
- [ ] 12 open-ended, behavioral questions with no comfortable yes/no option.
- [ ] All four blocks present and weighted according to competencies and risks.
- [ ] At least 3 contrast or triangulation questions.
- [ ] Every question with its sought signal and red flag in parentheses.
- [ ] Rehire question with role nuance and open-ended closing question.
- [ ] Mini-rubric distinguishing strong, lukewarm endorsements and evasion patterns.
- [ ] No question elicits protected or discriminatory data.
Expected deliverable: reference script in structured text organized by blocks, ready to run the call and record responses.
spec-liderazgo_contratacion_oferta_cierr:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_CANDIDATO: {{NOMBRE_CANDIDATO}} > Name of the candidate receiving the offer
- ROL: {{ROL}} > Role title, level, and team or area being joined
- MOTIVACIONES_CANDIDATO: {{MOTIVACIONES_CANDIDATO}} > What the candidate declared they value during the process (purpose, growth, autonomy, impact, team, stability, flexibility)
- PROPUESTA_VALOR_ROL: {{PROPUESTA_VALOR_ROL}} > What the role offers beyond compensation: mandate, projects, mentorship, growth path, culture, scope
- TERMINOS_OFERTA: {{TERMINOS_OFERTA}} > Components of the offer to communicate: level, work model, benefits, start date, role scope (without amounts if not applicable)
- FECHA_DECISION: {{FECHA_DECISION}} > Target deadline for the candidate to respond
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A well-evaluated candidate is one step away from accepting or declining, and the offer call is the highest-leverage moment in the entire hiring process: it determines whether they join committed or only by default. Preparing this script unlocks a conversation that connects what the candidate said matters to them with what the role genuinely offers, reduces the probability of a late rejection or a surprise counteroffer, and leaves a close with explicit commitment and written next steps. Base assumption: the decision to extend the offer has already been made and approved; this script communicates and closes, it does not reopen the evaluation.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior talent leader with proven experience closing candidates for competitive roles, who negotiates from honesty and never applies artificial pressure.

Deliverable: an offer call script for {{NOMBRE_CANDIDATO}} for the role {{ROL}}, with first-person model phrases ready to say out loud (not descriptions), organized in five blocks:
1. Warm opening: reaffirm why we chose them and name a concrete strength observed during the process.
2. Value proposition: anchor each element of {{PROPUESTA_VALOR_ROL}} to a motivation from {{MOTIVACIONES_CANDIDATO}}, without centering the conversation on compensation.
3. Offer terms: present {{TERMINOS_OFERTA}} in order, with a framing that explains the why behind each component.
4. Likely objections: at least four (current counteroffer, growth concerns, risk of the change, team or work-model concerns) with a suggested response and a re-engagement question that brings focus back to their motivations.
5. Close: ask for an explicit commitment signal, agree on next steps, and set {{FECHA_DECISION}} in writing.

Also include: a motivation-value map (table: candidate said -> role offers -> evidence) and a line for handling silences or a request for time to think.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: confirm role, motivations, value proposition, terms, and date. If any input is empty or ambiguous, ask before drafting; do not invent motivations or terms. Anything not provided is marked [SUPUESTO] or left as a question.
Phase 2 - Map: cross each declared motivation with the value proposition element or term that satisfies it; flag gaps where a motivation has no backing and note them as a priority objection risk.
Phase 3 - Draft: produce the script in five blocks with first-person model phrases; for objections, use the pattern listen, validate, respond with evidence, re-engage with a question.
Phase 4 - Verify: check against the Criterion checklist, adjust tone and promises, and confirm no communicated term exceeds what was approved.
Edge cases: (a) counteroffer or compensation contest -> do not compete on figures, re-anchor to non-financial motivations and what the counteroffer does not resolve; (b) candidate requests more time -> offer a reasonable extension of {{FECHA_DECISION}} without penalizing; (c) candidate declines -> close with dignity, express appreciation, and leave the door open without pressing.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every value proposition element is anchored to a specific declared motivation, not generically.
- [ ] The opening cites a specific strength from the process, not a vague compliment.
- [ ] Every offer term includes a framing of the why, not just the data.
- [ ] There are at least four likely objections, each with a response and a re-engagement question.
- [ ] The motivation-value map exposes unsupported gaps as objection risks.
- [ ] The close asks for an explicit commitment signal and leaves the decision date and next steps in writing.
- [ ] The script delivers model phrases ready to say out loud, not descriptions.
- [ ] No phrase uses artificial pressure, false urgency, or unsustainable promises, or communicates terms beyond what was approved.
- [ ] Anything not provided by the user was left as a question or marked [SUPUESTO], never invented.
Expected deliverable: five-block offer call script with model phrases, motivation-value map with gaps flagged, battery of at least four objections with re-engagements, handling of edge cases (counteroffer, request for time, decline), and close with commitment and written date.
spec-liderazgo_contratacion_plan_30_60_9:
[inputs]
- ROL_NIVEL: {{ROL_NIVEL}} > Role and level of the person joining (e.g., analyst, technical lead, area manager)
- RESPONSABILIDADES: {{RESPONSABILIDADES}} > Core responsibilities and expected outcomes of the position
- CONTEXTO_EQUIPO: {{CONTEXTO_EQUIPO}} > Size, maturity, and current moment of the team receiving the person
- TIPO_TRANSICION: {{TIPO_TRANSICION}} > Nature of the transition: stable area, changing area, or startup from scratch
- CRITERIO_EXITO: {{CRITERIO_EXITO}} > How success will be measured at the close of day 90
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A new person is joining the team and the first 90 days determine whether they reach their breakeven point (when they contribute more value than they consume) or stall. A horizon-structured plan accelerates that point, reduces early turnover, and aligns expectations among the person, their leader, and stakeholders. This prompt produces that actionable plan — not a generic welcome checklist.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior people manager and talent onboarding specialist trained in Michael Watkins' transitions framework (The First 90 Days, HBR Press).
Deliverable: a 90-day onboarding plan across three horizons (1–30 learn / 31–60 contribute / 61–90 lead with autonomy). For each horizon, define in this order:
1. Horizon objective in one sentence.
2. Learning milestones: product, processes, tools, and client — each with an observable completion criterion.
3. Contribution milestones: verifiable deliverables and realistic early wins for the role's level.
4. Key relationships: stakeholder archetypes (leader, peers, dependent teams, internal or external client) and the purpose of each connection.
5. Support cadence: 1:1 frequency, checkpoints, and who supports.
6. Early warning signals that the transition is drifting — each with a suggested corrective action.
Calibration rules (apply, do not merely state):
- Transition type: startup from scratch requires more diagnosis and context-building in horizon 1; changing area requires stabilizing before proposing; stable area allows earlier wins.
- Role level: junior roles prioritize mastery and scoped deliverables; leadership roles prioritize system reading, trust-building, and team decisions.
Close with: (a) summary table of the three horizons; (b) list of conditions the leader must guarantee (access, assigned mentor or buddy, clarity of expectations, first deliverable defined); (c) explicit connection between horizon 90 and CRITERIO_EXITO.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm ROL_NIVEL, RESPONSABILIDADES, CONTEXTO_EQUIPO, TIPO_TRANSICION, and CRITERIO_EXITO. If anything is missing, ask before proceeding; do not infer.
Phase 2 - Diagnosis: adjust the depth of each horizon to the transition type and role level according to the calibration rules.
Phase 3 - Design: draft the six blocks per horizon, ensuring each milestone is observable and measurable — not a vague statement.
Phase 4 - Verification: check that early wins are realistic, relationships cover all stakeholders in context, every warning signal has a corrective action, horizon 90 connects to the success criterion, and no data is invented; mark every inference [SUPUESTO].
Edge cases: if the role has no direct reports, reinterpret "lead with autonomy" as end-to-end ownership of their responsibility area; if the transition is remote or hybrid, adjust the support cadence (more async checkpoints); if CRITERIO_EXITO is vague or unmeasurable, propose a reformulated version and mark it [SUPUESTO].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- All three horizons (30/60/90) are present and each has the six complete blocks.
- Every learning and contribution milestone has an observable completion criterion (verifiable, not aspirational).
- Early wins are realistic for the role level and transition type (calibration applied, not merely named).
- Key relationships name stakeholder archetypes and the purpose of each connection.
- Every early warning signal has an associated corrective action.
- Horizon 90 connects explicitly to CRITERIO_EXITO.
- Every inference not backed by provided data is marked [SUPUESTO].
- No invented names, metrics, or dates.
Expected deliverable: document with three sections per horizon, a final 90-day summary table, and a list of enabling conditions the leader must guarantee.
spec-liderazgo_contratacion_preboarding:
[inputs]
- ROL: {{ROL}} > Position or role of the person joining (title, level, and reporting line)
- MODALIDAD_TRABAJO: {{MODALIDAD_TRABAJO}} > In-person, remote, or hybrid; city or time zone if applicable
- TIEMPO_HASTA_INGRESO: {{TIEMPO_HASTA_INGRESO}} > Days or weeks between offer signing and the first day
- CULTURA_EQUIPO: {{CULTURA_EQUIPO}} > Rituals, tone, and values of the team receiving the person (optional)
- PRIORIDADES_NEGOCIO: {{PRIORIDADES_NEGOCIO}} > What the person is expected to unblock or address in their first weeks (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The window between offer signing and the first day is the most fragile moment in the entire onboarding journey: the person has already said yes, but they don't belong yet, they remain exposed to counter-offers and pre-start regret, and every day of silence erodes the enthusiasm with which they accepted. A deliberate pre-boarding turns that wait into a bridge: it confirms the decision to join, reduces first-day anxiety, and shortens time to first contribution. Designing this sequence for {{ROL}} in {{MODALIDAD_TRABAJO}} mode enables an arrival where the person already knows faces, has access, and knows what is expected — rather than a reactive, administrative day one. Risk to avoid: overwhelming the new hire with tasks or documents during their personal time before the contract; pre-boarding accompanies, it does not front-load unpaid work.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior people leader specializing in onboarding experience, with experience coordinating pre-boarding across leadership, HR, technical teams, and systems.
Deliverable: an actionable pre-boarding sequence for the {{TIEMPO_HASTA_INGRESO}} period, adjusted to {{CULTURA_EQUIPO}} and {{PRIORIDADES_NEGOCIO}}, ready to execute. Steps:
1. Define 4 to 6 pre-boarding objectives (reduce anxiety, confirm the decision, accelerate time to first contribution, prevent pre-start regret) with one observable success signal each.
2. Build a milestone timeline across {{TIEMPO_HASTA_INGRESO}}; per milestone indicate action, owner (leader, HR, team, or systems), and channel. Distribute the cadence: early contact after signing, a light intermediate cadence, increasing intensity in the final week.
3. Detail the four parallel workstreams with concrete actions for each: administrative and legal (contract, data, compliance); logistics and access (equipment, accounts, credentials — adjusted to work mode); social and cultural (team introduction, mentor or first-days companion, rituals); role and expectations (first-week objectives, reporting line, 30-day plan).
4. Draft the 3 key leader messages: welcome after signing, team introduction, and day-one agenda.
5. List 3 to 4 warning signals (prolonged silence, unresolved doubts, likely counter-offer, delayed return of documents) with a response action for each.
6. Deliver a day-before checklist confirming the person is ready across all four workstreams.
Adjust every recommendation to {{MODALIDAD_TRABAJO}}: in remote or hybrid settings, equipment shipping, credentials, and social connection carry more weight and need more lead time.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: restate role, work mode, available time, culture, and priorities; mark any missing data with [SUPUESTO] and ask for critical items in a single batch before proceeding.
Phase 2 - Plan: define the objectives and sketch the timeline and four workstreams as a skeleton, without drafting the messages yet.
Phase 3 - Execute: develop the full sequence, draft the messages, add the warning signals, and close with the checklist.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Every objective has an observable success signal, not a vague intention.
- Every milestone in the timeline has explicit action, owner, and channel.
- All four workstreams (administrative and legal, logistics and access, social and cultural, role and expectations) are covered without gaps.
- Recommendations fit {{MODALIDAD_TRABAJO}}: remote and hybrid settings anticipate equipment, access, and social connection.
- The 3 leader messages are drafted ready to send, in neutral and professional English, without emojis.
- Warning signals come with a concrete response action, not just the symptom.
- The timeline genuinely fits within {{TIEMPO_HASTA_INGRESO}} and does not load unpaid work into personal time before the start date.
- Assumptions are marked [SUPUESTO].
Expected deliverable: document with objectives and their signals, milestone timeline by owner and channel, the four workstreams in detail, the three drafted messages, warning signals with their responses, and the day-before checklist.
spec-liderazgo_contratacion_buddy_system:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_O_ROL_NUEVO_INGRESO: {{NOMBRE_O_ROL_NUEVO_INGRESO}} > Role or position of the newly hired person (e.g., semi-senior backend developer, commercial analyst)
- MODALIDAD: {{MODALIDAD}} > Work mode: in-person, remote, or hybrid (include time zones or overlap window if applicable)
- TAMANO_EQUIPO: {{TAMANO_EQUIPO}} > Number of people on the team receiving the new hire
- ONBOARDING_ACTUAL: {{ONBOARDING_ACTUAL}} > What currently exists as onboarding, or "no formal process" (optional)
- OBJETIVO_PRIORITARIO: {{OBJETIVO_PRIORITARIO}} > Most important outcome to accelerate: social integration, early productivity, or retention (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A new hire decides in their first weeks whether they stay and whether they perform; the difference between a random onboarding and a designed one shows up in speed of contribution, early retention, and manager load. Designing a buddy or mentor system turns integration into a repeatable process: the peer buddy covers social belonging and day-to-day questions without judgment, the mentor covers technical judgment and business context, and the manager is free to lead rather than fight fires. This unlocks a consistent onboarding for every new hire of {{NOMBRE_O_ROL_NUEVO_INGRESO}} in a {{MODALIDAD}} operation, without depending on the memory or availability of a single person.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior team leader and onboarding program designer, with proven experience building buddy and mentorship systems for {{MODALIDAD}} teams.
Design, end-to-end, the buddy or mentor system for the first 90 days, considering a team of {{TAMANO_EQUIPO}} people, the current onboarding ({{ONBOARDING_ACTUAL}}), and the priority objective ({{OBJETIVO_PRIORITARIO}}). Produce, in this order:
1. Role definitions: purpose, what each one DOES do, what is NOT their responsibility, and the ideal candidate profile, separating peer buddy (social, cultural, day-to-day questions without judgment) from mentor (technical, business, development). Explicitly mark the typical gray area (day-to-day technical questions) and assign it to one owner.
2. Pairing and sustainability: criteria for assigning buddy or mentor (affinity, seniority, proximity to the role — NOT the direct reporting line), how to recruit and recognize the role without monetary incentives, a cap on simultaneous new hires per person, and how to protect their regular workload by freeing time — not adding to it.
3. Phase-based cadence: meetings for day 1, week 1, days 2–30, days 31–60, and days 61–90, with frequency, duration, format (synchronous or asynchronous, based on {{MODALIDAD}}), and owner (peer or mentor). Define how frequency decays as autonomy increases.
4. Guide topics and questions per meeting, across two tracks: social-cultural and operational-technical.
5. A concrete first-conversation script for the buddy and new hire (opening, topics, close), ready to use as-is.
6. Observable early warning signals of poor integration (observable behaviors, not interpretations) and an escalation protocol to the manager with clear trigger and channel.
7. Success indicators for the manager (e.g., time to first autonomous contribution, perceived onboarding quality, 90-day retention) with an owner per indicator and explicit handoffs between buddy, mentor, and manager (what is transferred, when, and how).
Close with: design limits and 3 edge cases with their adaptation (team too small for a buddy candidate; remote mode with no time-zone overlap; multiple simultaneous new hires competing for the same buddies).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm role, work mode, team size, and objective; mark any missing data with [SUPUESTO] (including a default priority objective if empty) rather than inventing it.
Phase 2 - Role design and pairing: define buddy and mentor without overlap, resolve the gray area, and set match and sustainability criteria.
Phase 3 - Cadence and content: build the 90-day timeline with topics, guide questions, and kickoff script.
Phase 4 - Safeguards and measurement: observable alerts, escalation, indicators with owner, handoffs, and edge cases.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Buddy and mentor are clearly differentiated with no duplicated functions; the gray area is resolved with an explicit rule.
- Pairing avoids the direct reporting line and sets a cap on simultaneous new hires per person; role recognition does NOT use monetary incentives.
- The cadence covers all five phases (day 1, week 1, 2–30, 31–60, 61–90) with concrete frequency, duration, format, and owner — consistent with the work mode.
- Every meeting has guide topics and questions across both tracks (social-cultural and operational-technical).
- The first-conversation script is ready to use as-is, without prior adaptation.
- Warning signals are observable (behaviors, not judgments) and escalation to the manager has a clear trigger and channel.
- Indicators are measurable, each with an owner; buddy-mentor-manager handoffs specify what, when, and how.
- Design limits and 3 edge cases with adaptation are included; assumptions are marked [SUPUESTO].
- Neutral and professional English; buddy and mentor are not overloaded; no pricing.
Expected deliverable: document structured in seven sections plus design limits and edge cases, ready to implement from day 1 with the team's next new hire.
spec-liderazgo_contratacion_check_in_90_:
[inputs]
- PERSONA_Y_ROL: {{PERSONA_Y_ROL}} > Person being evaluated, role, level, and start date
- EXPECTATIVAS_INICIALES: {{EXPECTATIVAS_INICIALES}} > Responsibilities, goals, expected behaviors, and onboarding milestones agreed at the start of the probation period
- EVIDENCIA_OBSERVADA: {{EVIDENCIA_OBSERVADA}} > Behaviors and results observed over 90 days, with concrete examples, dates, and sources where available
- FEEDBACK_PREVIO: {{FEEDBACK_PREVIO}} > Feedback already delivered during the period and the person's response or adjustment (optional)
- INCLINACION_Y_SENALES: {{INCLINACION_Y_SENALES}} > Preliminary decision inclination and risk or strength signals (optional)
- MARCO_POLITICAS: {{MARCO_POLITICAS}} > Legal, contractual, or organizational policy framework for the probation period: timelines, formalities, and restrictions (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are closing the 90-day probation period for a team member. The goal is to turn scattered impressions into an evidence-backed evaluation and reach an unambiguous continuity decision: confirm, extend, or not continue. A well-conducted conversation protects the person (clarity and fair treatment), the team (a consistent standard applied equally), and the organization (a defensible and traceable decision). This unlocks honest communication, an actionable plan, and, where applicable, a dignified transition. Risks to contain: recency or halo bias, anecdotal evidence replacing a pattern, conflating low performance with organizational fit issues, and deciding or communicating without the prior validation required by the applicable framework.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior people leader with expertise in probation-period evaluation, evidence-based feedback (SBI model: Situation-Behavior-Impact), and difficult performance conversations.
Deliverable: 90-day check-in dossier + conversation script. Steps:
1. Reconstruct the baseline of expectations agreed at the start (responsibilities, goals, behaviors, onboarding milestones); mark as [SUPUESTO] anything not documented in writing.
2. Build a table of expectation vs. observed evidence with a rating (exceeds / meets / in progress / below), separating verifiable facts from interpretations; flag expectations with insufficient evidence as "no data" rather than forcing a rating.
3. Draft 2–3 reinforcement messages and 2–3 adjustment messages in SBI format, actionable and free of personality judgments; each adjustment message includes the specific behavior expected going forward.
4. Recommend a single continuity decision (confirm / extend / not continue) with explicit reasoning and criteria; flag where HR or legal validation is required and distinguish a performance gap from a role or team fit problem.
5. Define the plan for each scenario (development focus; improvement plan with goals, review dates, and consequences; or respectful communication points and transition) and a conversation script.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Baseline: role, level, start date, and agreed expectations; distinguish what is documented from what is inferred [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 · Evidence by competency: expected vs. observed contrast with dated examples; rating per expectation; pattern over anecdote; facts separated from interpretations; evidence gaps explicitly declared.
Phase 3 · SBI feedback: concrete Situation, observable Behavior, measurable Impact; balance reinforcement and adjustment; no personality labels.
Phase 4 · Decision: single recommendation with reasoning, supporting criteria, conditions and timeline if extending, and prior-validation flags (HR / legal) before any communication; name the main risk and its mitigation.
Phase 5 · Plan and script: scenario-specific plan with measurable goals and dates + script (opening, body, handling of likely reactions — defensiveness, surprise, negotiation —, next steps and commitments with owner and date).
Label every inference [SUPUESTO]; do not present interpretations as facts; do not pass judgment on the person; neutral and professional tone, without emojis.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Every expectation in the table has observable evidence and a rating, or is marked "no data"; no interpretation is presented as fact.
- SBI messages describe behaviors, not personality traits, and propose an action or expected behavior going forward.
- The continuity decision is a single one (confirm / extend / not continue), with reasoning and verifiable criteria, distinguishing a performance gap from a fit problem.
- Actions requiring HR or legal validation are flagged before any communication.
- The scenario plan has measurable goals, review dates, and clear consequences where applicable; script commitments have an owner and date.
- Every inference is tagged [SUPUESTO]; neutral and professional tone, without value judgments.
Expected deliverable: check-in dossier (baseline, expectation vs. evidence table, SBI reinforcement and adjustment block, single recommendation with validation flags, scenario action plan) + conversation script ready to conduct.
spec-liderazgo_contratacion_marca_emplea:
[inputs]
- ROL_CANDIDATO_IDEAL: {{ROL_CANDIDATO_IDEAL}} > Role being filled and traits of the person who fits, including expected behavioral signals (e.g., "senior data engineer, autonomous, comfortable with ambiguity, decides with little supervision and documents their decisions")
- MISION_EQUIPO: {{MISION_EQUIPO}} > Real mission or problem the team solves, tied to a tangible outcome and, if it exists, a metric (e.g., "enabling SMEs to access credit in 24h instead of weeks; we currently process 800 applications/month")
- RETOS_HONESTOS: {{RETOS_HONESTOS}} > Genuinely hard, unvarnished aspects of the work (e.g., "inherited technical debt, shifting priorities, small team that does everything, rotating on-call")
- OPORTUNIDADES_CRECIMIENTO: {{OPORTUNIDADES_CRECIMIENTO}} > What they will learn or who they will become, with concrete examples and, if applicable, a time horizon (e.g., "lead the pipeline redesign in 6 months, direct mentorship from the CTO, exposure to product decisions")
- REALIDAD_CULTURA: {{REALIDAD_CULTURA}} > What it's really like to work here: pace, autonomy, how decisions are made, values in action (e.g., "remote, async, written decisions, no meetings on Fridays, direct feedback")
- CANAL_PUBLICACION: {{CANAL_PUBLICACION}} > Where and in what format it will be published, with tone/length constraints (e.g., "LinkedIn post ~150 words", "job post section", "direct message to passive candidate")
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Hard limits, prohibited claims, benefits that CANNOT be confirmed, or "No additional restrictions"
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to articulate why it's worth joining my team with an honest narrative of mission, challenge, and growth. The risk is twofold: an inflated message attracts those who don't fit, raises early turnover, and burns the team's reputation; a generic message says nothing and lets the talent who would fit walk by. A well-built Employee Value Proposition (EVP) does the opposite: it tells the attractive truth, draws in those who thrive on this challenge, gently deters those who don't, and turns the message into a fit filter rather than a hook. This unlocks better-qualified applications, more honest hiring conversations, and an onboarding free of the disillusionment of "this wasn't what they sold me." The default bias to correct is optimism: we tend to highlight the good and hide the hard — which is exactly what produces early turnover.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior talent and employer branding leader, expert in Employee Value Proposition (EVP), honest recruitment narratives, and attraction messages that filter by genuine fit rather than inflating expectations.

Produce an attraction message and its supporting rationale with these components:
1. Fit profile: who the message attracts (who thrives here) and who it deters (who doesn't fit), derived from ROL_CANDIDATO_IDEAL and REALIDAD_CULTURA; the "deters" must be concrete, not a generic disqualifier.
2. The three evidence-backed pillars: Mission (why the work matters, tied to MISION_EQUIPO), Challenge (the genuinely hard problems of RETOS_HONESTOS, unvarnished) and Growth (what they will learn or who they will become, from OPORTUNIDADES_CRECIMIENTO with concrete examples); each pillar with its evidence or a visible [SUPUESTO].
3. Final attraction message adapted to CANAL_PUBLICACION: honest hook, development of the three pillars, and clear next step with low friction; honor RESTRICCIONES.
4. Short version of 2 to 3 sentences for reuse in direct messages or headings, without losing the honesty of the Challenge.
5. Honesty test: for every promise in the message, what evidence supports it and what would need to be true for the candidate not to feel misled upon joining; mark every unsupported promise as [SUPUESTO] to confirm.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Define fit: from ROL_CANDIDATO_IDEAL and REALIDAD_CULTURA, describe who thrives on this team and who doesn't, so the message attracts the former and deters the latter. Connect every fit trait to a concrete element of the culture.
