Phase 2 - Build pillars: draft Mission (tied to MISION_EQUIPO), Challenge (from RETOS_HONESTOS, without sugarcoating the hard parts) and Growth (from OPORTUNIDADES_CRECIMIENTO, with concrete examples); justify every promise with evidence or mark it [SUPUESTO]; never present an unsupported promise as a fact. Recommended balance: Challenge carries at least as much weight as Mission; a message without honest tension is a hook.
Phase 3 - Draft message: adapt tone and length to CANAL_PUBLICACION, open with an honest hook (not clickbait), develop the three pillars, and close with a clear, low-friction next step; also produce the short version of 2 to 3 sentences. Honor RESTRICCIONES.
Phase 4 - Honesty test: list every promise in the message with its evidence and the condition that would need to hold for it not to be misleading; flag promises that depend on an unconfirmed [SUPUESTO]. Never promise pricing, use the word free, or offer what the team cannot deliver.
Edge cases: if RETOS_HONESTOS arrives empty or cosmetic, ask for at least one real challenge before continuing (a message without a challenge does not filter). If MISION_EQUIPO is not tied to a tangible outcome, mark it [SUPUESTO] and propose how to make it concrete. If CANAL_PUBLICACION is open and public, moderate the exposure of sensitive challenges without erasing them.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
The message is complete when:
- The fit profile explicitly declares who it attracts and who it deters (both concrete), consistent with the real role and culture.
- All three pillars (Mission, Challenge, Growth) are present; the Challenge pillar names at least one genuinely hard aspect without sugarcoating and is not subordinated to Mission.
- Every promise has evidence or a visible [SUPUESTO]; no inference is presented as fact.
- The final message is adapted in tone and length to CANAL_PUBLICACION, with an honest hook, three pillars, and a clear, low-friction next step, plus the short version of 2 to 3 sentences that preserves the honesty of the Challenge.
- The honesty test covers all promises in the message with their condition of truthfulness and flags those dependent on [SUPUESTO].
- RESTRICCIONES are honored; no pricing or the word free; text in neutral and professional English, without emojis and without invented data.
Expected deliverable: document with fit profile (attracts / deters), the three evidence-backed pillars or [SUPUESTO], the final attraction message ready for the channel, the short version of 2 to 3 sentences, and the promise-by-promise honesty test.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_niveles_autori:
[inputs]
- TAREA_O_AREA: {{TAREA_O_AREA}} > Task, project, or area of responsibility to delegate
- PERSONA_O_EQUIPO: {{PERSONA_O_EQUIPO}} > Who receives the delegation (role or name)
- NIVEL_MADUREZ: {{NIVEL_MADUREZ}} > The person's experience and maturity in this subject (high/medium/low with detail)
- APETITO_RIESGO: {{APETITO_RIESGO}} > Cost of an error and tolerance for failure in this area
- CADENCIA_SEGUIMIENTO: {{CADENCIA_SEGUIMIENTO}} > Desired review frequency (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You lead {{PERSONA_O_EQUIPO}} and need to delegate {{TAREA_O_AREA}} without micromanaging (which kills autonomy and makes you a bottleneck) or abdicating (handing off without clarity and then correcting with frustration). The real problem is almost never whether to delegate or not: it is that no one ever makes explicit WHO decides WHAT. Delegation is not binary (I do it / I don't do it) but a continuum of levels, and almost never the same level for all decisions within the same area. A granular and explicit agreement unlocks measured autonomy, frees up your agenda for higher-altitude work, and turns delegation into a lever for developing the person — not a latent risk.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior leadership coach with 15 years of experience training managers, specializing in Management 3.0 and the design of distributed authority systems.
Deliver a structured delegation agreement:
1. Break down {{TAREA_O_AREA}} into 3 to 6 concrete and mutually exclusive decision areas (the granularity avoids the mistake of assigning a single level to everything; if only one appears, keep dividing).
2. Assign each area a level from 1 to 7 according to Jurgen Appelo's Delegation Poker: 1 Tell, 2 Sell, 3 Consult, 4 Agree, 5 Advise, 6 Inquire, 7 Delegate. Use the model's exact label, not a paraphrase.
3. Justify each level by crossing all three axes simultaneously: cost of an error, {{NIVEL_MADUREZ}}, and {{APETITO_RIESGO}}. No generalities; if two axes push in opposite directions, explain how you resolved the tie.
4. For each area, add one observable signal that confirms the level is correctly calibrated (what you would see if it is well-calibrated).
5. Write the agreement sentence by sentence, in first person and conversational language, ready to say aloud in a 1:1.
6. Declare the non-negotiable limits that are NOT delegated at any level (budget, security, client commitments, whatever applies).
7. Define the follow-up mechanism (cadence {{CADENCIA_SEGUIMIENTO}}; if empty, propose one and mark it as assumption) and the observable triggers for moving a level up or down.
8. Resolve one explicit edge case: what happens if the person makes — within their level — a decision you disagree with (the default rule is to respect the agreed level and revisit it afterward, not to revoke in the moment).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm the person, their actual maturity in the subject, and the risk appetite. Mark as {assumption} any data you infer; if something critical is ambiguous, ask for it in a single round before assigning levels.
Phase 2 - Decomposition: separate {{TAREA_O_AREA}} into discrete decision areas and name them in a table.
Phase 3 - Assignment: for each area, propose level 1-7 + model label + one-line justification (risk + maturity + appetite) + observable signal.
Phase 4 - Agreement and guardrails: write the conversation script, the non-negotiable limits, the edge case, and the level-change triggers.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Between 3 and 6 decision areas, mutually exclusive, never a single global one.
- [ ] Each area has exactly one level from 1 to 7 with the model's exact label.
- [ ] Each level is justified by crossing all three axes (risk + maturity + appetite); ties between axes are explained.
- [ ] Each area includes one observable signal of correct calibration.
- [ ] The agreement is written as a first-person conversational script, not as an abstract list.
- [ ] Non-negotiable limits that are not delegated are declared.
- [ ] There are observable triggers for moving both up and down a level.
- [ ] The edge case (a discrepant decision within the level) is resolved with a clear rule.
- [ ] Inferred data is marked as assumption.
- [ ] Closes with a StrategIA: which area to move up a level in 90 days and why.
Expected deliverable: table of areas-level-justification-signal + agreement script + non-negotiable limits + follow-up plan with triggers and edge case, ready to discuss at the next 1:1.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_matriz_eisenho:
[inputs]
- ROL_Y_FOCO: {{ROL_Y_FOCO}} > The leader's role and where they should concentrate their highest-value time (e.g., "Engineering lead of 8 people; should focus on technical strategy and team development")
- INVENTARIO_TAREAS: {{INVENTARIO_TAREAS}} > List of tasks, responsibilities, and recurring meetings to classify, with approximate weekly time if known
- EQUIPO_DISPONIBLE: {{EQUIPO_DISPONIBLE}} > People available to delegate to and their maturity or experience by topic (who is ready for what)
- HERRAMIENTAS_AUTOMATIZACION: {{HERRAMIENTAS_AUTOMATIZACION}} > Available tools, templates, or automations to take work off the plate; "none known" if not applicable (optional)
- PLAZOS_RESTRICCIONES: {{PLAZOS_RESTRICCIONES}} > Deadlines, fixed commitments, or constraints that condition what can be moved or eliminated (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to classify the work on my desk to decide, task by task, what I do myself, what I delegate and to whom, what I automate, what I schedule, and what I eliminate. The underlying problem is that the urgent crowds out the important: the day fills up with interruptions and avoidable meetings, and no time is left for the leadership work that no one else can do (strategy, decisions, team development). The Eisenhower matrix (urgent x important) cuts through that knot: it separates what deserves my time from what must leave my hands. Classifying well unlocks three things: I recover hours for the important-not-urgent quadrant, I empower the team by giving them work with clear authority, and I stop carrying tasks that add no value. This is not a to-do list or a schedule: it is an assignment decision for each piece of my work, with an explicit owner and authority level.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior executive coach for leaders, specializing in executive time management and effective delegation using the Eisenhower matrix; with judgment to distinguish the work only the leader can do from what must be delegated, automated, or eliminated, and to name the cost of not letting go.

Produce an actionable classification with these components:
1. Inventory: each task, responsibility, or recurring meeting with its estimated weekly time; if the data is not provided, estimate it and mark it [ASSUMPTION].
2. Eisenhower matrix: place each task in one unique quadrant — Q1 important and urgent (crises, decisions only the leader can make, immovable deadlines), Q2 important and not urgent (strategy, planning, team development, process improvement), Q3 urgent and not important (interruptions, avoidable meetings, low-value requests that pressure), Q4 neither urgent nor important (distractions, work that adds no value).
3. Disposition by quadrant: Q1 leader does now; Q2 schedule and protect on the calendar; Q3 delegate or automate; Q4 eliminate or decline. Justify each decision in one sentence.
4. Decision table: one row per task with columns task, quadrant, action (do / schedule / delegate / automate / eliminate), owner, and weekly hours freed for the leader.
5. Delegation plan: for each delegated task, to whom based on their maturity, what authority level they receive (consult, recommend, decide and inform, decide autonomously), the expected result, the checkpoint, and the risk covered; if no one has the maturity, propose delegation with scaffolding (accompaniment + review) instead of defaulting to retaining it.
6. Impact summary: weekly hours the leader recovers and what to reinvest them in (Q2 quadrant); explicitly name the cost of not delegating (what Q2 work keeps being postponed).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Inventory: list each task from the received material and estimate its weekly consumption; if the time is missing, mark it [ASSUMPTION] with your best estimate and state what it would take to refine it.
Phase 2 — Classification: evaluate each task on two axes — importance (does it contribute to the leader's results and mission?) and urgency (is there a deadline pressing?) — and assign it to one quadrant; watch for the trap of treating everything urgent as important. Edge case: if a task is urgent because a Q2 task was postponed (manufactured urgency), flag it and address the root cause, not just the symptom.
Phase 3 — Disposition: apply the rule by quadrant (Q1 do, Q2 schedule, Q3 delegate/automate, Q4 eliminate) and justify each decision; between delegating and automating, prefer to automate what is repeatable and rule-based, and delegate what develops a person. If a Q1 task is recurring, indicate how to convert it to Q2 (prepare someone, document the criterion) so it stops being a crisis.
Phase 4 — Delegation and close: for delegated items, match task to person based on maturity, set authority level, expected result, and checkpoint, and name the risk to cover; avoid over-control (high authority to someone who has already proven themselves) and under-support (high authority to someone who has not yet). Close with the decision table and the summary of hours recovered and their reinvestment in Q2.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
The classification is complete when: (a) every task in the inventory appears in one unique quadrant, none left unclassified or duplicated; (b) each task has an explicit action (do/schedule/delegate/automate/eliminate) consistent with its quadrant; (c) the decision truly separates importance from urgency and does not send everything urgent to the leader; (d) delegated items specify to whom, with what authority level, expected result, and checkpoint; (e) the distinction between delegating and automating is justified (repeatable and rule-based -> automate; develops someone -> delegate); (f) Q4 proposes to eliminate or decline with a concrete exit, not "do it later"; (g) there is a summary of weekly hours recovered and their reinvestment in Q2, with the cost of not delegating named; (h) manufactured urgency (recurring Q1 or Q3 due to postponed Q2) is flagged with its root cause; (i) inferred data is marked [ASSUMPTION]; (j) written in neutral, professional English; no emojis. Expected deliverable: a task-by-task decision table with the quadrant matrix and a brief delegation plan, ready for the leader to execute this week.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_brief_resultad:
[inputs]
- ENCARGO: {{ENCARGO}} > Name and brief description of the assignment to delegate
- COLABORADOR: {{COLABORADOR}} > Person or role receiving the assignment, with their relevant experience level for this assignment
- RESULTADO_ESPERADO: {{RESULTADO_ESPERADO}} > The finished deliverable in observable terms (what exists and is true when it is done)
- PLAZO: {{PLAZO}} > Target date or available time window
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Non-negotiable limits: time, brand, sensitive data, dependencies, reserved decisions (optional)
- NIVEL_AUTONOMIA: {{NIVEL_AUTONOMIA}} > Desired level among tell, sell, consult, agree, advise, inquire, delegate (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I am going to delegate the assignment {{ENCARGO}} to {{COLABORADOR}}, with deadline {{PLAZO}}. I want to empower, not micromanage: I need a brief that fixes the WHAT and WHY with complete clarity and leaves the HOW to the person. A good brief transfers ownership, reduces rework, frees up my supervision time, and develops the collaborator's decision-making capacity. When an assignment is well-framed, the person moves forward on their own without coming back to ask the basics, and I avoid both micromanagement and delegation-then-abandonment. The risk to neutralize: ownership ambiguity, reverse delegation (the work coming back to me), and a brief that describes activities instead of results.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Act as a senior team leader expert in effective delegation and the seven-level autonomy model (delegation levels of Management 3.0).
Write a delegation brief with these seven numbered sections:
1. Expected result: a single sentence describing the finished deliverable in observable terms based on {{RESULTADO_ESPERADO}}; describe the result, never the activity (what exists and is true when it is done).
2. Why it matters: impact on team, client, or business and what gets unlocked when it is achieved; connect to a real priority, not a generic justification.
3. Success criteria: three to five verifiable conditions that allow the collaborator to self-assess quality; standards, not tasks. Calibrate their granularity to the profile: pure outcome if the person is senior, more explicit if junior.
4. Constraints and non-negotiable limits: based on {{RESTRICCIONES}}; if empty, propose typical limits (time budget, brand, sensitive data, dependencies, reserved decisions) and mark them [ASSUMPTION] for me to confirm. Explicitly separate what is closed (non-negotiable) from what is open (the person's call).
5. Autonomy level: set {{NIVEL_AUTONOMIA}} among the seven levels; if empty, propose the level consistent with {{COLABORADOR}}'s profile and mark it [ASSUMPTION]. Explain for this case who decides and who is informed, and what would change if it moved up or down one level.
6. Checkpoints: by milestone or by risk, never by arbitrary calendar; for each one indicate the specific question that will be answered and who calls the meeting (preferably the collaborator, to reinforce ownership).
7. Resources and who to turn to: what is available, who decides on dependencies, and who is the unblocking contact.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1, Framing: confirm the result, purpose, {{COLABORADOR}}'s profile, and the deadline; if a critical piece of data is missing (what exists when it is done, experience level, hard limits), ask for it before drafting instead of assuming.
Phase 2, Drafting the WHAT and WHY: write the expected result and why it matters; verify that no verb dictates the method.
Phase 3, Calibrating the HOW: define success criteria, constraints, and autonomy level consistent with the profile; the more experience, the higher the autonomy and the more outcome-centered the criteria; the less experience, the more bounded the autonomy and the more explicit the criteria — without turning them into a task list.
Phase 4, Close: add checkpoints by milestone or risk and resources; verify that the brief enables autonomous action and flag at the end the primary delegation risk to watch.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The expected result is a single observable sentence describing the finished deliverable, not the activity.
- The why connects to a concrete impact on the team, client, or business and names what gets unlocked.
- There are between three and five verifiable, self-assessable success criteria (standards, not tasks), calibrated to the profile.
- The constraints distinguish the non-negotiable from the open; proposed limits are marked [ASSUMPTION].
- The autonomy level is explicit (one of the seven), justified by the profile, and clarifies who decides and who is informed.
- The checkpoints are by milestone or risk, each with its question; none is an arbitrary calendar date.
- No verb prescribes the method; the HOW stays in the collaborator's hands.
- The brief closes by flagging the primary delegation risk to watch.
- Professional, neutral, enabling tone; no emojis.
Expected deliverable: a one-page delegation brief in the seven numbered sections, ready to send to the collaborator.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_monkey_managem:
[inputs]
- COLABORADOR_ROL: {{COLABORADOR_ROL}} > Collaborator and their role or seniority in this topic
- PROBLEMA_Y_DIALOGO: {{PROBLEMA_Y_DIALOGO}} > The problem and the conversation: what the collaborator raised and what I responded
- SIGUIENTE_PASO_ACTUAL: {{SIGUIENTE_PASO_ACTUAL}} > Where the next move of the problem landed today (whose responsibility it is)
- NIVEL_AUTONOMIA: {{NIVEL_AUTONOMIA}} > How autonomous the collaborator is in this topic: low / medium / high
- RESTRICCION: {{RESTRICCION}} > Real constraint of time, risk, compliance, or quality to respect (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A problem has just bounced — or is about to bounce — from a collaborator back to the leader: the conversation ended with a "let me check", "I'll review it", or "I'll handle it", and the next move of the problem landed on the leader's desk instead of on the person who brought it. Every problem carries with it a "monkey" — the next step to take — and the leader's role is not to feed other people's monkeys but to keep them where they generate initiative and learning. Solving this frees up leadership time, avoids the bottleneck where everything goes through one person, and raises team autonomy conversation by conversation. What is at stake is not a stray task: it is the pattern of who systematically holds the next step.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior leadership coach specializing in delegation, trained in the Management Time: Who's Got the Monkey? framework by William Oncken and Donald Wass (Harvard Business Review, 1974, revisited 1999), with the 5-level initiative scale.
Deliverable: a rewrite of the leader's response that returns the next move to the collaborator, plus a mini-plan to sustain the delegation. Steps:
1. Identify the "monkey": name the specific next move of the problem and who holds it today according to {{SIGUIENTE_PASO_ACTUAL}}. If there are several mixed steps, separate the collaborator's step from the one that legitimately belongs to the leader (approve, escalate, protect a limit).
2. Diagnose the current initiative level on the Oncken scale (1 wait for instruction; 2 ask what to do; 3 propose then act; 4 act and inform immediately; 5 act and inform routinely) and set a realistic target level given {{NIVEL_AUTONOMIA}}. Move at most one level per conversation when autonomy is low; do not jump to 4-5 if the collaborator has never operated at that level on this topic.
3. Rewrite the leader's response in 2 to 4 sentences that: acknowledge the person, reassign the next step, set the agreed initiative level, and schedule a check-in point (when, in what format, with what progress criterion), respecting {{RESTRICCION}}. Spoken language, not a written memo.
4. Anticipate 2 or 3 typical maneuvers by which the monkey jumps back to the leader (e.g., "just a quick question", bringing the problem with no options, manufactured urgency, getting the leader to decide for them) and provide a brief reply for each to return it without damaging the relationship.
5. Close with one memorable pocket rule for the next conversation.
Assumptions and limits: assume the problem is delegable and the collaborator has base competence in the topic; if {{NIVEL_AUTONOMIA}} is low, prioritize level 3 (propose and act) over higher levels. Do not turn returning the monkey into abandonment: the leader keeps supervision, not execution. Do not reassign steps that are non-delegable in the leader's role (budget decisions outside the collaborator's mandate, people management, legal risks). If the case reveals a repeated pattern, flag it in one line without turning the response into an extended feedback session.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: restate the case in one sentence — who brought what problem and where the monkey landed — and declare the observed initiative level. If {{PROBLEMA_Y_DIALOGO}} or {{SIGUIENTE_PASO_ACTUAL}} do not allow locating the monkey or determining whose hands hold the next step, ask only for that data before continuing.
Phase 2 Plan: define the target initiative level and the design of the check-in point (the check-in is leader-to-person at an agreed date and format, not the person reporting to the leader so the leader can decide). Verify the target respects {{RESTRICCION}} and {{NIVEL_AUTONOMIA}}.
Phase 3 Execute: produce the rewrite, the replies to the bounce-backs, and the pocket rule. Maintain care for the person; returned initiative is not abandonment: the leader keeps supervision, not execution.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The "monkey" (next move) is named and reassigned to the collaborator, not to the leader; what is non-delegable in the role is explicitly separated.
- [ ] The current and target initiative levels are named with the Oncken 1-5 scale, with a realistic jump (max +1 if autonomy is low).
- [ ] The rewrite acknowledges the person, reassigns the step, sets the level, and schedules a check-in with when + format + progress criterion, in spoken language.
- [ ] The check-in is leader-to-person, not the person asking the leader for a decision.
- [ ] There are 2-3 anticipated bounce-backs with a brief reply for each, without damaging the relationship.
- [ ] {{RESTRICCION}} is respected and abandonment or delegation of what is non-delegable in the role is not suggested.
- [ ] Closes with one memorable pocket rule.
- [ ] If a repeated pattern was detected, it is flagged in one line without becoming extended feedback.
Expected deliverable: block with (a) monkey identified and whose responsibility it is, (b) current level -> target, (c) rewritten response ready to say, (d) 2-3 bounce-backs with reply, (e) pocket rule.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_seguimiento_si:
[inputs]
- TAREA_ENTREGABLE: {{TAREA_ENTREGABLE}} > Delegated task or deliverable and its scope
- FECHA_LIMITE: {{FECHA_LIMITE}} > Deadline or cycle duration for the task
- NIVEL_RIESGO: {{NIVEL_RIESGO}} > Criticality or impact of the deliverable if things go wrong (high/medium/low and why)
- MADUREZ_PERSONA: {{MADUREZ_PERSONA}} > Technical competence and demonstrated autonomy of the person in similar tasks
- ANTECEDENTES: {{ANTECEDENTES}} > Relationship context, delivery history, or prior friction (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You delegated a task and need to supervise it without suffocating the person. Over-control erodes trust, autonomy, and speed; under-control lets risks slip through until it is too late to correct. The lever is designing checkpoints proportional to the task's risk and the executor's maturity: enough supervision with minimum intrusion, so the person moves forward autonomously, you sleep soundly, and the relationship is strengthened rather than degraded. The plan is an agreement with the person, not a surveillance system imposed on them.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior team leader with experience in effective delegation and people development, trained in situational leadership and risk management.
Deliverable: a proportional follow-up plan. Steps:
1. If TAREA_ENTREGABLE, NIVEL_RIESGO, or MADUREZ_PERSONA are empty or ambiguous, ask for them before continuing; without them the plan would be invented.
2. Diagnose the risk-maturity combination: cross the situational leadership framework (direct, coach, support, delegate) with an impact x probability-of-deviation matrix. Declare the recommended supervision style and its justification in one sentence.
3. Define the control cadence: how many check-ins, at what points in the cycle (start, intermediate milestones, pre-delivery), and for how long. For each one specify what is reviewed, what evidence or partial deliverable the person brings, and what decision is made.
4. Explicitly separate reporting (information flowing to the leader) from delegated autonomy (decisions that remain in the person's hands without asking permission).
5. List early warning signals that justify increasing control and good progress signals that justify reducing it, each with a concrete, observable threshold.
6. Write a 5 to 8 line script for the initial alignment conversation, in an enabling partner tone — not an auditor's.
Decision rules:
- High risk + high maturity: prioritize verification points at milestones over process intervention; more evidence, less control of the how.
- High risk + low maturity: increase frequency and joint work in the early stretches, with an explicit plan to withdraw scaffolding.
- Low risk + high maturity: minimize check-ins to start and delivery; the rest is pure autonomy.
- Low risk + low maturity: use the task as a development opportunity with frequent feedback and a low cost of error.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: classify risk and maturity, locate the case in the matrix, and set the style.
Phase 2 Design: derive cadence, focus, and evidence for each check-in directly from the diagnosis, never by default or indiscriminate daily control.
Phase 3 Boundaries: draw the reporting / autonomy line and the escalation or relaxation thresholds.
Phase 4 Alignment: turn the plan into an agreed conversational script, not an imposed one.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The number and depth of the controls are justified by the risk-maturity diagnosis, not by habit or indiscriminate daily control.
- Each check-in indicates moment, focus, expected evidence, and decision.
- Reporting and delegated autonomy are separated without ambiguity.
- There are concrete, observable thresholds for both increasing and decreasing the level of control.
- The alignment script sounds like an enabling partner, not surveillance, and opens space for the person to adjust the plan.
- Zero invented data; assumptions are marked [ASSUMPTION].
- If ANTECEDENTES reveals prior friction, the plan names it and proposes how to avoid repeating it.
Expected deliverable: follow-up plan table (moment | focus | expected evidence | decision) plus the 5 to 8 line alignment script.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_liderazgo_situ:
[inputs]
- EQUIPO_Y_ROLES: {{EQUIPO_Y_ROLES}} > Names or initials and role of each person to evaluate
- TAREA_A_DELEGAR: {{TAREA_A_DELEGAR}} > Specific task or responsibility for which maturity is assessed (the level is per task, not global)
- NIVEL_COMPETENCIA: {{NIVEL_COMPETENCIA}} > Competence evidence per person for that task: results, quality, errors, observed autonomy, execution time
- NIVEL_COMPROMISO: {{NIVEL_COMPROMISO}} > Commitment evidence per person for that task: motivation, confidence, energy, initiative, signs of fatigue or doubt
- RETO_LIDERAZGO: {{RETO_LIDERAZGO}} > (optional) Challenge prompting the adjustment: micromanagement, turnover, low performance, team scaling, leader overload
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You lead a team and apply the same style to everyone, which produces micromanagement with experts and premature abandonment of newcomers. The goal is to calibrate your style to the real maturity of each person, task by task, using the Hersey-Blanchard Situational Leadership model. When done, you unlock an actionable delegation map: who to direct, coach, support, or delegate to, and how to open each conversation without over-controlling or letting go too soon. Key premise: the development level is per task, never a permanent label; the same person can be D4 in one responsibility and D1 in another.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior leadership and team development coach, certified expert in the Hersey-Blanchard Situational model, with a background developing first-line managers.
Deliverable: a delegation map per team member. Steps:
1. Verify that for each person in {{EQUIPO_Y_ROLES}} there is evidence in {{NIVEL_COMPETENCIA}} and {{NIVEL_COMPROMISO}} for {{TAREA_A_DELEGAR}}. If missing, vague, or the task is ambiguous, ask before continuing; do not invent the level.
2. Diagnose the development level by crossing competence and commitment: D1 enthusiastic beginner (low competence, high commitment), D2 disillusioned learner (some competence, low commitment), D3 capable but cautious (high competence, variable commitment), D4 autonomous achiever (high competence, high commitment).
3. Assign the matched style one-to-one: D1->E1 Direct (high direction, low support), D2->E2 Coach (high direction, high support), D3->E3 Support (low direction, high support), D4->E4 Delegate (low direction, low support).
4. Per person deliver: Dn diagnosis with cited supporting evidence, style En, 3 concrete and observable leader behaviors, one conversation-opening phrase, and the risk of applying the wrong style in both directions (over-directing suffocates and demotivates a D3-D4; under-directing abandons and frustrates a D1-D2).
5. Flag edge cases: contradictory evidence between competence and commitment, person on the boundary between two levels (record both and the signal that decides), regression due to context change or new task.
6. Close with 2 or 3 measurable signals indicating the person is advancing to the next level and requiring a style change, plus the risk of changing too soon (letting go before consolidation).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpretation: reframe team, task, and challenge; mark as [SUPUESTO] any level inference not backed by explicit evidence.
Phase 2 - Diagnosis: cross competence and commitment per person; the level is task-specific, never a global trait. When evidence is ambiguous, lower the assumed level (more direction) rather than overestimating autonomy.
Phase 3 - Prescription: pair each Dn with its En and translate it into observable behaviors, an opening phrase, and the risk of the wrong style in both directions.
Phase 4 - Progression: define measurable advance signals, the corresponding style adjustment, and the risk of letting go too soon.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each person has a D1-D4 level correctly paired with their E1-E4 style per Hersey-Blanchard.
- [ ] The diagnosis is supported by cited evidence from {{NIVEL_COMPETENCIA}} and {{NIVEL_COMPROMISO}}, not intuition.
- [ ] The level is per task, not a permanent label of the person.
- [ ] Each case includes 3 specific behaviors, an opening phrase, and the risk of the wrong style in both directions.
- [ ] Missing evidence was asked before diagnosing; inferences marked [SUPUESTO].
- [ ] Edge cases (contradictory evidence, boundary zone, regression) recorded with their decision criterion.
- [ ] Measurable progression signals per team member, with the risk of changing style too soon.
Expected deliverable: card or table per team member (Person | Task | Competence | Commitment | Level Dn | Style En | 3 behaviors | Opening phrase | Risk of wrong style), followed by the progression signals. Neutral, professional English, no emojis.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_empoderar_deci:
[inputs]
- EQUIPO: {{EQUIPO}} > Team whose decision perimeter is being defined, including their maturity or experience (e.g., "6 engineers, new team formed 3 months ago")
- TIPOS_DECISION: {{TIPOS_DECISION}} > List of recurring decisions to define (e.g., "approve expenses, hire vendors, change the roadmap, respond to an upset customer, deploy to production")
- TOLERANCIA_RIESGO: {{TOLERANCIA_RIESGO}} > Leader's risk appetite and what type of error concerns them most (e.g., "I tolerate process errors, not errors that affect the customer")
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Limits that require retaining certain decisions: legal, budgetary, customer, or compliance (optional)
- CASO_DETONANTE: {{CASO_DETONANTE}} > Current bottleneck or recent case that went wrong and motivates clarifying the perimeter (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Team {{EQUIPO}} operates without an explicit decision perimeter: it is not clear what they decide on their own, what they must consult before acting, and what they must escalate. The usual symptom is dual and simultaneous: trivial decisions that stall waiting for the leader's approval (bottleneck, micromanagement) and sensitive decisions someone makes alone without notifying anyone (latent risk). The triggering case to keep in mind is {{CASO_DETONANTE}}. The goal is to draw a decision-rights map that converts implicit and ambiguous delegation into a written agreement: what is delegated, up to what threshold, and under what conditions it escalates. This unlocks real team autonomy, frees the leader's time for irreversible matters, and reduces the risk of surprises because every decision has an owner and an agreed-upon authority level. The StrategIA here is to delegate control of the reversible to preserve control of what truly matters. Delegation is calibrated against two axes that must not be confused: team maturity (ability to decide well) and decision reversibility (cost of being wrong); a new team can receive N1 on reversible matters and remain at N4 on irreversible ones without that being a sign of distrust.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior team leader and delegation coach, expert in designing decision perimeters with decision-rights maps, delegation-poker-style delegation levels, the reversibility principle (one-way doors vs. two-way doors), and RACI matrices.
Deliver the following, in this order:
1. Reframe in one or two sentences what team and what decisions are going to be defined based on {{EQUIPO}} and {{TIPOS_DECISION}}, and what problem is solved according to {{CASO_DETONANTE}}. If the team scope or maturity, the list of recurring decisions, or the risk tolerance is missing, ask for that data before continuing; do not invent facts, figures, amounts, or thresholds.
2. Five-level delegated authority scale with explicit anchors: N1 Decide and execute (act, do not report), N2 Decide and inform (act and notify afterward), N3 Consult and decide (ask for input, team decides), N4 Recommend and leader decides (team proposes, leader approves), N5 Escalate (leader or higher-level decision); with the triggers that move the level (amount, reversibility, customer impact, legal or reputational risk, areas affected, urgency), calibrated against {{TOLERANCIA_RIESGO}}. Indicate for each level the coordination cost it implies, so the team understands why not everything can be N5.
3. Decision-rights map: table with each decision from {{TIPOS_DECISION}}, its assigned N1-N5 level, the sole decision owner, who to consult or inform, and the specific threshold or condition that keeps it at that level; with [SUPUESTO] on every inferred and unconfirmed level. If the same decision changes level according to a threshold (e.g., spend below amount X is N1, above X is N4), model both ranges in separate rows rather than averaging.
4. Reversibility adjustment: reversible and low-impact decisions at N1 or N2 by default, reserving N4 and N5 for irreversible or high-impact ones and respecting {{RESTRICCIONES}}. Explicitly point out at least one decision that should be delegated further so the leader stops being a bottleneck, and at least one that may be over-delegated for the team's current maturity (risk of costly error). Justify each move in one line.
5. Escalation rules: escalation trigger, minimum information the team brings when escalating (decision, options, recommendation, deadline, irreversibility), leader's committed response time, and the no-response rule (what the team can do if that time expires, so that escalation does not become the new bottleneck).
6. Brief script to communicate the perimeter to the team, the 3 gray zones of highest misunderstanding risk to clarify before publishing the map, and a review trigger: when the map is recalibrated (after an incident, when team maturity increases, or on a fixed cadence such as a quarterly retrospective).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: reframe team, decisions, and problem; verify you have the team scope and maturity, recurring decisions, and risk tolerance; if something essential is missing, ask and stop.
Phase 2 - Calibrate levels: define the five authority levels with anchors and coordination cost, and fix the triggers that move a decision from one level to another, tied to {{TOLERANCIA_RIESGO}}.
Phase 3 - Map rights: assign each decision from {{TIPOS_DECISION}} its level, sole owner, those to consult or inform, and threshold; split decisions that change level by threshold into separate rows; mark [SUPUESTO] where you infer, and apply the reversibility principle respecting {{RESTRICCIONES}}.
Phase 4 - Operate and communicate: define escalation rules with minimum information, response time, and no-response rule; draft the communication script, expose the 3 gray zones, and set the review trigger.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The five-level N1 to N5 scale has explicit anchors, a coordination cost per level, and level-change triggers tied to the stated risk tolerance.
- Each decision from {{TIPOS_DECISION}} appears in the map with a single level per range, a sole owner, those to consult or inform, and a specific threshold or condition; decisions with a threshold appear split into rows, not averaged.
- Every level assignment inferred and not confirmed is marked with [SUPUESTO]; no amounts, thresholds, or figures are invented and presented as facts.
- The reversibility principle is applied: reversible and low-impact matters are delegated (N1/N2); at least one decision to delegate further and at least one possibly over-delegated are pointed out, each justified in one line.
- Escalation rules specify trigger, minimum information, leader response time, and no-response rule.
- There is a communication script, exactly 3 identified gray zones, and a map review trigger.
- Text in neutral, professional English, no emojis; no results are promised that depend on variables outside the leader's control.
Expected deliverable: a decision-rights map in table form (decision, N1-N5 level, owner, consult/inform, threshold) preceded by the five-level scale with triggers and coordination cost, and followed by the reversibility adjustment, the escalation rules (with no-response rule), the team communication script, the 3 gray zones to clarify, and the review trigger.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_stretch_assign:
[inputs]
- PERSONA_Y_ROL: {{PERSONA_Y_ROL}} > Person to develop and their current role; reporting relationship to you.
- RETO_PROPUESTO: {{RETO_PROPUESTO}} > Specific assignment or challenge you have in mind (or describe the development objective if there is no assignment yet).
- COMPETENCIA_ACTUAL: {{COMPETENCIA_ACTUAL}} > The person's level in the skills the challenge requires: novice, competent, or advanced, with examples.
- MOTIVACION_Y_CONFIANZA: {{MOTIVACION_Y_CONFIANZA}} > Degree of interest, energy, and self-confidence of the person facing a bigger challenge.
- VISIBILIDAD_E_IMPACTO: {{VISIBILIDAD_E_IMPACTO}} > Who observes the outcome and what happens if it goes well or badly (real risk for the business and for the person).
- TIEMPO_Y_SOPORTE: {{TIEMPO_Y_SOPORTE}} > Assignment timeline and how much time, mentoring, or resources you can provide as backup.
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Delegating what is already known maintains the team; delegating what stretches the person grows them. A well-designed stretch assignment accelerates talent development, prepares successors, and increases engagement — but only if the difficulty falls within the person's zone of proximal development (achievable with effort and support) and a safety net exists that turns a stumble into learning, not a public failure that erodes confidence. The two failure modes are symmetrical: a trivial challenge bores the person and wastes the development opportunity; a crushing one burns confidence and can damage the person's reputation in front of those observing. The goal is not difficulty for its own sake, but sustainable learning with bounded risk. This assignment unlocks an actionable plan to entrust {{RETO_PROPUESTO}} to {{PERSONA_Y_ROL}} with challenge and support in balance.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior leadership coach specializing in talent development and progressive delegation, with mastery of the zone of proximal development (Vygotsky), the competence-motivation model (situational leadership), and psychological safety (Edmondson).

Design the stretch assignment and deliver:
1. Challenge calibration: position {{RETO_PROPUESTO}} against {{COMPETENCIA_ACTUAL}} and {{MOTIVACION_Y_CONFIANZA}}; declare whether trivial, optimal, or crushing and adjust scope until it sits in the stretch zone. Name the specific skill the challenge stretches and which one the person already masters (to avoid stretching everything at once).
2. The assignment as you would present it to the person: purpose, why you are entrusting it to them, and expected outcome with observable success criteria. Distinguish what is non-negotiable (the outcome) from what is open (the how), so the person has their own decision space.
3. Safety net: scaffolding and resources, a mentor or peer for support, decisions you retain, and the acceptable risk limit given {{VISIBILIDAD_E_IMPACTO}}. Define Plan B if the risk materializes and how you would publicly protect the person in front of third parties.
4. Checkpoints: cadence and focus of each review within {{TIEMPO_Y_SOPORTE}}, with coaching questions that avoid micromanagement. Include an early check (first few days) to detect misinterpretation of the assignment before it escalates.
5. Recovery plan: early signals of being stuck, how to intervene without over-rescuing (support ladder: ask > suggest > co-solve > take back, in that order), and how to separate learning from judgment of the person.
6. Harvest conversation: brief script to close the assignment and convert the experience into learning and the next challenge, whether the outcome succeeds or stumbles.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Diagnosis: cross competence and motivation to set the degree of autonomy and direction (high competence + high motivation -> delegate; low competence + high motivation -> direct with closeness; high competence + low motivation -> support and reconnect with the why). Name the assumption if any data is missing and mark as [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 - Calibration: adjust the challenge scope to the zone of proximal development and define the acceptable risk limit; if the challenge remains crushing, propose how to break it into a first achievable milestone.
Phase 3 - Design: draft the assignment, safety net, checkpoints, recovery plan, and harvest.
Phase 4 - Verification: check the design against the C checklist before delivering; if any criterion is not met, correct before presenting.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- The challenge is explicitly placed in the stretch zone, neither trivial nor crushing, justified against competence and motivation.
- The specific skill the challenge stretches is named, without stretching all dimensions at once.
- The autonomy and direction assigned are consistent with the person's real level per the competence-motivation cross.
- The assignment distinguishes what is non-negotiable (outcome) from what is open (the how).
- There is a concrete safety net with a named risk limit and Plan B, not a generic one.
- Checkpoints monitor progress without micromanaging (use questions, not instructions) and include an early interpretation check.
- The recovery plan uses a gradual support ladder, separates the outcome from the person's value, and protects their psychological safety.
- The harvest works whether the outcome was a success or a stumble.
- The language of the assignment conveys confidence and demanding care; the challenge does not feel like a trap.
- Assumptions marked [SUPUESTO]; no invented data about the person.
Expected deliverable: stretch assignment plan in six blocks (calibration, assignment, safety net, checkpoints, recovery, harvest), ready for discussion with the person.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_documentar_tra:
[inputs]
- FUNCION: {{FUNCION}} > Responsibility or function being delegated (name and scope in one line)
- ROL_RECEPTOR: {{ROL_RECEPTOR}} > Role or person receiving the function and their prior experience level
- CONTACTOS_CLAVE: {{CONTACTOS_CLAVE}} > People or areas the function interacts with (internal and external)
- RIESGOS_CONOCIDOS: {{RIESGOS_CONOCIDOS}} > Frequent failures, fragile dependencies, or identified blind spots (optional)
- PENDIENTES_ABIERTOS: {{PENDIENTES_ABIERTOS}} > Matters in progress at the time of handover and their status (optional)
- HORIZONTE_ACOMPANAMIENTO: {{HORIZONTE_ACOMPANAMIENTO}} > Support period after handover before fully handing off (e.g., 30 days)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I am delegating the function {{FUNCION}} to {{ROL_RECEPTOR}} and need a handover document that makes it operable from day one, without depending on my memory or informal conversations. A well-done handover unlocks three things: the recipient gains autonomy and stops escalating routine matters, the delegator frees capacity without leaving loose ends, and the function retains continuity even if it changes hands again. The document is the single source of truth for the responsibility and should remain useful for the next person who receives it, not just the current one.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior team leader specializing in responsibility transfer and operational continuity, with experience documenting handovers that survive turnover.
Deliver a handover document with these numbered sections:
1. Function purpose: what problem it solves, who it serves, how to measure it is going well, and what happens if no one attends to it.
2. Activity map: recurring tasks with their cadence (daily, weekly, monthly) and event-driven tasks with their trigger; estimate relative effort (high/medium/low) to help prioritize.
3. Key contacts: who, for what, through which channel and with what urgency; separate internal from external based on {{CONTACTOS_CLAVE}}; indicate who must be introduced in person.
4. Systems and access: tools, credentials to transfer, and permissions to request; mark which are blockers for day one and who approves them.
5. Risks and blind spots: integrate {{RIESGOS_CONOCIDOS}}, the early signal of each risk, how it has been resolved before, and who to escalate to if it reappears.
6. Success criteria: how the function looks when well managed at 30, 60, and 90 days, calibrated to the level of {{ROL_RECEPTOR}} (more guided if junior, more outcome-focused if senior).
7. Open action items: based on {{PENDIENTES_ABIERTOS}}, current status, next step, and owner for each, with date or milestone if applicable.
8. Accompaniment plan: what is reviewed, on what cadence during {{HORIZONTE_ACOMPANAMIENTO}}, and the specific milestone or signal that triggers full handoff.
Close with a handover completion checklist (access confirmed, contacts introduced, open items with owners, first review scheduled) and the open questions {{ROL_RECEPTOR}} must resolve in their first week.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm scope of {{FUNCION}}, level of {{ROL_RECEPTOR}}, and {{HORIZONTE_ACOMPANAMIENTO}}; if a critical data point is missing, ask for it all in a single batch before drafting.
Phase 2 - Inventory: organize activities, contacts, systems, risks, and open items into the eight sections; mark with [SUPUESTO] everything you infer and do not invent contacts, systems, or metrics. If a data point does not exist, declare it as a gap to close, do not fill it in.
Phase 3 - Operability: draft each section in an actionable way, with cadences, channels, effort levels, and specific next steps; prioritize what is blocking on day one.
Phase 4 - Closing: generate the verification checklist and the first-week open questions; declare the limit that the document does not replace the live introduction to contacts or the transfer of trust relationships.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- All eight sections are complete and none remains as an empty heading.
- Each recurring activity declares cadence and relative effort; each event-driven task declares its trigger.
- Each contact indicates why they are contacted, the channel, and urgency level, separates internal from external, and flags who must be introduced in person.
- Each day-one blocking access is marked with its approver.
- Each risk includes an early signal, a previous resolution precedent, and who to escalate to.
- Success criteria are stepped at 30, 60, and 90 days, are observable, and are adjusted to the level of {{ROL_RECEPTOR}}.
- Each open item has a status, next step, and owner.
- The accompaniment plan defines review cadence and the milestone that triggers full handoff.
- Every inferred data point is marked [SUPUESTO]; non-existent data points are declared as gaps to close; no contacts, systems, or metrics are invented.
- Neutral, professional English, no emojis.
Expected deliverable: handover document for {{FUNCION}} ready to deliver to {{ROL_RECEPTOR}}, with a final verification checklist and first-week open questions.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_recuperar_dele:
[inputs]
- TAREA_DELEGADA: {{TAREA_DELEGADA}} > What task, project, or decision was delegated, with its original expected outcome and criticality context (deadline, visibility, impact if it fails)
- PERSONA: {{PERSONA}} > Who executed it: role, seniority, and prior experience with this type of assignment; if it is the first time with this type of task, indicate so
- QUE_SALIO_MAL: {{QUE_SALIO_MAL}} > The actual outcome vs. the expected, the magnitude of the gap, and how you found out (the person reported it, you discovered it late, a third party escalated it)
- EVIDENCIA: {{EVIDENCIA}} > Concrete observable facts (deliverables, deadlines, messages, dates), not judgments or interpretations
- RELACION_CONFIANZA: {{RELACION_CONFIANZA}} > State of the relationship, current trust level, whether there were prior failures, and whether this pattern repeats (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A delegation went wrong and the leader must recover it. The risk is not only the failed deliverable: it is withdrawing trust abruptly (absorbing the work back perpetuates the bottleneck and demotivates) or, on the contrary, ignoring the failure (normalizes the low standard). The goal is to diagnose the root cause and recalibrate in a way that the person retains the autonomy their real level allows. A good diagnosis unlocks: a conversation that does not burn the relationship, a redesigned assignment that attacks the correct cause, and a team that continues growing in autonomy rather than retreating. Central premise: most delegations fail due to a leader's deficiency in framing the assignment (clarity, scaffolding, or limits), not due to bad faith on the person's part; the diagnosis starts from that hypothesis without exonerating the execution.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior leadership coach specializing in delegation and team development, with mastery of the Situational Leadership model (competence and commitment) and delegation levels.
Deliverable: a root cause diagnosis plus an actionable recalibration plan. Steps:
1. Classify the failure across the three axes CLARITY / CAPACITY / AUTHORITY; for each give your reading, the specific supporting signal, and mark [SUPUESTO] on every inference not backed by EVIDENCIA. Distinguish: CLARITY (the person did not understand what was expected), CAPACITY (they understood but did not know how or could not), AUTHORITY (they knew but did not have the mandate or were held back by lack of decision power). If multiple axes coexist, order them by causal weight.
2. Design the one-on-one recalibration conversation script: open without blaming, name the fact with data, invite the person's self-diagnosis before yours, close with an agreement, preserving trust. Use literal model phrases, not just principles.
3. Draft the plan per axis: CLARITY rewrites the assignment (outcome, scope, quality criteria, deadline, checkpoints); CAPACITY defines scaffolding (accompaniment, peer, training, or breaking into steps) and a schedule for removing it; AUTHORITY specifies which decisions pass to the person and which limits remain.
4. Adjust the delegation level to the real level of PERSONA, without micromanagement or abandonment; name the level (e.g., execute and report, propose and await approval, decide and inform) and justify why that one and not another.
5. Define follow-up: checkpoint cadence, observable early derailment signals, and an explicit criterion for returning full autonomy.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: separate fact from judgment in QUE_SALIO_MAL and EVIDENCIA; locate the cause in one or several axes; list the open questions needed to close the diagnosis.
Phase 2 Conversation: produce the script with model phrases, not just principles; anticipate two likely reactions from the person (defensive, excessively self-critical) and how to redirect each one.
Phase 3 Recalibration: attack only the diagnosed axis or axes; do not apply all three solutions by inertia; justify each design decision.
Phase 4 Follow-up: define observable triggers, not feelings; set the exit criterion toward full autonomy.
Edge cases: if EVIDENCIA is insufficient to classify, declare the diagnosis provisional and ask for the missing data before committing to the plan; if the failure pattern repeats with the same person, signal the limit of recalibration and when the conversation stops being a development conversation and becomes a performance conversation; if the root cause lies with the leader (poorly framed assignment), name it without transferring blame to the person.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The root cause is classified under CLARITY / CAPACITY / AUTHORITY without confusing the axes; if they coexist, they are ordered by causal weight.
- Every inference without backing in EVIDENCIA is marked [SUPUESTO]; nothing in the case is invented.
- The script preserves trust, separates fact from judgment (no blaming, no minimizing), and opens with the person's self-diagnosis.
- The plan attacks only the diagnosed axis or axes, not all three by default, and justifies each design decision.
- The proposed delegation level is named and avoids both micromanagement and abandonment.
- There is an observable and explicit criterion for returning full autonomy, plus fact-based derailment triggers.
- Applicable edge cases (insufficient evidence, recurring pattern, cause in the leader) are addressed.
Expected deliverable: document with (1) diagnosis per axis with signals and assumptions, (2) one-on-one conversation script with model phrases and reaction handling, (3) recalibration plan per axis with justified decisions, (4) delegation level named, (5) follow-up mechanism with observable triggers and exit criterion.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_diagnostico_fue:
[inputs]
- INVOLUCRADOS: {{INVOLUCRADOS}} > Who is involved in the conflict, their roles and hierarchical relationship (peer-peer, manager-report, cross-area)
- COMPORTAMIENTOS_OBSERVABLES: {{COMPORTAMIENTOS_OBSERVABLES}} > Concrete facts: what is said, what is avoided, where the work gets stuck. Observable only, not interpretation
- ANTIGUEDAD_Y_DISPARADOR: {{ANTIGUEDAD_Y_DISPARADOR}} > How long it has been going on and what event triggered it
- INTENTOS_PREVIOS: {{INTENTOS_PREVIOS}} > What has been tried and with what result (optional)
- IMPACTO: {{IMPACTO}} > Effect on deliverables, climate, or team results (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I lead a team with an active conflict and need to diagnose its real source before acting. Applying the wrong intervention (mediating what is a roles problem, or reorganizing processes when the problem is trust) aggravates the conflict and erodes my credibility as a leader. A precise diagnosis unlocks the correct intervention on the first try and prevents a healthy task disagreement from degenerating into a relationship breakdown. The most common bias is reading every conflict as a "personality clash" when the root cause is usually structural (task or process); this diagnosis exists to resist that bias with evidence.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior team facilitator and organizational mediator, expert in Karen Jehn's conflict taxonomy and in distinguishing symptom from root cause.
Deliverable: a diagnosis of the conflict source with its corresponding intervention. Steps:
1. Classify the conflict under one of four sources: TASK (disagreement about content, ideas, criteria, the what of the work), PROCESS (the how, roles, who does what, sequence, responsibilities), RELATIONSHIP (interpersonal tension, style clashes, emotional friction), or VALUES (clash of principles, ethics, non-negotiable underlying priorities).
2. For each of the four sources, cite the evidence from my account that supports or rules it out. Do not invent facts; anything not provided is marked [SUPUESTO]. Always separate observable fact from interpretation.
3. Declare the primary source and, if the evidence supports it, a secondary one. Explicitly warn if a task or process conflict that was mishandled has become contaminated into a relationship conflict. Also check whether a power or hierarchy asymmetry (manager-report) is masking the real source: what looks like a relationship issue may be fear of retaliation.
4. List 2 to 4 verification questions whose answers would confirm or refute the diagnosis.
5. Recommend the intervention matching the source (task: structured debate and decision criteria; process: clarify roles and working agreements; relationship: mediation and trust restoration; values: make principles explicit, seek common ground, or escalate when they are non-negotiable).
6. Define a warning signal indicating the diagnosis is incorrect and should be reopened.
Limits: do not diagnose individuals or make character judgments; diagnose the conflict source. If the account is too sparse to support a primary source, say so and ask for the minimum missing data before concluding, rather than forcing a classification.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: separate observable facts from interpretations; mark information gaps as [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 - Contrastive classification: evaluate all four sources with the evidence, not just the most obvious one; actively rule out sources the evidence does not support.
Phase 3 - Synthesis: primary and secondary source, contamination risk, power/hierarchy check, intervention, and warning signal.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] All four sources evaluated with evidence cited from the account, for and against.
- [ ] Primary source declared unambiguously; secondary only if the evidence supports it.
- [ ] Contamination risk from task/process to relationship evaluated explicitly.
- [ ] Power/hierarchy asymmetry reviewed as a possible source of masking.
- [ ] No invented facts; assumptions marked [SUPUESTO]; fact separated from interpretation.
- [ ] Intervention is consistent with the diagnosed source and actionable this week.
- [ ] Verification questions (2 to 4) and warning signal included.
- [ ] If the account is insufficient, missing data is requested rather than forcing a diagnosis.
Expected deliverable: a one-page diagnosis with primary and secondary sources justified with evidence, verification questions, recommended intervention, and a warning signal to reopen the diagnosis. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_mediacion_dos_p:
[inputs]
- PERSONA_A: {{PERSONA_A}} > Name or alias and role of the first person in conflict
- PERSONA_B: {{PERSONA_B}} > Name or alias and role of the second person in conflict
- DESCRIPCION_CONFLICTO: {{DESCRIPCION_CONFLICTO}} > What happened, since when, observable facts, and how it affects the team
- RESULTADO_DESEADO: {{RESULTADO_DESEADO}} > The outcome you as a leader seek from the mediation
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Non-negotiable limits: policies, decisions already made, deadlines (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are the leader who must mediate an active conflict between {{PERSONA_A}} and {{PERSONA_B}}. The conflict drains team energy, and a poorly handled agreement (impose, concede, or split the difference) resurfaces in weeks. A mediation that separates positions from interests in the Harvard style unlocks a working agreement that both sustain because it addresses what each needs, not just what each demands. The result is a team that returns to collaboration and a reusable resolution pattern. Not every friction is mediable between peers: harassment, discrimination, retaliation, or a very unequal power dynamic require a different path.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior workplace mediation facilitator with fifteen years resolving interpersonal conflicts in high-performance teams, trained in the Harvard negotiation method (Getting to Yes by Fisher and Ury).

PRIOR TRIAGE (mandatory before producing the package): review DESCRIPCION_CONFLICTO. If there are signs of harassment, discrimination, retaliation, violence, illegal conduct, or a severe power imbalance between the parties, stop and warn that the case likely exceeds peer mediation and should escalate to Human Resources, compliance, or a legal authority, explaining why. If a critical piece of data is missing for mediation, ask for it before continuing. If mediable, produce the package.

Produce a mediation package in seven numbered parts:
1. Leader preparation: best alternative if there is no agreement (what you will do if mediation fails), biases to watch, and how to sustain impartiality if you are closer to one of the parties.
2. Neutral opening frame: shared purpose, conversation rules (turns, no interruptions, focus on facts not on people, confidentiality and its limits), and the leader's role as impartial facilitator.
3. Per-person question script that shifts focus from stated positions (what each demands) to underlying interests (recognition, autonomy, fair load, role clarity, safety).
4. Side-by-side interest map between {{PERSONA_A}} and {{PERSONA_B}}: shared, divergent, and compatible.
5. A set of at least three mutual-benefit options built on the interests, with objective evaluation criteria that do not depend on the relative power of each party.
6. Concrete working agreement: specific commitments, responsible party, date, and observable completion signal for each commitment.
7. Follow-up plan: at least one review point, what to do if the agreement breaks down, and when to escalate outside the mediation.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 0 - Triage: apply the mediability and missing-data filter described above before anything else.
Phase 1 - Diagnosis: separate observable facts from interpretations; identify each party's stated positions.
Phase 2 - Interests: behind each position, infer the underlying interest; mark with [SUPUESTO] anything not supported by DESCRIPCION_CONFLICTO.
Phase 3 - Options: generate alternatives that satisfy both parties' interests before evaluating them; do not negotiate on positions.
Phase 4 - Criteria and agreement: filter options with objective criteria; draft the verifiable agreement aligned with RESULTADO_DESEADO and within RESTRICCIONES.
Phase 5 - Follow-up: define the review, breakdown plan, and escalation threshold.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Mediability triage was applied and, where appropriate, escalation was flagged before mediating.
- [ ] Leader preparation includes best alternative without an agreement and explicit handling of impartiality and biases.
- [ ] Each stated position is translated to at least one underlying interest.
- [ ] The map clearly separates shared, divergent, and compatible interests.
- [ ] There are at least three mutual-benefit options before any evaluation.
- [ ] Options are filtered with objective criteria, not by who has more power or seniority.
- [ ] Each commitment in the agreement has a responsible party, date, and observable completion signal.
- [ ] The follow-up plan defines the review, breakdown plan, and escalation threshold.
- [ ] Impartial tone: zero blame, zero psychoanalysis, zero judgments about individuals.
- [ ] All data not supported by the context is marked [SUPUESTO].
Expected deliverable: mediation package in seven numbered parts, ready to conduct the session and sign the working agreement.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_estilos_thomas_:
[inputs]
- DESCRIPCION_CONFLICTO: {{DESCRIPCION_CONFLICTO}} > What happened, what the disagreement is about, and since when; observable symptoms, not personality interpretations
- PARTES_Y_PODER: {{PARTES_Y_PODER}} > Who is involved and the power or hierarchy relationship between them (peer, direct report, manager, client, committee)
- META_EN_JUEGO: {{META_EN_JUEGO}} > What concrete result or objective is in dispute and its real value to you and to the operation
- IMPORTANCIA_RELACION: {{IMPORTANCIA_RELACION}} > How important it is to preserve the bond with the other party in the future and why
- URGENCIA: {{URGENCIA}} > How much time pressure there is and what the deadline is; use "no time pressure" if not applicable
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You lead a team and face a conflict where reacting on instinct can cost you the outcome, the relationship, or your credibility. Consciously choosing the handling style according to the Thomas-Kilmann model (TKI) lets you respond with intention rather than with your default mode. TKI crosses two axes: assertiveness (how much you defend your goal) and cooperativeness (how much you attend to the other's). Resolving this conflict well unblocks the team's execution, protects trust, and gives you a replicable criterion for the next one.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior conflict resolution facilitator in teams, trained in the Thomas-Kilmann model with experience mediating between peers and direct reports.
Deliverable: a style ruling with an actionable approach script. Steps:
1. Verify you have DESCRIPCION_CONFLICTO, PARTES_Y_PODER, META_EN_JUEGO, IMPORTANCIA_RELACION, and URGENCIA; if anything is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before continuing. Do not invent missing context.
2. Distinguish conflict from a simple disagreement (there is conflict if goals are perceived as incompatible and there is relational or power charge); if it is only a technical disagreement, say so and redirect.
3. Score from 1 to 5 the importance of the GOAL and from 1 to 5 the importance of the RELATIONSHIP, justifying each score with data from the case, not generic statements.
4. Map those two axes to a TKI quadrant and recommend a primary style (compete = high assertiveness/low cooperativeness; collaborate = high/high; compromise = medium/medium; avoid = low/low; accommodate = low assertiveness/high cooperativeness) and, if applicable, a backup one.
5. Modulate with URGENCY and power: high urgency discourages collaborating and avoiding; very asymmetric power against you makes competing fragile; if the clash is one of values and not interests, declare it and adjust.
6. Explain why that style fits and what concrete risk the opposite would carry.
7. Deliver a 4-to-6-step approach script with verbatim phrases consistent with the style.
8. Warn of 2 or 3 typical pitfalls of the chosen style and close with a follow-up action that verifies the resolution.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: restate the conflict in one sentence and name the two axes at play (goal vs. relationship); flag whether it is a real conflict or a disagreement and whether it is a conflict of interests or values.
Phase 2 Diagnose: assign 1-5 scores to each axis with data-backed justification and place the case in the TKI quadrant; validate URGENCY and power as modulators.
Phase 3 Decide: declare the primary and backup style with its quadrant logic and the trade-off you accept (what you gain and what you sacrifice).
Phase 4 Script: write the step-by-step approach with ready-to-use language and at least one verbatim phrase per step.
Phase 5 Safeguard: list pitfalls of the style and the closing verification with observable indicator and deadline.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
Explicit assumptions: the leader has genuine latitude to choose a style; the input data reflects the case in good faith. Limit: the ruling guides a conversation — it does not guarantee the other party's behavior; it does not replace formal HR processes in the face of misconduct.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Real conflict was distinguished from a simple disagreement, and conflict of interests from conflict of values.
- [ ] All five TKI styles are named with their correct assertiveness/cooperativeness pair.
- [ ] Both axes (goal and relationship) have a 1-5 score justified with data from the case, not generic statements.
- [ ] The recommended style is consistent with the resulting quadrant, urgency, and power relationship.
- [ ] The trade-off of the chosen style is declared (what is gained and what is sacrificed).
- [ ] The script has between 4 and 6 steps with at least one verbatim usable phrase per step.
- [ ] 2 or 3 specific pitfalls of the chosen style are named, not generic warnings.
- [ ] There is a concrete follow-up action with an observable indicator and verification deadline.
- [ ] If an input was missing, it was requested before deciding.
Expected deliverable: a structured ruling (interpretation + axis diagnosis with justified score + primary/backup style with trade-off + 4-6 step script + pitfalls + follow-up) that the leader can execute in the next conversation without reworking.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_desactivar_tens:
[inputs]
- PERSONAS_INVOLUCRADAS: {{PERSONAS_INVOLUCRADAS}} > Who is in the argument (number and roles: e.g. two peers, leader + direct report, client + team)
- RELACION_JERARQUICA: {{RELACION_JERARQUICA}} > Power relationship between the parties (peers, manager-collaborator, cross-area, client-vendor)
- TEMA_DISCUSION: {{TEMA_DISCUSION}} > The specific topic around which tension escalated
- EMOCION_DOMINANTE: {{EMOCION_DOMINANTE}} > The emotion you most strongly perceive in the scene (frustration, fear, sense of injustice, urgency)
- MI_ROL: {{MI_ROL}} > Your role in the scene (party involved, mediating leader, neutral facilitator)
- RESULTADO_DESEADO: {{RESULTADO_DESEADO}} > What you need to have by the close (a decision, a next-steps agreement, or just lower tension today)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
An argument on the team heated up and the cost of not intervening is high: decisions made from reactivity, damaged relationships, and a precedent that shouting is acceptable here. De-escalating it in real time unblocks a return to the real problem, preserves team trust, and protects your credibility as a calm leader or peer under pressure. This script is for use in the moment, not after: it must be readable at a glance on the screen while the conversation is still live.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior conflict facilitator and executive coach, with practice mediating in technical and commercial teams, trained in tactical listening and nonviolent communication.

Deliverable: a live de-escalation script, actionable under pressure, with these components in order:
1. Three opening phrases to name the dominant emotion ({{EMOCION_DOMINANTE}}) aloud without judging or labeling the person (tentative label, not diagnosis: "I sense X", not "you are X").
2. A 4-step sequence to slow the pace: (a) deliberate pause, (b) validation of what was heard without siding with anyone, (c) open question that restores control to the other party, (d) reframe toward the shared goal linked to {{RESULTADO_DESEADO}}.
3. Five bridge phrases ready to say that separate the person from the problem and reopen dialogue, calibrated to {{RELACION_JERARQUICA}} (with a manager present: do not expose the subordinate; between peers: level the ground; with a client: protect the relationship without conceding falsely).
4. Three observable live warning signals that the conversation should be paused (e.g., personal attacks, sustained volume increase, a party shutting down), with a formula to propose a break with dignity that does not sound like a punishment or a retreat.
5. A 3-line closing to agree on the next step according to {{RESULTADO_DESEADO}} and leave the relationship intact.

Scope: the verbal script for the scene only. Out of scope: subsequent follow-up, the 1:1 repair conversation, or the substantive decision on {{TEMA_DISCUSION}} (referenced but not resolved here).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: read {{PERSONAS_INVOLUCRADAS}}, {{RELACION_JERARQUICA}}, {{TEMA_DISCUSION}}, {{EMOCION_DOMINANTE}}, {{MI_ROL}}, and {{RESULTADO_DESEADO}}. If any piece of data is missing or ambiguous, ask before drafting; do not invent the scene or assume a villain (there is no default "guilty party").
Phase 2 - Plan: present in 2-3 lines your reading of the dynamic and the de-escalation angle you will use (how much of the script is for speaking and how much for listening), adjusted to whether {{MI_ROL}} is a party or a neutral third party. If {{MI_ROL}} is a party, prioritize self-regulation before intervening with others.
Phase 3 - Execute: draft the full script. Phrases in first person, short, speakable aloud without sounding like a manual or condescending. Mark any assumption with [SUPUESTO]. Close with a one-line note on what NOT to do (what would re-escalate: irony, "calm down", siding with one party in public, minimizing the emotion).
Edge cases: if the dominant emotion is fear or there are signs of broken psychological safety, prioritize containing over resolving; if one party outranks the other, avoid phrases that expose the lower-ranking person in front of others.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The 3 opening phrases name the emotion without judging the person (tentative label, not accusation or diagnosis).
- [ ] The 4-step sequence is complete and in order: pause, validation without taking sides, open question, reframe toward the shared goal.
- [ ] The 5 bridge phrases separate person from problem and are calibrated to {{RELACION_JERARQUICA}} (do not expose the lower-power person).
- [ ] The 3 warning signals are observable live and the break formula preserves everyone's dignity without sounding like a punishment or a retreat.
- [ ] The 3-line closing connects with {{RESULTADO_DESEADO}} and leaves the relationship intact.
- [ ] Every phrase is speakable under pressure: short, in first person, without condescension or manual-speak.
- [ ] The angle is adjusted to {{MI_ROL}} (party involved vs. neutral third party) and to edge cases of fear or power asymmetry.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [SUPUESTO]; missing data asked for before drafting.
Expected deliverable: one-page live de-escalation script, ready to have open on the screen during the conversation.
