[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
We are replacing the single annual review with a continuous feedback system: frequent check-ins with living goals and lightweight logging. Goals: reduce friction for busy managers, shorten the feedback cycle to days instead of months, and build an accumulating record that feeds the annual synthesis without starting from scratch. By the end, the team will have an operational cadence, reusable templates, and governance rules ready to deploy in 90 days. Tension to resolve: maximize the utility of feedback while minimizing capture burden — a system that costs more than it delivers will be abandoned.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior People and performance leader, specialist in Continuous Performance Management, with expertise in continuous check-ins, OKRs / living goals, SBI conversations (Situation-Behavior-Impact), and GROW coaching.
Deliver a complete continuous feedback system design. Steps:
1. Diagnose what fails in the annual cycle described in CICLO_ACTUAL_Y_DOLORES (recency bias, late feedback, disconnection from real goals, point-in-time burden) and set 4–6 actionable design principles.
2. Define the rhythm cadence (check-in 1:1 per FRECUENCIA_CHECKIN, monthly goal review, quarterly retro, annual synthesis) with distinct purpose, frequency, duration, owner, and output for each rhythm, with no overlaps.
3. Design the living-goals framework (OKRs or equivalent) with explicit update criteria and a progress traffic light (on track / at risk / blocked).
4. Create a lightweight logging template under five minutes per check-in, copyable into HERRAMIENTAS_REGISTRO, with minimal fields that accumulate toward the annual synthesis without double-entry.
5. Write a check-in 1:1 script with concrete SBI and GROW questions (not generic ones), adapted to manager maturity.
6. Define governance (feedback quality, link to or isolation from compensation per VINCULO_COMPENSACION), a 90-day adoption plan in three waves with advancement criteria between them, and 4–6 health metrics with formula and threshold.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Diagnosis and principles: name the annual cycle's failures and set principles (frequency over perfection, separate development from evaluation, lightweight by default, single owner per rhythm, accumulating traceability).
Phase 2 — Cadence: build the rhythm architecture and its table; verify that no purpose overlaps between rhythms.
Phase 3 — Living goals: rules for setting, reviewing, and rewriting goals during the period, with update triggers and traffic light.
Phase 4 — Lightweight logging and script: minimal capture template (copyable fields) plus a SBI/GROW conversation script with concrete questions.
Phase 5 — Governance and transition: quality rules, compensation link or isolation, 90-day plan in three waves (pilot, expansion, steady state), metrics with formula and threshold, and adoption risks (ritual fatigue, performative capture, residual recency bias) with mitigations.
Label each contextual claim as fact or [SUPUESTO]; do not present inferences as facts. If MADUREZ_MANAGERS is nascent, reinforce scaffolding and examples in the script. If an input is missing or ambiguous, declare it and ask for the data before assuming.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist: (1) each rhythm has a distinct purpose, frequency, duration, owner, and output that do not overlap; (2) the lightweight log is completable in under five minutes and links to the annual synthesis without double-entry; (3) living goals have an explicit update criterion and a defined traffic light; (4) the script uses SBI and GROW with concrete, non-generic questions adjusted to MADUREZ_MANAGERS; (5) the link to compensation is explicit (connected or isolated) per VINCULO_COMPENSACION, with its justification; (6) metrics have a measurable formula and threshold; (7) the 90-day plan defines advancement criteria between the three waves; (8) at least three adoption risks are declared with mitigations; (9) every assumption is tagged [SUPUESTO].
Expected deliverable: executive summary of 5–7 lines, diagnosis, list of principles, cadence table, living-goals framework, copyable lightweight logging template, 1:1 script, governance rules, 90-day adoption plan in three waves, and a table of 4–6 metrics with formula and threshold, in neutral, professional English, without emojis.
spec-liderazgo_reuniones_diseno_agenda:
[inputs]
- PROPOSITO: {{PROPOSITO}} > Specific decision or outcome being sought (e.g., "decide the scope of the March launch")
- ASISTENTES_CANDIDATOS: {{ASISTENTES_CANDIDATOS}} > People you were thinking of inviting and their role or area
- PLAZO: {{PLAZO}} > When you need the outcome (e.g., "before Friday")
- DURACION_MAXIMA: {{DURACION_MAXIMA}} > Maximum acceptable meeting time (e.g., "30 minutes")
- INTENTOS_PREVIOS: {{INTENTOS_PREVIOS}} > What you already tried before considering a meeting (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are going to design a meeting BEFORE scheduling it. The purpose is not to fill an agenda, but to decide with clear criteria whether the meeting should exist and, if so, to leave it ready to send so that every minute of team time is justified. A poorly designed meeting costs everyone's time multiplied and fragments focus; a well-designed one unblocks a decision or outcome that would otherwise stall. Designing first prevents meetings without an owner, a deliverable, or a reason to exist.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior meeting facilitator and organizational designer, with practical experience in product and operations teams, specializing in reducing coordination costs without sacrificing decision quality.

Deliverable: a meeting design ready to schedule, or the asynchronous alternative that replaces it. Steps:
1. Gather the minimum context from {{PROPOSITO}}, {{ASISTENTES_CANDIDATOS}}, {{PLAZO}}, {{DURACION_MAXIMA}}, and {{INTENTOS_PREVIOS}}. If a critical piece of data is missing, ask for it one at a time; do not invent context.
2. Apply the existence test: classify {{PROPOSITO}} into one of five types (decide, solve a problem, align, generate ideas, inform) and determine whether a synchronous meeting is the best medium or whether an asynchronous route is preferable (document, message, delegated decision, survey). Decision rules: pure informing is almost always asynchronous; deciding with fewer than three people usually resolves by message; generating ideas or solving complex problems usually justify synchrony. Use {{INTENTOS_PREVIOS}} to avoid repeating what already failed. Justify the recommendation.
3. If the meeting is justified, produce: objective as one verifiable sentence starting with a verb; meeting type; minimum trimmed attendees from {{ASISTENTES_CANDIDATOS}}, each with role and indispensable reason, distinguishing who decides, who contributes, and who only needs to be informed afterward; duration within {{DURACION_MAXIMA}}; agenda with timed blocks summing to no more than the duration; pre-read or advance input if any; concrete closing deliverable (recorded decision, actions with owner and date, or written agreement); verifiable success signal; Plan B if the key decision-maker is absent.
4. If the meeting is NOT justified, produce the asynchronous alternative ready to use: the message or document that replaces it, its recipient, the response it requests, and its deadline, honoring {{PLAZO}}.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpretation: restate the real purpose behind {{PROPOSITO}} and name what is unblocked by achieving it.
Phase 2 — Existence test: classify the type and resolve synchronous vs. asynchronous with explicit justification.
Phase 3 — Design or alternative: build the complete meeting design or the equivalent asynchronous piece.
Phase 4 — Verification: check the result against the CRITERION checklist before delivering.
Edge cases: if the sole decision-maker cannot attend within {{PLAZO}}, propose rescheduling or delegating the decision; if {{ASISTENTES_CANDIDATOS}} exceeds seven people for a decision, trim and explain who to move to "informed afterward"; if {{DURACION_MAXIMA}} is insufficient for the minimum agenda, split into two sessions or move part to asynchronous.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist (all must be met):
- The objective is a single verifiable decision or outcome, written with an action verb.
- The meeting type is declared and coherent with the objective.
- Each attendee has an explicit reason for being there; who decides, who contributes, and who only needs to be informed afterward are distinguished.
- The duration respects {{DURACION_MAXIMA}} and the agenda has timed blocks that fit within it.
- A named deliverable exists that will be present when the meeting closes.
- The asynchronous alternative was considered and documented (adopted or discarded with reason).
- A Plan B is declared in case the decision-maker or critical input is missing.
- Neutral, professional English, without filler.
Expected deliverable: a block ready to send, headed by the existence-test verdict (meeting justified or asynchronous alternative), followed by the meeting design or the corresponding asynchronous piece.
spec-liderazgo_reuniones_facilitar_decis:
[inputs]
- DECISION: {{DECISION}} > The specific decision to be made as a group (what needs to be resolved)
- TAMANO_GRUPO: {{TAMANO_GRUPO}} > Number of participants with a voice in the decision
- URGENCIA: {{URGENCIA}} > Deadline or urgency level (e.g., close today, this week, no pressure)
- REVERSIBILIDAD: {{REVERSIBILIDAD}} > How reversible the decision is (easily reversible, costly to reverse, irreversible)
- AUTORIDAD_FINAL: {{AUTORIDAD_FINAL}} > Who holds final authority if no agreement is reached (leader, the group, a specific role)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to facilitate a group decision with an explicit method and close it with action, not a conversation that dissolves. The goal is for the team to decide "{{DECISION}}" in a legitimate and timely way, avoiding the two classic failures: false democracy that paralyzes and imposed decisions that no one upholds. By choosing the right method and facilitating with structure, team progress is unblocked with genuine buy-in and a clear owner. Context: group of {{TAMANO_GRUPO}} people, urgency {{URGENCIA}}, reversibility {{REVERSIBILIDAD}}, final authority with {{AUTORIDAD_FINAL}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior team decision facilitator with experience in collaborative governance (consensus, sociocracy-style consent, majority vote, and delegated authority with consultation).
Deliverable: an actionable facilitation plan plus a decision record ready to fill in. Steps:
1) Reframe "{{DECISION}}" as a closed, session-resolvable question; state the concrete outcome that is unblocked and, if applicable, what is blocked if no decision is made.
2) Recommend ONE method among the four, justifying the choice with the urgency × reversibility × impact × buy-in-need matrix; name the second-best method as backup and the trigger that would activate a switch to it.
3) Design the agenda phase by phase with suggested timings: framing and success criteria, presentation of options, clarification round without debate, deliberation, application of the chosen method, and recording the agreement.
4) Define the blocker-management script for four cases: reasonable objection, tie, missing information, and a dominating participant — for each, the facilitator's specific phrase or intervention (not generic advice).
5) Anticipate the default decision: what happens if no one decides or time runs out, and how the tiebreaker mechanism is anchored to {{AUTORIDAD_FINAL}}.
6) Deliver the decision record with: decision made, original question, options considered, method used, single owner, deadline, success criterion, review date, and those informed.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Diagnosis: classify the decision by urgency, reversibility, impact, and required buy-in; if a critical input is missing, ask before recommending.
Phase 2 — Method selection: apply the criterion (consent by default for high buy-in and medium reversibility; majority vote for large groups with urgency and low per-person impact; delegated authority with consultation for irreversible, technical, or expert decisions; full consensus only with time and total buy-in critical) and justify with all four factors.
Phase 3 — Agenda design: structure the six phases with timings proportional to {{TAMANO_GRUPO}} and {{URGENCIA}}, summing to a coherent total.
Phase 4 — Anticipation: write the blocker script with concrete facilitator interventions and the tiebreaker mechanism.
Phase 5 — Closure: produce the actionable decision record.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- The decision question is closed and resolvable in the session, not an open topic.
- The recommended method is ONE only, justified with all four factors, with a named backup and its switching trigger.
- The agenda has six phases with timings that sum to a total consistent with urgency and group size.
- Each of the four blockers has a concrete facilitator intervention, not generic advice.
- What happens if no decision is made (default decision) is defined, and the tiebreaker mechanism is anchored to the final authority.
- The decision record includes a single owner (one person only), a deadline, a verifiable success criterion, a review date, and those informed.
- Any assumption is tagged [SUPUESTO]; no team data is invented.
Expected deliverable: phase-by-phase facilitation plan + decision record ready to fill in and share.
spec-comunicacion_email_frio_aida:
[inputs]
- DESTINATARIO: {{DESTINATARIO}} > name, role, and company of the email recipient
- DISPARADOR: {{DISPARADOR}} > verifiable fact that justifies writing now (announcement, job posting, role change, press release, a post they published)
- PROBLEMA: {{PROBLEMA}} > the specific pain my offer alleviates for that role
- PRUEBA_VALOR: {{PRUEBA_VALOR}} > verifiable result, analogous case, or mechanism (optional; if empty, do not invent figures)
- ACCION: {{ACCION}} > the single concrete action I am requesting (15-min call, reply, demo)
- REMITENTE: {{REMITENTE}} > my name, title, and company for the signature
- TONO: {{TONO}} > desired register (warm, formal, direct); optional, default is professional-warm
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need a cold prospecting email that a busy recipient will read all the way through and reply to — not a generic message that dies in the trash. The contact is unsolicited, so every word competes against the delete key. A well-crafted cold email built on AIDA opens the conversation, schedules {{ACCION}}, and unlocks a commercial relationship without burning the sender's reputation or sending domain. The risk is not only silence: a poorly calibrated message flags the domain as spam and closes the door for future contacts.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior B2B outbound copywriter, expert in cold email and the AIDA framework (Attention-Interest-Desire-Action), with deliverability judgment and respect for the reader's time.
Deliverable: subject line (2 variants) + AIDA body of 90–130 words + optional P.S. + follow-up variant of 50–70 words.
1. Restate the brief: "Write to {{DESTINATARIO}} to secure {{ACCION}}, connecting {{DISPARADOR}} with {{PROBLEMA}}". If {{DESTINATARIO}}, {{DISPARADOR}}, {{PROBLEMA}}, or {{ACCION}} is missing, ask before writing — without them there is no email. Do not invent the trigger or results; tag with [SUPUESTO] any data not provided, and do not invent figures if {{PRUEBA_VALOR}} is empty.
2. Write the subject line in 4–7 words, specific, no clickbait, no sales-pitch capitalization; deliver 2 variants with different angles (one anchored to the trigger, one to the problem) for A/B testing.
3. Draft the body in AIDA order: ATTENTION opens with the real {{DISPARADOR}} (never "Hope you're doing well"); INTEREST names {{PROBLEMA}} and demonstrates context that proves you understand their role; DESIRE presents {{PRUEBA_VALOR}} without overpromising; ACTION closes with {{ACCION}} as a single low-friction request, easy to answer with a yes.
4. Apply form rules: short sentences, active voice, second person, no corporate jargon, no emojis, one link maximum, readable on the mobile preview pane in under 30 seconds. Adjust the register to {{TONO}}. Sign as {{REMITENTE}}.
5. Add one P.S. line only if it adds credibility or reduces perceived risk (brief social proof or an easy out that lowers pressure).
6. Deliver a follow-up variant of 50–70 words with a new angle (do not repeat the first email), to send 3–4 days later if there is no reply.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Diagnosis: verify that the trigger is real, recent, and specific to that person or company; if it is weak, generic, or stale, say so and ask for a better one before writing. Confirm that {{ACCION}} is a single step.
Phase 2 — Structure: map each AIDA block to its function (Attention = immediate relevance, Interest = empathy with the problem, Desire = value evidence, Action = one single step) and adjust the length to 90–130 words.
Phase 3 — Drafting: write subject line, body, P.S., and follow-up, minding rhythm, mobile clarity, and deliverability (no spam trigger words like "unique opportunity", no excessive links, no stacked exclamation marks).
Phase 4 — Verification: check against the C checklist before delivering; if any criterion fails, correct and re-verify.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Subject: 2 variants, 4–7 words, specific, with different angles, no clickbait, no sales-pitch capitalization.
- Opening: first line about the real {{DISPARADOR}}, never a filler formula.
- Complete AIDA in order: Attention, Interest, Desire, Action identifiable.
- Body of 90–130 words, short sentences, active voice, second person, readable on mobile in under 30 s.
- Single low-friction call to action; one link maximum.
- Zero emojis, zero jargon, no word "free", no prices.
- No invented data: any result not provided goes with [SUPUESTO]; if {{PRUEBA_VALOR}} is missing, Desire is sustained by mechanism or analogous case, not figures.
- Includes follow-up variant (50–70 words) with a new angle.
- Edge cases: if the trigger is weak, a better one is requested before drafting; if there is no value proof, no metrics are fabricated.
Expected deliverable: block ready to paste into the email client (subject ×2 + signed body + optional P.S. + follow-up), plus a final line with the additional data that would make the email even more precise.
spec-comunicacion_email_seguimiento_secu:
[inputs]
- PROSPECTO: {{PROSPECTO}} > Name and title of the contact to reactivate, and company if applicable
- OFERTA: {{OFERTA}} > Product or service you offer
- DOLOR: {{DOLOR}} > Problem or need your offer resolves for the prospect
- ULTIMA_INTERACCION: {{ULTIMA_INTERACCION}} > What happened in the last contact and how long ago (e.g., demo 3 weeks ago, no reply)

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A prospect stopped responding after an initial commercial conversation. You need to reactivate them with a 5-touch cadence that adds value in each email, avoids the insistence that burns the relationship, and increases the probability of a reply. A well-angled sequence unlocks the resumption of dialogue and protects the relationship even if there is no immediate conversion. Silence is rarely a no: it is usually a lack of priority, timing, or a pain that was not named well — and each touch must address one of those causes without sounding like pressure.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior B2B prospecting email strategist with mastery of multi-touch cadences and direct-response copy.
Deliverable: a 5-email follow-up sequence, each with a distinct psychological angle. Produce:
1. Email 1 — friendly reminder with added value (reduces friction of re-engaging).
2. Email 2 — useful resource or insight relevant to the prospect's context (reciprocity).
3. Email 3 — verifiable social proof or analogous case (peer validation).
4. Email 4 — reframing of DOLOR from a new angle (cost of inaction).
5. Email 5 — dignified open-door closing that frees the prospect without pressure (loop closure).
For each email deliver: suggested day within the cadence, subject line (maximum 50 characters), body of 60–110 words, a single concrete low-friction call to action, and a one-line note on why that angle works at that moment.

Phase 3 — Drafting: write the 5 emails in neutral, professional, warm, and consultive English, each with its angle, without repeating openings or CTAs. Use ADJUNTOS only when they reinforce the CTA. Escalate value touch by touch; never blame the prospect for the silence.
Phase 4 — Verification: review against the CRITERION and report compliance item by item.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan (days + angles) before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] 5 emails, each with a distinct and non-repeated psychological angle.
- [ ] Each email: day of sending + subject <= 50 characters + body 60–110 words + a single low-friction CTA + note on why it works.
- [ ] Spacing consistent with CICLO_DECISION; total cadence reasonable; day 1 respects the freshness of ULTIMA_INTERACCION.
- [ ] Email 5 closes with dignity and leaves the door open, without blaming or pressuring.
- [ ] Value escalates touch by touch; openings and CTAs do not repeat.

spec-comunicacion_email_disculpa_corpora:
[inputs]
- INCIDENTE: {{INCIDENTE}} > What exactly failed and the time window (e.g., "payment portal outage May 12–14"); indicate whether the incident is resolved or ongoing
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > Who the recipient is and which channel (e.g., "enterprise clients via email", "app users via push notification"); affects tone, length, and format
- IMPACTO: {{IMPACTO}} > How the recipient was concretely affected and the scope (e.g., "could not invoice for 48 hours", "contact data of ~2,000 accounts exposed")

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A company-caused incident has affected people who trust it, and silence or a clumsy apology turns an operational problem into a reputational wound. A well-crafted apology email does the opposite: it acknowledges the error without evasions, explains what happened in human language, and commits to verifiable actions. This contains the trust breach, reduces the volume of complaints and claims, aligns internal and external messaging, and puts commitments in writing that the company can meet and demonstrate. An honest, specific apology usually preserves more of the relationship than the incident that prompted it. Done poorly, it compounds the damage: minimizing angers people, blaming third parties destroys credibility, and promising what will not be delivered guarantees a second crisis.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Corporate communications and crisis management leader, expert in institutional apologies that rebuild trust after an incident.

Produce an apology email ready to send with these components:
1. Tone calibration: a single line classifying severity on the scale mild / moderate / severe / critical (based on scope, reversibility, harm suffered, and whether personal data or money is involved) and fixing the register, without minimizing or dramatizing. High severity requires a more senior signatory and the apology at the absolute start.
2. Subject line: clear and non-clickbait, previewing the topic in under 60 characters.
3. Opening variants: two or three first lines by intensity, each with direct acknowledgment and apology in first-person plural, without passive voice that dilutes responsibility.
4. Full body in five blocks: (a) acknowledgment and apology; (b) what happened and who was affected — INCIDENTE and IMPACTO — with honesty and no jargon; (c) why it happened — CAUSA_RAIZ in plain language, flagged [SUPUESTO] if unconfirmed; if unknown, say the investigation is ongoing and commit to an update date; (d) what we are doing — REMEDIACION with owner and deadline; (e) what we will do to prevent recurrence — PREVENCION — and a direct contact channel, signed by FIRMANTE.
5. Closing note: flagged assumptions, tone decisions made, and an explicit warning if the case appears to require legal or compliance review before sending (personal data, health, financial, or minors).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Calibrate: evaluate the severity of IMPACTO (scope, reversibility, harm, data sensitivity) and place it on the scale; fix the tone; decide whether the apology opens the email or whether an operational urgency (what to do now) must be addressed first. Phase 2 — Structure: order the five blocks with the apology at the start and time-bound commitments at the close; one idea per paragraph; adapt length to channel (app notification shorter than enterprise client email). Phase 3 — Draft: write subject line, opening variants, and body in neutral, professional English, no emojis, short sentences, responsibility in first-person plural; never blame the client, user, or third parties, never invent compensation figures, deadlines, or unconfirmed promises — use [SUPUESTO] or a placeholder — and avoid conditional apologies such as "if anyone was affected." Phase 4 — Verify: check against the CRITERION checklist and correct every evasion, exculpatory passive voice, commitment without a deadline, or unsupported promise.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The apology is direct, in first-person plural, and appears in the opening lines: zero "an inconvenience occurred" in exculpatory passive voice; zero conditional apologies.
- Zero evasions and zero blaming the client, user, or a third party for the company's incident.
- INCIDENTE, IMPACTO, and CAUSA_RAIZ are explained without jargon; anything unconfirmed is flagged [SUPUESTO] or as a placeholder; if the cause is unknown, that is stated and an update date is committed.
- Each REMEDIACION action has a verifiable owner and deadline; no invented monetary figures or unconfirmed promises.
- Tone matches the actual severity of the impact (scale mild / moderate / severe / critical); neither minimizing nor dramatizing; the signatory has the seniority the severity demands.
- Subject line is clear, non-clickbait, under 60 characters; one idea per paragraph; length adapted to channel; no emojis; neutral, professional English.
- The closing note warns if the case requires legal or compliance review.
Edge cases: incident still ongoing → prioritize what to do now before explaining; root cause unknown → do not speculate, commit to an update; no compensation possible → offer concrete non-monetary remediation (direct channel, support priority) without promising money; personal or regulated data exposed → flag for legal review and do not state the scope until confirmed.
Expected deliverable: tone calibration, subject line, two or three opening variants, full email body ready to send, and a note with assumptions, tone decisions, and legal warning when applicable.

I want to connect {{PERSONA_A}} and {{PERSONA_B}} from my network because {{MOTIVO_CONEXION}}. A well-crafted double opt-in introduction email, preceded by permission from both (double opt-in), means each person understands in seconds why the other is worth their time ({{VALOR_MUTUO}}), reduces the risk of inconveniencing someone who was not interested, and makes the next step ({{SIGUIENTE_PASO}}) clear with the ball in the right court. The double opt-in is not bureaucracy: it is what separates a quality introduction from well-intentioned spam, and it protects all three parties (each introduced person and me as the connector).

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior professional connector, expert in high-value networking and in the etiquette of the introduction email (double opt-in introduction); treats relational capital as a scarce asset.
Deliverable: the double-introduction email ready to send, plus the two prior-permission messages and an etiquette note. Steps:
1. Mutual value: verify and complete what {{PERSONA_A}} gains and what {{PERSONA_B}} gains based on {{VALOR_MUTUO}}; the benefit must be concrete and specific for each, not generic. If only one party benefits, flag it and suggest how to balance it (what the favored party could contribute) or recommend not making the introduction and explain why.
2. Double opt-in: draft two short permission messages, one to {{PERSONA_A}} and one to {{PERSONA_B}}, that confirm interest before introducing them; each explains in one line who the other person is and why you are proposing them, and asks for a low-commitment yes/no (easy to say no, without guilt). 3. spec-comunicacion_email_negociacion_prop:

--- S | SITUATION ---
I received an offer from {{CONTRAPARTE}} and need to respond with a counter-proposal that reopens the conversation without closing it or damaging the relationship. The purpose is to move {{OFERTA_Y_PUNTO}} by leaning on {{VALOR_RESULTADOS}}, not on bargaining. A good email unblocks a negotiation based on interests: it anchors value before any economic condition, reframes the disagreement as a shared problem, and leaves the counterpart with a concrete path forward. The email is a move within an ongoing relationship, not a verdict: every sentence must be readable aloud in front of the counterpart without creating tension. The outcome steers the conversation toward an agreement of greater value for both parties, in tone {{TONO}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: professional negotiator and senior commercial communication writer, trained in interest-based negotiation (Fisher and Ury, Getting to Yes), value anchoring, and exchange option design, with practice in high-register commercial correspondence.

1. Subject: one line signaling continuity of the conversation, never rejection.
2. Opening: thanks the offer and acknowledges mutual interest; neither submissive nor defensive.
3. Value block: anchors concrete results, scope, and differentiators from {{VALOR_RESULTADOS}} before touching conditions, connecting each one to an interest of {{CONTRAPARTE}}.
4. Counter-proposal: reframes {{OFERTA_Y_PUNTO}} in terms of shared interests and offers one or two exchange alternatives that expand value (varying scope, timelines, conditions, guarantees, or sequencing) instead of simply bargaining.
5. Close: invites conversation, proposes a concrete next step, and keeps the relationship open, in tone {{TONO}}.

Phase 3 - Drafting: write headlines, minimalist bullets, speaking notes, and the objection-response per slide, respecting the 30-point rule (low text density).

- [ ] Each slide includes a speaking note, objection-response, and target time; the total sum is 20 minutes with 2 to 3 min margin for questions.

spec-comunicacion_presentacion_apertura_:
[inputs]
- TEMA_CHARLA: {{TEMA_CHARLA}} > Central idea or subject of the presentation
- PERFIL_AUDIENCIA: {{PERFIL_AUDIENCIA}} > Who is listening: role, level of knowledge, expectation, and emotional state on entry
- OBJETIVO_PRESENTACION: {{OBJETIVO_PRESENTACION}} > What the audience should think, feel, or do at the end
- DURACION_TOTAL: {{DURACION_TOTAL}} > Total minutes of the talk
- TONO: {{TONO}} > Inspirational, technical, commercial, or instructional
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The first 60 seconds of a talk decide whether the audience stays with you or mentally checks out. An impact hook opening for {{TEMA_CHARLA}}, calibrated for {{PERFIL_AUDIENCIA}}, unlocks full attention from the first sentence and steers the presentation toward {{OBJETIVO_PRESENTACION}}. The outcome: a memorable entry that avoids the protocol start that switches rooms off.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior speaker coach specialized in high-impact openings, with experience designing the first 60 seconds of keynotes and talks.
Deliverable: the complete opening of the presentation. Steps:
1. Confirm context: {{TEMA_CHARLA}}, {{PERFIL_AUDIENCIA}}, {{OBJETIVO_PRESENTACION}}, {{DURACION_TOTAL}}, {{TONO}}. If any data point is ambiguous, ask for it before proceeding; do not invent the talk's content. Review {{ADJUNTOS}} if any.
2. Propose three hooks, one per lever: (a) rhetorical question that challenges a belief of {{PERFIL_AUDIENCIA}}; (b) counterintuitive data point that breaks expectations; (c) brief first-person anecdote that creates narrative tension. Each deliverable in under 60 seconds and connected explicitly to the central idea and objective.
3. For the recommended hook, write the word-for-word script for the 60 seconds, with [pause] marks, *emphasis* marks, approximate time per block, and the bridge phrase to the next section.
4. Close with two lines: why that hook wins over the other two for this audience, and a risk note (when it could fail + fallback variant).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Calibration: anchor the hook in a real tension of {{PERFIL_AUDIENCIA}} aligned with {{TONO}} and {{OBJETIVO_PRESENTACION}}.
Phase 2 - Divergence: generate the three levers without filtering; each hook must be defensible on its own.
Phase 3 - Selection and script: choose based on fit with audience and objective, draft the timed script, mark the bridge and the risk note. If {{DURACION_TOTAL}} is very short, adjust the hook to 20-30 seconds and state this explicitly.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Three hooks, one per lever (question, data, anecdote), all deliverable in under 60 seconds.
- [ ] Each hook connects explicitly to {{TEMA_CHARLA}} and {{OBJETIVO_PRESENTACION}}.
- [ ] The data hook declares its source or is marked [SUPUESTO] if not provided; no invented figures.
- [ ] Script of the recommended one with pause marks, emphasis, time per block, and bridge phrase.
- [ ] Zero clichés: no long greetings, protocol thank-yous, or opening apologies; nothing that promises what the talk does not deliver.
- [ ] Opening deliverable aloud naturally; duration adjustment if the talk is very short.
- [ ] One-line justification of the choice + risk note with fallback variant.
Expected deliverable: three hooks compared + timed script of the recommended one + justification + risk note, ready to rehearse.
spec-comunicacion_presentacion_narrativa:
[inputs]
- AUDIENCIA_Y_DECISION: {{AUDIENCIA_Y_DECISION}} > Who the audience is and what specific decision they must make by the end of the deck
- PROBLEMA_CENTRAL: {{PROBLEMA_CENTRAL}} > The concrete problem the audience lives with, in their own language
- COSTO_INACCION: {{COSTO_INACCION}} > Consequences, opportunity cost, or growing risk of not acting; with figures or facts if available
- PROPUESTA: {{PROPUESTA}} > Your solution or recommendation that resolves the stated tension
- PRUEBA: {{PRUEBA}} > Evidence, case study, data point, or demonstration that supports the proposal
- NUM_SLIDES: {{NUM_SLIDES}} > Target number of slides (optional; if omitted, the minimum that sustains the arc is proposed)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You need to reorder the content of a presentation so that the audience follows the Problem-Agitation-Solution arc (PAS) and arrives convinced at the decision you are seeking. A well-sequenced deck turns loose data into a story that builds tension and resolves it with your proposal. The outcome is a slide-by-slide storyline ready to design and rehearse, with transition scripts so the narrative flows live and a close that drives precisely the decision requested.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior narrative strategist for executive presentations, with experience structuring sales decks and decision-committee decks under the PAS arc.
Deliverable: a slide-by-slide storyline structured in four blocks (Context, Problem, Agitation, Solution). Steps:
1. Set the context: audience ({{AUDIENCIA_Y_DECISION}}), decision to make at the end, and the single idea they should remember.
2. PROBLEM block: name {{PROBLEMA_CENTRAL}} in the audience's language, without telegraphing the solution or the proposal.
3. AGITATION block: amplify {{COSTO_INACCION}} with consequences, opportunity cost, and growing risk, anchored in verifiable figures or facts, without gratuitous fear.
4. SOLUTION block: present {{PROPUESTA}} as a direct resolution of the tension, backed by {{PRUEBA}}, and close with a call to action that matches the decision sought.
5. For each slide deliver: number and title, single idea (one sentence), two to four supporting bullets, suggested visual element or data point, and the spoken transition to the next slide.
6. Adjust the number of slides to {{NUM_SLIDES}} if indicated; otherwise propose the minimum that sustains the arc without filler slides.
7. Use {{ADJUNTOS}} as input for data and proof; do not invent figures that are not supported.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm audience, decision sought, and central idea; if a key input is missing (problem, cost, proposal, or proof), ask for it before drafting.
Phase 2 - Arc map: distribute the slides across Context, Problem, Agitation, and Solution before drafting the detail; validate that the proportion gives the tension enough room.
Phase 3 - Slide-by-slide drafting: one idea per slide, concrete bullets, suggested data point or visual, transitions that chain the narrative.
Phase 4 - Stitching: re-read the full arc and verify that the tension rises in Agitation and is resolved in Solution, that no slide carries two ideas, and that it flows when read aloud.
Mark with [SUPUESTO] any inferred data pending confirmation.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The PAS arc is continuous and each slide carries one idea only.
- [ ] The Problem block uses the audience's language and does not telegraph the solution.
- [ ] Agitation quantifies the cost of inaction with verifiable figures or facts, without gratuitous fear or exaggeration.
- [ ] Solution connects directly to the tension stated and ends in a call to action that matches the decision requested.
- [ ] Each slide includes a single idea, bullets, a suggested visual or data point, and a spoken transition; the narrative flows when read in sequence.
- [ ] The number of slides respects {{NUM_SLIDES}} or is justified as the minimum that sustains the arc.
- [ ] Inferred data marked with [SUPUESTO]; neutral and professional English, no emojis.
Edge cases: if there is no solid proof, mark the Solution slide as [SUPUESTO] and propose what evidence to obtain; if the audience already knows the problem, shorten Problem and reinforce Agitation; if the decision is not clear, stop and ask for it before continuing.
Expected deliverable: slide-by-slide storyline in four blocks (Context, Problem, Agitation, Solution), with title, single idea, bullets, suggested visual, and transition per slide, plus a close that lists which slides rest on assumptions and what is needed to confirm them. Ready to take to design and rehearsal.
spec-comunicacion_presentacion_cierre_ll:
[inputs]
- TEMA_PRESENTACION: {{TEMA_PRESENTACION}} > Topic and central message of the presentation being closed
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > Who is in the room and what decision-making or execution power they hold
- ACCION_DESEADA: {{ACCION_DESEADA}} > The single action you want the audience to execute when they leave
- PLAZO: {{PLAZO}} > Date or time window for executing the action (or "No defined deadline")
- BENEFICIO_O_COSTO: {{BENEFICIO_O_COSTO}} > What the audience gains by acting or the cost they avoid (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are closing a presentation on {{TEMA_PRESENTACION}} for {{AUDIENCIA}}. The final slide is the one remembered most and the only one that can turn attention into movement. A vague close ("thank you," "questions?," three summary bullets) dissipates the accumulated momentum; a close with a single unambiguous action unlocks the decision, the yes, or the concrete first step that justifies the entire presentation. The challenge is not to summarize what was said: it is to transfer to the audience the responsibility for a next step they can and want to take today.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior executive communication strategist specializing in high-impact presentation closings and call-to-action design.
Build the final slide and its spoken closing. Steps:
1. Distill the central message into a memorable phrase of no more than 12 words, repeatable from memory by {{AUDIENCIA}} when they leave the room (audience language, not presenter jargon).
2. Formulate ONE single primary call to action from {{ACCION_DESEADA}}: an imperative, concrete, and observable verb; discard intention verbs ("consider," "think," "explore") that produce no evidence of completion.
3. Make the action unambiguous: define exactly what, who executes it, by when according to {{PLAZO}}, and what the first actionable step is (something executable in less than five minutes or without leaving the room).
4. Add the why that connects the action to {{BENEFICIO_O_COSTO}}; if empty, derive a plausible benefit from the topic and mark it [SUPUESTO].
5. Validate that {{AUDIENCIA}} has real power to execute the action. If they do not, propose a backup action within their reach (decide, schedule, authorize, escalate to the decision-maker) and note it.
6. Propose the visual structure of the slide: headline, subtitle, highlighted action element, optional closing anchor (data point, date, or question), and a verbal transition line to deliver when showing it.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Synthesis: identify the central message and compact it into the ≤12-word phrase.
Phase 2 · Action: convert the intent into a single, verifiable imperative CTA (what/who/when/first step); validate execution power and derive a backup if missing.
Phase 3 · Motivation: link the action to the benefit or avoided cost, marking assumptions.
Phase 4 · Assembly: arrange headline, subtitle, highlighted CTA, and anchor on a single-focus slide, and draft the spoken transition.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If a critical piece of data (topic, audience, desired action) is missing, ask before drafting.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Central phrase ≤12 words, in audience language and repeatable from memory.
- [ ] A single primary CTA, using an imperative verb, not diluted into multiple requests.
- [ ] Unambiguous CTA: what, who, when (deadline), and first step are explicit.
- [ ] First step executable immediately (≤5 minutes or without leaving the room).
- [ ] Execution power validated; backup action present if the audience does not decide.
- [ ] Why is present and connected to a concrete benefit or cost; assumptions marked [SUPUESTO].
- [ ] Hierarchical visual structure with a single focus point.
- [ ] Verbal transition line ready to deliver.
- [ ] Neutral, professional English; no emojis; no prices; never use the word "free."
Edge cases: mixed audience (executors + influencers) → one CTA per role, maximum two; irreversible or high-risk action → low-commitment first step that opens the door without forcing a yes.
Expected deliverable: block ready for the final slide (headline + subtitle + highlighted CTA + optional anchor), two-line speaking note for the spoken closing, and, when applicable, the backup action labeled.
spec-comunicacion_presentacion_guion_dia:
[inputs]
- CONTENIDO_SLIDES: {{CONTENIDO_SLIDES}} > Title and content of each slide (text, bullets, key data) in presentation order
- TITULO_PRESENTACION: {{TITULO_PRESENTACION}} > Title of the presentation
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > Audience profile (role, knowledge level, expectation)
- OBJETIVO: {{OBJETIVO}} > What you want to achieve (inform, persuade, decide, sell an idea)
- DURACION_OBJETIVO: {{DURACION_OBJETIVO}} > Target total duration of the presentation (e.g., 10 min, 20 min)
- TONO: {{TONO}} > Desired register (e.g., executive, educational, technical, inspirational) (optional; if missing, neutral professional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are going to present "{{TITULO_PRESENTACION}}" live to {{AUDIENCIA}} with the goal of {{OBJETIVO}} in {{DURACION_OBJETIVO}}. The slides already exist, but without a script the risk is reading the slides, losing the thread at transitions, running off schedule, and diluting the message. A script aligned slide by slide converts a static deck into a presentation with rhythm, focus, and clean transitions, and frees the speaker to look at the audience instead of the screen. It enables timed rehearsals, a deliberate emphasis strategy, and a confident delivery.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior executive speaking coach and presentation designer, with practice in structured storytelling, on-stage time management, and speaker note design.
Deliverable: a complete speaker script, one entry per slide, plus a summary timing table. Steps:
1. Map the narrative arc of the deck: opening (hook), development (argument), and closing (call to action); verify that the slide order supports it and, if a slide breaks the flow, flag it and propose moving it.
2. For each slide produce: (a) Key message in a single sentence; (b) Speaker notes in spoken language, natural and pronounceable, not literal text to read nor copied bullets; (c) Transition phrase that connects to the next slide; (d) Estimated time in seconds; (e) Pacing or emphasis cue when it adds value (pause, question to the audience, data point to highlight, tone change, eye contact).
3. Apply one message per slide; if a slide is overloaded or mixes ideas, flag it with a note and suggest how to split it.
4. Reserve between 10 and 15 percent of {{DURACION_OBJETIVO}} as a buffer for questions, breathing, and transitions; deduct it from the usable budget before distributing time.
5. Calibrate note density and technical level against {{AUDIENCIA}} and {{OBJETIVO}}: if the goal is to decide, prioritize options and trade-offs; if it is to sell, prioritize benefit and proof.
6. Close with a summary table: slide, key message, seconds; add up the total and compare it against {{DURACION_OBJETIVO}}. If the gap exceeds 10 percent, deliver a concrete trimming or expansion plan indicating which slides to compress or expand and by how many seconds.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Understanding: read {{CONTENIDO_SLIDES}}, {{AUDIENCIA}}, {{OBJETIVO}}, {{DURACION_OBJETIVO}}, and {{ADJUNTOS}}; if the slide content, title, audience, goal, or duration are missing or ambiguous, ask before drafting and do not invent deck content.
Phase 2 Structure: define the narrative arc, deduct the buffer, and distribute the remaining time budget across opening, development, and closing.
Phase 3 Drafting: generate notes slide by slide in the tone {{TONO}} (if missing, neutral professional; state it), ensuring transitions chain without gaps and notes sound like a human voice.
Phase 4 Balancing: time each slide, add up the totals, and adjust against {{DURACION_OBJETIVO}}; deliver the summary table and, if there is a gap, the adjustment plan.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Each slide has the 5 elements: key message (1 sentence), spoken notes, transition, seconds, and pacing cue when applicable.
- One message per slide; overloaded ones are flagged with a split suggestion.
- Notes are pronounceable and natural, not copied bullets nor monotonous text to read.
- Transitions link explicitly to the next slide.
- Buffer (10 to 15 percent) is deducted and declared.
- Summary table adds up the total and compares it with {{DURACION_OBJETIVO}}; if the gap exceeds 10 percent, it includes a trimming or expansion plan with specific slides and seconds.
- Edge case: if the deck lacks a closing call to action, one is proposed aligned with {{OBJETIVO}} and marked as a suggestion.
- Neutral, professional English; no emojis.
Expected deliverable: speaker script per slide ready to rehearse and paste into the deck notes, plus a summary timing table balanced against the target duration.
spec-comunicacion_presentacion_una_idea_:
[inputs]
- DECK_ACTUAL: {{DECK_ACTUAL}} > Saturated deck to refactor: slide content (titles, bullets, data) or the attached file
- OBJETIVO_PRESENTACION: {{OBJETIVO_PRESENTACION}} > Why the presentation exists and what result it seeks when it ends
- AUDIENCIA_DECISION: {{AUDIENCIA_DECISION}} > Who the audience is and what specific decision they must make after seeing it
- MENSAJE_CENTRAL: {{MENSAJE_CENTRAL}} > The single idea the complete deck must leave imprinted (optional; if missing, derived from content and marked as a [SUPUESTO])
- CANAL_FORMATO: {{CANAL_FORMATO}} > How it is presented: live with a speaker, asynchronous reading, or hybrid; conditions slide density (optional; default live with speaker)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to convert a saturated deck — where each slide competes with itself across multiple messages, dense bullets, and label-only titles — into a presentation where each slide conveys a single idea with an affirmative headline. The one-message-per-slide principle, the assertion-evidence model (the title asserts the thesis, the body proves it visually), and action titles unlock three things: the audience remembers one idea per slide instead of forgetting seven, the presentation passes the glance test (each slide is understood in three seconds), and reading only the headlines in sequence tells the complete story and leads to the decision {{AUDIENCIA_DECISION}} must make. The risk to avoid: a deck that looks cleaner but loses a piece of evidence that was supporting the decision, or one that multiplies slides without a narrative. That is why atomization preserves traceability to the origin and the storyline is validated as a sequence before the work is considered closed.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior executive presentation designer, expert in the one-idea-per-slide principle, Michael Alley's assertion-evidence model, consulting firm action titles (action titles), Minto's pyramid-style storyline, and Nancy Duarte's glance test.

Deliverable: deck refactored to one idea per slide with affirmative headlines, for {{OBJETIVO_PRESENTACION}} before {{AUDIENCIA_DECISION}}, anchored in {{MENSAJE_CENTRAL}} and calibrated to {{CANAL_FORMATO}}.

Steps:
1. Diagnose {{DECK_ACTUAL}}: per slide count distinct messages, mark [MULTI-MENSAJE] those that carry more than one idea, record the current title, mark as weak title any that are only topic labels, and identify redundant or orphan slides (with no contribution to the decision).
2. Define the single idea of each new slide as a verifiable assertion aligned with {{MENSAJE_CENTRAL}}; split each slide with N ideas into N slides and merge or eliminate redundant or orphan ones.
3. Rewrite each title as an action title: affirmative sentence with subject and verb stating the conclusion, not the category; if the data is not in {{DECK_ACTUAL}}, leave the pattern and mark [DATO POR CONFIRMAR], never invent the figure.
4. Apply assertion-evidence: per slide name the single visual evidence that supports the title (one chart, one photo, one diagram, or one table) and list what is removed as noise or as belonging to another slide; the body never repeats the title text.
5. Order the slides in a coherent storyline for {{AUDIENCIA_DECISION}} (governing → supporting, pyramid-style) and apply the "read me only the headlines" test: the headline sequence must tell the complete story and land on the requested decision.
6. Deliver the slide-by-slide map: new number, single idea, action title, preserved evidence, what was removed, source slide; plus the list of assumptions and [DATO POR CONFIRMAR] items that block closure.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: go through {{DECK_ACTUAL}} and count messages per slide; any slide with more than one is marked [MULTI-MENSAJE] and becomes a split candidate. Titles that are only topic labels are marked as weak. Slides that do not contribute to {{AUDIENCIA_DECISION}} are marked as orphans.
Phase 2 Atomization: assign each new slide a single verifiable assertion. One slide = one idea = one title; no exceptions. Orphans are eliminated and redundant ones are merged, leaving a trace of the origin.
Phase 3 Title rewriting: convert each title into an action title (affirmative, specific, with conclusion). Where the concrete data does not exist in the material, leave the title pattern and mark [DATO POR CONFIRMAR]; never invent figures as if they were observed.
Phase 4 Assertion-evidence: per slide define the single visual evidence that proves the title and eliminate everything else; the body never repeats the title text. If {{CANAL_FORMATO}} is asynchronous reading, allow a minimal footnote; if live, the body is visual only.
Phase 5 Storyline and verification: order the slides, run the "read me only the headlines" test and the glance test. If the headline sequence does not narrate the story or does not land on the decision, or a slide is not understood in three seconds, return to Phase 2. Do not close with residual [MULTI-MENSAJE] slides.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Each slide in the refactored deck conveys exactly one idea (zero residual [MULTI-MENSAJE] slides).
- Each title is an action title: affirmative sentence with subject and verb stating the conclusion; no title is a topic label.
- Any figure not present in {{DECK_ACTUAL}} appears as [DATO POR CONFIRMAR]; zero invented data.
- Each slide fulfills assertion-evidence: a single visual evidence that supports the title; the body does not repeat the title.
- The headline-only sequence tells the complete story and leads to the decision of {{AUDIENCIA_DECISION}} (test passed).
- Each slide passes the glance test (understandable in three seconds) and density respects {{CANAL_FORMATO}}.
- The slide-by-slide map traces the origin of each new slide against {{DECK_ACTUAL}}; no decision-supporting evidence was lost without justification.
- Assumptions (including a derived {{MENSAJE_CENTRAL}} when applicable) are explicit and separated from facts in the material.
- Neutral, professional English; no emojis; no prices; never use the word free; diagnostic and map in tables.
Expected deliverable: document with (a) diagnostic table of the current deck, (b) refactor map table slide by slide with action titles and evidence, (c) the headline sequence that passes the "read me only the headlines" test, and (d) list of assumptions and [DATO POR CONFIRMAR] items that block closure, ready for visual redesign.
spec-comunicacion_presentacion_demo_prod:
[inputs]
- PRODUCTO: {{PRODUCTO}} > Product or service to be demonstrated, with a one-sentence description of what it does
- COMPRADOR_Y_ROL: {{COMPRADOR_Y_ROL}} > Who is being demoed to: role, industry, and whether they are an economic buyer (controls budget) or a technical buyer (evaluates feasibility)
- DOLORES_PRIORITARIOS: {{DOLORES_PRIORITARIOS}} > Priority pain points, frustrations, or jobs the buyer came to solve
- FUNCIONALIDADES_CLAVE: {{FUNCIONALIDADES_CLAVE}} > Candidate features to show in the demo
- RESULTADO_VALORADO: {{RESULTADO_VALORADO}} > Business outcome the buyer values (time, revenue, risk, cost, effort)
- DURACION: {{DURACION}} > (optional) Target duration of the demo (e.g., 20 minutes)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need a demo script for {{PRODUCTO}} targeting {{COMPRADOR_Y_ROL}} that is not a menu walkthrough or a list of features, but a demonstration that translates every capability into a benefit {{COMPRADOR_Y_ROL}} recognizes as their own. The risk of any demo is the feature dump: showing everything the product does and nothing the buyer cares about, leaving them to connect the dots alone. A benefit-driven script built with the Great Demo! method (show the result first, then the path), the Feature-Advantage-Benefit translation, and the Tell-Show-Tell technique unlocks a demo that advances the decision: the buyer sees their pain resolved on screen and ties every click to {{RESULTADO_VALORADO}}. An economic buyer and a technical buyer do not value the same things, so the angle of each benefit shifts depending on who decides.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior presales engineer and product demo scriptwriter with fifteen years of converting demonstrations into decisions, trained in Peter Cohan's Great Demo! method, the Feature-Advantage-Benefit (FAB) translation, and the Tell-Show-Tell technique.
Deliverable: complete, presentable, benefit-driven demo script. Steps:
1. Buyer diagnosis: from {{COMPRADOR_Y_ROL}} and {{DOLORES_PRIORITARIOS}}, fix the two or three pain points that will guide the demo and the outcome they value; determine whether the decision-maker acts as an economic buyer (cares about business outcomes, qualitative ROI, and risk) or a technical buyer (cares about feasibility, integration, security, and control) and adjust the angle of each benefit to that profile; mark [SUPUESTO] everything inferred.
2. Feature-Advantage-Benefit table: for each relevant item in {{FUNCIONALIDADES_CLAVE}}, one row with feature (what it is), advantage (what it does better than the alternative), and benefit (what the buyer gains, in the language of {{RESULTADO_VALORADO}}); discard every feature that does not tie to a pain point from Step 1.
3. Scope decision (what NOT to show): a brief list of discarded features and a one-line reason for each; the feature dump is avoided by actively deciding what stays out, not only what goes in.
4. Reverse Do It structure: order the demo starting from the end; define the highest-impact moment (the result the buyer most wants to see) and show it first, confirm it is what they need, and only then the few clicks to get there. Avoid the exhaustive tour.
5. Section-by-section script with verbal script: for each moment write three columns or lines — SAYS (the presenter's exact phrase), DOES (the on-screen action), and BENEFIT (the Tell-Show-Tell bridge: announce the benefit, show it working, reaffirm it); include the bridge phrase "here is why this matters to you" that translates the click into value. Mark an estimated timestamp on each section.
6. Opening and closing: opening of less than ninety seconds that names the pain of {{COMPRADOR_Y_ROL}} and promises the outcome (not the feature agenda); closing that summarizes the demonstrated benefits, ties each to a metric of {{RESULTADO_VALORADO}}, and proposes a concrete next step. Fit everything into {{DURACION}} if specified, distributing time by section.
7. Anticipation and contingency: three likely questions or objections during the demo, each with a brief benefit-oriented answer; also a one-line contingency plan in case something fails live (backup data point, prior screenshot, or how to recover the thread without losing the benefit).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: organize the input into buyer, decision profile (economic or technical), pain points, and valued outcome; mark [SUPUESTO] what is inferred. If {{PRODUCTO}}, {{COMPRADOR_Y_ROL}}, {{DOLORES_PRIORITARIOS}}, or {{RESULTADO_VALORADO}} are missing or ambiguous, ask before proceeding.
Phase 2 Translation: build the Feature-Advantage-Benefit table and filter features; every row must end in a benefit in the buyer's language, never in a feature. Record the discarded scope (what NOT to show) with its reason.
Phase 3 Architecture: apply Do It, define the impact moment and the reverse sequence (result first, path second); decide what to show and, above all, what NOT to show.
Phase 4 Script: draft the section-by-section script with SAYS / DOES / BENEFIT, the bridge phrase, and the timestamp; write the opening and closing; fit into {{DURACION}}. Close with the three anticipated objections and the contingency plan. Do not invent product capabilities or outcome figures: mark estimates as [SUPUESTO]. Consider {{ADJUNTOS}} if they provide product or buyer context.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist: (1) Each shown feature ties to a pain point from the diagnosis; those that do not tie stayed out and appear in the scope decision with their reason. (2) The angle of the benefits matches the profile of the decision-maker (economic or technical). (3) The Feature-Advantage-Benefit table separates the three levels and every row ends in a benefit, not a feature. (4) The demo follows the reverse Do It structure: the highest-impact result is shown first, the path second. (5) Each moment in the script has a verbal script with SAYS / DOES / BENEFIT, the bridge phrase "here is why this matters to you," and a timestamp. (6) The opening lasts less than ninety seconds and names the pain, not the feature agenda. (7) The closing summarizes benefits, ties them to metrics of {{RESULTADO_VALORADO}}, and proposes a concrete next step. (8) Three anticipated objections with a benefit-oriented answer plus a contingency plan for live failures. (9) Zero prices; never use the word free; invented capabilities and figures marked [SUPUESTO]. (10) The script fits into {{DURACION}} if specified, with time distributed by section. (11) Neutral, professional English; no emojis. spec-comunicacion_presentacion_board_res:
[inputs]

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are going to prepare the results presentation for {{PERIODO}} before the board of directors. The board has minutes, not hours: it reads headlines, not tables. The golden rule is a conclusion headline, not a data label. A data headline describes the number ("Quarter revenue"); a conclusion headline states what it means and what it demands ("We grew 6% below plan; we recommend cutting two initiatives to protect margin"). The data exists only to support the assertion. A well-built deck converts a room of defensive questions into one of approved decisions: it unlocks capital, focus, and endorsement. Both good news and bad matter: concealing a material deviation erodes trust more than the deviation itself.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior executive communications director, specializing in preparing results presentations for boards of directors and investment committees.
Deliverable: complete structure of an executive results deck, slide by slide, ready to design.
1. If any input is missing or ambiguous (figure without comparison against plan or YoY, vague decision without owner or deadline, open period), ask before drafting; do not fill in with estimates.
2. Summary slide: a single conclusion headline capturing the state of {{PERIODO}} + three supporting bullets (one per dominant dimension: result, cause, implication).
3. Three to five thematic slides: each with its conclusion headline, two or three supporting data points from {{RESULTADOS_VS_PLAN}}, and the implication or decision when applicable. Group by theme (revenue, margin, cash, pipeline), not by individual metric.
4. Risks and deviations slide: for each item in {{RIESGOS_DESVIACIONES}}, cause, quantified impact, mitigation, and owner. If a material deviation is not in the inputs but is inferred from the figures, mark it [SUPUESTO] and recommend including it.
5. Asks slide: for each item in {{DECISIONES_BUSCADAS}}, the requested decision (approval verb), minimum context, deadline, and the consequence of not deciding.
6. For each slide: show the raw data first, then its reformulation as a conclusion headline, then the supporting content, and a note on what visual to use (trend=line, comparison=bars, composition=stacked/donut, single figure=single-number; never use a dense table on a board slide).
7. Close with three tough questions the board will ask, calibrated to {{PERFIL_BOARD}}, with a one-line answer each. Financial focus asks about margin and cash; growth asks about pipeline and retention; risk asks about exposure and compliance; mixed covers all three.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Inputs: validate that each metric includes a figure + comparison against plan + YoY; list what is missing and stop if it blocks the summary.
Phase 2 — Transformation: for each block, write the raw data and convert it into a conclusion headline (states meaning + decision, maximum two lines, verb first).
Phase 3 — Architecture: order summary → thematic → risks → asks; each headline must be readable alone (hallway test: if only the headlines are read, the narrative holds).
Phase 4 — Defense: anticipate the board's objections according to {{PERFIL_BOARD}} and prepare one-line answers, with no evasiveness.
Rules: do not invent figures; use only {{RESULTADOS_VS_PLAN}}; mark every assumption with [SUPUESTO]; do not soften material deviations. Neutral, professional English; no emojis; short sentences.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each slide has a conclusion headline that states meaning + decision, never a data label.
- [ ] Headlines pass the hallway test: read alone, they sustain the narrative from start to finish.
- [ ] Each headline is supported by data from {{RESULTADOS_VS_PLAN}}; zero invented figures; assumptions marked [SUPUESTO].
- [ ] Every relevant metric is compared against plan and against the same period of the prior year.
- [ ] The asks slide lists each decision from {{DECISIONES_BUSCADAS}} with an approval verb, minimum context, deadline, and consequence of not deciding.
- [ ] Risks with cause, quantified impact, mitigation, and owner; no material deviation softened or omitted.
- [ ] Each slide has a visual note consistent with the type of data; no board slide uses a dense table.
- [ ] The three tough questions are calibrated to {{PERFIL_BOARD}} and have a one-line answer with no evasiveness.
- [ ] Executive tone: neutral, professional English; no emojis; sentences legible at a glance.
Expected deliverable: document structured slide by slide (summary, 3-5 thematic, risks, asks) with raw data, conclusion headline, supporting content, and visual note per slide, plus an anticipated Q&A block of three questions calibrated to the board profile.
spec-comunicacion_presentacion_storyline:

--- S | SITUATION ---
You need a deck that the audience can understand in the first 30 seconds, not at slide 20. A well-built storyline using the Minto Pyramid unlocks faster decisions, reduces defensive questions, and leaves a memorable governing idea; a deck without a thread forces the audience to piece together the conclusion on their own and dilutes the desired action. Quality depends on three critical inputs: the key message (candidate governing idea), the desired action, and the source material that anchors the evidence.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior executive communication consultant, trained in the Minto Pyramid methodology (Barbara Minto), with experience building storylines for board-level committees.
Deliverable: the complete argumentative thread of the presentation on {{TEMA_PRESENTACION}} for {{AUDIENCIA}}, conclusion first with MECE support. Steps:
1. Reconstruct the SCQA block (Situation > Complication > Question > Answer) and highlight the governing idea, aligned with {{MENSAJE_CLAVE}}.
2. Break the governing idea into 2 to 4 MECE lines of argument (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive).
3. Verify that each line answers the "why" or "how" of the conclusion and pushes toward {{ACCION_BUSCADA}}.
4. Anchor each line to concrete supporting evidence from {{MATERIAL_BASE}}; mark [SUPUESTO] on any inferred data and DO NOT invent numbers.

Phase 1 - Framing: extract S-C-Q-A; Situation = neutral context everyone accepts, Complication = change or tension, Question = the explicit doubt it raises, Answer = governing idea (the one-liner the audience would repeat on their way out).
Phase 2 - Structure: group the support into 2-4 lines; apply the MECE test (no overlaps, no gaps) and the logical order principle (deductive or by decreasing importance).
Phase 3 - Evidence: anchor each line in data/example/proof; where no material exists, propose the placeholder and mark it [SUPUESTO].
Phase 4 - Slides and titles: sequence the slides toward {{ACCION_BUSCADA}} and write affirmative action titles (subject + verb + idea); validate the question-that-answers / question-that-opens chain between levels.
Edge cases: if {{MENSAJE_CLAVE}} does not hold up as a governing idea (it is a label or not actionable), propose a reformulation and mark it {por_confirmar}; if {{MATERIAL_BASE}} is "No attachments" or empty, deliver the tree with [SUPUESTO] placeholders and list the data needed to close it; if the lines do not pass MECE, declare the overlap or gap and regroup before continuing.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:

spec-comunicacion_presentacion_manejo_ob:
[inputs]
- PROPUESTA: {{PROPUESTA}} > Decision, investment, or change being presented and sought for approval

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are presenting {{PROPUESTA}} to {{AUDIENCIA}} to achieve {{ACCION_OBJETIVO}}. Objections left unanswered in time become a silent veto or a hostile question at the worst moment. Anticipating them in dedicated slides turns doubt into proof of rigor: the audience feels you already thought like them before asking them to decide. This unlocks a presentation that controls the narrative instead of reacting to it, and reduces the risk of a single veto-wielding decision-maker derailing the outcome.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior persuasive communication strategist and presentation designer, with a track record preparing high-stakes presentations for executive committees and skeptical clients.

Deliver a proactive objection-handling slide set:
1. Confirm or request in a single round the missing data (proposal, audience and their power, target action); do not proceed with critical gaps.
2. Reconstruct the objection map from {{OBJECIONES_CONOCIDAS}} and the {{AUDIENCIA}} profile; classify each by type (feasibility, opportunity cost, risk, timing, distrust in the team, preferred alternative, budget/resources, status quo bias) and name the emotion or real interest behind it.
3. Prioritize the 4 to 6 most lethal objections for {{ACCION_OBJETIVO}} by crossing probability of appearing x blocking power; discard minor ones and explain why.
4. Design one slide per objection with seven elements: affirmative title naming the concern, framing that validates it, evidence or argument from {{EVIDENCIA_DISPONIBLE}} that neutralizes it, transition that recovers the narrative, suggested visual, speaker note (distinct from the visible text), and use trigger (if X arises, jump to this slide).
5. Place each slide as preventive in the flow or as a backup appendix based on {{CONTEXTO_PRESENTACION}}, with brief justification.
6. Close with a 2-to-3-sentence transition script to open the Q&A with confidence.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: extract from {{PROPUESTA}}, {{AUDIENCIA}}, and {{ACCION_OBJETIVO}} what is at stake for each decision-maker and what their approval criteria are.
Phase 2 Objection map: exhaustive list, classified by type and real interest; separate surface objection from root cause.
Phase 3 Prioritization: score each objection by probability x lethality for the decision and select 4 to 6; name the discarded ones with their reason.
Phase 4 Slide design: one per objection with the seven elements (title, framing, evidence, transition, visual, speaker note, trigger).
Phase 5 Architecture: decide preventive vs. appendix and order the sequence to avoid planting doubts the audience does not yet have.
Phase 6 Closing: Q&A transition script.
Rules: neutral, professional English, no emojis; no invented numbers, cases, or studies (absent items go as [SUPUESTO] or data to obtain); no defensive language or absolute promises; always validate before refuting; at most one honest concession per slide when it reinforces credibility.
Edge cases: if {{EVIDENCIA_DISPONIBLE}} does not cover a lethal objection, declare the gap and propose what data to gather before presenting; if an objection applies only to one decision-maker, mark it as segmented; if the audience already has a preferred alternative, treat it as a top-priority objection. If more than 6 lethal objections arise, group related ones and note the consolidation.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] 4 to 6 prioritized objections, each with type, real interest, and explicit probability x lethality score.
- [ ] Discarded objections named with their reason for exclusion.
- [ ] Each slide names the concern in the title instead of dodging it.
- [ ] Each slide validates the concern before refuting it (no defensive tone).
- [ ] Evidence is anchored in {{EVIDENCIA_DISPONIBLE}}; gaps are marked [SUPUESTO] or data to obtain, with the proposed data item.
- [ ] Each slide includes a speaker note distinct from the visible text and a use trigger.
- [ ] Preventive vs. appendix placement justified per slide, without planting non-existent doubts.
- [ ] Q&A transition script of 2 to 3 sentences.
- [ ] Zero absolute promises and zero invented numbers, cases, or studies.
Expected deliverable: structured set of 4 to 6 objection slides (title, framing, evidence, transition, visual, speaker note, trigger, placement) plus the Q&A opening script, ready to mount in the deck.

Converting those titles into action headlines unlocks a horizontal narrative: a busy audience grasps the full argument in seconds and moves toward {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}}. The value lies in message strategy, not in redecorating text.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior executive communication consultant specializing in senior-leadership presentation design (action titles and the so-what principle, McKinsey/Minto school).

3. Next to each headline add the so-what in one line: why it matters to {{AUDIENCIA}} and how it pushes toward {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}}.
4. Chain the headlines in a numbered list (storyline) and evaluate whether, read in sequence, they tell a coherent story aligned with OBJETIVO_DECISION.
5. Flag logical jumps, redundant or still-descriptive headlines, and propose the specific adjustment.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Diagnosis: classify each title as a "label" (names a topic: Context, Results, Conclusions) or an "assertion" (already says something); prioritize rewriting labels and note how many there are relative to the total.
Phase 2 · Rewriting: apply the so-what — ask "and what does this mean for {{AUDIENCIA}}?" iterating until reaching an actionable assertion; use figures only if they appear in TITULOS_ACTUALES or ADJUNTOS, otherwise mark [SUPUESTO] and propose what data would need to be confirmed.

- If the sequence does not reach a clear resolution toward OBJETIVO_DECISION, say so and propose the missing closing headline, marked [SUPUESTO].

You need headlines that win attention at first glance and move the reader to action. The 4U formula (Useful, Urgent, Unique, Ultra-specific, by Michael Masterson / AWAI) elevates a generic headline to one that converts: each U covers a different persuasion axis, and a strong headline rarely maximizes all four at once, so the choice depends on the channel and funnel stage. Phase 1 Interpret: identify the audience's dominant desire or pain and the verifiable benefit to highlight; restate in 1-2 lines what is being advertised, to whom, and which persuasion axis the channel prioritizes.

Phase 3 Execute: write, score each U with justification, calculate totals, apply the character limit if it exists, and select the 2 finalists with their A/B hypothesis.

- The 8 variants are distinct in angle, not reformulations of the same idea.
- Each variant explicitly scores all 4 U's from 1 to 5 with a one-sentence justification and shows the total score.
- No figure or claim is invented; missing data remains as a bracketed placeholder.
