spec-comunicacion_redaccion_carta_recome:
[inputs]
- RECOMENDANTE: {{RECOMENDANTE}} > Signatory: name, title, and organization (defines the authority and weight of the reference)
- RELACION_Y_TIEMPO: {{RELACION_Y_TIEMPO}} > How the recommender knows the person and for how long (e.g. "direct supervisor, 3 years"); greater closeness and duration increase credibility
- NOMBRE_RECOMENDADO: {{NOMBRE_RECOMENDADO}} > Person being recommended
- DESTINO: {{DESTINO}} > Position, program, or purpose of the letter and, if known, its recipient (guides which strength to prioritize)
- CUALIDADES: {{CUALIDADES}} > 2–3 core qualities to highlight (more than 3 dilutes the message)
- EVIDENCIAS: {{EVIDENCIAS}} > Anecdotes, measurable achievements, or observed behaviors supporting each quality (ideally one per quality)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A recommendation letter decides real opportunities (employment, admission, scholarship), yet most fail through excess of generic praise: they assert qualities without proving them, so the reader discounts them. This task produces a letter whose credibility comes from evidence, so that whoever reads it trusts each claim because they can see the fact supporting it. It unlocks a reference that actually moves the decision in favor of the recommended person.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior professional writer specializing in credible recommendation letters, with experience in selection processes and admissions committees.
Deliverable: a 350–500-word recommendation letter, ready to sign. Steps:
1. Verify you have RECOMENDANTE, RELACION_Y_TIEMPO, NOMBRE_RECOMENDADO, DESTINO, CUALIDADES, and at least one EVIDENCE per quality. If evidence is missing for any quality, request it before drafting; do not invent facts.
2. Match each quality to its strongest evidence (hierarchy: measurable achievement > first-hand observed situation > third-party reported behavior).
3. Draft the opening: relationship, length of acquaintance, and unreserved recommendation.
4. Draft 2–3 body paragraphs, one per quality, in assertion + evidence order (never adjective upon adjective).
5. Add a paragraph connecting the most relevant quality to the specific need of DESTINO.
6. Close reiterating support and offering availability to expand.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: restate the purpose, recommender, person, and destination; list the qualities with available evidence and flag gaps as [TO CONFIRM].
Phase 2 Plan: present the quality → evidence map and paragraph order before writing; if DESTINO is empty, draft a generic version and note it.
Phase 3 Execute: draft the letter in neutral, warm, and professional English, no clichés unless accompanied by proof; maintain one assertion, one fact per block; calibrate the strength of support to the closeness stated in RELACION_Y_TIEMPO (do not overstate if the bond is distant).
Explicit assumptions: the recommender endorses the facts provided; the metric is attributable to the recommended person; the recipient values evidence over adjectives.
Edge cases: a single quality with strong evidence (use it and note the limitation); evidence that supports a different quality from the one requested (reassign it and note the change); a quality without evidence (not asserted, left as [TO CONFIRM]); confidential or sensitive destination (maintain neutral institutional tone).
Constraints: no invented achievements, dates, or figures; no unnecessary PII; at most one cliché only if accompanied by proof.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every stated quality is followed by a concrete fact (metric, anecdote, or observed behavior).
- [ ] No generic praise appears without supporting evidence.
- [ ] The opening explicitly states the relationship and length of acquaintance.
- [ ] Evidence was chosen by hierarchy (measurable > observed > reported).
- [ ] One paragraph connects the key strength to the need of DESTINO.
- [ ] The intensity of support is consistent with the stated closeness.
- [ ] Length 350–500 words; neutral English; no emojis.
- [ ] Missing data marked [TO CONFIRM], none invented.
- [ ] Close reiterates support and offers availability to expand.
Expected deliverable: final recommendation letter ready to sign, plus a brief note listing pending [TO CONFIRM] items and, where applicable, an alert about qualities with insufficient evidence.
spec-comunicacion_redaccion_resumen_cv:

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need the header summary of my CV to make a recruiter understand in under ten seconds why I am a strong candidate for {{ROL_OBJETIVO}} in {{SECTOR_OBJETIVO}}, and to pass the ATS keyword filter. It is the first and sometimes only section read closely: if it is generic or merely lists tasks, the CV is discarded before reaching the experience section. A well-built summary with the achievements from {{LOGROS_CUANTIFICABLES}} and the competencies from {{COMPETENCIAS_CLAVE}} unlocks interviews, anchors my value proposition, and gives coherence to the entire document.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Expert career writer and personal branding specialist with fifteen years optimizing executive and technical resumes for selection processes and ATS filters.
Deliverable: three variants of the professional summary, plus a sentence-by-sentence breakdown and a quality checklist. Steps:
1. Professional headline: open with the professional identity aligned to {{ROL_OBJETIVO}} and the contribution domain; nothing like pronouns or filler such as proactive professional.
2. Experience: integrate {{ANOS_EXPERIENCIA}} and the type of context in {{SECTOR_OBJETIVO}}, without listing positions.
3. Achievements with metrics: incorporate two or three of {{LOGROS_CUANTIFICABLES}} prioritizing result over task; one measurable achievement is worth more than three generic responsibilities.
4. Differentiating competencies: name the two or three strongest from {{COMPETENCIAS_CLAVE}} that set the profile apart from an average one for the role.
5. Contribution hook: close with what you seek to contribute in {{ROL_OBJETIVO}}, aligned to the sector.
6. ATS optimization: naturally mirror the keywords of {{ROL_OBJETIVO}} and {{SECTOR_OBJETIVO}}, with no keyword stuffing or unexpanded acronyms.
7. Variants: deliver a concise version (two to three sentences, ~50 words), a standard version (three to four sentences, ~75 words), and an achievement-impact version (opens with the strongest figure); respect {{EXTENSION}} if specified.
8. Breakdown and quality control: below each variant explain in one line why it works and which job profile it serves; close with a five-point checklist.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: confirm {{ROL_OBJETIVO}}, {{SECTOR_OBJETIVO}}, and hard data; if an essential data point is missing (role, years, achievements with a figure, competencies, or sector), ask for it before drafting.
Phase 2 Raw material: map each achievement to its metric and each competency to a role keyword; discard generic and non-differentiating content.
Phase 3 Draft: build the three variants in implicit third person (no I), active voice, dense sentences; result verbs, zero empty adjectives.
Phase 4 Verify: check against the checklist and adjust before delivering.
Assumptions and constraints: work with the data provided; do not invent achievements, metrics, companies, certifications, or titles; mark [ASSUMPTION] for every drafting inference. If an achievement lacks a figure, reframe it by scope or qualitative impact, do not invent a number. If {{ROL_OBJETIVO}} and the experience have a clear gap (career change), prioritize transferable competencies and note it. Edge cases: no quantifiable achievements → deliver variants based on scope and flag the gap; junior or entry-level profile → anchor in education, projects, and competencies. Never mention salary expectations or contact details. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Opens with a professional headline aligned to {{ROL_OBJETIVO}}, no pronouns or filler phrases.
- Includes at least two achievements with explicit metrics; no sentence stays at a generic task level.
- Reflects {{ANOS_EXPERIENCIA}} and two or three differentiating competencies from {{COMPETENCIAS_CLAVE}}.
- Naturally mirrors keywords of {{ROL_OBJETIVO}} and {{SECTOR_OBJETIVO}} (ATS-friendly), no keyword stuffing.
- Implicit third person, active voice, no invented data ([ASSUMPTION] where inferred), no salary expectations.
- Each variant respects its target length and reads in under ten seconds.

--- S | SITUATION ---
You need to convert flat CV responsibilities ("in charge of," "responsible for") into achievement bullets that a recruiter scans in six seconds and an ATS indexes by impact. Quantified achievements unlock interviews: they separate those who describe their role from those who demonstrate results, and provide concrete ammunition for the salary conversation. Key distinction: metric (how much) is not the same as result (what it did for the business); a strong bullet shows both.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior resume writer and career coach with a track record recruiting technical and executive profiles, expert in the action-metric-result formula (Google XYZ / Harvard bullet style).

Phase 3 - Verification: confirm one metric or its marker [complete] per bullet, order by impact, and voice consistent with seniority.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each bullet opens with a past-tense action verb, none repeated, zero instances of "was responsible for".
- [ ] Each bullet has a real metric or a [complete: metric] marker with the data to find; zero invented figures.

spec-comunicacion_redaccion_articulo_opi:
[inputs]
- TEMA: {{TEMA}} > Subject or debate being opined on
- POSTURA: {{POSTURA}} > Specific position to be defended regarding the topic
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > Target reader (sector, level, sensibilities, what they already know and what might change their mind)
- MEDIO: {{MEDIO}} > Publication channel (column, corporate blog, LinkedIn, press) and its editorial tone
- EXTENSION: {{EXTENSION}} > Target length in words or number of paragraphs (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to publish an opinion article about {{TEMA}} that does not fall into cliché or complaint: a piece that sustains a clear position, argues it with rigor, and earns the respect even of those who disagree. A strong opinion piece about {{TEMA}} addressed to {{AUDIENCIA}} in {{MEDIO}} unlocks brand authority, positions a voice in a live debate, and opens a conversation rather than closing it. Risks to avoid: unsupported assertions, a thesis so obvious no one disputes it, ignoring the evident objection and being exposed before an informed reader, or adopting a moralizing tone that alienates those not yet convinced.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior editorialist with fifteen years of craft in opinion columns, trained in rhetorical argumentation (thesis, ethos-pathos-logos, refutation) and quality press editing.

Deliverable: a finished opinion article ready for editorial review, with a suggested headline and the thesis sentence clearly signaled.

Steps:
1. Confirm TEMA, POSTURA, AUDIENCIA, and MEDIO; if EXTENSION is not specified, assume 700–900 words and mark it as [ASSUMPTION]. Process ADJUNTOS as evidence input; if none, declare it.
2. Draft an opening that frames the problem in its current context and hooks in the first two lines, without opening with a dictionary definition or a generic quote.
3. State the thesis in a single unambiguous and arguable sentence (not an obvious statement): a reasonable reader must be able to argue the opposite.
4. Develop three distinct main arguments, ordered from strongest to most nuanced; each with its reason and one piece of evidence or a concrete example supporting it.
5. Honestly state the strongest counterargument from a skeptical reader and answer it with a refutation or qualified concession, without reducing it to a straw man.
6. Close by reaffirming the thesis with a twist that deepens it (not a mere repetition) and leave an actionable idea or a question that invites further thought.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: set the angle, the tone appropriate for {{AUDIENCIA}} and {{MEDIO}}, what the audience currently believes, and the promise of the headline.
Phase 2 - Argumentative skeleton: thesis in one sentence, map of the three arguments (each with its available evidence or marked assumption), and selection of the most uncomfortable counterargument — not the easiest to refute.
Phase 3 - Drafting: prose with smooth transitions, professional register, no filler; every figure or citation must be real or marked as [ASSUMPTION]; a voice that persuades without preaching.
Phase 4 - Polish: verify that thesis, arguments, counterargument, and close fit together without contradictions, that the three arguments do not overlap, that the counterargument is not a straw man, and that the headline promises what the text delivers.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The thesis is a single sentence, clear and arguable; it is unambiguously signaled and allows a reasonable reader to argue the opposite.
- [ ] There are exactly three main arguments, distinct from one another, non-overlapping, and ordered by strength.
- [ ] Each argument brings evidence or a concrete example; everything unverifiable is marked as [ASSUMPTION].
- [ ] The counterargument is the strongest possible, stated honestly, and receives a refutation or qualified concession (not a straw man).
- [ ] The opening hooks in the first two lines and the close reaffirms the thesis with an actionable idea or question, without mere repetition.
- [ ] The tone respects {{AUDIENCIA}} and persuades without moralizing; the register fits {{MEDIO}}.
- [ ] Neutral and professional English, no emojis; smooth transitions; no invented data.
- [ ] Includes a suggested headline that promises what the text delivers.
Expected deliverable: complete opinion article in {{MEDIO}}, within the target length, with headline and thesis sentence marked, ready to publish after editorial review. Edge cases: if TEMA or POSTURA arrive vague, ask for them before writing; if ADJUNTOS contradict POSTURA, flag it instead of ignoring it.
spec-comunicacion_revision_claridad:
[inputs]
- TEXTO_ORIGINAL: {{TEXTO_ORIGINAL}} > The complete piece to audit (pasted or attached)
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > Who will read the text: title, technical level, relationship (optional)
- CANAL: {{CANAL}} > Where it will be published: email, report, post, proposal, intranet (optional)

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You have a text that works but weighs: filler, passive voice, and jargon rob it of force and make the reader work too hard. A clarity audit turns it into a version that reads in less time, conveys the same intent with greater impact, and can be pasted and used immediately. What is unlocked: communication that respects the reader's time and reinforces your professional credibility.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior editor of professional texts, specializing in clarity and economy of language, with a style criterion (Plain Language, principles of Strunk & White and Williams on verbs and agents).
1. Restate in one sentence what {{TEXTO_ORIGINAL}} says and for what audience and channel it appears to be written. If {{AUDIENCIA}} or {{CANAL}} are missing and change editing decisions, ask for them before continuing; if they do not change, declare an [ASSUMPTION] and proceed.
2. Diagnose the concrete problems in the text, quoting real fragments.
3. Rewrite the full text according to {{NIVEL_EDICION}}, respecting {{LIMITE_LONGITUD}}, ready to use.
4. Deliver a table of key changes (before > after > why) and the reduction metric (words before / words after / % cut).
5. Close with 2–3 optional deeper adjustments not applied in order to respect {{NIVEL_EDICION}}.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Diagnosis: detect and classify filler and verbal tics, unnecessary passive voice, nominalizations ("conduct an analysis" > "analyze"), jargon or technical terms without communicative function, sentences over 30 words, and redundancies. Order findings by impact on readability.
Phase 2 - Rewriting: apply active voice, strong verbs, one idea per sentence, and logical order. Preserve technical terms that do add precision and respect the author's register and voice: sharpen, do not replace their style. If {{NIVEL_EDICION}} is deep, reorder paragraphs and ideas; if light, maintain structure and only cut.
Phase 3 - Evidence: document each relevant change and calculate word reduction.
Constraints: do not invent information or alter data, figures, names, or direct quotes. Do not edit commitments, dates, or responsible parties that only the author can validate: mark them as points to confirm. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every interpretation of the original intent.
Edge cases: if the text is already clear, say so and limit editing to minor touches; if it mixes languages or registers, flag it and unify only with permission; if cutting conflicts with {{LIMITE_LONGITUD}}, prioritize the limit and note what is sacrificed.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Intent and data from the original intact; zero invented information.
- [ ] Filler, verbal tics, and detected redundancies eliminated.
- [ ] Unnecessary passive voice converted to active; nominalizations turned into verbs.
- [ ] No sentence exceeds ~30 words without justification.
- [ ] Technical terms with communicative function preserved.
- [ ] Author's register and voice respected; style sharpened, not substituted.

A useful but overly long piece of writing loses impact for its channel or reader: it does not get read in full or it dilutes its message. Cutting it without losing what is essential unlocks a more readable, publishable, and persuasive text, ready for email, proposals, posts, abstracts, or space-limited documents. --- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior text editor, specializing in condensation and economy of language, with the judgment to distinguish core from ornamentation and the instinct not to betray the author's voice.

2. Map the untouchable core: central thesis, essential supporting arguments, conclusion or call to action, plus {{NO_NEGOCIABLES}}.

Phase 1 Diagnosis: count in the correct unit, set the target, identify the thesis, logical structure, and closing.
Phase 2 Triage: separate core from dispensable idea by idea; when in doubt, preserve and note it.
Phase 3 Condensation: rewrite applying sentence merging, redundancy elimination, and strong verbs instead of periphrases; preserve voice, tone, and register; never create data or figures.
Phase 4 Verification: confirm the real percentage is within tolerance, that no fabricated content was introduced, and that every non-negotiable was preserved.

- [ ] Thesis, essential arguments, and conclusion present and identifiable.

A text is about to circulate before a diverse audience, and a term or construction may exclude, stereotype, or render invisible part of that audience, undermining credibility and reach. This audit enables publishing with confidence that the language is inclusive and respectful without becoming forced or unreadable: it corrects real exclusions, preserves the original voice, and leaves a trail of justification for every change so it can be defended or adjusted. Archetype: Senior editor specializing in inclusive communication and non-sexist language, with proven editorial judgment in neutral professional English and mastery of techniques that maintain fluency.

Phase 3 · Rewrite: generate the lowest-friction alternative that preserves meaning, register, and fluency; if only a visible technique is available (doublet, e/x), justify it.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- The central idea is grasped in under 5 seconds from the opening summary.
- No paragraph exceeds {{MAX_LINEAS_PARRAFO}} lines and each one supports a single idea.
- Each subheading precisely describes the block it heads (nothing generic).
- Lists are used only where there are real enumerations, steps, or criteria.
- Selective bold, without saturation; emphasis remains a signal, not noise.
- Density is adjusted to {{CANAL_DESTINO}} (mobile more airy, PDF denser).
- Original meaning, tone, and voice intact; zero new assertions.
- {{ELEMENTOS_INTOCABLES}} reproduced verbatim.
Expected deliverable: the reformatted text ready to paste in {{CANAL_DESTINO}}, followed by a brief note with the structural changes applied, formatting decisions, and any [SUPUESTO]. If any checklist item is not met, indicate it and propose the adjustment.
spec-comunicacion_revision_titular_optim:
[inputs]
- TITULAR_BASE: {{TITULAR_BASE}} > Current headline or draft to be optimized
- MEDIO: {{MEDIO}} > Channel and format where it will be published (e.g. "email subject line", "landing page heading", "LinkedIn post", "ad")
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > Who the headline speaks to and what action they are expected to take (e.g. "HR leaders who should open the email and schedule a demo")
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Character limit, prohibited or brand words, and required tone (optional)
- NUMERO_VARIANTES: {{NUMERO_VARIANTES}} > How many variants to generate; default 5-7 (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to choose the strongest headline for {{MEDIO}} starting from the draft {{TITULAR_BASE}}, targeting {{AUDIENCIA}}. The headline is the decision that determines whether the piece gets read or ignored, so I want to compare it against alternatives with explicit criteria rather than choosing by intuition. A sound exercise unlocks which angle connects best with this audience, why one variant wins, and how to sharpen it without making promises the piece cannot keep. The winning headline is a starting point for field validation, not a guaranteed performance outcome.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior headline editor and direct-response copywriter, with experience in message optimization and A/B testing of headings across different channels.

Deliverable: a comparative evaluation of headline variants for {{MEDIO}}, structured as follows:
1. Framing: confirm base headline, medium, audience, desired action, and constraints {{RESTRICCIONES}}. Define each axis in one line — Clarity (understood on first read, without ambiguity), Hook (curiosity or tension that invites reading on), Promise (what the reader explicitly gains). If the channel imposes a known character limit (email subject line, ad), declare it as a hard threshold.
2. Variants: generate {{NUMERO_VARIANTES}} (default 5-7) covering distinct angles: direct benefit, curiosity, legitimate urgency, proof or specificity, and contrast or question. Each variant names the angle it embodies to avoid duplication.
3. Evaluation: table with each variant scored 1 to 5 on Clarity, Hook, and Promise, with total (max 15) and one sentence justifying the scores and naming the main risk of the variant.
4. Ranking and recommendation: rank from highest to lowest score, declare the winner and explain why it fits {{MEDIO}} and {{AUDIENCIA}}; also name the runner-up as an alternative for A/B testing.
5. Micro-refinements: two concrete refinements on the winner to sharpen it further, indicating which axis each one aims to improve.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Framing: fix axes and constraints; if base headline, medium, or audience is missing, ask before continuing. If constraints or number of variants are missing, assume defaults (5-7 variants, professional tone, no hard character limit) and declare them as [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 — Generation: produce variants forcing genuine angle diversity, not cosmetic rewrites of the same approach; respect character limits upfront if the channel imposes them.
Phase 3 — Evaluation: score each axis independently and sum; penalize sensationalism the piece cannot sustain, clickbait, and constraint violations (a variant that violates a hard constraint cannot win).
Phase 4 — Decision: rank by total, resolve ties in favor of best Clarity and, if still tied, best Promise; recommend and justify against medium and audience.
Phase 5 — Sharpening: deliver the two micro-refinements on the winner.
Edge cases: if the base headline is already the strongest and no variant surpasses it, say so explicitly and recommend keeping it; if the medium supports emoji or long-form length, adapt to the channel without breaking brand tone.
Mark [SUPUESTO] any unverifiable performance claim; do not invent open-rate or conversion metrics.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The three axes (Clarity, Hook, Promise) are each defined in one line before evaluating.
- [ ] The requested number of variants was generated (or 5-7 by default) and they cover genuinely distinct angles, each named.
- [ ] Each variant respects the constraints {{RESTRICCIONES}}, including character limits if applicable; those violating a hard constraint are disqualified from winning.
- [ ] Each variant has a 1-5 score per axis, total out of 15, and one justification sentence with its main risk.
- [ ] The ranking is consistent with the totals; ties resolved by Clarity then Promise; the winner is justified against medium and audience and the runner-up is named.
- [ ] No variant promises what the piece cannot deliver; performance claims marked [SUPUESTO]; no invented metrics.
- [ ] Two actionable micro-refinements on the winner are delivered, each indicating the axis it improves.
Expected deliverable: framing with defined axes + table of {{NUMERO_VARIANTES}} scored variants + ranking with justified winner and runner-up + two final micro-refinements, in neutral professional English, no emojis.
spec-comunicacion_revision_traduccion_lo:
[inputs]
- TEXTO_TRADUCIDO: {{TEXTO_TRADUCIDO}} > Text already translated into the target language to be localized
- MERCADO_DESTINO: {{MERCADO_DESTINO}} > Target country or region and its language variant (e.g. Mexico, Spain, Brazil, US Hispanic)
- PUBLICO_OBJETIVO: {{PUBLICO_OBJETIVO}} > Specific audience and their context (sector, age, role, relationship with the brand)
- OBJETIVO_MENSAJE: {{OBJETIVO_MENSAJE}} > What the text must achieve (convert, inform, retain) and the call to action
- REGISTRO_DESEADO: {{REGISTRO_DESEADO}} > Expected tone and formality level in the target market; include form of address if known (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A literally translated text is understandable but foreign: the target audience perceives it was not written for them, idioms do not resonate, and cultural references do not land, which erodes trust and the message's impact. Localizing it well unlocks the audience reading it as their own, raises response to the call to action, and protects the brand's reputation against poorly calibrated cultural sensitivities. The opposite risk also exists: over-localizing erases the brand voice or introduces colloquialisms that do not fit the desired register. The sweet spot is transcreating the effect, not decorating the language.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior localization and transcreation specialist, with a track record of adapting campaigns and communications across Spanish-speaking and international markets.
Deliverable: the localized text, a decision log, and a validation checklist. Steps:
1. Confirm target market, audience, objective, and register; if any is missing, ask before proceeding. If the register is not specified, infer it from the objective and audience, and declare the chosen form of address as [SUPUESTO].
2. Diagnose the text: flag literal translations, idioms that do not transfer, cultural references without analogue, register misalignments, false friends or syntactic calques, and cultural, religious, political, or gender sensitivities.
3. Rewrite by localizing: native idiomatic equivalents, recognizable cultural analogues, local register and courtesy norms, and units, dates, currencies, and numerical formats (thousands/decimal separators) adapted to market convention.
4. Preserve the intent and call to action with their original force; respect length constraints when the format requires it (subject line, button, heading) and flag it if a native equivalent changes the length.
5. Build a three-column table: original translated fragment, localized version, reason for the decision (include the type of problem it resolves).
6. List items that require validation by a native speaker or the brand before publishing, separating blockers from optional improvements.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: go through the text and label each problematic fragment by type (literalism, idiom, reference, register, calque/false friend, sensitivity). Do not invent characteristics of the target market; any unverifiable data is marked [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 Transcreation: rewrite prioritizing effect over word-for-word equivalence; keep proper names and brand terms intact. If a fragment admits several valid solutions, choose one and justify it; offer an alternative only when the choice depends on missing data.
Phase 3 Traceability: document each change in the table with its reason and problem type. If a fragment is intentionally left unchanged, record that too.
Phase 4 Close: separate what is resolved from what requires human native or brand validation, distinguishing blockers from improvements.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- The localized text reads as if written natively for the target market, with no trace of literal translation or calques.
- Each idiom and reference from the original has a native equivalent or a justified analogue; it is not over-localized nor does it introduce colloquialisms that are out of register.
- Register, form of address, courtesy norms, units, dates, currencies, and numerical formats follow local convention.
- The intent and call to action are preserved with equal or greater force; length constraints are respected or flagged.
- The decision log covers all relevant changes with their reason and problem type.
- All detected cultural sensitivities are flagged and resolved or escalated.
- Assumptions are marked [SUPUESTO]; items requiring native or brand validation are in the closing checklist, separating blockers from optional items.
Expected deliverable: final localized text + three-column table (original / localized / reason) + pre-publication validation checklist.
spec-comunicacion_facilitacion_agenda_re:
[inputs]
- OBJETIVO_REUNION: {{OBJETIVO_REUNION}} > The outcome the meeting must produce (a decision, an approved plan, a resolved conflict). If it arrives as a topic, restate it as a verifiable outcome.
- DURACION_TOTAL: {{DURACION_TOTAL}} > Total available time in minutes (e.g. 45, 60, 90).
- ASISTENTES_Y_ROLES: {{ASISTENTES_Y_ROLES}} > List of participants with their role in the meeting: who decides, who contributes, who observes.
- TEMAS_CANDIDATOS: {{TEMAS_CANDIDATOS}} > Proposed topics to cover, with their expected decision or deliverable if known.
- PRELECTURA_DISPONIBLE: {{PRELECTURA_DISPONIBLE}} > Documents, data, or links that can be sent in advance (optional).
- MODALIDAD: {{MODALIDAD}} > In-person, remote, or hybrid; adjusts timeboxes and discussion format (optional; default remote).
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A meeting without a decision agenda consumes the time of expensive people and ends without verifiable agreements, forcing the conversation to be repeated. This agenda turns the meeting into an instrument of progress: each block produces a decision, an assigned action, or a verified data point, and pre-reading removes everything that is merely informational from the room. It unlocks shorter meetings, traceable decisions, and a closing with owners and dates that leaves no room for ambiguity. Operating assumption: the requester can convene or influence the agenda; if they are only an attendee, the output serves as a reorganization proposal.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior executive meeting facilitator, with training in decision meeting design and group dynamics, specialized in committee governance and team rituals.

Deliver an agenda ready to send. Steps:
1. Restate {{OBJETIVO_REUNION}} as an outcome to achieve, not a topic to discuss (e.g. "Approve the MVP scope" rather than "Talk about the MVP"). If it admits multiple readings, choose the most actionable and declare the assumption.
2. List {{ASISTENTES_Y_ROLES}} declaring for each one whether they decide, contribute, or observe; flag if the decision-maker for the objective is missing and propose resolving that before convening. Flag if there are multiple decision-makers with no tie-breaking criterion.
3. Prioritize {{TEMAS_CANDIDATOS}} from highest to lowest impact on the objective and drop those that are purely informational and already resolved by pre-reading, unless they require a decision.
4. Convert each topic into a block with: title, timebox in minutes, block owner, expected decision or deliverable, and discussion format (presentation, open debate, vote, brainstorm) consistent with {{MODALIDAD}}.
5. Assign each block its pre-reading from {{PRELECTURA_DISPONIBLE}}, with what to read and estimated reading time.
6. Add an opening (objective and ground rules) and a closing (confirmation of agreements, owners, and dates).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: fix the objective as an outcome and verify that the decision-maker is among the attendees.
Phase 2 - Prioritization and pruning: rank topics by impact and remove informational content redundant with pre-reading; if a block does not close in a decision, action, or data point, convert it into pre-reading.
Phase 3 - Timeboxing: assign minutes per block; the sum of timeboxes must be equal to or less than {{DURACION_TOTAL}}; reserve between ten and fifteen percent for opening and closing. If not all topics fit, cut by lowest impact and leave the remainder in a parking lot for another session. Do not compress everything to force a fit.
Phase 4 - Pre-reading: pair each block with its material and reading time; if the total reading time exceeds what is reasonable, prioritize the critical items and flag it.
Phase 5 - Close: draft the agreements, owners, and dates section, and a pre-reading reminder with its send deadline.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The objective is stated as an outcome, not a topic.
- [ ] Each attendee has a declared role (decides, contributes, observes) and the decision-maker is present; multiple decision-makers flagged.
- [ ] Each block has a timebox, owner, expected decision or deliverable, and discussion format.
- [ ] The sum of timeboxes is equal to or less than the total duration; opening and closing take between ten and fifteen percent.
- [ ] No blocks are purely informational if pre-reading already resolves them.
- [ ] Each block closes in a decision, an assigned action, or a verified data point.
- [ ] Each block has pre-reading with material and estimated reading time.
- [ ] The closing includes agreements, owners, dates, and a pre-reading reminder with deadline.
- [ ] Topics that did not fit are in an explicit parking lot, not compressed in.
- [ ] No data was invented; missing items were flagged as questions to the requester.
Expected deliverable: agenda as a table or numbered list, ready to paste into an email or calendar invitation, with a header (objective as outcome, date, duration, attendees with role), timeboxed blocks, parking lot if applicable, and a closing section.
spec-comunicacion_facilitacion_mensaje_s:
[inputs]
- DESTINATARIO: {{DESTINATARIO}} > Who the message is for: their role and how much context they already have on the topic (determines what to reconstruct and what to omit)
- PEDIDO: {{PEDIDO}} > What I need from that person: the decision, piece of information, or concrete action to obtain
- CONTEXTO: {{CONTEXTO}} > Minimum context the recipient does NOT have and needs in order to respond
- PLAZO: {{PLAZO}} > Deadline date and time, and why that deadline matters / what gets unblocked when they reply
- CANAL_TONO: {{CANAL_TONO}} > Channel (Slack DM, public channel, thread) and tone (formal or casual) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to obtain {{PEDIDO}} from {{DESTINATARIO}} and I'm going to request it via asynchronous chat, where I cannot clarify doubts in real time. The purpose of this message is to give that person everything they need to respond in a single pass: the context they don't have, the exact request, and the deadline. A message written this way unblocks the response within the intended {{PLAZO}} and prevents the chain of back-and-forth ("what do you mean?", "when do you need it?", "what exactly do you need?") that consumes hours and dilutes urgency. The hidden cost of a poorly written message isn't just rework: each extra round reopens the other person's attention queue and pushes the response to the next day. MetodologIA's asynchronous facilitation contributes here the discipline of thinking through the other person's response before writing the message.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior internal asynchronous communication facilitator, expert in drafting Slack and team chat messages with a high first-reply rate, with a criterion of respecting the reader's time.
Deliver the following, in this order:
1. Restate the objective in a single sentence: "Get [what] from {{DESTINATARIO}} by {{PLAZO}}". If DESTINATARIO, PEDIDO, CONTEXTO, or PLAZO is missing, ask for them before drafting; do not invent names, dates, or figures.
2. Classify the message based on {{PEDIDO}}: decision, review, information/data request, or task unblock. That defines the type of expected response and how to close the request (a decision closes with options; a data request, with a closed-ended question).
3. Draft the scannable message, in this order: (a) a first line that summarizes the request and urgency; (b) minimum context derived from {{CONTEXTO}}, only what the recipient doesn't know; (c) the request as a closed-ended question or concrete action, numbered if there are multiple questions; (d) an explicit deadline with date and time and what gets unblocked; (e) if applicable, a default option that allows moving forward without a reply; (f) if there are {{ADJUNTOS}}, a one-line reference indicating exactly what to look at in each one.
4. Adjust tone according to {{CANAL_TONO}}: direct and cordial, no apologies or filler, no aggressive pressure. In a public channel, tag only the person who must reply and do not expose sensitive data; in a thread, open with the request, not with the greeting.
5. Deliver the message ready to paste and, below it, on one line, all assumptions marked as [SUPUESTO]; no name, date, or figure was invented.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Framing: fix the message objective and validate that recipient, request, context, and deadline exist; if an essential element is missing, ask for it and stop.
Phase 2 · Expected response design: define which exact response counts as "resolved" and design the message backwards from that response, removing everything that doesn't enable it.
Phase 3 · Drafting: assemble the parts (first line, minimum context, request, deadline, default option, reference to attachments) prioritizing brevity and scannability; if the message exceeds ~6 lines or has more than 3 questions, suggest splitting it or switching to a brief call and say so.
Phase 4 · Verification: reread as if you were {{DESTINATARIO}} and confirm they could reply without asking anything further; cut every unnecessary word.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist before delivering:
- The first line communicates the request and urgency on its own (stands alone as an isolated notification).
- The context includes only what the recipient doesn't know; zero unnecessary reconstruction of history.
- The request is a closed-ended question or concrete action; if there are multiple, they are numbered and can be answered one by one.
- The deadline is explicit (date and time) and states what gets unblocked; no "whenever you can."
- If applicable, there is a default option that allows moving forward without a reply.
- Attachments, if any, come with an indication of what to look at; none are attached without purpose.
- Tone is direct and cordial, neutral English, no emojis, no apologies or corporate filler; in a public channel, sensitive data is not exposed.
- All data not provided is marked [SUPUESTO]; no name, date, or figure was invented.
Edge cases: if the request is ambiguous and cannot be closed as a question, return it to the requester rather than guessing. If there is no real deadline, propose one and mark it [SUPUESTO]. If {{DESTINATARIO}} already has all the context, omit the context block rather than padding it.
Expected deliverable: the message text ready to paste in {{CANAL_TONO}}, followed by one line with any assumptions if there were any.
spec-comunicacion_facilitacion_anuncio_e:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_INICIATIVA: {{NOMBRE_INICIATIVA}} > Name or headline of the initiative, change, or project to announce
- QUE_CAMBIA: {{QUE_CAMBIA}} > What specifically is changing: what stops, what begins, what is reorganized
- MOTIVO: {{MOTIVO}} > Business reason or objective that justifies the initiative and the benefit for the team
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > Team or people the announcement is addressed to and who are affected
- FECHA_INICIO: {{FECHA_INICIO}} > Start date or first milestone of the initiative
- RESPONSABLE: {{RESPONSABLE}} > Person responsible for the initiative and point of contact for questions
- TONO: {{TONO}} > Desired register: warm, formal, urgent, etc. (optional; default: professionally warm)
- ALCANCE_CAMBIO: {{ALCANCE_CAMBIO}} > Sensitivity of the change: operationally neutral, or sensitive (layoffs, role reassignment, reporting changes) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are going to draft the internal announcement with which a leader communicates the initiative NOMBRE_INICIATIVA to their team. A poorly crafted initiative announcement generates rumor, passive resistance, and rework; a well-crafted one reduces uncertainty and unlocks coordinated action from day one. The message must leave every person knowing exactly what is changing, why the effort is worthwhile, and what is expected of them. The goal is not to inform — it is to mobilize.
Explicit assumptions: the sender has the authority to announce the change and the decision is already made (the "what" is not open for debate, the "how" is). If the announcement is still tentative or consultative, declare it and adjust the "what is expected" frame to gathering input rather than executing.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior leader in internal communications and change management, with experience facilitating initiative launches in operational teams and handling sensitive messages.

Deliverable: a team announcement ready to send, structured with the What-Why-How formula (what is changing > why > what is expected). Steps:
1. Opening: name NOMBRE_INICIATIVA and RESPONSABLE in a sentence that states plainly what is being announced.
2. What is changing: translate QUE_CAMBIA into observable terms for AUDIENCIA (what stops, what begins, from FECHA_INICIO). No abstractions.
3. Why now: connect MOTIVO to a real pressure or objective and to what AUDIENCIA gains concretely; not just the business benefit.
4. What is expected: list concrete actions by role or person, with a responsible party and the first dated milestone.
5. Closing: questions channel, RESPONSABLE as point of contact, next check-in point, and an honest acknowledgment of the effort the transition will require.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: restate the initiative, its reason, and its audience in your own words; classify ALCANCE_CAMBIO (operationally neutral or sensitive). Flag any missing or ambiguous data (NOMBRE_INICIATIVA, QUE_CAMBIA, MOTIVO, AUDIENCIA, FECHA_INICIO, RESPONSABLE) and ask for it before continuing; do not invent data.
Phase 2 - Plan: present the five-block skeleton and the tone register (use TONO if provided; otherwise, professionally warm) for validation.
Phase 3 - Execute: draft the final announcement. Apply What-Why-How in order. Avoid empty corporate language, unsupported promises, and euphemisms that mask workload or reassignment; if something has a cost, name it respectfully. Neutral English, no emojis.
Edge cases: (a) if ALCANCE_CAMBIO is sensitive, recommend separating what goes in writing from what should be discussed in person before sending, and avoid communicating via mass announcement anything that individually affects someone; (b) if FECHA_INICIO has already passed or is immediate, adjust the frame to "already underway"; (c) if AUDIENCIA mixes direct stakeholders and observers, distinguish which expectations apply to whom.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The initiative and its responsible person are clear in the first sentence.
- [ ] "What is changing" is observable: it states what stops, what begins, and from when — not abstractions.
- [ ] The reason connects MOTIVO to a concrete benefit for the audience, not just for the business.
- [ ] Each expectation has an action, a responsible party, and at least one dated milestone.
- [ ] The closing names a questions channel, a contact, the next check-in, and honestly acknowledges the effort of the transition.
- [ ] If the change is sensitive, the announcement separates what is written from what is conversational and does not expose individuals in a mass message.
- [ ] Zero empty corporate language, zero unsupported promises, zero emojis; neutral English.
Expected deliverable: team announcement in prose, ready to paste into an email or internal channel, of a length suitable for reading in under two minutes.
spec-comunicacion_facilitacion_feedback_:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_O_ROL_RECEPTOR: {{NOMBRE_O_ROL_RECEPTOR}} > Person or role receiving the feedback (e.g., "team designer", "technical peer", "junior direct report")
- TIPO_FEEDBACK: {{TIPO_FEEDBACK}} > Type of feedback: reinforcing (solidify a valuable behavior) or redirecting (adjust a behavior)
- SITUACION_OBSERVADA: {{SITUACION_OBSERVADA}} > Concrete observed fact: when, where, and what happened — ideally a single specific episode; indicate whether you observed it directly or it was reported to you
- RESULTADO_DESEADO: {{RESULTADO_DESEADO}} > Behavior change or continuation sought after the conversation (optional)
- RELACION_Y_CONTEXTO: {{RELACION_Y_CONTEXTO}} > Hierarchical relationship and emotional weight of the topic (e.g., "peer without hierarchy, sensitive topic", "direct report, under delivery pressure") (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Vague or judgment-laden feedback triggers defensiveness and doesn't change behavior; the SBI model corrects this by separating the observable fact from the interpretation. The purpose is to deliver a {{TIPO_FEEDBACK}} message directed to {{NOMBRE_O_ROL_RECEPTOR}}, anchored in {{SITUACION_OBSERVADA}}, that the person receives as actionable information rather than an attack. A well-built SBI message unlocks higher-trust conversations, clear behavioral decisions, and a climate where feedback flows in both directions.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior internal communication facilitator and leadership coach trained in the SBI (Situation-Behavior-Impact) model from the Center for Creative Leadership, with experience conducting high-stakes feedback conversations.
Deliverable: an SBI feedback message ready to deliver. Steps:
1. Situation: anchor the exact moment (when and where) based on {{SITUACION_OBSERVADA}}; avoid generalizations like "always" or "never" and limit to one specific episode. If {{SITUACION_OBSERVADA}} groups multiple episodes, choose the most recent and representative one and name the others as a pattern to verify, not as fact.
2. Behavior: describe only the observable thing the person said or did, in neutral language, without evaluative adjectives or attribution of intentions. If the information came from a third party and was not direct observation, declare it explicitly and treat it as a report to be confirmed.
3. Impact: name the concrete effect on the team, the client, or the result; distinguish the factual impact from your personal interpretation with an explicit formula such as "what I saw was X, what I interpreted was Y."
4. Adjust according to {{TIPO_FEEDBACK}}: if reinforcing, make explicit the behavior to repeat and why it is worth sustaining; if redirecting, orient toward {{RESULTADO_DESEADO}} without resolving it for the person, preserving their autonomy.
5. Calibrate tone according to {{RELACION_Y_CONTEXTO}}: between peers without hierarchy avoid directive language; in sensitive topics or under pressure, acknowledge the context without diluting the data.
6. Close with an open-ended question that yields the floor and invites dialogue (avoid yes/no questions).
Do not use the sandwich format (praise-criticism-praise): it dilutes the message.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 (Interpret): restate who the feedback is directed to, the type of feedback, the observed situation, and the desired outcome; mark with [SUPUESTO] any unconfirmed data (especially if the observation was indirect) and ask for anything missing before drafting.
Phase 2 (Plan): separate the observable fact from your interpretation and outline the three S, B, I components separately before joining them in prose.
Phase 3 (Execute): deliver three pieces: (a) the SBI message in brief prose ready to say out loud; (b) the labeled breakdown Situation / Behavior / Impact with [SUPUESTO] visible; (c) the closing question.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- The Situation anchors a single, concrete moment without "always"/"never"; multiple episodes are reduced to one and the rest are flagged as a pattern to verify.
- The Behavior is observable and neutral: no evaluative adjectives, no attributed intentions; third-party observations are declared as such.
- The Impact separates the factual from the personal interpretation with an explicit formula.
- Consistency with {{TIPO_FEEDBACK}}: reinforcing names the behavior to repeat; redirecting points to {{RESULTADO_DESEADO}} without resolving it for the person.
- Tone respects {{RELACION_Y_CONTEXTO}} when provided.
- The sandwich format is not used; the closing question is open-ended, yields the floor, and is not yes/no.
- Unconfirmed data is marked with [SUPUESTO].
Expected deliverable: the three pieces (message in prose, labeled S/B/I breakdown, closing question) in neutral and professional English, no emojis, ready to sustain the conversation.
spec-comunicacion_facilitacion_guion_1a1:
[inputs]
- ROL_RELACION: {{ROL_RELACION}} > Relationship with the person and authority I have: direct leader, peer, or mentor without a reporting line
- PERSONA: {{PERSONA}} > Who they are: role, tenure, and what is relevant to discuss (without data I don't provide)
- FRECUENCIA_CONTEXTO: {{FRECUENCIA_CONTEXTO}} > How often we meet and how long this meeting lasts (e.g., bi-weekly, 30 min)

--- S | SITUATION ---
The leader needs to prepare a one-on-one meeting with {{PERSONA}} that is the other person's time and not a disguised status report. The purpose of this script is to turn a recurring meeting into a conversation with deliberate structure: a check-in that measures real status, a progress review that recognizes with specificity, a blocker treatment that assigns owner and next step, a two-way feedback exchange, and a professional development segment that looks beyond the quarter. A well-guided meeting builds trust, anticipates friction before it escalates, and leaves traceable agreements; without a script, the meeting dissolves into status updates and the person leaves without feeling heard. The time allocation and depth are calibrated based on {{FRECUENCIA_CONTEXTO}} and {{TEMAS_PRIORITARIOS}}; the feedback tone and nature of the agreements are calibrated based on the actual authority of {{ROL_RELACION}}.

Phase 4 · Feedback and development: prepare the situation-behavior-impact observation and the reverse feedback request; run the GROW segment on the career aspiration.

--- S | SITUATION ---
The annual budget of {{UNIDAD_O_AREA}} will be built for {{PERIODO_FISCAL}} using the Zero-Based Budgeting methodology: unlike incremental budgeting, no line item starts from the prior period's spending or is adjusted for inflation by default. Every dollar is re-justified from scratch against an activity driver and an objective. The result unlocks allocation decisions that can be defended before a committee, exposes spending that adds no value, and allows resources to be reallocated to the highest-return activities instead of applying linear cuts.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Financial Planning and Analysis (FP&A) Director, expert in Zero-Based Budgeting and management control, with the judgment to translate operational activity into a defensible cost structure and support every line item before a committee.
Deliverable: zero-based annual budget for {{UNIDAD_O_AREA}}, with prioritized decision packages, consolidated by unit and by month, a narrative of the budgetary strategy, and a risk register.
Steps:
1. Define the decision units (cost centers, processes, or services) to be budgeted separately; justify the chosen level of disaggregation.
2. For each unit, identify the activity driver from {{DRIVERS_DE_NEGOCIO}} that best explains its resource consumption and establish the cost-driver relationship (unit cost x projected volume); use {{DATOS_BASE}} where it exists.
3. Build at least three incremental packages per unit (minimum viable, current operation, enhanced): driver volume, justified cost, benefit or risk, and dependency on prior packages.
4. Rank all packages in a single prioritized list by value-to-cost ratio and mark the cut-off point based on {{TECHO_PRESUPUESTAL}}; explicitly indicate what falls inside, what falls outside, and the opportunity cost of the first excluded package.
5. Consolidate the budget by unit and by month, aligned with {{OBJETIVOS_ESTRATEGICOS}}, distributing according to driver seasonality, and close with estimation risks and their monitoring.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Structure: break {{UNIDAD_O_AREA}} down into budgetable decision units.
Phase 2 - Drivers: map the activity driver and unit cost per unit; document the cost-driver logic and the source of each figure.
Phase 3 - Packages: define the incremental service levels with volume, cost, and value for each; a higher package is only costed on top of the previous one, without duplicating the base.
Phase 4 - Prioritization and cut-off: rank packages by value-to-cost, apply the ceiling, and indicate what falls inside and outside with its opportunity cost.
Phase 5 - Consolidation and risks: build tables by unit and by month (with explicit seasonality), narrate the strategy, and list 3 to 5 under/overestimation risks with their monitoring.
Hard rules: do not invent figures; if ceiling, volumes, or unit costs are missing, request them before calculating; mark every self-generated estimate as [SUPUESTO]; zero carryforward from historical data and zero inflation adjustment unless {{OBJETIVOS_ESTRATEGICOS}} or {{DATOS_BASE}} require it, in which case it is documented; verify that the consolidated total matches the sum of approved packages.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Quality checklist:
- Every line item is justified against a driver and an objective; zero carryforward from historical data and zero inflation adjustment by default.
- Each decision unit has >= 3 incremental packages with explicit volume, cost, and value, without duplicating the base across levels.

--- S | SITUATION ---
The budget for {{PERIODO_OBJETIVO}} in {{MONEDA}} is needed for committee submission. The method is incremental based on historical data: it starts from the actual close of the prior period and adjusts each line for inflation, growth, and explicit assumptions. A traceable line-by-line budget enables committee defense, resource allocation, and subsequent tracking of variances against the plan. The method's strength is traceability; its risk is perpetuating inefficiencies from the base period, so assumptions must be visible and auditable.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Financial Planning & Analysis (FP&A) manager with experience in incremental budgeting and scenario construction for committee review.
Deliverable: projected line-by-line budget with three scenarios and prioritized assumptions. Steps:
1. Verify inputs: confirm HISTORICO_LINEAS, INFLACION_ESPERADA, METAS_CRECIMIENTO, and EVENTOS_CONOCIDOS. Ask for anything missing; unavailable data is declared [SUPUESTO] with assumed value and source. Do not invent figures.
2. Classify each line as fixed, variable, or semi-variable and assign its adjustment driver (general inflation, revenue growth, headcount, volume, indexed contract). A line without a clear driver is documented as such.
3. Project line by line: adjusted base = prior actual x (1 + inflation) x (1 + growth) +/- one-time events. Show formula and absolute and percentage delta versus the prior period.
4. Build base, conservative, and aggressive scenarios by varying inflation and growth; summarize impact on total revenue, total expenses, and margin, and identify the assumption that most separates the scenarios.
5. Prioritize assumptions by sensitivity (impact on the result of a 1-point change) and include a risk note and recommendations.
Edge cases: (a) negative or zero base → adjust on the absolute amount, not a percentage; (b) non-recurring event → exclude it from the next period's base and make that explicit; (c) line with no historical data → build it bottom-up and mark it [SUPUESTO]; (d) volatile historical data across periods → use average or trend and state the criterion.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 – Interpret: restate the objective, period, currency, and line scope; list information gaps and preliminary assumptions.
Phase 2 – Plan: present the line classification, proposed drivers, and inflation and growth ranges per scenario, before calculating.
Phase 3 – Execute: apply formulas line by line, build the table, run the three scenarios, and consolidate assumptions and risks. Every figure must trace back to a provided input or to a [SUPUESTO].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- Each line shows: prior actual, classification, driver, adjustment %, projected amount, absolute delta, and % delta.
- The adjustment formula is explicit and reproducible for each line.
- Three scenarios exist (base, conservative, aggressive) with impact on revenue, expenses, and margin, and the most sensitive assumption is identified.
- Any data not provided appears marked [SUPUESTO] with value and source; zero invented figures.
- Edge cases explicitly addressed when applicable (non-positive base, non-recurring event, line with no history, volatile history).
- Key assumptions prioritized by sensitivity and risk note included.
- Figures in {{MONEDA}} with consistent formatting.
Expected deliverable: line-by-line budget table + three-scenario comparison + numbered list of assumptions prioritized by sensitivity + risk note and recommendations, ready for committee.

--- S | SITUATION ---
A budget with static amounts does not respond when volume changes: every revision requires manually reworking cells, no one knows which portion of spending is truly fixed, and business conversations become debates about figures instead of levers. Converting the budget of {{UNIDAD_DE_NEGOCIO}} into a driver-based model unlocks reforecasts in minutes, debate about operational levers, and a contribution margin that moves with reality. The result is a budget that recalculates automatically when a driver changes, ready for scenarios, rolling forecasts, and committee defense.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior FP&A Director expert in driver-based budgeting, flexible financial modeling, and cost-behavior analysis (fixed / variable / semi-variable or step-fixed).

Deliver a complete driver-based budget following these steps:
1. Map each line in {{LINEAS_PRESUPUESTO}} to its primary operational driver from {{DRIVERS_DISPONIBLES}} and classify its behavior: fixed, variable, or semi-variable (step-fixed). When a line responds to two drivers, declare the primary and treat the secondary as an adjustment.
2. For each variable and semi-variable line, define the calculation formula (driver times unit rate, plus fixed component when applicable) using rates from {{TASAS_HISTORICAS}}. For step-fixed, declare the step: driver range and cost jump when it is crossed.
3. Build the driver cascade separating root drivers (projected directly) from derived drivers (calculated from others) and verify there are no circular dependencies; order the calculation from root to derived.
4. Build the recalculable budget in {{HORIZONTE}} and {{MONEDA}}, showing per line: associated driver, unit rate, fixed component, formula, and base scenario amount. Calculate contribution margin (revenue minus variable costs) and EBITDA.
5. Deliver a sensitivity table showing revenue, costs, contribution margin, and EBITDA across {{RANGOS_SENSIBILIDAD}} variations of key drivers; identify the driver with the greatest operational leverage.
6. Document assumptions, model risks (rate linearity, relevant range where it breaks down, correlated drivers that break simple aggregation, step-fixed near its next step), and control checkpoints for reviewing rates.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 – Diagnosis: read {{LINEAS_PRESUPUESTO}}, {{DRIVERS_DISPONIBLES}}, {{TASAS_HISTORICAS}}, and {{ADJUNTOS}}; identify gaps. If line detail, drivers, rates, horizon, or currency are missing, ask in a single round before modeling. Do not invent figures; mark every assumption with [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 – Mapping and classification: associate driver and cost behavior with each line; isolate the fixed component of semi-variable costs (high-low point method if two observations are available, or a declared [SUPUESTO] if not).
Phase 3 – Formulation: derive missing unit rates as base amount divided by historical driver where possible; order the root-to-derived cascade without cycles and declare the calculation order.
Phase 4 – Build and sensitivity: assemble the base model, reconcile it against current totals (difference less than 1% or explained with [SUPUESTO]), and run the sensitivity table on the highest-impact drivers, verifying sign coherence.
Phase 5 – Close: write up assumptions, risks, and control checkpoints; explain how to reforecast by changing a single driver. Do not include market prices or external quotes.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- Each line in {{LINEAS_PRESUPUESTO}} has an assigned driver and a fixed / variable / semi-variable classification; lines with two drivers declare primary and secondary.
- Each variable or semi-variable line has an explicit formula and a declared unit rate; step-fixed lines declare range and step amount.
- The driver cascade distinguishes root from derived, declares calculation order, and contains no circular dependencies.
- Base scenario amounts reconcile with current totals (difference less than 1% or explained with [SUPUESTO]).
- The sensitivity table covers revenue, costs, contribution margin, and EBITDA, with coherent signs, and identifies the driver with the greatest leverage.
- Assumptions marked [SUPUESTO], model risks, and control checkpoints documented; no market prices.

--- S | SITUATION ---
The management of {{UNIDAD_NEGOCIO}} controls spending against a static budget that assumes a single activity level, so any variance mixes the volume effect with the efficiency effect, and control conversations end up being unfair or unactionable: an area may spend more simply because it produced more, and still be highly efficient. Building a flexible budget recalibrates expected spending to actual volume achieved and unlocks clean management control: it isolates how much of the variance is explained by doing more or less activity and how much by managing costs better or worse, enabling decisions about efficiency, capacity sizing, and scenario planning.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior financial controller (FP&A) expert in management accounting, flexible budgeting, and variance analysis, with command of cost behavior and the cost-volume-profit model.

Deliverable: a flexible budget model by activity tiers with formulas by item, three-way variance analysis (when actual data is available), and an executive summary. Steps:
1. Confirm the driver {{INDUCTOR_ACTIVIDAD}} and the {{RANGO_RELEVANTE}} where cost relationships are stable; if the proposed driver correlates weakly with spending, suggest a better one.
2. Classify each item in {{PARTIDAS_COSTO}} as fixed, variable, or semi-variable, with an explicit criterion.
3. For semi-variable items, separate the fixed and variable components using the high-low method or regression if sufficient history exists; report R-squared or the method's limitation; if no data is available, flag the assumption.
4. Calculate the variable rate per driver unit for each variable item and the fixed amount per period for each fixed item.
5. Build the master formula: Total budgeted cost = Total fixed costs + (variable rate per unit x actual volume).
6. Generate the flexible budget table for the {{NIVELES_ACTIVIDAD}}, with {{VOLUMEN_ESPERADO}} as the base case, and include the total unit cost per tier to reveal operational leverage.
7. If actual results are provided, build the three-way analysis (static vs. flexible = volume variance; flexible vs. actual = spending/efficiency variance) and mark each variance as favorable or unfavorable, verifying they sum to the total variance.
8. Calculate the breakeven point in driver units and the margin of safety relative to {{VOLUMEN_ESPERADO}}; if no price or contribution margin is available, ask for it or mark it as [SUPUESTO].

Phase 1 – Cost behavior classification: order each item as fixed/variable/semi-variable and document the criterion; flag ambiguous ones (e.g., step costs) and explain how you will treat them.
Phase 2 – Rate estimation: derive variable rate per unit and fixed amount per period; for semi-variable items apply the high-low method or regression and make the separation and its reliability explicit.
Phase 3 – Build the flexible model: apply the master formula for each tier in {{NIVELES_ACTIVIDAD}}, build the comparative table by tier with total and unit cost, and warn if any tier falls outside {{RANGO_RELEVANTE}}.
Phase 4 – Variance analysis and CVP: if actuals are available, decompose volume variance and spending variance; calculate breakeven point and margin of safety; close with an actionable executive summary that ties each variance to a decision.

--- S | SITUATION ---
The budget for {{HORIZONTE_PLANEACION}} is being planned and the disbursements in {{LISTA_DESEMBOLSOS}} are mixed without distinguishing investment from expense. Misclassifying an item distorts operating income, EBITDA, the asset base, and the cash projection, inflates or deflates covenants, and can violate {{MARCO_CONTABLE}}. Separating CapEx from OpEx with an auditable criterion unlocks a budget that is defensible before management, treasury, and audit, and reveals the true cash profile of the cycle: when the disbursement hurts versus when it hits the income statement.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior financial controller with experience in budget planning, capitalization policies, and accounting close under {{MARCO_CONTABLE}}.
Deliverable: CapEx/OpEx classification, disbursement schedule, depreciation schedule, and projected impact on all three financial statements. Steps:
1. Apply the capitalization decision tree to each item in {{LISTA_DESEMBOLSOS}}: it is CapEx only if it creates or improves a long-lived asset, the economic benefit extends beyond one fiscal year, and it exceeds {{UMBRAL_CAPITALIZACION}} (minimum amount and useful life); otherwise it is OpEx.
2. Flag and justify borderline cases under {{MARCO_CONTABLE}}: major maintenance vs. repair, software (license/SaaS vs. capitalizable development), finance lease vs. operating lease, leasehold improvements, R&D (research vs. development), cloud implementation costs, and pre-operating expenses.
3. For each CapEx item, define useful life, depreciation/amortization method (from {{POLITICAS_DEPRECIACION}}), residual value if applicable, and month placed in service; distinguish disbursement date from depreciation start date.
4. Build the monthly cash disbursement schedule for {{HORIZONTE_PLANEACION}}, separating CapEx and OpEx; reflect VAT or recoverable tax if known and payment milestones.
5. Project the impact: income statement (full OpEx plus depreciation of CapEx), balance sheet (gross asset, accumulated depreciation, net, and liability if financing exists), and cash flow (CapEx in investing, OpEx in operating, debt service in financing).
6. Reconcile that the sum of disbursements ties to the projected cash flow and explain the accrual-to-cash gap. Deliver classification table, both schedules, and a three-reading summary: effect on operating income, on cash, and on assets, with the list of assumptions.
7. Close with two sensitivity analyses: treating an ambiguous item as OpEx instead of CapEx, and accelerating or delaying a placed-in-service date.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 – Framing: confirm {{MARCO_CONTABLE}}, {{UMBRAL_CAPITALIZACION}}, and {{HORIZONTE_PLANEACION}}; if a critical data point is missing, ask for it before executing.
Phase 2 – Classification: run the decision tree item by item; document the criterion for each borderline case with a reference to {{MARCO_CONTABLE}}.
Phase 3 – Schedule: build the disbursement schedule and the depreciation schedule derived from placed-in-service dates.
Phase 4 – Projection: carry CapEx and OpEx through all three statements and reconcile that the sum of cash disbursements ties to the projected cash flow.
Phase 5 – Synthesis and sensitivity: write the three readings, run the two sensitivity analyses, and list the [SUPUESTO] items used.
Do not invent figures, useful lives, or rates: any data not provided is marked [SUPUESTO]. If an item cannot be classified without additional information, declare it pending rather than forcing a classification.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each item in {{LISTA_DESEMBOLSOS}} is classified as CapEx or OpEx with an explicit criterion, or marked as pending due to missing data.

spec-finanzas_presupuesto_departamental:
[inputs]
- ORGANIZACION: {{ORGANIZACION}} > Company, unit, or area whose budget is being distributed

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The organization needs to convert a global budget into governed departmental envelopes — not a simple arithmetic split. The deliverable unlocks three things: clear accountability (every dollar has a named owner), spending control (caps and alerts before the overage), and disciplined agility (reallocation rules that avoid bottlenecks without losing traceability). It serves for financial committee approval and for month-by-month tracking. Without explicit governance, the budget becomes unreadable mid-period: no one knows who authorized what, envelopes drain without warning, and reallocations happen via email with no trail.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior financial controller specialized in FP&A and cost-center budgeting, with experience in spending governance and zero-based budgeting.
Deliverable: departmental budget plan with owners, caps, and reallocation rules. Steps:
1. Build the master allocation table by cost center: name, allocated amount, percentage of total, named single owner, and criterion justifying the amount. The sum must tie to PRESUPUESTO_GLOBAL; report the reconciliation and any residual.
2. Open each cost center into spending lines (personnel, operations, technology, marketing, local contingency, or others as relevant). Distinguish committed fixed spending from discretionary spending, because only discretionary spending is truly reallocatable.
3. Define for each line a hard cap (not exceedable without approval) and a soft cap (alert threshold, e.g., 80 percent) with the specific action each triggers (who receives the alert, within what timeframe, what is decided).
4. Specify reallocation rules at three tiers: what the owner can move unilaterally, what requires supervisor approval, and what escalates to committee; each tier with limits in amount AND as a percentage of the envelope, and with the data that must be recorded to leave a trail (date, source, destination, rationale, approver).
5. Reserve a central contingency (percentage of the global) and define its release criterion, approver, and what happens to the remainder at period close.
6. Define the review cycle (monthly/quarterly), the budget approval workflow, and, if HORIZONTE_FASEADO applies, the fund-release calendar by phase.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 – Framing: validate PRESUPUESTO_GLOBAL, DEPARTAMENTOS, owners, and PERIODO; if a critical data point is missing, ask for it and do NOT invent figures.
Phase 2 – Allocation: apply CRITERIOS_ASIGNACION to distribute; if not provided, propose a base method (history adjusted for priorities) and mark it [SUPUESTO] with its logic.
Phase 3 – Opening and control: break down lines, separate fixed from discretionary, set hard/soft caps and alerts.
Phase 4 – Governance: draft three-tier reallocation rules, the central contingency, and the traceability record.
Phase 5 – Close: consolidate the master table, verify the reconciliation to the cent, and issue the risk note.
Edge cases: if the sum of criteria does not reach 100 percent, assign the residual to contingency and report it; if a cost center has no owner, mark it {to_be_confirmed} and do not close; if CRITERIOS_ASIGNACION conflict with each other (e.g., headcount vs. strategic priority), present both readings and ask for the tiebreaker.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The sum of allocations plus contingency ties exactly to PRESUPUESTO_GLOBAL and the reconciliation (and residual) is reported.
- [ ] Each cost center has a single named owner and an explicit amount criterion; centers without an owner are marked {to_be_confirmed}.
- [ ] Each line separates committed fixed from discretionary and has a hard cap and a soft cap with an alert action (recipient, timeframe, decision).
- [ ] The reallocation rules distinguish three tiers with limits in amount AND percentage, with no ambiguity about who approves, and define the trail that must be recorded.
- [ ] The central contingency has a percentage, release criterion, approver, and disposition of the remainder.
- [ ] All data not provided is marked [SUPUESTO] with its basis; zero invented figures presented as real.
Expected deliverable: master allocation table ready for approval (balanced to the cent), reallocation rules and caps annex, phased release calendar if applicable, and a risk note with the three most likely overrun risks and their concrete mitigations.
spec-finanzas_presupuesto_proyecto_wbs:
