Expected deliverable: table by segment (revenue, gross margin, each cost-to-serve block, net margin, % over revenue) + true profitability ranking + the 3 drivers that most explain the differences + quadrant matrix + 3 to 5 prioritized actions with assigned segment and estimated margin impact.
spec-finanzas_optimizacion_costos_estruc:
[inputs]
- ALCANCE_GASTO: {{ALCANCE_GASTO}} > Scope of the cost base to optimize: unit, area, categories or accounts included, with amounts if available
- PERIODO_BASELINE: {{PERIODO_BASELINE}} > Reference period against which savings are measured (e.g. last 12 months, fiscal year)
- OBJETIVO_AHORRO: {{OBJETIVO_AHORRO}} > Savings target as a percentage or amount, and the time horizon
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Non-negotiable limits: untouchable areas or contracts, service levels to preserve, workforce sensitivities (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Linear cuts destroy value: they cut muscle along with fat and the cost returns in one or two quarters. A structural optimization program is needed to reduce the cost base sustainably, protecting operational capacity and service levels. A well-designed program unlocks reinvestable margin, improves resilience under revenue pressure, and gives leadership a defensible roadmap with quantified savings and explicit risk — rather than a reactive slash.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Finance and Operations Director, specialized in cost transformation, with expertise in zero-based budgeting, value lever analysis, and StrategyAI applied to prioritization.

Deliverable: a prioritized, wave-based cost optimization program. Steps:
1. Decompose ALCANCE_GASTO by category, nature (fixed/variable, direct/indirect, discretionary/committed), and process; identify concentrations (80/20 rule) and avoidable spending pools against PERIODO_BASELINE.
2. Build the inventory of structural lever candidates: contract renegotiation, supplier consolidation, process redesign and automation, portfolio/SKU rationalization, energy efficiency, workforce reallocation, elimination of duplicates, demand and specification (should-cost) optimization.
3. Quantify each lever: estimated annual savings, recurring vs. one-time, implementation cost (one-off), effort, time to first impact, and risk level (operational, contractual, service, reputational).
4. Prioritize using an impact-effort matrix; separate quick wins (high impact, low effort) from structural initiatives (high impact, high effort) and discard traps (low impact, high effort).
5. Organize the program into waves (0–3, 3–9, 9–18 months) with a cumulative savings target against OBJETIVO_AHORRO, dependencies, suggested owner, and a tracking signal per lever.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Mapping: structure the cost base and locate where spending lives.
Phase 2 Diagnosis: match each spending pool with applicable levers and rule out anything that violates RESTRICCIONES.
Phase 3 Quantification: estimate net savings (gross minus implementation cost) and risk per lever; every figure not provided by the user is marked [SUPUESTO] with its calculation logic and range.
Phase 4 Prioritization: apply the impact-effort matrix and sequence the waves until the gap against OBJETIVO_AHORRO is closed; if it does not close, declare the shortfall and propose additional levers or a target adjustment.
Phase 5 Packaging: consolidate the program, dependencies, residual risks, and follow-up plan (KPIs and cadence).
Edge cases: if ALCANCE_GASTO comes without amounts, work with percentages and structure and request the data for quantification; if OBJETIVO_AHORRO is unachievable without touching RESTRICCIONES, state it explicitly and show the trade-off.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Cost base decomposed by category, nature, and process, with concentrations flagged.
- [ ] Each lever quantified by annual savings, recurring vs. one-time, implementation cost, effort, time to impact, and risk.
- [ ] Net savings (not just gross) used for prioritization; every figure not provided marked [SUPUESTO] with logic and range; zero invented amounts.
- [ ] Impact-effort matrix with quick wins, structural initiatives, and traps separated.
- [ ] Wave plan with cumulative savings against OBJETIVO_AHORRO, dependencies, and owner per lever.
- [ ] RESTRICCIONES respected; gap against the target resolved or declared; residual risks explicit.
Expected deliverable: prioritized lever table + impact-effort matrix + wave plan with cumulative savings targets and suggested owner, ready for committee decision.
spec-finanzas_cost_to_serve_logistico:
[inputs]
- ALCANCE: {{ALCANCE}} > Channel/segment and period to cost (e.g. "B2C e-commerce, Q1 2026"). Defines the costing unit (one order) and the time window of costs.
- VOLUMEN_PEDIDOS: {{VOLUMEN_PEDIDOS}} > Number of orders in the period and average ticket; include contribution margin per order if available.
- COSTOS_LOGISTICOS: {{COSTOS_LOGISTICOS}} > Cost pools for the period: storage, picking/labor, last-mile, reverse logistics. Indicate whether they are direct costs or include allocated fixed costs.
- DRIVERS: {{DRIVERS}} > Volumes for distributing each pool: sq-ft-day or stored units, lines per order, shipments, processed returns. Ideally actual volume for the period, not installed capacity.
- TASA_DEVOLUCIONES: {{TASA_DEVOLUCIONES}} > % of orders returned and the cost of processing each return (collection + inspection + reconditioning + shrinkage).
- SEGMENTOS: {{SEGMENTOS}} > Cut dimensions for the profitability cross-reference: channel, region, ticket range, SKU type (optional).
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
An average logistics cost per order hides where margin actually goes: two orders with the same ticket can cost very differently depending on how much warehouse space they occupy, how many picking lines they have, which zone they ship to, and whether they end up returned. Costing each order by activity unlocks decisions on shipping pricing, returns policy, network design, and profitable customer segmentation. This analysis converts aggregate operating figures into an actionable unit cost per component, with the traceability needed to defend every figure to finance and operations.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior cost-to-serve and logistics operations analyst, expert in activity-based costing (ABC) applied to e-commerce fulfillment and distribution.
Deliverable: the unit logistics cost per order broken down into storage, picking, last-mile, and returns, with a profitability cross-reference by segment and prioritized optimization levers. Steps:
1. Restate the scope: "Calculate the unit logistics cost per order for {{ALCANCE}}, broken down into storage, picking, last-mile, and returns." Verify that you have {{VOLUMEN_PEDIDOS}}, {{COSTOS_LOGISTICOS}}, {{DRIVERS}}, and {{TASA_DEVOLUCIONES}}; if something essential is missing, ask for it before calculating and do not invent figures (mark every estimate [SUPUESTO] with its value and source).
2. Verify consistency: confirm that the pools and drivers cover the same period and that the sum of assigned costs reconciles against the total logistics spend for the period. If the drivers reflect capacity rather than actual volume, separate the cost of used vs. idle capacity and do not load idleness onto the order without flagging it.
3. For each of the 4 components choose a defensible activity driver from {{DRIVERS}}: storage by sq-ft-day or unit-day; picking by line or unit; last-mile by shipment (adjusted for zone/weight if data is available); returns by returned order including collection, inspection, reconditioning, and shrinkage. Justify in one line why that driver and not another.
4. Calculate the rate for each activity (pool cost / driver volume) and the unit cost per order for each component, showing the formula and numbers.
5. Sum the total unit logistics cost per order and express it in absolute terms, as a % of ticket from {{VOLUMEN_PEDIDOS}}, and as a % of contribution margin per order.
6. Deliver the decomposition table (component, driver, rate, unit cost, % of total) sorted by weight and flag the 2–3 dominant components.
7. Cross-reference profitability by {{SEGMENTOS}} with the actual logistics cost loaded and flag which segments are served at a loss; use {{TASA_DEVOLUCIONES}} to detect segments distorted by reverse logistics. If a segment concentrates returns, recost it with its own rate, not the average.
8. Close with 3 to 5 levers prioritized by impact/effort: component attacked, mechanism (consolidate shipments, minimum ticket for free shipping, picking slotting, zone-based fee, returns policy), estimated unit savings, assumption to validate, and side effect to monitor (e.g. a minimum ticket raises margin but may trim volume).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: fix the costing unit (one order), the period, and the 4 cost pools; validate completeness and reconciliation against total spend.
Phase 2 - ABC assignment: map each pool to its driver, justify the choice, calculate activity rates and unit costs per component.
Phase 3 - Consolidation: build the total unit cost, its weight on ticket and margin, and the sorted decomposition table.
Phase 4 - Diagnosis and levers: run the profitability cross-reference by segment, recost segments distorted by returns, and derive prioritized levers with savings and side effects.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- All 4 components (storage, picking, last-mile, returns) are costed with an explicit, justified driver and a visible formula.
- The sum of assigned costs reconciles against the total logistics spend for the period; any gap (idle capacity, unassigned cost) is named.
- Every figure not provided by the user is marked [SUPUESTO] with value and source; in particular unmeasured unit return costs and all allocated fixed costs.
- The total unit cost is expressed in absolute terms and as a % of ticket and of contribution margin.
- The decomposition table is sorted by weight and identifies the dominant components.
- The profitability cross-reference names at least one segment served at a loss (or confirms that none is, with evidence) and recosts segments distorted by reverse logistics.
- Levers are prioritized by impact/effort, each with estimated unit savings, assumption to validate, and side effect to monitor.
Expected deliverable: report with unit cost per order decomposition table, profitability reading by segment, and 3 to 5 actionable optimization levers.
spec-finanzas_make_vs_buy:
[inputs]
- ACTIVIDAD_O_COMPONENTE: {{ACTIVIDAD_O_COMPONENTE}} > Activity, part, or service being evaluated under make-vs-buy (e.g. manufacturing a sub-assembly, tier-1 technical support, payroll, content moderation)
- VOLUMEN: {{VOLUMEN}} > Relevant volume and horizon for the decision (units, transactions, or hours per period); indicate whether stable, seasonal, or growing
- COSTOS_VARIABLES_INTERNOS: {{COSTOS_VARIABLES_INTERNOS}} > Variable costs of producing internally: materials, direct labor, energy, waste; express per unit or as a total at a known volume
- COSTOS_FIJOS_EVITABLES: {{COSTOS_FIJOS_EVITABLES}} > Fixed costs that truly disappear if production stops (dedicated supervisor, specific equipment maintenance, exclusive license); exclude common fixed costs that persist and sunk costs
- PRECIO_PROVEEDOR: {{PRECIO_PROVEEDOR}} > Unit or total price from the external supplier and conditions (minimums, volume tiers, validity); include or describe transaction costs (logistics, inbound QA, safety stock, contract management) if known
- CAPACIDAD_Y_USO_ALTERNATIVO: {{CAPACIDAD_Y_USO_ALTERNATIVO}} > (optional) Available internal capacity and contribution margin of the best alternative use if freed up; basis for the opportunity cost. If capacity would remain idle with no profitable use, the opportunity cost is zero
- FACTORES_CUALITATIVOS: {{FACTORES_CUALITATIVOS}} > (optional) Quality control, supplier dependency and bargaining power, intellectual property, confidentiality, flexibility for peak demand, labor impact, service continuity
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You face a make-vs-buy decision for {{ACTIVIDAD_O_COMPONENTE}}: produce internally or outsource. Most of these decisions are made poorly due to three errors: (a) comparing total accounting costs (with common fixed and sunk costs included) rather than relevant costs (only those that change with the decision); (b) ignoring the opportunity cost of freed-up capacity; and (c) looking only at the supplier price without adding the transaction costs of outsourcing. A correct analysis produces a defensible recommendation to finance and operations, prevents margin destruction from outsourcing what should have stayed in-house, and reveals the volume at which the decision reverses.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior cost and operations analyst, expert in relevant cost accounting and make-vs-buy decisions in manufacturing and services.
Deliver:
1. Restate the activity evaluated, the volume and its horizon, and the available data; list the essential missing data and ask for it before calculating. Do not proceed with calculation if a critical variable is missing (supplier price, internal variable costs, or volume).
2. Classify costs as avoidable vs. non-avoidable: isolate {{COSTOS_VARIABLES_INTERNOS}} and {{COSTOS_FIJOS_EVITABLES}}; explicitly declare which sunk costs (investments already made) and common fixed costs (those that persist in both scenarios) are excluded, with one line of justification per relevant exclusion.
3. Incorporate the opportunity cost of capacity: if making internally occupies {{CAPACIDAD_Y_USO_ALTERNATIVO}} with margin, add it to the cost of making; if capacity would remain idle with no profitable use, declare it at zero and justify.
4. Calculate the relevant unit and total cost of MAKING and BUYING ({{PRECIO_PROVEEDOR}} plus transaction costs: logistics, inbound QA, safety stock, contract management, non-compliance risk) for {{VOLUMEN}}. If the supplier has volume tiers or minimums, reflect the effective price at the evaluated volume.
5. Calculate the indifference point in units where the cost of making equals the cost of buying, and interpret which side the current volume falls on and how close it is to the crossover (safety margin).
6. Build a recommendation that weighs {{FACTORES_CUALITATIVOS}} and risk factors, with the quantitative and qualitative conditions under which it would change.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: restate the activity, volume, horizon, and assumptions; request missing data and do not invent critical ones.
Phase 2 - Relevant costs: separate avoidable from non-avoidable; discard sunk and common fixed costs with explicit justification per exclusion.
Phase 3 - Capacity: quantify opportunity cost only if capacity has a profitable alternative use; if idle, justified zero.
Phase 4 - Comparison: relevant cost table (unit and total) per option at the given volume, with subtotals by component (variable, avoidable fixed, opportunity, transaction).
Phase 5 - Indifference point and sensitivity: solve the crossover, express the safety margin against the current volume, and move the 2–3 highest-impact variables (supplier price, internal variable costs, volume) showing how the decision shifts.
Phase 6 - Decision: recommendation with quantitative + qualitative + reversal conditions (price, volume, or quality that would reverse the decision).
Rules: mark every estimate of your own as [SUPUESTO]; do not invent market prices or monetary figures; use only those provided or leave as variables. Distinguish a one-time decision from a long-term contract: the longer the horizon, the more fixed costs become avoidable. If data comes as totals, normalize to unit (and vice versa) declaring the base volume.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Sunk costs and non-avoidable common fixed costs are explicitly excluded, with justification per exclusion.
- [ ] The opportunity cost of capacity is included only if there is a profitable alternative use; otherwise declared at zero with justification.
- [ ] The cost of buying incorporates transaction costs, not just the supplier price; volume tiers or minimums are reflected at the evaluated volume.
- [ ] The indifference point is calculated and interpreted against the current volume, with safety margin.
- [ ] The sensitivity analysis covers the 2–3 highest-impact variables and shows the shift in the decision.
- [ ] Every estimate of your own is marked [SUPUESTO]; no invented monetary figures or market prices.
- [ ] The recommendation integrates qualitative and risk factors and defines concrete reversal conditions.
- [ ] If applicable, a one-time decision is distinguished from a long-term contract and its effect on which costs are avoidable.
Expected deliverable: comparative table of relevant costs per option (unit and total, with subtotals by component), indifference point in units with safety margin, sensitivity analysis on key variables, and actionable make-vs-buy recommendation with change conditions.
spec-finanzas_spend_analysis_compras:
[inputs]
- PERIODO: {{PERIODO}} > Time range of the analysis (e.g. fiscal year, last 12 months, quarter); must be a single period
- DIVISA: {{DIVISA}} > Single reporting currency; if the data contains multiple currencies, the exchange rate is requested and not assumed
- FUENTE_DATOS: {{FUENTE_DATOS}} > Source of the spend data (purchase orders, invoices, ERP, general ledger, attached file) and level of granularity available
- UNIDAD_NEGOCIO: {{UNIDAD_NEGOCIO}} > Organizational scope (full company, business unit, region, cost centers) (optional)
- TAXONOMIA_FAMILIAS: {{TAXONOMIA_FAMILIAS}} > Spend family or category scheme to use; if none exists, one is proposed and documented (optional)
- OBJETIVO_AHORRO: {{OBJETIVO_AHORRO}} > Savings and consolidation target or focus that guides prioritization (optional)
- CONTRATOS_VIGENTES: {{CONTRATOS_VIGENTES}} > Suppliers or families with an active contract or framework agreement, to distinguish off-contract spend (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Procurement spend is typically fragmented across many suppliers and families with no unified view, which hides concentration risk, duplication, tail spend, and price leakage. Consolidating spend into a spend cube unlocks category decisions: who to negotiate with, which suppliers to rationalize, and where to capture savings without disrupting operations. The result enables an evidence-based sourcing strategy conversation and a prioritized consolidation initiative backlog.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior procurement and category management analyst with experience in spend analytics, spend cube construction, and supplier base consolidation strategies.
Deliver a procurement spend analysis for {{PERIODO}} covering {{UNIDAD_NEGOCIO}}, in {{DIVISA}}, from {{FUENTE_DATOS}}, with these steps:
1. Validate the data: period coverage, single currency, line-level granularity (quantity, unit price, item, date), and supplier and family completeness; list gaps and assumptions before calculating.
2. Normalize suppliers (consolidate legal names, branches, and subsidiaries under a parent supplier) and classify each line into a family according to {{TAXONOMIA_FAMILIAS}} or a proposed taxonomy; report the percentage of unclassified spend.
3. Build the spend cube in three dimensions: supplier x family x business unit or cost center.
4. Calculate total spend, spend by family and by supplier, 80/20 Pareto ranking, and ABC classification of suppliers and families.
5. Measure concentration by family using the HHI (with interpretation threshold: low / moderate / high) and identify single-supplier critical dependencies.
6. Detect tail spend, maverick or off-contract spend against {{CONTRATOS_VIGENTES}}, supplier duplication within a family, and leakage (inconsistent prices for the same item, order splitting, dispersed buying).
7. Estimate consolidation and savings opportunities as a reasoned percentage range per family against {{OBJETIVO_AHORRO}}, separating compliance savings (capturable internally) from negotiated savings (requires counterparty) and marking each estimated figure with [SUPUESTO].

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Cleansing: clean, deduplicate, and normalize suppliers and families; document mapping rules and percentage unclassified.
Phase 2 Cube: aggregate spend in the three dimensions and produce views by family and by supplier.
Phase 3 Diagnosis: apply Pareto/ABC, calculate HHI by family with its threshold, and isolate tail spend and leakage signals.
Phase 4 Opportunity: translate findings into consolidation initiatives with estimated impact, effort, dependency, and lever (consolidation, volume negotiation, item standardization, contract compliance), prioritized by impact over effort.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- A single period and a single currency; multiple currencies are flagged and the exchange rate is requested, not assumed.
- Suppliers normalized to group level and each line classified into a family; percentage of unclassified spend reported.
- 80/20 Pareto and ABC present for both suppliers and families.
- HHI calculated by family with interpretation threshold and critical dependencies flagged.
- Tail spend, off-contract spend, and leakage (price, splitting, dispersion) identified with evidence, not just stated.
- Every savings figure marked [SUPUESTO] with explicit logic and classified as compliance or negotiated; zero invented figures.
- Data gaps listed as actionable questions.
Edge cases: if currency is not single, stop aggregate calculation and request rate; if granularity does not reach item level, limit price leakage detection and declare it; if period coverage is partial, annualize only with an explicit [SUPUESTO].
Expected deliverable: (1) executive summary with the three highest-impact findings, (2) spend cube table by family and top supplier, (3) HHI concentration matrix with critical dependencies, (4) prioritized backlog of consolidation and leakage-reduction opportunities with impact, effort, dependency, and lever, (5) questions and missing data to close the analysis.
spec-finanzas_sop_proceso_estandar:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_PROCESO: {{NOMBRE_PROCESO}} > Name of the operational process to document (e.g. monthly bank reconciliation, supplier onboarding)
- DUENO_PROCESO: {{DUENO_PROCESO}} > Role or area that owns the process and approves the SOP
- DISPARADOR: {{DISPARADOR}} > Event or condition that initiates the process (e.g. month-end close, received request)
- SISTEMAS: {{SISTEMAS}} > Systems, tools, and repositories involved (ERP, spreadsheet, shared folder)
- FRECUENCIA: {{FRECUENCIA}} > How often the process is executed (daily, weekly, monthly, event-based)
- CONTROLES_REGULATORIOS: {{CONTROLES_REGULATORIOS}} > Applicable regulations, internal policies, or audit requirements (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A critical operational process currently lives in the memory of a few people and is not documented: it creates individual dependency, handoff errors, audit findings, and delays when onboarding new staff. Documenting it as a standard SOP standardizes execution, enables safe delegation, sustains traceability for audits, and frees the process owner to focus on improvement rather than firefighting. The SOP must serve equally to train a new hire, to execute under period-close pressure, and to respond to an internal controls finding.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior operational excellence manager with experience documenting auditable standard procedures (SOPs) in finance and operations, trained in internal control discipline and process improvement.
Deliverable: a complete, publish-ready SOP for the process {{NOMBRE_PROCESO}}, owner {{DUENO_PROCESO}}, initiated by {{DISPARADOR}}, executed using {{SISTEMAS}}, frequency {{FRECUENCIA}}, subject to {{CONTROLES_REGULATORIOS}}. Structure it in these 10 numbered sections:
1. Control header: code, title, version, effective date, owner, approver, and next review.
2. Purpose and scope: the problem it solves, start and end boundaries, and explicit exclusions (what it does NOT cover).
3. Roles and responsibilities: RACI matrix (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) by key activity, with a definition of each role.
4. Inputs and prerequisites: inputs, accesses, systems, and data required before starting, and how to obtain them.
5. Step-by-step procedure: numbered steps with executing role, concrete action in imperative form, system, and target time; mark decision points with their criterion (yes/no) and resulting path.
6. Outputs and deliverables: what the process produces, format, storage location, and retention period.
7. Quality controls and checkpoints: validations, acceptance criteria, segregation of duties (the executor does not approve), and evidence retained (what, where, how long).
8. Exception handling and escalation: what to do in the event of common failures, threshold that triggers escalation, to whom to escalate, and expected response time.
9. Indicators: 2 to 4 measurable metrics with name, formula, target, and measurement frequency.
10. Change log: table of version + date + author + description of change.
Use imperative and verifiable language; each step with one unambiguous responsible party. NEVER include amounts, prices, or cost figures: document the flow and controls, not monetary values.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Mapping: reconstruct the end-to-end flow from {{DISPARADOR}} to the final output, identifying actors, systems, data, and decision points.
Phase 2 - Structure: assign RACI by activity, with no two Responsibles for the same step; separate duties where there is a control risk (executor distinct from approver).
Phase 3 - Drafting: write steps in imperative form, one per atomic action, with role, system, and target time; resolve each decision with its explicit criterion.
Phase 4 - Hardening: incorporate quality controls, acceptance criteria, retained evidence, exception paths with escalation threshold; define actionable indicators with formula and target.
Phase 5 - Closing: complete the control header and change log. Mark every inference as [SUPUESTO]; if an essential process data point is missing, ask before drafting rather than inventing it. Flag the points where you recommend additional evidence or process owner validation.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Complete control header (code, version, effective date, owner, approver, next review).
- Scope with explicit start and end boundaries and exclusions.
- Unambiguous RACI: one single Responsible per activity and at least one Accountable; segregation of duties where applicable.
- Each step is imperative, atomic, with executing role, system, and target time; decision points with explicit criterion.
- Controls include acceptance criteria, segregation of duties, and retained evidence (what/where/how long).
- Exception paths and escalation defined with threshold, recipient, and response time.
- 2 to 4 measurable indicators with formula, target, and frequency.
- No amounts, prices, or cost figures.
- Zero invented data; every inference marked [SUPUESTO]; gaps converted into questions.
Expected deliverable: SOP for {{NOMBRE_PROCESO}} in 10 sections, ready to publish and train the team, capable of withstanding an internal controls audit.
spec-finanzas_mapeo_proceso_sipoc:
[inputs]
- PROCESO: {{PROCESO}} > Name of the process to map and what it does (what it transforms and for what purpose)
- FRONTERAS: {{FRONTERAS}} > Event that triggers the process (start) and deliverable that closes it (end); defines scope
- PASOS_CONOCIDOS: {{PASOS_CONOCIDOS}} > Steps or areas the requester already knows (optional; if missing, the model proposes high-level steps and marks them as proposed)
- CLIENTE_REQUISITOS: {{CLIENTE_REQUISITOS}} > Primary customer of the output and what they expect from it to accept it (voice of the customer / CTQ)
- PROPOSITO: {{PROPOSITO}} > Reason for mapping the process and what is unlocked by agreeing on scope (measure, redesign, document SOP, automate)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The requester needs to delimit the process {{PROCESO}} before measuring or intervening in it: without clear boundaries, any diagnosis, SOP, or automation is built on sand. The purpose of this mapping is to produce a SIPOC, the bird's-eye view that fixes what enters, what exits, who supplies it, and who consumes it, and puts in writing where the process starts and where it ends. Agreeing on this scope ({{PROPOSITO}}) unlocks the following phases (time measurement, bottleneck analysis, redesign) without later disputes about what was or was not included, and aligns stakeholders on a single page. EstrategIA contributes the rigor of the Lean framing before touching the process.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior process and operations analyst, expert in Lean Six Sigma, SIPOC mapping, and voice of the customer (CTQ), with a focus on delimiting scope before measuring.
Deliver the following, in this order:
1. Restate {{PROCESO}} in one sentence: "Process of [verb + object], which starts at [start] and ends at [end]", using {{FRONTERAS}}; if the name, start, or end is missing, ask for them before executing.
2. Declare the explicit boundaries (start/stop) and name at least one element outside scope.
3. Describe the PROCESS as 4 to 7 high-level steps in sequence (verb + object) from {{PASOS_CONOCIDOS}}; if they are empty, propose them and mark them as proposed. Altitude test: if a step describes a click, a screen, or a sub-task, raise its altitude or merge it. Do not descend to sub-tasks.
4. List the tangible, nameable OUTPUTS (products, documents, decisions) the process delivers.
5. Assign CUSTOMERS to each output and, for the primary customer, derive 2 to 4 measurable or verifiable CTQ requirements from {{CLIENTE_REQUISITOS}}; no generic CTQs such as "fast" or "quality".
6. List the INPUTS the process consumes to start and operate.
7. Assign SUPPLIERS to each input (internal, external, or systems).
8. Build the SIPOC table with 5 columns (Suppliers | Inputs | Process | Outputs | Customers) and verify traceability: each input with a supplier, each output with a customer; flag the gaps.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: define the process in one sentence and set start/stop; if the name or any boundary is missing, ask before executing and do not invent steps. If a boundary is fuzzy, propose one and mark it as a decision to confirm with the owner.
Phase 2 - Process (P): describe 4 to 7 high-level steps in sequence; no sub-tasks or clicks. If more than 7 emerge, add them; if fewer than 4, reconsider whether scope is too narrow.
Phase 3 - Working backward (O and C): identify OUTPUTS and their CUSTOMERS first, and derive CTQs for the primary customer. SIPOC is best completed from right to left: the customer defines what constitutes a valid output, which prevents inventorying inputs that nobody uses. If an output serves multiple customers with different expectations, separate CTQs by customer.
Phase 4 - Inputs and suppliers (I and S): identify the INPUTS the process consumes and the SUPPLIER for each. If an input is also the output of a previous step in the same process, do not list it as an external input: it is an internal flow.
Phase 5 - Table and traceability: assemble the 5 aligned columns, verify that each input has a supplier and each output has a customer, mark [SUPUESTO] on everything inferred, and flag the gaps detected.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- The process was restated in one sentence with an action verb, with explicit start and end, before assembling the SIPOC.
- Boundaries (start/stop) are declared and at least one element outside scope is named.
- The PROCESS has between 4 and 7 high-level steps in sequence, without descending to sub-tasks, clicks, or screens.
- OUTPUTS are tangible and nameable; each has at least one CUSTOMER assigned.
- The primary customer has 2 to 4 measurable or verifiable CTQ requirements derived from the voice of the customer, not generic ones.
- Each INPUT has an identified SUPPLIER; no orphan inputs or outputs without a customer; internal flows are not listed as external inputs.
- The SIPOC table presents the 5 aligned columns and traceability is verified with gaps flagged.
- Everything inferred is marked [SUPUESTO] and the deliverable closes with the agreed scope in one sentence, 2 to 3 assumptions to confirm with the process owner, and the boundary-validation question.
Expected deliverable: SIPOC table with 5 columns, explicit boundaries, and customer CTQ requirements, plus the agreed scope in one sentence and the assumptions to confirm, in neutral professional English.
spec-finanzas_value_stream_mapping:
[inputs]
- PROCESO: {{PROCESO}} > Operational process to map (e.g., billing, customer onboarding, monthly close)
- DISPARADOR_INICIAL: {{DISPARADOR_INICIAL}} > Event that triggers the process (e.g., "approved purchase order arrives")
- SALIDA_FINAL: {{SALIDA_FINAL}} > Deliverable or state that closes the flow (e.g., "invoice collected and reconciled")
- UNIDAD_DE_VALOR: {{UNIDAD_DE_VALOR}} > What moves through the flow and the customer values (e.g., an invoice, an order, a request)
- PASOS_Y_TIEMPOS: {{PASOS_Y_TIEMPOS}} > List of steps with responsible area and known PT/LT times (optional)
- OBJETIVO_MEJORA: {{OBJETIVO_MEJORA}} > Goal prioritizing improvements (e.g., reduce lead time, lower rework) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to see my operational process as a value flow, not as a task list. Today I cannot distinguish which portion of the total time actually transforms the unit of value and which portion is waiting, queuing, redundant control, or rework. Building the value stream map (VSM) of the current state unlocks evidence-based redesign decisions: it shows where lead time concentrates, how much of that duration is eliminable waste, and how low cycle efficiency is, providing a measurable baseline to justify and prioritize the future state. A weak VSM occurs when waits are hidden inside steps, when times are invented without marking them, or when everything is labeled as value; this assignment prevents all three failures by design.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior lean process engineer with experience in Value Stream Mapping (VSM) under the Toyota / Rother-Shook approach (Learning to See) and Lean metrics (PCE, lead time, takt).
Deliverable: the VSM of the current state of process {{PROCESO}}, with value classification, times, and cycle efficiency, plus prioritized improvement focus areas. Steps:
1. Define scope: {{DISPARADOR_INICIAL}}, {{SALIDA_FINAL}}, and {{UNIDAD_DE_VALOR}}. If multiple units of value are mixed, choose a single family and declare it.
2. List each step in sequence with its responsible area or role, starting from {{PASOS_Y_TIEMPOS}}.
3. For each step capture process time (PT, effective work) and lead time or elapsed time (LT, including prior waits and queues), in a consistent unit.
4. Classify each step as: value-added (transforms the unit and the customer would pay for it), non-value-added but currently necessary (control, compliance, handoff, legal requirement), pure eliminable waste (rework, wait, redundant approval, information transport, overproduction).
5. Model waits and queues between steps as explicit nodes, not embedded in the steps.
6. Calculate total value-added time, total lead time, and cycle efficiency: PCE = value-added time / total lead time. Declare the unit of time and the assumptions used.
7. Present the map as a sequential table and as a textual flow diagram with waits interspersed.
8. Close with the 3 to 5 highest-impact waste focus areas against {{OBJETIVO_MEJORA}} and a future-state hypothesis for each, naming the lean lever (eliminate, automate, parallelize, level, move control upstream).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm scope, unit of value, and step granularity level; if the process has branches or cycles, fix the dominant path.
Phase 2 Data collection: sequence steps, assign responsible parties, and record PT and LT; if a time is missing, use a range and mark it [SUPUESTO], never invent a point-in-time figure; if PT and LT come in different units, normalize before calculating.
Phase 3 Classification: label each step (VA / NVA-necessary / waste) and model waits between steps as nodes.
Phase 4 Metrics: calculate value-added time, total lead time, and PCE with its formula and source data.
Phase 5 Synthesis: prioritize waste focus areas by impact on {{OBJETIVO_MEJORA}} and propose future state with its lean lever; note relevant branches as variants with estimated frequency.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If an essential datum is missing, ask for it specifically before continuing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Explicit scope: trigger, output, and unit of value defined; single family if there were multiple.
- [ ] Each step has a responsible area, PT and LT in a consistent unit.
- [ ] Waits and queues appear as separate nodes, not hidden inside the steps.
- [ ] Every activity is classified as VA / NVA-necessary / waste.
- [ ] PCE calculated and shown with its formula, unit, and source data.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [SUPUESTO]; no invented times (ranges when missing).
- [ ] 3 to 5 prioritized focus areas with an actionable future-state hypothesis and named lean lever.
Expected deliverable: sequential VSM table (step, responsible, PT, LT, classification) + textual flow diagram with waits + metrics block (VA, lead time, PCE) + prioritized list of focus areas with future state, in professional English.
spec-finanzas_rediseno_proceso_bpr:
[inputs]
- PROCESO: {{PROCESO}} > Process to redesign with its trigger and final result (e.g., accounts payable, from invoice receipt to payment)
- OBJETIVO_MEJORA: {{OBJETIVO_MEJORA}} > Priority radical measurable goal (e.g., reduce cycle time 70%, cut cost per transaction in half)
- VOLUMEN: {{VOLUMEN}} > Volume, frequency, and seasonality of the process (e.g., 1,200 invoices/month, peaks at month-end); "(optional)" if not yet known
- SISTEMAS: {{SISTEMAS}} > Systems, tools, and data involved (ERP, spreadsheets, email, RPA) and whether they are integrated or siloed; "(optional)"
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Non-negotiable regulatory and internal-control constraints (segregation of duties, audit traceability, mandatory approvals, document retention)
- CONTEXTO_DOLOR: {{CONTEXTO_DOLOR}} > Symptoms and cost of the current state (rework, waits, errors, complaints, fines) and the trigger for redesign; "(optional)"
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to reconfigure the process {{PROCESO}} from scratch to unlock radical, not incremental, improvements in cost and cycle time. The priority goal is {{OBJETIVO_MEJORA}}. The current process has accumulated steps, controls, and inherited handoffs that nobody has questioned again; the symptom is {{CONTEXTO_DOLOR}}: rework, waits, and hidden cost. Designing the correct TO-BE releases operational capacity, shortens cycles, and delivers an auditable, scalable process without adding headcount. The challenge: gain speed without breaking {{RESTRICCIONES}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior business process reengineering (BPR) consultant, trained in Michael Hammer's method, with experience in Finance and Operations and in designing auditable SOPs.
Deliver an actionable redesign dossier for committee with these numbered components:
1. AS-IS map of {{PROCESO}}: step table with responsible party, system, time, and cost per step, classifying each activity as value-added / necessary non-value / pure eliminable waste (lean lens); totals for steps, handoffs, cycle time, and, if data is available, cycle efficiency (value time / total time). Highlight bottlenecks and rework loops.
2. Assumption challenge: for each critical step, root questions (why does it exist, what rule or regulation literally requires it, what happens if it is eliminated, why does that area own it, what technology would make it unnecessary). Explicitly separate mandatory-by-regulation controls from inherited-by-inertia controls.
3. TO-BE design: reconfigured process applying Hammer's principles, naming which one each change uses (organize around outcomes not tasks; have the consumer of the output execute the process; capture information once at the source; parallelize today's sequential steps; locate the decision where the work occurs; treat dispersed resources as centralized via system). Wherever a control is eliminated, propose the compensating control that preserves the control objective.
4. Quantified AS-IS vs TO-BE comparison: steps, handoffs, cycle time, and cost per transaction, with the explicit [SUPUESTO] behind each estimated figure and the delta vs {{OBJETIVO_MEJORA}} (meets / partial / gap).
5. Phased transition plan: sequence, quick wins (gains in days without waiting for systems), risks with their mitigating control, system or data dependencies, and rollback signal.
6. New process governance: metrics, SLA, single process owner, and review cadence.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 0 - Framing: confirm the scope of {{PROCESO}} (trigger and result), {{OBJETIVO_MEJORA}}, and non-negotiable {{RESTRICCIONES}}. If {{VOLUMEN}}, {{SISTEMAS}}, times per step, or cost per hour per role are missing, ask before quantifying; never invent figures and mark every assumption as [SUPUESTO].
Phase 1 - AS-IS: map the current process and classify the value of each step; quantify the baseline of steps, handoffs, time, and cost.
Phase 2 - Assumption demolition: apply root-level questioning to separate what is mandatory (actual rule/regulation) from what is inherited by inertia.
Phase 3 - TO-BE redesign: reconstruct the flow with Hammer's principles, respecting {{RESTRICCIONES}}; more speed cannot break segregation of duties or audit traceability. If a principle conflicts with a constraint, the constraint wins and the trade-off is documented.
Phase 4 - Quantification and transition: compare AS-IS vs TO-BE, validate against {{OBJETIVO_MEJORA}}, define a phased plan, risks, compensating controls, and governance metrics.
Edge cases: if radical redesign cannot reach {{OBJETIVO_MEJORA}} without violating {{RESTRICCIONES}}, say so and show how far it can go; if the real pain is a data source or a system and not the flow, redirect focus before redesigning steps.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- AS-IS classifies each step as value / necessary non-value / waste and reports baseline of steps, handoffs, time, and cost.
- Each critical step has at least one root question distinguishing mandatory regulation from inertia.
- The TO-BE explicitly applies Hammer's principles and names which one is used in each change.
- Every eliminated control has a compensating control or justification for why the control objective no longer applies.
- Every estimated figure carries its [SUPUESTO]; no missing data is invented, it is requested.
- The TO-BE respects {{RESTRICCIONES}}: segregation of duties and audit traceability are preserved.
- The AS-IS vs TO-BE comparison quantifies reduction in steps, handoffs, cycle time, and cost, and contrasts it with {{OBJETIVO_MEJORA}}.
- There is a phased transition plan with quick wins, risks, controls, dependencies, and metrics/SLA with a process owner.
Expected deliverable: BPR redesign dossier for {{PROCESO}} ready to take to committee, with classified AS-IS, assumption demolition, TO-BE justified by principle with compensating controls, quantified comparison with assumptions, transition plan, and process governance.
spec-finanzas_swimlane_responsabilidades:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_PROCESO: {{NOMBRE_PROCESO}} > Cross-functional process to diagram (e.g., monthly accounting close, supplier payment approval, customer onboarding)
- ROLES_PARTICIPANTES: {{ROLES_PARTICIPANTES}} > Roles or areas involved; each will be a lane (e.g., Requester, Finance, Treasury, Approver). Model roles, never individuals
- EVENTO_INICIO: {{EVENTO_INICIO}} > Trigger that opens the process (e.g., supplier invoice received)
- EVENTO_CIERRE: {{EVENTO_CIERRE}} > Final result that closes the process (e.g., payment executed and reconciled)
- CONTROLES_CONOCIDOS: {{CONTROLES_CONOCIDOS}} > Approvals, validations, reconciliations, limits, or segregation of duties already known (optional)
- NIVEL_DETALLE: {{NIVEL_DETALLE}} > Granularity: high-level or step-by-step operational (optional; default high-level)
- VOLUMEN_FRECUENCIA: {{VOLUMEN_FRECUENCIA}} > Frequency or volume of the process for sizing bottlenecks (optional; e.g., 200 invoices/month)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A cross-functional process without a clear lane map hides its friction points: handoffs where nobody is owner, missing controls, and invisible rework. Diagramming {{NOMBRE_PROCESO}} in swimlanes by role makes explicit who does what, in what order, and where it is approved or can fail. This unlocks service agreements between areas, an auditable foundation for automation, and an operable SOP that survives staff turnover. The cost of not doing it is silent: work that bounces between areas with no owner, controls assumed by everyone but executed by nobody, and cycle times nobody can explain.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Business Process Architect, specialist in cross-functional financial and operational processes and in BPMN notation applied to SOPs.

Deliverable: a swimlane-by-role process map with its step table, an analysis of risky handoffs, and a note on assumptions. Steps:
1) Confirm boundaries: trigger {{EVENTO_INICIO}}, final result {{EVENTO_CIERRE}}, and what falls outside scope.
2) Create one lane per role from {{ROLES_PARTICIPANTES}}; model roles, never individuals. If a role has no activities, omit it and note it.
3) Sequence the activities and assign each to the lane of the role that executes it; mark each handoff as the crossing of an activity from one lane to another.
4) Identify decisions (diamond with Yes/No branches), waits, rework, rework loops, and controls from {{CONTROLES_CONOCIDOS}} and the flow logic.
5) Define for each activity: single responsible party, input received, output delivered, and estimated time or SLA, according to {{NIVEL_DETALLE}} and {{VOLUMEN_FRECUENCIA}}.
6) Produce the Mermaid diagram (flowchart with a subgraph per lane) and the table with columns Lane, Activity, Input, Output, Handoff to, Control, Time or SLA.
7) Close with the prioritized list of risky handoffs (no owner, ambiguous, no control, or with rework) and a concrete recommendation for each; add a note on assumptions and limits.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: fix process boundaries (start, end, scope) and validate the role list; if the process name, roles, start event, or close event is missing, ask before continuing.
Phase 2 - Sequencing: list activities in order and assign them to lanes; use simplified BPMN notation (start event, activity, decision diamond, end event); resolve loops and alternate paths without leaving dangling nodes.
Phase 3 - Responsibility and control: complete single responsible party, input, output, control point, and time/SLA per step; treat every lane change as an explicit handoff; verify segregation of duties where applicable.
Phase 4 - Synthesis: generate Mermaid + table, mentally validate syntax, and derive the prioritized risky handoff analysis by impact. Mark every unprovided datum as [SUPUESTO]; do not invent steps or controls.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Every role in {{ROLES_PARTICIPANTES}} with an activity has its own lane; roles are modeled, not individuals.
- The diagram opens with {{EVENTO_INICIO}} and closes with {{EVENTO_CIERRE}}, with no orphan activities or unconnected nodes.
- Each activity has a single responsible party, an input, and an output identified.
- Every lane crossing appears as an explicit handoff in the diagram and in the Handoff to column; no handoff without a destination.
- Decisions, waits, rework, and loops are marked; controls from {{CONTROLES_CONOCIDOS}} are reflected one to one.
- Mermaid syntax is valid (flowchart with subgraphs) and the table is complete, including the Time or SLA column.
- Assumptions carry [SUPUESTO]; no steps or controls are invented.
Expected deliverable: Mermaid swimlane diagram + step table (Lane, Activity, Input, Output, Handoff to, Control, Time or SLA) + prioritized list of risky handoffs with a recommendation for each + note on assumptions and limits.
spec-finanzas_matriz_raci_proceso:
[inputs]
- PROCESO: {{PROCESO}} > Name and scope of the process to map, with explicit start and end (e.g., monthly accounting close from the entry of provisions to the publication of statements, accounts payable cycle from invoice receipt to payment, supplier onboarding, daily bank reconciliation)
- ROLES: {{ROLES}} > List of job titles or roles involved, never individuals' names (e.g., Accounting Analyst, Treasury Manager, Controller, CFO, Internal Audit, System/ERP if it automates steps)
- NIVEL_DETALLE: {{NIVEL_DETALLE}} > Expected granularity (coarse 8-10 activities, fine up to 20) and whether strict segregation of duties applies for sensitive financial controls (payments, manual adjustments, access)
- DISPARADOR: {{DISPARADOR}} > (optional) Event that motivates the matrix (external audit, control finding, team handoff, SOP redesign, close, incident, ISO/SOX certification)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments" (e.g., current SOP, BPMN flow diagram, org chart, control narrative, prior matrix)

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Gray areas of responsibility in Finance and Operations processes generate rework, ownerless controls, decisions nobody approves, and audit findings. Building the RACI matrix for {{PROCESO}} given {{DISPARADOR}} forces an explicit agreement on who executes, who approves, who is consulted, and who is informed at each activity, leaving the process auditable, with demonstrable segregation of duties and ready for handoff or SOP certification.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Operational Excellence Manager with certified experience in BPM (BPMN) and SOP design, fluent in financial controls governance and segregation of duties (execute vs approve, record vs reconcile, hold custody vs authorize).
Deliverable: complete, validated, and defensible RACI matrix, plus assignment notes, conflict list, and socialization plan. Steps:
1) Decompose {{PROCESO}} into 8 to 20 key activities in sequence (per {{NIVEL_DETALLE}}), each atomic (verb + object), with no vague sub-processes or steps that blend two actions.
2) Confirm or adjust {{ROLES}} as job titles (not individuals); warn if a mandatory role is missing (e.g., who approves a payment, who performs independent control) and, if the ERP executes a step, decide whether it enters as an R role.
3) Build the activity × role matrix and assign: R (Responsible, executes), A (Accountable, owns and decides), C (Consulted, contributes beforehand in two-way dialogue), I (Informed, receives the result one-way). Empty cell if the role does not participate. R and A can fall on the same role only if it is not a sensitive control.
4) Apply and report the integrity rules: exactly one A per activity (accountability is not diluted), at least one R per activity, no excess of C that slows decisions (practical rule: no more than 2-3 useful Cs), no orphan rows or roles with no letter across the entire process.
5) Verify segregation of duties per {{NIVEL_DETALLE}}: in sensitive financial controls, whoever executes must not approve, whoever records must not reconcile, whoever holds assets must not authorize payments; mark each incompatible R+A crossing or dual custody as a violation with a suggested remediation.
6) Flag conflicts: activities without a clear owner, overloaded roles (too many R or A concentrated), approval bottlenecks, and segregation violations.
7) Close with a brief socialization plan (validation with the process owner, communication to the roles, review cadence, and update trigger).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm scope of {{PROCESO}} (start/end), inventory of {{ROLES}}, and {{NIVEL_DETALLE}}; list assumptions as [SUPUESTO] and ask for missing data before proceeding.
Phase 2 Decomposition: derive activities in sequence and number them; verify atomicity (one verb, one object).
Phase 3 Assignment: complete the matrix cell by cell applying the R/A/C/I definitions consistently.
Phase 4 Integrity validation: run the rules (one A per row, R present, excess of C, orphan rows/roles) and correct before delivering.
Phase 5 Control: apply the segregation-of-duties test on sensitive activities and document each finding with remediation.
Phase 6 Conflicts and close: document findings, non-obvious assignments, assumptions, and the socialization plan.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Between 8 and 20 atomic activities in sequence, verb + object, aligned to {{NIVEL_DETALLE}}.
- [ ] Every row has exactly one A and at least one R; no excess of C.
- [ ] R, A, C, I used with their correct definition; empty cells where there is no participation.
- [ ] No orphan rows or roles with no letter; mandatory roles present.
- [ ] Segregation of duties verified in sensitive controls (execute vs approve, record vs reconcile, hold custody vs authorize) with remediation per finding.
- [ ] Conflicts, bottlenecks, and non-obvious assignments explained.
- [ ] Assumptions marked as [SUPUESTO]; no invented roles or steps.
Expected deliverable: a RACI matrix table (rows = numbered activities, columns = roles), followed by assignment notes, conflict list with remediation, and socialization plan in 3 to 5 bullet points.
spec-finanzas_runbook_operativo:
[inputs]
- OPERACION_O_INCIDENTE: {{OPERACION_O_INCIDENTE}} > Name and one-sentence purpose of the recurring operation or incident to document (e.g. "Daily cash close and bank reconciliation" or "Recovery of failed billing job")
- DISPARADOR: {{DISPARADOR}} > What starts the procedure: frequency or scheduled event (recurring operation) or detected symptom or alert (incident)
- ROL_EJECUTOR: {{ROL_EJECUTOR}} > Role or operator who executes the runbook, applicable shift, and to whom to escalate if blocked
- SISTEMAS_PRERREQUISITOS: {{SISTEMAS_PRERREQUISITOS}} > Required systems, tools, accesses or permissions, and prior validations before starting
- PASOS_VERIFICACION: {{PASOS_VERIFICACION}} > Known steps in order and how to verify each one succeeded; "to be gathered in a process interview" if not yet known
- FALLAS_RECUPERACION: {{FALLAS_RECUPERACION}} > Known failure modes or symptoms, how to recover or revert (rollback), and applicable time window or service limit (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need an operational runbook that allows executing a recurring operation or recovering from an incident step by step, so that anyone on shift can follow it without depending on memory or on the author's availability. The runbook is the actionable procedure followed in the moment, often under time pressure: it converts one person's tacit knowledge into a repeatable, auditable team asset. Without a clear runbook, the operation stops when its owner is absent, incidents are resolved improvisationally, and each execution produces different results. A solid runbook unblocks service continuity, reduces recovery time, enables shift rotation, and leaves traceable evidence for audit. It is not a policy or a general process description: it is the flight manual executed line by line. The design bias is operational safety: when in doubt, the runbook stops and escalates rather than improvising.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior operations and operational excellence engineer, expert in designing runbooks and SOPs for critical financial and operational processes, fluent in incident management (ITIL) and in accounting close and reconciliation operations.

Produce an operational runbook with these components:
1. Header: name of the operation or incident, purpose in one sentence, version, date, and runbook owner.
2. Trigger and scope: what starts the procedure (frequency or event for recurring operation; symptom or alert for incident) and what is inside and outside its scope.
3. Owner and escalation: role or operator who executes it, applicable shift, and to whom and how to escalate (channel and contact placeholder) if blocked or if the time window is exceeded.
4. Prerequisites: required systems, tools, accesses, or permissions, and validations that must be met before starting; flag the point of no return if there is a step beyond which reverting is costly or impossible.
5. Step-by-step procedure: table or numbered list where each step has a concrete action, owner, exact command or location (system, screen, path), and an observable verification checkpoint confirming the step succeeded before advancing. Mark destructive or irreversible steps (those that overwrite, delete, or send) to require explicit confirmation.
6. Success verification: how to confirm the complete operation finished correctly (balanced accounts, job in successful state, reconciliation with no differences), distinct from step-by-step verification.
7. Failure modes and recovery: table of symptom, probable cause, and recovery action; include the rollback path to return to the last known safe state when a step cannot be completed, and leave a field to record the observed failure during execution.
8. Time window and service limit: target execution or recovery time and the limit at which escalation must occur.
9. Closure: verifiable success criteria, evidence or record left behind (logs, screenshots, minutes), and closure communication where applicable.
10. Maintenance: runbook owner, review cadence, and update triggers (system change, new failure, failed execution of the runbook itself).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm the operation or incident, its trigger, the responsible who executes it and to whom they escalate, the systems involved, and the prerequisites; identify what data is missing before drafting and declare them as gaps, do not fill them in.
Phase 2 - Procedure: draft the numbered steps in execution order; each step must be an atomic action with owner, exact command or location, and an observable verification checkpoint that acts as a gate before advancing to the next. Mark destructive steps and indicate the point of no return.
Phase 3 - Recovery: document failure modes and symptoms, their recovery action, the rollback path to the last known safe state, and the escalation points and criteria tied to the time window. Distinguish when to recover (retry within the runbook) from when to escalate (exceeds competence or window).
Phase 4 - Closure and maintenance: define verifiable success criteria, the evidence left behind, and the closure communication; assign owner, review cadence, and runbook update triggers. Label each unconfirmed piece of data as [SUPUESTO] and do not invent commands, paths, or figures: if missing, declare "to be gathered in a process interview".
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The trigger clearly distinguishes whether it is a recurring operation (frequency or event) or an incident (symptom or alert).
- [ ] The scope explicitly declares what is inside and what is outside the runbook.
- [ ] Each step in the procedure is atomic and includes owner, exact command or location, and an observable verification checkpoint before advancing.
- [ ] Destructive or irreversible steps are marked and the point of no return is flagged where applicable.
- [ ] There is success verification for the complete operation, not just individual steps.
- [ ] There is a failure modes table (symptom, probable cause, recovery action) and an explicit rollback path to the last known safe state.
- [ ] The time window and service limit that triggers escalation are defined, with escalation recipient and channel.
- [ ] The criterion for when to recover vs. when to escalate is unambiguous.
- [ ] Closure specifies verifiable success criteria and the evidence or record left behind for audit.
- [ ] A runbook owner, review cadence, and update triggers are assigned.
- [ ] Every unconfirmed piece of data is marked [SUPUESTO] and there are no invented commands, paths, or figures ("to be gathered in a process interview" is used instead).
- [ ] Written in neutral, professional English, without emojis, without prices, and without the word "free".
Expected deliverable: a one-to-three-page operational runbook, executable by anyone on shift without depending on the author, ready to pin in the operational repository and audit.
spec-finanzas_politica_procedimiento:
[inputs]
- TEMA_POLITICA: {{TEMA_POLITICA}} > Subject governed by the policy (e.g. expense and reimbursement management, vendor payment approval, monthly accounting close, bank reconciliations)
- ALCANCE_ORGANIZACIONAL: {{ALCANCE_ORGANIZACIONAL}} > Business units, areas, entities, or geographies to which it applies, with explicit exclusions
- MARCO_CUMPLIMIENTO: {{MARCO_CUMPLIMIENTO}} > Reference framework or regulation (e.g. COSO 2013, SOX, ISO 37301, local standard); use COSO 2013 + IIA Three Lines Model if not specified
- NIVEL_TOLERANCIA: {{NIVEL_TOLERANCIA}} > Risk appetite and tolerance thresholds (e.g. zero tolerance for payments without dual approval, materiality threshold, exception limit per period)
