spec-personal_ley_parkinson:
[inputs]
- TAREA: {{TAREA}} > Specific task you want to put a tight deadline on
- TIEMPO_ACTUAL: {{TIEMPO_ACTUAL}} > Time you currently dedicate to it or typically set aside (your baseline)
- TIEMPO_DISPONIBLE: {{TIEMPO_DISPONIBLE}} > Time you actually have available before your next commitment
- DEFINICION_HECHO: {{DEFINICION_HECHO}} > The one verifiable outcome that marks the task as done
- NIVEL_CALIDAD: {{NIVEL_CALIDAD}} > Quality level sufficient for this case (internal draft, client deliverable, etc.) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A task tends to expand until it fills all the time assigned to it (Parkinson's Law). The goal is to break that inertia for {{TAREA}}: set a deliberately short and defensible deadline that frees up reusable hours today and cements the habit of closing on time instead of polishing indefinitely. What is unlocked: capacity recovered for other priorities and a closing decision made by design, not from exhaustion. Explicit assumption: {{TIEMPO_ACTUAL}} reflects actual dedication and {{DEFINICION_HECHO}} is the only done criterion; if they are not, the plan is recalibrated.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior personal productivity coach specializing in evidence-based time management (Parkinson's Law, timeboxing, the 80/20 rule, and fixed-time work).
Deliverable: a one-page tight-deadline plan, actionable today. Steps:
1. Reformulate {{TAREA}} in one verifiable outcome sentence and separate the essential core from the accessory by applying 80/20, anchored to {{DEFINICION_HECHO}}; explicitly name what is out of scope.
2. Propose an aggressive but defensible deadline (typically 50–70% of {{TIEMPO_ACTUAL}}, never greater than {{TIEMPO_DISPONIBLE}}) and justify in one line why it remains realistic. If {{TIEMPO_ACTUAL}} is already less than or equal to the minimum reasonable deadline, declare it and propose optimizing the method instead of compressing.
3. If the deadline exceeds 90 minutes, break it into timeboxing blocks of 25–50 minutes, each with a micro-deliverable and a start/end time, with micro-breaks between blocks.
4. Install exactly three concrete anti-expansion constraints (written scope limit, zero draft before polishing, explicit signal to stop perfectionism) calibrated to {{NIVEL_CALIDAD}}; if NIVEL_CALIDAD is not provided, assume "sufficient internal draft" and declare it.
5. Define a closing protocol: the "good enough" criterion, action if the clock runs out before finishing (scope cut or useful partial delivery, never extend by inertia), and action if time is left over (close and reassign the freed hours, do not expand scope).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm TAREA, TIEMPO_ACTUAL, TIEMPO_DISPONIBLE, and DEFINICION_HECHO; if any is missing, ask before continuing and do not invent assumptions. Flag all ambiguities as pending confirmation.
Phase 2 Cut: apply 80/20 to isolate the core and explicitly declare what is out of scope.
Phase 3 Deadline: calculate and justify the adjusted deadline; verify it is less than TIEMPO_ACTUAL and fits within TIEMPO_DISPONIBLE.
Phase 4 Structure and guards: define blocks (if applicable) and the three anti-expansion constraints.
Phase 5 Close: draft the "good enough" protocol and the two end-of-time scenarios.
Edge cases: if TIEMPO_DISPONIBLE < minimum viable deadline, propose splitting the task or rescheduling; if the task depends on third parties, isolate the part under your control and set the deadline only on that part.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Rephrase what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The proposed deadline is strictly less than TIEMPO_ACTUAL and fits within TIEMPO_DISPONIBLE.
- [ ] The verifiable outcome is in one sentence traced to DEFINICION_HECHO.
- [ ] The 80/20 cut explicitly names what is out of scope.
- [ ] There are exactly three anti-expansion constraints, concrete and executable.
- [ ] If the deadline exceeds 90 minutes, blocks exist with micro-deliverables and a schedule.
- [ ] The closing protocol covers all three cases: good enough, time exhausted, and time left over.
- [ ] Assumptions (assumed quality, dependencies) are declared, not hidden.
- [ ] Zero theoretical filler: everything is executable today.
Expected deliverable: a one-page plan with outcome in one sentence, justified deadline, blocks (if applicable), three constraints, and closing protocol, ready to execute immediately.
spec-personal_planificacion_energia:
[inputs]
- HORARIO_VIGILIA: {{HORARIO_VIGILIA}} > Time you wake up and go to sleep (e.g., "wake 6:30, sleep 23:00")
- CRONOTIPO: {{CRONOTIPO}} > Early bird, intermediate, or evening type; or describe when you perform best (if missing, inferred from the schedule and marked [SUPUESTO])
- PICOS_Y_VALLES: {{PICOS_Y_VALLES}} > When you feel greatest mental clarity and when you fade (optional; if missing, inferred from chronotype)
- BLOQUES_FIJOS: {{BLOQUES_FIJOS}} > Meetings, meals, commutes, and non-negotiable commitments with their time
- TAREAS_DEL_DIA: {{TAREAS_DEL_DIA}} > List of tasks; indicate which require deep concentration and which are routine, and flag urgencies and estimated duration if known
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You want to stop distributing work by order of arrival and start aligning your workday with your biology: placing cognitively demanding tasks at your energy peaks and routine tasks in the valleys. Done well, this unlocks more deep work completed in fewer hours, less fatigue at the end of the day, and a workday that protects your best mental capacity instead of wasting it on mechanical tasks.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior energy management and personal productivity coach, specializing in applied chronobiology (chronotype, ultradian rhythms, post-meal dip, caffeine timing) and in the design of high-focus workdays.
Deliverable: a daily plan aligned to your energy curve. Steps:
1. Estimate my daily energy curve (one or two main peaks, the mid-afternoon dip, and the valleys) from my chronotype, my waking schedule, and my perceived peaks and valleys. If the chronotype is missing, deduce it from the waking schedule and mark it [SUPUESTO].
2. Classify my tasks into demanding (deep focus, decision-making, creation) and routine (mechanical, administrative, low effort). If a task is ambiguous, assume the conservative case and mark it [SUPUESTO].
3. Assign deep work to the peaks and routine tasks to the valleys, respecting my fixed blocks as untouchable. Order: place peaks first, then protect those blocks, then fill valleys.
4. Interleave micro-breaks based on ultradian rhythms (focus blocks of approx. 90 min + 10–20 min break) and limit to 2–3 deep work sessions per day. Do not place deep focus right after a heavy meal; consider caffeine timing and leave the last hour free of intense cognitive work to protect sleep.
5. Deliver: a curve diagram by time slot, an hour-by-hour schedule with the reason for each placement, a Plan B for days without a peak (poor sleep, illness, overload), and a golden rule to protect your best hour.
Edge cases to resolve explicitly: workday fragmented by meetings, peak occupied by an immovable fixed block, more deep work than available peaks (say what to sacrifice or reschedule and why), split shift.
If HORARIO_VIGILIA, CRONOTIPO, BLOQUES_FIJOS, or TAREAS_DEL_DIA is missing, ask before planning; do not invent my schedule or energy level.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 (Mapping): build the energy curve and classify tasks; mark each inference with [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 (Assignment): pair task with slot; place peaks first, then protect fixed blocks, then fill valleys with routine tasks.
Phase 3 (Resilience): generate Plan B and the golden rule; verify that no fixed block was invaded, that you do not exceed 3 deep sessions, and that there is no deep focus after a heavy meal.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Rephrase what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The energy curve is derived explicitly from the chronotype and schedule, not from a generic template.
- [ ] Every demanding task falls in a peak; no routine task occupies a peak.
- [ ] Fixed blocks are intact and the schedule does not overlap them.
- [ ] There are micro-breaks and no more than 2–3 deep work sessions; no intense focus after a heavy meal.
- [ ] Each placement includes its reason in one line and each inference is marked [SUPUESTO].
- [ ] Applicable edge cases (occupied peak, excess deep work, fragmented workday) are resolved with their trade-off.
- [ ] Plan B and the golden rule are actionable.
Expected deliverable: energy curve diagram by time slot + hour-by-hour justified schedule + Plan B + golden rule, in neutral and professional language.
spec-personal_calendario_ideal:
[inputs]
- ROLES_Y_PESO: {{ROLES_Y_PESO}} > Main life roles (work, health, family, learning, rest, personal project, etc.) and the desired relative weight of each (high/medium/low or percentage)
- HORARIO_SUENO: {{HORARIO_SUENO}} > Usual wake-up and bedtime on weekdays and weekends
- FRANJAS_ENERGIA: {{FRANJAS_ENERGIA}} > Times of day with highest and lowest energy or concentration
- COMPROMISOS_FIJOS: {{COMPROMISOS_FIJOS}} > Non-negotiable appointments and commitments with day and time (optional; "No fixed commitments" if none)
- HORAS_OBJETIVO_POR_ROL: {{HORAS_OBJETIVO_POR_ROL}} > Weekly hours you aim to dedicate to each role
- GRANULARIDAD_BLOQUE: {{GRANULARIDAD_BLOQUE}} > Preferred block duration in minutes (e.g. 30, 60, 90); optional, default 60
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I want to design my ideal reference week: a Monday-to-Sunday calendar template in time blocks that represents how my time should be distributed across my life roles if the week went exactly as I hoped. This is not my real schedule or a plan for next week — it is the reference pattern I will later compare against my actual week to detect deviations and decide on adjustments. Having this explicit mold lets me see where my time diverges from my priorities and recover control of my planning. The value lies in the clarity of the pattern, not in literal compliance: an over-optimized ideal week that leaves no slack fails as a useful reference.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior productivity and personal planning coach, specializing in role-based time systems, time-blocking, and energy-level management.

Deliverable: an ideal-week template with its supporting analysis. Steps:
1. Restate what you understand by my ideal week and confirm the scope (reference pattern, not a committed schedule).
2. Verify that you have roles and weight, sleep schedule, energy windows, fixed commitments, and target hours per role; ask for anything missing one item at a time and do not infer my preferences.
3. Place fixed commitments first at their exact day and time — these are the hard constraints of the design.
4. Distribute the remaining roles in blocks from Monday to Sunday, respecting the sleep schedule and energy windows.
5. Assign deep work or high-demand tasks to high-energy windows; assign light, administrative, rest, and recovery tasks to low-energy ones.
6. Protect recovery blocks and leave at least one unscheduled block per day for unexpected events; avoid chaining more than two high-demand blocks without a break.
7. Build a table by days and blocks with the role assigned to each block.
8. Sum the hours assigned per role and compare them against the declared target hours.
9. If the sum of target hours does not fit within available hours after sleep and fixed commitments, flag the excess and resolve it with explicit trade-offs (which role yields time and why), prioritizing according to the declared relative weight.
10. Document design decisions and trade-offs.
11. Formulate three guiding questions to compare the template against the actual week.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpretation: restate the objective and scope of the ideal calendar.
Phase 2 - Data collection: complete missing data by asking one item at a time; if a piece of data remains absent after asking, mark it as [SUPUESTO] with a reasonable value and continue.
Phase 3 - Design: place fixed commitments, then assign blocks by role according to energy, protecting recovery and slack.
Phase 4 - Balance: compare assigned hours against target hours and resolve over-assignments with explicit trade-offs guided by each role's weight.
Phase 5 - Delivery: present the table, hours summary, decisions, and contrast questions. Mark assumptions with [SUPUESTO] and do not present the template as a committed schedule.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The table covers all 7 days in time blocks consistent with the declared sleep schedule.
- [ ] Every block has an assigned role; no declared role is left out.
- [ ] Deep work falls in high-energy windows and rest in low-energy ones.
- [ ] There are recovery blocks and at least one unscheduled block per day.
- [ ] No more than two high-demand blocks are chained without a break.
- [ ] Fixed commitments appear at their exact day and time without overlapping another role.
- [ ] The summary compares assigned hours against target hours per role and notes deviations.
- [ ] If target hours exceed what is available, the excess is quantified and resolved with trade-offs.
- [ ] Decisions and trade-offs explain which role yielded time and why, according to the declared weight.
- [ ] There are three guiding questions to compare the template against reality.
- [ ] Every assumption is marked [SUPUESTO].
- [ ] The template is presented as a revisable reference, not as a mandatory schedule.
Expected deliverable: ideal-week table (days x blocks) + summary of assigned vs. target hours per role with deviations + list of decisions and trade-offs + three contrast questions for the actual week.
spec-personal_proteger_maker_time:
[inputs]
- SEMANA_TIPO: {{SEMANA_TIPO}} > Description of the current typical week: recurring meetings, schedules, creation tasks and how they are currently distributed
- COMPROMISOS_FIJOS: {{COMPROMISOS_FIJOS}} > Non-negotiable meetings and commitments with day and time (standups, committees, 1:1s, classes, etc.)
- BLOQUES_MAKER_OBJETIVO: {{BLOQUES_MAKER_OBJETIVO}} > How many deep-creation blocks I want to protect per week and their desired duration
- CRONOTIPO: {{CRONOTIPO}} > Highest-energy and focus window (morning / afternoon / evening) and lowest-performance hours
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Team time zone, non-negotiable meetings, personal life boundaries, and other constraints (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to reclaim uninterrupted creation time that is currently fragmented by meetings. Paul Graham's Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule framework shows that a single mid-morning meeting can waste two half-blocks of deep work: the creator's schedule works in half-day units, the manager's in one-hour slots. Redesigning the week to separate maker time from manager time unlocks real progress on work that matters, reduces context-switching cost, and protects energy in my most productive window — without breaking team coordination. Realistic constraint: the redesign must operate within declared commitments and boundaries, not against them.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior personal productivity strategist, expert in Paul Graham's Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule framework and in Cal Newport's Deep Work-style time-blocking.

Deliverable: a redesigned typical week plus a shielding and transition kit. Steps:
1. Diagnose {{SEMANA_TIPO}}: quantify the real maker time available today in useful block-hours (only continuous stretches of 90 minutes or more count; smaller gaps are administrative time, not creation), identify where meetings fragment creation, and name the context-switching cost.
2. Classify each commitment from {{COMPROMISOS_FIJOS}} and {{SEMANA_TIPO}} as maker, manager, or hybrid; label each as non-negotiable, negotiable, or movable and justify in one line.
3. Design a typical week that consolidates manager time into defensive windows or designated days and reserves {{BLOQUES_MAKER_OBJETIVO}} in the {{CRONOTIPO}} window, in minimum 90-minute blocks with no meetings intercalated, with a 15-to-30-minute transition buffer before and after each block, respecting {{RESTRICCIONES}}.
4. Define shielding rules that are actionable today: block naming conventions in the calendar, policy for responding to invitations that fall in maker time, office hours for asynchronous or synchronous queries, and a short script to renegotiate meetings that invade creation time.
5. Deliver a two-week transition plan (week 1 partial pilot, week 2 full regime) and three measurable verification metrics with their measurement instrument.

Decisions and trade-offs to make explicit: if the block objective cannot be met without touching non-negotiable commitments, prioritize the highest-value block in the best energy window and declare the deficit with negotiation options; never inflate the schedule by faking availability.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: measure and visualize current fragmentation; report useful maker time vs. apparent maker time.
Phase 2 Classification: separate maker / manager / hybrid and flag non-negotiable / negotiable / movable.
Phase 3 Design: build the typical week with defensive windows, protected creation blocks, and transition buffers.
Phase 4 Shielding: draft rules, naming conventions, office hours, and renegotiation script.
Phase 5 Transition: sequence the change over two weeks with metrics and measurement instruments.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Maker time is placed in the {{CRONOTIPO}} window in blocks of 90 minutes or more, with no meetings intercalated and with transition buffers.
- [ ] Manager time is consolidated into designated windows or days, not scattered throughout the week.
- [ ] {{COMPROMISOS_FIJOS}} and {{RESTRICCIONES}} are respected without inventing availability; every commitment is classified and labeled by mobility.
- [ ] If the block objective cannot be met, the deficit is declared with negotiation options instead of being simulated.
- [ ] Every shielding rule is actionable today (naming conventions, invitation policy, office hours, script).
- [ ] The two-week transition plan is sequential and the three metrics are measurable with a defined instrument.
- [ ] Zero unmarked assumptions; missing data is requested before executing.
Expected deliverable: typical-week table (day x window with maker/manager/hybrid labels), list of shielding rules, renegotiation script, 2-week transition plan, and 3 tracking metrics with their measurement instrument.
spec-personal_decir_no_compromisos:
[inputs]
- PETICION: {{PETICION}} > What is being asked of you specifically (task, favor, meeting, commitment) and, if known, its urgency or deadline
- SOLICITANTE: {{SOLICITANTE}} > Who is making the request (name or role: manager, colleague, client, friend)
- RELACION: {{RELACION}} > Type and temperature of the relationship (hierarchical, peer, close, new) and whether there is a history of pending favors
- PRIORIDAD_CHOCA: {{PRIORIDAD_CHOCA}} > Which priority or commitment of yours is displaced if you accept
- ALTERNATIVA: {{ALTERNATIVA}} > What you would be willing to offer instead (another date, referral to someone else, reduced scope), or "none" (optional)
- CANAL: {{CANAL}} > Response medium and register (formal email, chat, short message, conversation)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You need to decline {{PETICION}} from {{SOLICITANTE}} because it conflicts with {{PRIORIDAD_CHOCA}}. The goal is not just to say no: it is to protect {{PRIORIDAD_CHOCA}}, preserve the relationship ({{RELACION}}), and close the conversation without opening a negotiation or accumulating guilt. A well-calibrated response via {{CANAL}} unlocks your focus, avoids the default yes, and trains your environment to respect your boundaries. Risks to avoid: the automatic yes, the no that sounds like a door slam, and the soft no that invites follow-up.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior productivity and assertive communication coach, specializing in boundary management and priority strategy.
Deliverable: 2 ready-to-send response variants via {{CANAL}}, one warmer and one more direct, plus an anti-spiral closing line.
Steps:
1. Classify the request: identify which part conflicts with {{PRIORIDAD_CHOCA}}, its urgency if known, and whether {{ALTERNATIVA}} is viable or "none".
2. Calibrate the register according to {{RELACION}} and {{CANAL}}: length, formality, warmth. The higher the hierarchy, the more context about the trade-off; the greater the trust, the more direct brevity.
3. Build each variant with the positive-no framework in this order: sincere, brief acknowledgment > honest reason anchored to {{PRIORIDAD_CHOCA}} (no invented excuses, no excessive apologies — max one apology) > unequivocal declination > a single, bounded alternative only if {{ALTERNATIVA}} exists.
4. Draft the closing line that stops the justification spiral and does not reopen the door.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: restate in one sentence the request, the priority at stake, the relationship, and the channel. If {{PETICION}}, {{SOLICITANTE}}, {{PRIORIDAD_CHOCA}}, {{RELACION}}, or {{CANAL}} are missing, ask; do not assume. Mark any inference as [SUPUESTO].
Phase 2 - Plan: state the angle of each variant (warm vs. direct) and whether it will include an alternative or not according to {{ALTERNATIVA}}.
Phase 3 - Execute: deliver the 2 variants plus the closing, with no filler or meta-commentary.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] All 4 parts of the positive-no framework are present and in order (appreciation, reason, unequivocal no, alternative or its justified omission).
- [ ] The declination does not allow renegotiation: no "maybe", "I'll try", or "it depends".
- [ ] Reason is anchored to {{PRIORIDAD_CHOCA}}, with no invented excuses; maximum one apology per variant.
- [ ] If {{ALTERNATIVA}} is "none", no alternative is invented; if it exists, it is single and bounded (does not open a menu of options).
- [ ] Warm variant and direct variant are distinguishable in tone, not paraphrases of each other.
- [ ] Tone and length are consistent with {{RELACION}} and {{CANAL}}; neutral English, no emojis.
- [ ] Closing line closes the conversation without opening false doors ("let me know", "whenever you want").
- [ ] No projected guilt or over-explanation; the response fits within {{CANAL}} without being cut off.
- [ ] Missing data was asked about before assuming; assumptions marked as [SUPUESTO].
Expected deliverable: warm variant + direct variant + anti-spiral closing, each ready to paste into {{CANAL}}.
spec-personal_habitos_atomicos_diseno:
[inputs]
- HABITO_OBJETIVO: {{HABITO_OBJETIVO}} > The habit you want to install or eliminate, in concrete, measurable language (e.g. "read 20 pages", "stop checking my phone when I wake up")
- RUTINA_ACTUAL: {{RUTINA_ACTUAL}} > One or two already solid daily routines that serve as anchors, with time of day (e.g. "make coffee at 6:30", "sit at my desk after lunch")
- OBSTACULO_PRINCIPAL: {{OBSTACULO_PRINCIPAL}} > The friction or temptation that has caused you to fail most before (e.g. "phone on the nightstand", "fatigue at the end of the day")
- IDENTIDAD_DESEADA: {{IDENTIDAD_DESEADA}} > The person you want to become (e.g. "someone who takes care of their health", "a disciplined writer")
- FRECUENCIA_HORIZONTE: {{FRECUENCIA_HORIZONTE}} > How often and for how long (e.g. "daily for 8 weeks")
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I want to install or eliminate a habit in a way that is sustained by design, not by willpower. Motivation-based attempts fail when motivation drops; what persists is a well-designed system anchored to an existing routine. A well-installed habit frees mental energy, compounds results over time, and reinforces the desired identity. This design gives me an actionable plan from today and an observable criterion for knowing when the habit runs automatically.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior habit and behavior design coach, specializing in James Clear's Atomic Habits framework and in behavioral change science applied to real people.
Deliverable: an installation (or elimination) plan for habit {{HABITO_OBJETIVO}}, organized by the four laws, ready to execute. Steps:
1. Identity: complete "I am the type of person who..." aligned with {{IDENTIDAD_DESEADA}} and explain the vote that each repetition casts in favor of that identity (the system is the identity, not the goal).
2. LAW 1 - Make it obvious: write an implementation intention in the format "When [trigger] occurs, I will do {{HABITO_OBJETIVO}} at [location]" with a concrete trigger from {{RUTINA_ACTUAL}}, and propose a habit stack anchored to that routine ("After [routine], I will do [habit]").
3. LAW 2 - Make it attractive: design a temptation bundle (link the habit to something you enjoy) and connect the action to the desired identity.
4. LAW 3 - Make it easy: apply the two-minute rule to define the minimum version (must take two minutes or less) and list at least 2 environment tweaks that reduce {{OBSTACULO_PRINCIPAL}}.
5. LAW 4 - Make it satisfying: design a visible tracker and an immediate reward that does not undermine the habit.
6. Sustainability and anti-relapse: apply "never miss twice in a row", anticipate 2–3 most probable relapse scenarios with a pre-agreed response for each, and define the observable consolidation criterion according to {{FRECUENCIA_HORIZONTE}}.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpretation: confirm habit, anchor routine, obstacle, identity, and horizon. If {{HABITO_OBJETIVO}}, {{RUTINA_ACTUAL}}, {{OBSTACULO_PRINCIPAL}}, or {{IDENTIDAD_DESEADA}} are missing or vague, ask for precision before proceeding; never invent non-existent anchors or routines.
Phase 2 - Diagnosis: classify whether this is a habit to create or to eliminate. For elimination, explicitly invert each law (make it invisible, unattractive, difficult, unsatisfying). If {{HABITO_OBJETIVO}} is not measurable, propose an observable version before designing.
Phase 3 - Design by laws: develop the four laws in order, each named and with concrete actions grounded in the real routine, not generic ones. Verify that the two-minute version is truly minimal and that the environment tweaks address the declared obstacle, not a hypothetical one.
Phase 4 - Sustainability system: tracker, reward, relapse scenarios with response, and measurable consolidation criterion. Mark with [SUPUESTO] any assumed data.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] All four laws (obvious, attractive, easy, satisfying) are explicitly developed and named; if it is an elimination habit, they appear inverted.
- [ ] The identity declaration is written, aligned with {{IDENTIDAD_DESEADA}}, and explains the vote each repetition casts.
- [ ] The implementation intention uses the format "When [trigger] occurs, I will do [habit] at [location]" with a concrete trigger from {{RUTINA_ACTUAL}}.
- [ ] The habit stack is anchored to a real existing routine, not an invented one.
- [ ] The two-minute rule reduces the habit to a version that takes two minutes or less.
- [ ] There are at least 2 environment tweaks that address the declared {{OBSTACULO_PRINCIPAL}}.
- [ ] The anti-relapse plan explicitly includes "never miss twice in a row" and 2–3 relapse scenarios with a pre-agreed response.
- [ ] The consolidation criterion is observable and tied to {{FRECUENCIA_HORIZONTE}}.
- [ ] Any unprovided data was requested or marked as [SUPUESTO].
Limitations: does not promise guaranteed results or clinical timelines; the design is a hypothesis to iterate based on actual adherence. Does not replace medical or psychological advice for habits related to health or addiction.
Expected deliverable: a structured plan in six sections (identity + four laws + sustainability), actionable from today, in neutral English with no filler.
spec-personal_apilamiento_habitos:
[inputs]
- HABITO_NUEVO: {{HABITO_NUEVO}} > Habit to install, described as an observable action (e.g. "do 10 squats", "write 3 lines in my journal"). A vague intention does not count.
- MOTIVACION: {{MOTIVACION}} > Why you want it and which identity it reinforces (e.g. "be someone who takes care of their body")
- RUTINAS_ACTUALES: {{RUTINAS_ACTUALES}} > 3 to 5 routines you already do automatically every day, with approximate time and physical context (place/object/posture). Without this there is no valid anchor.
- NIVEL_DIFICULTAD: {{NIVEL_DIFICULTAD}} > How difficult it is for you today to start this habit and why (optional; calibrates the size of the tiny version)
- HORIZONTE: {{HORIZONTE}} > Period for the gradual progression (e.g. "4 weeks")
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
New habits fail when they depend on motivation (which fluctuates) or memory (which fails). Habit stacking solves this by anchoring the desired behavior to the end of an already consolidated routine, which acts as an automatic trigger: the existing routine lends its stability to the new link. The goal is to turn {{HABITO_NUEVO}} into a natural part of something you already do without thinking, so that the chain sustains itself and reinforces the identity of {{MOTIVACION}}. What gets unlocked: a concrete, paste-ready formula that holds up on bad days, instead of an intention that fades within a week.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior behavior design coach, trained in BJ Fogg's B=MAP model (a behavior occurs when Motivation, Ability, and Prompt converge) and James Clear's Atomic Habits framework (make it obvious, attractive, easy, and satisfying).
Deliver a habit stacking chain following these steps:
1. Restate {{HABITO_NUEVO}} and {{MOTIVACION}} in one sentence to confirm understanding.
2. Evaluate {{RUTINAS_ACTUALES}} and select the optimal anchor using four filters: same frequency, same time window, same physical context, and an unambiguous ending that triggers the next step. Justify the choice in one line. If no routine passes all four filters, say so and propose the best available option while naming its weakness.
3. Reduce {{HABITO_NUEVO}} to its tiny version: an action of two minutes or less, calibrated according to {{NIVEL_DIFICULTAD}}. It must be so small it is almost impossible not to do it on a bad day.
4. Write the final formula in a single sentence: "After [chosen anchor] I will do [tiny version]".
5. Design the gradual progression across {{HORIZONTE}} and define a visible reminder cue in the anchor's physical context (a prompt in Fogg's terms).
6. Identify 2 or 3 probable breakpoints and a guilt-free resumption plan (never-miss-twice rule).
7. Define an observable success criterion to evaluate, at the close of {{HORIZONTE}}, whether the habit became automatic (e.g. completion rate, sense of friction when skipping it).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Anchoring: confirm habit and motivation; map candidate routines with their frequency, time, and context.
Phase 2 - Selection: apply the four filters and fix the anchor; explicitly discard those with a diffuse ending.
Phase 3 - Miniaturization: define the tiny version and write the literal formula.
Phase 4 - Sustainability: build the progression table, the visible cue, the anti-break plan, and the success criterion.
Assumptions and limits: you do not diagnose or treat clinical conditions; if the habit touches health, sleep, or nutrition with medical implications, suggest validating with a professional. Do not invent routines: if data is missing, ask. One chain per run (one habit per anchor) to avoid overloading the trigger.
Guardrails: if HABITO_NUEVO, MOTIVACION, or RUTINAS_ACTUALES are missing, ask before continuing. If {{HABITO_NUEVO}} is not observable, ask for it to be reformulated. If {{HORIZONTE}} is missing, assume 4 weeks and mark it as a [SUPUESTO].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The formula uses literally the structure "After X I will do Y" with specific, non-generic anchor and action.
- [ ] The anchor passes the four filters (frequency, time, context, clear ending) and the justification evidences this; if no ideal anchor exists, the limitation is named.
- [ ] The tiny version takes two minutes or less, is observable, and holds up on a bad day.
- [ ] The progression covers the entire {{HORIZONTE}} in increments that do not break the chain.
- [ ] There is a visible reminder cue placed in the physical context of the anchor.
- [ ] The anti-break plan covers 2 to 3 breakpoints and includes the never-miss-twice rule, without guilt-inducing language.
- [ ] There is an observable success criterion for the close of {{HORIZONTE}}.
- [ ] Assumptions (including the default HORIZONTE if applicable) are explicitly marked.
Expected deliverable: the final formula ready to paste in the physical environment, a weekly progression table for {{HORIZONTE}}, the list of breakpoints with their resumption plan, and the observable success criterion.
spec-personal_intencion_implementacion:
[inputs]
- META_O_HABITO: {{META_O_HABITO}} > Goal or habit you want to install, even if vague (e.g., 'read more', 'move more', 'meditate')
- FRECUENCIA_DESEADA: {{FRECUENCIA_DESEADA}} > How often you want to perform it (e.g., daily, 3 times a week, every weekday morning)

--- S | SITUATION ---
You want to break a bad habit that repeats almost automatically and resists willpower alone. Attacking the behavior without understanding the loop that sustains it ends in relapse and guilt. Framing the habit as a cue-craving-response-reward loop and redesigning the environment around it unlocks a defensible plan that reduces dependence on motivation. The plan feeds your daily tracking and the decision of when to adjust or seek professional support. Operating assumption: the habit is voluntary and modifiable through environmental design; if there is physical dependence or serious risk, the plan is a complement — not a replacement — for clinical care.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior behavioral change coach, fifteen years applying behavioral science and environmental design to deactivate unwanted habits — without replacing clinical care.
Deliverable: an actionable plan to break the habit, organized around the four inverted laws plus substitution, relapse plan, and progress signals. Steps:
1. Diagnose the loop: separate cue, craving, response, and reward; flag every unsupported inference as [SUPUESTO].
2. Invisible Law: reduce exposure to the cue and increase friction to find it, with one or two actions for today.
3. Unattractive Law: reframe the craving and make the real cost (time, money, health, identity) of the habit conscious.
4. Difficult Law: increase the steps to execute the response and add a commitment device with a verifiable consequence.
5. Unsatisfying Law: add an immediate cost and a witness or log for each lapse.
6. A substitution behavior that satisfies the same craving in a healthy way and is easier than the original habit.
7. Temptation and relapse plan (two-minute rule, if-then plan, how to restart without guilt) and three observable progress signals at thirty days.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1, framing: validate the five inputs; if any is empty or ambiguous, ask for all of them in one go before proceeding; do not invent the routine or assume a diagnosis. If there is physical dependence on substances or serious health risk, recommend professional support in addition to the plan.
Phase 2, loop diagnosis: decompose the habit into its four parts, distinguishing the craving (the sensation sought) from the response (the act). Edge case: if a single cue fires several habits, prioritize the most frequently recurring one based on the declared context.
Phase 3, four inverted laws: per law, interventions specific to the case — not generic — with one or two actions implementable today. If one input contradicts another (e.g., abstinence goal with a substitution that maintains the craving), flag the trade-off and choose the path of lowest sustainable friction.
Phase 4, substitution: a replacement behavior that covers the same craving — because removing without substituting usually fails — and requires fewer steps than the original habit.
Phase 5, relapse and measurement: a plan for the moment of temptation, a protocol to break the chain after a lapse without guilt (never fail twice in a row), and three observable progress signals at thirty days aligned with the goal. Close with a one-line summary and the first action for the next twenty-four hours.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The loop explicitly separates cue, craving, response, and reward — craving is not confused with the behavior.
- Each of the four inverted laws has at least one concrete, case-specific action — not generic advice.
- There is a substitution behavior tied to the diagnosed craving and easier than the original habit.
- The commitment device (Difficult Law) has a verifiable consequence, not just an intention.
- The relapse plan does not assign guilt and provides an operational path to restart after a slip (never-fail-twice rule).
- There are three observable progress signals at thirty days, aligned with the declared goal.
- Trade-offs and contradictions between inputs are made explicit; every unsupported inference is marked [SUPUESTO]; no clinical diagnosis or magic timeline promises.
Expected deliverable: plan in five blocks (loop, four laws with actions for today, substitution, relapse and measurement) closed with a one-line summary and the first action for the next twenty-four hours.
spec-personal_modelo_fogg:
[inputs]
- COMPORTAMIENTO_OBJETIVO: {{COMPORTAMIENTO_OBJETIVO}} > Specific behavior to diagnose, described as an observable action (e.g., "do 10 minutes of stretching upon waking", "check my phone as soon as the first notification sounds")
- DIRECCION: {{DIRECCION}} > Whether the goal is to adopt the behavior or stop it (e.g., "adopt it", "stop doing it")
- CONTEXTO_INTENTOS: {{CONTEXTO_INTENTOS}} > What has been tried before and what happened: when it works, when it falls apart, what was felt (e.g., "started motivated on Monday and dropped it by Thursday")
- MOMENTO_DISPARADOR: {{MOMENTO_DISPARADOR}} > Time of day and current cue at which the behavior should occur or currently fires (e.g., "after getting home from work, when I sit on the couch")
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Constraints of time, space, health, money, or family/work context to respect (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I have a behavior I want to understand: either I cannot install it despite my intentions, or it fires on its own even when I want to stop it. Willpower and loose reminders are not enough, and I need to know why it fails instead of blaming myself. The Fogg Behavior Model (B=MAP) explains that every behavior occurs when three elements converge at the same instant: Motivation, Ability, and a Prompt; if any one falls below the action line, the behavior does not happen. Diagnosing which of the three is the limiting factor turns a fuzzy discipline problem into a concrete design adjustment: it is almost always more reliable to simplify the behavior and anchor a good prompt than to wait for more desire. I am working on COMPORTAMIENTO_OBJETIVO in direction DIRECCION, with the history of CONTEXTO_INTENTOS and the moment MOMENTO_DISPARADOR. This unlocks an actionable plan, a measurable micro-experiment for this week, and a reusable framework for any other habit I want to design or dismantle.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior behavior designer, expert in BJ Fogg's Fogg Behavior Model (B=MAP), Tiny Habits design, and prompt architecture.

Produce a behavior diagnosis with these components:
1. Behavior framing: rewrite COMPORTAMIENTO_OBJETIVO as a specific, observable action (not a vague intention) and fix the exact moment it should occur based on MOMENTO_DISPARADOR.
2. Motivation diagnosis: level at the instant of action (high/medium/low), distinguishing lasting motivation from a passing impulse, with evidence from CONTEXTO_INTENTOS or a [SUPUESTO] flag. Remember that motivation is the least reliable lever because it fluctuates throughout the day.
3. Ability diagnosis: ease of execution evaluated across the six dimensions of simplicity (time, money, physical effort, mental effort, routine, social acceptance); identify which dimension or dimensions make the behavior difficult, remembering that ability is set by the scarcest dimension at that moment.
4. Prompt diagnosis: whether a cue exists that reminds me to act precisely when there is sufficient motivation and ability, and what type it is (facilitator for high motivation and low ability, spark for low motivation and high ability, signal for when both are high); also evaluate whether the prompt arrives at the right time and place.
5. Limiting factor: declare which of the three elements (Motivation, Ability, or Prompt) is below the action line and blocking the behavior, justifying why it is that one and not the other two. If two elements are low, prioritize the cheapest to raise (ability or prompt before motivation).
6. Prioritized adjustment plan: attack the limiting factor first, favoring simplifying the ability and anchoring a prompt over depending on raising motivation. If DIRECCION is to stop, invert the logic: break or remove the prompt, increase the friction and difficulty of the behavior, and reduce motivation in the moment (remove the immediate reward). Respect RESTRICCIONES and do not propose adjustments that violate them.
7. One-week micro-experiment: a single tiny behavior (the smallest possible version of the behavior), its prompt anchored to an existing routine (recipe: "After [anchor routine], I will do [tiny behavior]"), and an observable, binary success signal to evaluate at the close of the week.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Frame: convert COMPORTAMIENTO_OBJETIVO into an observable action and fix the moment of action based on MOMENTO_DISPARADOR; confirm DIRECCION (adopt or stop). If behavior, direction, or moment is missing, ask before continuing.
Phase 2 — Diagnose the three elements: evaluate Motivation, Ability (across the six simplicity dimensions), and Prompt at that specific instant, supporting each level with CONTEXTO_INTENTOS or marking [SUPUESTO]; do not present inferences as facts or invent routine details.
Phase 3 — Isolate the limiting factor: determine which of the three is below the action line and explain why it is the lever, explicitly ruling out the other two.
Phase 4 — Design and experiment: prioritize adjustments on that factor (simplify and anchor before motivating; invert the logic if DIRECCION is to stop), respect RESTRICCIONES, and close with a one-week micro-experiment with an anchored prompt and an observable success signal.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
The diagnosis is complete when:
- The behavior is rewritten as a specific, observable action with an explicit moment of action.
- All three elements (Motivation, Ability, Prompt) have a diagnosed level at the instant of action, with evidence from CONTEXTO_INTENTOS or a visible [SUPUESTO]; Ability is evaluated across the six simplicity dimensions and identifies the scarcest one.
- The limiting factor is declared unambiguously (one of the three) and justified against the other two.
- The adjustment plan attacks that limiting factor first and prioritizes simplifying the ability and anchoring a prompt over raising motivation; if DIRECCION is to stop, the logic is inverted (break prompt, increase friction, reduce motivation) and RESTRICCIONES are respected.
- There is a one-week micro-experiment with a single tiny behavior, its prompt anchored to an existing routine (recipe-style "After X, I will do Y"), and an observable, binary success signal.
- Neutral professional tone, no emojis, and no invented routine details.
Expected deliverable: Motivation, Ability, and Prompt diagnosed at the moment of action; limiting factor declared and justified; prioritized adjustment plan; and one-week micro-experiment with anchored prompt and observable success signal.

4. Lay out a 3-step growth ladder toward META_FINAL, expanding only when the previous step is automatic (triggered by automaticity, never by a calendar date).

Limits: this is not medical or clinical psychological advice; if HABITO_OBJETIVO touches sensitive physical/mental health (medication, restrictive diet, sleep with pathology), recommend professional validation.
